stories.title: Ida May Merry: enrollment and the Golden post office
stories.hook: Her mother’s affidavit records her birth; a later obituary follows Ida’s work serving the community of Golden.
body: On 27 April 1899, Bessie Merry signed an affidavit in an application to the Commission to the Five Civilized Tribes. She gave her age as 19, named her husband Lewis Merry and their daughter Ida May Merry, and identified herself as a Choctaw citizen by blood and Lewis as a citizen by marriage. The record gives Ida’s birth as 12 June 1898. The clerk’s note on census card 5754, in a hand that can be read as 17 or 12, is the only place a different day might appear; the mother’s and midwife’s sworn affidavits, Ida’s 1993 obituary and her gravestone all give 12 June, so 12 June is used. Midwife Eliza Jones signed a separate affidavit on the same page confirming that she had attended the birth.

On 6 October 1902, the Commission replied to J. L. Merry at Glover about bringing his family and witnesses to support their enrollment application. The letter bears the reference Choctaw D 128. The next year’s response to Lewis Merry at the same place bears 7-D 128 and names Louis, Bessie and Ida May. The shared case reference, address and subject support a probable identification of J. L. with Lewis/Louis; they do not prove it or establish a full first name for the initials.

A commissioner’s letter dated 24 October 1903 answered the family’s question about why enrollment was still pending. The commissioner stated that the application had not yet been decided; this letter is not a final enrollment decision. Addressed to Lewis Merry at Glover, Indian Territory, it describes the application of Louis Merry, his wife Bessie and their minor child Ida May. The same original document therefore uses both Lewis and Louis for the applicant, strengthening the connection between those spellings. A letter of 18 January 1908, addressed to Louis, records the return of his and Bessie’s marriage license and certificate after a copy was retained; it does not supply their wedding date.

Ida’s own obituary in the February 1993 Bishinik names her parents as J. L. and Bessie Durant Merry and repeats the birth date of 12 June 1898. This directly supplies her mother’s Durant surname, strengthening the connection between the Bessie Merry of the affidavit and Bessie Durant in the 2008 family notice. The father’s initials differ from Lewis in the affidavit, but the 1902–1903 correspondence provides a probable connection between those names.

The obituary remembers Ida as a former postmaster at Golden. After her husband died in 1941, she worked as assistant postmaster and then postmaster, retiring at 72. It names a surviving son Lewis O. Whitfield, supporting the later family connection, and calls her husband Clinton O. C. Whitfield. The 1920 census instead lists Oliver C. Whitfield, Ida M. and a son Oliver L.; those variations remain explicit rather than being silently standardized.

A second obituary, for Ida’s daughter Catherine Ouida Carroll in May 2007, gives the parents’ names as Oliver Clinton and Ida May Merry Whitfield. It names her deceased brothers as Omagene Clinton and Oliver Lewis Whitfield. This supplies fuller names that help explain the census initials, although Lewis Oliver and Oliver Lewis still appear in different orders. Catherine continued the family’s postal work: her obituary says she served 22 years at the post office in Golden and retired as postmaster in 1990.

Elma Severn’s separate obituary in the December 2011 Biskinik gives the same father’s full name, Oliver Clinton, and names her mother Ida Mae Merry Whitfield. Born at Glover in 1918, Elma taught and worked in education for 30 years in Oklahoma and New Mexico. This second notice strengthens the identification of the family while preserving May/Mae and the other recorded name variations.

The Oklahoma Historical Society’s official final-roll index places Louis Merry, Bessie Merry and Ida May Merry together on Choctaw card 5754. It records Bessie under roll 15526 and Ida May under roll 15527. These are historical enrollment records; they do not measure anyone’s DNA or establish present-day tribal citizenship.

The final-roll index records more than names. It lists Bessie Merry, 21, as three-quarters Choctaw by blood, roll 15526; Ida May, 4, as three-eighths, roll 15527; and Louis Merry, 30, as “IW,” an intermarried white citizen, roll 1363. Ida’s three-eighths is exactly half of her mother’s fraction, which is what the Commission recorded when one parent was white. The card itself, dated 26 April 1899, gives the three ages as 27, 19 and 1; the ages in the index are the later ones. Of all the families in this part of the tree, only the Merry household appears on the Dawes rolls. No Sandridge, Box, Whitfield, Cash, Logan of this family, Kernell or Nelson of this family is enrolled. The only Choctaw-roll Sandridges are a Freedmen family on card 81, with no known connection.

The index does not give Bessie’s parents, but the census card does, and it has since been read. Card 5754, dated 26 April 1899, names her father and mother as Peter and Ellen Durant of Bok Tuklo County, both dead, and gives Louis’s parents as Calvin and Elizabeth Merry, also dead and not Choctaw citizens; the story “Card 5754 read: Peter and Ellen Durant” sets out the card. Durant was a prominent Choctaw name, and the 1898–1914 rolls list more than a hundred Durants, many recorded as full-blood, so it is the card, not the surname, that ties Bessie to her parents.

Ida’s 1993 obituary adds a detail about her childhood: “She spent her childhood visiting her parents and attending Indian Boarding Schools.” Her parents had separated. Bessie’s gravestone at Denison Cemetery, Idabel, reads “Bessie E. Kernell, Nov. 11, 1879 – Mar. 22, 1950,” the name of her later husband. A newspaper clipping of county marriage licenses lists “Joshua L. Merry to Mrs. Mattie Erwin, Glover.” It is undated, the newspaper is not identified, and a memorial alone dates that marriage to 1908 and spells the name Ervin. The Mattie in the Dawes jacket for card 507 is Mattie E. Clay, Abner Clay’s wife, whom the Commission’s letters address under the name Clay through March 1904; no record read for the Clay and Gibbs stories, including the jackets for cards 507 and 966, names an Erwin or ties the clipping’s Mattie to her, so the clipping’s identification is left open.

That clipping and the Glover Cemetery stone together suggest the answer to the riddle of the initials. The stone reads “In sacred memory of J. L. Louis Merry, Apr. 10, 1872 – July 1, 1932,” with the line “Dear Papa, we miss you.” The J. L. of the 1902 letter and the 1993 obituary, and the Lewis or Louis of the 1899 affidavit and the rolls, were probably Joshua Louis Merry. His memorial calls him the first postmaster at Glover. Glover’s post office opened in 1901, but his appointment has not been checked. If it is confirmed, three generations of the family ran local post offices: J. L. at Glover, Ida at Golden, and Ida’s daughter Catherine at Golden. The memorial gives his birthplace as Sevier County, Arkansas, and his parents as John Calvin Merry and Eliza Jane McGregor; both are leads.

Ida’s husband appears on his own stone at Glover Cemetery as “O. C. (Clint) Whitfield, July 27, 1893 – Mar. 21, 1941.” That explains why the 1993 obituary calls him Clinton O. C. and the children’s obituaries call him Oliver Clinton: he was Oliver Clinton, and people called him Clint. His memorial gives Chapel Hill, Sevier County, Arkansas, as his birthplace and William Franklin “Frank” Whitfield and Emma Ward as his parents. Those parents are leads. Ida’s own stone gives her death as 28 January 1993, a Thursday, which matches the obituary’s “passed away Thursday.” The stone reads “Her children rose up and called her blessed.”

Post Office Department records now confirm the memorial’s claim. Grant Foreman’s 1928 list and George H. Shirk’s 1948 list both give Joshua L. Merry as Glover’s first postmaster, appointed on 26 June 1901, and the Official Registers of 1903, 1905 and 1907 list him there by that full name. The story “Joshua L. Merry, first postmaster at Glover” sets out those records.

stories.note: The 1993 original obituary directly names Bessie Durant Merry as Ida’s mother and Lewis O. Whitfield as her son. Her father is J. L. in that obituary, Lewis in the 1899 affidavit and Louis in the final-roll index; the 1903 letter supports Lewis/Louis as variants for the same applicant, while the 1902 J. L. letter shares the case reference and Glover address with the 1903 response. This supports a probable identification, not proof or a full first-name expansion. Her husband appears as Clinton O. C. in the obituary and Oliver C. in the census. The 1920 son Oliver L. is a probable match to Lewis Oliver. The final-roll index and census card 5754 have been checked, and several original application letters have been reviewed; the card names Bessie’s parents as Peter and Ellen Durant. Her death date, 28 January 1993, comes from her gravestone and agrees with the obituary’s “Thursday.” Catherine’s 2007 obituary supplies Oliver Clinton for her father and Oliver Lewis for her brother; the earlier recorded variants are retained. Elma’s 2011 obituary is another child obituary naming Oliver Clinton; that fuller display name is supported, while the census identification and earlier variant remain qualified.

stories.title: Alfreda Whitfield Sandridge and her Choctaw family
stories.hook: A family anniversary notice connects Alfreda’s story to Choctaw enrollment and her grandparents’ generation.
body: Alfreda Whitfield was born in 1939 at Wheelock, Oklahoma, to L. O. and Violet Box Whitfield. She married Larry Sandridge in 1958 at First Assembly of God in Broken Bow. Her family remembered her love of gardening, fishing and time with her grandchildren, and her work at the Choctaw Casino in Idabel.

Violet grew up in McCurtain County: the 1930 census records nine-year-old Violet as a daughter of Tyro Box and his wife Annie. A family-contributed transcription of Violet’s obituary names her father as T. S. Box and says she and her husband ran a grocery in Golden. The initials fit Tyro in the census, but the identification remains probable. Annie’s maiden name is taken up below, and the original published obituary has not yet been located.

The 1900 census in Van Zandt County, Texas, lists twelve-year-old Tyro Box as a son of Alonzo and Emma Box. A World War I draft registration for Tyro Stevens Box in McCurtain County gives a matching May 1888 birth and a Texas birthplace. The 1930 household, however, reports Tyro’s birthplace as Oklahoma. His unusual name and matching birth month support the connection, but the difference in birthplace leaves the identification and his parents’ relationship to Violet probable rather than proven.

Their 50th anniversary notice in the Choctaw Nation’s Biskinik identifies Alfreda’s grandmother as Ida Merry Whitfield and her great-grandmother as Bessie Durant, both original enrollees. A 1899 application contains an affidavit by Bessie Merry identifying herself as the mother of Ida May Merry and naming Lewis Merry as the father. The family notice and the affidavit together support identifying Bessie Merry with Bessie Durant, though the connection remains a probable match.

The 1920 census lists a child named Oliver L. Whitfield in the McCurtain County household of Oliver C. and Ida M. Whitfield. His age and family context fit Lewis Oliver Whitfield, Alfreda’s father, but the reversed name order makes the identification probable rather than certain. A later Biskinik family notice names the late Lewis Whitfield and Ida Merry Whitfield among this branch’s elders.

Later notices clear up the Box questions. Violet’s 1962 obituary names her father as T. S. Box of Millerton. Annie F. Box’s 1959 notice names her daughter Mrs. Louis Whitfield of Golden. Tyro Stephen Box’s 1967 notice gives his birth as 22 May 1888 at Pittsburg, Texas, the same month and year as the 1900 census and the draft card. Annie’s maiden name was Logan: her notice names her brothers Rob and Walter Logan and her sister Mrs. Bell Culpepper of Dallas. The Wheelock Cemetery card file at the Broken Bow library names her parents as Dudley Logan and Annie Wedgeworth Logan. Dudley Timothy Logan came to Titus County, Texas, from Greene County, Alabama, and died there in 1898. That was eight years before Annie moved from Mount Pleasant to McCurtain County.

A family note on Tyro’s memorial gives his mother as Emillie Wilkerson. That matches the Wilkerson maiden name suggested for Emma Box in a collaborative tree, but it is still not an independent original record.

stories.title: Audrey Sandridge: wartime work and a community switchboard
stories.hook: From a McCurtain County childhood to wartime work and the telephone office, Audrey Nelson Sandridge’s life connected work and community.
body: Audrey Inez Nelson was born in 1917 in the Redland area of McCurtain County, Oklahoma. The 1920 census lists two-year-old Audrey as a daughter in the household of William and Julia Nelson. A family memorial identifies her parents as William Nelson and Julia Robbins; the original obituary it reproduces has not yet been located.

During the 1940s, Audrey and her husband Lemuel Sandridge worked at the Red River Arsenal plant making ammunition. Audrey also worked the switchboard there. After they returned to Broken Bow, she worked as one of the early telephone operators at Pine Telephone Company.

Her community life included service at Broken Bow First Assembly of God: the reproduced obituary describes work with young people, Sunday school and fellowship meals. Audrey and Lemuel’s son Larry carried the family story into another generation in McCurtain County.

stories.title: Alice Walker’s Illinois beginnings
stories.hook: Census households and a Texas death certificate offer a path back to the Walker family, with one important disagreement to resolve.
body: The 1860 and 1870 censuses list an Alice M. Walker in the Illinois household of Wm P. and Abigail Walker. The records place the family in Washington County, Illinois; those censuses did not identify the relationships between people in a household.

By 1900 Floyd and Alice Livesay were living in Brazoria County, Texas, with children who included Lester W. Livesay. A 1912 Texas death record for their son Walter names Floyd Livesay and Alice Walker as his parents. In 1920, Floyd H. and Alice M. Livesay were recorded together in Houston.

Alice May Livesay’s original death certificate records her death in Houston on 23 October 1922. It describes her as a married housewife born in Illinois, with burial at Pearland the following day. The informant’s signature reads F. C. Livesay, rather than F. H. Her father is indexed as Wm P. Walker; the handwritten surname is less clear.

The mother’s name on the original reads Addie Bruce, with Illinois as her birthplace; the index transcribes the surname as Brace. The earlier census household includes Abigail Walker. These are distinct recorded names, and no record yet establishes whether they identify the same woman. No mother is attached to Alice’s profile.

The certificate also contains a birth-date conflict. Its date-of-birth field gives 11 January 1860, but the age is 67 years, 9 months and 12 days, which would imply 11 January 1855. The matching census child points instead to about 1859, and her headstone at Pearland, described in her father’s story, reads 11 January 1859. The tree retains that approximate census date and presents all three indications rather than choosing a precise birth year from the conflicting certificate.

Abigail Walker and any proposed Abigail Schanck identity have not been merged with Addie Bruce or attached as Alice’s mother. This could concern the later census household, but the groom’s middle initial differs from Wm P. and the bride’s surname differs from Addie Bruce. The original marriage record has not been examined; neither this couple’s identity with the census household nor Schanck’s identity with Alice’s recorded mother is established.

stories.title: From Illinois to the Texas Gulf Coast
stories.hook: Census records trace Floyd and Alice Livesay’s family from Illinois to Brazoria County, where later generations put down roots.
body: In 1900, Floyd and Alice Livesay lived in Brazoria County, Texas, with children born in Illinois and Texas. Their son Lester W. was listed as born in Illinois in November 1894. The census points to a family move from Illinois to Texas between the births of their Illinois-born children and their Texas-born daughter Ruth, about 1898; it does not reveal the reason for the move.

Floyd ran a grocery in Pearland. A 1932 Houston Chronicle notice places his move from Illinois to Pearland about 37 years earlier, suggesting the mid-1890s; the estimate fits the birthplaces in the 1900 household. The notice names a son L. W. Livesay among his survivors.

Lester W. Livesay and Sadah H. McCormick married on 10 October 1911, according to the original Harris County marriage register. The 1920 census places them in Harris County with their young children, including a son Lester Jr. The younger Lester’s obituary later identified his parents as Lester W. Sr. and Sadah McCormick. His railroad career and ranches carried the story into Pearland and East Texas.

A Texas death record for Walter Livesay, also listed in the 1900 household, names his parents Floyd Livesay and Alice Walker. Floyd’s own death certificate identifies him as a widowed, retired groceryman who died in Houston on 5 May 1932 and was buried at Pearland the next day. It gives his birth as 5 February 1857 in Illinois, while the 1900 census gives February 1856. The 1900 entry for Lester also gives a birth month and year that do not agree with his recorded age.

An 1860 census records a four-year-old Floyd H. Livesay in Washington County, Illinois, in a household headed by Lydia Livesay that also included David Livesay, 28. Ten years later, a fourteen-year-old Floyd H. appeared in David’s household in the same county. A FamilySearch collaborative tree proposes David and Tabitha Flannigan as Floyd’s parents, but the two censuses did not state household relationships and the 1860 household did not list a Tabitha. Those entries offer a promising path for research; they do not establish his parents.

Floyd’s death certificate leaves both parents’ names and birthplaces unknown. The informant, E. W. Livesay, supplied no parentage that could connect him to the earlier Illinois household. David Livesay and Tabitha Flannigan therefore remain research leads rather than attached parents.

Within three years of Floyd and Alice’s move to Pearland, the Handbook of Texas counted 75 residents and twelve businesses there. The 1900 hurricane “destroyed fruit trees and slowed growth for a period of time,” and a 1918 freeze ended a later revival based on oranges and figs.

Floyd and Alice outlived two grown sons. Walter, their eldest, died on 26 January 1912, aged 31. The Houston Post reported that he “died Friday afternoon in a sanitarium in Houston” and was buried from the Sid Westheimer parlors “under the auspices of Magnolia Camp No. 13, Woodmen of the World,” in Evergreen Cemetery. A note on his memorial gives the cause as renal tuberculosis. William Paul Livesay died in San Antonio on 13 April 1915, aged 32, and was buried at Pearland. Alice died in 1922 and Floyd in 1932. They lie side by side in the Old Settlers Cemetery at Pearland.

stories.title: The Sandridge family of Broken Bow
stories.hook: Oklahoma records follow the Sandridges from a farm near Broken Bow to service aboard a Navy helicopter carrier.
body: Larry Lamar Sandridge grew up in Broken Bow, Oklahoma, where he graduated from high school in 1956. His obituary says he served in the Army and Navy as an aviation electrician, including service aboard the helicopter carrier USS Thetis Bay. It names his parents as Lemuel Lamar Sandridge and Audrey Inez Nelson.

In 2008 Larry and his wife Alfreda Whitfield Sandridge celebrated their 50th wedding anniversary. Their anniversary notice appeared in the Choctaw Nation’s Biskinik along with a photograph. Alfreda’s obituary names their daughter and her parents, connecting the Sandridge and Whitfield families.

A 1961 McCurtain Gazette notice identifies Lemuel Sandridge of Broken Bow as a son of Clinton Lamar Sandridge. The notice says Clinton was born in Arkansas and moved to McCurtain County in 1919, where he farmed. These records offer a path into an earlier generation of a Sandridge family in the region.

A funeral-home obituary index names a daughter whose identity was confirmed by the family. The 1930 census lists Lemuel in the household of Clinton and Maggie; Clinton’s recorded age there differs from the birth years on his obituary and his gravestone, and Maggie’s maiden name needs more research.

stories.title: Railroad and ranch: the Livesays in East Texas
stories.hook: Lester Livesay worked on the Southern Pacific Railroad and ran cattle ranches in Pearland and Carthage.
body: Lester Woodrow Livesay Jr. was born in Houston in 1916, the son of Lester W. Livesay Sr. and Sadah McCormick. He grew up in Pearland and became a Southern Pacific Railroad engineer. He also operated a cattle ranch there, then began another ranch after moving to Carthage in 1961.
His 2001 obituary names his wife, Barbara Phillips Livesay, and identifies members of several generations. It gives a useful starting point for tracing an East Texas Livesay family into Oklahoma.

A Texas birth index names Lester and Barbara as the parents of Wayne Woodrow Livesay. The next generation is supported by a Texas birth index and family confirmation; living relatives appear on this site only by their family roles.

Railroading ran on into the next generation. Wayne Woodrow Livesay, born in Houston on 13 February 1940, became a locomotive engineer. His memorial says he worked “for Burlington Northern Santa Fe Railroad for 30 years and retired in 2000.” He died in April 2013 at Cushing, Nacogdoches County, close to his mother’s birthplace, and is buried in McKnight Cemetery there.

stories.title: The air commander behind the Andrews name
stories.hook: From the Stevenson family in Tennessee came Frank Maxwell Andrews, a pioneer of American air power and the namesake of Joint Base Andrews.
body: Frank Maxwell Andrews was born in Nashville on 3 February 1884, the son of James David Andrews and Lula Adaline Maxwell. He graduated from West Point in 1906 and began his Army career in the cavalry. During the First World War he entered aviation and earned his pilot’s wings in 1918.

In 1935 Andrews took command of the newly organized General Headquarters Air Force. He argued for a modern long-range bomber force and supported developing and buying the Boeing B-17. By 1943 he was commanding United States forces in the European theater, where American and Allied forces were preparing for the campaigns ahead.

When his father died in 1937, Frank recalled how the family had traveled to a world’s fair by train under oil lamps when he was a boy. Years later he flew his father to the Chicago fair in an amphibious airplane, landing on Lake Michigan.

On 3 May 1943 Andrews was killed when the B-24 bomber Hot Stuff crashed in Iceland. In 1945 Camp Springs Army Air Field in Maryland was renamed Andrews Field in his honor; it became Andrews Air Force Base in 1948 and is now part of Joint Base Andrews.

The family connection runs through the Stevenson line. Elam and Lydia Stevenson’s sons included Abner Arrington Stevenson, our ancestor, and his brother James Calvin. James’s daughter Eliza Catherine married William Thomas Andrews; their son James David was Frank’s father. Elam and Lydia are the shared ancestors.

stories.title: A minister’s memoir that connected two families
stories.hook: In 1912 William Thomas Andrews set down the names of his wife’s parents and their children, preserving a link between the Stevensons and the Andrews family.
body: William Thomas Andrews grew up in Giles County, Tennessee, after his mother brought the family there from Limestone County, Alabama. He was licensed to preach in 1856. On 30 November of that year he married Eliza Catherine Stevenson, daughter of the Rev. James C. and Margaret C. Stevenson.

In the autobiography he included in his 1912 volume of Methodist conference memorials, Andrews named their five sons and daughter. The first son named was James David Andrews of Nashville, the future father of Frank Maxwell Andrews. James David’s later newspaper memorial also identified William Thomas and Eliza as his parents.

Andrews spent his first fourteen years in ministry as a local preacher, then joined the North Alabama Conference. His assignments took him to Limestone, Scottsboro, Florence, Gadsden, Talladega and other communities. His published account lists those appointments across decades of church work.
The book includes his portrait as a frontispiece. Its printed caption identifies him; the original page and the autobiography can be viewed with this story.

stories.title: Junior Thompson, from Jeter to Speer
stories.hook: A childhood in a household of several generations, and a marriage that joined the Thompson and Hulsey families.
body: William “Junior” Thompson Jr. grew up on his parents’ farm at Jeter in Choctaw County, Oklahoma. In 1940 he was six, sharing the household with Simon and Frances Thompson, his brothers and sisters, and his Pisachubbe grandparents.

At sixteen, he was still at home in Jeter. His father worked his own farm, and his Pisachubbe grandmother remained part of the household. The two censuses place Junior in a family whose children and elders lived together.
By December 1956, William was living at Speer. His marriage license with Mary Ellen Hulsey of Hugo appeared in the local newspaper that month, joining the Thompson and Hulsey branches of the family.

He remained connected to Hugo through the years. His father Simon’s surviving family included William Thompson Jr. of Hugo in 1990, and his sister Ethel Hamill’s family included him there in 2002. William died in 2007.

He and Mary Ellen share one granite marker at Woodlawn Cemetery in Choctaw County, under a scroll lettered THOMPSON: "Mary E. / Aug. 22, 1938 / Nov. 4, 2002" on one side and "William, Jr. / Mar. 14, 1934 / Feb. 17, 2007" on the other.

stories.title: Lizzie’s road from Alabama to Apache
stories.hook: Married in Alabama in 1889, she made her later home near her children in southwestern Oklahoma.
body: Lizzie Newton was born in Etowah County, Alabama, on 20 February 1873. She married John M. Shackleford there on 1 December 1889. Her father Balas Newton’s written consent to the marriage is told in “The consent folded into their marriage book”.

An 1880 Etowah County census lists seven-year-old Elizabeth in the household of Balus Newton and his wife Mary. The rare name, place and age make this a probable match for Lizzie and her father in the 1889 marriage papers. Mary Ann Dockery, who married a Bailus Newton in 1867, is a probable mother; the census does not explicitly state Elizabeth’s mother.

The family’s travels eventually took Lizzie to Texas. In 1933 she moved from Dawson County to the Apache community in Caddo County, Oklahoma. She belonged to the Baptist church, and several of her grown children also made their homes in or around Apache.
She spent her final days at the home of her son Ed, six miles southwest of town, and died there on 8 November 1951, aged seventy-eight. She was buried in Fairview Cemetery at Apache.

Her family had grown across Oklahoma, Texas and California. At her death it included nine surviving children, forty-two grandchildren and sixteen great-grandchildren. Sons Ed and John and daughters Mrs. Joe Haskell and Helen Josey lived at Apache; other children had settled in Lawton, Texas and California.

stories.note: The 1951 obituaries and her grave marker agree on 20 February 1873; the 1900 census gives February 1872. The newspaper spelling “Etowak” is normalized to Etowah. Both obituaries place daughter May/Mary Moffett at Granite; that place has not been silently changed to Grant. The funeral time was tentative when the notices were printed. Mary Ann Dockery is a probable mother, based on the 1880 household and the 1867 marriage; no record naming Lizzie’s mother directly has been located.

stories.title: A miner’s household in the Ouachitas
stories.hook: In 1880 B. F. Hulsey worked as a miner and raised a young family in Montgomery County, Arkansas.
body: B. F. Hulsey was thirty-two when the census taker reached Center Township in June 1880. Born in Georgia, he was working as a miner in the Ouachita country of western Arkansas. His wife Sarah G., thirty, had been born in Arkansas.

B. F. was not the only miner on the page: William W. Gleason and C. W. Dyer also gave that occupation. The entries place mining within the local community, although they do not show that the men worked together.

Three children were at home: Margaret M., six; George W., four; and Charles F., five months. The household offers a likely childhood home for the later George Washington Hulsey of Story. George’s own draft registration gives a December 1875 birth, consistent with the four-year-old on this census.

The census calls Margaret M. a daughter and George W. and Charles F. sons of B. F. Margaret had been born about 1874, George about 1875–76, and Charles early in 1880. Sarah G. appears as B. F.’s wife. Those relationships establish the household, but they do not expressly establish that Sarah was every child’s biological mother.

A later family query in the Arkansas Family Historian connects a Benjamin F. Hulsey with a son George Washington and children named Charles, Mary and Francis. It also gives a wife named Margaret Partain and dates that conflict with other accounts. The overlapping names are useful clues, but the query does not resolve the mother’s identity or prove that all the Benjamin Hulsey records concern one man.

Of Sarah G. herself the census says a little more than her age and her Arkansas birth. The enumerator recorded her father as born in North Carolina and her mother in Tennessee, which outlines her own family without naming either parent. Her maiden name and full given names are still unknown. She is not Sarah Rebecca Graves, whom George later married, and nothing yet identifies her with Sylvania Susane Partain, the name a descendant's photo caption gives for George's mother.

stories.note: The original 1880 census records B. F. Hulsey, 32, born Georgia, with wife Sarah G., 30, born Arkansas, and son George W., 4, in Center Township, Montgomery County, Arkansas. George’s December 1875 birth in the 1900 Sulphur Springs census and 24 December 1875 birth on his 1918 draft card are consistent with the child’s age. A 1977 family query associates a Benjamin F. Hulsey with a son named George Washington. The connection remains probable: no record yet explicitly connects the adult George, husband of Sarah Rebecca Graves, to the named 1880 parents. This household has not been securely identified with the separate Benjamin Franklin Hulsey biography or with Sylvania Partain. The 1977 query is an unsourced family-research submission with conflicting names and dates; it calls the wife Margaret Partain and gives a 1921 death. It is supporting evidence, not proof of the connection or of a mother’s identity. Sarah G. is recorded as B. F.'s wife, not explicitly as George's mother, so she is a probable mother or stepmother. This story now includes the shorter entry about Sarah G.; its old link opens this page.

stories.title: Moonshine and federal court in Hugo
stories.hook: An October arrest report and later federal court notices preserve a different side of life in Hugo.
body: On a Saturday night in October 1961, two men looking for whisky visited John W. Moffitt in Hugo. They left without a purchase, but Moffitt later caught up with them in town and offered a half-gallon. When he handed it over, the buyers showed their badges: one was a federal alcohol-tax agent and the other worked for the state liquor board.
Moffitt, thirty-six, was arrested and brought before U.S. Commissioner Lon Kile on Monday. His bond was set at $1,000.

The following spring, federal court news named John Winfred Moffitt of Hugo. In May 1962 he pleaded guilty to two counts of violating the federal liquor stamp law. A June sentencing list recorded John Winfred Moffitt of Choctaw County receiving two years’ probation for operating a still.
src: The Hugo Daily News, 31 Oct 1961, p. 1, https://www.newspapers.com/image/602946181/; Muskogee Times-Democrat, 25 Apr 1962, p. 9, https://www.newspapers.com/image/631019234/; The Ada Weekly News, 17 May 1962, p. 2, https://www.newspapers.com/image/667017065/; Muskogee Daily Phoenix and Times-Democrat, 23 Jun 1962, p. 2, https://www.newspapers.com/image/631077697/.
stories.note: Identification as the family’s John Winfred Moffitt is probable: the 1962 reports give his full name and Hugo/Choctaw County; the October 1961 report gives John W. Moffitt’s age as 36, matching his 25 October 1925 birth. None names a wife, relative or street address. The court file has not been examined, so the 1961 arraignment and 1962 prosecution have not been proved to be the same case. The newspaper records establish what happened to the men they name; the remaining uncertainty is their identification with this family member and the link between cases.

stories.title: The consent folded into their marriage book
stories.hook: A father’s permission survived with John and Lizzie’s Alabama marriage papers.
body: John M. Shackleford and Lizzie Newton obtained their marriage license in Etowah County, Alabama, on 30 November 1889. A small note was kept over the page: permission from her father, Balas Newton, for the couple to marry.

The consent is dated 28 November. John certified two days later that he had written and signed it at Balas’s direction. In a separate statement, sworn before the probate judge, he presented the permission and explicitly identified Lizzie as Newton’s daughter. The marriage index dates the wedding to 1 December 1889.

By 1900 John and Elizabeth were raising their family in Gilbert Precinct, Etowah County. Their daughter Mary Tinsley later married Woodford Grady Moffitt, carrying this Alabama branch into the Moffitt family in Oklahoma.

Etowah County had been created only 23 years before the wedding, and for two of those years, 1866 to 1868, it was called Baine County. The 1900 census household at Gilbert lists John, 37, Elizabeth, 28, and five living children: “Balous” 8, Myrtle 6, May 5, Robert 3 and Eddie 8 months. Mary, born 4 June 1895, was the “May, 5.” Family trees give her brothers and sisters as Balis Anthony (1892-1982, who died in Los Angeles County), Robert Yates (1897-1961), John Newton (1906-2002), Hazel Marzee King (1908-1980), Edward Richard (1910-1988) and Helen Elizabeth Josey (1915-1997). Two later obituaries (Chico Enterprise-Record, 23 June 1961; Lamar County Echo, 1 January 1981) also name sisters Josephine Haskell, Eulah Tillman and Beulah Hutchins, who do not fit the 1900 list.

Hazel was born at Rattan in Delta County, Texas, so the family was in northeast Texas about 1908 before reaching Martin County. By 1930 John Morgan was there with his wife and children, and Grady and Mary and their six boys were living with them. The 1930 census gives his birth year as 1863; his marker says 1862.

John Morgan Shackleford's grave in Evergreen Cemetery at Stanton, Martin County, Texas, lies on the far north side, to the right of the first gate. The flat granite marker is carved with a bird and flowers and reads "John M. Shackleford / Sept. 30, 1862 / May 22, 1930." Lizzie, who outlived him by twenty-one years, is buried in Oklahoma at Apache. His own parents are not named in any record yet examined; his 1930 Texas death certificate is the document most likely to name them.

In 1933 Lizzie moved from Dawson County, Texas, to Apache, Caddo County, Oklahoma, where several of her grown children lived. She died at her son Ed’s home southwest of town on 8 November 1951 and is buried at Fairview Cemetery, Apache.

The Shackelfords of Virginia trace to an immigrant, Roger, who received a grant in Gloucester County in 1658. A Shackleford family history of 1940 says the family had no coat of arms, and Mary’s descent from Roger is not proved.

stories.title: A father’s permission, preserved on paper
stories.hook: Named as Lizzie Newton’s father in the original papers for her 1889 marriage.
body: In November 1889 Balas Newton gave written permission for his daughter Lizzie to marry John M. Shackleford in Etowah County, Alabama; the consent and John’s sworn statement are told in “The consent folded into their marriage book”.

The 1880 census lists a Balus Newton in Etowah County with wife Mary and daughter Elizabeth, aged seven. Their uncommon names, location and Elizabeth’s age make them a probable match for the Balas and Lizzie named in the later marriage papers. The census records Mary as Balus’s wife but does not explicitly identify her as Elizabeth’s mother.

The 1880 home held nine people. Balus was forty-four and farming; Mary, thirty-six, was recorded as keeping house. The seven children listed as Balus’s sons and daughters ranged from a twelve-year-old son, whose occupation was farm hand, to an eight-month-old daughter born in November. Between them were Ann, ten; Lindsey, nine; Elizabeth, seven; Hezekiah, four; and Amanda, three. The census records Alabama as the birthplace of Balus, Mary and all seven children.

In March 1901 the Gadsden Times-News reported that a Balus Newton had made final proof on land before the county clerk. The brief notice gives no age or family names, so its subject’s identification with Lizzie’s father remains a lead.

stories.title: Singing, holidays and a house full of family
stories.hook: From a Jeter farm childhood to a family of children, grandchildren and Christmas gatherings.
body: Faye Smith was the youngest child of Charles Oscar and Artie Pearl Smith, born at Forney, Choctaw County, on 23 March 1929. She appears as "Fay May," 2, in the 1930 census at Jeter and as "Fay," 12, in 1940. She married John W. Moffitt at Paris, Texas, on 12 June 1947, died at Paris on 23 December 2014 and is buried at Grant Cemetery.

She made her home around family life. Singing, shopping, visits with friends and trips to the Nutrition Center filled her days. Holidays were a particular pleasure, and her Christmas portrait catches her smiling beside the tree.

John had returned from Navy service the year before their marriage. By her death in 2014, the family had grown to 20 grandchildren, 38 great-grandchildren and two great-great-grandchildren. Her funeral was held in Hugo, with burial at Grant Cemetery beside John.

stories.title: Edith, the Thompson daughter who was proud to be Choctaw
stories.hook: Junior's younger sister was the baby of the house in 1940, and she was proud of her Choctaw heritage all her life.
body: Edith Irene Thompson was born at Hugo on 27 December 1939, one of the children of Simon and Frances (Pisachubbe) Thompson, and grew up in the same crowded farmhouse at Jeter as her brother William “Junior” Thompson, the grandfather of this family. She was the baby of the household when the 1940 census taker arrived the next spring.

Her obituary in the Choctaw Nation's newspaper, the Biskinik, in May 2012, says she loved her family very much, enjoyed spending time with them, and was “especially proud of her Choctaw Indian Heritage.” She married twice. Her first husband, Bert Jones, died before her; at her death she was married to Cleatus Williams. Her children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren lived around Hugo and Blackwell.

Edith died at Durant on 12 April 2012, aged 72. By then she had buried both parents, her brothers Leonard and Junior, and her sisters Ethel Hamill and Norma Homer. Only one brother, Bernie of Grant, was named among her survivors. The Biskinik printed her color portrait beside the notice.

stories.title: A Regulator the Governor wouldn't pardon
stories.hook: One of thirteen men left out of Governor Tryon's 1768 pardon.
body: The Regulators were backcountry farmers in North Carolina who rose up (1766–1771) against corrupt officials and illegal fees. William Moffitt of Deep River was in the movement from its start: in August 1766 the inhabitants of Deep River chose "Wm Cox and Wm Masset" (a misreading of Maffet) to attend the Regulators' first general meeting. In 1768 he signed their petitions alongside the movement's leaders, Herman Husband and James Hunter, and on 21 May 1768 he was named first on the committee to carry their grievances to the Governor.

On 3 October 1768, at Hillsborough, Royal Governor William Tryon pardoned the Regulators except thirteen named men, and "William Moffitt" is one of them. He was never outlawed, and a general pardon in 1769 covered "all persons concerned in the said late Insurrection." His name is on the memorial trail at Alamance Battleground, and James Otis listed him among "the patriots of upper Carolina" in his 1901 boys' novel The Boy Spies with the Regulators.

William married Mary Davies at Cane Creek Quaker Meeting on 2 April 1763, when he was 23. He and Hugh Moffitt, probably his brother, married sisters, and Hugh ran the first mill on Richland Creek, which gave the community of Moffitt, North Carolina, its name; the Moffitt's Mills post office lasted from 1823 to 1935.

His will, dated 13 March 1796, begins “I William Moffitt of Randolph County in the province of North Carolina, being weak in body.” He gave his sons Robert, William and David land, and his daughters Naomi (Neomi Macky), Catharine Cox, Hannah Cox, Mary Wilkinson and Margaret £3 each, with Margaret also getting cows, sheep and a bed.

Robert, our ancestor, received the 250 acres William had bought of William Cox, except “the new field that is cleared upon the River,” which his mother kept for life. William got the 225-acre plantation where his father lived, with a share reserved for Mary while she was a widow. David, who was clearly under age, got land on Tibs Run, wagon iron “brought from Pig River,” and a quarter of a lot in Campbelltown in Cumberland County. If David died young, his brothers inherited and each sister would get £15.

“My Loveing Wife Mary Moffitt” received the wagon, the still, the plantation tools and the stock, and was named executrix with “my son Robart Moffitt” as executor. The witnesses were Hugh Moffitt and Charles Moffitt. The Quaker records of Center Meeting show Robert, “son of William & Mary,” marrying Martha Chamness in 1797.

William and Mary had eight children: Naomi (born 11 June 1763), Catharine (1765), Hannah (22 December 1771), Mary (1773), Margaret (1774), Robert (1778), William (1781) and David (4 February 1785). All five daughters and three sons are named in Mary's will.

Family legend says the Moffitts came from Dumfriesshire, Scotland, descended from a "Robert Bruce Moffitt" born in 1716. No record names such a man. The Alamance Battleground Book of Remembrance instead says William was born about 1740 in Donegal, Ireland, to Robert and Martha Steward Moffitt and came through Philadelphia, which fits Ulster Scots, but that entry has no citations.

His part in the committee's account of the deputy sheriff's missing Act is told in "The Act nobody could find," and his name on the Regulators' letter, address and indictment of September 1768 in "Four documents, one name: William Moffitt in 1768." A Cox family history of 1955 adds two earlier court-record items: a deed proved by "Wm. Moffitt" in May 1765 and his witnessing of William Cox's will, proved at Hillsborough in February 1767.

The Moffitt Genealogy of 1928, compiled by Frank Moffitt for the descendants of Silas Moffitt of Hamilton County, Indiana, gives that family's own tradition of William's origins: sons of "Robert and Margaret Moffat" who "migrated to Donegal County, Ireland," and whose children included James, Charles, William, Adam, Margaret, Catharine, Robert, Mary, Hugh, Patrick and John. It says that "William married Mary Davis and Hugh married Hannah Davis, both being daughters of Charles Davis," and that Mary Moffitt Wilkinson, "our own foremother," was "said to have been their fifth child," married to William Wilkinson, "an Englishman, on the 26th day of the 3rd month, 1795." This agrees with the "Mary Wilkinson" of William's will, and the two witnesses to that will, Hugh and Charles Moffitt, match two of the brothers in the book's list. The parents differ from the Book of Remembrance's Robert and Martha Steward Moffitt, so the Donegal family is tradition, not record.

The book also repeats a story about "the Davis millions." Hamilton County heirs, it says, raised money to send an agent to the old country to look into an inheritance, but "this supposed wealth, like the fortune at the foot of the rainbow, was always just out of reach."

WikiTree quotes the Bible Record of Abijah Moffitt for William's parents: Robert Moffitt, born in Scotland and later of County Donegal, and Margaret Stuart, with eleven children, six of whom came to America. It adds that William and his brother Hugh both married Davis daughters in North Carolina, which matches William's 1763 marriage to Mary Davies. The Alamance Battleground Book gives the mother as Martha Steward. Both accounts are family-based, not contemporary records.

In an 1853 letter, Hugh's son Joseph Moffitt named his father's brothers, including William, and said their parents were Robert Moffitt and Margaret Stewart. Joseph also named his mother Hannah Davis and said her sister Mary married a Moffitt. This fits the William and Mary Davies of Randolph County, though the letter does not explicitly name Mary's husband as William. The surviving account is a 1924 printed transcription, not the original manuscript. Hugh's 1799 Chatham County will independently names his wife Hannah and son Joseph, strengthening the identification of the letter's family.

stories.title: The baby on the Dawes card
stories.hook: Enrolled at 7½ months. A 19-year-old farmer on his 1918 draft card. Three generations under his roof in 1940.
body: Simon was the youngest person on the family's 1899 Choctaw enrollment card, listed at 7½ months old. His mother Betsy and his grandmother Emeline Tims, who was the midwife at his birth on 4 May 1899, both swore affidavits so he could be enrolled. He was given Dawes Roll No. 3492 and his own land allotment near his parents'.
On his WWI draft card (12 September 1918) he was 19, a farmer working for his father at Corinne, of medium height and build, with black hair and brown eyes.

By 1940 he and Frances owned a $400 farm at Jeter, in a county where nearly three of every four farmers were tenants, and were raising five children: Ethel 13, Leonard 10, Junior 6, Bernice 3 and a baby daughter. Frances's parents Robert and Lizzie Pisachubbe lived with them, with Robert and Lizzie's orphaned niece and nephews, Frances's double first cousins. Simon had three years of schooling and had worked all 52 weeks of 1939. His 1990 obituary called him a retired farmer and a Methodist who had lived in the Hugo area for 64 years; he left 17 grandchildren and 20 great-grandchildren. He and Frances, who married in 1925, are buried at Long Creek Cemetery near Hugo, also called Choctaw Cemetery.

The card shows how close the timing was. His mother's family applied on 1 May 1899, three days before the birth date given in the enrollment affidavits, so his birth affidavit was added later. His 1990 obituary instead gives 14 May 1899. The affidavits date much closer to his birth, but the discrepancy remains. His enrollment was recorded on 19 December 1899; the affidavit was returned for correction and the corrected one filed on 20 February 1900. At four he received a 160-acre homestead, the northeast quarter of Section 11, Township 5 South, Range 19 East, and he was issued a citizenship certificate at Hugo on 6 December 1907.

His wife's family on the Dawes cards: her mother Lizzie was Roll No. 3738 on Card 1363, written there as the 7-year-old daughter of Legion and Molsey Austin of Fowlerville, and her father Robert Pisachubbe was Roll No. 4467 on Card 1580 at Goodland. The two families lived forty miles apart in 1899 and joined in 1925 when Simon married their daughter Frances.

stories.title: Neighbors at Hagansport
stories.hook: In 1910 Oscar Smith, 19, and Pearl Satterfield, 11, lived a few doors apart in the same Texas farm community. Four years later they married.
body: Charles Oscar Smith was born on 29 May 1889 at Hagansport, Franklin County, Texas, a farm community that grew up around a Sulphur River crossing called Hagan's Port. In the 1880s it had about 150 people, a gin, a mill, four churches and a one-room school.

In June 1900 the census found "Oscar," 10, in the Franklin County household of John and Emma Smith, with Vera, Luina, Lona, Allie and baby Jimmie. John owned his farm free of mortgage. Emma died on 15 March 1905, at 37, and her stone at Hagansport reads "Emma / Wife of / J.B. SMITH / Gone but not forgotten."

By April 1910 John B. Smith had remarried, and Oscar, 19, was working on the home farm. The same census taker, on the same day, recorded the Satterfield family a few doors away: John C. and Samantha, lately from Kentucky, and their daughter Pearl, 11. Oscar and Artie Pearl Satterfield married in 1914.

They later crossed the Red River to Choctaw County, Oklahoma. Charles died on 17 August 1971 and Artie on 21 July 1983, and they are buried together in Grant Cemetery, south of Hugo. John B. Smith died in 1918 and lies beside Emma at Hagansport, in a grave "marked with a wooden stob."

His 1942 draft card gives his name as Charlie Oscar Smith, 52, of Forney in Choctaw County, with mail at Hugo Route 1, working on a farm. He gives his birthplace as 'Higgensport, Texas,' the Franklin County community more often spelled Hagansport, and names Mrs. Pearl Smith as the person who would always know his address.

The census pages follow Charles and Pearl from Texas to the Choctaw County farms. Their first daughter, Nellie Mae, was born at Talco, Texas, on 3 April 1917, three years after their marriage; by the 1920 census, enumerated as "C O Smith," 28, they were renting a farm at Oakes Township in Choctaw County, Oklahoma. In 1930 they were at Jeter with four children, and in 1940 the census taker wrote his name as "Oscar Msith," 50, a farmer on rented land on Hugo Route 1 who had worked all 52 weeks of 1939 for an income of $105. Nellie's 1973 death certificate names her parents as "Charley O. Smith" and "Pearl Satterfield."

stories.title: Judge and Choctaw senator
stories.hook: Spencer Academy, Mount Hermon and Roanoke College, then county clerk, legislator and judge in Cedar County.
body: A full-blood Choctaw (Dawes Roll No. 3487), born in Cedar County in December 1861, two miles west of High Hill church. His Dawes card names his parents as John and Betsy Thompson, both dead by 1899; his son Joel said John died when Joseph was nine.

A sketch of Joseph printed in 1891, while he was still a young man, says he was educated at Spencer Academy and at 'Mount Harmon Institute, Northfield' (D. L. Moody's Mount Hermon School for boys in Massachusetts), and finished at Roanoke College in Salem, Virginia, where he stayed until 1886. Joel remembered it in a different order: three years at Roanoke, then three years at a college in Massachusetts studying law.

The 1885 Choctaw census shows him at 24 in Cedar County, farming 20 acres of his own with a horse, six cattle and 30 hogs. The 1891 sketch says he began as a schoolteacher, was appointed county clerk of Cedar County in 1889, and the next year was elected to the lower house of the Choctaw Council, 'one of the youngest members of the legislature.' Joel said he later served as County Judge of Cedar County, holding court at Sulphur Springs near present-day Rattan, and about six years as a Senator.

He married Betsy Tims in 1889. They started in a one-room log house. In 1901 he built a big white house with two front rooms, a wide hall, an L-shaped kitchen and dining room, and lots of porches, 300 yards from High Hill Methodist Church. He sat on the school board, raised an orphan boy named Wister Davis, and had a son named Peter Pitchlyn Thompson.

The 1910 census, taken on the special Indian schedule, shows Joseph at 48 farming his own allotment free of mortgage in Wilson Township, Choctaw County. He gave both his parents' birthplace as Mississippi, which fits a family that came west on the Removal. Living with them was 19-year-old "David Wister," the orphan the family raised, whom Joel remembered as Wister Davis. Their nearest neighbors included Henry W. Thompson and two Tims households, one headed by James Tims, very likely Betsy's brother Jimmie. Henry's Dawes card names Simon and Lucy Thompson as his parents, while Joseph's card names John and Betsy.

Joel said his father was 'second of nine children' and that the 1901 house stood on a farm that raised 'plenty of hogs' and 'lots to eat.' He added that his father 'was always interested in the government of his people.' The county officers Joel named were Robert S. Frazier, High Sheriff, and Noah Frazier, Clerk, with James Brown Tims as a representative in the Council.

Joseph's name is in the federal record again after statehood. He filed a petition on 27 August 1908 from Fort Towson, and again on 10 September 1915 from Corinne; the Secretary of the Interior approved removal of restrictions on his land on 28 March 1916. In 1903 he had gone to Atoka to pick out the allotments for his wife and children.

The Mount Hermon part of the 1891 sketch fits the school's own history. A handbook of Northfield Seminary and the Mount Hermon School printed in 1889 records that by 16 October 1883, as the boys moved into the new brick cottages, "four Indians had arrived as pupils from the Indian Territory." It does not name them or their nation, so it does not prove Joseph was among them. The council records that name a J. P. Thompson are told in a separate story.

stories.note: The 1891 sketch heads him 'Joseph B. Thompson,' probably a printer's error; everything else in it fits. It also calls his father 'Rev. John Thompson,' a Presbyterian minister in Cedar County for twenty years, which does not fit Joel's memory that John died about 1870. Roanoke College had about 35 Choctaw students between 1876 and 1896, but Joseph does not appear in the 1881-82 catalog; that fits the sketch, which has him at Mount Hermon first, but the 1882-86 catalogs have not been seen. Joseph's terms as judge and senator have not yet been found in Choctaw Nation records. A Find a Grave memorial gives his birth as 1862 and has him at High Hill, but his burial there is unverified; his death in 1927 comes from family files. The orphan he raised is 'Wister Davis' in Joel's interview.

stories.title: Home from the Navy, lost in the Red River
stories.hook: John's older brother cooked for the Navy through the war, then died two summers after coming home.
body: Dois was the "Dais, 19" of the 1940 census, born 16 February 1921, the third of Grady and Mary's sons. He joined the U.S. Navy on 3 September 1942 and served as a Ship's Cook until 27 January 1946, the same years his younger brother John spent in the Navy in the Pacific.

On Thursday afternoon, 21 August 1947, he dove into shallow water in the Red River at Arthur City and broke his neck. A companion, Mac Davidson, pulled him out, and an ambulance took him to the Sanitarium of Paris. He died days later, at 26.
His funeral was at Grant Baptist Church, and he is buried at Shoat Springs Cemetery near Hugo. In October 1947 his father Grady signed the application for his military headstone.

His Texas death certificate lists him as single, 26 years, 6 months, 9 days old, a discharged U.S. Navy man, born in Choctaw County, Oklahoma, and living at Grant. It gives the cause as a fracture of the fifth cervical vertebra with a severed spinal cord, from an accident on 21 August at the Red River bridge north of Paris, and he lived four days. His father Grady Moffitt signed as informant and the certificate gives his mother's maiden name as Mary Shackelford, born in Alabama.
The Shoat Springs listing gives his rating as SC1C, Ship's Cook First Class, U.S. Naval Reserve, and the date 25 August 1947 that appears on his death certificate.

stories.title: Killed in France, 1918
stories.hook: A runner in the Choctaw Code Talkers' regiment, awarded the Croix de Guerre.
body: Judge Tims's son by Willie Jane Maxwell, enrolled Choctaw by Blood No. 4012 and listed as "Edmund, 3" in the 1896 Choctaw census. He served first in Co. L, 1st Oklahoma Infantry, then as a company runner in Co. D, 142nd Infantry, 36th Division. On 9 October 1918, near St. Étienne, France, a fellow runner spoke with him at 8 a.m. and an hour later found him killed by shrapnel.

He was posthumously awarded the French Croix de Guerre with Palm and lies in the Meuse-Argonne American Cemetery. The 142nd was the regiment of the Choctaw Code Talkers. The report pictured here, written by the regiment's commander, describes how Choctaw speakers were first used to send messages in this same St. Étienne fighting. Edmond is not listed as a code talker, but he served alongside them.

Two books printed in 1920 carry his name. Capt. Ben H. Chastaine of the 142d Infantry, in Story of the 36th: The Experiences of the 36th Division in the World War (Oklahoma City, Harlow Publishing Company), closes with an Honor Roll of the division's dead. Under "142d Infantry" it lists "TIMS, EDMOND, Private, Co. D," with the date October 8, 1918 (p. 287). The same year the War Department's casualty lists were printed state by state in Soldiers of the Great War, vol. 3. In the Oklahoma section, among the privates killed in action, the entry reads "TIMS, Edmond, Hugo" (p. 31).

The Honor Roll gives 8 October 1918 where the company runner's account in the regiment's report puts his death on the morning of the 9th. The two dates fall within the same two days, 8 and 9 October 1918, of the 142d Infantry's fighting at St. Étienne.

Chastaine's narrative of the morning of 8 October gives Edmond's battalion a hard start. The First Battalion lost its commander, Capt. Charles Kuhlman, and "half of the battalion headquarters group, including several runners," to a single shell before the jump-off, and Company D "wandered into the French sector to the left" and stayed there. The longer account is told under "The runner's morning: Company D at St. Etienne."

stories.title: In the Navy in the Pacific
stories.hook: Born at Frogville. Enlisted in the Navy at 18 and served on a floating drydock that came under air attack at Leyte.
body: Born 25 October 1925 at Frogville, Oklahoma, a Red River community of about 40 families, to Grady and Mary Moffitt; his older brothers were Alvin, Odis and Dois. In 1930 the family was living with his mother's parents in Martin County, Texas, and in 1940 he was "Johnnie," 14, at 411 North H Street in Hugo.

He enlisted in the U.S. Navy on 17 December 1943, at 18. Training as a corpsman (medic) at the Navy Hospital Corps School in San Diego has been credited to him, but no record seen confirms it, and the one rating found in his papers, on USS Chief in November 1945, is F1c, fireman first class, an engineering rating. From the day it was commissioned, 22 March 1944, he served on ARD-19, a floating drydock towed across the Pacific to Manus and then to Leyte in the Philippines. In late November 1944, while ARD-19 held the mine-damaged destroyer USS Ross, a Japanese fighter crashed into the dock and started gasoline fires, and the crews shot down a second attacker. ARD-19 earned a battle star for Leyte, then moved to Subic Bay on Luzon, where it kept repairing ships until after the war. For nearly all his time aboard, its commanding officer had a name much like his: Lieutenant Commander Allan P. Moffat.

Chief had a war behind her before he joined. She was an 890-ton Auk-class minesweeper, commissioned on 9 October 1943. In June 1944 she swept mines ahead of the Saipan and Tinian landings, and she was at Okinawa from late May to late August 1945. In September 1945 she swept minefields at Wakayama, Japan, ahead of the occupation forces and helped salvage the minesweeper YMS-418. Chief’s report of changes for the month ending 1 December 1945 shows him received aboard on 7 November from the commander of Mine Squadron Four (“COMINRON FOUR”), rated F1c; his muster-roll entries begin on 1 December 1945 or 1 January 1946. Where he came aboard, in the Philippines or in Japan, is not stated.

From November 1945 he was aboard the minesweeper USS Chief, which had swept mines off Japan and was on occupation duty at Nagoya and Sasebo until March 1946, when she sailed home to San Francisco. He was discharged on 9 May 1946 and married Faye Renee Smith in Paris, Texas, on 12 June 1947. He belonged to Emanuel Baptist Church in Hugo and died at Choctaw Memorial Hospital on 19 September 1990. His funeral followed two days later at Grant Cemetery.

Chief arrived at San Francisco in April 1946. His rolls run to 31 May, past his discharge, a gap that is probably just how the muster index records report dates. She went out of commission in reserve at San Pedro on 17 March 1947, was recommissioned for the Korean War, and was sold to Mexico in 1973 as ARM Jesus Gonzalez Ortega. The muster index’s label for her, MCM 14, belongs to a 1990s ship named after her.
His flat bronze marker at Grant Cemetery names the service first: "John W Moffitt / US Navy / World War II / Oct 25 1925 / Sep 19 1990."

stories.title: The school where 'Swing Low' was written down
stories.hook: Joseph Thompson's boarding school north of Doaksville gave the world a famous spiritual.
body: Spencer Academy was the first school created under the Choctaw Council's school law of 1842. It opened on 1 February 1844, a quarter mile north of present-day Spencerville on the old Fort Smith–Fort Towson military road, and was named for Secretary of War John C. Spencer, who gave it a 250-pound bell. Presbyterian missionaries ran it from 1846. Its three two-story halls had long porches, and the dining room served tanfula, a Choctaw crushed-corn dish.

The school closed in 1861. During the Civil War its buildings served as a Confederate hospital and sheltered homeless Choctaw families. It reopened in 1871 and ran until 1881, when a new Spencer Academy opened at Nelson, near Antlers. Joseph Thompson, born in 1861, was of school age during the reopened years. Among Spencer's earlier students was Allen Wright, later Principal Chief, who gave Oklahoma its name.

Before the war, Wallace and Minerva Willis, enslaved people hired out to the academy, sang their songs at their cabin door. Superintendent Alexander Reid wrote them down, and in 1871 he spent a day in Brooklyn teaching them to the Fisk Jubilee Singers: 'Steal Away to Jesus,' 'I'm a Rolling,' and 'Swing Low, Sweet Chariot.' Whether Wallace Willis composed the songs himself is debated.
src: National Register of Historic Places nomination, Spencer Academy (NRIS 75001562); Robert E. Flickinger, The Choctaw Freedmen and the Story of Oak Hill Industrial Academy (1914); O'Beirne, Leaders and Leading Men of the Indian Territory (1891).

stories.title: Henry and Hannah in the Ozarks
stories.hook: From Randolph County to the Stone County hills: a farm owned free and clear, and a widow who kept going for 22 years.
body: Henry was born in August 1855 in Lawrence County, Arkansas, the son of Nathan and Rebecca Moffitt, and appears as "Henry, 4" in their 1860 household. He and Hannah Grimes married about 1876. In June 1880 they were farming in Janes Creek Township, Randolph County, with daughter Josephine, 3, and son Jesse, 1.

By 1889 they were in Stone County, where son Tom was born at St. James, the old Buck Horn settlement. In May 1864 Buck Horn had seen the county's bloodiest Civil War fight, when Jo Shelby's Confederates attacked a band of bushwhackers. Grady was born near Mountain View in 1891, the year after the town incorporated.

The 1900 census, taken in Franklin Township, shows Henry as a farmer who owned his farm free of mortgage, with Hannah and five children at home: Jesse, Gimsa, Bertha, Tom and Woodford (Grady), 8. Henry died at Mountain View the next year, at 46. No grave has been found for him.

Hannah, who could not read or write, kept the family going. In 1910 she was a widow renting a house with Tom, a railroad section hand, and Grady, who worked in the timber. She had borne seven children, six still living. She died at Herpel, a Rocky Bayou settlement east of Mountain View, on 4 April 1923, and her stone in Herpel Cemetery reads "Wife of Henry H Moffitt."

stories.title: Quakers and the first Indy 500
stories.hook: A New Jersey Quaker family that moved west, a grandson who fought for the Union, and a cousin whose firm won the first Indianapolis 500.
body: The Nordykes were Quakers from Burlington County, New Jersey. Henry Nordyke married Rebecca Perkins there in 1731. Their descendants moved to Guilford County, North Carolina, then on to Ohio and Indiana with the Quaker migration away from slavery.

Aden was the oldest son of Abraham Nordyke and Mary Rogers, born in Burlington County in 1762. An Ohio county history says that while the family lived in Georgia he was shot in the arm during an Indian attack. He married Martha Johnson at Deep River, Guilford County, in 1787, and later moved on to Indiana, where he died in 1842.

An 1899 biography of Captain Adin Nordyke of the 63rd Indiana calls his father Robert Nordyke "son of Adin and Sarah Nordyke," and his mother Elizabeth Shaw. If this is our Aden, the captain was his grandson. Raised a Quaker, he "still holds to that doctrine," yet he fought at Resaca, Atlanta, Allatoona, Franklin and Nashville. Since our Sicily Nordyke married Noble Shaw, the two Guilford County families were probably linked twice.

Aden's brother Micajah moved to Clinton County, Ohio, in 1806 and gave the land for the East Fork Friends burying ground at New Vienna. Micajah's son Ellis, born in 1807, was a Quaker millwright who founded a flour-mill machinery works at Richmond, Indiana, with his son Addison. Daniel W. Marmon joined in 1866, and the firm moved to Indianapolis in 1876 as Nordyke & Marmon. On 30 May 1911 Ray Harroun drove its yellow No. 32 Marmon "Wasp" to victory in the first Indianapolis 500, averaging 74.6 miles per hour.

Hinshaw's Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy, vol. 1, carries a Quaker entry dated 12 December 1787: "Martha, dt Robert & Cecilia, Surry Co., m Adin Nordyke." If this is Aden's wife, her parents were Robert and Cecilia of Surry County, and the Quaker entry for the marriage is dated 12 December 1787. The name would also fit Aden's daughter Sicily, a form of Cecilia. The entry as printed gives no surname for Martha, so the link to Martha Johnson stays a lead. Hinshaw also lists Aden's children with Martha beginning "Sicily b. 8-2-1790. Mary 2-15-1792."

Deep River Monthly Meeting recorded the marriage intention of Adin Nordyke and Martha Johnson on 12 December 1787, naming his parents as Abraham and Mary Nordyke. It ties Aden to the Abraham Nordyke and Mary Rogers household that had come south from Burlington, New Jersey.

stories.title: The blue-and-white coverlets in Mary's will
stories.hook: Mary Moffitt divided a household among eight children: pewter, bedding, a coffee mill, her big Bible, and the work of settling her estate.
body: On 23 September 1820, Mary Moffitt made a will that records her household almost object by object. She was weak in body but declared herself sound in sense and memory. For each of her five daughters she set aside a pewter dish, six plates and two basins. Bedding received the same careful attention: white sheets, checked sheets, blankets, a blue-and-white flowered coverlet and a blue-and-white double-diamond coverlet. These were separate possessions to be passed to particular people, rather than an anonymous lot to sell.

Naomi Mackie was to have Mary's saddle and best cloak. Catharine Cox received the dresser and cupboard. Hannah Cox received the walnut chest and the big Bible. Mary Wilkinson was left the copper kettle and a five- or six-gallon pot. Margaret Moffitt received a feather bed, bedstead and pillows, the case of drawers, pewter teapot, coffee mill, square walnut table, flax and cotton, provisions and forage, and half the cattle, sheep and hogs. Mary was dividing the tools of cooking, sleeping, dressing and keeping a farm household.

Her sons Robert and William each received bedding and fifty dollars; David received the still, livestock, plantation utensils, cider vessels and 150 dollars. Leftover money was to be divided equally among all eight children, or the gifts reduced equally if the estate fell short. Mary directed the remaining household furniture and clothing to her daughters and the jack screw to her three sons. She appointed Margaret executrix alongside David as executor, and William Cox and Stephen Cox witnessed. The daughter who received the coffee mill would also share responsibility for carrying out the whole plan.

Mary had married William Moffitt at Cane Creek Monthly Meeting on 2 April 1763. His 1796 will had left her the wagon, still, household goods, farming tools and livestock, with rights in the home plantation during her widowhood. More than twenty years later, her own choices show how those broad provisions had become a detailed set of gifts to Naomi, Catharine, Hannah, Mary, Margaret, Robert, William and David. She dated the will “the 23rd day of the 9th month, 1820,” in the Quaker style, and her son Robert, our ancestor, was alive when she wrote it. The preserved file is indexed 1822. Her death is given as February 1822 in one account; the filing date alone does not establish it.

She was a daughter of Charles and Hannah (Matson) Davies. Her family had followed the Quaker road from Pennsylvania through Virginia to Cane Creek, North Carolina. Her sister Hannah married Hugh Moffitt, joining the Davies sisters to two Moffitt households. Mary's will brings that large family down to a smaller scale: one saddle, one Bible, particular coverlets and the people she wanted to have them.

stories.title: The midwife of Doaksville
stories.hook: Her Dawes card names her parents as John Steadman and O-we-na. She attended the birth of her grandson Simon.
body: Born 26 January 1842, Emeline was enrolled as Choctaw by Blood, Roll No. 1947, one-quarter blood, with her sons Johnny and Calvin on Card 778. The card names her father John Steadman as a noncitizen and her mother O-we-na as deceased in Towson County; it does not state John's race or O-we-na's ancestry.

She and Vinson farmed in the High Hill neighborhood north of Doaksville. Their children included James, Mitchell, Betsy (Mrs. Joseph Thompson), John, Rev. Robert Tims, Willie, Rosie and Calvin, and several of them later lived around Spencerville.

When her grandson Simon was born on 4 May 1899, Emeline attended as the midwife. On 17 October 1899 she swore before a notary at Doaksville that "there was born to her on said date a male child… said to have been named Simon Thompson," the affidavit that put Simon on the rolls. She died on 16 March 1918 and is buried at High Hill Cemetery.

Her grandson Joel did not remember her maiden name ('Grandmother Tims first name was Emmaline'), so the name Steadman comes from the Dawes records, not family memory. Joel placed her home 'about four miles north and a little west of Doaksville,' in Towson County, 'known as the Charley Blankenship place now.' A local history says six or seven miles. Betsy and Joseph were married there in 1889.

Emeline and Vinson are 'buried there at the old place,' Joel said. A memorial at High Hill Cemetery for Emeline, created by the Choctaw County Genealogical Society, gives her dates, while a photograph of a Tims headstone in a local history is captioned Hampton Chapel Cemetery, which may belong to a child. Her husband's marker at High Hill is a cenotaph.

Her name is printed "Emiline" in the 1944 memoir of her son, the Rev. Robert James Tims, which says he was born six miles north of Fort Towson and was "the son of Vincent and Emiline Tims." The Methodist Indian Mission minutes also give the date and place of birth of another son, James Brown Tims: 25 June 1864, at Doaksville.

Her name is on more Dawes cards than her own. Card 778 enrolls her with Johnny and Calvin; the cards of her sons James B. (510), Robert (816), Mitchell (850) and Willie (1268) each name "Emiline Tims" as mother, and so do the cards of her daughters Rosanna (1281) and Betsy (1283). The men's father is written variously as "Vinson W. Tims," "Vincent Tims" and "Benson Tims," always dead by 1899. In the 1900s she kept being asked to vouch for births.

Her daughter Rosanna was first on her mother's Card 778, enrolled on 24 April 1899, and moved to her husband James Wilson's Card 1281 in October 1900; the notary who sorted out the name wrote that Rosanna's "mother name is Emaline Times." Emeline swore as midwife to the birth of Rosanna's son (23 March 1903) and, signing as "midwife" on 29 April 1905, of Betsy's son Joseph W. (5 March 1903), swore with Rosanna to the birth of Rosanna's daughter Candace (16 June 1905), and swore with Mildred to the birth of Mitchell's son Vincenta (1904; the Commission acknowledged the affidavits in April 1905).

stories.title: From Butler County to the Red River
stories.hook: A Kentucky farm family that moved to Texas about 1907 and ended up around Soper and Hugo.
body: John C. Satterfield was born in 1864 in Allen County, Kentucky. In 1880, at 16, he was a farm laborer at Renfrow, Butler County, in the household of his father, James H. Satterfield, with his brothers and sisters. His mother, Melissa Gibson, had died in 1877.

A widower with three children, Henry B. (born May 1883), Martha A. (August 1884) and John W. (January 1887), he married Samantha D. "Mantha" Johnson, about 20, in 1892. In 1900 they were farming at Horse Mill, Butler County, with seven children at home. Their son Wavey Lincoln was born near Morgantown on 28 December 1895 according to his draft cards; his headstone gives 9 January 1896. Artie Pearl followed in August 1898. Wavey later served as an Army private in World War I. A family account identifies an early son, Joseph, who died before 1910.

About 1907 the family moved to Franklin County, Texas. In April 1910 John, 46, was renting a farm at Hagansport, with Wavey, Pearl, James, Ira and little Stella. A family account says their last child was born in Texas in 1912. John died in Franklin County a few years later. On 28 July 1917 Samantha married Bird Alexander "Alex" Stephens at Mount Vernon, Texas, and they moved across the Red River to Choctaw County, Oklahoma. Wavey died at Soper in 1952. Their daughter Artie Pearl married Charles Oscar Smith in 1914; both are buried at Grant Cemetery. Samantha died in Choctaw County in 1928 and is buried as Samantha Stephens in Soper Cemetery.
His father's family is described under James Henry Satterfield and Melissa Gibson.

Samantha's husband John C. had a larger family than the two households show. His full brothers and sisters, children of James H. and Melissa, included Sidney Rufus (1865-1949), James Doiser (1867-1929, who went to Clay County, Arkansas) and A. M. (born in Minnesota in 1870, died 1892). His nine half-siblings by Lucinda Phelps lived mostly around Texarkana. He and his brother Sidney both married women of the Clark-Johnson family of Butler County.

The farm John C. Satterfield rented at Hagansport in 1910 was in a county where, by the government's 1908 soil survey, tenants on the usual share plan gave up half the crop, and farms averaged under 80 acres. The Hagansport soil was heavy clay that stayed sticky after rain and suited cotton better than corn. See the story on renting on shares at Hagansport.
