Wright, Oklahoma: A History of the State and Its People (1929), vol. 1, pp. 165-70 and note 17, archive.org/details/oklahomahistoryo01thob; Fort Coffee entry in the same volume's chapter on military posts
stories.note: No removal roll naming Joseph Pisachubbe has been seen. Fort Coffee was established in June 1834, so a settlement there in 1832 cannot be literal.
stories.place: Mississippi; Arkansas Post and Little Rock; the Arkansas River near Fort Smith and Fort Coffee

stories.title: Doaksville before the store: 1833 in the removal papers
stories.hook: A Choctaw district's letter of February 1833 complains of white traders in 'a small town below Kiametia' and names Doaksville as the place where annuities were received.
body: Doak & Tims is usually dated by its contracts of 1838-39. The removal correspondence puts Doaksville on the map five years earlier. In Senate Document 512, the printed correspondence on the emigration of the Indians, a letter dated at Horn Prairie on Red River on 6 February 1833 is signed by the treaty captains of Nittuckachee's district. They write that their people "are entirely satisfied with our new country" and ask that their annuity be delivered at Horn Prairie, because "at Doaksville, where we have generally received our arms and articles mentioned in the treaty, our horses have suffered much, as there is no winter range." There was a complaint too: "We have to inform you that we have too many white traders in our country, we wish you to have them removed. ... They have built a small town below Kiametia, consisting of white traders, with the exception of two." They would not object to "a few traders ... but we do not wish to be crowded."

The same volumes carry a smaller clue to the man the town was named for. In the account of Lieutenant J. R. Stephenson, the officer in charge of the subsistence depot at Fort Towson, a line lists Josiah S. Doak with "28 lbs. bacon and 4 lbs. sugar," for the first and third quarters of 1833. The printed columns are garbled in the scan, so what Doak was paid for is unclear, but it shows a Josiah S. Doak dealing with the removal's quartermasters on the Red River in the year of the letter.

Vincent B. Tims was a witness, with Doak, to the Treaty of Doaksville on 17 January 1837 and was feeding Chickasaw emigrants under contract by 1 January 1838, at thirteen cents a ration. His partnership with Doak was dissolved in 1844. A New Orleans advertisement in the Washington (Arkansas) Telegraph of 10 December 1845 lists references that begin with "Maj. Wm. Armstrong, Choctaw A[gency]" and include "Doak & Tims, Doaksville, C. Nation." Armstrong was the Choctaw agent, and his brother Francis had taken the 1831 census and run the removal; by 1845 the agent himself stood as a reference for the firm. The Oklahoma history of 1954 lists the Doak & Tims Mercantile Company among the stores of Doaksville, with a blacksmith shop and a hotel.

No document seen puts Tims himself at Doaksville in 1833. Family accounts say he was born in South Carolina in 1803 and had a Choctaw wife; his earliest record at Doaksville that has been seen is the January 1837 treaty. The 1833 letter shows what he walked into: a Red River town already built by white traders, already resented by the Choctaw districts around it, and already the place the government's goods and annuities were handed out.

quotes.c: Treaty captains of Nittuckachee's district, Horn Prairie, 6 February 1833, in Senate Doc. 512

stories.title: Peter Gaunt, who knew no visible worship in the world
stories.hook: Called before the Plymouth court in 1655 for staying away from church, Peter Gaunt of Sandwich said he knew no public visible worship in the world, and was fined in cattle for the Quaker meetings that followed.
body: Peter Gaunt settled at Sandwich on Cape Cod, in Plymouth Colony, with his wife Lydia, whose surname is unknown. One proposed identification links him to a Peter baptized at St Peter at Gowts, Lincoln, on 29 June 1610, son of Thomas Gaunt and Susan Bate. That identification remains unproved. Thomas and Susan married at Rotherham on 28 August 1609, and Susan's will calls Peter her only son.

The colony’s court books follow Peter Gaunt for six years. At the court of 6 March 1654/5 he was called in "to answare for neglecting to frequent the publick worship of God." Asked to speak to the charge, the record says, "Peter Gaunt affirmed hee knew noc publicke vizable worship now in the world, whereunto the said Ralph Allen assented, but Gorg Allen dissented; the case was left to further consideration." Within three years the same court was fining him for Quaker meetings.

On 2 March 1657/8 Gaunt, Daniel Wing, Ralph Allen Jr. and William Allin were summoned "for a tumultuose carriage att a meeting of the Quakers att Sandwich." The court cleared them of that charge, "notwithstanding, for theire vnreuerent carrying themselues before the Court, coming in before them with theire hatts on," it fined each of them twenty shillings. Thomas Butler, whose daughter Dorothy would marry Peter's son Hananiah in 1678, was summoned for the same disturbance and was "admonished and cleared."

The fines were collected in cattle. In June 1660 a note was entered in the court's record that Marshal George Barlow "tooke from Goodman Gaunt, for his fine of 24li, these particulares: seauen cowes & heifers, two steers, seauen bushells and an halfe of pease; and after, when one of the cowes died, hee tooke another liue one in stead therof, because Barlow had not the hide of the dead cow deliuered to him." Thomas Burgis Jr. owned in open court that he had made the report, and was himself fined thirty shillings for refusing to help the marshal. Joseph Besse's Sufferings of the People Called Quakers, in a list of goods taken from Plymouth Colony Friends about 1658, prints "Peter Gaunt 43 l. 14 s. 6 d."

The summonses kept coming. In October 1660 a long list of people "fined for being att Quakers meetings," ten shillings each, includes "Peter Gaunt, Dorithy Butler, Obadiah Butler." In February 1660/1 the Sandwich constable was ordered to bring Gaunt and nine others to Plymouth "to answare for theire tumultuouse carriages against the marshall and cunstable of Sandwich in the execution of theire offices in the cecuring of two Strang Quakers." A ten-shilling fine on Gaunt "was leuied vpon a mistake" and was given back. In 1661 a list given into the court of those who had sheltered visiting Friends reads: "Wiliam Allin entertained Christopher Holder. Wiliam Newland entertained one forraigne Quaker. Peter Gaunt entertained two forraigne Quakers."

Family trees date Peter’s death at Sandwich to 10 May 1678, the day of his son Hananiah’s marriage to Dorothy Butler, but the date needs independent confirmation. Lydia died in April 1692. Their sons included Israel and Hananiah, who went to New Jersey. A 1661 court case involving Thomas Burgis Jr. names a Lydia Gaunt; the record does not identify her as Peter’s wife, so it does not establish an event in this family. (Lead)

stories.title: The Butlers of Sandwich and the marshal
stories.hook: Thomas and Dorothy Butler were fined in cattle and money for Quaker meetings; their son Daniel was publicly whipped in June 1660.
body: Thomas Butler was at Sandwich, Plymouth Colony, soon after the town was founded in 1637. In March 1657/8 he was summoned with Peter Gaunt and others over a Quaker meeting and "admonished and cleared." In 1658-9 he was fined ten shillings "for refusing to assist the marshall, Barlow, in the execution of his office," and the court assigned another fine, fifty shillings for refusing to serve as constable, to Barlow himself.

In June 1660 the court passed two sentences on the family: "Daniell Butler, for rescuing a Strang Quaker, when apprehended by the marshall, Barlow, and for his breakeing away when taken p'soner, is sentanced to bee publickly whipt, which accordingly was pformed." The next reads: "Thomas Butler, and Dorithy, his wife, for turbulent cariages the same night that theire son Daniell was serched for att theire house, fined forty shillings." In October 1660 Dorothy Butler, almost certainly the mother, was fined ten shillings for being at Quaker meetings.
The court later returned twenty shillings taken from Thomas for his wife and son attending a Quaker meeting. Its October list also names Obadiah Butler among those fined.

Thomas was also a land-hunter. In 1665 the court sent Richard Bourne and William Bassett "to view and purchase some lands desired by Edmond Freeman and Thomas Butler lying towards Saconeesett," and when the Indians would not part with that parcel it gave them leave to buy other land for him. In 1667 the court granted Butler "a necke of land called Tassacausett, lying neare to Edmond Freemans land," which he had "bought ... of an Indian called Charles, alias Pampmumitt, for a yoake of oxen," provided the Indian returned three pounds to Butler.

Dorothy died on 9 August 1675 and was buried the next day. Thomas died on 12 March 1690. Their daughter Dorothy, born 23 January 1649/50, married Hananiah Gaunt at the Quaker meeting at Sandwich in 1678, and they carried the Quaker family to New Jersey. Thomas's origin and Dorothy's maiden name are not known.

stories.title: Thirty-five head of cattle: Sandwich in December 1658
stories.hook: A magistrate's letter to a friend in London, printed by Joseph Besse, describes the town where the Gaunts and Butlers lived as nearly all Quaker and being stripped of its cows.
body: In December 1658 J. Cudworth (James Cudworth of Scituate), a Plymouth Colony magistrate who had lost his seat on the bench and his militia captaincy for "entertaining some of the Quakers at my House," wrote to a friend in London. Joseph Besse printed the letter in his Sufferings of the People Called Quakers. Of Sandwich, Cudworth said: "almost the whole Town of Sandwich is adhering towards them: And give me leave a little to acquaint you with their Sufferings, which is grievous unto, and saddens the Hearts of most of the precious Saints of God."

He described the method. The Quakers would not swear, so the old law that every man take the oath of fidelity was revived: refuse it and pay five pounds or leave the colony. "When the Time is come, they are the same as they were; then goes out the Marshal, and fetches their Cows and other Cattle ... On this Account thirty five Head of Cattle, as I have been credibly informed, have been, by the Authority of our Court, taken from them the latter Part of this Summer." Some families had one cow, some two, "and many small Children in their Families, to whom, in Summer-time, a Cow or two was the greatest outward Comfort they had for their Subsistence."

A poor weaver with seven or eight small children, lame himself, had two cows, and both were taken. "The Marshal asked him, What he would do, he must have his Cows? The Man said, That God that gave him them, he doubted not, but would still provide for him." The court then fixed fines for the meetings themselves, ten shillings a meeting, which Cudworth reckoned at one hundred and fifty pounds for Sandwich men, "Newland ... for himself and his Wife" being twenty-four of it and the weaver twenty.

The town was watched. "Sandwich Men may not go to the Bay, lest they be taken up for Quakers," Cudworth wrote, and a man who went on business was put in prison for twenty-four hours while witnesses were sent for. By the colony's newest law, anyone who entertained a Quaker "if but a Quarter of an Hour" forfeited five pounds. Besse follows the letter with a list of other people whose goods were taken at about the same time, for refusing to swear or for absence from public worship. It includes "Peter Gaunt 43 l. 14 s. 6 d.," and the whole list amounts, Besse says, to about six hundred and sixty pounds.

Peter Gaunt's goods and the Butler family's fines are in the colony's own court books, told under “Peter Gaunt, who knew no visible worship in the world” and “The Butlers of Sandwich and the marshal.” Twenty years later Peter's son Hananiah and Thomas Butler's daughter Dorothy were married at the Sandwich Friends meeting, and within a few years they left for New Jersey.

stories.title: A "madman" at the table: William Dewsbury and Richard Browne
stories.hook: The Nottingham Friends' family memorandum says our Browne ancestor became a Quaker when William Dewsbury shared his table, and that his landlord then made him pay his rent twice.
body: In 1786 East Nottingham Monthly Meeting entered into its book of births and burials an account of the English father of William Brown the emigrant, written down from the stories of a great-nephew of William's in his eightieth year. It places the father in "Puddington" near Wellingborough, today's Podington, and says he had been "some time in communion with the Baptists, afterwards joining with the sect called Puritans, and is said to have been a teacher among both, and a seeking, religious man." The memorandum calls him William, but the Wellingborough Quaker registers give the father's name as Richard. Other register transcriptions describe Richard as of Boasworth (see “Stripped of their property for fines”), so the family's English home is given two ways.

The story is that William Dewsbury, "about the first going forth" of that minister, came to the town, and the man noticed "the solidity of his countenance" and asked him in to "break bread." When they sat down the host said grace. Dewsbury sat in a grave manner and answered, "if thou wilt first partake with me I shall be free to partake with thee." After a short silence he was moved to speak, "beginning with these words, 'O Earth! Earth! hear the word of the Lord,'" and the host was convinced. When he came home with Dewsbury his wife asked why he had brought "that madman" to their house. "Why woman," he answered, "he hath brought the Eternal Truth of God to us." She thought it over and was convinced too.

The cost came quickly. The landlord, "a wild airy man and given to sporting," sent his tenant two young hounds to feed and raise. The tenant would not, and the landlord waited. Rent had been paid every half year to a steward without a receipt, so the landlord demanded it again, and said, "except you will take your oath that it is paid, you shall pay it to me." Browne held that Christ had forbidden swearing, so "this Friend had to pay his rent over again," and was then turned off the farm. It took him a considerable time to find another, where he did well. Dewsbury came back, the memorandum adds, and Browne got him leave to speak in the parish church, where "many people were convinced."

Richard died about 1664 by the memorandum's reckoning (a Quaker burial record in the registers gives 1662), and on his deathbed told his wife, "thou shalt live to bring up all our children, and they shall be blessed and be all favoured to keep their habitations in the Truth." The memorandum makes William, born about 1656 in its reckoning, the youngest of nine, six other sons and two daughters. The original Wellingborough register instead gives his birth as the twenty-ninth day of the first month 1658 and names his father Richard; it does not name his mother. The same pages say that when Penn's province was proposed, some Friends doubted whether to go, and Dewsbury, preaching among the Brownes in Northamptonshire, told them: "The Lord is about to plant the wilderness of America with a choice vine or noble seed which shall grow and flourish."

Besse's Sufferings of the People Called Quakers records, in its Northamptonshire section, a meeting at Findon where Daniel Brown and Joane Brown, both "of Puddington in Bedfordshire," were taken with some forty other Friends, held overnight in an alehouse, fined forty shillings each, and sent with the rest to the county gaol for six weeks. Nothing in either source ties them to Richard, and the match rests only on the village name, so it remains a lead.

stories.title: Lots 23 and 33: William Brown on the Nottingham Lots
stories.hook: William Brown is said to have cut the first tree on the Nottingham Lots in 1701; the plat gives him Lots 23 and 33 and his sons the lots beside them, and the first meeting was held in his house.
body: Before Nottingham there was Marcus Hook. William Brown came over about 1682 or 1683 with a first wife, Dorothy, who “could not give up to it cheerfully.” The Nottingham memorandum says he felt a clear sense of duty and that “the Lord wonderfully made way for and assisted him,” and adds that on the voyage his wife died at sea. (The memorandum dates his landing “about the year 1696,” which Cope marks as wrong.) Their son Joseph had been born in England on 12 June 1682. William went first to his older brother James, a weaver, who was already at Marcus Hook on the Delaware. James had been in Pennsylvania before Penn’s grant, by Gilbert Cope’s reckoning. He married Honor Clayton, whose father William Clayton came in 1677, and on the 20th of the 12th month 1683 (February 1683/4 in modern reckoning) he took a patent for 115 acres on Chichester Creek, which he named “Podington” after the home village. He conveyed it to his son William in 1706.

About 1692 George Keith, once a leader among Friends, split the Quakers of the Delaware. At Chichester meeting Keith “spake or preached largely, using some arrogant and lofty expressions, beyond the simplicity of the gospel.” James Brown, “having at first a favourable opinion of Keith,” asked his brother afterwards “what he thought of George Keith now; was not he satisfied?” William, “a deep feeling man,” answered, “I am satisfied, but it is in this, that he is in a wrong spirit.” James took it badly and started to leave. William stepped after him and asked whether he remembered “how they used to feel at their meetings when in England, though they were but as lads,” and went on: “In this country we have come under a different dispensation ... We have been looking out and allowed to provide towards an outward inheritance, and settlements for ourselves and families, free from disturbance or persecution; but let us remember that the truth is still as precious as ever.”

The next day Keith held a meeting at the house of Henry Reynolds and called at James’s door on the way. James hesitated; Keith got down from his horse and went in, saying that if James was growing dissatisfied he would satisfy him, but “though he used many words, all did not avail, for James went not to meeting.” James later settled in the same neighborhood at Nottingham and died about 1715, “a religious man and of a good character, but not favoured with a capacity or talent equal to his brother William.” William’s son Richard married Hannah Reynolds of Chichester in 1717.

The Nottingham Lots were thirty-seven rectangular lots of Penn's land laid out in 1701-02 on the border with Maryland. A 1902 bicentennial history of the Brick Meeting House at Calvert, Maryland, says "all agree that William Brown was the first Friend to settle on the Nottingham lots." The family memorandum says he moved his family there in 1702, "accounted far back in the wilderness." The bicentennial history adds a tradition that Penn himself rode out in the early spring of 1701 with a party that included William Brown, James Brown, John Churchman, Edward Beeson and Henry Reynolds, and that in the fall the two Brown brothers went to the site on pack horses from New Castle to clear ground for corn.

The plat as the history gives it assigns "No. 23 to William Brown" and "No. 33 to William Brown," with "No. 14 to James Brown" and Nos. 26 and 27 to James, and "No. 28 to Messer Brown." Messer is William's son Mercer, born in February 1685/6, whose first name was his mother Ann Mercer's maiden name; the history prints it as Messer, as it was commonly written. William's lot was beside a spring about a mile east of the present Rising Sun, near the road to the Brick Meeting House.

Tradition, "which is now upon record," says William "was the first to take his axe in hand and strike it into a tree, one of the monarchs of the forest," and said, "In humble trust we commence our labor." The spring is said to have been an Indian camping ground on the trail from Pennington to the mouth of the Susquehanna, which an old resident, Jesse Pugh, remembered tracing as a boy.

The records are firmer about the meeting. At Concord Monthly Meeting in the 2nd month of 1705, "two Friends of Nottingham desires on behalf of the rest a First Day meeting at the house of William Brown, and a Fourth Day meeting once a month," and Concord Quarterly Meeting on 9 April 1705 "approves of until further order." The first brick meetinghouse followed in 1724. Penn's spoken gift of forty acres for a meetinghouse, burial ground and school in 1701 was the only title Friends had until 1765, when his sons Thomas and Richard Penn issued a patent to William Brown, Timothy Kirk, William Churchman and Benjamin Chandlee in trust.

William Brown the emigrant died, by the family memorandum, on the 23rd of the 6th month 1746 (23 August), "in the 91st year of his age," having lived at Nottingham about 44 years "in good repute for his integrity; being an elder in the Church, and a substantial Friend." Ninety-one would put his birth near 1655; the Wellingborough register gives 1658. Another account gives his death as 1 October 1746; the memorandum’s 23 August (Old Style) is the date written down by the family. His great-nephew and namesake William Brown, a minister, traveled in Europe with John Churchman from 1750 to 1754 and was the man in whose eightieth year the memorandum was written down.

stories.title: Three cows, two mares and 500 acres: Thomas and Agnes Croasdale on the Neshaminy
stories.hook: Two inventories preserve a family’s Pennsylvania household: livestock, bedding, tools and a 500-acre holding on Neshaminy Creek.
body: Thomas Croasdale of New Hay, Yorkshire, married Agnes Hawthornthwaite of Wyresdale on 1 May 1664. The marriage was recorded by Lancaster Monthly Meeting. Eighteen years later, the couple prepared to leave England with six children. The certificate issued at Settle on 7 June 1682 names the whole household, placing their move within a group of Quaker families rather than an isolated voyage.

Before leaving, Thomas arranged to buy land in Pennsylvania by deeds dated 21 and 22 April 1682. The family history describes a purchase of a thousand acres, but the estate papers later describe a 500-acre holding; in Pennsylvania 500 acres of the purchase were laid out on Neshaminy Creek near the present Langhorne. The records concern different stages of acquiring and settling land; they should not be treated as two measurements of an unchanged farm.

One of those documents survives. The Friends Historical Library at Swarthmore College catalogs the 21 April 1682 indenture from William Penn to Thomas Croasdale as a vellum document with a red seal, signed by both men. The catalog describes a yearly rent of one peppercorn. The document was made before the family crossed the Atlantic; its catalog does not itself describe their voyage.

Thomas died on 2 November 1684, about two years after the move. Agnes became administrator of his estate. On 8 December, James Dillworth and Thomas Constable valued his belongings: clothing, bedding, pewter and brass, cushions, wooden vessels, chests, linen, ironware and hogs. Two mares were worth £8 10s; three cows, a calf and a yearling were valued at £12. The goods totaled £47 9s. The 500 acres were listed but left unvalued.

The inventory of “Agnes Crossdale of Neshaminah Widdowe” was taken by Nicholas Waln, who signed with his mark, and Robert Heaton. It gives the household another outline: brass and pewter, pots, a bed and bedding, a chest, a saddle, hogs, three cows, two bullocks, a heifer, two mares and a colt. This time the land was valued at £50, nearly half the £106 5s total. Small things also survived into the account: a blanket, nails and the tools used around the house and farm, or in its own words, “one Blankit Some nails all the husbandrie Tooles & hustlement about the House.”

Agnes died on 20 October 1686, according to the family account, and sons William and John received administration on 1 November. The printed inventory is dated the 10th of the 9th month 1685 but registered on the 1st of the 9th month 1686; neither fits a death in October 1686, so one of the printed years is off, and the transcript does not resolve it. The children’s list names William (born 7 February 1664/5), John, Elizabeth (who died in 1683), Mary, Bridget (30 August 1671) and Alice. Alice married David Potts, and Mary, William Smith. William, who stayed in Bucks County, made his will on the 30th of the 1st month 1715 (30 March), naming his sisters Mary Smith with eight children and Alice Potts with ten. Bridget’s marriage to John Cowgill carries this branch into the Brown, Norton, Chamness and Moffitt families.

The same archive preserves a later trace of the family’s land. In 1728 John Wildman and his wife Mara, the widow of Thomas and Agnes’s son John Croasdale, transferred land in Middletown to a Thomas Croasdale identified in the catalog as John’s son. He was Bridget’s nephew. Other documents in the collection describe a debt involving a Thomas Croasdale and a sheriff’s sale in 1733; whether this was the same nephew requires further research.

Agnes’s maiden name may link her to a Friend who was jailed. Besse lists a “William Hathornthwaite” among forty-three Friends arrested at Swarthmoor in January 1660 for refusing the oath and committed to Lancaster Castle (Lancashire section, p. 308). Nothing yet ties him to Agnes, so this is a lead only.

stories.note: Thomas Maxwell Potts’s 1895 book reproduces the inventories and meeting entries; these are printed transcriptions, not images of the original manuscripts. Thomas’s inventory supports his death in 1684 rather than 1682. Agnes’s printed inventory year conflicts with the reported 1686 death and administration. Their own birth dates and parents remain unverified. The ship name is disputed in later accounts. The Swarthmore finding aid describes the 1682 and 1728 documents; their original text has not been independently examined. The 1733 debtor’s identity is not established.

stories.title: Ellen Cowgill, widow of Giggleswick, and the sons who came as servants
stories.hook: The 1682 Settle certificate calls her "Ellen Cowgill widow & her children"; two of her sons landed in Pennsylvania in service.
body: On 7 June 1682 Settle Monthly Meeting, in the Yorkshire dales, issued a certificate for a party of Friends bound for Pennsylvania. It lists Cuthbert Hayhurst "his wife & family," Thomas Wrigglesworth and Alice, Thomas Walmsley and Elizabeth, Thomas Croasdale "Agness his wife & six children," Thomas Stackhouse and his wife, Nicholas Waln "his wife & three children," William Hayhurst, and "Ellen Cowgill widow & her children." No child is named. Ellen was born near Giggleswick about 1639, so she was about forty-three. Later genealogical research, working from Middletown Meeting records and the Board of Property minutes, identifies her children as Edmund, Jennet, John, Jane and probably Ralph; the certificate does not name them.

Her husband's name is not documented. Many trees name Ralph Cowgill, said to have been hanged in 1682 as a Quaker, but that has no documentation, and the Cowgill family association thinks Edmund Cowgill, baptized in 1634 at Thornton in Craven, more likely. Her maiden name is also disputed: some books give Stackhurst, and several Stackhouse histories say she was not a Stackhouse, so a Thomas Stackhouse of Giggleswick and Anna Evans are not added as her parents.

John, probably about seventeen, came as a servant to Cuthbert Hayhurst. Hayhurst, born at Easington in Yorkshire about 1633, had been among the Friends imprisoned in the West Riding in the 11th month of 1660 for refusing the oath of allegiance. In 1668 he held a meeting at the house of Richard Betteris in Oxford and was arrested while speaking and held for a month by the vice-chancellor. His neighbor Nicholas Waln wrote that "he went through many great exercises and imprisonments." He died in the first month of 1683, only months after landing in Bucks County.

Ralph Cowgill came by a different ship, landing about 28 September 1682. Under Randolph Blackshaw of Hallingee, Cheshire, a list of Bucks County residents prints: "These servants below came in the ship the 'Friend's Adventure.' The Mr., Thomas Wall. Arrived in this river the 28th 7th M., 1682. Servants to Randulph Blackshaw, William Beasy, Ralph Nuttall, and Ralph Cowgill, each to serve 4 years, and to have 50 acres of land apiece." Passengers and Ships Prior to 1684 (1970) lists both John and Ralph as apparently Ellen's children: John, "servant to Cuthbert Hayhurst" and a probable passenger on the Lamb of Liverpool, and Ralph, who came on the Friend's Adventure.

Which ship carried the Settle families has been told two ways. Potts's Our Family Ancestors (1895) and the 1915 Stout family history say they sailed in Penn's own Welcome, and Potts adds that smallpox killed thirty on that ship. The later study says at least four of the seven Settle families sailed on the Lamb of Liverpool, and a Watson family history lists the Lamb, "John Tench, master, from Liverpool," as arriving on 22 October 1682. The party's own certificate does not name a ship.

Ellen settled at Middletown, Bucks County, and is buried in the Middletown Friends cemetery; she died in 1705. John served his time, married Bridget Croasdale at Neshaminy in 1693, and had four children by her before her death in 1701, among them Elizabeth, born in 1694, who married William Brown Jr. John married Rachel Bunting in 1703/4. Jennet married Bernard Lane at Burlington on 2 February 1688. Elizabeth's daughter Elizabeth Brown married Edward Norton, and the line came down through the Nortons and Chamnesses to the Moffitts.

stories.title: Carted through Dover: John Cowgill of Little Creek, 1776
stories.hook: Elizabeth Cowgill's nephew refused Continental paper money on conscience, was declared an enemy to his country by the Kent County Committee in January 1776, and was driven to Dover in a cart with a paper pinned to his back.
body: John Cowgill of Little Creek Hundred was the son of John Cowgill and Lydia Clayton, and the grandson of the tanner John Cowgill of Black Bird's Creek, which makes him a nephew of Elizabeth (Cowgill) Brown, our ancestor. On 4 January 1776 the Committee of Inspection and Observation for Kent County, Caesar Rodney and Thomas Rodney among its members, resolved "that it appears to this Committee, by the confession of John Cowgill, a residenter of Little Creek Hundred, in this County, that he has refused, and, from conscience, shall refuse, to take said Continental money in discharge of debts, or for other purposes, when tendered to him." The committee decided he was "an enemy to his country, and ought to be treated as such by every friend of American liberty; and that they ought to have no further dealings with him."

His daughter Mary Corbit described the arrest in a letter of 1824 to her brother John, who passed it on to Samuel R. Fisher. It began when he asked a tenant to pay rent in specie. He was taken before the Assembly at Dover and threatened with "a heavy fine," and, when he declined to take any part in encouraging war, was let go. Later "going to Meeting on a fifth day, mother and I being in the chaise, and my father on horseback with one of my little brothers behind him," a man in regimentals rode with him half a mile where armed men were waiting. "The child was taken from behind him, and he was ordered to dismount and get into a cart." Friends coming to meeting followed as far as the meetinghouse, where "my father called out and bid us farewell." "A paper was pinned to his back."

Before they entered the town the officer stopped the cart, and, taking his calm for ignorance, said, "Mr. Cowgill you are not aware of the danger you are in!" He answered: "I fear not them that can kill the body, and after that have no more power that they can do; but I fear Him who after he hath killed the body, hath all power." At the liberty pole in Dover it was proclaimed that he had no protection and that anyone dealing with him did so at their peril; "the miller was threatened with the destruction of his mill if he ground for his family, and the school-master forbid receiving his children at school."

The man was let go, and many Friends rode home with him. His daughter wrote, "When we went to bed at night we did not know what would be the issue before morning, and in this way we lived for several years." She told of one of the party who took him that day. The roads were wet and muddy, and Cowgill, seeing the man walking beside the cart, said, "Thee had better get up and sit with me, as the walking is wet and I am fearful thee will take cold." The man said long afterward that he never regretted any act of his life more than being concerned in the affair against "one of the best of men."

Duck Creek Monthly Meeting, on 27 June 1778, received "an account of the sufferings of John Cowgill for refusing Continental Currency" and sent it to the Quarterly Meeting committee. John married Mary Worrell and had a large family; his daughter Mary married William Corbit of Odessa, Delaware.

stories.title: A cane and a sword
stories.hook: Wills and inventories from 1731–32 trace three generations of a Perkins family and their connection to the Nordykes.
body: In May 1731 administration of the estate of Jacob Perkins of "Wellenborrow," Burlington County, who died without a will, went to his son Jacob Perkins, yeoman. The inventory, made on 20 May by Robert Lucas and Joseph Fenimore, comes to 91 pounds 18 shillings 5 pence and "includes cane and sword, £1.10; debt of 14 shillings from Benja. Perkins; 8 years rent due from Benja. Perkins and Wm. Makintass, £1."

The son, Jacob Perkins Jr., made his own will on 26 October 1731. He left his wife Sarah and his children "Abraham, Rebeckah, David, Mary, Ann, Susannah, Hannah, Sarah, Bethseda and Martha." He disposed of "land in Chester, which I bought of John Ward March 15, 1728," and listed bonds due him "from James Smith, Esq., John Shinn and Henry Nordike." He also left ten pounds to St. Mary's Church, Burlington, the Church of England parish, which points to Church of England ties. His son David was executor and the witnesses were Joseph Fenimore, Eliza Fenimore and Sam. Scattergood. The will was proved on 7 December 1731, and the inventory of 6 December, by Fenimore and Scattergood, was 205 pounds 14 shillings 6 pence.

Henry Nordyke had married Rebecca Perkins at Willingboro on 6 January 1731, the same year. He appears in her father's will as a man who owed him money. Then David died too. His will, made in January 1731/2 "of Wellingborrow, yeoman," leaves his brother Abraham "plantation in Wellingburrow, which came to me by will of my father, Jacob Perkins, dated Oct. 26, 1731," and names his "Sister, Rebecca, wife of Henry Nordike" and "Mother, Sarah Perkins." It was witnessed by Joseph Fenimore, Sam'l Scattergood and Henry Nordike, and was proved on 4 March 1731/2.

So within about a year the Perkins household of Willingboro lost a grandfather, a father and a son, and the new son-in-law Henry Nordyke witnessed the last of the wills. Henry and Rebecca's descendants are the Nordykes of the family tree. Abraham, to whom David left the plantation, was also his executor.

stories.title: Soldiers on the road to Huntsville: Giles County, 1862-1863
stories.hook: Abner Stevenson's son Gilbert was five months old when the first Federal troops marched into Pulaski.

subject.name: Giles County in the Civil War

body: Gilbert Franklin Stevenson was born near Pulaski on 17 November 1861, to Rev. Abner Stevenson and Martha. Goodspeed's county history says what the next four years were like around the family farm. "The county was continually overrun with both Federal and Confederate soldiers throughout the war, being on the line of march from Nashville to Huntsville, Ala. Pulaski, Lynnville, Elkton and Prospect were each visited by Federal troops in large numbers, and Pulaski and Lynnville were fortified." On Fort Hill above Pulaski "a formidable fort or earth-work was erected."

The first Federals to come in any number arrived in April 1862, when Col. Mark Monday brought a detachment of Gen. Negley's brigade from Columbia to drive off John Morgan's cavalry, who were plundering the Federal wagon trains. Gilbert was then about five months old. Monday camped at Pulaski until September 1862. In August 1863 Col. Hayes raided the county with a regiment of cavalry and camped a day and a night in Pulaski. In the same year, in Goodspeed's words, "Lynnville and Elkton were both raided by the Federals, the whole county, in fact, being relieved of horses, cattle and grain."

That October Gen. Wheeler retreated south through the county with Gen. Wilder after him, and in November "Gen. W. T. Sherman and his entire army passed through Giles County, en route to Chattanooga, making a short stop at Elkton." Bee Spring, the Methodist church Elam Stevenson helped found, stood in the Twentieth Civil District with Mount Pisgah and Mount Zion.

The book does not name Abner's household. What it gives is the setting: a Methodist preacher with a farm, a wife, and a new baby on a road that three armies used. Abner's nephews Coleman and Wilbur Stevenson served the other side from their own farms nearby, in the 32nd Tennessee.

stories.title: John Milton Garrison, a Mecklenburg boy who ended up in the legislature's Acts
stories.hook: Born at Cowans Ford in 1788, married in Wilson County at twenty-one, and divorced by the Kentucky General Assembly at fifty-nine.
body: John Milton Garrison was born on 4 October 1788 at Cowans Ford in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina, and came as a boy with his parents to Warren County, Kentucky. On 6 December 1809 he married Martha "Patsey" Cannon in Wilson County, Tennessee. Patsey is said to have been born about 1788 in Mecklenburg County. John’s daughter Mary, born 17 October 1811, married Henry Satterfield; whether Patsey was her mother remains a lead because the records examined do not name Mary’s mother. In 1815 Allen County was formed from Warren and Barren counties, placing the family in a newly named county.

WikiTree transcribes the census index entry for "John M Garreson" in Warren County in 1810, and the transcription gives "Numbers of Slaves 1" in a household of five. That is one enslaved person in the household of a man of about 21. The transcribed returns for Allen County in 1820, 1830 and 1840 show no slaves: in each the total of all persons equals the total of free white persons (7, 11 and 7). The 1850 census shows him at 62, a farmer, with real estate valued at $2,250. No 1850 or 1860 slave schedule has been checked, so it is not known whether he held anyone after 1810. The 1810 count rests on a WikiTree transcription of an index, not on the schedule page itself.

The marriage ended in the legislature, by statute. The printed Acts of the 1847-48 session, section 6 on page 410, read: "That the marriage contract now existing between John M. Garrison, and his wife, Patsey Garrison, be and the same is hereby dissolved, and they are hereby restored to all the rights and privileges of unmarried persons." The chapter was approved on 29 February 1848. The section gives no reason. The volume's index lists it twice, once under "Garrison, Patsey, an act to divorce" and once, apparently by a slip, under "Harrison, John M."

WikiTree gives a reason from other records, but names no source for it. Its biography says that during the marriage he "fathered children by Sarah Stamps who lived nearby," that he "had the KY legislature declare those children legitimate," and that after the divorce he married Sarah. The 1850 census, as WikiTree transcribes it, lists J. M. Garrison, 62, with an "S" aged 57 and three younger Garrisons aged 21, 19 and 6. The legitimation act has not been located in the volumes searched, so that part is a lead. He died in Allen County on 18 September 1860. WikiTree gives Patsey’s death as about 1850 in Allen County; the estimate has not been independently verified.

Mary Garrison married Henry Satterfield and bore twelve children. The 1885 sketch of her son James calls her father "John M. Garrison, of Allen County, Ky." and adds "(now living at the age of seventy-five years)"; because John died in 1860, the parenthesis most likely describes Mary, who would have been 73 or 74 in 1885. His parents were probably Samuel and Esther (Alexander) Garrison, who came to Warren County from Mecklenburg: Samuel's family record book, as copied by the compiler Floyd C. Stuart, lists John Milton, born 4 October 1788, among their nine children (see “Nine children from a family record”), though no county record names him as their son.

His grave is in the Mount Pleasant United Methodist Church Cemetery near Scottsville, in Allen County, under a modern flat granite marker: "In memory of John Milton Garrison 1788-1860." His daughter Mary is buried far from him, in Wayne County, Iowa, where she died in 1896.

stories.title: What a rented farm at Hagansport meant in 1910
stories.hook: The government's 1908 soil survey says what tenants paid, what the land near Hagansport grew, and why the north end of the county was held back.
body: In April 1910 John C. Satterfield, 46, was renting a farm at Hagansport, and John B. Smith and Emma Liza Langley Smith had farmed there in 1900. The U.S. Bureau of Soils surveyed Franklin County in 1908 and wrote about farming in just that corner, without naming any family.

On renting, the survey says that "the rental paid is on the usual share plan, by which the tenant furnishes everything but the land and buildings and receives one-half the crops. When the tenant furnishes only the labor he is given one-third of the corn and one-fourth of the cotton." In 1900 only 44.1 percent of the county's farms were run by their owners, and the average farm was 77.9 acres. Most land could be bought for $5 to $10 an acre, more in the Sulphur River bottoms. The authors add that "since that date many of the tenants have acquired title."

On Hagansport itself: the town sits on a divide between the Sulphur River and White Oak Creek, with bodies of Wilson clay loam "in the vicinity of Hagansport and Lavada." The survey calls that soil "somewhat better adapted to cotton than to corn," says it was nearly all in cultivation, and gives the cotton yield as "from one-third to three-fourths bale per acre." The bottoms along the river were "more or less subject to overflow." Of the north end of the county, the survey says: "Other small centers in the northern part of the county are Daphne, Lavada, and Hagansport. In this part of the county development is seriously hindered by the absence of adequate shipping facilities."
This is a general portrait. It does not say whether the Smiths owned or rented, or whether the Satterfields farmed on halves or thirds, but it describes the terms on which families like them worked.

quotes.t: The rental paid is on the usual share plan, by which the tenant furnishes everything but the land and buildings and receives one-half the crops.
quotes.c: Soil Survey of Franklin County, Texas (1908), p. 931

src: A. E. Kocher and W. S. Lyman, Soil Survey of Franklin County, Texas, in Field Operations of the Bureau of Soils, 1908 (USDA, 1909), pp. 931-947; archive.org: usda-soil-survey-of-franklin-county-texas-1908.

stories.title: Fifteen children at Bee Spring
stories.hook: Frank Stevenson was one of fifteen children of a farming preacher, and a twin; the 1870 census lists eleven of them under one roof.

subject.name: The fifteen children of Abner and Martha Stevenson

body: Rev. Abner A. Stevenson and Martha S. Watson were married on 8 December 1838. A family history compiled from the Stevenson family sketches of the 1950s lists their fifteen children, all born in Giles County: Lucinda C. (3 May 1840), William Elam Fletcher (9 April 1842), Lydia Mary Eliza (20 December 1843), Catherine M. Frances (10 January 1846), Augustus Summerfield (30 October 1847), Ellen Tillman and James Willis (twins, 30 January 1850), Larkin Henry (12 October 1852), Amanda Elizabeth (21 October 1854), Julia Ann Desdemona (July 1857), John Edward Thomas (16 September 1859), the twins Gilbert Franklin and George Washington (both 17 November 1861), Wilson McAlister (15 August 1864) and Manerva Jane (22 July 1866).

The 1870 census, as printed on the WikiTree page for Frank, finds the household in District 10 with A. A. Stevenson, 54, Martha, 47, and eleven children: Lucinda 28, James 20, Ellen 20, Larkin 18, Amanda 16, Julia A. 14, John E. 12, George W. 8, Gilbert 8, Mack 5 and Manerva J. 3. The two eight-year-olds are the twins. By 1880 the house was nearly empty: Abner, 63, "Farming Preacher," Martha, 56, Gilbert F., 18, Wilson M., 16 and Jane M., 12, with three hired or fostered Whittaker children and a one-year-old grandchild named Berry Andrew, born in Alabama. The Andrew grandchild was probably the youngest son of Abner's daughter Eliza, who had died in November 1878 (lead).

Several of the dates check against the Bee Spring graveyard. W. Mack Stevenson is on the cemetery list as born 15 August 1864 and dead 30 June 1940, which matches Wilson McAlister. Nathan A. Stevenson, 12 November 1870 to 21 July 1936, is Abner's grandson Nathaniel, William's son. Werner W. Stevenson, 4 March 1880 to 23 June 1974, is James Willis's son. Abner himself lies there, as does Martha S., 19 February 1823 to 12 July 1887.

The children scattered. Lucinda married Perry Pittman Williams and died in 1920; Eliza Mary married John Newton Andrew on 20 December 1870 and died in 1878; Frances married J. M. Whitaker and died on 18 April 1889; Summerfield went to Arkansas and was buried near Crowley's Ridge; Ellen married James Marion Britton; Julia went to Texas as John Newton Andrew's third Stevenson wife; Edward died in El Paso; George became a judge at Lubbock; James Willis became a Methodist minister; Manerva married Andrew R. Merrill and moved to Ardmore, Tennessee. Frank went to Indiana.

quotes.t: Farming Preacher
quotes.c: Abner A. Stevenson's occupation, 1880 U.S. census, 10th District, Giles County, Tennessee

src: Robert Casey, Interactive Family Histories, "Stevenson, Arrington and Tucker Families," Master Publication pp. 3-98 to 3-120 (http://www.rcasey.net/master/steelam.htm and steabner.htm); WikiTree profiles (api.wikitree.com) for Gilbert Franklin Stevenson (Stevenson-12558), Parsis Jane O'Neal (O'Neal-3514) and Daniel Waters O'Neal (O'Neal-2667), with the 1870, 1880 and 1910 census transcriptions printed there; Bee Spring Cemetery listing, Giles County, Tennessee (Giles Co. TNGenWeb cemetery page); Goodspeed list of Elam Stevenson's children, p. 872.
stories.note: The Casey family history names the fifteen children and their births; the 1870 and 1880 census households and the cemetery dates fit it, but the family history has no sources for the exact days.
stories.place: Giles County, Tennessee, with branches in Alabama, Arkansas and Texas

stories.title: Two Stevenson brothers go to Texas
stories.hook: One brother became a judge at Lubbock and the father of thirteen; another died of smallpox at El Paso in June 1886, working for the railway.
body: Frank Stevenson had a twin. George Washington Stevenson was born on the same day, 17 November 1861, and the 1870 census lists both as 8 years old in the same Giles County household. In May 1881 the Pulaski Citizen noted that "Judge Geo. Stevenson, son of Rev. A. Stevenson, returned from Texas last week." The family history says that George later lived at Lubbock, Texas, where he was a judge, and that he was the father of thirteen children. It names none of them.

John Edward Thomas Stevenson, born on 16 September 1859, appears in the 1870 census as "John E," 12. The family history says Edward "moved to Texas where he worked for the Texas and Pacific Railway" and "died of smallpox in El Paso, Texas on June 26, 1886." He would have been 26. The Texas and Pacific reached El Paso in 1881, so the job fits the date.

The pull of Texas runs through this family. In January 1881 their father "abandoned the idea of going to Texas." Their sister Julia Ann followed her husband John Newton Andrew there, and by the 1870s their sister Ellen Britton's growing family was moving between Giles County and Texas. When Frank and Parsis lived there in the 1890s and 1900s, three of their children were born in Texas.

quotes.t: Edward Stevenson moved to Texas where he worked for the Texas and Pacific Railway. Edward Stevenson died of smallpox in El Paso, Texas on June 26, 1886.
quotes.c: Casey family history, Master Publication 3-109

quotes.t: Judge Geo. Stevenson, son of Rev. A. Stevenson, returned from Texas last week.
quotes.c: The Pulaski Citizen, 5 May 1881, p. 2

src: The Pulaski Citizen, 5 May 1881, p. 2 (Library of Congress); Robert Casey, Interactive Family Histories, "Stevenson, Arrington and Tucker Families," Master Publication pp. 3-98 to 3-120 (http://www.rcasey.net/master/steelam.htm and steabner.htm); 1870 U.S. census, District 10, Giles County, as transcribed on the Frank Stevenson WikiTree page.
stories.note: The El Paso death and the Lubbock judgeship come from the family history alone, which has no source for them. A Texas death record or a Lubbock County court record would settle both.
stories.place: Giles County, Tennessee; Texas

stories.title: One widower, three Stevenson wives
stories.hook: John Newton Andrew of Giles County married a Stevenson cousin, then a Stevenson sister, then Frank's other sister; the last wife took him to Texas.
body: John Newton Andrew was born in Giles County on 20 February 1841. His first wife was Mary Hamilton, a granddaughter of Rev. Elam Stevenson through Elam's daughter Catherine. His second, on 20 December 1870, was Eliza Mary Stevenson, Frank's sister, who bore him four sons (Baxter, Abner, Truman and Perry) and died on 16 November 1878. His third was Eliza's younger sister Julia Ann Desdemona Stevenson, born in July 1856 or 1857. The family history notes that Julia was thus "John's third marriage to a Stevenson woman."

Julia and John had four children, Ray, George, Tina Tisha and Alice. WikiTree places a son, Roy Jackson Andrew, at Rockwall, Texas, on 30 July 1893 and at his death at Wilbarger County, Texas, in 1964. John died on 28 March 1909 and Julia on 3 July 1928 at Vernon, Wilbarger County, according to WikiTree; its biography page gives 1925 as her death year, so the date is not settled.

Rockwall comes up again in this family. A WikiTree profile for the possible first husband of Parsis O'Neal, Frank's wife, puts his death in Rockwall County in 1901. If Frank and Parsis were among the Giles County Stevensons around Rockwall in the 1890s, the Texas births of their children Willie, Frank and Elisha would be explained (lead; see the Louderback story).
src: Robert Casey, Interactive Family Histories, "Stevenson, Arrington and Tucker Families," Master Publication pp. 3-98 to 3-120 (http://www.rcasey.net/master/steelam.htm and steabner.htm); WikiTree profiles Stevenson-5863 (Julia Ann Desdemona), Andrew-1921 (John Newton Andrew) and Andrew-1917 (Roy Jackson Andrew).
stories.note: Julia's death year is given as 1925 and 1928 in different WikiTree fields, and her birth as 1856 and 1857. A Texas death certificate or Vernon cemetery record would settle it.
stories.place: Giles County, Tennessee; Rockwall and Wilbarger Counties, Texas

stories.title: Ellen Stevenson and the Brittons
stories.hook: A twin born in 1850 who married a Giles County farmer, went to Texas and back, and raised seven children.
body: Ellen Tillman Stevenson was born on 30 January 1850, the twin of James Willis. On 24 December 1871 she married James Marion Britton, born on 3 March 1840 in Giles County, the son of Wilson Britton and Elizabeth Ragains. His brother John Frank Britton died in Collin County, Texas, in 1890.

The family history names seven children: Logan Harwell, Sarah Beulah, Amanda Elizabeth, an infant daughter, Wilson Arrington, James Wilson Lafayette "Fate," and Carlos Erskine. In the 1880 census of Friendship, Crockett County, James and Ellen's household included son L. H., age seven, and daughters B. V., age five, and M. E., age three. The family history gives Logan's birth as 17 September 1872 and Sarah Beulah's as 24 January 1873; these dates are only four months apart and cannot both be accepted without further evidence. By 1900 Ellen and James were back in Giles County.

James died on 18 September 1913 in Giles County and Ellen on 4 March 1927 (Find a Grave gives 4 February); both lie at Mount Zion (New Zion) Cemetery near Pulaski. Their daughter Amanda married Eli Bascom Pitts on 2 March 1892 and had eleven children. Sarah Beulah married Samuel McNeese and had eight, including twins who died the day they were born, 10 June 1902.
src: Robert Casey, Stevenson, Arrington and Tucker Families, pp. 3-98 to 3-120 (https://www.rcasey.net/acrobat/ste0301b.pdf); 1880 U.S. census, Friendship, Crockett County, Tennessee (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:MDQY-F5F); 1900 U.S. census, Logan Britton (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:MSCB-B5Z); Sarah Bulah McNeece, Tennessee death record, 1957 (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QKM9-KRS9); Find a Grave memorial 88644767; WikiTree profiles Stevenson-3637, Britton-1643 and Britton-2364.
stories.note: Birthplaces and the month of Ellen's death differ between the sources. The family history's 17 September 1872 birth date for Logan and 24 January 1873 date for Sarah Beulah are only four months apart. The 1880 census records a son L. H., age seven, and daughter B. V., age five; Logan's 1900 census gives September 1872. Sarah Beulah's 1957 death record names her parents James Britton and Ellen Stevenson but estimates her birth year as 1873; her grave memorial gives 24 January 1872. The exact dates and the identification of B. V. with Beulah remain unresolved.
stories.place: Giles and Crockett Counties, Tennessee; Texas

stories.title: A third-generation preacher with three wives
stories.hook: Frank's brother James Willis, a twin of Ellen, became a Methodist minister, married three times, and lived until 1943.
body: James Willis Stevenson, born on 30 January 1850, was the twin of Ellen. The family history calls him a Methodist minister. His first wife was a cousin, Nancy J. Stevenson, and their only son was Werner Wesley, born on 4 March 1880. After Nancy died he married Elizabeth A., and then Beatrice, born in October 1870 in Alabama. The 1900 census finds James and Beatrice in Giles County, and he later lived at Ardmore, Tennessee.

His second and third marriages gave him another ten children: Bessie (1885), Bertha (1887), Coleman (1893), Cletis Z. (1897), Lydia M. (1898), and Nore, Clower, Elizabeth, Charlie and Talmadge Dewitt. He died on 9 November 1943 and was buried at Bee Spring, the church his grandfather founded.

Werner Wesley (1880-1974) stayed in Giles County and married Lila Mitchell. Their daughter Nannie married Robert Hulsey, born in January 1904; a family letter of 1997 from "Nannie (Stevenson) Hulsey" is one of the sources for the family history. No connection between this Giles County Hulsey and Katie Stevenson's husband Oscar Hulsey has been shown (lead).
src: Robert Casey, Interactive Family Histories, "Stevenson, Arrington and Tucker Families," Master Publication pp. 3-98 to 3-120 (http://www.rcasey.net/master/steelam.htm and steabner.htm) (James Willis Stevenson, Werner Wesley Stevenson); Bee Spring Cemetery listing, Giles County, Tennessee (Giles Co. TNGenWeb cemetery page); 1900 and 1920 censuses, Giles County, as cited in the family history.
stories.note: The 1943 death date comes from the family history; the cemetery list used here has no matching entry for him.
stories.place: Giles County, Tennessee

stories.title: A preacher with soldier sons and a short-lived brood
stories.hook: Elam's oldest son had nine children on a Giles County farm, buried six of them young, and sent two sons into the Confederate 32nd Tennessee.

subject.name: Rev. William Payne Stevenson and Malinda (Rowe)

body: William Payne Stevenson was born on 27 September 1810 in North Carolina, the oldest son of Rev. Elam Stevenson. On 14 October 1830 he married Malinda Rowe in Giles County. Goodspeed (1886) says he "has four brothers who are ministers of the gospel," and that he settled on his farm in 1838. He lived to 14 January 1892; Malinda died on 21 January 1888. He is buried at Bee Spring.

The family history lists nine children: an infant son who lived and died in 1831; Coleman Lafayette (26 December 1832); Elam R. (1835); Joseph J. (1837); Sarah Ann P. (10 March 1840); Wilbur Marion (20 January 1841); Presley W. (8 September 1847); William F. (19 January 1853); and John Henry (1856). Six of the nine did not reach adulthood. The family history gives Presley W.'s death as 30 June 1849 (the cemetery list reads 30 July), Elam R. on 2 August 1854, William B. F. on 19 August 1854 and Joseph J. on 15 February 1856. Sarah died on 10 February 1846.

The two grown sons went to war. Goodspeed says Coleman "enlisted in the Thirty-second Tennessee Regiment of Volunteers" in 1862 and "served until the close of the war," taking part "in most of the principal battles." The same book says the 32nd was organized at Camp Trousdale in the summer of 1861, with four Giles County companies, and went first to East Tennessee and Kentucky. Goodspeed's orders of battle for the Army of Tennessee place the 32nd in Brown's Brigade of the division of Gen. C. L. Stevenson (no kin), and the county chapter says it was reorganized at Jackson, Mississippi. Wilbur Marion served in the same regiment until the fall of 1864, "when left the service due to ill health."

Coleman raised not only his own sons but three orphaned Jackson nieces of his wife (Martha V., Nancy M. and Mary J.). He died on 24 October 1908. Wilbur married Martha Jane Hampton on 9 November 1865. She died on 28 December 1918 and he died the next day, 29 December 1918, in Giles County. The sources do not give a cause, but their dates fall in the winter of the great influenza epidemic (lead).

quotes.t: He has four brothers who are ministers of the gospel, and his father was also a very prominent Methodist Episcopal minister.
quotes.c: Goodspeed, History of Tennessee (1886), Giles Co., sketch of Coleman L. Stevenson, p. 872

quotes.t: In 1862 Mr. Stevenson enlisted in the Thirty-second Tennessee Regiment of Volunteers, and served until the close of the war.
quotes.c: Goodspeed, p. 872

src: Goodspeed, History of Tennessee (1886), Giles County, Biographical Appendix, pp. 871-872; Goodspeed, Giles County military chapter, p. 758-759; Robert Casey, Interactive Family Histories, "Stevenson, Arrington and Tucker Families," Master Publication pp. 3-98 to 3-120 (http://www.rcasey.net/master/steelam.htm and steabner.htm) (William Payne Stevenson, Coleman Lafayette, Wilbur Marion); Bee Spring Cemetery listing, Giles County, Tennessee (Giles Co. TNGenWeb cemetery page).
stories.note: The influenza suggestion is only a guess from the dates. Neither source states a cause for the 1918 deaths.
stories.place: Giles County, Tennessee

stories.title: "They who bear the cross shall bear the crown"
stories.hook: Elam's eldest child moved to Alabama with her husband, raised nine children, and is quoted on her gravestone; her sons went on to Texas and Arkansas.
body: Catherine A. Stevenson was born on 2 October 1808 in North Carolina, the oldest of Elam and Lydia's eleven children. She married William B. Hamilton, born in 1808 or 1809 in South Carolina. Their nine children were Lydia J. (1832), Mary A. (1834), James (1839), Elam Carr (1 February 1842), Clatinda I. (20 January 1844), George Worth (1846), Thomas C. (1848), Gilbert William (1850, in Alabama) and John Baxter (30 April 1853, in Limestone County, Alabama). The family was in Limestone County in 1860, 1870 and 1880.

William died on 8 September 1872 and was buried in the Wallace Cemetery in Limestone County. Catherine died on 2 December 1888, and the same cemetery has her stone: "Mrs. C.A. Hamilton born October 2, 1808 died in great peace December 2, 1888. They who bear the cross shall bear the crown." A grandson, Robert J. Hamilton of Ripley, Alabama, described her as "a short, chubby, and very cheerful little lady."

Her children moved west. Her son George became a Methodist minister. Clatinda never married and died on 4 March 1892. Gilbert William married Martha J. Thorpe and lived in Greene County, Arkansas, where their daughter Bessie was born on 31 March 1880; Martha died on 19 May 1881, Gilbert on 6 June 1896, and both were buried at Pruetts Chapel. John Baxter married Mary Arantha Lynch in Kaufman County, Texas, on 31 January 1884 and had nine children there. Her daughter Mary A. became the first wife of John Newton Andrew, who later married two of Frank's sisters.

quotes.t: Mrs. C.A. Hamilton born October 2, 1808 died in great peace December 2, 1888. They who bear the cross shall bear the crown.
quotes.c: Gravestone, Wallace Cemetery, Limestone County, Alabama, as quoted in the Casey family history, p. 3-99

src: Robert Casey, Interactive Family Histories, "Stevenson, Arrington and Tucker Families," Master Publication pp. 3-98 to 3-120 (http://www.rcasey.net/master/steelam.htm and steabner.htm) (Catherine A. Stevenson, pp. 3-99 to 3-103); WikiTree Stevenson-8354 (Catherine A. Stevenson) and Hamilton-23815.
stories.note: A 1950 Skinner family genealogy on archive.org (ancestryofcaroly00skin) prints a chart of Elam Stevenson (1787-1875) and what appears to be the opening of his will in Giles County Court, 1875, via the Hamilton line; the book is not available in full text and was seen only in search snippets.
stories.place: Giles County, Tennessee; Limestone County, Alabama

stories.title: A doctor and preacher who moved to Arkansas in 1858
stories.hook: Abner's younger brother carried the family trade to Arkansas, taught his sons the pulpit, and is buried at Booneville, not far from Danville where Frank later lived.
body: Elam Augustus Stevenson was born on 3 February 1829 in Giles County, the son of Rev. Elam and Lydia. He joined the Tennessee Conference of the Methodist Episcopal Church, South. The Minutes of the 1858 Conference record "Elam A. Stevenson, transferred to Wachita Conference" (Ouachita, in Arkansas). A 1930 Arkansas biography of his son says he "came to Arkansas and became pastor at El Dorado and Princeton" in 1858. His son James Baxter was born at Richmond, Arkansas, on 24 October 1860, and WikiTree puts Thomas Elam's birth at Booneville in April 1857, a year before the Minutes record the transfer, so he was in Arkansas earlier than 1858 (lead).

Ten years later he was back in Tennessee, where the 1870 census shows "E A Stephenson," 40, with Alabama-born wife H. S., 27, and sons Thomas, James and John. In 1875 the Minutes list him as "readmitted" and then "transferred to White River Conference," and appoint "Wittsburg, E. A. Stevenson," in the White River Conference of northeast Arkansas. The 1880 census finds him at Addison, Winston County, Alabama, aged 51 and married to Hannah, listed as a "Doctor & Preacher" with seven children at home. Hannah Celia Carolan, born in 1844 at Somerville, Alabama, died on 26 October 1884 at Carolan, Logan County, Arkansas. Elam A. died on 17 April 1886 and is buried at Oak Hill Memorial Cemetery, Booneville.

The 1930 biography says he "was a graduate of the Vanderbilt University" at Nashville. Vanderbilt did not open until 1875, when he was already 46, so the claim must be a family exaggeration. It also names his wife as "Earl (Cook)," which none of the census records supports, so the sons by his first marriage and by Hannah are not yet separated (lead).

quotes.t: Elam A. Stevenson, transferred to Wachita Conference.
quotes.c: Minutes of the Annual Conferences of the Methodist Episcopal Church, South, 1858 (archive.org item 27838123.1858.emory.edu)

quotes.t: Wittsburg, E. A. Stevenson.
quotes.c: Minutes of the Annual Conferences, MECS, 1875, appointments (archive.org item 27838123.1875.emory.edu)

src: Minutes of the Annual Conferences of the Methodist Episcopal Church, South, 1858 and 1875 (Emory/Internet Archive 27838123.1858 and .1875); Arkansas and Its People (1930), vol. 4, sketch of James Baxter Stevenson (archive.org arkansasitspeopl0004vari); WikiTree Stevenson-15611 and Stevenson-15610 with the 1870 and 1880 census transcriptions; Goodspeed list of Elam's children, p. 872.
stories.note: This Elam A. Stevenson is called "Elam A., Jr." in the Casey family history, which gives his wife as Mrs. Hannah Celia Wright.
stories.place: Giles County, Tennessee; Arkansas; Winston County, Alabama

stories.title: Frank's cousin the Arkansas Methodist
stories.hook: A cousin of the Hulsey ancestor Frank preached in Yell County in 1883, was the first pastor of Oklahoma City's Methodist church, and is the Rev. J. B. Stevenson whose 1932 letter is quoted for the family's years of preaching.
body: James Baxter Stevenson was born on 24 October 1860 at Richmond, Arkansas, the son of Rev. Elam A. Stevenson. His 1930 biography says he "grew up in Tennessee, to which State his father had returned when he was six," and that at nineteen he "returned to Arkansas and settled in Booneville, Logan County" (the 1930 text is hyphenated across a line). He was licensed to preach on 21 September 1881. In 1883 "the Arkansas Conference sent him to Yell County, where he remained for two years" and then to the Mulberry Circuit and to Paris, Logan County.

He became "the first pastor of the Methodist church in Oklahoma City" and later served at Guthrie, Fort Smith, Conway, Batesville, Morrillton, Dardanelle, Fayetteville, Paragould, Russellville and Ozark. The Conference Minutes confirm some of this: "Conway Station, J. B. Stevenson" in 1892, "Van Buren Station, J. B. Stevenson" in 1896, "Morrillton Station, J. B. Stevenson" in 1900. From 1927 he was pastor at Atkins. He married Lulu Briggs on 14 May 1885. They had four children, among them Eugene Hendrix, a Rhodes Scholar who studied at Oxford and took a doctorate at the University of Pennsylvania.

This is the J. B. Stevenson who wrote in 1932 that "Uncle Jimmie preached 63 years, Uncle Abner 54 years, Uncle John 48 years, my father E. A. Stevenson 38 years, Uncle Gilbert 25 years." The Giles County site that printed the letter calls it a letter to "Eugene Hendricks Stevenson," which fits his son Eugene Hendrix (lead). His Yell County parish of 1883-85 is the county where Frank Stevenson was living at Danville in 1910, and his father's burial place at Booneville is in the next county.

quotes.t: Uncle Jimmie preached 63 years, Uncle Abner 54 years, Uncle John 48 years, my father E. A. Stevenson 38 years, Uncle Gilbert 25 years.
quotes.c: Rev. J. B. Stevenson, 1932 family letter, Giles County TNGenWeb

quotes.t: In 1883 the Arkansas Conference sent him to Yell County, where he remained for two years.
quotes.c: Arkansas and Its People (1930), vol. 4

src: Arkansas and Its People: A History 1541-1930, vol. 4, sketch of James Baxter Stevenson (archive.org arkansasitspeopl0004vari); Minutes of the Annual Conferences, MECS, 1892, 1896 and 1900 (archive.org 27838123.1892, .1896, .1900 emory); letter of 1932 listed in the Giles County TNGenWeb Stories index.

stories.place: Richmond, Booneville and Atkins, Arkansas; Oklahoma City

stories.title: Golden-wedding preacher, and a general in the family
stories.hook: A Tennessee preacher’s family connects the Stevenson line to an Army Air Forces commander.

subject.name: Rev. James Calvin Stevenson and Margaret Caroline (Brown)

body: James Calvin Stevenson was born on 23 June 1813 in North Carolina and brought to Giles County as a babe. On 19 November 1835 he married Margaret Caroline Brown, born on 8 December 1816. County marriage returns of the 1850s and 1860s name "James C. Stevenson" as the officiating minister at several weddings, among them Swinney-Dyer on 19 January 1852, Young-Huff on 3 November 1852, Stovall-Stephenson on 3 September 1860 and Woodard-Barnfield on 25 August 1862.

On 20 August 1885 the Pulaski Citizen's county correspondent visited "our old friends, Rev. and Mrs. Jas. C. Stevenson of near Bryson," who "speak of celebrating their golden wedding in October." Margaret died on 11 February 1886. James lived until 23 February 1899 and is buried beside her at Bee Spring. His ten children included Catherine Eliza (1838; her husband's 1912 autobiography calls her Eliza Catherine) and another daughter, Sarah, who married James Hollon.

Eliza Catherine Stevenson married the Rev. William Thomas Andrews in 1856. In his 1912 autobiography he named her as the daughter of James C. and Margaret C. Stevenson and listed their son James David Andrews. James David’s 1937 memorial names his son Major General Frank M. Andrews; the Nashville Public Library’s family papers identify him as Frank Maxwell Andrews. He became a lieutenant general and the namesake of Andrews Field, now Joint Base Andrews.

His wife's family was one of the best known in Tennessee. F. T. M'Laurine's “Old Times in Giles,” printed in the Pulaski Citizen in 1884, says James “married a daughter of Mr. Duncan Brown, sister of ex-Gov. N. S. and J. C. Brown,” and the Bee Spring Cemetery transcription of her grave, Margaret Caroline Brown Stevenson (8 December 1816 – 11 February 1886, married 19 November 1835), adds the same note. Her brother Neill Smith Brown was the twelfth governor of Tennessee, from 1847 to 1849, and later United States minister to Russia; her brother John Calvin Brown was a Confederate major general, the nineteenth governor, from 1871 to 1875, and afterward president of the Texas and Pacific Railway. Both were born in Giles County to Duncan and Margaret Smith Brown. The kinship rests on the 1884 recollection and the cemetery note rather than on a will naming Margaret among Duncan Brown's children.

quotes.t: speak of celebrating their golden wedding in October
quotes.c: The Pulaski Citizen, 20 Aug 1885, p. 3

quotes.t: Frank Andrews was a general and died off the coast of Iceland.
quotes.c: Casey family history, p. 3-107

src: Robert Casey, Interactive Family Histories, "Stevenson, Arrington and Tucker Families," Master Publication pp. 3-98 to 3-120 (http://www.rcasey.net/master/steelam.htm and steabner.htm) (James Calvin Stevenson, Catherine Eliza Stevenson); The Pulaski Citizen, 20 Aug 1885, p. 3; Bee Spring Cemetery listing, Giles County, Tennessee (Giles Co. TNGenWeb cemetery page); Giles County marriage returns (Giles Co. TNGenWeb marriage index, grooms S-Y); Wikipedia, "Frank Maxwell Andrews," early life.; W. T. Andrews, Memorial Sketches (1912), pp. 340–341, https://archive.org/details/memorialsketches00andr/page/340/mode/1up; The Pulaski Citizen, 10 Mar 1937, https://tngenweb.org/gilestn/obituaries/GC1930-1939_Obits.html; Nashville Public Library, James D. Elam Stevenson’s will and the 1886 Goodspeed sketch support the connection between James Calvin and his brother Abner, the direct ancestor.
