stories.title: Parsis's brothers stayed home
stories.hook: Five of Daniel and Vashti O'Neal's sons and their youngest daughter lived out their lives in or near Gibson County, Indiana, while Parsis and Mary went west.

subject.name: The O'Neal brothers of Gibson County

body: Daniel Waters O'Neal and Vashti Pearson had ten children, and WikiTree traces eight of them to adulthood: Parsis, her sister Mary and the six told here. William Allen was born on 15 April 1863 in Tennessee (WikiTree; the 1880 census says Indiana), and died on 11 September 1933 in Pike County, Indiana, with burial at Blackfoot Cemetery. His wife was Nancy Jane Mason, born in 1865 at Oakland City, who died there on 20 June 1923.

John Sherman was born on 15 January 1866, a few months after the regiment mustered out, and died at Somerville on 19 July 1940. He married Jane Minerva Mitchell. George Johnson was born on 16 August 1875; the 1880 census says in Missouri, so the family spent some time there in the 1870s (WikiTree says Tennessee). He lost his first wife, Adella Douglas (born 1875), on 27 February 1906, married Sarah Eleen Reed, and died at Somerville on 12 June 1965 at 89. Daniel Clinton, born 9 June 1878, married Flora Nellie McGregor and died on 3 March 1954. David Commodore, born at Somerville on 22 March 1881, married Birdie Viola Rembe and died at Evansville on 7 May 1955.

The youngest, Charity Louisa, born on 19 December 1887, was the only daughter besides Parsis and Mary to live to adulthood. She married Fred Skomp, born on 7 May 1884 in Greene County, Indiana. He died at Hobart, Indiana, on 5 August 1949, and she died at Valparaiso on 15 November 1979. Vashti's 1919 obituary named her five living sons as William, John, George, Clinton and Commodore, and the daughters as Mrs. Frank Stevenson of Valiant, Oklahoma, and Mrs. Fred Skomp of Somerville.
src: Obituary of Vashti O'Neal, Jan 1919 (Find a Grave 24711779); WikiTree profiles O'Neal-3565, 3566, 3567, 3568, 3569, 3570 and spouse pages; 1880 U.S. census, Columbia Twp, Gibson Co., Indiana, as printed on the Parsis O'Neal WikiTree page.
stories.note: Death dates after 1900 are taken from WikiTree and are not checked against Indiana death certificates.
stories.place: Gibson and Pike Counties, Indiana; Missouri

stories.title: A hundred years from Indiana to Oklahoma
stories.hook: Parsis's oldest sister married three times, raised her children in Arkansas, and was feted at 100 by the Tuttle Times.
body: Mary Elizabeth O'Neal was born on 16 November 1860 in Gibson County, Indiana, the first child of Daniel and Vashti, ten months after their marriage. By 1878 she had married David Raliegh Farris, born in 1856 in Indiana. Their son Elmer Cooper Farris was born on 25 September 1878 at Princeton and died in Sequoyah County, Oklahoma, in 1948. A second son, Daniel Riley, born in Arkansas on 23 March 1881 and recorded as Fairce, died at Mead, Oklahoma, in 1968.

On 10 February 1884, in Arkansas, Mary married Joseph McConnell Rinker, 29, born in Iowa. WikiTree lists their children: Lydia Bell (1885, Sunset, Arkansas), Armenda Mae (1888), Cynthia Jane (1890), Joseph Jonathan (1892, Fayetteville), Vasha (1895, died 1897), Oscar Ashel (1897), Letha Agnes (1900) and Alta (1902, died 1906). Joseph was in Roger Mills County, Oklahoma, in 1910 and died on 27 May 1919 at Wapanucka.

Her obituary in the Tuttle Times of 22 December 1960 says Mrs. Mary Elizabeth Wilson, 100, "was born in Gibson County, Indiana, near Evansville, and spent most of her early life in Missouri, and raised her children in Arkansas. She first came to Oklahoma in 1907 and moved to Tuttle, from Faxton, in 1926." She "celebrated her 100th birthday in Nov 16, 1960, and passed away at her home on Wednesday, Dec 14, 1960." Survivors included "3 sons, 3 daughters, 51 grandchildren, 150 great-grandchildren, & 73 great great grandchildren." She was buried in Fairlawn Cemetery. Her third husband, James Calvin Wilson, born in 1867 at Princeton, Indiana, is listed with her on WikiTree.
Katie's brother Eddie was born in McCurtain County, Oklahoma, in July 1907, the same year Mary first came to Oklahoma.

quotes.t: She first came to Oklahoma in 1907 and moved to Tuttle, from Faxton, in 1926.
quotes.c: Tuttle Times, 22 Dec 1960, obituary of Mrs. Mary Elizabeth Wilson, as transcribed on WikiTree O'Neal-2666

src: Tuttle Times, 22 Dec 1960 (transcribed in Find a Grave 41943603 and WikiTree O'Neal-2666); WikiTree Rinker-451, Farris-3080, Wilson-112326 and the children's profiles.
stories.note: Names and dates for her children and husbands are from WikiTree; the Rinker and Wilson marriages are not checked against a county marriage register.
stories.place: Gibson County, Indiana; Missouri; Arkansas; Tuttle, Oklahoma

stories.title: Seven children in the 1910 census
stories.hook: The 1910 census at Danville, Arkansas, lists Katie, the baby, with six older brothers and sisters born in Indiana, Texas and Oklahoma.
body: The 1910 census, enumerated at Danville, Yell County, on 18 April, lists Frank Stevenson, 51, "Clergyman," his wife Jane, 41, and these children: Delphia, 18, born in Indiana; Willie, 16, Texas; George, 12, Indiana; Frank, 8, Texas; Elisha, 6, Texas; Eddie, 2, Oklahoma; and Katie, under one year, Arkansas. Frank and Jane told the enumerator they had been married 25 years and that seven children had been born. These are the seven.

Delphia was the oldest daughter. In her own obituary in 2009 Katie was said to have been preceded in death by "daughters Delphia and Mary," so she named a daughter for her sister. Willie was born in Texas about 1894. George Sherman Stevenson died on 3 June 1978 at Kilgore, Gregg County, Texas, and his mother Parsis Jane (O'Neal) Stevenson is named on the Texas death certificate cited in WikiTree. Frank, born about 1902 in Texas, is "Frank Lester" in other trees. WikiTree's list of the children calls the sixth one "Allen" where the census has Elisha.

The youngest brother, Horace Edward "Eddie," was born on 13 July 1907 in Garvin, McCurtain County, Oklahoma. He married Edith Marie Shunkey (born 29 July 1911 at Muskogee, died 2 April 2003 at King City, Oregon), and he died on 1 February 1998 at Portland, Oregon.

Other trees give a different list for the same parents: Iva Myrtle (1884), Adison Galiton (1886), Nellie Vashti (1889), Frank Lester (1902), Horace Edward (1907) and Katie. Iva Myrtle, Adison and Nellie would have been 26, 24 and 21 in 1910, so they could have been grown and away; WikiTree's list does not include them, and their link to this family is not documented (lead).
src: 1910 U.S. census, Danville, Yell Co., Arkansas, as transcribed on the WikiTree pages for Parsis Jane O'Neal (O'Neal-3514) and Gilbert Franklin Stevenson (Stevenson-12558); WikiTree Stevenson-5100 (Horace Edward Stevenson); Texas death certificate 1978, George Sherman Stevenson, cited on WikiTree O'Neal-3514.
stories.note: Delphia, Willie, George, Frank, Elisha and Eddie are the names on the 1910 census page; the later given names in other trees are not proven. The census is also the only record yet seen for Willie and Delphia.
stories.place: Indiana, Texas, Oklahoma and Arkansas

stories.title: A sixteen-year-old bride in Pulaski County
stories.hook: An Arkansas marriage index records Parsis J. O'Neal, 16, marrying a 40-year-old Otho Louderbank on Christmas Day 1884, and her grave memorial still carries the Louderback name.
body: The WikiTree page for Parsis Jane O'Neal quotes a FamilySearch index of "Arkansas Marriages, 1837-1944": "Parsis J O Neal and Otho Louderback were married 25 December 1884 in Pulaski County, Arkansas. Otho was 40, Parsis, 16 years old." The index spells the groom "Louderbank." Pulaski County is Little Rock. In Gibson County, Indiana, at the 1880 census, Parsis, 11, had been in her father's household. Parsis's sister Mary was also in Arkansas by February 1884.

William Ortho Louderback was born about 1836 to 1844 at Princeton, Gibson County, the same county as the O'Neals. WikiTree gives his death in 1901 in Rockwall County, Texas, and lists a daughter, Henrietta Louderback, born in Illinois and dead in Texas in 1955, as a child of Parsis and him.

The Find a Grave memorial that WikiTree cites for her grave at Hugo is titled "Parsis Jane O'Neal Louderback (26 Mar 1868-26 Jan 1956)," so she was remembered under the Louderback name to the end, while the same WikiTree page lists the Stevenson children after the note "Marriage to Stevenson ..... Citation Needed." The 1910 census says Frank and Jane had been married 25 years, which would put that wedding in 1885, months after the Louderback record. Either the 1910 answer is loose, or the Stevenson household began without a recorded marriage, or the Louderback marriage ended early. No record seen settles it. Willie, Frank and Elisha Stevenson were born in Texas after 1894, where Otho Louderback died in 1901 (lead).
src: WikiTree O'Neal-3514 (Parsis Jane O'Neal), Louderback-86 (William Ortho Louderback) and Louderback-85 (Henrietta Louderback), quoting "Arkansas Marriages, 1837-1944," FamilySearch F73Z-LQF; 1910 census, Danville, Yell Co., Ark.
stories.note: The marriage record itself has not been seen. Both the Louderback surname index and the bride's age should be checked against the Pulaski County, Arkansas, marriage register for 25 December 1884.
stories.place: Pulaski County, Arkansas; Illinois; Rockwall County, Texas

stories.title: A juror in Cherokee County, the year of the roundup
stories.hook: In November 1838 Gilliam Graves sat on a county jury a few months after soldiers emptied the Cherokee farms of his county into a stockade.

subject.name: Gilliam Graves in Cherokee County, Georgia

body: Gilliam Graves is on the Cherokee County, Georgia, jury lists twice, in December 1835 and on 5 November 1838. The county had been carved out of the Cherokee Nation's Georgia land, and the state gave that land to white men by lottery in 1832. Its seat, first called Etowah, is Canton today.

In May 1838 the rest of the story arrived. Gen. Winfield Scott set up at the Cherokee capital, New Echota, and on 10 May told the Cherokee that "before another moon had passed every Cherokee man, woman, and child must be in motion" for the West. About 7,000 regulars, militia and volunteers were used. Stockade forts were built to hold the people until they could be moved, and Mooney lists five in Georgia: Fort Scudder in Lumpkin County, Fort Gilmer in Gilmer County, Fort Coosawatee in Murray County, Fort Talking Rock in Pickens County and "Fort Buffington, near Canton, in Cherokee county."

Mooney, who gathered the story from people who had lived it, wrote: "Families at dinner were startled by the sudden gleam of bayonets in the doorway and rose up to be driven with blows and oaths along the weary miles of trail that led to the stockade. Men were seized in their fields or going along the road, women were taken from their wheels and children from their play." Looters followed the soldiers, and many families, looking back from a ridge, "saw their homes in flames." A Georgia volunteer later said: "I fought through the civil war and have seen men shot to pieces and slaughtered by thousands, but the Cherokee removal was the cruelest work I ever knew."

When about seventeen thousand people had been gathered into the stockades the removal began. Mooney says "hundreds died in the stockades and the waiting camps," mostly from the rations, and that "over 4,000" Cherokee died as a direct result of the removal.

Nothing in the record says what Gilliam saw or did that summer. The jury lists place him in the county; they do not say where he lived in it. But when he was called to serve on 5 November 1838, the Cherokee families of his county had been gone from their farms for some months. By 1853 he was on the tax lists of Montgomery County, Arkansas, and in January 1864 he volunteered as a Union private at the age of 45.

quotes.t: I fought through the civil war and have seen men shot to pieces and slaughtered by thousands, but the Cherokee removal was the cruelest work I ever knew.
quotes.c: A Georgia volunteer, quoted in James Mooney, Myths of the Cherokee (1900), p. 130

src: Gilliam Graves's Cherokee County jury service (Dec 1835 and 5 Nov 1838) as given on his own page; James Mooney, Myths of the Cherokee, 19th Annual Report of the Bureau of American Ethnology (1900), "The Removal, 1838-39," pp. 130-133, and the note "Removal forts, 1838" (https://archive.org/details/mythsofcherokee00moon); Wikipedia, Cherokee County, Georgia (land lottery of 1832; Etowah, now Canton, county seat 1833)

Montgomery Co., Ark., tax lists by 1853; Union volunteer 1864
stories.note: Gilliam's jury service comes from the Graves family compilation cited on his own page; Mooney does not mention him or any juror. The page numbers are those of the Annual Report edition. This is a place-and-time story: nothing seen says Gilliam took any part in the roundup.
stories.place: Cherokee County, Georgia

stories.title: "Hung up to the first limb": Doaksville, June 1861
stories.hook: In the first week of June 1861 a Northern missionary learned that a meeting at Doaksville, the town where Vincent Tims kept store, had called for hanging men who would not take the South's side.
body: John Edwards, a Presbyterian missionary from New York, had taught at Spencer Academy and since 1853 ran Wheelock Seminary for Choctaw girls. In 1861, as the Choctaw Nation was pressed toward the Confederacy, he refused to pledge himself to take up arms for the South. His account of what followed was printed by the Oklahoma Historical Society a century later, with the editor's remark that a writer at Goodland had told her of the story, "It just would not do to print!"

A few weeks earlier, riding back from Pine Ridge, Edwards had come through Doaksville and found that "The Confederate flag was flying over the town." On 1 and 2 June the Principal Chief, George Hudson, and Peter Pitchlynn stayed with the Edwardses on their way to a special council at Doaksville. Hudson carried a message recommending neutrality; Edwards later heard "that he was compelled by a vigilance committee to change it recommending the Choctaws to join the South."

Then, he writes, "On Thursday afternoon I learned that on Wednesday a public meeting had been held at Doaksville, the capital, at which Capt. Robert M. Jones, the wealthiest Choctaw, took the ground that 'every man that was not with them must be hung up to the first limb between heaven and hell.'" The next morning a neighbor, Mrs. Dukes, came to say "the committee are to be here today to hang you." He handed his keys to a friend, had his pony Jerry saddled, prayed with his wife and was on the road "probably within 15 minutes of the time the word came." His plan was that Mrs. Edwards would follow with the children, and the editor credits her with managing the family's escape.

Jones, the editor's note says, owned about 500 enslaved people, plantations on the Red River and "a large store at Doaksville." His house, Rose Hill, stood east of present Hugo; the state encyclopedia says it burned in 1912.

Vincent B. Tims had been a trader at Doaksville since the late 1830s, in the firm of Doak & Tims, and in 1864 he signed Confederate mail contracts there as "V. B. Tims, P. M." The Edwards account never names him, and nothing seen says what Tims said or did that week. It records only the town where he did business and the climate in it.

quotes.t: every man that was not with them must be hung up to the first limb between heaven and hell.
quotes.c: Capt. Robert M. Jones, as reported by John Edwards, Chronicles of Oklahoma 43 (1965), p. 72

quotes.t: The Confederate flag was flying over the town.
quotes.c: John Edwards, Chronicles of Oklahoma 43 (1965), p. 70

src: John Edwards, "My Escape from the South in 1861," The Chronicles of Oklahoma 43, no. 1 (Spring 1965), pp. 58-89, esp. 70-73 and the editor's notes 13-15 (https://archive.org/details/chroniclesofokla4319okla); Chronicles of Oklahoma 41 (1963), Doaksville postmaster letters of 1864 (https://archive.org/details/chroniclesofokla4119okla); Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture, Choctaw County and Hugo (okhistory.org, entries CH051 and HU010)

Rev. John Edwards, superintendent of Wheelock girls' seminary

stories.place: Doaksville, Choctaw Nation

stories.title: The logging train that ran away, 25 June 1915
stories.hook: A log hauler jumped from a runaway train on the Pine Belt Lumber Company's railroad near Fort Towson and broke his leg; the company said he had signed away his right to sue.

subject.name: The Pine Belt logging train, 25 June 1915

body: The Pine Belt Lumber Company ran a mill, dry kilns and planers at Fort Towson and a railroad about 15 miles north into the woods, along which it logged. Clifford Riggs hauled logs by wagon and team and was paid $2 a day. His petition says the company gave its workers passes to ride the train between Fort Towson and the woods.

On 25 June 1915, Riggs says in his petition, he boarded a train near his work and "the train in going down a steep grade got out of the control of the train men operating the same and ran away down the grade." He "believed that the only chance to save his life was by jumping." He landed with a compound fracture of the right leg and ankle, was in bed 32 days, and said his injuries were permanent. He sued in the Choctaw County district court for $6,000, charging that the air brakes and steam brakes were old, worn and insufficient, and had been for a long time.

The company answered that its track was only a tramway for hauling logs and not a common carrier, that Riggs had been careless and had accepted the risk, and that before boarding he had signed a paper releasing it from any claim for injuries on the train. A jury found for Riggs.

On 6 April 1920 the Oklahoma Supreme Court affirmed. A contract, it said, "whereby the servant, in consideration of the employment, or of the wages, agrees to release and discharge his master from liability on account of injuries caused by the negligence of his master" is forbidden by the state constitution and "void as against public policy." The opinion does not state how much the jury awarded.

Two years after Riggs jumped, Grady Moffitt, 25, put "timberman" and "C. D. Neese, Ervin, Oklahoma" on his draft card in the same county. Which sawmill bought his timber is not recorded, and the county's biggest sawmill was the Pine Belt company's at Fort Towson. Nothing links Riggs to the family. The case shows what a timber hand's day could end in, and what a signed paper did not protect against.

quotes.t: the train in going down a steep grade got out of the control of the train men operating the same and ran away down the grade
quotes.c: Petition of Clifford Riggs, as summarized in Pine Belt Lumber Co. v. Riggs, 80 Okla. 28 (1920)

src: Pine Belt Lumber Co. v. Riggs, 80 Okla. 28 (1920), Supreme Court of Oklahoma, on appeal from the District Court of Choctaw County (https://static.case.law/okla/80/); Grady Moffitt's 1917 draft card and the Pine Belt company as given on the family pages

$6,000; compound fracture of right leg and ankle; 32 days in bed
Pine Belt Lumber Company, Fort Towson; logging railroad about 15 miles long
Oklahoma Supreme Court, 6 April 1920 (rehearing denied 14 Dec 1920)
stories.note: The injury is Riggs's allegation as stated in the opinion; the jury found for him and the court affirmed. The link to Grady is the lumber industry of the same county.
stories.place: Fort Towson, Choctaw County, Oklahoma

stories.title: A Sunday in August 1898: the Austin murder at Hagansport
stories.hook: In August 1898 a farmer near Hagansport was shot on his way to his field by a man hired at the sawmill; the court cases ran until 1906.

subject.name: J. P. Austin, killed near Hagansport

body: On Sunday, 28 August 1898, J. P. Austin walked from his house toward his field in the bottom, "across the lake," and did not come home. His wife Ella took the children to church at Hagansport, a mile or a mile and a half away. That night he was still gone. On Monday morning she went back to Hagansport and asked a neighbor named Martin to look for him, and told him to try the trail from the lake to the field.

He was found there, killed. The Texas Court of Criminal Appeals later said the killing occurred "twelve or thirteen miles north" of Mount Vernon. Ella Austin, by then Mrs. Johnson, told the jury why she knew where to send Martin. She said that H. J. Carbough "wanted me to take the life of my husband so that he and I could marry," and that she refused. Weeks later he said he would not do it himself, "but would get some one that would." In July he told her "there was a man at the sawmill by the name of T. C. Wallace and that he would be all right to do the work," for "seventy-five or a hundred dollars." The week before the killing, she said, Carbough warned her not to let the oldest little boy go with his papa.

On the evening of the killing, she testified, Wallace came to her house on foot, carrying a long bundle wrapped in a sack, and said: "Your man is down yonder; the work is done; the man is down yonder between the fields on the trail. You know me by Carbough."

Wallace was held in jail for months before he was indicted, and was tried in Franklin County five days after the indictment, some five years after the killing. The jury gave him death. On 8 June 1904 the Court of Criminal Appeals reversed, finding that he should have had a continuance to bring in witnesses and that the prosecutor had urged the jury that if he was not at the scene, "in God's name he should have told where he was." The case was moved to Camp County and tried again; on 31 May 1905 the court reversed that verdict too, for errors in instructing the jury about the testimony of accomplices. Carbough was tried in Camp County as an accomplice and given life in the penitentiary, and on 7 March 1906 the court affirmed.

The opinions do not say what became of Wallace after the second reversal, or whether the widow was ever charged. They place the murder in the Hagansport neighborhood during the years the Smiths were farming there: Charles Oscar was nine in the summer of 1898, and by 1900 his father owned the farm. Nothing seen connects the family to anyone in the case.

quotes.t: Your man is down yonder; the work is done; the man is down yonder between the fields on the trail.
quotes.c: T. C. Wallace to Mrs. Austin, as she testified; Wallace v. State, 46 Tex. Crim. 341 (1904)

quotes.t: He wanted me to take the life of my husband so that he and I could marry.
quotes.c: Ella (Austin) Johnson, testimony quoted in Wallace v. State, 46 Tex. Crim. 341 (1904)

src: Wallace v. State, 46 Tex. Crim. 341 (8 June 1904); Wallace v. State, 48 Tex. Crim. 318 (31 May 1905); Carbough v. State, 49 Tex. Crim. 452 (7 Mar 1906), Court of Criminal Appeals of Texas, on appeal from the district courts of Franklin and Camp counties (https://static.case.law/tex-crim/46/, /48/, /49/); Handbook of Texas, Hagansport; Charles Oscar Smith's page for the Smith farm

stories.place: Hagansport, Franklin County, Texas

stories.title: A quarrel over the log count at the Frogville sawmill
stories.hook: In July 1912 a log cutter shot the scaler at the Frogville sawmill five times over a pay settlement, thirteen years before John Moffitt was born there.
body: Frogville, on the Red River in Choctaw County, was a place of about forty families when John Winfred Moffitt was born there in October 1925. Thirteen years earlier it had a sawmill, and the sawmill had a log scale. Sloan Pool kept it; a man named Wyrick was the sawyer. The log count in the scaler's book was what a cutter's settlement was figured from, so what he wrote was money.

On 18 July 1912 Pool went out to scale logs with Jess Allen and the old logger A. F. Buxton. A. F. Buxton's son John joined them. Allen, an eyewitness, said they all sat on a log while Pool showed John the book, with every log set down. John said he did not want it to be "like the last month's pay day," and the two argued about whether Pool had "figured" him out of money. Allen said that Pool replied, "in that way I mean to dispute your word," and "John shot him." Pool was hit five times. Allen swore that John stood over the body and said, "the next log you scale will be in hell," and shot him again. Then, Allen said, John took Pool's knife from his pocket, asked "how are you going to swear about this?", cut his own arm with it and pressed the knife into the dead man's hand.

Witnesses said Buxton had been talking for weeks. On the day, a man heard him say he would have his settlement from "those damned fellows over there." At the start of July another had heard him say that "the company was beating him" and that he meant to kill Pool. Buxton swore the opposite: that Pool had cut him once on the breast and twice on the arm with "a little old pocket knife," that he had been carrying the pistol because he was told two men were waiting in the woods to kill him, and that "I shot him to keep him from killing me." His sister, Mrs. Ruth Holden, said Allen had told her in jail that he had sworn falsely against her father.

The jury in the Choctaw County district court found John Buxton guilty of murder on 21 November 1912 and set his punishment at death; his father was found not guilty. The judge sentenced him on 27 November to be hanged. On 22 September 1914 the Criminal Court of Appeals affirmed. Because a new state law on executions had taken effect while the appeal was pending and the date fixed had passed, it sent the case back to Choctaw County to set another day. The opinion says nothing about what followed.

The Moffitts were not yet in the county in 1912; at the 1910 census Grady, 18 or 19, was in Stone County, Arkansas, making barrel staves. By 1917 he was a timberman at Ervin, in this same timber country. The record shows what a day at a mill in Choctaw County could come to when the scale and the pay disagreed.

stories.title: Jesse and Hannah: a license, a grant and a widow who remarried
stories.hook: Jesse Blackshear bought a marriage license in Jones County about 1788, took up 77 acres in 1796, and vanishes from North Carolina; his widow Hannah is the one who shows up in Tennessee court in 1814.
body: Jesse's North Carolina paper trail is short. A 1954 Blackshear genealogy lists him as a chain-bearer on a Jones County survey in 1782 and again in 1789. Between 1787 and 1789 he paid ten shillings for a marriage license in Jones County, with no bride named. The 1790 census for Jones County counts him as one man over sixteen with two females in the house. In 1794 he entered a plea for land, and in 1796 he was granted 77 acres on the south side of the Trent River (Grant Book 91). After 1796 the book says he was 'not found in N.C.'

The Tennessee record picks him up. In October 1814 the Williamson County court settled the estate of 'Jesse Blackshare, Dec'd.' His widow and administrator, by then 'Hannah Mairs, wife of Isaac Mairs,' showed a balance of $227.30 'subject to a division between Penny Blackshare and James Blackshare and the above named Legatees,' who are named as Ezekiel, Elisha, Luke, David, Elijah, Jacob and Jesse. So Jesse had at least nine living children in 1814, and one of them is called Penny, the name Penelope Blackshear Grimes went by.

Jesse moved to Williamson County between 1800 and 1810; two of his sons stayed in North Carolina until after 1810. The 1954 Blacksheariana traces some of the sons named in the settlement. Ezekiel (born 13 July 1792) lived in Williamson County in 1820, in Haywood County in 1830, and died at Brownsville on 23 April 1837; his widow, Isabella Dobson, was “bur. in the Ozarks” in 1882. Elisha (about 1794) farmed in Marshall County in 1840. Jacob (born 26 January 1802) moved to McNairy and Obion counties. The first child in the book’s list is “A dau., m. Grimes.”

Hannah was a Huggins. A WikiTree profile gives her birth as 20 May 1771 in Jones County and her death as 4 June 1829 in Wayne County, Tennessee, buried in Brown Cemetery, with a second husband, Isaac Mairs or Marrs, and a child by him born about 1807. Her youngest Blackshear child is given as born in March 1804, so Jesse's death and her second marriage fall between 1804 and about 1807. Her father is very probably the Luke Huggins whose Jones County will of 1784 names a daughter Hannah.

The two families were tied twice. Jesse’s father, Elisha Stout Blackshear, whose wife was Susannah, named 'James Huggins' as a son-in-law and his granddaughter 'Susanna Huggins' in his will, so a Huggins had already married a Blackshear daughter; Hannah, a Huggins, married a Blackshear son. Both families lived in Jones County.

The book names no wife for Jesse; Hannah Huggins rests on WikiTree and a Texas family website. WikiTree's date of 26 July 1803 for Jesse's death sits oddly beside an estate settled in 1814, and WikiTree's 1814 death for Penelope is wrong if she was alive in 1850. Hannah Huggins, born in Jones County in 1771, outlived him, remarried, and died in Wayne County, Tennessee, in 1829. Their daughter Penny is the probable wife of John Grimes.

stories.title: Luke Huggins and his 1784 will
stories.hook: A Jones County planter's will leaves a shilling each to his older children and the rest to the youngest, and one of the youngest is Hannah.
body: Luke Huggins was born about 1715, probably in North Carolina, and was a planter in Jones County, which was cut off from Craven County in 1779. He made his will on 8 March 1784 and it was proved in December of that year.

A published abstract of the Jones County wills reads: to his wife Nelly, the plantation where he lived 'as long as she is a widow or as long as she lives'; to daughters Phebe Shelfer, Sarah Standley and Nelly Littleton, and sons James, Luke and Isaac, one shilling each; to his son Jacob, the land where he lived 'with all the rest of my lands'; and the remainder of the estate to 'my youngest children, namely: Esther, Hannah, Thomas, Charles, and Temperance Huggins,' at his wife's death. Simon Spight and John Parry were executors, and Nathan Bryan, Waxel Parry and Adonijah Parry witnessed.

Hannah was about thirteen. She married Jesse Blackshear a few years later, and the Jones County papers show other ties between the two families: Jesse's father named a James Huggins as son-in-law. A James is also among Luke's sons, so the two families may have married in both directions.

stories.title: Elisha Stout Blackshear's will: a black horse named Pal
stories.hook: Elisha's 1808 will leaves a granddaughter a black horse called Pal and a bed, and gives two grown sons nothing but their clothes because they had already had their share.
body: Elisha Stout Blackshear was born near Little Creek in Kent County, Delaware, about 1736, the son of Alexander and Agnes Blackshear, who left Delaware for Craven County, North Carolina, in the 1740s. His wife was Susanna. A 1954 Blackshear genealogy calls her 'probably Ward': Enoch Ward of neighboring Carteret County named a daughter Susannah in his will, and Elisha's youngest son Jacob later named a son Enoch and lived beside an Enoch Ward in Georgia. No marriage bond has been found for either of them.

He was his father's executor. When Alexander's will was proved in Jones County in September 1786, 'Elisha Blackshear one of the Executors herein named qualified.' His mother's will of 1793 left him 'one Stone Jug for the service he hath done,' and her granddaughter Agnes, 'Elisha Blackshear's Daughter,' eight barrels of corn and her pockets and silver clasps.

His own will, dated 11 December 1808 and proved in November 1810, starts: 'I lend to my wife Susanna Blackshier (during her life or widowhood) my black Horse called Jack and all my household & kitchen furniture.' His sons Moses and Jacob get 'all my wearing clothes only, they having had their proportionable part of my Estate'; the daughters Rebecca, Susanna and Agnes 'have received their proportionable' share; Nancy gets an enslaved man and a young horse called Ball, Elizabeth gets the sheep, and Temperance gets the cattle, the hogs and the rest. To granddaughter Susanna Huggins he leaves 'my black horse called Pal, and one bed & furniture,' and to a granddaughter Koonce a bed. His sons-in-law James Huggins, Samuel Westbrook and Elijah Koonce share his carpenter's and plantation tools.

Jesse, our line, is not named in the will. The genealogy lists Jesse among the eleven children, says he 'moved to Tenn., and had Ezekiel,' and explains that the sons not named in the will, Alexander, James and Jesse, were presumed to have gotten their share earlier and 'struck out to find their fortunes in other parts.' Jesse's birth about 1767 fits Elisha, who would have been about thirty-one.

stories.title: Alexander and Agnes: from Delaware to the Trent
stories.hook: A Delaware clerk took Agnes aside in 1741 to ask whether she really agreed to sell the family farm; her own will of 1793, made with her mark, remembers a stone jug and some silver clasps.
body: In 1735 Robert Blackshaw deeded 100 acres at Little Creek Hundred in Kent County, Delaware, to 'My Son Alexander Blacksliare,' for 'the natural love I bear him.' The land was part of a tract called Blackshier Range, and Alexander already held a proprietary grant to survey it. Robert had been born in New Jersey and had come down the Delaware.

On 12 February 1740 (old style) Alexander and 'Agnis his wife, of Little Creek Hundred,' confirmed the sale of the 100 acres to the executors of Robert Carter of Dover Hundred, who had bought it in his lifetime for fifty pounds. The deed was acknowledged in the Court of Common Pleas on 14 May 1741, when, the clerk wrote, Agnes 'being secretly examined out of the hearing of the said husband did declare that she freely & voluntarily became a party.' Alexander signed with his mark. By 1747 Alexander was witnessing a will in Craven County, North Carolina; in 1748 he petitioned the council at New Bern for a grant.

Over forty years he built up a farm on the south side of the Trent. In 1779 he was taxed in Jones County on 517 acres and five enslaved people. He also turns up in the North Carolina Revolutionary army accounts of 1777 and 1786, in small amounts. His will, dated 3 October 1785, leaves his wife all his estate for her life, 'one Large Bible and one pair of Brass-headed Hand Irons' to his son James, a small house and one acre to his daughter Eleanor Bailey, 100 acres on the south side of the Trent to his son Abraham and then to Abraham's son Alexander, and 82 acres to Elisha until 'my Grandson Jacob Blackshear son of my son Elisha' reached twenty-one. Elisha and Nathan Bryan were executors, and it was proved in September 1786.

Agnes outlived him by seven years. Her will of 6 July 1793 gives 'Elisha Blackshear, my son, one Stone Jug for the service he hath done,' Abraham 'one barrel of Vinegar and my Garden,' and her granddaughter Agnes, 'Elisha Blackshear's Daughter,' eight barrels of corn due from a neighbor and 'my pockits and Silver Clasps.' She signed it 'Agnes B. Blackshear, her mark.' Her maiden name is not recorded.

The book says 'probably Stout' (Elisha Stout is the son's name), and WikiTree makes her a daughter of Benjamin Stout and Agnes Truax of Delaware. Stillwell's Stout genealogy lists only sons Charles, Benjamin and Jacob for that Benjamin, a wife Agnes of unknown surname, and no daughter Agnes. That Stout daughter is not accepted here.
stories.place: Alexander was born in Kent County, Delaware, about 1708 and farmed at Little Creek Hundred. He and his wife Agnes sold their Delaware land in 1740, were in Craven County, North Carolina, by 1747, and settled on the Trent River in what became Jones County, where he died in 1786 and she in 1793.

stories.title: Robert Blackshaw, yeoman of Little Creek
stories.hook: The Blackshear name in this family began as Blackshaw and drifted to Blackshare, Blackshier and Blackshear through the spelling of clerks writing down what they heard.
body: Robert Blackshaw is the earliest of the line the Blacksheariana can follow through records. He was born at Piscataway, New Jersey, on 24 August 1677, 'son of Ellenor and Thomas Blackshaw.' By 1708 he had bought a lot on Second Street in Lewes, Delaware (Sussex County Deed Book A-1, p. 281), and in 1712 that purchase came up at the Court of Quarter Sessions. In 1716 the Proprietaries' commissioners at Philadelphia issued warrants for 200 acres and 200 more in Kent County, and a survey of 207 acres near the head of Dover River.

He is listed as a yeoman and a farmer. In 1725 he deeded 200 acres, the grant of 1716, to 'Son Randall,' and in 1735 100 acres of 'Blackshares Range' to 'Son Alexander.' The book remarks that his own surname 'began one of its many changes with this Robert, who started out with Blackshaw and ended with Blackshare; his sons went to Blackshere, Blackshier and Blackshear.'

Robert's wife is not named in any of the records the book cites. Robert's son Randall, who married Eve, stayed in Kent County, and Eve's will of 1762 is in the Kent County probate records; Alexander left for North Carolina after selling the land his father gave him.

stories.title: Thomas and Ellenor Blackshaw at Piscataway
stories.hook: Six babies in eleven years, four of them dead by 1688: all that is left of the first Blackshaw couple in the Delaware Valley.
body: The Blacksheariana says most American Blackshears descend from 'Robert Blackshaw, first documented as son of Thomas and Ellenor of Piscataway, N.J., 1677.' Thomas appears on a 1 January 1677-78 promissory note to Thomas Bloomfield of Woodbridge, for 'Good Merchantable Tobacco,' and as a freeholder in 1683 and again in a later list. He paid quit rents on 37 acres and is listed as an early patentee. He is not in the probate records of Middlesex or Monmouth counties.

The New Jersey Archives record the births: Robert on 24 August 1677; a Thomas on 5 January 1679-80, dead two days later; Joseph on 13 April 1681, dead in October 1687; Timothy on 22 December 1682, 'd. soon'; a second Thomas on 3 September 1685, dead 24 October 1687; and a second Joseph on 15 May 1688. Only Robert and the second Joseph outlived their father.

The author guesses that Thomas was the son of John Blackshaw and Maude Barlowe of the parish of Prestbury, Cheshire, whose son Thomas was baptised on 25 September 1631 in the parish of Prestbury, who 'could very well be the first Blackshaw to establish a family in America.' The author could not locate that Thomas's marriage or death in Cheshire.

stories.title: William and Viney Clark: a bond with Henry Willis
stories.hook: In 1808 a Pulaski County marriage bond was signed by the groom and by Henry Willis; a veteran named Henry Willis said in his pension application that he had lived with William Clark during the War of 1812.
body: A WikiTree profile for William Clark, built from the Kentucky War of 1812 soldiers list, the censuses of 1840 and 1850 for Butler County, and the 1856 Kentucky death register, gives his birth as 13 October 1785 in Granville County, North Carolina, and his death as 6 January 1856 in Butler County. His wife appears in the 1850 census as 'Vina Clarke' in his household and in the 1860 census as 'Luvina Clark.'

They married in 1808 in Pulaski County, Kentucky. The county marriage book (Book 1, 1799-1850, p. 28) has the couple's names in the wrong places in the index: 'William Willis & Livina Clark.' The Kentucky marriage index files the same record under 'Viny Willis' and 'William Clark,' 1808. A discussion on WikiTree's Henry Willis page says William Clark and Henry Willis stood as bondsmen.

Their first child, Lewis, was born in Pulaski County on 16 April 1809. The family moved to what became Butler County, where Mary (1815), Newton Jasper (6 August 1817), and Emeline (1820) were born, and then to what became Edmonson County, where Harvey was born in 1826. Lewis and Emeline died in Edmonson County and Mary and Harvey in Butler.

Original Butler County papers record Newton Clark and Polly D. Elms marrying on 24 January 1839, after a 20 January license; the return was signed on 25 January. Melvina’s death certificate names Newton Clark and Mary Dunn as her parents; identifying her mother with Polly Elms remains probable and the surname difference is unresolved. Melvina married a Johnson, and her daughter Samantha married John C. Satterfield, who is our line.

William Clark's gravestone, in the Clark-Whobrey Cemetery at Roundhill in Edmonson County, records the hour of his death: "In memory of William Clark consort of Vina Clark born Oct. the 13 1785 And departed this life Jan. 6 1856 on sunday morning 8 oo & 55 minutes." The sixth of January 1856 was a Sunday. The stone agrees with the dates given from the Kentucky death register and names his wife as Vina, the form the 1850 census uses.

The War of 1812 service credited to him is still unchecked. The Kentucky roster of 1891 lists several privates named William Clark or Clarke, all in companies from other counties. Captain Samuel Tate's Pulaski County company, the one in which a Henry Willis served in 1813, includes an Elisha Clarke but no William (lead).

Lavina, born in South Carolina about 1785, died in Butler County in 1877.

stories.title: Henry Willis: bondsman, levy-exempt, dead by 1818
stories.hook: The documents agree that a Henry Willis stood bond for Lavina Willis in 1808; they do not say whether he was her father.
body: A Henry Willis and his wife Mary sold land on the waters of Clifty Creek and Fishing Creek in Pulaski County, Kentucky, before 14 October 1800. In November 1807 the Pulaski County court excused Henry from the county levy because of old age and infirmity. The next year he is the Henry Willis who stood bond with William Clark for the marriage of Lavina Willis. By 1818, a Pulaski County tax record shows Mary alone, which is the basis for his death date. In the spring court of 1820 a suit named John, George and Daniel Willis as his heirs.

The WikiTree discussion of this family traces a Henry Willis through Washington County, Virginia, where he took title to 400 acres in Rich Valley in 1781-82 and was presented by a grand jury in 1773 for living with Mary Cochran, then to Greene County, Tennessee, and then to Kentucky. It calls the identification of these as one man 'most likely' but admits he disappears from each place just as a man of the same name shows up in the next.

That discussion lists Lavina among the children only as a presumption: 'Lavina (aka Viney) Willis married William Clark in 1808. William Clark and Henry Willis stood as bondsmen. The presumption is that Viney is Henry's daughter.' Another Henry Willis, born about 1793, lived later in Edmonson County, drew a War of 1812 pension, and said he lived with William Clark in Pulaski County; the WikiTree author reads that as showing that William Clark lived in the household of Henry and Mary, which is how he would have met Viney.

A Henry Willis is on a War of 1812 muster roll. The Kentucky adjutant general's roster of 1891 lists "Willis, Henry" among the privates of Captain Samuel Tate's company, Kentucky Mounted Volunteer Militia, "commanded by Colonel Michael Taul," with service from 23 August to 14 November 1813. The regiment was raised under Governor Isaac Shelby's address of 31 July 1813 and rendezvoused at Newport, Kentucky, on 31 August. Bennett H. Young's history of the campaign names the company's county: Taul's seventh regiment was made up of companies from Wayne, Cumberland and Knox, "and Captain Samuel Tate, of Pulaski."

Shelby's volunteers crossed into Upper Canada that autumn. At the Battle of the Thames on 5 October 1813, Young places General George E. King's brigade, the fifth and seventh regiments, "four hundred and fifty feet behind Trotter," in the second line. The roll does not say where each private was that day, and some men in Tate's company are marked "left behind," one of them "with lame horse."

The soldier was probably not the Henry Willis who stood bond in 1808. That man had been excused from the Pulaski County levy in November 1807 for old age and infirmity. The private of 1813 fits the younger Henry Willis, born about 1793, who later lived in Edmonson County, drew a War of 1812 pension and said he had lived with William Clark in Pulaski County (probable). No record seen states how he was related to Lavina.

stories.title: A family quarrel ends in a stabbing, January 1938
stories.hook: Oscar Hulsey, 27, was arrested after a two-day search in the mountains north of Millerton for stabbing his wife's brother.
body: In the last week of January 1938, Oscar Hulsey and Eddie Stevenson of Millerton, named as his brother-in-law, had a family quarrel that ended with Stevenson stabbed. The Valliant Tribune of 4 February 1938 put it in six sentences, and the McCurtain Gazette of 2 February ran the headline "Oscar Hulsey Arrested on Assault Count."

The Tribune says: "Oscar Hulsey faces a charge of assault with attempt to kill after his arrest Monday night by Deputies James Houston and Bud Butler. He was charged in connection with the stabbing Saturday night of his brother-in-law Eddie Stevenson of Millerton. Stevenson is in the Sanitarium of Paris, where his condition was reported as satisfactory Monday afternoon. The stabbing followed a family quarrel, officers said. Hulsey was arrested in a remote mountain area 30 miles north of Millerton after a two-day search." By its dates the stabbing was Saturday night, 29 January, and the arrest Monday night, 31 January.

The charge did not go away quickly. The McCurtain Gazette's published district court dockets of 17 and 28 September and 5 October 1938 list "the State of Oklahoma vs. Oscar Hulsey" as assault and battery with intent to kill for the October 1938 term, and the dockets printed on 16 and 20 September 1939 list it again, set for Saturday, 14 October 1939. No sentence, plea or dismissal was found in the pages that could be read. By April 1940 Oscar was back in Arkansas at South Fork in Montgomery County, working on a government job, and in 1941 his marriage to Katie ended in divorce.

stories.title: Killed on his bicycle, July 1947
stories.hook: Bennie George Hulsey, 13, turned in front of a pickup truck west of Hugo and died within the hour.

subject.name: Bennie George Hulsey and the pickup truck

body: The clipping reads: "Choctaw County's second highway fatality was suffered Tuesday night when Bennie George Hulsey, 13, died of injuries received when he turned in front of a pickup truck on his bicycle, the local highway patrol unit reported." Three eyewitnesses told the patrolmen that the boy turned directly into the path of a truck driven by Mack Flinn, 29, of Grant, on U.S. 70 two miles west of Hugo in front of Leon Griffin's store, about 7:30 p.m.

"The boy, son of Mrs. Katie Hulsey, Hugo Route One, was rushed to the Hugo hospital but he succumbed 45 minutes later from a compound fracture of the skull and internal injuries." The patrol said he was knocked 75 feet; Flinn's truck swerved off the road, jumped a four-foot fill and turned over once and a half. Flinn had only a few bruises and two other men in the truck were slightly hurt. The boy's death "marked the second road fatality in Choctaw County during 1947."

Services were set for 11 a.m. Thursday at the Coffey Funeral Home chapel, with burial at Mount Olivet. He was a member of the Assembly of God church and had been born in Danville, Arkansas, the paper says, and had moved with his mother and family to a place on Hugo Route One. The survivors named in the continuation are his mother, his father Oscar Hulsey of Wright City, two sisters, Mrs. Delphia Murphy of Oregon and Mary of Hugo, and four brothers, Leon, Glen, Charles and Willis, all of Hugo. Mary was his sister Mary Ellen, then eight years old.

The McCurtain Gazette of Idabel, where the Hulseys had lived, ran the story on its front page on Saturday, 26 July, under the headline “Former County Youth Dies in Bicycle Mishap.” It adds what the boys were doing. Pulling a home-made wooden sled and a toy wagon behind their bicycles, Bennie and the son of Leon Griffin had been riding back and forth between the Griffin home and the Griffin store. Bennie and the truck were both headed east when he turned north toward the store's driveway. Highway patrolman Cecil Snapp and Sheriff Bird Collins investigated. The Gazette names him as the son of Oscar Hulsey of Wright City and Mrs. Katie Hulsey of Hugo Route 1, and lists his injuries as internal injuries, a compound fracture of the skull and broken ribs.

stories.title: Two courthouses and a second wife
stories.hook: Oscar and Katie were divorced in Arkansas in 1941, he remarried five weeks later, and Katie filed again in Oklahoma in 1945.
body: Oscar and Katie Hulsey's marriage ended in two different courtrooms. The Arkansas divorce index records the divorce of "Oscar Hulsey" and "Katie Hulsey" on 26 September 1941 in Montgomery County. On 3 November 1941, five weeks later, the county marriage index shows Oscar Hulsey, 31, of Mount Ida, marrying Hester May Whittington; the state certificate gives his birth date as 27 October 1910.

Katie went back to Oklahoma and appears to have brought a second action there. In the McCurtain Gazette's court docket of 10 October 1945 the entry reads "Katie Hulsey vs. Os[car Hulsey], divorce," and from 24 November to 15 December 1945 the Gazette ran a notice by publication in the district court, case no. 12,652, with Katie Hulsey as plaintiff and Oscar Hulsey as defendant, addressed "To: Oscar Hulsey." The text of the petition itself was not readable.

By the 1950 census Katie, 40, is head of a household at Jeter in Choctaw County with her children Glen, Mary, Charley and Willis, marked "Separated" and "Keeping house." An Oscar Hulsey, "Divorced," lives alone as a farmer on the road between Wright City and Gloster in Sulphur Township, McCurtain County, the township where his parents had farmed; the index puts him at 38, born in Oklahoma, so the match is probable, not certain.
The records give no reason for either divorce.

stories.title: Lydia Payne's parents, in her son's words
stories.hook: The only direct statement of who Lydia Payne's parents were comes from her preacher son: William Payne, a six-month Revolutionary militiaman, and Catherine Arnold.
body: Rev. Elam Stevenson's wife Lydia is the mother of Abner and the grandmother of Frank Stevenson, but her own people were not named in any record the family kept. The answer comes from her son, Rev. John Baxter Stevenson, who wrote a short note about his mother. As the Casey family history and a Skinner family book print it: "My mother was born in Burke Co., N.C., Aug. 16. Her father was William Payne. Her mother was Catherine Arnold. Her ancestry were of English extraction. Her father belonged to the militia during the Revolutionary War, and was in the service six months." The Casey version adds that she joined the Methodist church in August 1802 and that "her parents were both of the Methodist Church." The Skinner book also cites a printed "Table of Descents," published at Nashville, for the same two names.

That makes the link a son's own written statement about his mother's parents, which is as direct as a family record gets, but it is a recollection and not a birth or marriage record, and no will or deed naming Lydia as William's daughter has been seen. The place fits the Stevenson story: the Skinner book says Elam married Lydia Paine in North Carolina in 1805, and Burke County lies in the same western North Carolina country as Elam's birthplace in what is now Alexander County.

A William Paine household, spelled "Wm Pain" in 1790, is on the Burke County censuses of 1790 and 1800 as WikiTree transcribes them (twelve people in 1790, thirteen in 1800), and a widow of the name is on the 1810 census. WikiTree gives William's death as 15 October 1807 and carries a gravestone memorial at Rocky Mount Cemetery, Granite Falls. It lists four children: Thomas; Abner Burgess Payne (1777-1845); Sarah, who married a Boyce; and Lydia C. Sarah's profile puts her at Bee Spring, Giles County, in the 1830 and 1840 censuses, with a grave in the Bee Spring Cemetery, so Lydia seems to have had a sister in the same church neighborhood. McFerrin's history of the Bee Spring society names a Rev. Meshach Boyce among its first members and says he is buried in the churchyard there; that he was Sarah's husband is a guess (lead).

WikiTree makes William a son of John Paine of Spotsylvania County, Virginia, whose 1764 will names a son William (see "A Spotsylvania will with six sons"). The same page says two different men named William Paine have been attached to Catherine Arnold's family and that more research is needed to rule one out, so the step back from William Paine of Burke County to John Paine is a lead.

stories.title: A Spotsylvania will with a daughter 'Catey'
stories.hook: A 1774 Spotsylvania will names a daughter Catey, and a tree makes her Catherine Arnold, wife of William Payne of Burke County.
body: WikiTree's page for Catherine Arnold says she was born about 1751 in Spotsylvania County, Virginia, a daughter of William Arnold (about 1714 to after 1774) and Lydia Bell. The one record it cites is Spotsylvania Will Book E, page 119, the will of William Arnold, who died there on 17 September 1774 and "names a daughter Catey." The page marks her marriage to William Payne "Citation Needed."

The Spotsylvania origin is the only thing that makes the link plausible: WikiTree also puts William Paine's own family in Spotsylvania, and says he and his wife sold his share of his father's estate there on 20 November 1777 before the family moved to Burke County, North Carolina. A daughter named Lydia (Lydia Stevenson) may echo Catherine's mother Lydia. None of this has been checked against the will, the deed or a record that gives Catherine's age or origin, so Catherine Arnold's parents are carried here only as a lead.

stories.title: A 1955 note on the Stevenson immigrant
stories.hook: A family compiler's 1955 notes say James Stevenson of Iredell County was the son of an Irish immigrant James, not of the William some trees give him.

subject.name: James Stevenson, immigrant from Ireland, & Sally Kelly

body: A family book on the Skinner ancestry covers the Stevensons because Rev. Elam Stevenson's descendants married into that line. Its Stevenson chapter first follows a chart that starts with William Stevenson, born in County Antrim, Ireland, who came to Pennsylvania in 1748 and to Iredell County, North Carolina in 1762. Then it adds a correction from "data received May 11, 1955": "The father of James Stevenson was not William Stevenson, immigrant, but was James Stevenson, immigrant from Ireland, who died in 1820. James I married Sally Kelly of Md., who died about 1820 or 1821. James Stevenson II, who m. Jane Stevenson, died in 1828. She died 1814."

James II is the James Stevenson whose 1828 will in Iredell County names his son Elam; his wife Jane is the Jane Stevenson of the next generation. The chapter also quotes McFerrin that Elam was the son of James Stephenson of Iredell, now Alexander County, "who was a Captain in the Revolutionary War." Another passage in the same book says James Stevenson "was born in Ireland. Settled in North Carolina about 1775" and had two other sons besides Elam, which does not agree with the 1955 note (James II would then be the immigrant).

The dates do not fit well: if James II was born about 1746, an immigrant father who died in 1820 and a mother who died about 1820 or 1821 would both have been very old. The 1955 note is therefore a family compiler's statement, not a record, and the parents of James Stevenson stay a lead until a will, deed or church record names them.

stories.title: Jane Stevenson's parents: John, and a Thompson
stories.hook: The same 1955 notes say Elam Stevenson's mother Jane was a Stevenson by birth, daughter of John Stevenson, who died in 1794, and a woman named Thompson.
body: Elam Stevenson's mother is only ever called Jane Stevenson, and the compiler of the Skinner book's Stevenson chapter noted that the wives' maiden names show "Stephenson was Jane's maiden name, and not a variation" of her husband's. In the same note: "James Stevenson II, who m. Jane Stevenson, died in 1828. She died 1814. Jane was the daughter of John Stevenson (d. 1794), and a Thompson."

Nothing more is given: no first name or dates for Jane's mother, no place, no will. This is the only place found that names Jane's parents, and it is a compiler's statement from 1955 with no source printed in the excerpts that could be read, so it stays a lead. Another passage of the book puts the marriage of James and Jane about 1765 and calls James a soldier of the Revolution.

stories.title: Jesse Hulsey, the wounded soldier of Hall County
stories.hook: A Revolutionary veteran with an Indian wound and a North Carolina pension lived in Hall County, Georgia, when Salathiel Hulsey did; whether he was Salathiel's father is open.
body: The Hall County, Georgia history of the Hulsey families, as the San Diego society reprinted it, says that Jesse Hulsey, "a veteran of the American Revolution," was still living in Greenville District, South Carolina, in 1800, one of only two of the family left in the state, was in Hall County in 1820, and drew a Revolutionary land lottery lot in Troup County in 1827 (granted 12 January 1829). In the 1840 pension census he is a Revolutionary soldier, age 81, in Hall County.

WikiTree adds his North Carolina pension: on 25 November 1822 Jesse, "of Hawl Co. Ga.," named Samuel Carson his attorney to collect the pension the North Carolina legislature allowed him "in consideration of a wound which I received by the Indians in the Revolutionary War"; he appointed another agent in 1826, and a man swore in Wake County in December 1835 that he had seen him alive in September in Hall County. WikiTree calls him Jesse Hamilton Hulsey, born 1760 in Goochland County, Virginia, and lists the blacksmith Salathiel Hulsey (born about 1807, Franklin County, Georgia) among his many children by Mary Tharp.

A contemporary North Carolina resolution supplies firmer evidence for the pension. The printed Acts of the General Assembly for the 1834–35 session direct the treasurer to pay all pension arrears to Jesse Hulsey, then living in Georgia, or his agent N. Edmonson, and to continue payments for Jesse's lifetime. The resolution says his pension had been allowed by an act passed in 1824. It names no wife, children or Georgia county, so it supports the pension account without proving that Jesse was Salathiel's father. Its 1824 date also leaves a question about the 1822 power of attorney reported on WikiTree; the earlier document has not been checked here against its original.

The link to our Salathiel is a family-tree assertion. The pieces that fit are place and names: Salathiel is on the 1840 census of Hall County, and his 1850 household in Union County has a Jesse, 10, and a Jennings, 8, while the Georgia history names a Jennings Hulsey who stayed in South Carolina with Jesse in 1800. The pieces that do not fit: the same WikiTree page says a son Jesse Jr. married Mary Tharp in "1779" in Franklin County, Alabama, which cannot be right; the Georgia history treats Jesse as possibly a brother of James Hulsey Sr. of Hall County; and no will, deed or census that lists Salathiel as Jesse's son has been found.

stories.title: A widower in Hopkins County
stories.hook: The 1880 census finds George W. Langley, 38, alone with two small daughters and his wife's brother and sisters in the house.
body: The 1880 census for Precinct 5 of Hopkins County, Texas, lists George W. Langley, 38, born in Georgia, as head of household. His daughters are Emma J., 12, and Eliza J., 8, both born in Texas. No wife is listed.

Living with him are Jacob Black, 29, called brother-in-law, and Sarah J. Quinton, 32, and Elizabeth Black, 23, called sisters-in-law. Two Black siblings under his roof and no wife make it likely that Mrs. Langley, a Black, had died before the count (lead).

Emma Elizabeth Langley, wife of John B. Smith, was born on 11 December 1867 in Texas, which makes her 12 in June 1880. The census gives the daughter as Emma J., so the identification rests on age, birthplace and neighborhood (Hopkins County lies beside Franklin County, where Emma died in 1905), not on a document naming Emma Elizabeth.

stories.title: Frances Thompson and the family at Jeter
stories.hook: Frances and Simon built a household at Jeter that included three generations of the family.
body: Frances Pisachubbe was born in 1907 to Robert Pisachubbe and Lizzie Austin. Her parents came from Choctaw families whose earlier generations appear in the Dawes enrollment records: Robert and his mother Eunice on Card 1580, and Lizzie with her parents Legion and Molsey on Card 1363.

The federal enrollment process was governed by dates set in law. An act approved on 26 April 1906 authorized a limited application period for eligible children who were minors living on 4 March 1906. Frances was born the following year; her family's earlier cards provide information about her relatives, but the cutoff helps explain why she was not enrolled as one of those children.

Frances married Simon Thompson in 1925. In the 1930 census the couple shared a household at Jeter, Oklahoma, with her parents. Ten years later the 1940 census recorded Simon and Frances on a farm they owned, valued at $400, with five children in the household.

The 1950 census again placed the family at Jeter. Frances, then recorded as 42, lived with Simon, five children and her mother Lizzie Pisachubbe. Lizzie's presence connects the household directly to the earlier Austin and Pisachubbe records. Frances died in 1979 and is buried at Long Creek Cemetery.

stories.title: Lizzie Austin and the two sisters who married two brothers
stories.hook: A seven-year-old on a Fowlerville card in 1899 became the grandmother who kept a twelve-person house at Jeter.
body: Lizzie Austin is Roll No. 3738 on Dawes Card 1363, which her father Legion filled out on 21 May 1899 for Towson County, post office Fowlerville. The clerk wrote her down as 7 years old, full-blood, the daughter of Legion and Molsey. Her 1896 census number was Towson No. 201, on the line after her mother's No. 200. The final roll, approved on 12 December 1902, carries her at 10. The age she gave the later censuses moved around as well: 42 in 1940, 58 in 1950. The roll ages point to a birth about 1892, and the 1950 age agrees.

Her small family was already losing members. The card enrolls her brother James, born 15 November 1898, with a note that he died in April 1899, and a younger sister arrived the next year: Adline, born 5 August 1900 and enrolled in June 1901. The two girls grew up to marry brothers. Adline married William Harrison Pisachubbe, and Lizzie married his younger brother Robert, the son of the widow Eunice Pisachubbe of Goodland. The children of the two marriages were double first cousins.

Lizzie's name turns up in the federal record once more before the 1920 census. In the 1916 House hearings on removal-of-restriction cases, a section for June to September 1915 lists "Lizzie Pisachubbee, nee Austin," an application to have federal restrictions lifted from her land. By 1917 Robert was 28, married with a child, and farming for himself at Speer. In 1920 Lizzie and Robert owned their farm in Jeter Township with their daughter Frances, Robert's widowed mother Eunice, and a young cousin.

The house grew crowded as the old generation died. Her mother Molsey died in 1924 and Eunice in 1927. Adline died at Speer in 1929 and her husband William Harrison in 1937, leaving their children, and the 1940 census at Jeter finds Lizzie and Robert in one household with Frances, her husband Simon Thompson and their five children, and Alice, Eli and Edward, the orphaned niece and nephews: twelve people. Frances had married Simon in 1925, and so the Austin and Pisachubbe families were joined with Joseph and Betsy Thompson's line. Lizzie was still in that household in 1950 and died in 1964. She is buried at Long Creek Cemetery near Hugo, the cemetery where Simon and Frances lie.
src: Dawes Card 1363; House Committee on Indian Affairs, Five Civilized Tribes of Indians, hearings (1916), list of removal-of-restriction cases, Choctaws.; James Austin birth affidavit, sworn 2 May 1899, Dawes Card 1363 enrollment jacket, National Archives; Dawes Card 1363. 1920, 1940 and 1950 U.S. censuses (Jeter, Choctaw Co., Okla.); Dawes Card 1363 (1896 census Nos. 199-201; final roll approved 12 Dec 1902); House hearing 1916 removal-of-restrictions list (June-Sept 1915).

stories.title: The old place north of Doaksville
stories.hook: Vinson Tims farmed north of Doaksville, where his daughter Betsy married Joseph Thompson in 1889 and where he is said to be buried.
body: Vinson W. Tims was born in 1838, the elder son of the Doaksville trader Vincent B. Tims. He and Emeline farmed in the High Hill neighborhood of Towson County, 'about four miles north and a little west of Doaksville,' on land later called the Charley Blankenship place. Their children included James, Mitchell, Betsy (Mrs. Joseph Thompson), John, Rev. Robert Tims, Willie, Rosie (Mrs. James Wilson) and Calvin.

Betsy married Joseph Thompson at that house in 1889. Joel remembered his grandparents as 'buried there at the old place,' which fits the marker at High Hill, a cenotaph that carries only his name and no dates.

A memorial for him at High Hill Cemetery gives 1838 to 25 October 1891. The 1896 Choctaw census, pictured here, appears to list Vinson with Emeline and their family in Towson County, and on the 1899 card Betsy's father is named 'Vincent Tims,' dead. So his death date is unsettled: 1891 on the memorial, after 1896 if the census line is his.

A memoir of his son Robert, printed in 1944 in the Methodist Indian Mission's minutes, says Robert was "the son of Vincent and Emiline Tims." That is the same first name the 1899 Dawes card gives for Betsy's father, so the family's own church record used "Vincent" for him where the High Hill marker says "Vinson."

Vinson never enrolled, because he was gone by 1899, but his name is on the cards of his children. Written by Dawes clerks in 1899, it appears as "Vinson W. Tims" on James B.'s card, "Vincent Tims" on the cards of Betsy, Robert and Willie, and "Benson Tims" on Mitchell's. In every case the column marks him dead and gives Towson County, where the family lived.
src: Find a Grave memorial 10596388; Joel J. Thompson interview #7392; 1896 Choctaw census, Towson County; Hughes (2020); Minutes of the Indian Mission of Oklahoma, 14-17 Sept. 1944, p. 31, memoir of Robert James Tims

His marker at High Hill is a cenotaph bearing only his name; an online memorial for it gives 1891 as his death year, but he appears to be on the 1896 Choctaw census. His grandson said he was buried at the old home place.

stories.title: Eunice Pisachubbe’s family and allotment
stories.hook: An enrollment card and a later court petition trace a Choctaw mother’s family and land across nearly three decades.
body: After Eunice died on 19 May 1927, her sons Robert and William H. Pisachubbe, "the lawful issue of the marriage between Joseph Pisachubbe and Eunice Pisachubbe," petitioned the Choctaw County court to approve the sale of her allotment of about 159 acres for $1,200. As full-blood Choctaw land, it could not be sold without a judge's approval. The petition also records that Joseph had died long before her and that she never remarried.

Eunice's Dawes card, 1580, was made out for Kiamitia County, post office Goodland, on 10 May 1899. It lists "Pisachubbe, Eunice," age 49, full-blood, Roll No. 4465, with her parents named as "Jackson Gardner" and "Viney Gardner," both dead, of Blue County. Her sons William H., 16 (on the 1896 roll as "William Harrison"), and Robert, 11, are on lines 2 and 3, fathered by "Joseph Pisachubbe," dead. Line 4 is not a son: Edward Pisachubbe, 17, is written as her ward, with his own dead parents named as Simpson and Sallie Pisachubbe of Jackson County, and the card notes that he was the husband of Frances Byington, Card 956.

The tribal-enrollment columns of Card 1580 add the 1896 census numbers: Eunice is Kiamitia County No. 10432, her son Robert No. 10433 and the ward Edward Pisachubbe No. 10434, the three of them on consecutive lines of one household. William is not with them. He appears on the same card as No. 5759, a far earlier number, with a note "No. 2 on 1896 roll as William Harrison," which fits the 1911 finding that he was also listed separately as a student at Armstrong Academy and enrolled twice. All four were approved by the Secretary of the Interior on 12 December 1902.

A note on the card sends the reader on for William's child: "For child of No. 2 see N.B. (Apr. 26, '06) Card No. 1203," the 1906 newborn card for his son Colbert. On the back of the 1911 duplicate-enrollment file, the Commissioner's letter of 1 August 1911 lists the testimony of four witnesses taken to settle the question: William H. Pisachubbe, Eunice Pisachubbe, Harrison Nohio and Thomas Hunter.

The court petition describes Eunice’s land in Section 29 of Township 5 South, Range 17 East, and subtracts two strips for the St. Louis and San Francisco Railway’s right of way: 10.80 acres from one tract and .01 acre from another. It gives the remaining allotment as 159.19 acres. Robert and William asked the court to approve a $1,200 deed to L. C. Hudgens; the petition itself records the request and does not establish whether the court approved it.
src: Choctaw County Court, Estate of Eunice Pisachubbe, petition for approval of full-blood deed (1927); Dawes Card 1580; Dawes Card 1580 (1896 census numbers and marginal notes); Choctaw Commissioner's letter, 1 Aug. 1911 (jacket 7-1580); Choctaw County Court, Estate of Eunice Pisachubbe, Petition for Approval of Full Blood Deed, 1927; Choctaw by Blood enrollment card 1580, National Archives.

stories.title: Joseph Pisachubbe, the father who is on a card only as 'dead'
stories.hook: The Dawes clerk recorded him as the deceased father of two sons; probate records preserve more of his family.
body: On Dawes Card 1580, made out on 10 May 1899 at the Goodland post office in Kiamitia County, Joseph Pisachubbe holds a single word. The card is his widow Eunice's. Her two sons stand on lines 2 and 3, William H., 16, and Robert, 11, and in the father column of each the clerk entered "Joseph Pisachubbe," the year column reading "Dead" and the county Kiamitia. He is recorded as deceased when the card was made; no enrollment card of his own has been identified. His sons were born about 1883 and 1888, so he was alive into the late 1880s. Eunice, Robert and their ward Edward Pisachubbe are on consecutive lines of the 1896 census, Nos. 10432 to 10434, and he is not listed with them; that alone does not establish his date of death.

Eunice's widowhood is the rest of his record. When she died on 19 May 1927, her sons Robert and William H. petitioned the Choctaw County court as "the lawful issue of the marriage between Joseph Pisachubbe and Eunice Pisachubbe," and the petition adds that he died long before her and that she never remarried. The 159-acre allotment she asked to sell lay in Section 29, Township 5 South, Range 17 East, the same section where Robert's own allotment lies.

The only account of where the family came from is a family history printed in the Hugo Daily News on 11 May 1937 at William Harrison's death, given by his relative Judge T. W. Hunter: the Pisachubbes came from Mississippi in 1832 with the first group of Choctaw exiles and settled at Fort Coffee, near present-day Spiro. The date has to be read with care. Fort Coffee was established on the Arkansas River only in June 1834, so the family's "in 1832" and "at Fort Coffee" describe the neighborhood by the later landmark; by 1899 they were in Kiamitia County, where a Presbyterian mission had worked at Goodland since 1848. The family history does not say whether Joseph himself was born in Mississippi or among the first children born in the new Nation.

His own parents are unknown. Family trees give them as a man called Pisachubbe or Wilson and Nancy Te-hol-ba-ta-bi, but the Nancy on Dawes Card 1278 was listed as 69 in 1899, born about 1830. Her age alone does not establish or rule out a mother-and-son relationship; no examined record links her to Joseph (lead only). A "Case Pisachubbi" has his own jacket at Idabel, and a Sarah Pisachubbi is Roll 3471, but nothing connects either to Joseph. What his descendants can be certain of is the name, which they carry through Robert and Lizzie to Frances Thompson, and which the clerks spelled Pisachubbe, Pisachubbee and Pisachubbi from one document to the next.
src: Dawes Card 1580; Dawes jacket 7-1277 (Commission letter of 13 Sept. 1904 to Case Pisachubbi). Hugo Daily News, 11 May 1937; Choctaw County Court, Estate of Eunice Pisachubbe (1927); Chronicles of Oklahoma 17:2 (June 1939), on Goodland Mission (first work 1848, resident missionary 1850); Dawes Card 1278.

stories.place: Kiamitia County, Choctaw Nation. Named as the deceased father of William Harrison and Robert on Dawes Card 1580 in May 1899. A family remembrance places their ancestors’ arrival from Mississippi in 1832 and settlement near Fort Coffee, established in 1834.

stories.title: John and Betsy Thompson, Joseph's parents
stories.hook: Two names on the first line of a Dawes card, and a grandson's memory of a burial, are all that survive of the parents of Judge Joseph Thompson.
body: Joseph P. Thompson's card, No. 1283, was filled out on 1 May 1899 in Cedar County, post office Doaksville, and its first line, Joseph himself, names his parents: "John Thompson," dead, of Cedar County, and "Betsy Thompson," dead, of Cedar County. Joseph's wife shared his mother's first name, and both women were Betsy. Joseph was born in December 1861, two miles west of High Hill church, the year the Choctaw Nation sided with the Confederacy, and he gave the 1910 census taker Mississippi as the birthplace of both his parents.

His son Joel, interviewed in Hugo in 1937, supplied what the card does not. Joseph was the second of nine children. John died when Joseph was nine, about 1870, and was buried near the family home toward Spencer Academy. Spencer, which had closed in 1861, reopened in 1871, and Joseph, who had lost his father the year before, was of school age during its reopened years; the 1891 sketch of him says he was educated at Spencer, and from there he went east to Roanoke College in Virginia.

Betsy's side was a harder subject. Joel said his father's mother's people "had some sort of a Choctaw name" and never took a white man's name, which fits the pattern the Dawes cards show elsewhere on this line: surnames such as Thompson, Austin and Gardner came into use among the Choctaw after the 1830s, often borrowed from the given name of a respected white man, while others, like Pisachubbe and Ata-sa-ha-bi, kept their Choctaw names to the end.

The neighborhood that marked their lives was High Hill, where the Methodist church stood two miles east of their son's birthplace; Joseph later built his white house 300 yards from it, and Emeline Tims, his mother-in-law, is buried in its cemetery. Henry W. Thompson, who was enrolled on the next card the same day, is not their son: his parents are written as Simon and Lucy. The names of Joseph's eight brothers and sisters have not been found in the records cited here.
src: Dawes Card 1283; WPA interview #7392 (Joel J. Thompson, 1937); Dawes Card 1283. Dawes Card 1283; 1910 U.S. Census, Wilson Twp, Choctaw Co.; H. F. O'Beirne, Leaders and Leading Men of the Indian Territory (1891), p. 162; Spencer Academy NRHP nomination (NRIS 75001562).

stories.place: Full-blood Choctaw of Cedar County, named as Joseph's parents on his 1899 Dawes card, both dead. Joel said John died when Joseph was nine and was buried near the family home toward Spencer Academy, and that his grandmother's people "had some sort of a Choctaw name" and had not taken an English one.

stories.title: Legion Austin and a father’s affidavit
stories.hook: A birth form altered by hand records a Choctaw father, a neighbor and a child whose enrollment records do not agree.
body: Dawes Card 1363, line 1, lists 'Austin, Legion,' 33, male, full blood, on the 1896 census of Towson County as No. 199, living near Fowlerville. The card names his father as Ata-sa-ha-bi and his mother as Lotima, both dead and both of Towson County. His wife Molsey is on line 2, with her parents Brazil and Siney of Red River, also dead.
Fowlerville's post office was established on 7 July 1894 and renamed Valliant on 23 June 1902.

The application was filed on 21 May 1899 for Towson County, post office Fowlerville. The card lists five people: Legion, Molsey, their daughter Lizzie, a son James, whose date of death is recorded differently in the documents, and a baby daughter Adline, born on 5 August 1900. Legion himself wrote to the Commission from Garvin in October 1900 asking for a blank application for an infant child; the Commission sent it on 9 October. The baby was enrolled on 4 June 1901, as a Commission letter of 5 June 1901 to William Swink at Fowlerville records: "Adline Austin, the infant daughter of Leageon and Muley Austin, born August 5, 1900," the clerk's spellings of Legion and Molsey.

The enrollment card records that James died in April 1899 and that proof of death was filed; his enrollment was canceled in 1904. A birth affidavit signed by Legion and neighbor Leonidas Willis, dated 2 May 1899, retains the printed words that James was then living. The two documents therefore disagree, and the date on the form or the recorded death requires further checking.

The card's tribal-enrollment columns tie him to the 1896 Choctaw census: Towson County, No. 199, with Molsey at No. 200 and Lizzie at No. 201, and the clerk's note "No. 1 on 1896 roll as Legend Austin." The Commission approved lines 1, 2, 3 and 5 on 12 December 1902. On the final roll he is Choctaw by Blood No. 3736 and the age beside his name is 36, three years more than the 33 written on the 1899 card. The ages on one card do not agree with each other, or with his own testimony in November 1902 that he was "about fifty".

He signed by mark. On the affidavit for his infant son James, sworn at Fowlerville in early May 1899, the clerk crossed out the form's printed "Affidavit of Mother" and wrote "Father" above it, and Legion, "33 years of age and a citizen by blood," swore as the husband of Molsey that the boy was born 15 November 1898. The man who vouched for the birth was a neighbor, Leonidas Willis, who also signed with a mark and is written in as "a Neighbor," not a physician. Nobody named a doctor or midwife for that birth.
src: Dawes Card 1363; Foreman, 'Early Post Offices of Oklahoma' (1928); Dawes Card 1363 and jacket 7-1363 (letters of 9 Oct. 1900 and 5 June 1901); Dawes Card 1363 (front and back) and jacket 7-1363, NARA Dawes Enrollment Jackets (Choctaw by Blood); James Austin birth affidavit, sworn 2 May 1899, Dawes Card 1363 enrollment jacket, National Archives; Dawes Card 1363.
