stories.title: Molsey Austin and Adline’s birth affidavit
stories.hook: In 1901 Molsey and a midwife each made their mark on a record of her daughter’s birth.
body: On 19 April 1901, Molsey Austin signed an affidavit concerning the birth of her daughter Adline. The document records that Adline was born on 5 August 1900, and names her father as Legion Austin. It gives the family’s post office as Fowlerville, Indian Territory, and identifies both parents as citizens of the Choctaw Nation.

Molsey’s statement appears above a second affidavit made by Sinie Hall, the midwife who attended the birth. Both women signed by mark. J. R. Moore and Sallie Johnson witnessed the marks, and William Swink signed as notary. The page preserves a mother’s account and the name of the woman who helped at the birth.

The family’s enrollment card names Molsey’s parents as Brazil and Siney of Red River County. It also lists Molsey and Legion’s daughter Lizzie, their son James, who died in April 1899, and Adline. The name Siney appears both for Molsey’s mother and in a similar form for the midwife, but the surviving page does not establish whether the two women were related.

The federal enrollment records recorded the family under several spellings, including “Mulcy” for Molsey and “Leageon” for Legion. A later land-restriction list uses “Molsey Pisachubbi, Austin,” suggesting she later carried the name Pisachubbi.
src: House Committee on Indian Affairs, Five Civilized Tribes of Indians, hearings (1916), "Removal of restriction cases received in the Indian Office since Jan. 1, 1915," Choctaws, p. 93; Dawes Card 1363 (front and back) and jacket 7-1363, NARA Dawes Enrollment Jackets (Choctaw by Blood); Dawes Card 1363 and enrollment jacket 7-1363, Choctaw by Blood; Adline Austin birth affidavit sworn 19 April 1901, National Archives; House Committee on Indian Affairs, Five Civilized Tribes of Indians, hearings (1916), removal-of-restrictions list, p. 93.

stories.title: John Steadman on Card 778
stories.hook: The one name on a Choctaw card whose county column reads 'Non Citz': the father of the Doaksville midwife.
body: On Card 778, in the father column of line 1, the clerk wrote "John Steadman," with "Dead" and "Non Citz." in the adjoining columns. Emeline was enrolled as a Choctaw citizen by blood, and the card records her mother as O-we-na. The noncitizen label does not by itself establish John's race or birthplace. The card gives Emeline's recorded blood fraction as one-quarter, but does not record a fraction for either parent; it cannot establish O-we-na's ancestry on its own.

Emeline was born on 26 January 1842, while Fort Towson was still an army post and Doaksville a trading town. Her father's surname is Steadman on the Dawes card; her own grandson Joel Thompson could not recall her maiden name when he was interviewed in 1937, so the name comes from the card and not from family memory. Her 1896 census entry is Towson County No. 12116, written there as Emeline Tims, and the clerk gave her age as 57 against a final-roll age of 60.

He may have been Irish (lead). The card gives no birthplace, residence or death year, only that he was dead by 1899. What the card does show is how far his line traveled from him. His daughter married Vinson W. Tims, a son of the Doaksville trader Vincent B. Tims, and bore eight children, among them Betsy, who married Judge Joseph P. Thompson in 1889. Emeline herself lived to see her grandson Simon born on 4 May 1899, attended his birth as midwife and swore the affidavit that put him on the roll.

The law John Steadman married under was strict on paper. An act of October 1840 barred any white man from marrying in the Choctaw Nation until he had been a citizen for two years and required a license from a judge or the district clerk and a ceremony by a minister "before he shall be entitled and admitted to the privilege of citizenship." It forbade a white husband to dispose of his Choctaw wife's property without her consent. Emeline was born in January 1842, so her parents' marriage falls close to the passing of that act. No license or marriage record for John and O-we-na has been found, and the Dawes clerk's "Non Citz." in 1899 records only how the Commission classed him, not whether he ever held Choctaw citizenship.

stories.title: O-we-na, the mother who is a name and a county
stories.hook: Emeline Tims’s mother is named on an 1899 enrollment card, with Towson County beside her name.
body: O-we-na is the only parent on Dawes Card 778 who has a Choctaw county beside her name. The clerk wrote her in the mother column of line 1, the year marked "Dead," the county Towson, the same county in which her daughter Emeline Tims was counted in 1896 (No. 12116) and lived near Doaksville in 1899. Emeline's father, John Steadman, is the one parent on the card marked "Non Citz". The card identifies O-we-na as Emeline’s mother but does not provide a separate enrollment entry for her.

The hyphens are the clerk's. Dawes clerks wrote Choctaw names by ear and broke them into syllables, and O-we-na may have been spelled differently by the person who said it. Its meaning is not recorded. The card gives no year of birth or death for her. Emeline's birth on 26 January 1842 is the one date that frames her.

The commission recorded Emeline as one-quarter Choctaw and listed John Steadman as a noncitizen. It did not record O-we-na’s ancestry or a fraction for her, so the card cannot by itself establish those details. Through Emeline, O-we-na is an ancestor of the Tims and Thompson families of High Hill.
src: Dawes Card 778 (National Archives).

stories.title: Jackson and Viney Gardner of Blue County
stories.hook: Eunice Pisachubbe's parents, written 'dead' on an 1899 card, lived in the county that held Armstrong Academy.
body: Their daughter Eunice's Dawes card names them in the parents' columns of line 1: "Jackson Gardner," dead, of Blue County, and "Viney Gardner," dead, of Blue County. The card was made out on 10 May 1899 at Goodland in Kiamitia County, when Eunice was 49, which puts her birth about 1850. Her own number, 10432 on the 1896 census in Kiamitia, comes from her husband's county, not from her parents'.

Blue County in the Choctaw Nation lay in the Pushmataha District, and Armstrong Academy, the Choctaw boys' school where Eunice's son William Harrison's name turned up on a student list in August 1899, stood in it. By the 1894 printed laws Blue sent one senator, like Kiamichi, Atoka and Jack's Fork. In 1886 the Council cut a new Jackson County from Kiamitia, Blue and Atoka. Samuel G. Gardner of Blue County was a probate judge, but nothing connects Jackson and Viney to him (lead).

The family tree suggests that Jackson was born in Mississippi around 1820, but no examined record establishes his birthplace or birth year (lead). A Carney maiden name and other given names for Viney also appear in trees and need independent evidence. Their daughter Eunice married Joseph Pisachubbe and lived at Goodland, where she raised two sons and a ward. After her death on 19 May 1927, her sons petitioned to sell her 159-acre allotment in Section 29, Township 5 South, Range 17 East.

The Dawes card points to an older set of Choctaw Nation records. The Nation conducted its own censuses decades before the federal commission compiled its rolls; a surviving 1860 Towson County census, for example, records households, ages, occupations and places of birth. These records may help trace earlier generations, but a name match alone does not establish that a person is this Jackson or Viney. The Choctaw Nation Genealogy Department recommends following evidence through census records, application packets and other records to verify each link.

stories.title: Brazil and Siney of Red River County
stories.hook: Dawes Card 1363 records the names of Molsey Austin's parents, Brazil and Siney, in the Choctaw Nation's Red River County.
body: Dawes Card 1363 names them in the parents' columns on line 2, the line of their daughter Molsey Austin: "Brazil," dead, of Red River, and "Siney," dead, of Red River, with the clerk setting the mother's name in quotation marks. The quotation marks may mean the clerk was unsure of the spelling or that it was a nickname. Brazil is written with no surname.

Red River County was one of the Choctaw Nation's counties along the Red River on the Texas border. Molsey was counted in Towson County in 1896 (No. 200), after her husband Legion Austin, so she had moved from Red River County to Towson. Molsey was 22 on the 1899 card and swore she was 25 in April 1901, which puts her birth about 1876 or 1877.

A midwife named Sinie Hall attended the birth of Molsey's daughter Adline on 5 August 1900, and signed the affidavit with her mark at Fowlerville. The two spellings may be the same name; the affidavit does not state any kinship. What Brazil and Siney left is Molsey, who signed with her mark as "Mulcy Austin" and was later listed in the 1916 hearings as "Molsey Pisachubbi, Austin," and the children on Card 1363: Lizzie, James and Adline.

stories.title: Ata-sa-ha-bi and Lotima of Towson County
stories.hook: Legion Austin's parents survive only as two Choctaw names copied from the 1896 census.
body: Legion Austin's parents are on Dawes Card 1363 in the parents' columns of line 1: "Ata-sa-ha-bi," dead, of Towson County, and "Lotima," dead, of Towson County. The card writes "Ded" beside both, gives no year of death, and gives neither a roll number. Because Legion was already on the 1896 Choctaw census as "Legend Austin" (Towson No. 199), the clerk had the parents' names from that roll and not from fresh testimony in 1899.

The first name ends in abi, which the Choctaw linguist Ovid Vickers calls a war-name element; "a great proportion of those who had earned second names as a result of participation in a war were given names carrying the termination abi signifying killer." The Choctaw Nation's language staff cautions against reading the ending simply as "killer," and the meaning of Ata-sa-ha-bi is not recorded.

Legion himself bore an English surname, Austin, and signed by mark. The 1899 card gave his age as 33, but in November 1902 he testified he was "about fifty," so his birth falls somewhere between about 1852 and 1866. He had a grown daughter, Viny, born about 1879 to an earlier wife named Betsy, and he raised his nephew Nicholas Greenwood, so the household was wider than the card shows. His daughters Lizzie and Adline married the Pisachubbe brothers Robert and William Harrison, and the line runs through Frances Pisachubbe Thompson.
src: Dawes Card 1363 (NARA); Dawes Card 1363. Dawes Card 1363 and jacket 7-1363; Ovid Vickers, 'Mississippi Choctaw Names and Naming' (Names).

stories.title: The fifth child, who was eight the summer her brother died
stories.hook: Born at Broken Bow in 1938, Mary Ellen Hulsey grew up between two courthouses and married into the Thompson family of Choctaw County.
body: Mary Ellen Hulsey was born on 22 August 1938 at Broken Bow, Oklahoma, the fifth child of Oscar and Katie Hulsey. Broken Bow had grown up around the Dierks lumber company and was incorporated in 1911, a mill town in the pine hills of McCurtain County; her father's work in the Ouachita timber country is told in "A WPA laborer in the Ouachitas." In April 1940 the census found her at 2, with her parents and four older brothers and sisters, at South Fork in Montgomery County, Arkansas.

Her parents' marriage came apart in her childhood. An Arkansas divorce was entered in Montgomery County on 26 September 1941, when she was 3, and Katie filed again in McCurtain County, Oklahoma, in 1945 (see "Two courthouses and a second wife"). In July 1947 her brother Bennie George, 13, was killed on his bicycle west of Hugo; she was 8. By April 1950 she was 12 and living at Jeter in Choctaw County with her mother, enumerated as head of household and "Separated," and three brothers, Glen, Charley and Willis.

She married William 'Junior' Thompson Jr. (1934-2007), which joined the Hulsey line from Arkansas and Georgia to the Thompson family of Choctaw County. She died at Hugo on 4 November 2002, aged 64, and is buried at Woodlawn Cemetery in Choctaw County beside her husband. Her mother Katie outlived her by more than six years, and when Katie died in 2009, Mary was among the children she had already buried.

stories.title: Katie, who lived to ninety-eight
stories.hook: Born at Danville, Arkansas, in 1910 and married at 17, Katie Stevenson Hulsey raised her children alone at Jeter and Hugo and outlived five of her seven children.
body: The census taker at Danville, Arkansas, wrote down seven children in Frank Stevenson's rented house, and the last was "Katie, a baby." She was Katie Cornelia Stevenson, born 15 October 1910, the youngest of Gilbert Franklin 'Frank' and Parsis Jane (O'Neal) Stevenson. (The census day was in April and her recorded birthday is in October, so one of the two is off by months; the 1920 census, which gives her as 'Kate, 9,' agrees with a birth in 1910.) Danville was a Yell County seat laid out in 1841 and named for a steamboat on the Petit Jean River; her father was a Methodist clergyman there and had children born in Indiana, Texas and Oklahoma before her.

By 1920 the family was farming a rented place on the South Millerton Road in Kirk Township, McCurtain County, Oklahoma, near Valliant, a railroad town founded in 1902 in the Choctaw Nation. On 27 October 1927, twelve days after her seventeenth birthday, Katie married Oscar Hulsey, the son of the Rev. George Washington Hulsey and Sarah Rebecca Graves. Two preachers' families, one from Tennessee and Indiana, the other from Georgia and Arkansas, were joined, and their children grew up in the Ouachita hills at places like South Fork, Montgomery County, where the 1940 census found them.

The 1930s were hard on the marriage. Oscar was charged after a stabbing in January 1938 that involved Katie's brother Eddie Stevenson ("A family quarrel ends in a stabbing"). An Arkansas divorce was entered on 26 September 1941, and Katie filed in McCurtain County in 1945 (suit no. 12,652). In July 1947 her 13-year-old son Bennie George died after turning his bicycle in front of a pickup truck west of Hugo, and she moved to Hugo that year. In April 1950 she was enumerated at Jeter, Choctaw County, as "Kattie," 40, "Separated," head of household, with Glen, 14, Mary, 12, Charley, 9, and Willis, 6.

She died at Hugo on 30 January 2009, aged 98, with services on 2 February and burial at Mount Olivet Cemetery, where her parents lie in Block 2. Her obituary counted 16 grandchildren, 32 great-grandchildren and 26 great-great-grandchildren, and named daughters Delphia and Mary and sons Willis, Bennie and Glen as having died before her. Her daughter Mary Ellen's marriage into the Thompson family connects this line to the Choctaw County side of the tree.

stories.title: From Arkansas to the Oregon coast
stories.hook: Sarah Rebecca Graves arrived on 5 May 1884, married a Hulsey at 17, bore ten children, and ended her life on the Oregon coast.
body: Sarah Rebecca Graves was born on 5 May 1884. A family genealogy identifies Margaret Crumpton as her mother and says Margaret died the same day, but neither claim has been confirmed by a primary record. A 1977 family-history query names Jesse Graves as Sarah's father and lists Margaret as one of his wives, without stating which wife was her mother. An 1884 Garland County marriage record names a Jesse Graves and Margaret Crumpton; the groom's recorded age differs from other accounts of Jesse, so the identification needs more research.

On 22 December 1901, at 17, she married George Washington Hulsey in Arkansas. They farmed in Sulphur Township and between 1904 and 1925 had ten children, from Roy, the eldest, to George Paul, the youngest, with Oscar, the fourth, among them ("The oldest of the ten Hulsey children"; "George Paul, the last child"). By 1920 the family was in McCurtain County, Oklahoma. In September 1918 George Washington was a laborer at Camp Pike near Little Rock while she was at Story, Montgomery County; he died in 1935 and she was a widow at 51.

An index to an Arkansas Gazette obituary for Abe N. Graves, published on 4 February 1943, lists Mrs. Rebecca Hulsey as his sister. It is consistent with the family's account of her Graves relatives, but does not name her parents. The Graves family genealogy says Jesse was the son of Gilliam Graves, who came from North Carolina by way of Georgia and Alabama to Cedar Glades in Arkansas and volunteered for the Union army in January 1864.

She died on 23 December 1972 at Bandon, on the Oregon coast, at 88, and is buried at Hawthorne Memorial Gardens, Grants Pass. Her grandson Glen, Oscar and Katie's son, died at Veneta, Oregon, in 2001, so more than one branch of the Hulsey family ended up in Oregon.

Her bronze marker at Hawthorne Memorial Gardens in Grants Pass, Oregon, reads "In Loving Memory / S. Rebecca Hulsey / Mother / May 5, 1884 Dec. 23, 1972." She went by her middle name in Oregon, as the 1943 obituary index for her brother Abe had it: Mrs. Rebecca Hulsey.

stories.title: The preacher's son who followed the road west
stories.hook: Born in 1861 at Pulaski, Tennessee, Frank Stevenson was one of fifteen children of a Methodist preacher and went on to preach and farm in Indiana, Texas, Oklahoma and Arkansas.
body: In April 1910 the census taker at Danville, Arkansas, wrote "Clergyman" after Frank Stevenson's name. He was 51, renting, married for 25 years, and his seven children had been born in Indiana, Texas, Oklahoma and Arkansas. He had begun life in a Tennessee circuit preacher's household: Gilbert Franklin Stevenson was born on 17 November 1861 near Pulaski, Giles County, one of fifteen children of Rev. Abner Arrington Stevenson and Martha Still Watson, and the twin of George Washington Stevenson.

He was five months old when Federal troops first reached Pulaski in April 1862. Goodspeed's county history says Giles County was "continually overrun with both Federal and Confederate soldiers" and that in 1863 the Federals relieved the county of "horses, cattle and grain." His first cousins Coleman and Wilbur Stevenson served in the Confederate 32nd Tennessee. Giles County itself had been formed only in 1809, from Maury County, four years before his grandfather Elam came. In 1870 he and George, both 8, were in their father's household with younger children; in 1880 he was 18 and a farmer. In January 1881 The Pulaski Citizen reported that his father had "abandoned the idea of going to Texas," and that May that "Judge Geo. Stevenson, son of Rev. A. Stevenson, returned from Texas last week." Texas was in the family's talk before Frank himself lived there.

He went north to Gibson County, Indiana, where the family of his wife, Parsis Jane O’Neal, lived; her grandparents Archibald and Parses O’Neal had come to the county from Tennessee in 1839. The 1910 census gives Indiana as the birthplace of their children Delphia and George. Other family trees give them three older children, Iva Myrtle (1884), Adison Galiton (1886) and Nellie Vashti (1889), whose link to this family is not documented (lead). The order of the Texas and Oklahoma births between 1889 and 1902 is not established from the sources seen.

He married Parsis Jane O'Neal of Gibson County, Indiana, whose father Daniel had served in the 42nd Indiana. Their older children were probably born in Indiana; later ones were born in Texas (Willie, Frank and Elisha) and Oklahoma (Eddie), and the youngest, Katie, at Danville in 1910. By January 1919 his mother-in-law's obituary placed his wife as "Mrs. Frank Stevenson of Valiant, Oklahoma," and in 1920 he farmed a rented place on the South Millerton Road in Kirk Township, McCurtain County. Yell County, where he was preaching in 1910, had been organized on 5 December 1840, and the 1894 Ozark history notes that it had two county seats, Danville and Dardanelle. Katie Cornelia’s birth is given as 15 October 1910 at Danville, which does not fit her appearance as the baby in the census taken there that April; the two have not been reconciled.

He died at Hugo on 9 May 1950, aged 88, and lies in Block 2 of Mount Olivet Cemetery next to Parsis. The stone, as canvassed in 2000, reads 'Stevenson, Frank N., 1860-1950.' The year of birth is a year off the family record, and the census ages of 1870, 1880 and 1910 range from 1859 to 1862. His youngest daughter Katie married Oscar Hulsey, a Hot Springs native, in 1927, and she outlived her father by almost sixty years; their daughter Mary Ellen (1938-2002) is buried in Choctaw County beside William Thompson Jr. A photograph of the grave shows a stone reading 'Gilbert Franklin Stevenson, November 17, 1861 – May 9, 1950', which agrees with the family record; the 2000 canvass reading may come from an older marker or a misreading.

stories.title: The farming preacher of Bee Spring
stories.hook: For 54 years Rev. Abner Stevenson rode the Giles County circuits, and in 1880 he gave the census taker his trade as "Farming Preacher."
body: When the census taker came to District 10 of Giles County, Tennessee, in 1880, Abner Arrington Stevenson gave his occupation as "Farming Preacher." The census taker wrote his age as 63. He had been born on 16 March 1816, the fourth of eleven children of the Rev. Elam Stevenson and Lydia Payne, in a family that produced five Methodist-preaching brothers; Elam had organized the Bee Spring church in 1815 and moved to Tennessee in 1813. A grandnephew's letter of 1932 gave the family totals as years in the pulpit, and set down "Uncle Abner 54 years." The 1956 Methodist history of middle Tennessee calls him "a Godly man" who "lived to be very old."

On 8 December 1838 he married Martha Still Watson, born 19 February 1823, and between 1840 and 1866 they had fifteen children. The twins Gilbert Franklin and George Washington were the twelfth and thirteenth; one son, James Willis, became a minister and lived to 1943 ("Fifteen children at Bee Spring"). A son-in-law, John Newton Andrew, married three Stevenson women in turn. The household was a farm first and a pulpit second: The Pulaski Citizen of 21 November 1878 gave him "Blooming Grove, 4th Sunday, 11 a. m." on the Mt. Pisgah circuit, and on 29 May 1884 a column noted two sermons at Rocky Point, "one by Abner Stevenson."

The war came to his farm. His twins were infants when Federal troops reached Pulaski in April 1862, and Goodspeed says the county was "continually overrun with both Federal and Confederate soldiers." His nephews Coleman L. and Wilbur M., sons of his brother William P., served in the Confederate 32nd Tennessee. His own sympathies are not recorded. In January 1881 the Citizen reported that he had "abandoned the idea of going to Texas and will remain where he is now living," and that May his son "Judge Geo. Stevenson" had "returned from Texas last week." Another son, Frank, lived in Texas himself in the 1890s.

Martha died on 12 July 1887, and her stone at Bee Spring gives her name and dates and an epitaph. Abner died on 30 July 1896 and was buried at Bee Spring, the church his father founded. The church was destroyed by a tornado on 29 April 1909 and the congregation rebuilt at Bryson; the 1956 history says "All that remains of this today is the cemetery." His son Frank carried the preaching and the road west to Arkansas and Oklahoma, where Frank's youngest daughter Katie married a Hulsey.

stories.title: A blacksmith in the old Cherokee gold country
stories.hook: The 1850 census records a Georgia blacksmith and a household that may connect to the Hulseys later recorded in Arkansas.
body: The original 1850 census of Union County, Georgia, records Salathiel (indexed as Salathel Halsey), 43, a Georgia-born blacksmith with $50 in real estate. In dwelling and family 998 are Elizabeth, 35; Maryan, 19; Robert, 17; Elizabeth, 12; Jesse, 10; Jennings, 8; a girl transcribed as Lillean, 6; Benjamin, 3; and Nancy, 1. Arminda Burnett and J. C. Bell are listed in the same household. The page was enumerated on 11 November. The census did not record family relationships, so the apparent spouse and child relationships are inferred. In 1840 Salathiel was counted in Hall County, and in the 1830 Hall County Hulsey list he is one of seventeen men named Hulsey, living among the Hulseys of Charles and Adler.

The original page also corrects the published San Diego Genealogical Society extract, which had reversed two ages: Benjamin is three on line 34, and the girl immediately above him is six on line 33. Three is consistent with the family’s 1847 birth year for Benjamin, although the census does not give his exact birthday. It was the compiler of that extract who suggested that Robert in this household was the Robert Hulsey recorded in Hempstead County, Arkansas, in 1860.

Union County, in the northern mountains, was formed in 1832 from the country the Cherokee had held until their removal in 1836-39, once a gold-rush district; settlers there were hardscrabble farmers, mostly from Virginia and North Carolina, and few kept slaves. A blacksmith in such a place shod horses and mended plows. The census gives Salathiel's birth about 1807 and Elizabeth's about 1815, but it does not establish how Elizabeth and Maryan were related. He is gone by the early 1850s.

The original 1860 Hempstead County, Arkansas census records a Georgia-born Robert Hulsey, 27, with Sarah A., 20, and an infant male. His age and birthplace fit a possible continuation of Robert in the Georgia household, but neither census gives him a middle initial. The infant’s name, indexed as Selatha G., is uncertain in the handwriting; the published reading Salathel G. cannot securely link him to Salathiel. Family accounts also place Benjamin in Story, Arkansas, with a son named Martin Salatheil. The original 1850 age of three removes the apparent conflict with Benjamin’s reported 1847 birth, but neither his identity with the Arkansas man nor his relationship to George Washington Hulsey is established.

Salathiel's father may be Jesse Hulsey, the wounded Revolutionary pensioner of Hall County; online trees say so, but they also name Jesse Hamilton Hulsey and Mary Tharp, and no record supports either (lead).

stories.title: Eleven in the census, a bride at sixteen
stories.hook: Parsis O'Neal was 11 and "works at home" in Gibson County in 1880; by 1884 an Arkansas index has her a bride, and she died at Hugo in 1956.
body: In the Columbia Township, Gibson County, Indiana, census of 1880, Parsis J. O'Neal, 11, is listed as "Works At Home" in her father's house. She was the fourth of the ten children of Daniel Waters O'Neal, a veteran of Company F, 42nd Indiana, and Vashti Pearson. Her grandmother Parses (Shaw) Watt, widow of Archibald O'Neal, was on the old home farm near Oakland City, and her brothers in the household were William (16), John (13), George J. (4, born in Missouri) and Daniel G. (2). She was born on 26 March 1868, three years after her father came home from the war.

At 16 she may already have left. A marriage index for Arkansas records "Parsis J O Neal and Otho Louderback" married on 25 December 1884 in Pulaski County, Otho 40 and Parsis 16, and the Find a Grave memorial for her grave at Hugo carries the name Louderback (lead). Her sister Mary was in Arkansas by February 1884. The 1910 census says she and Frank Stevenson had been married 25 years, which puts the Stevenson household in 1885, and the oldest children, Delphia and George, were born in Indiana ("A sixteen-year-old bride in Pulaski County").

The Stevensons then followed the work. Willie, Frank and Elisha were born in Texas between about 1894 and 1904, Eddie in Oklahoma about 1907, and Katie at Danville, Arkansas, on 15 October 1910, when Parsis was 42. By January 1919 her mother's obituary called her "Mrs. Frank Stevenson of Valiant, Oklahoma," and in 1920 the family farmed a rented place in Kirk Township, McCurtain County. Her son George Sherman died at Kilgore, Texas, in 1978, and the death certificate names her as his mother.

She died at Hugo on 26 January 1956, aged 87, and lies in Block 2 of Mount Olivet Cemetery beside Frank. The stone, as canvassed in 2000, reads 1887-1956; every record made in her lifetime, from the 1880 census to her children's births, puts her birth in 1868, and a photograph of the stone shows 1868, so the 1887 is a misreading or comes from another marker. Her brothers stayed in Gibson County and her sister Mary lived to 100 at Tuttle, Oklahoma ("A hundred years from Indiana to Oklahoma").

stories.title: Vashti O'Neal's six hours of apoplexy
stories.hook: Married at 15 in 1860, Vashti Pearson O'Neal raised ten children in Gibson County, Indiana, sent a husband to the Union army, and died there in 1919.
body: Vashti Elizabeth Pearson was born on 18 May 1844 and married Daniel Waters O'Neal on 5 January 1860, when she was 15 and he 21. Daniel's father Archibald had come to Gibson County, Indiana, from Tennessee in 1839 and died in 1841, leaving his widow Parses on the farm. In October 1861, with Vashti 17 and their first child, Mary Elizabeth, a year old, Daniel enlisted in Company F of the 42nd Indiana, the company raised at Oakland City, and the war carried much of the regiment from Perryville to Atlanta ("Union soldier, 42nd Indiana"). A family biography has him discharged for disability at Nashville in March 1862.

Between 1860 and 1887 she bore ten children: Mary Elizabeth (1860, who lived to 100), William Allen (1863), John Sherman (1866, born the year after the war), Parsis Jane (1868), J. A. (1871, an infant death), George Johnson (1875), Daniel Clinton (1878), David Commodore (1881), Nora (1884, an infant death) and Charity Louisa (1887). The 1880 census shows the family in Columbia Township, with George, the child born in 1875, listed as born in Missouri. Her five surviving sons lived into their fifties or later, and three of them died at Somerville.

She died at Somerville on 16 January 1919, of "apoplexy, 6 hrs." She professed faith early in life and was a faithful member of Somerville's United Brethren Church. Her obituary named her husband, her five sons William, John, George, Clinton and Commodore, two daughters, "Mrs. Frank Stevenson of Valiant, Oklahoma," and Mrs. Fred Skomp of Somerville, and a brother, James Pearson of Elberfeld. Her eldest daughter Mary Elizabeth was in Oklahoma in 1919 but is not named in the notice, and Parsis's marriage to Frank Stevenson tied the O'Neals to the Stevenson family of Arkansas and McCurtain County.

The 1884 county history shows a Pearson family in Columbia Township long before she was born: in 1827 "Solomon Brown and William Pearson had charge of the poor." No record ties that William to her father John. Her restored family stone stands with Daniel's at Somerville, and her own marker reads "Vashti, 1844-1919."
src: History of Gibson County, Indiana (1884), Columbia Township, p. 213. Obituary of Vashti O'Neal, January 1919 (family transcription); History of Gibson County, Indiana (1884), p. 213.

stories.title: Martha Still Watson, fifteen children and a preacher's stone
stories.hook: Married at 15 in 1838, Martha Watson Stevenson bore fifteen children in Giles County; her stone at Bee Spring speaks of a better world and the Resurrection morn.
body: The Stevenson family history says that on 8 December 1838 Abner Stevenson "married Martha S. Watson," born 19 February 1823 in Tennessee, "the daughter of Mary Watson." She was 15. Between 1840 and 1866 she had fifteen children, the last of them about the time she turned 43, among them the twins Gilbert Franklin and George Washington in November 1861, five months before Federal troops reached Pulaski.

For a Methodist circuit preacher's wife that meant a farm and a houseful of children during the years her husband was riding to Blooming Grove, Rocky Point and the Mt. Pisgah circuit (see "Fifteen children at Bee Spring"). She died on 12 July 1887, and the Nashville Christian Advocate abstracts of 20 August 1887 carry the notice of her death. Her online grave memorial calls her "Wife of Rev. A. A. Stevenson."

Her mother is given only as Mary Watson. WikiTree names William Watson and Mary Brown as her parents; no record is cited and the middle name Still is unexplained, so her ancestry stops at Mary (lead). Her son Frank carried the line to Arkansas, where Frank's youngest daughter Katie married Oscar Hulsey.

Her stone in the Bee Spring churchyard is a plain round-topped tablet. It reads "Martha S. Stevenson / Born / Feb. 19, 1823 / Died / July 12, 1887," and below a carved rule: "She started in early life for a better world & has stopped at this Inn until the Resurrection morn, where we will meet again." The cutter's letters read "stated" and "sopped," with the r and t evidently left out. The stone's 1887 agrees with the family dates against the 1886 of the published newspaper abstract. The phrase "Wife of Rev. A. A. Stevenson" belongs to the online memorial's biography; it is not carved on this face of the stone.

The 1880 census of the 10th Civil District of Giles County, taken on 11 June, lists her as Martha S., 56, keeping house, wife of A. A. Stevenson, a farmer and preacher, with Gilbert F., 18, Wilson M., 16, and Jane M., 12, at home. She was born in Tennessee, and the census gives Virginia as the birthplace of both her father and her mother.

A Find a Grave family link makes her a daughter of David Milton Watson (1791-1843) and Mary Ann Gary of Mountain Creek, Anderson County, South Carolina, and lists her among their eight children. The memorial cites no record for the link. That couple were born, lived and died in South Carolina, whereas Martha was born in Tennessee to parents who, by her own household's 1880 entry, were Virginians. The link does not fit and is not adopted (lead, doubtful). Her mother remains the "Mary Watson" of the Stevenson family history.

The Isham Brown of Giles County lead noted elsewhere remains unchecked. The published abstract of her notice in the Nashville Christian Advocate of 20 August 1887 gives her death as 12 July 1886 and her marriage as 6 December 1837. Family compilations and the existing grave-memorial dates instead give death in 1887 and marriage on 8 December 1838. The original newspaper notice and marriage entry have not been examined, so these conflicts remain unresolved; the tree’s existing dates are retained pending verification. stories.title: The Pearsons behind Vashti
stories.hook: John and Elizabeth Pearson are known only through their daughter's 1919 obituary, a grave memorial, and a son in Elberfeld.
body: John and Elizabeth Pearson were the parents of Vashti Elizabeth, born 18 May 1844, who married Daniel Waters O'Neal in Gibson County, Indiana, on 5 January 1860. Both were dead by January 1919, when Vashti's obituary appeared. The only brother it names is James Pearson of Elberfeld, Indiana, a Warrick County town a few miles from Gibson County. Elizabeth's maiden name, Carman, comes from the memorial for her grave.

The 1884 History of Gibson County shows that a Pearson family had been in Columbia Township since at least 1827, when "Solomon Brown and William Pearson had charge of the poor." No document names that William as John's father or brother. Their daughter's story, with ten children and a husband in Company F of the 42nd Indiana, is told under Vashti's name.
src: Obituary of Vashti O'Neal (1919), family transcription on Find a Grave. History of Gibson County, Indiana (1884), Columbia Township, p. 213.
stories.note: The family tree carries dates for them (John 1803-1850; Elizabeth 1807 to 1 October 1879) that no record seen for this story confirms.
stories.place: Named as Vashti's parents in her 1919 obituary, both dead by then. Her only surviving brother was James Pearson of Elberfeld, Indiana. The maiden name Carman comes from her grave memorial.

stories.title: A Tennessean who lived two years on the Gibson County farm
stories.hook: Archibald O'Neal came to Gibson County, Indiana, in 1839 and was dead by April 1841, leaving a widow, a small son, and a farm that stayed in the family for decades.
body: The 1884 History of Gibson County, Indiana, puts it in one plain paragraph: "Archibald O'Neal was an early settler. He came here in 1839. He was a Tennesseean by birth. He died April 25, 1841." He farmed in Columbia Township with his wife Parses, whom the book calls "a native of Lawrenceburg, Ohio." Their son Daniel Waters had been born in Tennessee in October 1838, the year before the move.

The book prints his death date twice, and the two differ. The township narrative (p. 212) gives 25 April 1841; the directory on p. 239, listing him under his widow, reads "Died Ap'l 22,'41," "First Husband of Mrs. P. W." The year is certain, the day is not. His widow Parses then married Hugh Watt, an Irishman from County Down, who died in September 1871. In 1884 she was still on the old home farm, and she died in 1901 ("Parses Watt and the old home farm").

Online trees give Archibald a birth in Virginia in 1796 and parents named Charles and Martha, which rests on an uncited memorial; the county history says Tennessee. His son Daniel enlisted in Company F, 42nd Indiana Infantry, in October 1861, married Vashti Pearson, and had ten children, among them Parsis Jane, who married Frank Stevenson.

stories.title: Parses Watt and the old home farm
stories.hook: In an Indiana township directory, a widow and farmer appears alongside the names of both her husbands.
body: In 1884, a Gibson County directory listed “Mrs. Parsis Watt” as a farmer in Section 32 near Oakland City, Indiana. The entry gave her birthplace as Lawrenceburg, Ohio, and the year she came to the county as 1839. The directory set two more names immediately below hers: Archibald O’Neal, her first husband, and Hugh Watt, her second.

Archibald O’Neal came to Gibson County in 1839 and farmed there. He died in April 1841, leaving Parses a widow. She later married Hugh Watt, an Irishman from County Down. The county history says that, decades after Archibald’s death, she was still living on the old home farm.

The directory records Hugh’s death in September 1871. By the time the book appeared thirteen years later, Parses was listed under her own name and occupation. Its pairing of a widow’s farming entry with the names of two deceased husbands preserves a compact account of a household that had changed over more than forty years.

The same book gives conflicting dates for Archibald’s death: its biographical sketch says April 25, 1841, while the directory says April 22. Both agree on the year. Parses died in 1901, according to the family record.

stories.title: The Iredell Presbyterians who raised a Methodist preacher
stories.hook: James and Jane Stevenson lived out their lives in Rowan and Iredell counties, North Carolina, and their son Elam took the family into Methodism and Tennessee.
body: James Stevenson was born in 1746 and died in 1828. His will of June 1828, made in Iredell County, North Carolina, names his son Elam among his heirs, and the State Records of North Carolina list him in the Rowan County militia in 1781. He and Jane Stevenson, Presbyterians, were married in 1781, though a compiler's note puts the marriage about 1765 and calls James a soldier of the Revolution. Jane died in 1814, fourteen years before her husband.

Their son Elam was born on 24 September 1787 in what is now Alexander County, North Carolina. He was the first of the family to join the Methodists, married Lydia Payne in Burke County, was licensed to preach in 1813 and that year moved his family to Giles County, Tennessee (by pack horse, in family tradition; his own letter mentions a wagon). In 1869 he wrote his own account of those years ("In his own words, 1869"), and the Christian Advocate printed his obituary in April 1875. Three to five of his sons, depending on the source, became preachers; Abner, whose farm and pulpit were near Pulaski, is the next generation of this line.

The Sons of the American Revolution list him as patriot P-297560: born 27 May 1746 (a descendant's biography on the same record says 1747) in Bladen County, died 3 September 1828 in Iredell County, a private in the militia under Captain Joseph Sharpe and Colonel Francis Locke, with a wife Jane and children James, William, Elam and Phineas. The record places his grave in the Stevenson, or Lackey-Stevenson, Cemetery at Vashti, in what is now Alexander County, where his father had taken up 640 acres. Phineas, who does not appear elsewhere in this archive, is listed as Elam's brother. These details come from lineage-society applications rather than from his own papers, so they are secondary; the descendant's sketch also credits him with Ramsour's Mill and later battles that no muster record seen here confirms. A Captain James Stevenson of Rowan and Cabarrus counties, an elder at Poplar Tent who died in 1832, was a different man.

A 1955 note in a family book gives James's father as another James, an Irish immigrant who died in 1820, and his mother as Sally Kelly of Maryland; it gives Jane's parents as John Stevenson (d. 1794) and a Thompson. These are compilers' statements only (lead). The dates are strained: a father who died in 1820 and a mother in 1820 or 1821 would both have been very old. See the entries for each.
src: Will of James Stevenson, Iredell Co., NC (1828); State Records of North Carolina, vol. 17; Christian Advocate obituary of Elam Stevenson (1875). SAR Patriot Research System, James Stevenson, P-297560: https://sarpatriots.sar.org/patriot/display/297560.
stories.place: Presbyterians of Rowan, later Iredell County, North Carolina, married in 1781. James's will of June 1828 names his son Elam among his heirs. He served in the Rowan County militia in 1781.

stories.title: Noble Shaw's 268 acres at Oak Ridge
stories.hook: A Quaker farmer of Guilford County, North Carolina, Noble Shaw died on Christmas Day 1855, and his widow sold his land in the spring of 1857.
body: On Thursday, 26 March 1857, The Times of Greensboro carried a notice headed "Land Sale." Having qualified as administrators on the estate of Noble Shaw, with a will annexed, J. H. Leak and Sicily Shaw would sell on 16 April "a tract of land, consisting of 268 acres, well timbered and well watered, convenient to the Oak Ridge Institute, and on the direct road from Danville, Va., to Salisbury," on credit. It is signed at Oak Ridge, 24 March 1857.

The full notice adds that the sale would be held “at the dwelling of said deceased,” and the same notice ran again in the issue of 2 April 1857, p. 4. “With a will annexed” is the old legal phrase for administrators who carry out a written will when the executor it names cannot or does not act. So the notice tells us two things: Noble left a will, and Sicily, then 66, was one of the two people the court trusted to settle his estate and sell his land.

The farm lay near the Oak Ridge Institute, the academy in northwestern Guilford County, on the road that runs from Danville, Virginia, down to Salisbury. Sicily was born on 2 August 1790; she outlived the sale by four years.

Noble was born on 22 April 1787 and was a member of Dover Monthly Meeting, whose register lists his wife Sicily and children Aaron (16 December 1809), Parris (7 July 1817, died 30 May 1818) and Mary (17 November 1820). He died on 25 December 1855. The Dover register fits a time when Friends were leaving for Ohio and Indiana: Weeks counts seventy-one certificates from Dover between 1816 and 1860, nearly all of them to Indiana. The Shaws stayed.

Parses Watt of Gibson County, Indiana, who was born about 1811 and died in 1901, is thought to be the Shaws' daughter, but the Dover register shows only a Parris who lived a year; she would have to be an earlier child missing from the page (lead). If she is theirs, her son Daniel O'Neal's Union service and her great-granddaughter Katie Stevenson's marriage to a Hulsey tie the Guilford County Quakers to the Ouachita hills of Arkansas and Oklahoma.

His small stone stands among the leaves in the Dover Friends Meeting burying ground near Colfax, Guilford County. Lichen covers most of the face; "Noble Shaw," "Died," "25 Dec. 1855" and an age beginning "68" can still be read in the photograph, matching the Dover register's birth date of 22 April 1787.
src: Hinshaw, Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy, vol. 1 (Shaw family entry); U.S., Quaker Meeting Records, 1681-1935 (Dover MM birth and death of Noble Shaw); U.S., Quaker Meeting Records, 1681-1935 (Dover MM register, Noble Shaw family) The Times (Greensboro, N.C.), 26 March 1857, p. 3, and 2 April 1857, p. 4; Weeks, Southern Quakers and Slavery (1896).; Find a Grave memorial 18148137, Noble Shaw, Dover Friends Meeting Cemetery, Colfax, Guilford Co., N.C., photo by NCDave (2011): https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/18148137/noble-shaw; The Times (Greensboro, N.C.), vol. 2, no. 13, 26 March 1857, p. 3, and no. 14, 2 April 1857, p. 4.

stories.title: The widow who signed the land sale
stories.hook: Sicily Nordyke Shaw, born in 1790 to Quaker parents in North Carolina, outlived her husband Noble by five years and signed the notice that sold his farm.
body: Hinshaw's Quaker records list "Sicily b. 8-2-1790" first among the children of Aden and Martha Nordyke, which gives 2 August 1790 for her birth. Her father Aden had been born in Burlington County, New Jersey, in 1762, shot in the arm in a Georgia attack, and married Martha Johnson in 1787 at Deep River Meeting in Guilford County. Sicily married Noble Shaw of Dover Monthly Meeting and lived out her years in Guilford County while her father went to Indiana.

In the spring of 1857, aged 66, she and J. H. Leak signed, as administrators, the notice in the Greensboro Times offering Noble Shaw's 268-acre farm at Oak Ridge at public sale on 16 April (“Noble Shaw’s 268 acres at Oak Ridge”). The court trusted her, with Leak, to carry out her husband's will. She died on 16 May 1861, four years later.
src: Hinshaw, Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy, vol. 1 (Nordyke family entry); U.S., Quaker Meeting Records, 1681-1935 (Union MM birth of Sicily Nordyke) Weeks, Southern Quakers and Slavery (1896); The Times (Greensboro, N.C.), 26 March 1857.

stories.title: The Quaker bride at Deep River, 1787
stories.hook: Martha Johnson was born at Deep River in the Quaker country of Guilford County and married Aden Nordyke there in December 1787.
body: On 12 December 1787 a Quaker marriage entry in Hinshaw's index reads: "Martha, dt Robert & Cecilia, Surry Co., m Adin Nordyke." She was Martha Johnson, born in 1766 and living with her family in the Quaker settlements of the North Carolina piedmont. Another genealogy gives her parents as Robert Johnson and Virginia C. Elmore, daughter of Thomas Elmore and Cecilia Ellyson; Cedar Creek Meeting in Virginia recorded the couple as moving to North Carolina on a certificate dated 29 March 1766. Hinshaw's index gives her mother as Cecilia, while the Cedar Creek minutes name Robert's wife as Virginia, and the minutes do not name Martha at all (lead).

Her husband Aden was born in 1762 in Burlington County, New Jersey, the oldest son of Abraham Nordyke and Mary Rogers. Their daughter Sicily, born 2 August 1790, married Noble Shaw. Martha died in 1844, two years after Aden, who is said to have died in Indiana in 1842.
src: Hinshaw, Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy, vol. 1, Nordyke family entry and 12 December 1787 marriage; U.S., Quaker Meeting Records, 1681–1935, Deep River Monthly Meeting, 12 Dec 1787 (as cited in Aden Nordyke’s profile). The proposed Cedar Creek parentage remains a lead.
stories.place: Born at Deep River, North Carolina.

stories.title: Six homes in forty-four years
stories.hook: Abraham Nordyke and Mary Rogers married in a New Jersey Quaker meeting in 1761 and kept moving, through Virginia, Georgia, North Carolina and Tennessee, until they reached Ohio in 1805.
body: Abraham Nordyke and Mary Rogers were married on 1 June 1761 in Burlington County, New Jersey, and were members of Chesterfield Monthly Meeting. Mary was the granddaughter named in her grandfather Thomas Staples's will of 1758, where he left bequests to "Mehetable and Mary Rogers", the daughters of his daughter Ann and her husband Thomas Rogers. Abraham was probably the son of Henry Nordyke and Rebecca Perkins, who married at Willingboro in 1731.

The Terrell-Nordyke Genealogy of 1960 gives their moves in order. In 1771 they transferred to Hopewell Monthly Meeting near Winchester, Virginia. They then lived for eight years in Georgia, where their son Aden was shot in the arm in an Indian attack (Ohio county history), and where their son Micajah, born in 1771 in Stafford County, Virginia, hid through a night in the woods at the age of four when an invasion was feared. In 1788 they joined Deep River Meeting in North Carolina, where their son Aden had married Martha Johnson the December before. In 1798 they moved to Lost Creek Meeting near Knoxville, a settlement whose Friends had been refused leave to meet in 1787 because the land title was still disputed with the Indians, and in 1805 to a farm near New Vienna in Clinton County, Ohio, where they helped start East Fork Meeting.

Lost Creek, near New Market a few miles north of Knoxville, was already a settlement with a history of trouble. Weeks reports that in 1787 Friends there, near the Holston River, asked New Garden Monthly Meeting for the right to hold meetings and were refused, because they had “settled on lands the title to which was still in dispute with the Indians,” and were told to move off. The Western Quarterly Meeting added in 1792 that no Friend should “remove and settle out of the limits of a Monthly Meeting without first applying to and having consent.” A meetinghouse went up at Lost Creek in 1796. The Nordykes reached it two years later, and it was from there that Weeks says many Tennessee Friends “drifted on, like Charles Osborn and William Williams, to the Northwest.”

The last move put Micajah, then 34, his wife Charity, 26, with an infant in her arms and children of three, five and seven, and the “aging grandparents” on the road north. They bought land near what became New Vienna and “helped start a Friends Meeting which was called East Fork,” on a lot that was part of the Nordyke farm. “Micajah had to go to Chillicothe, forty miles distant, to get flour and sugar,” and Charity kept wolves off with brimstone on the fire. Terrell dates this move to 1805; the tree entry for Abraham gives Clinton County in 1806.

Their children included Aden, Israel, Benajah, Beulah, Micajah, Daniel, Phebe and Hiram, and the Quaker habit of recording the hour of birth survives: "Aden was born at 7:00 P.M.; Israel at 3:00 P.M.; Benajah at 9:00 P.M." Mary died in 1814 and Abraham’s burial at East Fork was recorded in 1825, at 89; the tree gives 1822, so the death year is unsettled. Aden's daughter Sicily, born in 1790, married Noble Shaw in Guilford County, North Carolina; if Parses Shaw of Gibson County, Indiana, was their daughter, the line runs on to the O'Neals, the Stevensons and the Hulseys of Arkansas.
src: C. B. Weeks, Southern Quakers and Slavery (1896), pp. 251-54, archive.org/details/southernquakerss00week

stories.title: The man who owed Jacob Perkins money
stories.hook: Henry Nordyke married Rebecca Perkins at Willingboro, New Jersey, on 6 January 1731, and the Perkins estates were settled around him that same year.
body: A New Jersey marriage license was granted on 6 January 1731/2 for Henry Nordyke of Burlington County and Rebecca Perkins of Wellingborough. The document records permission to marry, not the ceremony or its date. Her father’s will of 26 October 1731 names his daughter Rebeckah without a husband; her brother David’s will, dated January 1731/2, calls her Henry’s wife. A compiled family page places Henry’s birth on 2 January 1710 in the Netherlands, but no ship or church record has been found; his Dutch origin remains a lead.

Henry's name appears again in the estates of his wife's family. Her father, Jacob Perkins Jr., made his will on 26 October 1731, naming his wife Sarah and ten children, among them Rebeckah, and listing bonds due him "from James Smith, Esq., John Shinn and Henry Nordike." He left ten pounds to St. Mary's Church, Burlington. The will was proved on 7 December. Rebecca's brother David then died too; his will of January 1731/2 names "Sister, Rebecca, wife of Henry Nordike" and was witnessed by Henry himself, and it was proved on 4 March 1731/2 ("A cane and a sword").

Their son Abraham, who died at 89 in 1825, was born about 1736; he was a member of Chesterfield Meeting when he married Mary Rogers in 1761. From there the line goes to Guilford County, North Carolina, to Ohio and Indiana ("Six homes in forty-four years").
src: New Jersey State Archives, marriage license for Henry Nordyke and Rebecca Perkins, 6 January 1731/2 (copy supplied by family); Jacob Perkins Jr. will, 26 October 1731, and David Perkins will, January 1731/2, Calendar of New Jersey Wills, Lib. 3 p. 102 and Lib. 8 p. 184.

stories.title: Mamie: from Gadsden to the Red River, with eleven children
stories.hook: Born in Alabama, raised in Texas, married into the Moffitts, and called Mamie by the people who knew her.
body: Mary Tinsley Shackleford was born on 4 June 1895 in Alabama, a daughter of John Morgan and Lizzie (Newton) Shackleford. Her obituary would call her a native of Gadsden, Etowah County. In June 1900 the census found her as “May, 5” in her parents' household at Gilbert, Etowah County. Where the name Tinsley came from is still unknown.

The family did not stay in Alabama long. Her brother Robert was born at Gadsden in 1897, but her sister Hazel was born in 1908 at Rattan in Delta County, Texas, so the family had crossed to northeast Texas by then. About 1914 Mary married Woodford Grady Moffitt, and by June 1917 Grady was working as a timberman at Ervin in Choctaw County, Oklahoma, supporting a wife, his mother and a child. Their first son, Alvin, had been born in September 1915.

She had at least eleven children, and two died as toddlers. The family moved where the work was. In 1920 they were tenant farmers in Wilson Township, Choctaw County. In April 1930, with six boys, they were living with her parents on a farm near Stanton in Martin County, West Texas, where Grady was an out-of-work road laborer. By 1940 they were renting in Hugo, and in 1950 the census listed her as “Mamie,” 54, at Grant in Choctaw County, with Grady and three of the children still at home.

“Mamie” was the name her family used too. When her brother Robert died in California in 1961, his obituary listed “Mamie Moffett” of Oklahoma among his six sisters. Mary died the next year, on 26 August 1962, at Paris, Texas, still living at Grant. The Southeast Oklahoman of 30 August 1962 called her 67, the wife of Grady and the mother of John Moffitt. She is buried beside Grady at Shoat Springs Cemetery near Hugo, on a stone that reads “Mary Tinsley — Jun 4, 1895 – Aug 26, 1962.”

stories.title: Twenty-two years a widow at Herpel: Hannah Grimes Moffitt
stories.hook: Her birthplace is a Mississippi River landing or Illinois, depending on the tree, but her stone is in the Rocky Bayou hills and reads "Wife of Henry H Moffitt."
body: The 1910 census finds Hannah Moffitt, a widow of 53, renting a house in Franklin Township, Stone County, Arkansas. Two sons live with her: Thomas, who works as a railroad section hand, and Grady, who makes barrel staves. The census asks every mother how many children she has borne and how many are living, and Hannah's answer is seven and six. The household was already nine years into her widowhood: her husband Henry H. Moffitt had died at Mountain View in 1901, and she lived on without him until 1923.

Henry, a farmer who owned his land free and clear in the 1900 census, died at Mountain View in 1901 at 46. Family records give the date as 9 September; no original has been seen, and the Stone County Record newspapers for September 1901 would be the likeliest check. No grave has been found and he has no memorial of his own; Arkansas did not register deaths in Stone County until 1914. That May, on 26 May 1901, Henry’s brother Patrick had lost his wife, Alice Ann (Cole) Moffitt, who is buried at Levisy Flat Cemetery in Stone County. Hannah could not read or write, but she kept the family together for another two decades.

Henry and Hannah were the same age. Henry was born in 1855, when his father Nathan Moffitt, the wheelwright, and Rebecca Williams were farming in Lawrence County; Hannah was born in July 1855, the daughter of David H. Grimes of Wayne County, Tennessee. Their children were Josephine, Jesse Gee (1879-1957), Gimsa, Bertha, Thomas Berry (1889-1953) and Grady (1891-1972). Jesse Gee went to Texas and died in Amarillo in 1957; Tom died in Paris, Texas, in 1953. The 1900 census, taken in June 1900, gives her birth as July 1855 in Arkansas, with both of her parents born in Tennessee; her 1910 age of 53 would put it nearer 1857. Where in Arkansas is in dispute: a family tree gives Arkansas City, Desha County, and a second WikiTree profile gives Illinois instead; WikiTree lists only Tom and Grady as her children. The Desha County name cannot be right as written. In 1855 the Mississippi River landing that became Arkansas City lay in Chicot County and had seen little growth; the town was not incorporated until 1873 and was not in Desha County until the boundary moved in 1879.

What the records do show is where she ended up. By 1910 she was among the Moffitts of Stone County, a county only 37 years old. It was created in 1873; its seat, Mountain View, had 99 residents in 1880, got its first wooden courthouse in 1888 and was incorporated on 14 August 1890. Her brother-in-law Patrick Moffitt also lived in Stone County. After Henry's death Hannah kept a household of grown sons going on rented ground, and the two sons at home worked for wages, Tom on the railroad and Grady making barrel staves.

She spent her last years at Herpel, a Rocky Bayou community about six miles east of Mountain View, with a grist mill, a cotton gin, a stave mill and a sawmill. Its post office ran from 1907 to 1957. The Herpel Missionary Baptist Church laid its cornerstone on 5 March 1923, and Hannah died on 4 April 1923, about a month later. She is buried in Herpel Cemetery. Bertha May Moffitt Barham (1888-1930), also buried at Herpel, may be her daughter Bertha, whose birth the 1900 census gives as March 1886, but that is not proved (lead). Her stone reads "Wife of Henry H Moffitt," the only memorial the couple have, since Henry's own grave has not been located.

Hannah’s marriage connected the Grimes and Moffitt families. Through her husband she was the daughter-in-law of Nathan and Rebecca, whose road led from Randolph County, North Carolina, to Arkansas and Missouri; through her father David she belonged to the Grimes family of Hardin Creek in Wayne County. Her youngest son Grady carried both lines to Hugo, Oklahoma, where he raised his family.

stories.title: Rebecca's bond: a £500 promise in Randolph County, 1835
stories.hook: On 13 October 1835 two Moffitt brothers put up £500 to the Governor of North Carolina so that Nathan could marry Rebecca Williams.
body: The paper that proves the marriage is a printed form from the North Carolina Governor's office, filled in by hand. "KNOW all men by these presents, that we Nathan Moffitt & David Moffitt are held and firmly bound unto David L. Swain Esquire, Governor, &c.... in the full sum of five hundred pounds current money," and it is dated the 13th of October 1835. The condition reads that Nathan "hath made application for license for marriage to be celebrated between him and Rebecca Williams of the County aforesaid." The bond would be void if no lawful impediment appeared. Both men signed with seals. David Moffitt was almost certainly Nathan's older brother, born in 1802, one of Robert and Martha's nine children.

The form names her "Rebecca," and so does every later record. She is Rebecca Moffet in Nathan's household in Strawberry Township, Lawrence County, Arkansas, in 1850 and Rebecca Moffit in his household again in 1870. The county marriage index (FHL film 2,447,732) lists the marriage as Rebecca Williams to Nathan Moffitt, 13 October 1835. The profile title carries "Mary Rebecca," but every record calls her Rebecca. Her birth is given as 1814 in the dates above and as about 1816 in other tables, in Randolph County. No document names her parents. Ancestry suggests James S. Williams and Polly Garner, but the Williams families of Randolph County were numerous and none can be tied to her.

Her husband's family surrounded her. Nathan's mother Martha Chamness, who was born in 1778 and lived until 1865, was in the same county when Rebecca married, and Rebecca's sister-in-law Thalitha Williams (born 1804 at Deep River) had married Nathan's brother William C. on 7 August 1827. Whether the two Williams women were sisters is not shown. A son, Calvin Vestal, was born in Randolph County on 4 December 1841. By 1850 the couple were in Arkansas, where Patrick Green was born in May 1853, and in 1860 Nathan was a wheelwright with 1,200 dollars in land. Nathan's sister Sarah went to Iowa with her husband, Rev. Beeson Barker, and his brother Robert followed him to Strawberry Township by 1860.

Her last move was to Missouri. In 1870 she and Nathan were farming in Dent County, Missouri, with no land of their own, and she was still living in June of that year. She died in Oregon County, Missouri, in 1871 by the family tree, a year after the census date this profile carries, and Nathan married the widow Nancy (Rowe) Cole that same year. Her sons were Calvin Vestal (1841-1913) and Patrick Green (1853-1905), among others, and one of the others, Henry, married Hannah Grimes and raised the Moffitts of Stone County.

stories.title: David Grimes of Wayne County, and the daughter born on the river
stories.hook: Born in 1829 into a Tennessee farm family on the Highland Rim, David H. Grimes is known to us mainly through the daughter who married a Moffitt.
body: David H. Grimes was born in 1829 in Wayne County, Tennessee, a young county on the western edge of the Highland Rim. The legislature created Wayne County in 1817 and had to pass the act again in 1819 because the clerk never signed it; its first county court met at the home of Benjamin Hardin on Factor's Fork, where the old Natchez Trace crosses Shoal Creek. It was wooded country of ridges and hollows with iron deposits, and Clifton, on the Tennessee River, became its main commercial town and shipped cotton, livestock, lumber and cross ties downriver. David's world was the Hardin Creek farm of John Grimes and Penelope Blackshear, his probable parents, whose children were James B., Elisha S., John Anderson and William Jasper.

His father John died on 14 June 1844 and was buried on the Haggard farm, when David was about fifteen. His brothers stayed. John Anderson was farming on the home place in 1860 and 1900, and in 1872 William Jasper left a will naming "John A. Grimes, my brother, as executor." David is not named in that will. His birth in 1829 fits the unnamed son the Grimes family site lists between William Jasper (1826) and the end of the children, and a family tree names John Grimes as his father, but the link is unproved.

The rest of his life is in his daughter's records. A family tree has Hannah born in July 1855 at Arkansas City, Desha County, and David dying there in 1876. The place name is a later label: in 1855 the Mississippi landing now called Arkansas City was in Chicot County, and Desha County took in the area only in 1879. Hannah's 1910 age of 53 would put her birth nearer 1857, and a second profile gives Illinois. Whatever the town, the tree puts David in the lower Mississippi country of Arkansas by the mid-1850s, a long way from Hardin Creek, and has him dying in 1876. Hannah's 1900 census entry gives both of her parents' birthplace as Tennessee, which fits a father from Wayne County. His daughter's stone in Herpel Cemetery reads "Wife of Henry H Moffitt."
src: Tennessee Encyclopedia, 'Wayne County' (tennesseeencyclopedia.net/entries/wayne-county/); Encyclopedia of Arkansas, 'Arkansas City Commercial District'; Genealogy.com Grimes forum postings of P. Bryant (2002-2003)

stories.title: The recorder of Cane Creek, and eleven children in twenty years
stories.hook: Joseph Chamness wrote the Cane Creek marriage certificates from 1764, lost his wife the year the youngest was born, and lived to see every child married.
body: Joseph Chamness was in his twenty-third year when he married Margaret Norton at Cane Creek Meeting on 17 March 1763. Their certificate, which all four parents signed as witnesses, is told in full in “Two weddings at Cane Creek, sixteen days apart”. The next year, in 1764, the meeting made him its Recorder of Marriage Certificates, and the certificate book in his handwriting was kept in the vault at Guilford College when Zimri Hanson wrote the family's history in 1922. He was born in Baltimore County, Maryland, in 1740, and had come south with his father at the age of nine.

Eleven children were born to Joseph and Margaret between 1764 and 1784, the first three in Orange County and the rest in what became Randolph. Hanson lists Sarah (1764), William (1766), Elizabeth (1768), Mary (1770), Joseph (1771), Anthony (1773), Margaret (1776), Martha (1778), Lydia (1780), Edward (1782) and Mourning (1784). Joseph later took a certificate of removal from Cane Creek to Providence meeting in Randolph County, where he owned a farm. Martha, the eighth child, married Robert Moffitt at Providence in 1797, joining the Chamness and Moffitt families.

On the 12th of Fourth month 1784 Margaret died, with the youngest of her eleven, Mourning, a newborn. Hanson's account is that the eldest daughter, Sarah, then in her twentieth year, took charge of the infant and was the guiding star of the household until a stepmother appeared; some three years after her mother's death she married Obadiah Elliott in Randolph County and took the little sister into her own home. Joseph's second wife was Hannah Beeson, daughter of William and Mary Beeson, and they were married at Deep River meeting on 6 March 1786. Their daughter Susanna, born in 1788, was the twelfth child. Hanson counts twelve Beesons among the relatives of the bride when Joseph's son William married Isabel Beeson in Providence meeting, and records that William's stepmother signed that certificate too.

Joseph died on 17 May 1818 in Randolph County and is buried at Providence Cemetery. By Hanson's count he lived to see all his children married and settled, the youngest, Susanna, then about thirty. His own wedding certificate, printed in Hanson's book (pp. 17-18), is the document that ties the Chamness line to the Nortons, and his daughter's marriage to Robert Moffitt in 1797 tied both to the Moffitts.

stories.title: Pearl's family across the Red River
stories.hook: A Kentucky-born girl became a Texas farm neighbor, married Oscar Smith, and raised four children in southeastern Oklahoma.
body: Artie Pearl Satterfield was born in Butler County, Kentucky, in 1898, into the household of John C. and Samantha Johnson Satterfield. By 1910 the family had moved to Hagansport in Franklin County, Texas. Eleven-year-old Pearl and nineteen-year-old Oscar Smith appeared a few households apart on the same census route. They married in 1914. Their first daughter, Nellie Mae, was born at Talco, Texas, on 3 April 1917.

The Smiths crossed the Red River to Choctaw County, Oklahoma. In 1920, Pearl, Oscar and little Nellie were living on a rented farm in Oakes Township. By 1930 they were at Jeter with four children: Nellie, Robert Lee, Virgil and Faye. Faye had been born at Forney on 23 March 1929. The 1940 census still placed the household on rented farmland along Hugo Route 1. Pearl's family had gone from Kentucky to Texas to Oklahoma in one generation; the children's records preserve the different stops.

Pearl outlived Oscar and her eldest daughter. Nellie Mae Choat died in Paris, Texas, on 7 July 1973, aged 56, after breast cancer; her death certificate names her parents as Charley O. Smith and Pearl Satterfield. She was brought home to Hugo for burial at Mount Olivet Cemetery. Pearl lived until 1983 and was buried beside Oscar at Grant Cemetery. Her youngest daughter Faye lived until 2014, carrying the Smith and Satterfield connection into the Moffitt family.

stories.title: John B. Smith, who owned his Hagansport farm free and clear
stories.hook: A farmer on the Sulphur River divide who buried his wife at thirty-seven and lay beside her under a wooden stob.
body: The June 1900 census for Justice Precinct 2 of Franklin County, Texas, finds John B. Smith, 44, farming land he owned free of mortgage. With him were his wife Emma, their son Oscar, 10, daughters Vera, Luina, Lona and Allie, and a baby, Jimmie. The family lived around Hagansport, a community that grew up at a Sulphur River crossing called Hagan's Port and that by 1884 had about 150 people, four churches, a one-room school, a mill and a gin. Oscar, later Charles Oscar Smith, had been born there on 29 May 1889.

Emma Elizabeth Langley (Emma Liza on her Find a Grave memorial) was born on 11 December 1867 in Texas. The only census household that fits her is that of George W. Langley, a Georgia-born widower of Precinct 5 in neighboring Hopkins County in 1880, who had two daughters, Emma J., 12, and Eliza J., 8 (probable). She died on 15 March 1905, aged 37, and her stone in Hagansport Cemetery reads "Emma / Wife of / J.B. SMITH / Gone but not forgotten." Six children were in the house in 1900, the youngest a baby.

John did not stay a widower. By April 1910 he had remarried, and Oscar, 19, was working on the home farm. On the same census route, a few doors away, the census taker recorded John C. Satterfield, lately of Kentucky, with his wife Samantha and their daughter Pearl, 11. Oscar and Artie Pearl Satterfield married in 1914. Owning rather than renting set John apart in the county: in 1900 only 44.1 percent of Franklin County farms were run by their owners, and the usual tenant gave up half the crop.

John B. Smith died in 1918 and was buried at Hagansport beside Emma; his grave is marked with a wooden stob. His father was very probably Noah Smith, a Kentucky-born farmer and justice of the peace whose 1880 household in the same Franklin County precinct lists “John B. Smith, 20, son” (see “Noah Smith: Kentucky farmer, Franklin County justice of the peace, Confederate pensioner”). His mother is still unknown, and his own Texas death certificate is not indexed. His son Charles carried the farm tradition across the Red River to Choctaw County, Oklahoma, where he is buried at Grant.

Emma's marble stone at Hagansport gives her dates beneath "Emma / wife of / J. B. Smith" as "Born Dec 11 1869[?]" and "Died Mar 15 1905." In the photograph the last digit of the birth year looks like a 9, two years later than the 1867 used here; the 1880 census age of 12 fits 1867 or 1868 better, so the date above is kept.
src: 1900 and 1910 U.S. Census, Franklin Co., Tex.; Find a Grave (Hagansport Cemetery); obituary of Lona May Ottinger (1975). stories.title: Thomas Staples and Hananiah Gaunt's daughter
stories.hook: Thomas Staples's will of 1758 names a daughter Ann and two granddaughters, and through one of them the line passes to the Nordykes.
body: Thomas Staples of Burlington, New Jersey, wrote his will on 25 October 1758, naming his daughter "Ann, wife of Thomas Rogers" and his granddaughters "Mehetable and Mary Rogers." His wife Mehitable was the daughter of Hananiah Gaunt of Springfield Township, whose 1720 will names "Mahitable Staples" and "son-in-law Thomas Staples." Ann married Thomas Rogers at Upper Springfield Meeting on 30 October 1736.

A Burlington County administration of 6 December 1748 may belong to the next generation: "Staples, Thomas, Jun'r, of Burlington Co., innholder" died without a will, and administration went to Thomas Rogers, the husband of Ann Staples, with John Deacon and John Antram of the City of Burlington as bondsmen. The inventory was only 30 pounds 7 shillings. If this Thomas Jr. was Ann's brother, it fits Thomas Rogers acting for the estate (probable).
Granddaughter Mary Rogers married Abraham Nordyke on 1 June 1761 ("Three wills from Quaker New Jersey").

stories.title: John Rodgers and a third of the residue
stories.hook: John Rodgers of Burlington left his son Thomas one-third of the residue in a will proved in March 1767.
body: John Rodgers of Burlington, New Jersey, made his will on 23 January 1764. The published New Jersey will calendar abstracts his gift to his son Thomas as one-third of the residue. An inventory was made on 7 March 1767 and the will was proved on 26 March. The other thirds went to his daughter-in-law Elizabeth, then wife of William Lyndon, with her three daughters, and to the children of his daughter Martha, wife of Robert Hosier.

The son Thomas is identified in this family as Thomas Rogers, who married Ann Staples at Upper Springfield Meeting on 30 October 1736; their daughter Mary married Abraham Nordyke in 1761. The will abstract names Thomas but does not name his wife, and it gives no name for John’s own wife or parents.

The proposed connection to Martha Middleton and to the John Rogers born in 1687 to John and Mary Groom remains a lead. A separate calendar entry records John Rogers of Windsor, Middlesex County, whose will was dated 6 January 1769 and proved 10 April 1776. It names sons Isaac, Abraham, Joseph, John, Robert, Amos and Mathew, and daughters Mary and Martha; no Thomas is named in that abstract. Those dates and beneficiaries distinguish the Windsor estate from the Burlington estate proved in 1767. They do not establish which family belongs to the 1687 birth record.

Independently examined printed abstract: https://archive.org/details/calendarofnewjer04newj/page/360/mode/2up . Calendar of New Jersey Wills, vol. V, 1771–1780, p. 431, John Rogers of Windsor, will dated 6 Jan 1769, proved 10 Apr 1776; citing Lib. 17, p. 354. Independently examined printed abstract: https://archive.org/details/calendarofnewjer05newj/page/431/mode/1up . stories.title: Hananiah Gaunt: from a Quaker wedding at Sandwich to 500 acres at Hananicon
stories.hook: Hananiah Gaunt married a Quaker neighbor's daughter at Sandwich in May 1678, traded his Cape Cod land for New Jersey land the next day, and died on his own acres in Springfield Township.
body: On 3 May 1678 Hananiah Gaunt posted his intention to marry Dorothy Butler at the Sandwich Friends Meeting on Cape Cod. The next day he and his brother Israel exchanged their Sandwich land for land in New Jersey. On 10 May they were married. His father Peter Gaunt, who had been fined in cattle by the Plymouth Colony court for Quaker meetings, is recorded as dying on 10 May 1678, the same day; one of the two dates is probably wrong (“Peter Gaunt, who knew no visible worship in the world”). Dorothy's brother Daniel had been whipped for helping a Quaker in 1660 (“The Butlers of Sandwich and the marshal”).

The couple lived at Dartmouth, Massachusetts, until about 1685. On 11 May 1685 George Hutcheson of Burlington conveyed "to Hananiah Gaunt of Rhode Island, yeoman, for 500 acres in the First Tenth," and the proprietors' survey of July 1685 enters "500 a. near Honeonickon" (later Oneanickon, then Springfield Township). On 18 May 1687 "Hananiah Gaunt of near Oneanickon, yeoman," sold 100 acres to William Bustill, a carpenter of Shrewsbury, and in 1690 Hutcheson deeded him one twenty-fourth of a share of West Jersey, a proprietary right to land.

The 1685 deed calls him “of Rhode Island,” but an alphabetical list of Dartmouth land owners for 1684-1694 in Lands of Old Dartmouth carries his name, and a Ricketson family history notes undivided Dartmouth land he deeded to William Ricketson on 13 January 1684. Both of those are secondary accounts (probable).

He added to the farm. A later survey is entered for him “of 220 a. adjoining Samuel Houghton and Tho. Clark; incl. 9 a. of meadow on a brook near Mount Pisgah; 20 a. of the whole being an allowance for highways for other land.” A neighbor’s survey for Daniel Leeds of 188 acres at Oneanickon is described as lying beside “said Gaunts 9 a. lot,” the meadow ground on the brook.

The 1687 deed to Bustill describes the hundred acres as “N. grantor, E. Ralph Trenoweth, part of 500 a., bought of George Hutchinson May 11, 1685”: Hananiah’s own land lay on the north side and Ralph Trenoweth’s on the east. The West Jersey deed is dated 3 November 1690. It calls Hutcheson a distiller and Hananiah “of Burlington Co., yeoman,” and the share was one Hutcheson had bought of Godfrey Newbold of Handsworth, Yorkshire, on 22 August 1684, “excepting 200 acres.” A West Jersey share was a proprietary right to a portion of the province’s unsurveyed land, and such rights were bought and sold in England and Burlington before the land was laid out.

The county history, quoting Revel's Book of Surveys, shows him as a settled neighbor. Land "surveyed for William Biddle, at Oneanickon, 8th month, 1686, two hundred and seventy acres of land, and in 4th month, 1689, one tract of two hundred and thirty acres, and two other tracts, containing together three hundred and twenty-three acres" adjoined "lands of Hannaniah Gauntt, John Days, Peter Harvey, Charles Read, Samuel Barker, Daniel Leeds, Michael Buffin, John Browne, and John Shinn."

Dorothy died there on 26 April 1714. Hananiah made his will on 17 July 1720, naming his children Daniel, Zebulon, Mahitable Staples and Mary Webb, and his son-in-law Thomas Staples; it was proved on 17 November 1721. His daughter Mehitable's daughter Ann married Thomas Rogers in 1736, and Ann's daughter Mary married Abraham Nordyke in 1761, so the farm at Hananicon is where this line's New Jersey roots begin.
