stories.title: The charge against the women's minutes
stories.hook: In December 1766, Cane Creek Friends expelled Charles Davies after a dispute over the truth of the women's meeting record.
body: At Cane Creek Monthly Meeting on 6 December 1766, Charles Davies's name entered the minute book as a disciplinary matter. His complaint concerned the women's minutes: he had charged them with being mixed with an untruth. The record does not preserve the passage he disputed or explain his side of the argument. It records what the meeting decided to do about it.

Friends had already made repeated efforts to change his mind. Their minute says the labor had been to no purpose, and the meeting therefore disowned him. On the same page, ordinary business continued around the dispute: certificates of membership, a marriage report and appointments to attend the quarterly meeting. The break with Charles was entered in the same practical hand as those routine decisions.

Charles and Hannah Matson Davies had raised the family from which Mary Davies married William Moffitt in 1763. Charles owned 187 acres purchased in 1758 and was recorded as a minister in 1761. The 1766 decision shows a rupture within that Quaker community; it does not establish that he left North Carolina or ceased to believe. He lived until 1801. His daughter Mary's own will, written more than fifty years after the dispute, still used the numbered-month date familiar in Quaker records.
src: Radnor MM marriage certificate (1732/3); Davis, Davis: A Quaker Family (1985); Hinshaw vol. 1; U.S., Quaker Meeting Records, 1681-1935 (Cane Creek MM minutes, 6 Dec 1766); Cane Creek Monthly Meeting minutes, 6 December 1766, manuscript page 36, U.S. Quaker Meeting Records, 1681–1935.

Charles died in 1801 and Hannah in 1812.

stories.title: Married as an orphan at West Nottingham: Elizabeth Brown and Edward Norton
stories.hook: Elizabeth Brown was about eight when her father died. At twenty she married a Quaker born in Ireland, and their road ended at Cane Creek.
body: The Nottingham Monthly Meeting certificate of 16 October 1739 gives both sides in a few lines. The bridegroom was Edward Norton of West Nottingham, Chester County, son of the late Edward Norton of the Parish of Armagh in the Kingdom of Ireland. The bride was Elizabeth Brown, "dt William & Elizabeth (Cowgill), both dec." She had been born in the twelfth month of 1718, early 1719 by modern reckoning. Her mother died before her father married again in March 1721/2, and her father, William Brown Jr., died about 1727; her stepmother, Margaret Davis, then married William Kirk. Her grandfather, the emigrant William Brown, was an elder of the meeting.

Edward's own connections were tangled with hers from the start. His sister Mary Norton had married Elizabeth's uncle Richard Brown in November 1733, and both couples took certificates to Hopewell Monthly Meeting in Virginia, Edward and Elizabeth on 19 January 1739/40. Richard died before 1747, and when Fairfax meeting looked into the settlement of his will to protect his children, Mary married William Kirk, the widower of the same Margaret Davis who had been Elizabeth's stepmother.

From Hopewell the Nortons went on to Fairfax and then south. They reached Cane Creek in 1762, and the next March their daughter Margaret, born about 1740, married Joseph Chamness. The certificate calls the bride's parents "Edward Norton and Elizabeth, his wife, of Rowan County," and both signed as witnesses. Edward died in 1776 and is buried at Providence, Randolph County. Their granddaughter Martha married Robert Moffitt in 1797, which is how an orphan from West Nottingham and a family from Armagh come into the Moffitt story.

They were very likely the Edward Norton and Elizabeth Brown married at West Nottingham Meeting on 16 October 1739, who moved to Hopewell Meeting in Virginia, then Fairfax, and came to Cane Creek in 1762. Edward died in 1776 and is buried at Providence, Randolph County.

stories.title: John Matson of Merion, and the daughter who married at a justice's house
stories.hook: John Matson gave his consent in February 1733 for his daughter Hannah to marry Charles Davis; their daughter Mary married William Moffitt at Cane Creek.
body: The document that puts John Matson on record is his daughter's marriage certificate. In the twelfth month of 1732, by the Friends' count, Charles Davis of Blockley (Davies in the Cane Creek records) and Hannah Matson, "daughter of John Matson of Merion in the same county and province aforesaid with consent of her father," published their intentions under a Pennsylvania law against clandestine marriages and met at the house of Charles Read, Esq., a justice of the peace for Philadelphia. The witnesses were John Matson Jr. and Daniel Matson, probably Hannah's brothers, along with Evan and Jane George, Richard and Thomas George, Ellin Jones and Mary Andrew. Hannah was born about 1715.

John was a Quaker farmer of Merion, in the Welsh settlement west of Philadelphia. By the usual reckoning he was born about 1686 at Upper Merion and married a woman named Margaret before 1709. Their children were Daniel, Hannah, Morris, Catherine, John, Peter and Joseph. Matson is a Swedish name, and Swedes had farmed along the Schuylkill and the Delaware before Penn's grant, but the Swedish Colonial Society's study and the Mattson genealogy of 1983 do not make him a son of the Swede Johann Mattson; his parentage is undocumented. In 1742 he and his wife took a certificate from Chester Monthly Meeting to Goshen.

John Matson was buried on 3 May 1748, and his will was proved in Chester County on 16 July 1748. By then his daughter Hannah and Charles Davis had left Pennsylvania for Virginia and then Cane Creek, North Carolina, where Charles was disowned by the meeting in 1766 and died in 1801; Hannah lived until 25 October 1812. Their daughter Mary married William Moffitt there on 2 April 1763, sixteen days after the Chamness-Norton wedding, and her son Robert married Martha Chamness in 1797. John Matson of Merion is Robert Moffitt's great-grandfather on his mother's side.

stories.title: Joseph Cole's will, and the two-year-old who became Sarah Chamness
stories.hook: Joseph Cole made his will on 22 January 1720/1, leaving a widow and a daughter, Sarah, not yet three, who later married Anthony Chamness.
body: Joseph Cole of Baltimore County, Maryland, was the son of John Cole and Johanna Garrett. Barnes's Baltimore County Families lists him as "Cole, Joseph (6), s. of John (5) and Johanna." In November 1712 his father conveyed him part of a tract called "Daniel's Whimsey." His mother's father was Dennis Garrett, the early settler killed in 1691.

He made his will on 22 January 1720/1, and it names his wife Susanna and his daughter Sarah. Sarah was born on the 1st day of the 5th month 1718 in the Friends' register, so when her father wrote the will she was not yet three. The Cane Creek register later wrote her down as the "daughter of Joseph and Susanna Cole, of Baltimore Co., Md., now married to Anthony Chainness."

On 24 November 1735 Sarah married Anthony Chamness at St. Paul's Parish, Baltimore County. Anthony, a London-born servant who had finished his indenture, was about twenty-two, and she was seventeen. They went to Monocacy, then to Carver's Creek in 1749 and Cane Creek in 1751, and Sarah bore thirteen children. Zimri Hanson's 1922 history describes their farm, a mile west of the Cane Creek meetinghouse: a hewn-oak log house with a porch the length of the front, a grist mill on a small creek and large meadows on either side. Sarah died about 1773 and is buried in the Friends' graveyard at Cane Creek. Her son Joseph Chamness married Margaret Norton, and their daughter Martha was Robert Moffitt's wife.

stories.title: John Cole of Cole's Adventure: a witness at his father-in-law's trial
stories.hook: John Cole was about twenty-two when he was named as a witness in the Garrett case, and about sixty-seven when he gave evidence on the bounds of his own land in 1738.
body: John Cole's name is in the Provincial Court record of the death of his wife's father. The court's 1692 indictment of John Oldton for the sword blow that killed Dennis Garrett listed its witnesses: Philip Roper, Nicholas Hale, "John Cole (son-in-law of the deceased)," Thomas Stone, Abraham Vaughan and Barbara Garrett, the widow. John had married Dennis's daughter Johanna. Oldton was condemned to hang and was pardoned; he later served as captain of the county's rangers. John Cole was then about twenty-two.

The records that follow are surveys. William B. Marye's 1921 study of the old garrison roads of Baltimore County lists "Cole's Choice," surveyed for him on 28 July 1694 and never patented; "Cole's Addition," 67 acres surveyed on 29 May 1698 "on the north side of Patapsco River in the woods"; and "Cole's Adventure," surveyed in 1706 on a run called Gwin's Run. In March 1737/8, when a land commission sat on Cole's Adventure, "John Cole, Senior, aged about 67 years," testified that the beginning tree stood about a hundred yards east of Gwinn's Run.

Marye’s notes add detail to each tract. Cole’s Choice was later taken up again under the name “Orange,” and the same survey appears as “Cole’s Chance,” with a deed from John Cole to Robert Green dated 1702 (pp. 118, 242). Cole’s Addition lay beside the path called Darley Path, where Chase Street and the Bel Air Road now cross in Baltimore (p. 118). The 1737/8 commission on Cole’s Adventure was held by Thomas Demmett (p. 218, note 15).

In August 1750 another commission took depositions about Cole's Addition from men who had known him. John Ensor, Sr., aged 55, called him his father-in-law and said that about eighteen years earlier, around 1732, Cole had come with him to the spot and shown him where the boundary oak stood. William Green, aged 58, told the same story: “the aforesaid John Cole said there should have been a bounded tree of Coles Addition.” Ensor was born about 1695, and Marye’s note on the Garrett trial lists the Ensor family among the descendants of Dennis Garrett (pp. 118-119). By then Cole had died, in 1746, at about seventy-six. His land lay in and around the site of Baltimore, which was laid out as a town in 1729.

The family is easy to follow. His son Joseph made a will in 1720/1 and left a daughter, Sarah, who married Anthony Chamness in 1735; a son named Dennis Garrett Cole received land from his grandmother Barbara Garrett Broad in 1712. Sarah's son Joseph Chamness was the father of Martha, who married Robert Moffitt in 1797.

Marye, 'The Baltimore County Garrison and the Old Garrison Roads,' Maryland Historical Magazine 16:2-3 (1921), pp. 115-119, 214-242; William B. Marye, "The Baltimore County ‘Garrison’ and the Old Garrison Roads," Maryland Historical Magazine 16:2 (June 1921), pp. 118-119, and 16:3 (September 1921), pp. 214, 218, 242.

stories.title: Ann Mercer’s six children and her Quaker ministry
stories.hook: Ann Mercer bore six children with William Brown and was remembered among the Friends who spoke in meeting.
body: An original Ringwood Quaker entry records Ann Mercer, daughter of Thomas and Ann Mercer of Ringwood, born on the twenty-fourth day of the twelfth month 1666: 24 February 1666/7, or 1667 in modern year numbering. Her identification with Ann Mercer, William Brown’s second wife in Pennsylvania, remains probable. Later accounts place Thomas at Andover before he and his daughter crossed to Pennsylvania about 1682–83 and settled in Aston Township, Chester County. William’s original Wellingborough Quaker birth entry records him on the twenty-ninth day of the first month 1658 (29 March, Old Style), the son of Richard Browne; it does not name his mother. William had married Dorothy in England, and their son Joseph was born there on 12 June 1682. Dorothy died at sea on the voyage to the Delaware. William went first to his brother James, a weaver at Marcus Hook, and in 1684, when Ann was seventeen, he married her.

Gilbert Cope's 1864 list of the family, built from the Nottingham Monthly Meeting registers, gives the children Ann bore him: Mercer, born the 27th of the 12th month 1685; Ann, 1st of the 10th month 1687; William, 21st of the 7th month 1689; John, 3rd of the 5th month 1691; Richard, 31st of the 1st month 1693; and Thomas, 17th of the 11th month 1694. Mercer, named for her family and often written "Messer," was the first. Ann Mercer died in 1696; a 1709 Quaker list of Friends who died in Pennsylvania names her as "Ann Browne daughtr of said Thoms Mercer." Her father Thomas had died on 22 November 1694, eight weeks before her youngest, Thomas Brown, was born in January 1695.

Ann also had a public religious role. A catalog read at the Yearly Meeting in 1709 remembered Anne Browne among the deceased Public Friends, the people who spoke in meeting. It names her as Thomas Mercer’s daughter, says she crossed with her father and received a Testimony for Truth after arriving, and records her burial in 1696. Her place in that list preserves a part of her life beyond the names and dates of her children.

William married Catharine Williams of Philadelphia in 1699, and in 1702 he moved to the Nottingham Lots on the Pennsylvania-Maryland line, where Lots 23 and 33 were assigned to him. A 1902 history of the Brick Meeting House says that he "was the first Friend to settle on the Nottingham lots" and that the first meeting was held at his house in 1704. The meeting records put it a little later: Concord Monthly Meeting received the request for a meeting at his house in the 2nd month of 1705, and Concord Quarterly Meeting approved it on 9 April 1705, so meetings were held there by 1705. His fourth wife, whom he married in 1711, was Mary Matthews. The family memorandum entered at East Nottingham Monthly Meeting in 1786 calls him an elder and a substantial Friend, and puts his death on the 23rd of the 6th month 1746 (23 August, Old Style) in his ninety-first year (another account gives 1 October 1746); the Wellingborough register, which gives his birth in 1658, would make him about eighty-eight.

Ann Mercer’s descendants connect several branches of the family. Her sons William and Thomas married the Cowgill sisters Elizabeth and Ellin, as told in “Two Cowgill sisters, two Brown brothers, and a daughter left behind”; her son Richard married three times and ended with Mary Norton of Armagh in 1733; and William's daughter Elizabeth Brown married Mary's brother Edward Norton in 1739. Their daughter Margaret Norton married Joseph Chamness, and Margaret's daughter Martha married Robert Moffitt. Ann Mercer is Martha Chamness's great-great-grandmother, and so the ancestor of every child Martha bore Robert Moffitt.

stories.note: The original English birth entry names Richard as father and leaves the mother unnamed. The child’s identification with the later Pennsylvania emigrant remains probable. The Old Style date is retained; no Gregorian day conversion is implied. Ann Mercer’s original Ringwood birth entry names Thomas and Ann as parents; identifying that English child with the Pennsylvania wife remains probable. The elder Ann’s maiden surname is unknown. The 1709 catalog directly names the immigrant Anne Browne as Thomas Mercer’s daughter and was independently read in a later printed transcription; its original manuscript has not been examined. This corroborates the immigrant father-daughter relationship, while the identification with the Ringwood birth family remains probable.
stories.place: William Brown came from England in 1682 and was one of the first settlers of the Nottingham Quaker settlement on the Pennsylvania–Maryland line. Ann was his second wife.

stories.title: Chamniss of Wapping: the London parents of a boy bound for Maryland
stories.hook: John Chamness married Ann Weary at St John's, Wapping, in January 1704; twenty years later their son Anthony was bound as a servant for seven years in Maryland.
body: John Chamness and Ann Weary were married on 4 January 1704 at St John's Church, Wapping, the riverside parish beside the Thames, east of the Tower. The register spells the name "Chamniss," and Ann's surname Weary or Wearey. Online trees that call her Ann Jones have nothing behind them. Their children came steadily: at least eight between 1705 and 1717, baptized in the same parish. Anthony, the one who matters here, was baptized in February 1713 when he was eighteen days old. Cane Creek Meeting later wrote him down as "Anthony Chamness, s. John & Ann, b. about 2 mo. 1713, Est. Smithfield, London," so the family lived at East Smithfield, close to Wapping.

Anthony was bound as a servant on 9 February 1724/5. The indenture, which describes him as of Whitechapel, bound him for seven years to John Cooke, a London victualler, for service in "Maryland (his Majesty's Plantation in America)." It gives his age as fifteen; counted from his baptism he was about eleven. Either way he was out of his time by 1732 and was in Baltimore County, where on 24 November 1735 he married Sarah Cole, the great-granddaughter of the murdered Dennis Garrett.

The title of Zimri Hanson's 1922 family history, History and Genealogy of the American Descendants of John and Ann Chamness of London, England, names John and Ann as the founders of the American line. John and Ann themselves leave only the parish registers: no will, no trade and no death date. Their son, the boy sent to Maryland at the age of eleven or fifteen, became overseer of the Cane Creek meeting and in 1751 took up 490 acres there.

stories.title: Henry Satterfield, who died in 1861 with twelve children
stories.hook: A Tennessee-born farmer in Allen County, Kentucky, and the Garrison daughter who outlived him by thirty-five years.
body: The 1885 Butler County sketch of his son James names Henry Satterfield in one sentence: "a native of Maury County, Tenn.; died in 1861, at the age of fifty years." His death register entry, 24 December 1861, names his parents as Ephraim and "Rutha" Satterfield. He was born about 1811, two years after Ephraim Satterfield married Ruth Knowles in Warren County, and Maury County is where the sketch places the young couple. His son James was born in Allen County on 14 April 1838.

Henry married Mary Garrison, born 17 October 1811, the daughter of John M. Garrison of Allen County and of Martha "Patsey" Cannon (lead). The 1885 sketch names their twelve children: Louisa J. (Roy), David E., Samuel A., James H., Ruth M. (Massey), John E., Euphema P. (Liles), Hettie C. (Jones), Martha C. (deceased), Sarah E. (Hues), Joseph W. H. and Abraham W. Of the twelve, James H., born in 1838, married Melissa Gibson in 1859 and is the line to the Smiths. In 1861, the year his father died, James enlisted in the Ninth Kentucky, and an S. A. Satterfield, perhaps their son Samuel A., was sued with A. W. Garrison in 1871 in Warren Circuit Court over lot 74 in Bowling Green (Garrison v. Clark, 151 Ky. 565); the opinion gives only initials (lead).

Mary's parents' marriage ended in the legislature. By an act approved on 29 February 1848 the Kentucky General Assembly dissolved the marriage of her father John M. Garrison and Patsey; Mary was then 36. She outlived Henry by thirty-five years and died on 2 March 1896.

Mary did not die in Kentucky. Her stone stands in Big Springs Cemetery at Lineville, in Wayne County, Iowa, just north of the Missouri line, and reads: "M. C. Satterfield / Died / Mar 2, 1896 / Age 84 Ys 4 Ms 16 Ds." Counting back from the age gives a birth in mid-October 1811, which matches the 17 October 1811 birth given for Mary Garrison, and the initials fit Mary Cannon. The memorial links her to John Milton Garrison as her father (probable). No record seen says when or why she went to Iowa.

Her children's graves show how far the family spread. Memorials linked to hers place Samuel Addison (1835-1913) at Strawn in Palo Pinto County, Texas; James Henry (1837-1922) at Reed Cemetery in Bowie County, Texas; Ruth Melissa Massey (1840-1935) at Llano Cemetery in Amarillo; Euphema Lyles (1845-1922) near Stephenville in Erath County, Texas; Hettie Caroline Jones (1847-1907) at LeGrande in Hart County, Kentucky; and Abraham W. (1860-1933), the youngest, at Eldora in Hardin County, Iowa.

A studio portrait posted to her memorial is captioned "Age 78," which would date it to about 1889 or 1890 if the caption is right. It shows an elderly woman in a dark dress and a ruffled, lace-trimmed cap. Who identified the sitter is not stated, so the identification rests on the contributor's caption (probable).

stories.title: James and Cynthia Gibson of Allen County, Melissa's parents
stories.hook: Two names from a county history, and the daughter who married a Satterfield in 1859.
body: James and Cynthia (Woodcock) Gibson are named once, in the 1885 sketch of their son-in-law James H. Satterfield of Butler County: Melissa A., his first wife, was the "daughter of James and Cynthia (Woodcock) Gibson, of Allen County." The Allen County marriage register confirms Melissa's wedding to James Satterfield on 17 September 1859.

Allen County, created in 1815 from Warren and Barren, was where both families lived. Melissa and James had children together; the 1885 sketch names Henry W., John C., Sidney R., James D., Martha A. and Mary C., among them John C., born in February 1864. In 1867 the Satterfields left for Dakota County, Minnesota, and returned in 1875 to Warren County and then, in 1876, Butler County. Melissa died on 2 May 1877, the year after the move. A fire at the Allen County courthouse in 1902 destroyed some county records.

Melissa's son John C. Satterfield farmed at Horse Mill in Butler County and moved to Hagansport, Texas, about 1907. His daughter Artie Pearl Satterfield married Charles Oscar Smith in 1914, and their daughter Faye (Smith) Moffitt is the link to this family.

stories.title: Ephraim Satterfield, a Virginian by his grandson's account
stories.hook: One of thirteen children named in a Warren County will, he married a Knowles in 1809 and is gone by 1850.
body: The Butler County sketch of 1885 introduces Ephraim in a subordinate clause, as the father of Henry Satterfield and "a native of Virginia, who died about 1850." Warren County, Kentucky, supplies the documents. John Satterfield's will, recorded in Will Book D at page 262 and proved on 10 November 1847, names Ephraim among thirteen children: Uriah, Ephraim, Rebecca, Mary, Jeremiah, Phoebe, Nancy, Moses, Sarah, Jesse, Leah, Reuben and John. On 12 November 1809 Ephraim married Ruth Knowles in Warren County, and Ruth's father Joshua Knowles named "Ruth Saterfield" among his daughters in a will of 1824.

Their son Henry was born about 1811, in Maury County, Tennessee, by the 1885 account. Henry's own Kentucky death register entry of 24 December 1861 names his parents as Ephraim and "Rutha" Satterfield, and that is the document that ties Henry to this Ephraim and Ruth (probable). The sources disagree about Ephraim himself. WikiTree has him born in South Carolina in 1787 and dead in 1848, with Henry born in Warren County, while the 1885 sketch gives Virginia and Tennessee. A birth in South Carolina fits the will of his father John, who had lived in South Carolina before Kentucky.

By 1850 Ruth was a widow in Allen County, living with her daughter Elizabeth. Ephraim's death falls between his father's will of 1847 and that census, and the 1885 sketch dates it about 1850. His grandson James H. Satterfield, who supplied the sketch, was twelve in 1850.

stories.title: Melvina Clark: a birth date and age that disagree
stories.hook: Her 1929 death certificate names both parents, but its birth date and recorded age disagree.
body: Melvina’s original Kentucky death certificate uses the married spelling Johnston. It records her death at Big Reedy in Edmonson County on 17 January 1929, describes her as a widow, and names her father as Newton Clark, born in Kentucky, and her mother as Mary Dunn. Polly Nash of Big Reedy supplied the information. The space for her husband’s name is blank; this record does not identify him.

The certificate’s birth date is read and indexed as 10 November 1851, although the final year digits are not perfectly clear. It also records an age of 78 years, 2 months, 6 days. That age is inconsistent with the written birth and death dates. Both fields are preserved here without choosing a corrected birth year.

The original 1850 census for Newton Clark’s Butler County household lists Newton, 32; Polly, 32; Martha, 10; Granville, 9; Stanford, 8; Hester, 6; William, 5; a girl aged 3 indexed as Vina; and Mary, 11 months. The handwriting of the age-three girl’s name does not unambiguously identify her as Melvina. The former claim that this census establishes Melvina’s birth about 1847 is therefore withdrawn. The census has no relationship column, and the identification of Vina with Melvina remains open.

Original Butler County marriage papers name Newton Clark and Polly D. Elms: license issued 20 January 1839, ceremony 24 January, return signed 25 January. Melvina’s death certificate instead gives her mother’s name as Mary Dunn. The marriage does not reconcile Dunn and Elms or prove that the same woman bore both names. The identification of the mother named in 1929 with Polly in Newton’s 1850 household and with the 1839 bride remains probable. Compiled profiles link Newton to William and Lavina (Willis) Clark; that parental link is a separate question.

Her married name was Johnson; her husband's first name is not recorded on the memorials. Samantha D. was born on 28 March 1872 and Charlie in 1885. Samantha married John C. Satterfield in 1892, moved with him to Hagansport, Texas, about 1907, and crossed the Red River to Choctaw County, Oklahoma, after marrying Bird Alexander Stephens in 1917. She died on 1 October 1928 and is buried at Soper Cemetery.

The death certificate records burial at Mount Pleasant on 18 January 1929. The family memorial identifies this as Mount Pleasant Cemetery at Big Reedy. Samantha had died on 1 October 1928; the records examined do not establish that Melvina attended her Oklahoma burial. Charlie remained in Butler County and died in 1959.

stories.title: The Norton from Armagh who left a son and a daughter in Pennsylvania
stories.hook: Edward Norton of Armagh is known only from what his children's marriage certificates say of him, but it is enough to place his family in Ireland.
body: The Nottingham Monthly Meeting certificate of 16 October 1739 describes the bridegroom as "Edward Norton of West Nottingham, Chester County, son of Edward Norton of 'ye City and Parish of Armagh,' Ireland, deceased." That is all it says. His wife's name is not given, nor is his trade or the year of his death. He was dead by October 1739. Albert Cook Myers, who collected the certificates of Irish Friends settling in Pennsylvania between 1682 and 1750, prints the two Norton marriages together on p. 376 of his 1902 book, one under the other.

The other marriage is his daughter's. On 24 November 1733 (“9 Mo. 24, 1733” in the Irish certificate list), "Mary Norton, daughter of Edward Norton, 'of ye County of Armagh,' Ireland," married Richard Brown, son of William Brown of West Nottingham. Cope's genealogy of the Browns gives the same marriage as the 24th of the 5th month and calls her "dau. of Edward Norton of Co. Armagh, Irel'd." She was Richard's third wife. Together the two certificates put two adult children of the same Armagh Quaker in Chester County, near the Maryland line, within six years, part of the Irish Friends' emigration that Myers traced.

Richard, born in 1693, was the son of William Brown the emigrant and his second wife Ann Mercer; he had married Hannah Reynolds in 1717 and Rachel Beeson in 1730/1 before Mary Norton. The bridegroom of 1739, Edward Norton the younger, married Elizabeth Brown, daughter of William Brown Jr. and Elizabeth Cowgill, so he married his sister Mary’s husband’s niece. Elizabeth’s mother had died before March 1721/2 and her father about 1727, and she married at West Nottingham as an orphan; the meeting’s book calls her “dt William & Elizabeth (Cowgill), both dec.”

Both Norton marriages were into the Brown family, and both couples went on to Virginia. Edward Norton the younger and Elizabeth Brown are the Moffitt ancestors; their daughter Margaret married Joseph Chamness at Cane Creek in 1763, and Margaret's daughter Martha married Robert Moffitt. Mary and Richard Brown had three sons, Richard, Joseph and Mercer; Richard died before 1747, and in April 1747 Mary married William Kirk. The elder Edward, who stayed in Armagh as far as the certificates show, is the earliest Norton on this line.

Edward and Elizabeth Norton took a certificate to Hopewell Monthly Meeting in Virginia on 19 January 1739/40, and Richard and Mary Brown with their family took one to Hopewell too. Mary and Richard’s three children were Richard (born 18 September 1734, died 4 September 1738), Joseph (1 April 1736, died 19 May 1751) and Mercer (7 May 1740). Richard left a will. The editors’ abstract of the Nottingham minutes says that Fairfax Monthly Meeting appointed a committee on the 28th of the 12th month 1746/7 (28 February) to inquire into its settlement, to protect the children, and found it satisfactorily settled. On the 21st of the 1st month 1746/7 (21 March) Nottingham gave William Kirk, the widower of Margaret Davis, a certificate to Fairfax, clear to marry Mary Brown. Margaret Davis, who had died in February 1744/5, had been the second wife of Elizabeth’s father, so Mary Norton’s new husband was Elizabeth’s stepmother’s widower.

Edward and Elizabeth Norton later lived in Rowan County, North Carolina, according to their daughter Margaret’s marriage certificate of 1763, told in “Two weddings at Cane Creek, sixteen days apart”. That they are the couple of 1739 is probable, not proven, though the names and the Hopewell and Fairfax trail suggest it. If so, Margaret’s grandmother was Elizabeth Cowgill of Neshaminy, and the line from the Settle certificate of 1682 runs through Brown and Norton to the Chamness wedding that put the family into Robert Moffitt’s household.

stories.title: Two Cowgill sisters, two Brown brothers, and a daughter left behind
stories.hook: William Brown Jr. married a Cowgill in 1715, lost her within about six years, died himself about 1727, and left a daughter who married at West Nottingham as an orphan.
body: William Brown Jr. was born on the 21st day of the 7th month 1689, the third child of the Nottingham pioneer William Brown and Ann Mercer. In 1715 he married Elizabeth Cowgill, born on the 24th of the 6th month 1694 at Middletown, Bucks County, to John Cowgill and Bridget Croasdale. Her father had come from Yorkshire in 1682; accounts differ on which ship carried the Settle families. He was a tanner who moved about 1713 or 1714 to the Delaware shore, where on 10 May 1718 he asked for another hundred acres, "having erected a tan-yard on a branch of Black Bird's Creek." The marriage was recorded in Duck Creek Monthly Meeting, on 1 December 1715 by the Quaker count, as that of Elizabeth Cowgill, "daughter of John Cowgill, of Duck Creek in New Castle," and William Brown, "son of William Brown, of Nottingham."

Cope's list gives the couple two children. John was born on the 27th of the 2nd month 1717 and died on the 12th of the 7th month 1723, aged six. Elizabeth was born in the twelfth month of 1718, which in modern dating is early 1719. Her mother died within about three years of that birth, before March 1721/2, when William married Margaret Davis. That marriage produced William (1722) and Jacob (1724), and William Jr. himself died about 1727. His widow married William Kirk on the 6th of the 3rd month 1730. Her stepdaughter Elizabeth was eight or nine when her father died. In 1739 the Nottingham book called her "dt William & Elizabeth (Cowgill), both dec."

The Cowgill sisters had already made two marriages with the Browns. Elizabeth's sister Ellin, born on the 14th of the 10th month 1700, married William's brother Thomas Brown in 1718/9; Thomas died on 19 February 1746/7, and Ellin married again on 13 November 1768, to Lewis Clothier of Kent County, Maryland, and lived to 5 January 1772, aged 71. Two immigrant families, one from Yorkshire and one from Northamptonshire and Hampshire, had become a single network of cousins at Nottingham.

The child they left carried the line. Elizabeth Brown married Edward Norton at West Nottingham on 16 October 1739, her uncle Richard Brown having married Edward's sister Mary six years before, and their daughter Margaret married Joseph Chamness at Cane Creek in 1763. Through Elizabeth Brown, the Cowgill and Brown families became part of the Norton and Chamness lines.

stories.title: John Satterfield's will, with thirteen children in a single line
stories.hook: Born in Orange County, North Carolina, and dead in Warren County, Kentucky, at about eighty-one.
body: John Satterfield was born about 1766 in Orange County, North Carolina, a county formed in 1752 and since divided so that his birthplace lies in Person County. He lived in South Carolina and later settled in Warren County, Kentucky, where he made a will recorded in Will Book D at page 262 and proved on 10 November 1847. It lists thirteen children: Uriah, Ephraim, Rebecca, Mary, Jeremiah, Phoebe, Nancy, Moses, Sarah, Jesse, Leah, Reuben and John.

His wife Mary, born about 1768, is named in the will. Her maiden name is not settled: Find a Grave gives Jones, and a 1786 marriage record from Surry County, North Carolina, gives Haga. John's own father is disputed and is not shown here. Ephraim's place in the list is the link to this family. Ephraim's son Henry died on 24 December 1861, and the Kentucky register names Henry's father as Ephraim, which matches the Ephraim of the will (probable).
The sources differ on where Ephraim was born: WikiTree has South Carolina in 1787, where John had lived, while the 1885 sketch by his grandson calls him a Virginian.

His will was proved there on 10 November 1847. His wife Mary, born about 1768, is named in it, and their thirteen children included Ephraim.

stories.title: Ruth Knowles Satterfield, who died in Missouri at eighty-one
stories.hook: Born in Virginia, married in Warren County in 1809, widowed by 1850, and buried a long way from either.
body: Ruth Knowles was born about 1783 in Virginia, the daughter of Joshua Knowles, whose 1824 will names "Ruth Saterfield" among his five daughters. On 12 November 1809 she married Ephraim Satterfield in Warren County, Kentucky. Her son Henry was born about 1811 and his death register entry of 24 December 1861 names his parents as Ephraim and "Rutha" Satterfield.

By 1850 she was a widow in Allen County, living with her daughter Elizabeth. In 1860 the census found "Rutha Satterfield," about 77, in the household of Elizabeth and her husband Jesse Agee in Gasconade County, Missouri. She died there in 1864, having outlived her husband by about fourteen years and her son Henry by three.
Her reason for going to Missouri is not stated in any source. The identification of Ruth with our Ephraim's wife rests on Henry's death register and her father's will (probable).

stories.title: Joshua Knowles's will: a wife named Jemima and five daughters
stories.hook: A Warren County man, counted between 80 and 90 in 1830, who wrote his will in 1824 and lived about eight more years.
body: Joshua Knowles was born about 1747, and the 1830 census counted him in Warren County, Kentucky, between 80 and 90. He wrote his will on 11 November 1824, and it was proved in October 1832. It names his wife Jemima, his son Matthew as executor, his son John of Franklin County, Virginia, and five daughters: Sarah Hays, Polly Stephens, Leaner Jones, Ruth Saterfield and Elizabeth Bailey. Ruth was born in Virginia.

Ruth is the daughter that matters here. She had married Ephraim Satterfield in Warren County on 12 November 1809, and her father's will, written fifteen years later, calls her "Ruth Saterfield" in the clerk's spelling. The will does not say whether Jemima was Ruth's mother or a later wife.
His burial place is Knowles Cemetery at Motley in Warren County (Find a Grave). The will is cited from WikiTree and has not been read in the original (probable).

stories.title: Thomas Mercer of Andover, who crossed with his daughter Ann
stories.hook: A Hampshire Quaker widower brought his teenage daughter to Pennsylvania in 1682-83; she married at seventeen, and he died there in 1694.
body: Thomas Mercer and his wife Ann lived at Ringwood in Hampshire when their daughter Ann was born. The original Quaker register names both parents and dates the birth to the twenty-fourth day of the twelfth month 1666. In the Friends’ calendar then in use, this means 24 February 1666/7, or 1667 in modern year numbering. The entry gives the mother’s first name but no maiden surname. Later family accounts place Thomas at Andover before crossing to Pennsylvania with his daughter about 1682–83; identification with the Ringwood family remains probable.

He took up land in Aston Township, Chester County, and his daughter was married there in 1684 to William Brown, born in Northamptonshire, who had landed a year or two earlier. Ann was seventeen. Her first child, born in February 1685/6, was named Mercer for her family. Thomas Mercer lived long enough to see five grandchildren born, and died on 22 November 1694. A 1709 Quaker list of public Friends who died in Pennsylvania names him and "Ann Browne daughtr of said Thoms Mercer," who died in 1696.

Thomas Mercer's own parents are unknown. Through Ann his line runs to her son William Brown Jr., his daughter Elizabeth Brown, her daughter Margaret Norton and her daughter Martha Chamness, who married Robert Moffitt.

The two Anns belong to different generations: Ann, wife of Thomas, was the mother; Ann Mercer, who married William Brown, was the daughter. The elder Ann’s maiden surname and life dates remain unknown. Keeping those identities separate preserves the maternal link without supplying a name the birth entry does not give.

The 1709 catalog gives the immigrant father and daughter their own entries: Thomas Mercer of Andover, who arrived about 1682 or 1683 and died in 1694, and Anne Browne, his daughter, who came with him and was buried in 1696. It also remembers Anne’s public testimony after her arrival. The list names Andover’s county as Wiltshire, a discrepancy retained in the source citation; it supplies no further parents for Thomas or maiden surname for his wife.

stories.title: Mary Dockery and the Newton household
stories.hook: An 1867 marriage and an 1880 census offer a possible name for Lizzie Newton’s mother.
body: A St. Clair County, Alabama, marriage register records a license issued on 11 February 1867 for Bailus Newton and Mary Ann Dockery. The marriage return in a second entry places the ceremony at a Gibson residence; the day in the return is not clear enough to resolve the differing index dates.

In 1880 Balus Newton and his wife Mary lived in Etowah County with children including Elizabeth, seven. The original census image gives the surname Newton, though the index reads Keaton. Balus’s name, the county and Elizabeth’s age fit the father and daughter named as Balas and Lizzie in Lizzie’s 1889 marriage consent.

Mary’s work was entered as keeping house in a household of nine. The eldest boy, twelve, was already listed as a farm hand; the youngest child was an infant of eight months. Elizabeth stood between older children Ann and Lindsey and younger children Hezekiah, Amanda and the baby.

The 1880 census identifies Mary as Balus’s wife; it does not expressly identify her as Elizabeth’s mother. The earlier marriage to Mary Ann Dockery and the household make her a probable mother, but a record directly naming Lizzie’s mother is still needed. A death index for Oda Verbena Newton names parents Balous Newton and Mary Marzee Dockery; a similarly named young daughter appears in the 1880 home.

stories.title: A family name on the Armstrong school list
stories.hook: A school list preserves William Harrison Pisachubbe's name and points to a Choctaw education system built and funded by the Nation.
body: On 22 August 1899, a list of Armstrong Academy students was submitted to the Dawes Commission. It included Harrison Pisachubbe. Twelve years later, a federal official identified him as William H. Pisachubbe, son of Eunice and brother of Robert, the family's direct ancestor. The school list gave him a second enrollment number under his middle name; the 1911 letter and later roll notation document the correction. The letter does not describe his lessons or tell us how long he attended.

Armstrong Academy had opened in 1845 as part of the Choctaw Nation's school system. The Choctaw Council funded schools, often contracting with religious mission boards to operate them. The Civil War interrupted instruction, and the academy building later served as a Choctaw government meeting place before the Nation's capital moved to Tuskahoma.

In 1883 the Choctaw General Council passed an act establishing a school for orphan boys at Armstrong and appropriated money for its reopening. A separate act set a planned enrollment of fifty boys there and fifty girls at the Choctaw orphan school. The acts show the Nation making educational policy; a place on a later student list does not by itself explain a child's family circumstances or whether a parent was living.

The Oklahoma Historical Society dates the reopened orphan boys' academy to 1884. In 1898 the federal Curtis Act placed Choctaw Nation schools under United States government control. William's 1899 listing therefore belongs to a period when control over an institution begun by the Choctaw Nation was being transferred to the federal government. His own experience at the school remains to be researched.

stories.title: Clinton Sandridge: an Arkansas farmer in Broken Bow
stories.hook: A December 1961 newspaper notice follows Clinton’s move to McCurtain County and connects the family across Oklahoma, Texas and California.
body: Clinton Lamar Sandridge moved from Arkansas to McCurtain County in 1919. He farmed, belonged to the Assembly of God church and made his home in Broken Bow. His death notice appeared in the McCurtain Gazette on 20 December 1961, reporting that he had died at home early that morning.

The notice names Lemuel Sandridge of Broken Bow as a son, alongside another son, Jack, in Lake Jackson, Texas. Two daughters were in California and Houston. Clinton’s surviving brothers, Lon in Little Rock and L. P. in California, suggest routes for following the earlier Arkansas family, but the notice does not name Clinton’s parents.

His birth remains unsettled. The newspaper gives 25 September 1892, whereas the 1930 census records an age of 43, implying a birth around 1886–1887. The notice also leaves his widow unnamed. Maggie appears with Clinton and Lemuel in the census; her maiden name is still unverified.

The gravestone at Broken Bow Cemetery settles part of the date question. A double marker reads “Clinton L., Sept. 24, 1882 – Dec. 20, 1961” and “Maggie A., May 2, 1891 – July 15, 1982.” Carved between the two names is “Married June 19, 1910.” The 1961 newspaper printed 1892 for his birth year, and the stone has 1882. Maggie outlived Clinton by more than twenty years.

The newspaper gave his birthplace as “Burn, Arkansas.” That is probably Beirne, a small community in southern Clark County. A Find a Grave memorial records a Mary E. “Molly” Cole Sandridge (born 17 May 1861, died 1897) in an unmarked grave at Browns Cemetery near Beirne. It names her husband as William D. Sandridge, married 8 October 1877, and their sons Clinton (1882), Lon P. (1889), Joseph Burton (1892) and Lawrence Lafayette (1897). The 1961 notice independently names surviving brothers Lon, of Little Rock, and L. P., in California. Together these make William D. and Molly Cole Sandridge strong candidates for Clinton’s parents, but no original record yet names them as his parents. That link is a lead.

Clinton’s 1910 marriage to Maggie was his second. Memorials at Midway Cemetery near Prescott, in Nevada County, Arkansas, record his first wife, Esther Margaret Bolls Sandridge, as having died in 1909 at about 26. She left three children: Clinton Everett, called Chat, born in 1902; Nobie Jewel, born in 1904; and Mildred Marie, born in 1908. In June of the following year Clinton married Maggie. Lemuel, their only child together, was born on 4 December 1911. His memorial gives his birthplace as Prescott.

Chat did not live long. His government headstone at Midway Cemetery reads “Everett Chat Sandridge, Arkansas, Pvt. 1 Cl., U.S. Marine Corps,” and gives a death date of 18 April 1932. His memorial records the death in Kerr County, Texas, three days before his thirtieth birthday. The cause and circumstances have not yet been found.

A memorial for Maggie calls her Margaret Ann “Maggie” Cash, born at Prescott, a daughter of James L. Cash (1863–1946) and Maxie Ann McClure Cash (1865–1941), both buried at Midway. The 1930 census, however, gives her birthplace as Texas. Until a marriage record or Social Security application confirms the Cash name, it remains a lead.
Lemuel Lamar Sandridge died on 13 March 1979. His memorial records the death in Dallas. He is buried at Hochatown Cemetery beside Audrey, under a stone that names them “Mother” and “Father.”

stories.title: Barbara Phillips Livesay and the Pearland family
stories.hook: A local historical society remembered Barbara and Lester’s daughter, preserving a link between the Pearland and Carthage generations.
body: Barbara Phillips and Lester Woodrow Livesay Jr. belonged to a family with ties to Houston, Pearland and Carthage. A Texas birth index names Barbara Phillips and Lester as Wayne Woodrow Livesay’s parents. Lester’s later obituary identifies Barbara by her maiden name and records that she died before him.

In July 2014, the Pearland Historical Society remembered their daughter Carylon Livesay Bardwell. Its newsletter reports her death in Carthage on 18 June and names her parents as Lester and Barbara Livesay. It also identifies Wayne Livesay as her brother and Jimmy Bardwell as her husband, both of whom had already died.
The notice adds a daughter to the family preserved in the birth index and Lester’s obituary. It does not identify Barbara’s own parents; her 1995 obituary, below, does.

Barbara’s obituary in The Panola Watchman, 6 September 1995, fills in her own life. She was born on 7 April 1918 in Nacogdoches, “the daughter of Carl C. and Beulah Turner Phillips.” On 21 April 1935, aged seventeen, she married Lester W. Livesay. The date also appears in a heart carved between their names on their shared stone at Restland Memorial Park, Carthage. She had lived in Panola County for three years, “moving here from Mt. Enterprise,” and died on 2 September 1995 at Panola Nursing Home, aged 77.

The obituary lists her siblings: three brothers who died before her, R. Jay, Randall and Samuel Phillips; a sister, Glendale Baits, who also predeceased her; and a brother and a sister who survived her. The same brother and sister appear again among the survivors in Lester’s own 2001 obituary. Her parents, Carl and Beulah, have their own story, with their dates, their Houston years and Beulah’s Turner family.

stories.title: Julia’s changing names: the family behind Audrey
stories.hook: A marriage in Idabel and a daughter in Broken Bow help connect Julia Myers, Nelson, Stevens and Ratcliff.
body: Julia’s family appears under several surnames in the records of McCurtain County and neighboring Arkansas. A county marriage record names Julia Myers, forty, and William A. Nelson, forty-six, marrying at Idabel on 1 July 1916. The original page has been examined. Their names, place and ages make this a probable match for the parents in Audrey Nelson’s later household; the marriage does not establish that Myers was Julia’s birth surname.

In 1920, William and Julia Nelson were living in McCurtain County with two-year-old Audrey. William was recorded as forty-nine, born in Arkansas, and Julia as forty-seven, born in Texas. The household also included Homer, Willie and Edith Nelson, and Hattie Myres, indexed as William’s stepdaughter. Those entries suggest a family formed through more than one parental relationship. They do not identify Hattie’s father or prove who Julia’s own parents were.

Ten years later, the Broken Bow census places twelve-year-old Audry Nelson with a divorced, Texas-born parent indexed as Julian A. Stevens, fifty-four. The daughter’s name, age and birthplace make this a strong probable continuation of Audrey and Julia’s family. An original notice in The Broken Bow News on 10 October 1929, for Audrey’s older sister Hattie Myers Kilgore, names Hattie’s mother as Mrs. Stevens and her sister as Miss Audrey Nelson, providing another connection between the names.

An original Arkansas marriage record names Julia Ann Stevens, seventy-six, marrying Charles M. Ratcliff on 19 August 1950. An original notice in the McCurtain Gazette on 29 September 1956 names Mrs. Lemuel Sandridge and Homer E. Nelson among Mrs. C. M. Ratcliff’s children. Together these records strongly support Julia’s later identity. The notice reports a Bowie County, Texas, birth on 17 November 1873 and death on 26 September 1956, but its stated age of seventy-two conflicts with that birth date. The notice places her move to Broken Bow in 1921, after the 1920 census recorded the family elsewhere in McCurtain County.

Julia’s exact birth date and the circumstances of each surname change still need checking. The 1916, 1920 and 1930 ages imply different birth years. Robbins is the maiden name supplied by Audrey’s reproduced obituary, rather than a name established by these marriage records. Her parents remain unassigned while the conflicting records are investigated.

Part of the answer to why Julia’s name changed again lies in Redland Cemetery. A flat granite marker there reads “William A. Nelson, May 12, 1870 – Aug. 10, 1922.” The name and birth year match the William A. Nelson, 46, who married Julia Myers at Idabel in 1916, and the 49-year-old Arkansas-born William in the 1920 household. Audrey was five when he died. By 1930 Julia had married again, and the census lists her as divorced under the name Stevens.

The memorial for William A. Nelson lists two older children who would be Audrey’s half-siblings: Rosa Isabel Nelson Flowers (1894–1985) and Homer E. Nelson (1902–1999). Homer is named among Julia’s children in her 1956 notice. The same memorial names William’s parents as Aaron Burr Nelson (1815–1888) and Mary Elizabeth Anthony Nelson (1836–1916). No original record checked so far confirms that parentage, so Aaron and Mary Elizabeth remain leads.

stories.title: Hattie Myers Kilgore: Audrey’s older sister
stories.hook: A young woman’s 1929 death notice helps connect Audrey Nelson with her mother’s Stevens surname.
body: Hattie Myres was eleven in the 1920 Nelson household in Frisco Township, McCurtain County. The original census calls her William Nelson’s stepdaughter. Two-year-old Audrey Nelson was in the same household with William’s wife Julia. Hattie’s different surname preserves a clue to the family before Julia’s Nelson marriage.

Nine years later, a notice in The Broken Bow News on 10 October 1929 identifies Mrs. Gordon Kilgore as the former Hattie Myers. It names her mother as Mrs. Stevens of Broken Bow and Miss Audrey Nelson among her sisters. This recurring mother-and-sister combination strongly supports identifying her with the girl in the Nelson household. The notice does not say whether the sisters shared both parents, and Hattie’s father remains unknown.

The original Texas death certificate records Mrs. Gordon Kilgor’s death at the Sanitarium of Paris on 8 October 1929, at age twenty. Her usual residence was Idabel, Oklahoma, and the certificate records burial there. It gives 1909 as her birth year, with month and day unobtainable, and supplies no parental names. The memorial’s birth date, 23 September 1906, conflicts with both that certificate and her census age. The earlier date has therefore not been adopted as settled fact.

stories.title: A Camden visit brought three generations together
stories.hook: In 1940, Nona Alford’s visit to Broken Bow ended with her sister Audrey, Audrey’s young son Larry and the sisters’ mother Julia joining her in Arkansas.
body: Nona Alford and her married daughter traveled from Camden, Arkansas, to visit friends and relatives in Broken Bow. When they went home, the visiting party grew: Nona’s sister Mrs. L. L. Sandridge, her son Larry, and their mother Julia Stevens accompanied them for several days. The Broken Bow News recorded the trip on 7 March 1940. Audrey Sandridge and young Larry belonged to this same family, connecting the brief newspaper item with the direct maternal line.

Nona already had a family of her own. An original Bowie County, Texas, register records Wesley E. Alford and Nona Myers marrying on 20 June 1919. The 1930 Broken Bow census lists their daughters Mable and Gerldene, names later recorded as Mabel and Geraldine. Both daughters’ Social Security entries name Nona A. Myers and Wesley E. Alford as their parents, preserving the Myers surname behind Nona’s married name.

The newspaper calls Nona’s daughter Mrs. Edwin Chidester. A 1940 Camden census names Mabel as Edwin Chidester’s wife, and her Social Security record uses the name Mabel Alford Chidester, making this a strong identification. Mabel later appears under Crowl; an obituary index for Geraldine Forkner names Mabel Crowl as her sister. These separate records help keep the two daughters connected as their surnames changed.

Julia was the older generation traveling with her daughters and grandchildren between Broken Bow and Camden. The visit preserves her Stevens surname alongside Audrey’s Sandridge and Nona’s Alford names. It also gives Nona a clear place beside Audrey in the maternal family.

stories.title: Sadah’s Indiana beginnings
stories.hook: An Indiana census records Sadie’s birth in August 1893, matching the month and year later reported for Sadah; her parents’ identities still need a connecting record.
body: The 1920 census places Sadah and Lester W. Livesay in Harris County with their children. Their son Lester’s 2001 obituary names his mother as Sadah McCormick. The original Harris County marriage register records Lester W. Livesay and Miss Sadah H. McCormick: their license was issued on 10 October 1911, and the officer’s return records the marriage on the same day. The entry is on page 402 of volume 4; a handwritten number 22072 corrects the printed 21072.

An original Texas certificate records Sadah Livesay Vaughan’s death in Houston on 29 April 1978, aged 84. It gives her birth as 13 August 1893 in Anderson, Indiana, and names the informant as Alice Livesay Kauitzsch. The combination of the unusual given name, Livesay surname and informant supports the probable identification with Lester’s wife. Alice’s Social Security NUMIDENT index names her parents as Lester W. Livesay and Sarah H. McCormack and includes the Kauitzsch surname; Sarah and Sadah remain recorded variants rather than a silently corrected name.

The certificate names Sadah’s father as J. T. McCormack and gives her mother’s maiden name as Unknown. It does not expand his initials. The dates now shown in the tree come from this certificate, whose birth information was reported many decades after the event.

An earlier original census offers a possible family connection. On 18 April 1910, in Brazoria County’s Justice Precinct 5, Jay T. McCormick, 41, and his wife Frances, 40, were listed with a daughter Sadie, 17, born in Indiana. The father’s initials, daughter’s age and birthplace fit the later certificate, but no examined record yet establishes that Sadie and Sadah are the same person. Jay T. and Frances remain unattached research leads. The census supplies no maiden surname for Frances.

The original 1900 census brings that possible household closer to Sadah’s Indiana beginnings. On 5 June, in Stony Creek Township, Madison County, James McCormack and his wife Frances were listed with Cleveland, Hazel, Sadie, Pernell and Dewey. Sadie was recorded as their six-year-old daughter, born in Indiana in August 1893. That month, year and state agree with the later death certificate. Several names and the children’s sequence also match the 1910 Texas household, supporting continuity between those two census families.

The comparison leaves material conflicts. The 1900 head is James, born June 1863, rather than the Jay T., 41, recorded in 1910; Frances was born January 1862 and aged 38 in 1900, yet was listed as 40 ten years later. The census daughter has not yet been directly connected to Lester Livesay’s wife. James, Jay T. and J. T. are therefore not treated as an established full-name sequence, and Frances has no established birth surname. The original 1911 marriage entry has a margin note, “Consent of Mother on file,” but it does not identify the mother. The affidavit beneath the entry is blank and crossed out. The separately filed consent itself has not been examined; the margin note does not establish Frances as Sadah’s mother.

stories.title: Wm. P. Walker of the Beaucoup settlement
stories.hook: A government marker calls him a private of the Illinois militia; a shared family stone a few feet away records the wife who outlived him by four years.
body: Two stones stand for William P. Walker in Beaucoup Cemetery, Washington County, Illinois. A bronze veteran’s plaque reads “W P Walker, Pvt, Ill Militia, Civil War, 1831–1919.” A granite family stone carries “Wm. P. Walker 1831–1919” and, below it, “Abigail, his wife, 1833–1923.” The Find a Grave memorial gives his full dates as 15 March 1831 to 19 May 1919, both at Beaucoup, and his middle name as Pattison. Those details come from the memorial rather than a quoted record.

Beaucoup was one of the oldest settlements in the county. The 1879 county history says that pioneers from Tennessee settled “where the old Mud Prairie road enters the Beaucoup timber” from 1818, followed by the Whittenbergs, Whites, “Livisays” and others, among them “Rev. James Walker,” which made it “numerically the strongest in the county.” The same book lists James Walker among the pioneer Methodist ministers who “moulded” the area’s religious life and among the teachers who kept school there before 1824.

The Find a Grave memorial names Rev. James Walker (1800–1857) and Etheldra Jane Ballard as William’s parents. No record examined for this story states that relationship, so it was left a lead here; the 1850 census household told in a later story makes them his probable parents, and the tree now links them. One detail fits it: William and Abigail named their eldest daughter Mary Ellen Etheldra.

The 1879 history’s roster of Washington County soldiers lists a William P. Walker as a private in Company C of the 60th Illinois Infantry, the same company as Jackson L. and John W. Livesay. The state adjutant general’s roster for the company also includes a “Walker, William P.” among men from the Richview and Mount Vernon area. The 60th was raised in southern Illinois early in 1862. The veteran’s plaque, however, says “Ill Militia,” and the scanned roster columns are too garbled to give his enlistment date. Which service the plaque refers to, and whether the soldier is this William, were left open here; the later story “Private Walker of Company C” takes up both questions.

The Walker and Livesay families lived side by side at Beaucoup. David P. Livesay, the leading candidate for Floyd Livesay’s father, is buried in the same cemetery, and Alice Walker married Floyd about 1880. Alice’s own Pearland headstone reads “Jan. 11, 1859,” the same year implied by the 1860 census. Her 1922 death certificate gives 1860, and the age on it implies 1855. Two sources now support 1859.

The census households of 1860 and 1870 put Alice with Wm P. and Abigail Walker, and the family stone confirms that Abigail was William’s wife. Alice’s death certificate, however, gives her mother as Addie Bruce. “Addie” was a common nickname for Abigail, but the surname does not match the Schanck of an 1852 marriage-index entry. That entry, for a William F. Walker and Abigail Schanck in Washington County, is described on Alice’s page. Abigail is therefore not yet linked as Alice’s mother.

stories.title: Nine days: Tabitha Livesay’s stone
stories.hook: Floyd Livesay’s birth date is carved in Pearland; nine days later, by an Illinois stone, a young wife named Tabitha died.
body: In Gilead Cemetery, Grand Prairie Township, Jefferson County, Illinois, a lichen-covered marble stone under a carved weeping willow reads: “In memory of Tabitha J., wife of David P. Livesay, died Feb. 14, 1856, aged 27 yrs. 2 ms. 4 ds.” Floyd H. Livesay’s headstone at Pearland, Texas, gives his birth as “Feb. 5, 1856”, matching the February 1856 in the 1900 census. His Texas death certificate says 1857. If the stone is right, he was born nine days before Tabitha died.

The other records point the same way. In 1860 the census taker found four-year-old Floyd H. Livesay in Washington County in the household of Lydia Livesay, with David Livesay, 28. In 1870 Floyd H., 14, was living in David’s own household. A court paper filed in Washington County in 1856 names David P. Livesay as an heir at law of Robert Livesay, who had died in 1855. A family compiler’s sketch identifies Robert’s widow as Lydia (Fitzgerald) Livesay and gives David Pinkney’s birth as 1 January 1831, just after the family reached Illinois. On that reading, the motherless boy of 1860 was living with his widowed grandmother and his father.

The pieces fit together, but none of them names Floyd’s parents. The censuses do not state relationships, Tabitha’s stone does not mention a child, and the informant on Floyd’s 1932 death certificate wrote that both parents were unknown. David P. Livesay and Tabitha J. are therefore shown here as a strong lead, not as linked parents. A record that names them, such as Floyd’s 1880 Illinois marriage return, an 1880 census entry or David’s probate file, would settle the question.

The Livesays were among the oldest families in the county. The 1879 county history lists “Livisays” among the first families at Beaucoup, records that William B. Livesay laid out Old Richview in 1839, and lists Livesays among the founders of the Richview Methodist society. The same compiler’s sketch says Robert and Lydia came from Maury County, Tennessee, about 1830, in a move involving grandparents, parents, aunts and cousins from a family that had earlier come from Franklin County, Virginia. That account is secondary. Its claims beyond the 1856 court paper it transcribes have not been checked.

David P. Livesay remarried. His stone at Beaucoup Cemetery reads “D. P. Livesay 1831–1904” and “Elizabeth, his wife, 1846–1933.” Find a Grave lists Floyd’s younger half-siblings from that marriage, including Charles, Mary Ines, Clara and Ella. Floyd married Alice Walker, a Beaucoup neighbor, about 1880 and took his family to Texas in the mid-1890s.

stories.title: Lester W. Livesay Sr.: married at sixteen, buried at ninety-four
stories.hook: Lester Livesay married Sadah McCormick a month before his seventeenth birthday; each later married again, and they were buried apart, Sadah under her second husband’s name.
body: On 10 October 1911, a Harris County clerk issued a marriage license to Lester W. Livesay and Miss Sadah H. McCormick, and the marriage took place the same day. The register’s margin notes “Consent of Mother on file.” Lester’s headstone gives his birth as 8 November 1894, so he was a month short of seventeen. Sadah’s death certificate and headstone give 13 August 1893, making her eighteen. The note does not say whose mother gave consent, and, given Lester’s age, it may well have been his.

Lester had come to Texas as a small child. He appears as a son in Floyd and Alice Livesay’s Brazoria County household in 1900, while Pearland was still a young railroad town. The Handbook of Texas says the town got its name in 1893 “because of the abundance of pear trees.” It had 75 residents in 1898, and the 1900 hurricane “destroyed fruit trees and slowed growth for a period of time.” By 1920 Lester, 24, and Sadah, 26, were in Houston with their daughter Alice, 5, and son Lester Jr., 3.

The marriage did not last. Sadah is buried in South Park Cemetery, Pearland, under a flat stone reading “In loving memory, Sadah M. Vaughan, Aug. 13, 1893 – Apr. 29, 1978.” Her second husband, Jesse Pickard Vaughan, lies in the same cemetery. His government marker reads “Louisiana, Sgt, 155 Ambulance Co., World War I,” and Find a Grave records his death at Jacinto City in 1954. The date of the Livesays’ divorce and of Sadah’s remarriage has not been found.

Lester married Esther Voris, a native of Alvin born in 1910. Find a Grave dates the marriage to 1942. They share a double stone in the Confederate Cemetery at Alvin, Brazoria County, headed LIVESAY. His side reads “Lester W., Nov. 8, 1894 – Aug. 8, 1989.” A transcribed World War I draft list gives his birth year as 1895 instead, a conflict the story of the draft lists leaves unresolved. He outlived his father by 57 years and his son’s mother by eleven.

His daughter Alice A. “Nonnie” Livesay Kauitzsch (1914–1988) was the informant on her mother’s death certificate. His son Lester Jr. became a Southern Pacific engineer and cattleman. Lester Jr.’s 2001 obituary still named his parents as “Lester W. Sr. and Sadah McCormick Livesay.”

stories.title: Violet Box Whitfield and the Oak Hill road
stories.hook: In July 1962 a pickup loaded with watermelons left 400 feet of tire marks west of Golden, and Alfreda lost her mother.
body: At two o’clock on a Monday afternoon in late July 1962, Violet Whitfield was driving west on the Oak Hill road, two and a half miles outside Golden, in a 1960 GMC pickup loaded with watermelons. The McCurtain Gazette reported that she lost control coming down a hill. The truck left about 400 feet of tire marks, ran off the right side of the road and overturned once before landing back on its wheels. Violet was thrown out and landed about ten feet beyond it. Two Broken Bow boys riding bicycles watched it happen; they told the trooper they saw the pickup start weaving from side to side as it came down the hill.

Two doctors pronounced her dead at the scene of head and neck injuries. She was 41, and the paper counted her as the county’s second traffic death of the year. Her husband, Louis O. Whitfield, 46 by the paper’s count (45 by the birth date on his gravestone), had been riding as a passenger. He came out of it with a deep cut on his right cheek, bruises and scrapes. The paper put the damage to the truck at $500, and noted that the Whitfields had been in the grocery business at Golden for several years.

The obituary gives her birth as 21 September 1920 at Wheelock and says she had lived in McCurtain County all her life. The gravestone she shares with Lewis at Wheelock Cemetery reads 22 September 1920 to 30 July 1962. Among her survivors it names her married daughter Mrs. Larry Sandridge of Broken Bow, which is Alfreda, then 23. It also names her father T. S. Box of Millerton, two sisters and two brothers, two of whom lived at Baytown, Texas. That line ties the T. S. Box of earlier family accounts directly to Violet.

Her parents' own notices fill in the Box family. Annie F. Box died at Hugo Memorial Hospital on 28 December 1959. Her McCurtain Gazette notice says she was born 2 June 1886 at Collins, Texas, and came to McCurtain County in 1906 from Mount Pleasant. It lists her daughter Mrs. Louis Whitfield of Golden and her Logan brothers and sisters. Tyro Stephen Box died at the same hospital on 5 October 1967. His notice gives his birth as 22 May 1888 at Pittsburg, Texas, and says he had lived in the county for sixty years. He was a retired engineer and a member of the Valliant Masonic Lodge. Pittsburg is in Camp County, next to Titus County, where Mount Pleasant stands; the young couple came north from the same corner of northeast Texas.

Wheelock, where Violet was born and buried, is one of the oldest settled places in the Choctaw Nation. The Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture dates it to 1832, when the missionaries Alfred and Harriet Wright followed the removed Choctaw from Mississippi and set up a mission station, school and church northeast of present-day Millerton. Their congregation built a stone church in 1844–46. From 1884 to 1955 Wheelock Academy, beside the old mission, was a boarding school for American Indian girls, most of them Choctaw. Annie Box’s funeral was held in the Wheelock Presbyterian church. The Boxes themselves were Texas-born whites, and none of them appear on the Dawes rolls. The Choctaw ancestry in this branch came through Lewis’s mother, Ida May Merry, not through Violet.

Lewis Oliver Whitfield outlived his wife by 42 years. The bronze plaque at their grave identifies him as a private in the U.S. Army Air Forces in World War II and gives his dates as 24 August 1916 to 9 August 2004.

stories.title: Omagene Whitfield: a Golden boy on the Tablets of the Missing
stories.hook: Ida Merry Whitfield’s younger son is not buried in any grave. His name is carved on a wall above Omaha Beach.
body: Ida May Merry Whitfield’s 1993 obituary spends a single sentence on him: “Her younger son, Omagene Whitfield, was killed during World War II.” His sister Catherine’s obituary in 2007 lists him among her brothers who had died before her as Omagene Clinton Whitfield. The middle name was his father’s.

Omagene was born on 1 January 1922 at Golden, McCurtain County. His father, O. C. “Clint” Whitfield, died in March 1941, when Omagene was nineteen. Ida then went to work at the Golden post office. When Omagene entered the Army from Oklahoma, he became a Technician Fifth Grade in the 300th Engineer Combat Battalion. His service number was 38466149.

He died on 19 June 1944, thirteen days after D-Day. He has no grave. His name is on the Tablets of the Missing at the Normandy American Cemetery at Colleville-sur-Mer, the curved wall of the Garden of the Missing, on the bluff above Omaha Beach. The inscription for him reads: TEC 5, 300 ENGR COMBAT BN, OKLAHOMA.

At home the news came slowly and out of order. On 28 March 1945 the McCurtain Gazette ran a short item on its front page headed “County Man Listed As Dead, Relatives Are Not Notified.” Omagene's name had been in a War Department list released to newspapers the previous Saturday of men killed in action in Europe, but his mother, Mrs. Ida M. Whitfield of Golden, had received no such notice; the family knew only that he had been reported missing in France the previous June. Three weeks later, on 18 April, the paper printed his photograph in uniform and a fuller notice: he had been killed in action on 19 June 1944, according to a report his mother had received in March, and had been with the Army engineers since February 1942. It listed his survivors as his mother, his brother Louis O. Whitfield of Tulsa, his sisters Mrs. Elma Mae Henry and Miss Oudia Whitfield of Golden, his grandmothers Mrs. W. F. Whitfield of Golden and Mrs. Bessie Kernell of Glover, and an aunt, Mrs. J. B. Greenfield of Idabel. His mother had received his Purple Heart.

The date and unit point to a single event. On 19 June 1944 the tank landing ship LST-523 struck a mine off the Normandy beaches and sank. The Navy’s Dictionary of American Naval Fighting Ships records only that she was “sunk by an enemy mine” that day. Accounts of the 300th Engineers say the battalion was aboard, and one compiled account says the explosion split the ship in two, killing 94 men of the 300th and 41 of the crew. Several of the 300th’s dead from that day are listed as missing. Omagene’s own record has not yet been checked for a ship’s name, so his presence aboard LST-523 is probable rather than proven. A photograph of a model of LST-523 has been posted to his memorial page.
His older brother, Lewis Oliver Whitfield, Alfreda’s father, also served in the war, as a private in the U.S. Army Air Forces. Lewis came home to Golden and lived until 2004.

The War Department’s Honor List of Dead and Missing for Oklahoma, compiled to a cut-off date of 31 January 1946, lists him under McCurtain County as “Whitfield Omagene C, 38466149, TEC5, KIA.” Its foreword defines KIA as killed in action, and keeps a separate symbol, FOD, for men declared dead by a finding of death after being missing. So although his name is on the Tablets of the Missing, by early 1946 the Army counted him as killed in action. The list confirms his serial number and grade; it does not name his unit or ship.

stories.title: Betsy Tims, the Choctaw mother on Card 1437
stories.hook: Her son gave her name to the Dawes clerk in one line: "Betsy Tims," dead, of Towson County.
body: On 8 May 1899, at the Doaksville post office, the Dawes Commission made out Card 1437 for Edward W. Tims, 58. In the parents' columns of his line the clerk wrote his father as "Vincent B. Tims," dead, with "Non Citz" in the county column, and his mother as "Betsy Tims," dead, of Towson County. That line is the only record known that names the Choctaw wife of the Doaksville trader.

The card's blood column gives Edward as one-half Choctaw. Since his father is entered as a noncitizen, the Commission's fraction for Edward implies that it counted Betsy as a full-blood Choctaw; the card itself gives her no fraction, no age and no roll number. A history of Doaksville written from the Tims family's papers calls her Vincent's "full-blood Choctaw wife" and says the two stayed at Doaksville for the rest of their lives.

Three of her children are known from the family's records: Vinson W., born in 1838, Edward Ward, born in 1842 by family accounts (58 on his 1899 card), and a daughter, Phoebe, who died before the final rolls were made. Vinson's children were enrolled as Choctaws through him and through his wife Emeline Steadman, and his daughter Betsy, born in 1870, who married Joseph P. Thompson, carried her grandmother's name.

She married in the years when the Choctaw Nation was rewriting its marriage law. On 6 October 1836 the General Council abolished "the custom of not intermarrying with their own Iksa," the matrilineal clans, so that "all persons, without any distinction of Iksa, are left to make their own choice as to whom they shall marry." In October 1840 it ruled that no white man could marry in the Nation until he had been a citizen for two years, that he must take a license from a judge or the district clerk and be married by a minister, and that "no white man who shall marry a Choctaw woman, shall have the disposal of her property without her consent." A white man who left his wife "without just provocation" could be ordered to pay her damages and lose his citizenship. No marriage record for Betsy and Vincent has been found, so it is not known which of these rules applied to them.

Her husband's business ran through the removal years: Doak & Tims held the army contracts of 1838 and 1839 to feed arriving Chickasaw emigrants at thirteen cents a ration, and in January 1837 Vincent witnessed the Treaty of Doaksville. Family files give Betsy's birth as about 1800 in the old Choctaw Nation in Mississippi and her death as about 1860 at Doaksville. No record examined supports either date (lead), and no document cited here gives her Choctaw name or her parents.
