stories.title: Samuel Garrison's two discharges: Stono, 1779, and Frederick, 1782
stories.hook: A Mecklenburg elder who served two short terms in the North Carolina militia, then applied for a pension in Warren County, Kentucky, and died a few months after the certificate came.
body: Samuel Garrison was born on 24 August 1762, by his family's record on the Pennsylvania-Maryland line, though one account allows that it may have been Mecklenburg County, North Carolina. On 14 March 1786, in Mecklenburg County, he married Esther Alexander, a daughter of Hezekiah Alexander. Floyd C. Stuart, who compiled a large Garrison genealogy in 1979, worked from the family's record book and from five handwritten pages he obtained from the National Archives about Samuel's Revolutionary War pension, file S 31049. Those pages are the best account of what Samuel did as a teenager in the war.

He served two short terms as a private. His own declaration, made in Warren County, Kentucky, on 6 September 1832, says he served four months in Captain James Barr's company of Colonel Charles McDowell's regiment, General John Butler's brigade of North Carolina militia, and that “he was at the Battle of Stono,” the fight at Stono Ferry near Charleston on 20 June 1779, “in which Major Anderson was killed,” adding that Colonel Roberts of the artillery was killed too. (Stuart read the captain's name as Bass; the discharge is signed “Jas. Barr, Capt.”) The copied discharge certifies service “from the 20th of March till ye 20th of July” and is dated “2nd July 1779 Near Stono”; Samuel told the court the date should have read the 20th. Stono Ferry was a British victory: General Lincoln's attack on the British rear guard cost the Americans about 34 killed and more than a hundred wounded, and Colonel Owen Roberts of the South Carolina artillery was mortally wounded. The second discharge, signed by Lieutenant Conrad Doll at Frederick County, Maryland, on 14 January 1782, certifies five months in Captain Thomas Beatty's company of Select Militia, raised under a state act. Stuart wonders whether Samuel helped guard the British prisoners marched to Frederick after Yorktown, and repeats a claim that Samuel was at Yorktown. Samuel himself claimed nine months in all and said nothing of Yorktown.

Samuel applied for a pension in Warren County, Kentucky, where he gave his home as Hickory Grove and his age as 69. The certificate was issued on 6 November 1832 and counted four months in 1779 and five in 1781–82 on the strength of the two original discharges, at $30 a year from 4 March 1831. Samuel died on 27 March 1833, so he drew little from it. His death place is given both as Warren County and as Allen County, at a daughter's home near Scottsville; Allen County was later formed partly from Warren, so the two accounts may describe one place.

Between the war and the pension he was a church elder in Mecklenburg County (ordained 10 September 1793, by his record book) and the father of nine children. Their sixth child was born in Mecklenburg in September 1797 and the seventh at Bays Fork Creek in Warren County on 1 April 1800, so the move to Kentucky fell between those dates. Stuart adds that Samuel was Allen County's first member in the Kentucky legislature, in 1816; that was not checked here. One correspondent places his grave on his old home place south of Scottsville; another says he does not know where it is.

Two points stay open. First, Samuel's father: Stuart's 1979 text named John Garrison (born 1744), a son of a Baptist minister of Monmouth County, New Jersey. His 1981 corrections prefer a different John Garrison, said to be a son of David Garrison Sr., who came to Mecklenburg from Salem County, New Jersey. Stuart admits that positive proof of that John's relationship to David has not been found, and the link to Samuel is only "claimed." This site therefore stops at Samuel. Second, the earlier note on this site ("Samuel & Esther (Alexander) Garrison") took from WikiTree a private in the Continental Line and Esther's death in Coles County, Illinois. The pension papers as Stuart describes them show militia service, and the family record puts Esther's death in Allen County, Kentucky.

That this Samuel is the husband of Esther Alexander and the father of John Milton Garrison rests on Stuart's family record and a second compiled list (DAR Magazine, August 1952), not on a county record. Stuart's text is inconsistent in places: it calls the service both Continental and Colonial troops in different passages, though the discharges name the North Carolina militia, and it gives Esther's death year as 1827 once and 1829 elsewhere. Samuel's father is unresolved.

stories.title: Hezekiah Alexander's will names a daughter, Esther Garrison
stories.hook: A 1796 Mecklenburg will, abstracted in 1913, ties an Alexander daughter to a Garrison household and to a granddaughter named Caroline.
body: On 8 August 1796 Hezekiah Alexander of Mecklenburg County, North Carolina, made his will, and a codicil followed on 28 January 1797. The genealogical editor of the American Monthly Magazine abstracted all the early Alexander wills in the books at Charlotte and printed them in April 1913; this one is marked A20. The abstract names his wife Mary; sons William Semple, James R., Silas, Hezekiah, Amos, Joel and Ozwald; and two daughters, Kezia Alexander and "Esther Garrison," with "her husband" and "dau. Caroline Garrison and other ch. of Esther." William Semple and James R. were to serve as executors with their mother. The abstract does not name Esther's husband. A second abstract, in Walter O. Holliman Jr.'s 1997 genealogy of the Davidson family, cites Will Book A, p. 20, and likewise names Esther Garrison and her daughter Caroline; its own entry for Esther says only that she married "Unknown Garrison." So no printed abstract of the will names her husband. That name, Samuel Garrison, comes from the Garrison family record.

The Esther passage matters because it is a record made in Hezekiah's lifetime that ties an Alexander daughter to a Garrison household and to a child, Caroline, who matches the eldest child in Samuel and Esther Garrison's family record (born 9 January 1787). Floyd C. Stuart, who had a copy of the will, quotes the clause for Esther. It leaves a chest of drawers in trust for Caroline, and an enslaved woman named Jean with her children, whom his transcription lists as Siah, Frank and Nancy, for Esther's use for eighteen years, after which they were to be divided between Esther and her children, or, if she died first, among her children as her husband saw fit. His copy is partly garbled, so the names are as he read them. The same will gave four sons Hezekiah's tracts on the French Broad River, each to pay Esther 25 pounds as Stuart reads it. The codicil gave Charles Polk the property that Hezekiah's "late beloved dau. Mary" took with her when she married him.

Hezekiah himself is well documented. The Dictionary of North Carolina Biography gives his dates as 1728 to 16 July 1801 and names his parents as James Alexander, a Cecil County, Maryland, magistrate and Presbyterian elder, and Margaret McKnitt. He married Mary Sample on 12 June 1752, settled in Mecklenburg, and was appointed a county magistrate in 1768. He sat on the Committee of Safety, was one of thirteen members of the provincial council of 1776, and as a delegate to the Halifax congress that year was placed on the committees that drafted North Carolina's bill of rights and constitution. The entry counts seven sons and three daughters and notes that he enslaved people. Stuart reproduces a state Revolutionary Army Accounts entry of June 1776 in which Richard Caswell, treasurer of the Southern District, pays Hezekiah Alexander 1,200 pounds for supplies furnished to the militia, and says the family's stone house in Charlotte was built in 1774.

The sources disagree on small points. Stuart gives Hezekiah's birth as 13 January 1722 and his death as 10 January 1801, against 1728 and 16 July 1801 in the biography dictionary. For Mary Sample he gives death on 17 May 1806 at 71, while the earlier note on this site has 17 May 1805. Stuart names three daughters, Esther, Mary and Keziah, and repeats the family account that Mary was killed by a gun accident while her husband cleaned his rifle; the will says only "late beloved dau. Mary." The 1796 will is the one contemporary record here, and it proves only that Hezekiah had a daughter Esther Garrison with a daughter Caroline. Identifying her with Samuel Garrison's wife, and John Milton Garrison as her son, rests on the family record.

The will abstract is a 1913 editor's summary, not the will itself, and Stuart's quotation is partly garbled; all three agree that Esther Garrison and her daughter Caroline are named. The earlier notes on this site ("Hezekiah & Mary (Sample) Alexander" and "James & Margaret (McKnitt) Alexander") treat Esther's place in this family as a lead; the will and Stuart's copy of it support the daughter, while the tie to Samuel Garrison and John Milton Garrison stays probable.

stories.title: Nine children from a family record: the Garrisons of Bays Fork Creek
stories.hook: John Milton Garrison's brothers and sisters, from Mecklenburg County to Warren County, Kentucky, and on to Alabama.

subject.name: Children of Samuel and Esther (Alexander) Garrison

body: Samuel Garrison kept a record book of births, marriages and deaths, and the compiler Floyd C. Stuart held copies from it. His compilation, drawing on that book and on letters from descendants, lists nine children. The first six were born in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina: Caroline (9 January 1787), John Milton (4 October 1788), Hezekiah Alexander (February 1791), Mary (31 January 1793, who died on 26 October that year), Hannah (15 September 1794, born at her grandfather Hezekiah Alexander's home) and Samuel Young (September 1797). The last three were born at Bays Fork Creek in Warren County, Kentucky: Calvin Alexander (1 April 1800), Esther (22 February 1802) and Cynthia (19 April 1804). Caroline is the only one also named in a will: her grandfather's will of 1796 leaves a chest of drawers in trust for her.

The record follows several of them into adult life. Caroline married William Ray in 1814. On 10 June 1813 in Warren County, Hezekiah Alexander Garrison married Rebecca Lyle, a native of Loudoun County, Virginia. Nine of their children were born in Kentucky before the family moved to Morgan County, Alabama, where he died on 15 August 1846; she died near Moulton on 5 August 1873. Samuel Young Garrison married Eliza Pogue on 23 June 1829 and, in a second marriage, Chalia S. (Mitchell) Jones on 10 December 1840. Calvin married Mariah Neal and later Nancy Margaret Hawkins. Esther married Samuel Alfred Stubbins on 4 August 1825 and died on 13 December 1831, ten days after the infant son she had borne that November. Cynthia married John C. McPheeters on 22 June 1825.

John Milton Garrison was the first son, and Stuart's informants place him on Trammell Fork Creek in Allen County. They also speak of his burial alone in a field by an old cemetery there, which may not agree with the flat marker at Mount Pleasant cemetery described in his own story on this site, so the grave is unsettled. Stuart's 1981 corrections change an earlier date of 1814 for his marriage to Patsey Cannon to 1808 or 1809, in line with the 6 December 1809 Wilson County record cited on this site, and, from a descendant's letter, date the legislature's divorce to 29 February 1848 (the approval date printed with the act) and his marriage to Sarah Stamps to 30 March 1848. The same pages show how unsettled his own children are. One descendant counted ten children, five by Sarah Stamps, and named Nancy, Sidney, John, Charles and William Thurston as hers; another says all of them were born before the divorce; a third list gives Patsey children called John Jr., Samuel Jr., Calvin, Abram and Mary C. Stuart says he can neither prove nor disprove any of it.

Only that last list has a Mary, and Stuart gives no sign she is our Mary Cannon Garrison, born 17 October 1811; the list is unsourced and reached him through a chain of correspondents. The record that names John Milton as her father is the 1885 county-history sketch of her son James. A DAR Magazine lineage of August 1952 gives a second compiled list of Esther Alexander Garrison's children: Caroline, Milton, Hezekiah, Hannah, Esther, John and Samuel. It matches the family record for six of the nine names, omits Calvin, Mary and Cynthia, and adds a John who is not in the family record. The two compilations may share a source, so they count as one line of evidence, not two.

The nine children, their dates and spouses come from a family record book as copied by a twentieth-century compiler and from correspondents' letters; neither the record book nor a county marriage or birth record for these children was seen. Dates disagree inside Stuart's own text: Esther's birth is 23 or 28 September 1762, Hezekiah Alexander Garrison's 8 or 18 February 1791 and Samuel Young's 21 or 25 September 1797. stories.title: Two uniforms, two pension claims: Calvin Moffitt and David Grimes
stories.hook: A Lawrence County man's three failed tries at a Union pension and a Confederate lieutenant's widow's claim appear together on one page of an Arkansas research guide.

subject.name: Calvin V. Moffitt and David H. Grimes

body: A research guide to Arkansas Confederate pension records has a page on Union records, and it uses two examples that matter here. "Calvin V. Moffitt of Lawrence County served in two Arkansas Confederate units," it says, but when he applied for a pension he "claimed a few months' service in a Union unit and tried three times unsuccessfully to qualify for a Union pension." The guide adds that the files made by that process were far more rewarding for descendants than for Calvin. Its second example is "David H. Grimes," a third lieutenant in the 27th Arkansas Confederate Infantry whose widow applied for a Union pension, claiming he had briefly served in 1864 in a Union unit. The guide gives no dates, no wives and no place for Grimes, and it does not say Calvin's father's name.

Calvin V. Moffitt is the name this site already carries as Nathan Moffitt's son, born in 1841 and raised in Strawberry Township, Lawrence County. The National Park Service soldiers index, which gives only name, rank and unit, has a Calvin V. Moffitt as a private in Company G of the Confederate 25th Arkansas Infantry, and a Calvin V. Moffitt (also entered as Moffett and Moffat) as a private in Company L of the Union 4th Arkansas Cavalry. That pairing fits what the guide describes. The guide's remark that Union pensions turned on the unit, not the man's residence, also bears on a puzzle in the earlier notes: Company L was made up in Montgomery County, far from Lawrence County. According to Wikipedia, Company G of the 25th was enrolled at Pocahontas, in Randolph County, on 13 March 1862, and the 4th Arkansas Cavalry (Union) was organized at Little Rock in December 1863. The index also lists a C. V. Moffatt, private, Company K, 1st Arkansas Volunteers (30 days, 1861), which could be the guide's second Confederate unit, but nothing links him to Calvin.

David H. Grimes is harder. The index has a D. H. Grimes who rose from corporal to third lieutenant in Company I of the Confederate 27th Arkansas Infantry. Wikipedia says that company was organized on 6 July 1862 at Richwoods, Izard County, one of the four parent counties of Stone County, where Henry Moffitt and Hannah Grimes later lived. That fits the guide's wording about rank and regiment, but the earlier note on this site follows a family tree that has David Grimes living and dying in the Mississippi lowlands of southern Arkansas by 1876, and nothing here puts a David Grimes in Izard County. Whether Hannah Moffitt's father is this lieutenant is a lead.

The useful part is what the guide implies. A Union pension file is built from affidavits, and a widow's claim has to prove a marriage and a death. If these two men are ours, the National Archives pension files, found through the General Index to Pension Files, 1861–1934 (T288), could name Hannah's mother, and the children of both families, and could show where each man lived in the 1890s and 1900s. Calvin's three attempts may have left several sets of papers. Until someone orders them, the soldier index and a printed example are all the record there is.

The service files themselves are now online in the National Archives catalog, and they settle much of what the index could not. The Confederate file for "Calvin V. Moffitt" shows him enrolled at Pocahontas on 13 March 1862 by Captain Turnbull for twelve months, in a company first carried as Company E of Turnbull's Battalion and then Captain Sloan's company of the 30th Arkansas before it became Company G of the 25th. A roll dated 30 June 1862 gives his age as 21. He is marked present on the rolls from late 1862 through October 1863, and the roll for January and February 1864 ends his Confederate service in four words: "Deserted his company Feb 8, 1864." A separate file for "C. V. Moffatt" puts him in Captain L. W. Robertson's company of 30-day volunteers, mustered on 17 November 1861 and discharged on 17 December, with transportation due "from Pocahontas to Smithville," the Lawrence County seat. That is very likely the guide's second Confederate unit.

Ten weeks after leaving the 25th, on 20 April 1864, he enlisted in the Union army at DeValls Bluff for three years, signing the enlistment paper with his mark. The papers say he was born in Randolph County, North Carolina, was 22, and worked as a "Wagon Maker" ("Waggonmaker" on the enlistment), the trade of his father Nathan, the Strawberry Township wheelwright. He stood 5 feet 11 inches, with light eyes, dark hair and a light complexion. He was mustered in at Little Rock on 12 May 1864, paid a $25 bounty and $13 advance pay, assigned to Company L, and credited to the 1st Congressional District, Lawrence County, Strawberry. Every roll from the summer of 1864 onward repeats the same remark: deserted 20 August 1864 at Camp Fishback near Little Rock. A card dated 6 May 1909 shows the War Department pulling his cards under case number 2828098, which fits the guide's account of later pension attempts.

The D. H. Grimes file in the same catalog adds a little to the lieutenant's side. He was 33 in 1862, born in Tennessee and living in Izard County, and he enlisted at Richwoods on 6 July 1862; his rise from corporal to lieutenant and his dismissal by court-martial in April 1863 are told in "Elected at Richwoods, dismissed at court-martial."

Moffitt of Lawrence County" and the index has the matching unit entries; with the 1850 Strawberry Township household already on this site, that is probable, not proved, because the guide does not name his parents and the index carries no age or place. The guide's page is a printed example, not a record. The index is one man in the Confederate 25th and one in the Union 4th, while the guide says two Confederate units; the second unit was not identified. For David H. The Confederate enrollment and the Union enlistment are still two files joined by name, age and place rather than by a statement that they are the same man. Ages conflict slightly: 21 on a Confederate roll of June 1862 and 22 in April 1864, while a December 1841 birth gives 20 and 22. The pension files themselves remain unexamined.

stories.title: A brother and sister, a sister and brother: Dr. James R. Alexander and Dorcas Garrison
stories.hook: Hezekiah Alexander's son, a Princeton student turned army surgeon, married a Garrison in York District, South Carolina, and followed the family to Kentucky.

subject.name: Dr. James R. Alexander and Dorcas Garrison

body: Hezekiah Alexander's will of 1796 names a son James R. Alexander twice: first with "his children," then as co-executor with his brother William Semple. Walter O. Holliman Jr.'s 1997 genealogy of the Davidson family identifies him as Dr. James R. Alexander, born about 1756 in Cecil County, Maryland, who died after 1832 in Allen County, Kentucky, and says he married Dorcas Garrison on 26 November 1789. Harry Wright Newman's Maryland Revolutionary Records (1938) has an entry for the same pair and date in "York Dist., S.C." (a search snippet only; the page was not opened). A 1989 Simpson County, Kentucky, family history, also seen only as snippets, gives the same date, calls him a Revolutionary War surgeon, and says Dorcas, born 23 January 1766, was a daughter of John Garrison.

Holliman summarizes James's own pension application, file W-2901, dated 14 May 1833, when he gave his age as 76. James said he was born on the line between Pennsylvania and Maryland on 23 November 1756 and lived in Cecil County when the war began. He was a student at Princeton College in 1776, enlisted as a private in Captain Walter Alexander's "Flying Camp," was soon made a sergeant and was discharged on 1 December 1776. He then went back to medicine, joined his father in Mecklenburg County, and on 25 May 1780 volunteered again, this time as a surgeon. The W marks a widow's claim, and the full file, now transcribed, holds both his declaration and hers.

His own words fill in the outline. When the alarm reached Nassau Hall in 1776 he went home to Cecil County and joined the Maryland Flying Camp. He fell sick at Elkton, followed his company north by way of Philadelphia, Trenton, Princeton and Newark, and reached Fort Lee after dark on the eve of 16 November, so that he “saw the battle from Fort Lee but was not in it” when Fort Washington fell across the Hudson; he then retreated with the army through New Jersey before his discharge. In 1780, after Tarleton's men cut down Buford's regiment at the Waxhaws on 29 May, he nursed the wounded in a Presbyterian meeting house near the battlefield and then at Charlotte, until the British reached the town that autumn. He became surgeon to Colonel William Lee Davidson's Mecklenburg regiment and was with it until Davidson was killed at Cowan's Ford on the Catawba on 1 February 1781. He was allowed $103.33 a year from 1831 for four months as a private and four and a half as a surgeon. Dorcas applied on 9 May 1839, at seventy-two, giving their marriage as 26 November 1789 and his death as 11 March 1836; Mark Garrison, writing from Parke County, Indiana, placed the wedding in York County, South Carolina. The family record in the file lists ten children, from Silas, born 10 May 1791, to Dorcas Reese, born 28 December 1807.

Floyd C. Stuart's Garrison compilation says that James and Dorcas moved to Kentucky about 1795 or 1796, a few years before Esther and Samuel Garrison did, and that Dorcas was a widow in Allen County in the 1850 census. Stuart's own phrase for the pattern is a brother and sister Garrison who married a sister and brother Alexander. He admits that some question whether Dorcas was John Garrison's daughter, but reasons from dates and places that she was; the Simpson County snippet naming John Garrison as her father supports him, and York District, where she married, is where Stuart places John Garrison's family in the years before about 1795.

This does not prove that Dorcas and Samuel were brother and sister, and which John Garrison was their father is unsettled (see the note on Samuel Garrison). It does show that the Alexander and Garrison families were joined twice, and that both couples ended in the same part of Kentucky. Dates differ a little: Stuart once has James born about 1761 against his own 1756 statement, Holliman has his death only as after 1832, and the Simpson County snippet gives 11 March 1836 for his death and 1852 for Dorcas's.

stories.title: Elma Whitfield Severn: teacher, coach and principal
stories.hook: Ida Merry Whitfield’s daughter was born at Glover in 1918 and spent thirty years in Oklahoma and New Mexico schools.
body: Elma Mae Whitfield was born at Glover on 12 January 1918, the daughter of Oliver Clinton Whitfield and Ida Mae Merry Whitfield. Her own obituary in the Choctaw Nation’s Biskinik of December 2011 gives those names and calls her mother an original Choctaw enrollee. A second obituary, her sister Ouida Carroll’s in May 2007, lists “Elma Mae Severn of Valliant” among the survivors. Together the two notices place her firmly in the Whitfield household that Ida’s story follows from Glover to the Golden post office. She was the younger sister of Lewis Oliver Whitfield, Alfreda’s father, and the older sister of Omagene and Ouida.

Elma was a graduate of Southeastern State Teachers College, in Durant, and spent thirty years in education in Oklahoma and New Mexico. The obituary says she served as a teacher, basketball coach, 4-H leader and principal. It gives no years and no school names. Wikipedia lists the college under that name from 1921 to 1939, before it became Southeastern State College, so if the obituary uses the name in force when she studied there, she attended before 1939. That is an assumption, not a record. A transcript, a school list or a college yearbook would give the real dates.

Her second career was with the Department of Human Services, for seven years. For five of them she worked with older people. The last two were spent, in the notice’s words, “working through the court” with delinquent children, foster homes and adoptions. The notice says her training and schooling for that work were at the Hissom School for the Impaired and at Oklahoma University. She belonged to the National Retired Teachers Association and the Oklahoma Education Association.

Church was the other thread. She was a longtime member of Southern Baptist churches, where she taught Sunday school, directed Training Union and the Woman’s Missionary Union, and served as Sunday School superintendent, and she belonged to the National Association of Baptist Senior Adults. The obituary closes with her farewell, which begins “Love one another.”

Her husband, Mark Severn Jr., died before her. The notice lists her surviving children under other surnames, so she may have married earlier, but it does not say so and no marriage record has been found. Elma died on 31 October 2011, aged 93, and lived at Valliant; the notice does not say where she died. Among those who died before her it names her parents, her brothers Lewis and Omagene, her sister, printed as “Oulda” Whitfield Carroll, which is a variant of Ouida, and an aunt, “May Gimlim.”

Two details deserve a second look. “May Gimlim” is not in the tree. She is an aunt on either Ida’s or Oliver’s side, no record here places her, and she is a lead for a sister of Ida or of Oliver. And the two obituaries name the same two deceased brothers, one pair as Omagene Clinton and Oliver Lewis, the other as Lewis and Omagene. That fits the tree’s treatment of Lewis Oliver and Oliver Lewis as one man, a probable identification.

The National Archives’ World War II Army enlistment file has a card for a Mark Severn Jr. of McCurtain County, born in Oklahoma in 1918, Army serial number 20842194. He enlisted on 5 December 1941 as a private in the Air Corps, coming from the National Guard in federal service, and was then single, with a grammar-school education, and working as a general farm hand. He is the only Mark Severn Jr. in the file and came from Elma’s county, but the card cannot show that he is the husband her obituary names, so that link is probable at best.

Whitfield of the 1920 census remains probable, as Ida’s story explains. That story mentions only a son, Oliver L., in the 1920 household; Elma, born in January 1918, would have been two, so the census page is worth rechecking. The obituary prints her sister’s name as Oulda and her aunt’s as Gimlim; both are kept as printed. Living relatives named in the notices are not listed here.

stories.title: Ouida Carroll and the Golden post office
stories.hook: Ida Whitfield’s younger daughter spent twenty-two years at the Golden post office and retired as a postmaster in 1990.
body: Catherine Ouida Whitfield was born on 15 January 1924, the youngest of the Whitfield children recorded here, and went by Ouida. She died on 16 March 2007. Her obituary in the Choctaw Nation’s Biskinik of May 2007 calls her a retired postmaster who served 22 years at the post office in Golden, and says she belonged to NAPUS and the National League of Postmasters. It names her parents as Oliver Clinton and Ida May Merry Whitfield and her husband, Eugene Carroll Sr., who died before her.

The office she worked in was old by then. Jim Forte’s postal-history list shows a Golden post office in McCurtain County from 1911 to the present, and Wikipedia gives its opening as 13 March 1911 and says the community was named for its first postmaster, James M. Golden. Ida had gone to work there after her husband died in 1941, as her story relates, and Ouida retired from it in 1990.

The arithmetic of the two obituaries deserves a careful look. Twenty-two years ending in 1990 point to a start about 1968. Ida’s obituary, as her story summarizes it, says she retired as postmaster at 72, which for a woman born in June 1898 means between June 1970 and June 1971. Mother and daughter may therefore have worked at the same office for a few years, or Ouida’s twenty-two years may include time as a clerk or assistant before she became postmaster, or the notices may be rounding. Neither obituary gives an appointment date, so when each woman became and ceased to be postmaster is unknown. No appointment record has been examined.

Church and community filled the rest of her life. She was a nursery worker and a teacher of children and of senior women at Southwest Friendship Baptist Church in Oklahoma City and at Golden Baptist Church, and she belonged to the Woman’s Missionary Union at both for more than 57 years. After she retired in 1990 she volunteered at the Golden Community Center, the Golden Senior Citizens Center and Golden Baptist Church.
Her sister Elma’s obituary, in December 2011, prints her name as “Oulda.” The family’s notices also give her brothers’ names in two orders. Those variants are kept as printed in the tree.

stories.title: Card 5754: the record that may name Bessie’s parents
stories.hook: Bessie Merry’s Dawes card has been indexed but not read. National Archives guidance says such cards, and their application packets, usually name the enrollee’s parents.
body: The Oklahoma Historical Society’s Dawes Rolls index places Louis Merry, Bessie Merry and Ida May Merry together on Choctaw by Blood card 5754. Bessie and Ida May are on rolls 15526 and 15527, and Louis is listed as an intermarried white citizen on roll 1363. These are historical enrollment entries; they say nothing about anyone’s present status. The index gives names, ages, sex, blood degree and numbers, but not parents. Bessie’s own parents, the open question on her line, are therefore still unnamed.

The National Archives says three kinds of Dawes record could answer it. Census cards, also called enrollment cards, typically give the applicant’s name, relationship to the head of the family group, age, sex, blood degree and parents’ names, and they often refer to kin cards and note births, deaths or changes in marital status. They can also show whether the person appeared on an earlier tribal roll. The enrollment applications, the packets of testimony and letters, can contain the names of parents and extended family, a residence or nearby post office, and affidavits from relatives and neighbors. Land allotment jackets for approved enrollees can also list parents and extended family along with the location of the land. The same guidance says the Commission accepted enrollment applications from 1898 through 1907, with a handful in 1914, and that the final rolls were approved on or before 4 March 1907.

Earlier work on this family read the 1899 affidavit and several Commission letters from the application file. The card itself, the page that would carry the parents’ column, has not been read. The National Archives says the cards (series 251747) and the applications (series 617283) are digitized in the National Archives Catalog, where applications can be searched by name, tribe and card number, and that both are also on microfilm, M1186 for the cards and M1301 for the applications. The Kansas Historical Society’s reel list puts Choctaw by Blood cards 5141 to 5994, which includes 5754, on reel MS 2017. The Oklahoma Historical Society copies application packets for a fee and says each order includes the enrollment card.

Surname matching will not answer the question. The surname Durant comes from Ida’s 1993 obituary, and it was a large Choctaw family name with many Durants on the rolls, so linking Bessie to any one household without the card would be a guess. If the card names her parents, they can be added to the tree as proven, and the card may point to an earlier roll to check. If it does not, Bessie stays a brick wall. Either way, only what the record states should be written down. Update: the card was read on 3 November 2026, after this story was written, and it does name her parents; the story “Card 5754 read: Peter and Ellen Durant” tells what it says.

Kernell of Denison Cemetery, and the Durant surname, rest on Ida’s obituary and a gravestone as described in Ida’s story; both identifications are probable.

stories.title: The ordnance plants west of Texarkana
stories.hook: Audrey and Lemuel Sandridge worked at a “Red River Arsenal” in the 1940s. Texas records describe the two Army sites that stood west of Texarkana.
body: In the 1940s, according to a family memorial that reproduces Audrey Sandridge’s obituary, Audrey and her husband Lemuel worked at the Red River Arsenal plant making ammunition, and Audrey also worked its switchboard. The original obituary has not been seen, and the memorial gives neither the years nor the place. This story adds nothing about Audrey and Lemuel themselves. It asks what a “Red River Arsenal” was likely to be, using two Handbook of Texas entries.

The Red River Army Depot, also known as the Red River Ordnance Depot, was activated in August 1941 after the government bought 116 farms and ranches just west of Texarkana. Its mission was to receive, store and issue gun-motor carriages, ammunition, explosives, and supplies and equipment for combat vehicles and demolition work. The Handbook says construction was at first held back by a housing shortage and a lack of equipment. Wikipedia places the depot in Bowie County, Texas, 18 miles west of Texarkana.

Next to it stood the Lone Star Ordnance Plant, also called the Lone Star Army Ammunition Plant, on a tract nine miles west of Texarkana. It was an ammunition-loading plant for artillery shells, bombs, fuses, boosters and other items, run for the Army by the Lone Star Defense Corporation, a subsidiary of the B. F. Goodrich Rubber Corporation. Its contract was let on 23 July 1941 and its first small-caliber ammunition was sent out on 27 May 1942. In April 1943 the plant and the depot were consolidated as the Texarkana Ordnance Center.

Neither entry uses the name Red River Arsenal, so the memorial’s phrase may be shorthand for either site or for the combined center. Work remembered as making ammunition fits the loading plant most closely, but that is a guess: no record seen so far names the Sandridges’ employer, jobs or years. An employment record or a wartime newspaper notice would settle it.

One coincidence is worth recording without leaning on it. The depot is in Bowie County, Texas, and Julia Stevens Ratcliff’s 1956 death notice, as her story describes it, gives Bowie County as her birthplace. No record ties the Sandridges’ wartime work to that connection.

Wikipedia, Red River Army Depot (Bowie County, Texas; 18 miles west of Texarkana), read 2 Nov 2026: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_River_Army_Depot

The Sandridges’ work history rests on a reproduced obituary on a memorial page that earlier researchers read; it was not re-examined. Which installation, which years and which jobs remain unknown.

stories.title: Glover and De Queen: a thread to Sevier County, Arkansas
stories.hook: Two Glover-area families, and one later marriage, point to the same Arkansas county. None of it is proven yet.
body: Glover, where the Dawes Commission wrote to the Merry family in 1902 and 1903, lay close to Arkansas. R. L. Polk’s gazetteer for 1902–1903 lists it in the Choctaw Nation as a country post office about 40 miles from De Queen, Arkansas, and gives no postmaster or businesses for it. De Queen is the seat of Sevier County, and Wikipedia lists McCurtain County, Oklahoma, as the county on Sevier County’s western border.

Three items in these stories touch that county. The memorial for J. L. Louis Merry at Glover Cemetery gives his birthplace as Sevier County, and Clint Whitfield’s memorial gives Chapel Hill in the same county. Both come from Find a Grave pages that earlier researchers read, and both are leads. And in 1950 Julia Ann Stevens and Charles M. Ratcliff, both of Broken Bow, were married in Sevier County, according to the register page described in Julia’s story.

Put together, these do not prove that either family came from Sevier County, or that they knew one another before they reached McCurtain County. Two memorial birthplaces could match by chance, and a marriage in a nearby Arkansas county seat in 1950 may have little to do with births in the 1870s and 1890s. What the pattern does is point to where records for Louis Merry’s and Clint Whitfield’s parents should be looked for first: Sevier County marriage and probate files, and the county’s census schedules, 1880 for Louis and 1900 for Clint.

If those searches name Louis’s parents as John Calvin Merry and Eliza Jane McGregor, or Clint’s as William Franklin Whitfield and Emma Ward, which are only memorial leads now, the tree could finally attach them. Until then the Merry and Whitfield lines stop where they are. The Sandridge line’s Arkansas leads lie in other counties, so this thread belongs to the Merry, Whitfield and Stevens lines.

Wikipedia, Sevier County, Arkansas (county seat De Queen; McCurtain County, Oklahoma, on the western border), read 2 Nov 2026: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sevier_County,_Arkansas
Wikipedia, De Queen, Arkansas (seat of Sevier County), read 2 Nov 2026: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Queen,_Arkansas

stories.title: Private Walker of Company C
stories.hook: William P. Walker’s Civil War service, left open in his first story, can now be pinned down: a private in Company C, 60th Illinois, from March 1864 until the regiment mustered out in July 1865.
body: William P. Walker’s first story left two questions open: what his government marker meant by “Ill Militia,” and whether the William P. Walker of Company C, 60th Illinois Infantry, in the 1879 county history was this man. Two sources now answer most of both. The state adjutant general’s printed roster of the 60th Illinois (vol. 4, p. 184), read here on the scanned page, lists “Walker, William P.,” of Richview, among Company C’s recruits: date of enlistment 20 March 1864, date of muster 17 April 1864, and the remark “Mustered out July 31, 1865.” A volunteer-compiled abstract of the Illinois muster and descriptive rolls for Washington County veterans gives the same dates and adds the places: mustered in at Centralia, mustered out at Louisville, Kentucky. It also says he was born in 1831 in Washington County, died in 1919 and is buried at Beaucoup Cemetery, and describes a farmer from Richview, 5 feet 10 inches tall, with black hair, gray eyes and a dark complexion, citing the 1850 census, District 20, Washington County. That compilation was read, not the state database behind it.

Other sources agree. The Beaucoup Cemetery transcription lists his grave with the comment “PVT ILL MILITIA CIVIL WAR Co. C, 60th Ill. Inf.,” and the 1879 county history lists William P. Walker among the Washington County men of Company C. The same cemetery transcription uses the words “PVT ILL MILITIA” for Simeon Walker, whom it also calls a captain in Company C, and for two Mexican War veterans who were second lieutenants, so the phrase looks like a general marker label for Illinois volunteer soldiers and not a separate militia term.

Company C was raised in Jefferson and Washington counties, and William was one of a group of 1864 recruits. On the same printed page, Jackson L. Livesay, also of Richview, carries the same dates: enlisted 20 March 1864, mustered 17 April 1864, mustered out 31 July 1865. The compilation calls him a farmer born about 1846 in Jefferson County. John W. Livesay, listed under “Washington co.,” had joined earlier, on 29 August 1862, and was discharged for disability on 16 February 1865; the compilation calls him a mechanic born about 1834 in Washington County. The roster’s dates also show who commanded the company when William joined: Simeon Walker, listed among its captains from 19 December 1862 and mustered out on 14 March 1865. No record found so far says how either Livesay was related to Floyd Livesay’s family, who also came from the Richview area. The name was common there, and the question stays open.

Wikipedia’s summary of the regiment’s service, drawn from the National Park Service’s unit record, covers the months he served. The 60th was at Rossville, Georgia, until May 1864, then took part in the Atlanta campaign (1 May to 8 September), the March to the Sea (15 November to 10 December) and the siege of Savannah. It went through the Carolinas campaign from January to April 1865, marched in the Grand Review at Washington on 24 May, and moved to Louisville on 12 June, where it served as provost guard at 14th Corps headquarters until it was mustered out on 31 July 1865. William’s own muster-out place and date match the regiment’s last day. The records found so far do not say when he reached the regiment or which engagements he shared, so none are claimed for him.

Two later lists carry his name. The federal pension roll of 1 January 1883, as transcribed for Washington County, lists Walker, Wm. P., of Richview, pensioned at six dollars a month for chronic diarrhea and disease of the abdominal viscera. The transcription gives no regiment, so that match rests on his name and post office. And the 1914 Illustrated Roster of the Department of Illinois, Grand Army of the Republic, which prints post rolls as they stood on 1 January 1913, lists “Walker, W. P., Pr. C, 60 Ill. Inf.” under the Simon Walker Post, No. 629, at Richview. That line was read in the scanned book. William would then have been about 81.

Three Walkers appear in the regiment’s Washington County roll in the 1879 history: Simon Walker, a sergeant in Company C; William P., a private in the same company; and Levi S. Walker, the regiment’s chaplain. Which Simeon Walker the Richview post honors is not shown: the Department of Illinois roll of posts already lists “Simeon Walker Post, No. 629, Richview” in the proceedings of the Twenty-fourth Annual Encampment, held at Quincy in March 1890. Captain Simeon Walker (born 3 March 1831, according to both the cemetery transcription and the veterans compilation) is a candidate, but the two compilations disagree on his death: 11 October 1909 on the cemetery list against 29 April 1905 in the veterans compilation. The 29 April of the compilation’s date is also the day and month the cemetery list gives for Etheldra J. Walker’s death, in 1903, which may be a coincidence or a copying slip; no record opened here settles it. No record opened here says whether these men were kin to William. His own parents remain unproved; the story of the Walker graves at Beaucoup sets out the leads.

Identifying that soldier with the Beaucoup man is probable: the Richview residence, the compilation’s birth year, county and burial place, the cemetery transcription’s Company C comment, the 1879 county history and the 1913 G.A.R. roster all point the same way, but none gives parents or a full birth date. The state muster database and any pension file were not examined. The two compilations disagree on Simeon Walker’s death date. Kinship among the Company C Walkers is not established.

stories.title: The Walker graves at Beaucoup
stories.hook: Two Methodist Walker families lie in the old Beaucoup cemetery. County records show which stones belong to whom, and where the proof for William P. Walker’s parents still runs out.
body: Beaucoup Cemetery, in section 23 of Township 2 South, Range 2 West, was established in 1820, according to a volunteer transcription made in 1979 and rechecked in 2012. Its Walker entries include two stones that matter here. Rev. James Walker is listed with the years 1800 to 26 April 1857 and the age 57 years, 1 month, 16 days, which puts his birth about 10 March 1800. On the same stone, the transcription lists Etheldra, “wife of Rev. James,” as 1805 to 6 June 1878, aged 73 years, 8 months, 8 days. That age implies a birth about September 1804, so the printed year and the stated age differ by about a year, and her birth year stays approximate.

The 1879 county history supplies some of Rev. James Walker’s story. It lists a Rev. James Walker among the Methodist ministers who came to Beaucoup soon after 1820 and among the pioneer teachers who kept school before 1824, and it says the “Rock Chimney” farm, first settled by John Dees, was sold in 1827 to Captain James Burns, who afterwards sold it to Rev. James Walker. A transcription of the county’s early marriage register records a “James Walker, LE” (apparently a local elder) officiating at the marriage of Andrew White and Polly Ann Tate, license dated 18 February 1845. None of these sources names his children.

A second Methodist Walker family is easy to confuse with his. The Southern Illinois Conference’s 1880 memoir of Rev. Simeon Walker Sr. says he was born in Jackson County, Georgia, on 13 April 1802, was converted at Shiloh, St. Clair County, Illinois, in 1819, and died on 22 February 1880 at his son’s home in Carbondale. The marriage register lists a Simeon Walker “Jr.” marrying Etheldra Jane Walker on 15 September 1852. At Beaucoup, a Simeon Walker (3 March 1831 to 11 October 1909, a captain in Company C, 60th Illinois) and an Etheldra J. (31 July 1833 to 29 April 1903) are listed with several small children who died between 1854 and 1869, three of them marked “son of S. & E.” They are probably the same couple, but the records opened here do not say so. Nothing found shows how the two Walker families were related, or whether they were.

The younger Etheldra matters for the question of William P. Walker’s parents. Find a Grave, as noted in his first story, names his parents as Rev. James Walker and “Etheldra Jane Ballard.” The cemetery transcription shows two Etheldras: the older, wife of Rev. James, and the younger, Etheldra J., wife of Simeon. The “Jane” belongs to the younger woman, and the register gives her maiden surname as Walker, not Ballard. No Ballard record appears in the sources opened here, so the Find a Grave name may blend the two. There are echoes between the families: William named his eldest daughter Mary Ellen Etheldra, according to that first story, and Simeon and Etheldra J. named a son James H. (12 June 1855 to 21 August 1856). If Etheldra J. were a daughter of Rev. James and Etheldra, she would be William’s sister and Captain Simeon his brother-in-law. That was only a lead until the 1850 census household, told in a later story, put William P. and Etheldra J. in Rev. James and Etheldra’s house, which makes them probable, though not proven, children.

Abigail is documented, though her maiden name is not. The family stone reads “Abigail, his wife, 1833–1923,” and the transcription lists her as wife of Wm. P. A register transcription lists a license for William F. Walker and Abigail Schanck dated 25 February 1852, and the cemetery transcription has a son George W., 12 September 1853 to 24 October 1854, “son of Wm. R. & A.” The initials differ (F in the register, R in the cemetery list, P on the stones), but the dates fit a couple married in 1852 with a first child in 1853, so the marriage entry may be theirs. It stays an unlinked lead: Alice’s death certificate names her mother as Addie Bruce, and no Walker family record found here calls Abigail a Schanck.

The Walkers and Livesays of Beaucoup were already tied by marriage before Alice Walker married Floyd Livesay. The transcription lists Frances C. E. Walker (19 September 1849 to 18 February 1874), daughter of Rev. G. W. Walker and Elizabeth and “wife of Chas. M. Livesay.” Rev. G. W. Walker (1826 to 20 October 1902) is marked as a Mexican War lieutenant of the 2nd Illinois Foot Volunteers. The register lists Charles M. Livesay marrying Theresa E. Tate on 17 May 1877, three years after Frances’s death. The Livesay sketch story takes up what that means for Floyd’s family.

The transcriptions are volunteer work and contain visible slips (for example “Wm. R.” for a Wm. P. couple’s son); the stones themselves were not examined except through the photographs already on this site.

stories.title: The Livesay sketch against the county’s own records
stories.hook: A descendant’s sketch of Robert and Lydia Livesay’s family stands behind the lead that links Floyd to David P. Livesay. Volunteer transcriptions of Washington County’s own records confirm several of its details and leave the key link open.
body: Floyd Livesay’s possible Illinois ancestry rests largely on a family sketch of Jackson Monroe Livesay in the Orange County California Genealogical Society’s Livesay file. Written by a descendant from a family Bible, it names Robert and Lydia (Fitzgerald) Livesay, who came from Maury County, Tennessee, to Washington County, Illinois, about 1830, and their ten children, among them David Pinkney Livesay, born 1 January 1831. It is a secondary source, and the earlier story on Tabitha Livesay’s stone treated its claims as unchecked. Volunteer transcriptions of the county’s marriage registers and of Beaucoup Cemetery now allow several of them to be tested.

They hold up. The sketch gives Jackson Monroe Livesay’s marriage to Lucinda Ann Thompson on 15 November 1849, and the register transcription lists Jackson M. Livesay and Lucinda A. Thompson on that date. The sketch says Lorenzo M. married a Thompson; the register lists Lorenzo M. Livesay and Margaret Jane Thompson on 22 October 1845. The 1856 heirs’ paper it quotes names a James I. Logan as husband of Unity Jane; the register lists James L. Logan and Unity J. Livesay on 16 November 1849. The eldest son, William E., appears marrying Emily Goodner on 1 August 1844. At Beaucoup Cemetery, a stone for Jasper L. Livesay, who died 16 August 1841, is marked “son of Robert & Lydia,” and the sketch’s Jasper was born 15 February and died on 16 August 1841, to the day. These checks support the sketch’s account of Robert and Lydia’s family. They do not speak to David P. in particular.

David P. himself appears in two places. A stone at Beaucoup reads “D. P. Livesay 1831–1904” and, below, “Elizabeth, his wife, 1846–1933”; the photograph is reproduced in the earlier story. The register transcription lists a David B. Livesay and Elizabeth D. Jack with a license dated 28 July 1857, seventeen months after Tabitha J. Livesay’s death on 14 February 1856. If that is David P., it would be his second marriage. But a bride born in 1846 would have been eleven, so either the stone’s Elizabeth is a later wife, her year is wrong, or the register’s David B. is another man. This is not yet resolved, and the tree records Elizabeth as a lead.

The Livesays and Walkers were already tied by marriage. The cemetery transcription lists Frances C. E. Walker (19 September 1849 to 18 February 1874) as “wife of Chas. M. Livesay,” and the register lists Charles M. Livesay marrying Theresa E. Tate on 17 May 1877. The earlier story reports that Find a Grave lists a Charles among David P.’s younger children. A man widowed in 1874 and remarried in 1877 could be a child of David’s 1857 marriage only if he had married as a teenager, which seems unlikely, so this Charles may be a different Livesay. It is worth checking before anyone is added to Floyd’s family.

What would settle Floyd’s parentage is a record that names his parents: his 1880 Illinois marriage return to Alice Walker (later than the registers transcribed here), David’s 1904 obituary or probate file, or the family Bible the sketch cites. Until one turns up, David P. and Tabitha J. stay unlinked leads. The people added with this story record only what stones, registers and the sketch say about them, and none is connected to Floyd.
quotes: D. P. Livesay 1831–1904 / Elizabeth, his wife, 1846–1933 (headstone, Beaucoup Cemetery)
LIVESAY, Jasper L., 16 Aug 1841, son of Robert & Lydia (Beaucoup Cemetery transcription)

The 1857 register entry reads David B., not David P., and conflicts with the age implied by Elizabeth’s stone; it is not treated as established. The sketch’s dates and Fitzgerald parentage for Lydia were not checked against original records.

stories.title: Pearland on paper: 1914, 1950 and 1957
stories.hook: A 1914 business directory, a 1950 school annual and a 1957 stockmen’s journal each carry a Livesay name in Pearland’s corner of Brazoria County.
body: The 1914 R. L. Polk & Co. Texas State Gazetteer lists, under “Grocers, Retail,” a “Livesay F H” at Pearland, between the entries for Peacock and Pearsall. The printed page (numbered 1115 in the directory’s Texas Gazetteer section) was checked, not only the scan’s text, because the town names run in a separate column beside the merchants’ names. The initials, the town and the trade fit Floyd H. Livesay, whose 1932 death certificate calls him a retired groceryman and whom a 1932 Houston newspaper notice, cited in the earlier Illinois-to-Texas story, places in Pearland from the mid-1890s. A directory is not a household record, so the match is probable. The Handbook of Texas puts Pearland at twenty-three businesses and a population of 400 in 1914.

The 1950 Pearland High School annual, The Gusher, shows a later generation. A Wayne Livesay is in the fourth-grade pages and a Carolyn Livesay in the seventh-grade pages, and she also appears in the caption of the junior volleyball team’s photograph. The 2001 obituary of Lester Livesay Jr. names a son Wayne and a daughter Carolyn Jo, and says he was reared in Pearland; the Pearland Historical Society’s 2014 notice spells the daughter’s name Carylon. Wayne Woodrow Livesay, born 13 February 1940, would have been ten. The match with Floyd’s great-grandchildren is probable, not proven, because the annual names no parents.

A third record points to a Livesay working life in the same county, and it is a lead only. In its May 1957 issue, the Texas and Southwestern Cattle Raisers Association’s magazine The Cattleman ran a short item headed “Saddle Thief Sentenced.” It says a man was sentenced on 16 April to five years in the penitentiary, on a guilty plea, for stealing two saddles belonging to a man of Brazoria, and that the case was investigated by Deputy Sheriffs Lester Livesay and a colleague together with an association inspector. A 2006 book, Tales from the Brazos, appears in the Internet Archive’s search index with a passage about a Lester Livesay, “a former sheriff’s deputy who patrolled the Pearland area.” Only that search snippet could be read, because the book’s full text is not open.

Two Lester Livesays have ties to the county: Lester Jr., who bought a cattle ranch at Pearland in 1953, according to his 2001 obituary, and Lester Sr., who is buried at Alvin (he died in 1989). The obituary of Lester Jr., the only one read for this story, does not mention law enforcement, so the deputy could be either man or a different Lester Livesay altogether. The question is worth taking to the Brazoria County sheriff’s records and the county’s newspapers.

Lester Sr. is buried at Alvin on a double stone with Esther Voris, whose side reads “Esther Voris, Aug. 9, 1910” with no death year carved in the photograph. The tree now carries her as his later wife, with the birth date from the stone and nothing more.

The 1957 deputy is a lead only and is not attached to either Lester. Esther Voris’s later dates, birthplace and marriage year come from an earlier story and were not rechecked.

stories.title: The sisters in Hattie Kilgore’s notice
stories.hook: The 1929 Broken Bow News notice for Hattie Kilgore names more of her family than the first story used: a husband, a small son, her mother and three sisters, one of them in Chickasha.
body: Hattie Myers Kilgore’s first story used The Broken Bow News of 10 October 1929 to tie her to her mother, Mrs. Stevens, and her sister Audrey Nelson. The same front-page notice, headed “Mrs. Gordon Kilgore died Oct. 8th,” says more. She died on Tuesday afternoon at the Sanitarium of Paris, Texas, after an illness of several weeks. The body was taken to Idabel to the home of a Mr. and Mrs. W. S. Green, whose relation to her the notice does not give. The pastor of the First Baptist Church of Idabel conducted the funeral, and burial followed in the Denison cemetery there. The Texas death certificate agrees on the date, 8 October 1929, and on burial at Idabel. It gives her age as 20, calls her married, and says the illness was contracted at Idabel.

The notice lists her survivors: her husband, who is not named again after the heading; a son, four years old; her mother, Mrs. Stevens, of Broken Bow; and “three sisters, Mrs. Alfred and Miss Audry Nelson, Broken Bow, and Mrs. Joe Harrison, Chickasha.” Mrs. Alfred is probably Nona Myers Alford, whose married name the same paper spelled Alford in 1940, as the Camden story shows; the 1929 spelling looks like a slip, but that is an inference. The small son is not named here.

Mrs. Joe Harrison, of Chickasha, is the new name. She is not in the tree, and the notice does not say whether any of the sisters shared both of Hattie’s parents. She is a research lead: a Chickasha or Grady County record naming her parents, or her marriage to Joe Harrison, could show where she belongs.

Gordon Kilgore is the other gap. The notice’s heading and its first sentence are the only places that name him, and the certificate gives only “Mrs. Gordon Kilgor.” He is added to the tree as Hattie’s husband on that evidence alone, with no dates, birthplace or parents. A marriage record for Hattie Myers and Gordon Kilgore would be the next thing to look for.
quotes: three sisters, Mrs. Alfred and Miss Audry Nelson, Broken Bow, and Mrs. Joe Harrison, Chickasha (The Broken Bow News, 10 October 1929)

stories.title: Which Gardner was Eunice's brother? Five sketches from 1891
stories.hook: An 1891 book prints sketches of five Choctaw men named Gardner. Only one names his father as Jackson Gardner, the name on Eunice Pisachubbe's Dawes card, and the book never connects him to her.

subject.name: Gardner men of Blue County in the 1891 sketches

body: Eunice Pisachubbe's Dawes card, made out at Goodland on 10 May 1899, names her parents as Jackson and Viney Gardner, both dead, of Blue County. No other record of them has turned up. One place to look is H. F. O'Beirne's Leaders and Leading Men of the Indian Territory (1891), the same volume that prints Joseph P. Thompson's sketch on page 162. Its first volume has sketches of five Choctaw men named Gardner, and they do not share a father.

Josiah Gardner (page 67) was born at Wheelock in 1851, went to neighborhood schools until he was fifteen and lived with his parents until 1871, when he began farming for himself. At twenty-one he married Elizabeth Beajis, who was part Cherokee and lived three years. In 1877 he married Sallie Thunley, a Choctaw, and had no family by her. The sketch calls him "a fourth son of Jackson Gardner, of the Oklafalaya clan" and says he was a lawyer who practiced in the Choctaw courts. Eunice's card puts her birth about 1850, a year before Josiah's. If the two Jacksons are one man, Josiah would be her brother or half-brother.

James W. Gardner (page 93) was born in Blue County, Choctaw Nation, in 1849, if the scan's "18i9" is read that way, which is the reading that fits his 1870 marriage. His father died while James was a child, so he stayed home to look after his widowed mother and never had schooling. In 1870 he married Emily Cornwell, the widow of Wm. Lawson, and by 1891 he had a four-hundred-acre farm near Wynne Wood (now Wynnewood), about thirteen hundred head of cattle, part of the town site and four children. His father is not named. A Blue County birth, a father dead early and a widowed mother are all consistent with a Gardner household whose parents were both dead by 1899, but they are consistent with many households.

The other three can be set aside as sons of Jackson. William Gardner (page 124), born in 1830 on the Tombigbee River in Mississippi (the scan prints "Tom Bigby"), names his father as Jeremiah Gardner and his mother as Clarissa La Flore, and says the family reached Towson County in 1833. Judge G. W. (Green) Gardner (page 141), born at Little River in January 1844 (the scan reads "18-14"), was also a son of Jeremiah, "who came to the Indian Territory in 1833." Judge Jeff. Gardner (page 174 by the book's index), born near Wheelock, was the eldest son of "Noll Gardner," at one time an interpreter for the missionaries; John Bartlett Meserve's 1941 life of him, as Principal Chief from October 1894, names his parents as Noel and Hannah Gardner, mixed-blood Choctaws from Mississippi, and gives his birth near Wheelock on 12 July 1847 from his tombstone. Wheelock thus had at least two Gardner households in these years, Noel's and Jackson's. William's sketch also mentions a Tims: before he opened his own store at Hamilton, in Blue County, he worked for "E. B. Tims, the sutler at Doaksville," probably Vincent B. Tims (see his story).

What this does not show matters as much. The book is the only source here, every sketch is the man's own account, and it never links Jackson Gardner to Viney, to Blue County or to a daughter Eunice. Wheelock was a mission and academy, and the sketch does not say which county it lay in. A. D. Hefley's account of the Tobucksy County courthouse at McAlester, in the Chronicles of Oklahoma, also names a Josiah Gardner, a full-blood Choctaw lawyer who could neither read nor write; nothing seen shows whether he is the Wheelock-born Josiah. To test the lead, the next records to find are Josiah Gardner's own entries on the 1896 census and any Dawes card or probate that names his parents, and a card or probate for a Jackson Gardner of Blue County.

quotes.t: a fourth son of Jackson Gardner, of the Oklafalaya clan
quotes.c: H. F. O'Beirne, Leaders and Leading Men of the Indian Territory (1891), sketch of Josiah Gardner, p. 67

stories.title: Spencer Academy to Salem, Virginia: Joseph Thompson in company
stories.hook: Joseph Thompson's 1891 sketch has him at Roanoke College until 1886. Five other Choctaw men in the same book name the same college, and three of the six went there from Spencer Academy.

subject.name: Joseph Thompson and the Choctaw men who went to Roanoke

body: Joseph Thompson's sketch in O'Beirne's Leaders and Leading Men of the Indian Territory (1891, page 162) says he was educated at Spencer Academy and at "Mount Harmon Institute, Northfield," and completed his education at Roanoke College in Salem, Virginia, "where he remained until 1886." He then taught school, was appointed county clerk of Cedar County in 1889 and was elected to the lower house of the Choctaw Council the next year. The only other accounts of his college years are his son Joel's memory, which gives a different order, and the 1881-82 Roanoke catalog, which does not list him. A registrar's list from the right years has not been found.

The same volume shows he was not alone in making the trip. Jacob Jackson (page 207) was born about 1845, went to Fort Coffee Academy and, after the Civil War, to an academy at Little Rock and King's College in Tennessee, and in 1870 to Roanoke College, "where he spent four years." He began practicing law in 1874, served as senator for Skullyville County and was National Secretary of the Choctaw Nation by 1889. Napoleon B. Ainsworth (page 106), born at Skullyville in 1856, entered Roanoke at fifteen, "graduated after four years, in June, 1880," and won the orator's medal that year; the dates do not quite agree with each other, since four years from fifteen would be 1875. He went on to law school at the University of Virginia, served the Nation as auditor and in 1883 married Miss Emily K. Thompson at Roanoke, Virginia. Nothing in the sketch ties her to this Thompson family.

Three more followed the Spencer-to-Salem route Joseph took. Solomon E. Hotema (page 135), born near Grant in 1854, went to Spencer Academy and had his education "completed at Roanoke College"; he was elected Kiamichi County clerk in 1881, county judge in 1884, 1885 and 1886, representative in 1887 and senator in 1890. The Rev. William H. McKinney (pages 192-193), born in January 1861, was at Spencer until 1877, then spent five years at Roanoke, took his A.B. in 1883, went on to a divinity degree at Yale in 1886 and became a district school trustee and a Presbyterian minister. Don Juan Folsom (page 71), born in August 1866 in Atoka County, spent three years at Roanoke after Denison High School, returned to Atoka in 1884, and was elected Clerk of the House that year. His mother's maiden name was Thompson; no link to this family is known.

The pattern is the point. By 1891 a Spencer Academy education followed by college in Virginia was a recognized road to Choctaw office, and county clerk and then the House was a common first step; Hotema and Joseph both followed it. That makes Joseph's own sketch more believable. It does not confirm his years at Roanoke, which still rest on a sketch that Joseph supplied himself and on his son's memory, and the sketches of the other five are the same kind of source.

stories.title: A Hulsey pastor at Mount Ida
stories.hook: A Baptist minister named Hulsey served the Mount Ida church for twenty-two years while George Washington Hulsey lived and worked in the same county. No record seen ties the two families together.
body: The Chronicles of Oklahoma printed a short life of the Rev. John Washington Hulsey in 1952, in Herbert Miner Pierce's "Baptist Pioneers in Eastern Oklahoma." He was born on 17 March 1864 at Arkadelphia, Arkansas, the son of Lucretia Overall Hulsey and Dr. James Carroll Hulsey, a country doctor who practiced around Cameron, Williams, Spiro, Hartshorne and Wilburton in what became Oklahoma. John had little schooling. He was converted in the summer of 1889, at twenty-five, near Bengal in Latimer County, and was ordained by the Harlan's Chapel Baptist Church on 1 September 1889. The article says he could hardly read when he began to preach.

His pastorates run through two states. In Indian Territory and Oklahoma he served Bengal, Cameron and Poteau, organized the First Baptist Church of Wilburton in 1898 and was moderator of the Short Mountain Baptist Association in 1895, 1896 and 1898. In Arkansas he served Waldron, Parks, West Hartford and Mansfield from 1908 to 1913, then Norman, Caddo Gap and Mount Ida in 1914-1917. From 1922 to 1944 he was pastor at Big Fork, Cherry Hill, Antioch and Mount Ida, and his second term at Mount Ida lasted twenty-two years, "until his death." In 1919 he directed the $75 Million Campaign in Montgomery and Polk counties. He died at Little Rock on 17 November 1944, where he had gone to attend the state Baptist convention.

Why a Hulsey researcher cares is the geography. This site has George Washington Hulsey, a boy of four in the 1880 census of Montgomery County, living at Story in that county in 1918 and dying at Washita, in Montgomery County, in 1935, with his burial at Breashears Cemetery near Story. His son Louis Daniel died near Mena, in Polk County, in 1948. Mount Ida, Caddo Gap and Norman, where the Rev. John Hulsey was pastor, all lie in Montgomery County, and Big Fork, another of his churches, is in Polk County. Family usage calls George "Rev.," although the census, draft and work records seen name him a laborer and farmer. One thing to rule out is that a family memory of a Hulsey preacher at Mount Ida belongs to this man and not to George; that is an idea to test, with nothing yet found to support it.

A shared surname, a shared county and the middle name Washington are not evidence of kinship. Nothing seen connects Dr. James Carroll Hulsey of Arkadelphia to Benjamin F. Hulsey, born about 1848 in Georgia, or to the Salathiel Hulsey household in Union County, Georgia, in 1850. The records that could decide it are the 1870 and 1880 censuses for Dr. Hulsey's household and for any Hulsey households near Arkadelphia, probate for Lucretia Overall Hulsey, and a death certificate for George Washington Hulsey that names his parents.

stories.title: Where the cards were mailed: five post offices and their dates
stories.hook: A Dawes card gives each household a post office. The Postmaster General's dates, as compiled in 1948, show when Doaksville, Fowlerville and Alikchi opened and changed their names around the family.

subject.name: The post offices on the Thompson, Tims, Austin and Pisachubbe cards

body: Each Dawes card of 1899 names a post office for its household: Doaksville for Joseph and Betsy Thompson (Card 1283) and for Mitchell and Willie Tims (Cards 850 and 1268), Alikchi for James B. Tims (Card 510), Fowlerville for Legion and Molsey Austin (Card 1363) and Goodland for Eunice Pisachubbe (Card 1580). George H. Shirk's list of the first post offices in Oklahoma, printed in the Chronicles of Oklahoma in 1948, gives the dates from the Postmaster General's records for most of them. Shirk warns that the list shows the offices "on paper" and not always as they ran on the ground.

Doaksville's office opened on 11 November 1847, when the Fort Towson office, which dated from 7 September 1832 with George C. Gooding as its first postmaster, took the Doaksville name. Shirk names Joseph R. Bertholet (the Berthelet of the Doaksville store) as the first postmaster of Doaksville, and a descendant's letter quoted in the Chronicles in 1941 says Joseph was appointed postmaster in 1847. That bears on a family memory. Joel Thompson said that "Venson Brown Tims" was the first postmaster at Doaksville (see the story on Vincent B. Tims), but the list gives that place to Berthelet. The two men are linked in the same year: the 1941 article says that at the Red River Raft Convention held at Clarksville, Texas, in the winter of 1847, two Doaksville citizens, Berthelet and Vincent B. Tims, "took a prominent part," citing the Clarksville Northern Standard of 11 December 1847.

The office was not always open. Shirk records that it did not operate from 2 July 1866 to 28 May 1867 or from 15 September 1867 to 29 June 1869. A "V. B. Tims" is named as its postmaster on 17 May 1871 in the postmaster rolls, after the second reopening, and Edward Tims was appointed in 1887, as his story tells. On 12 June 1903 the name was changed back to Fort Towson, which explains the faint 1905 pencil note on Card 1283 that changes the family's address from Doaksville to "Ft. Towson, I.T." Corinne's office, the one the Thompsons used after 1904, opened on 24 August 1904 with Pearl Wynn as its first postmaster.

Fowlerville was the Austin family's office. It opened on 7 July 1894 with Nathaniel M. Fowler as postmaster and was renamed Valliant on 23 June 1902, with Hosea L. Fowler as the first postmaster under the new name. Legion Austin swore to his son James's birth at Fowlerville in May 1899, his wife's 1901 affidavit for their daughter Adline was sworn there too, and the family tree gives his death at Valliant on 8 April 1903, less than a year after the change. Alikchi, the address on James Tims's card, opened on 13 July 1888 with John Wooley as postmaster, almost eleven years before he applied. Spencerville opened on 17 May 1902, and the family tree gives Joseph Thompson's death there in 1927.

Goodland, the address on Eunice Pisachubbe's card, is the one gap. The scanned list has no Goodland entry that could be found, so which office served her household in 1899 is not shown here; the Presbyterian mission settlement of that name is told in other stories.

Morrison, ed., 'Notes from The Northern Standard, 1842-1849,' Chronicles of Oklahoma 19 (1941), pp. 273-274 and p. 277 n. 88: https://archive.org/details/chroniclesofokla1919okla (opened 2 Nov 2026); Dawes Cards 1283, 850, 1268, 510, 1363 and 1580 as described in this site's stories; Oklahoma Historical Society Dawes final roll index, index only: https://www.okhistory.org/research/dawesresults?fname=&lname=&tribe=Choctaw&rollnum=&cardnum=1283 (searched 2 Nov 2026).

stories.title: A farm near Pearland, May 1950
stories.hook: The 1950 census found Lester and Barbara Livesay with their two children on a farm in Brazoria County. Lester’s line is blank, and the entry for a railroad engineer sits one line below it.
body: On 3 May 1950 an enumerator who signed herself Mrs. L. M. Jones started sheet 24 of enumeration district 20-55 in Brazoria County, Texas. Dwelling 221 on that sheet is the Livesay household: Lester W., head, white, male, 33, married, born in Texas; Barbara, wife, 32, married, born in Texas; Carolyn Joe, daughter, 14; and Wayne W., son, 10, both born in Texas. The column asking whether the house was on a farm or ranch is marked yes.

The ages fit what other records say about this family. Lester Jr. was born on 8 May 1916, so he was five days short of his thirty-fourth birthday and still 33. Barbara was born on 7 April 1918 and had just turned 32. Wayne Woodrow was born on 13 February 1940. The census gives no birth date for Carolyn, but at 14 she was born between May 1935 and May 1936, the year after her parents’ April 1935 marriage. Lester’s 2001 obituary names this daughter Carolyn Jo; the Pearland Historical Society’s 2014 notice spells her name Carylon. The 1950 Pearland school annual, described in an earlier story, shows a Wayne and a Carolyn Livesay in the fourth and seventh grades of the same spring.

The work columns hold a small puzzle. Lester’s own line, 26, has nothing in them. The next line, 27, which is Barbara’s and is also one of the sheet’s sample lines, reads “Wk,” 40 hours, occupation “Engineer,” industry “Railroad,” private employer. Elsewhere on the sheet a wife’s line carries “H” for housework and her husband’s line carries his job. The entry almost certainly belongs to Lester, whose obituary says he was a Southern Pacific Railroad engineer, and was written one line too low. It is reported here as the enumerator wrote it.

The farm also fits. Lester’s 2001 obituary says he was reared in Pearland and that “in 1953, he purchased and operated” a cattle ranch there. The 1950 farm entry shows the family was already living on a place counted as a farm three years before that. The census does not say whether they owned it, how large it was, or what they raised.

The railroad occupation is written on Barbara’s line and is attributed to Lester here only by inference; the original is the authority. The sheet heading does not name the place within the county. stories.title: D. P. Livesay on paper, 1855 to 1933
stories.hook: A year before Floyd Livesay was born, the Illinois state census found D. P. Livesay at home with one young woman and one older one. County indexes add a loan, an estate file and a death date for his widow.
body: Illinois took its own census in 1855, and a volunteer transcription of the Washington County returns lists a household headed by D. P. Livesay. It counted only the head by name, and it counted the rest by sex and age group: one male aged 20 to 30, one female aged 20 to 30 and one female aged 50 to 60, three people in all, with one man of militia age and fifty dollars’ worth of livestock. David Pinkney Livesay, born on 1 January 1831 according to the family sketch, would have been 24. Tabitha J., who died on 14 February 1856 aged 27 years, 2 months and 4 days, would have been about 26. There is no child in the house, which fits a son born in February 1856.

The older woman is not named. Robert Livesay had died on 15 February 1855, and the sketch makes his widow Lydia the woman with whom Floyd was living in 1860. But the sketch gives Lydia’s birth as 16 October 1807, which would place her in the 40 to 50 column in 1855, not 50 to 60. The woman could be Lydia with a misreported age, Tabitha’s mother, or someone else. The transcriber also warns that the copy is faint and the script hard to read.

A second, independent transcription of Gilead Cemetery in Grand Prairie Township, Jefferson County, walked by Cindy Ford in 2000, lists “Livesay, Tabitha J., 2-14-1856, 27y2m4d, w/o David P,” agreeing with the stone photographed for an earlier story. Find a Grave, as reported there, gives her maiden name as Flannigen. The same transcription lists a Thomas H. Flannigan who died on 28 January 1853 aged 58 years and 11 days, a Martha Flennigen, “w/o Thomas,” who died on 9 July 1862, and a Mary L. Flanigan with a single date, 22 July 1846. Nothing in the transcription connects them to Tabitha, so they are only a lead for her family.

Gilead also holds Charles P. Livesay (4 October 1865 to 9 January 1915) and his wife, Mary Delona (21 September 1867 to 3 January 1948). The earlier sketch story reported that Find a Grave lists a Charles among David P.’s younger children and wondered whether he was the Charles M. Livesay widowed in 1874. A Charles born in 1865, buried in the cemetery where David’s first wife lies, fits a child of David’s second marriage far better. Charles P. is a different man from Charles M., but no record opened here names his parents, so he is added only as a lead and is not linked to David.

David appears in three other county records. A loan book from Hoyleton, presumed to be the Hoyleton Bank’s, records a personal note for D. P. Livesay dated 7 March 1879: sixty dollars for one year at ten percent. The county’s index to probate records before 1910 lists “Livesay, D. P. - Estate” (numbered 282 in the index) and “Livesay, D P - Bond” (262), as well as an estate for Robert Livesay (26). And the county’s index of death certificates from 1916 to 1950 lists Elizabeth Livesay, female, white, certificate 950123, on 15 October 1933 in Beaucoup Township, the year carved for “Elizabeth, his wife” on David’s stone.

The estate file is the record most likely to settle Floyd’s parentage. Estate papers often name a dead man’s heirs, and if Floyd was David’s son by Tabitha he could be named among them. The index shows that the file was made; its contents have not been seen. Until they are, David P. and Tabitha J. remain unlinked leads.
