The probate file, bond, loan and death certificate are known here only from indexes and transcriptions. Charles P. and Mary Delona Livesay and the Gilead Flannigans are leads, not linked to anyone in Floyd’s line. Floyd stays unlinked from David P. and Tabitha J.

stories.title: The Beaucoup Walkers in the 1855 census and the death index
stories.hook: The 1855 state census counts four Walker households that match the Beaucoup stones. The county death index then dates William P. and Abigail Walker’s deaths, and one date is a day off the one already in the tree.

subject.name: William P. and Abigail Walker and their Beaucoup neighbors

body: The 1855 Illinois state census for Washington County, as transcribed by a volunteer, counts several Walker households. That census named only the head and counted everyone else by sex and age group, so each entry is a shape, not a list of names. James Walker’s household holds a man aged 50 to 60, a woman aged 40 to 50 and two girls aged 10 to 20. Rev. James Walker was born about March 1800, and the older Etheldra, his wife, about 1804 or 1805, so both fit. Simeon Walker Sen.’s household holds a man and a woman in their fifties and a boy and a girl in their teens. Rev. Simeon Walker Sr. was born in 1802, according to the 1880 conference memoir cited in the earlier story on the Walker graves.

Simeon Walker Jun. heads a household of a man and a woman in their twenties and a boy under ten. The register shows Simeon Walker Jr. marrying Etheldra Jane Walker in September 1852, and the Beaucoup stones list a son of “S. & E.” who died young, so the shape fits that couple. G. W. Walker heads a household of a man in his twenties with three females, one under ten, one aged 10 to 20 and one in her twenties. The Beaucoup transcription gives Rev. G. W. Walker’s birth year as 1826 and his wife Elizabeth’s as 1829, and lists their daughter Eudora B. A., born on 7 July 1852. None of these entries names a relationship, and the shapes only show that the ages are consistent.

No household in the transcription is headed by a William P. Walker. The nearest is a William H. Walker with seven people, including a man and a woman in their twenties and five younger people. That does not look like a couple married about 1852 whose first child, George W., had died in October 1854. William P. may have been counted under another reading of his initials, living in someone else’s household, or missed by the transcriber, who notes that the original is faint.

The county’s index of death certificates for 1916 to 1950, drawn from Illinois State Archives data, has entries for both William and Abigail. “Walker, William P,” male, white, certificate 21461, is dated 20 May 1919 in Beaucoup Township. The Find a Grave memorial and the tree give 19 May 1919. The one-day difference may be a slip in either source; only the certificate can settle it. “Walker, Abigail,” female, white, certificate 950004, is dated 28 January 1923 at Richview, which agrees with the year on the family stone, “Abigail, his wife, 1833–1923.”

The same index lists Levi S. Walker, certificate 13125, on 6 April 1921 at Richview. The 1879 county roster, as cited in the earlier story on William’s service, names a Levi S. Walker as chaplain of the 60th Illinois, William P.’s regiment. The county’s pre-1910 probate index lists an estate for a James Walker (numbered 18 in the index), which may be Rev. James’s, who died in 1857. Neither the certificates nor that estate file have been examined. Either could name the next of kin needed to test whether Rev. James and Etheldra were William’s parents, and whether Abigail was the “Addie Bruce” of Alice’s Texas death certificate.

stories.title: Joshua L. Merry, first postmaster at Glover
stories.hook: The Post Office Department’s own lists answer a question Ida’s story left open: her father was appointed Glover’s first postmaster on 26 June 1901.
body: Ida Merry Whitfield’s story repeats a memorial’s claim that her father, J. L. Louis Merry, was the first postmaster at Glover, and notes that his appointment had not been checked. Two lists compiled from the records of the Postmaster General now answer it. Grant Foreman’s “Early Post Offices of Oklahoma,” printed in the Chronicles of Oklahoma in September 1928, lists Glover among the offices of the Choctaw Nation, with Joshua L. Merry as first postmaster and 26 June 1901 as the date of appointment. George H. Shirk’s revised list of 1948, made after the original records had reached the National Archives, gives the same office, nation, date and name.

Shirk explains how to read such a date. An office was formally established when its postmaster was appointed, and six weeks or more usually passed before the postmaster was set up and ready to open. That fits the federal Official Register, which printed every postmaster and his pay. Its list as of 1 July 1901 goes straight from Globe to Golconda in the Indian Territory section, with no Glover. In the register dated 1 July 1903 the line reads Glover, Choctaw, Joshua L. Merry, $24.94. The 1905 register lists him under District 24 at $56.93, and the 1907 register, the last before statehood, has “Merry, Joshua L, PM $90.”

The printed name helps with the family puzzle. The 1899 affidavit and the Dawes final-roll index call him Lewis or Louis, and the Commission’s 1902 letter went to J. L. Merry at Glover. The registers, compiled in Washington, spell out Joshua L. in 1903, 1905 and 1907, matching the Joshua L. Merry of Glover in the marriage-license clipping and the “J. L. Louis Merry” of his Glover gravestone. So the 1902 letter was addressed to the town’s own postmaster. That this Joshua L. Merry is the Louis Merry of card 5754 still rests on the shared place, initials and later family records, but no other Merry appears at Glover in any of these lists.

By 1911, after statehood, the register lists Glover in McCurtain County with G. W. Grigsby, born in Texas, as postmaster. When Merry gave up the office is not shown in the volumes checked; a 1909 postal register was not found online. The family’s postal work did run through three generations, as Ida’s story suggested it might: Joshua at Glover, Ida later at Golden, and Ida’s daughter Ouida, who retired from the Golden office in 1990.

One more glimpse of him is only a lead. A modern published transcription of Choctaw newborn enrollment applications under the Act of 1905, seen only as a search-result snippet, shows a J. L. Merry signing as notary public on an affidavit sworn 19 June 1905. The page has not been read, and the snippet does not say where the affidavit was made.

stories.title: Bessie Durant, in her granddaughter’s words
stories.hook: In 1997 Elma Whitfield Severn sent a short sketch of her grandmother to a book of Choctaw original enrollees. It adds a birthplace and a different birth year.
body: In 1997 Wesley and Charleen Samuels published Life and Times of the Choctaw Original Enrollees, a book of family stories sent in by enrollees and their descendants. The book says the stories were printed so that families could tell them “in their own words without substantive change,” and the staff of the Bishinik helped gather them. One short entry, on page 71, is headed “Bessie Durant” and was submitted by Elma M. Severn, granddaughter.

Elma wrote that Bessie Durant, roll number 15526, was born on 11 November 1878 in Choctaw County, Indian Territory, and died on 22 March 1950 at Golden, Oklahoma. Bessie married Louis (J.L.) Merry, roll IW 1363, who was born on 10 April 1872 and died on 1 July 1932 at Golden. They had one child, Ida May Merry Whitfield, roll 15527. In 1997, Elma wrote, Ida had three living children, Lewis O. Whitfield, Elma M. Severn and Catherine O. Carroll, and had lost a son, Omagene Clinton Whitfield, in the Second World War.

The roll numbers agree with the Oklahoma Historical Society’s final-roll index for card 5754, and Louis’s dates agree with his Glover gravestone. Bessie’s death date agrees with her Denison Cemetery stone. Her birth year does not: the stone reads Nov. 11, 1879, while Elma gave 1878. The index does not settle it, but Bessie’s Dawes records of April 1899 bear on it: her mother’s affidavit of 27 April 1899 and census card 5754, dated 26 April 1899, both give her age as 19. That fits a birth on 11 November 1879, as on the stone, and would be a year low for 1878, when she would have been 20. Ages on such records are approximate, so 1879 is preferred, not proven, and the sketch’s year is kept as a recorded variant.

The birthplace is new, and it needs care. Wikipedia’s article on Choctaw County, Oklahoma, says that county was created at statehood in 1907 from parts of the Choctaw Nation’s Jackson, Kiamichi, Cedar and Towson counties. A birth in 1878 or 1879 could not have been in “Choctaw County” under that name, so Elma was probably naming the place by its later Oklahoma county. The entry is kept as written and treated as a family statement, not an official record.

Just as important is what the sketch leaves out. It does not name Bessie’s parents, brothers or sisters, and it does not mention her later surname, Kernell, or the parting from Louis that Ida’s obituary implies. The sketch therefore names no parents; the census card for 5754, read in a later story, names them as Peter and Ellen Durant.

stories.title: Lewis Whitfield goes into the Army, July 1945
stories.hook: A year after his younger brother died off Normandy, Lewis O. Whitfield of McCurtain County was inducted at Oklahoma City.
body: The bronze plaque on Lewis Whitfield’s grave at Wheelock calls him a private in the U.S. Army Air Forces in World War II, but until now no record of his service had been found. The National Archives’ World War II Army enlistment file, which it publishes online in its Access to Archival Databases, has a card for Lewis O. Whitfield, Army serial number 38782151. It records that he lived in McCurtain County, was born in Oklahoma in 1916, and enlisted at Oklahoma City on 11 July 1945 as a private.

The card codes him as a selectee, a man who came in through the draft, enlisting for the duration of the war plus six months. He had no branch assignment yet on the day he enlisted. The other fields describe his life at home: he was married, had finished three years of high school, and gave his civilian occupation under the heading for plumbers, gas fitters and steam fitters. That trade appears nowhere else in his records; by 1950 he was keeping a general store near Golden.

The name, county and birth year all fit the Lewis Oliver Whitfield of the tree, born in August 1916, and his marriage to Violet Box fits the card’s “married.” The Air Forces service on his plaque is not on the card, which records only the day he came in. He was probably assigned to the Air Forces after induction, but no record seen so far shows it, or gives his discharge date.

His number has the same shape as his brother’s. The War Department’s 1946 honor list explains that men inducted through Selective Service received eight-digit numbers beginning with 3 or 4, the second digit standing for the service command. Omagene’s was 38466149 and Lewis’s 38782151. Omagene’s own enlistment card was not found in the online file, which the National Archives says does not hold records for every enlistee. When Lewis went in, Omagene had been dead for more than a year, and their widowed mother, Ida, was working at the Golden post office.

stories.title: A widow’s pension application from Titus County
stories.hook: The Texas index of Confederate pension applications lists a Mrs. A. E. Logan of Titus County, widow of Dudley Logan. It is the first record here to hint at Dudley’s war.
body: Annie Box’s mother is known so far only through other people’s records. The Wheelock Cemetery card file, quoted on Annie Box’s memorial, names her parents as Dudley Logan and Annie Wedgeworth Logan, and Dudley Timothy Logan’s memorial says he came to Titus County, Texas, from Greene County, Alabama, and died there in 1898. The tree gives his widow as Sarah Anne Elizabeth “Annie” Wedgeworth Logan, 1846–1923, dates that have not been checked against an original record.

The Texas State Library and Archives index to Confederate pension applications adds an entry of its own. Searching the surname Logan returns “Logan, A. E. (Mrs),” application number 30414, Titus County, with her husband’s name given as “Logan, Dudley.” The column for a husband’s own application number is blank. The library explains that this column is filled only when the husband himself received a pension, and its table of payments begins with the cash pension law of 1899, the year after Dudley died.

The same introduction explains who could apply. Texas paid pensions only to Confederate veterans, or their widows, who had lived in Texas since 1880 and were disabled or indigent. The index covers approved, rejected and home pensions issued between 1899 and 1975, and marks rejected and missing files. This entry carries neither mark. A widow’s application in Dudley’s name implies that she claimed Confederate service for him, and that she was poor enough to qualify, but the index gives no regiment and no date.

The initials A. E. fit Anne Elizabeth, the county is the one where Dudley died, and the husband is named Dudley, so this is probably Annie Box’s mother. The library says the application forms and any supporting papers are held in its archives, and the index links to a digital copy, but that copy sits behind a browser check that could not be passed for this research. Reading the file is the next step. It may state Dudley’s unit and the couple’s marriage, which no record here yet gives.

stories.title: Three households in the 1950 census
stories.hook: In April 1950 the census taker found Larry Sandridge in Broken Bow and Alfreda Whitfield near Golden, eight years before they married.
body: The National Archives’ 1950 census website lets the original pages be searched and read. Three pages from McCurtain County show both sides of the maternal grandmother’s family. On the first sheet of enumeration district 45-3, in Broken Bow, begun on 1 April 1950, the first household is Lemuel L. Sandridge, 38, born in Arkansas; his wife, written “Audry I.,” 32, born in Oklahoma; their son Larry L., 11; and a younger son, 8. Lemuel was working 40 hours a week as an electric service man for an electric company. Audrey was recorded as keeping house that week.

Clinton and Maggie Sandridge lived elsewhere in Broken Bow, on sheet 16 of district 45-8, begun on 10 April. The entry reads “Clenton L.” Sandridge, head, 66, and Maggie A., his wife, 58, both married and both born in Arkansas. The house was marked as being on a farm, and Clinton was not working that week. The ages add to the puzzles in Clinton’s story. Sixty-six in April 1950 points to a birth about 1883 or 1884, against 1882 on his gravestone and 1892 in his death notice. Maggie’s 58 fits the May 1891 birth on the stone, but her birthplace, Arkansas, differs from the Texas of the 1930 census. Arkansas agrees with the Prescott birthplace on the memorial that calls her Maggie Cash, though it does not prove the Cash name.

The third page is sheet 14 of district 45-46, in Sulphur Township, begun on 14 April. A note at the top says the enumerator was proceeding west from Golden one mile and south half a mile. There the head of one household is “Louis O.” Whitfield, 33, born in Oklahoma, a storekeeper working 72 hours a week in his own general store. Violet B., 29, worked the same 72 hours as a clerk in the store, recorded as unpaid family work. Their daughter Alfreda was 11. Two younger daughters, 7 and 4, were also at home; the older of them is recorded as born in California, a hint that the family spent part of the 1940s there, though no other record seen here places them in California. Violet’s 1962 notice says the Whitfields had been in the grocery business at Golden for several years; this page shows the store was already running in 1950.

The next dwelling on the same sheet holds a woman of 51, widowed, born in Oklahoma, listed as head of her household and working 54 hours a week as postmistress at the Golden post office, a government job. The name is written “James C. Whitfield.” Everything else fits Ida Merry Whitfield: she was 51 that spring, a widow since 1941, and her obituary says she became postmaster at Golden. The given name is probably a mistake by the enumerator, so the identification is probable rather than certain. If it is Ida, she was already postmistress, not assistant, by April 1950.
The children of these households who may still be living are described here without names. Larry and Alfreda, the eleven-year-olds of Broken Bow and Golden, married at Broken Bow in 1958.

stories.title: From Bays Fork to Cotaco Creek: the Garrisons who went to Alabama
stories.hook: John Milton Garrison's younger brother took his family south to Morgan County, and the family Bible he left kept their story.
body: Hezekiah Alexander Garrison was born at Cowan's Ford on the Catawba River in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina, in February 1791, and went with his parents, Samuel and Esther (Alexander) Garrison, to Warren County, Kentucky, about 1798 or 1799. On 10 June 1813 he married Rebecca Lyle there. The family list gives her birth as 25 October 1796 in Loudoun County, Virginia, and names her parents as Manasseh Lyle and Sarah Chaney (also written Chemey), who were first cousins; the Lyles had moved from Loudoun to Bedford County, Virginia, and then to Warren County. Rebecca's obituary, written by the Methodist preacher H. M. Welch, gives her birth as 18 August 1796 instead.

Their first nine children were born in Kentucky, in the part of Warren County that became Allen County: Esther Lyle, Samuel Newton (1816), Hillery Y. (1818), Simon Peter (1820), William Calvin, Hannah A., Nancy B., Sarah H. (1828, who died the next year) and Andrew Jackson (April 1830). Then the family went south. Stuart reasons that Morgan County, Alabama, was opened to settlement in 1830 and that Cynthia C., the tenth child, was born there on 3 April 1832, so the move fell between those dates, and he says a history of the county shows a Garrison among the settlers who filed land claims in 1830. The obituaries date the move about 1831 (Hillery's) and 1832 (Simon Peter's, and Rebecca's, which adds "I think"). An old section plat, as Stuart describes it, puts the family on a half-section of land straddling Cotaco Creek, about six miles east of Somerville, the county seat, near the Old Center Springs camp ground. The last child, Mary Rebecca, was born in Morgan County on 23 June 1835.

Samuel Newton, the eldest son, died in Morgan County on 27 July 1837, at twenty-one, and E. Welch wrote a long poem on his death "in his Mother's stead" that was kept with the family papers. Hezekiah died on 15 August 1846 by the Bible record; Rebecca's obituary says only that he went before her "about the year" 1846. In the 1850 census, as Stuart read it, Rebecca, 55 and born in Virginia, headed a Morgan County household with Andrew Jackson, Cynthia and Mary R., and her married sons Simon Peter and William Calvin lived beside her with their families. Cynthia married W. S. McClanahan on 4 January 1854 and died on 11 November 1856.

Rebecca outlived her husband by twenty-seven years. Her obituary says she was a Methodist for fifty years, that until she gave up keeping house "her house was the preacher's home," and that two of her sons became preachers. Stuart adds that during the Civil War she saw at least one son side with the Union while her youngest son was killed fighting for the Confederacy; he does not name the Union son. She died on 5 August 1873, after nine days in bed, at the home of her son-in-law S. W. Shackelford near Moulton, Alabama.

Nearly all of this comes from one book. Hezekiah's Bible, with handwritten births, marriages, deaths and burials and with newspaper obituaries pasted into its record pages, passed to his youngest daughter, Mary Rebecca, and then to her daughter Minnie, who gave it before her death to a great-granddaughter of Hezekiah's living in Decatur. That owner gave photocopies of the pages to the compiler Floyd C. Stuart in 1979, and his Garrison genealogy prints them in transcription. For the brothers who became preachers, see "Two preachers from Center Springs"; for Mary Rebecca and her brother Andrew Jackson, see "The youngest child, a carriage shop at Hartselle, and the Bible she kept."

quotes.t: Until she ceased to keep house to live with her children her house was the preacher's home.

The dates rest on the Hezekiah Alexander Garrison Bible as transcribed by Stuart from photocopies, and on obituaries pasted into it; the Bible itself, the 1850 Morgan County census page and the land-claim and plat records Stuart mentions were not seen. Rebecca's birth is 25 October 1796 in the family list and 18 August 1796 in her obituary. Andrew Jackson Garrison's birth is 2 April 1830 in the family list and 3 April 1830 in Stuart's narrative. The year of the move to Alabama varies from 1830 to 1832 among the accounts.

stories.title: Two preachers from Center Springs: Hillery and Simon Peter Garrison
stories.hook: Two of Hezekiah Garrison's sons became Methodist preachers: one rode Arkansas circuits through the Civil War, the other never left the neighborhood of the old camp ground.

subject.name: Rev. Hillery Y. Garrison & Rev. Simon Peter Garrison

body: Hillery Y. Garrison was born in Allen County, Kentucky, on 22 January 1818 and came with his father to Morgan County, Alabama, about 1831. His obituary, by H. M. Welch, was pasted into the family Bible. It says he professed religion at Barret's Camp-ground in the fall of 1837 under the Rev. William H. Johnston, was licensed to preach in 1842, joined the Tennessee Conference that fall, was transferred to the Alabama Conference and placed on the Coosa Circuit, and "located" (left the traveling ministry) when the year was out. He also studied and practiced medicine. In 1848 he married Jane Alexander, daughter of the Rev. Aaron Alexander of Lincoln County, Tennessee. Her own obituary, written for the Nashville Christian Advocate, says she died at her father's home on 10 October 1850, in her twenty-third year, a few weeks after her sister Martha, her father and her baby of about five months. Hillery's obituary prints her death year as 1830, an evident slip.

He married again, to Eliza C. Beale of Madison County, Alabama, and moved to Arkansas. The family list dates that marriage 28 December 1852; the obituary puts it in 1854, with the move soon after. From there the printed minutes of the Methodist Episcopal Church, South, take up his story. In the Arkansas Conference, Hilary Y. Garrison (so spelled) was a preacher on trial in 1862 and 1863 and was received into full connection at Jacksonport in October 1864. The minutes list him in the Helena District each year: at Prairie after the conference of November 1862, on the Helena Circuit after October 1863, on the Prairie Circuit after October 1864 and at Clarendon after the conference of 1865. These are wartime minutes kept by a church in the Confederacy, and they place him at work in the same district through all four years.

He died in Phillips County, Arkansas, on 8 December 1868, after about twenty-four hours of quinsy. Welch's obituary quotes his widow's letter and says he left a wife and one child in Arkansas, "an aged, widowed mother in Alabama," and several brothers and sisters.

Simon Peter Garrison, born in Allen County on 10 January 1820, moved with his parents to Morgan County in 1832 and, as his son Simon R. Garrison wrote, "settled near Old Center Springs' Camp ground." He joined the church at seventeen. On 18 December 1844 he married Louisa Glover, born in Northampton County, North Carolina, on 9 July 1828, whose widowed mother had moved to Morgan County near the same camp ground. They had seven children. Louisa died near Somerville of consumption in February 1874; her obituary says two of her sons had just entered the ministry. In 1875 Simon Peter married Annie E. Orme, and they had three children, two of whom died as infants.

Simon Peter was an exhorter and class leader for years before he was licensed to preach in 1862. He was ordained deacon at Florence and elder at Decatur, the latter in 1876, and his preaching stayed mostly in his own neighborhood and county; his son called him one of the "old-time" Methodist local preachers. Stuart describes him as a wealthy farmer. He died at Somerville on 13 May 1896 after a long illness and lived to see his two oldest sons preach. He and Louisa are buried in a family cemetery near Center Springs Methodist Church.

quotes.t: He leaves a wife and one child in Arkansas; an aged, widowed mother in Alabama.

stories.title: The youngest child, a carriage shop at Hartselle, and the Bible she kept
stories.hook: Mary Rebecca Garrison married a Morgan County wagon maker, lost a brother in the last weeks of the war, and handed her father's Bible down to her daughter.

subject.name: Mary Rebecca (Garrison) Shackelford & S. W. Shackelford

body: Mary Rebecca Garrison, the youngest of Hezekiah and Rebecca Garrison's eleven children, was born in Morgan County, Alabama, on 23 June 1835. She was still at home with her widowed mother in 1850, by Stuart's reading of the census. On 29 September 1858 she married S. W. Shackelford. Her mother died in August 1873 at the Shackelfords' home near Moulton; Stuart notes that S. W. Shackelford also lived at Moulton, but the couple's longer home was Hartselle, in Morgan County, where both were buried.

A trade paper gives a glimpse of his work. The Manufacturers' Record of 12 March 1887, in a weekly department of industrial news arranged by state, noted under Alabama that "S. W. Shackelford is building a wagon and carriage shop at Hartselle, Ala." The notice says nothing more about him, but the name, the initials and the town agree with the family record.

The family list in the Bible names four Shackelford children. Fannie Laura, born on 10 March 1863, died on 1 April. Robert James, born on 28 August 1864, married Sallie C. Bennet at Zion, Kentucky, on 12 July 1886 and made his home in Nashville. Hillery Sather, born on 12 May 1873, was living at Wynnewood in the Indian Territory when his mother died. Minnie Ann Emma, born on 6 August 1876, married R. L. Cox of Hartselle and lived to be 102; she died in 1978 in a nursing home at Athens, Limestone County, and was buried beside her husband in the Shackelford lot at Hartselle.

Mary Rebecca's brother Andrew Jackson Garrison, born in Allen County, Kentucky, in April 1830, married Sarah Sanders in Morgan County on 30 January 1862. The Bible records in longhand that he "was killed by our Federal Enemys, April 1865, near Crutchers shop, Madison Cty., Ala.," and that he was "a member of Col. Meads Confederate Guerillers." No service record for him was found. The National Park Service soldiers index lists an Andrew J. Garrison as a sergeant in the 1st Alabama Reserves, but nothing in the index ties that man to this one.

Mary Rebecca died at Robert's home in Nashville. Her death notice, clipped from a Hartselle paper and kept in the Bible, says her body was brought home on a Sunday, her funeral was held at the Methodist church, and she was buried in Hartselle cemetery beside her husband. Stuart's copy does not give the date of the notice. She had inherited her father's Bible, with its handwritten records and pasted obituaries, and it passed to Minnie, who gave it to a Garrison cousin in Decatur; that is how the Garrison family record reached the compiler in 1979.

stories.title: School District No. 95, Marshan Township, 1874
stories.hook: A Minnesota county history of 1881 puts a James H. Satterfield on a new school board in 1874, the first record outside his own biography of the family's years in Dakota County.

subject.name: James H. Satterfield in Marshan Township, Minnesota

body: James H. Satterfield's 1885 biography says he moved from Allen County, Kentucky, to Dakota County, Minnesota, in 1867 and went back to Kentucky in 1875. His daughter A. M. was born in Minnesota in 1870, by her Find a Grave memorial. Until now nothing else on this site placed him there.

The History of Dakota County and the City of Hastings, published in 1881, has a chapter on each township. In the one on Marshan Township it tells how School District No. 95 began. The district was organized on 31 March 1874 at a school meeting at the house of W. B. Mather, which voted to raise $400 for a schoolhouse; the building went up on the northeast quarter of section 8, on land owned by Peter Huneicker. "The first trustees of the district were elected at this meeting, and were as follows: James H. Satterfield, director; L. D. Massey, clerk; William R. Mather, treasurer." Ella Gilkey taught the first term, four months in the winter of 1875-76, to about twenty-seven pupils. A 1910 history of Dakota and Goodhue counties repeats the passage with the same names.

Marshan, by the 1881 description, was bounded on the north by Nininger, Hastings and Ravenna, on the east by Ravenna, on the south by Douglass and on the west by Vermillion. Its soil was mostly sandy, and the Vermillion River crossed its western sections.

The name, the county and the years agree with his own account, and the school meeting falls a year before he says he left. The clerk's name is a second point of contact. James's sister Ruth M. Satterfield married a Massey, by the 1885 list of Henry Satterfield's children, and the memorials linked to her mother's place her burial, as Ruth Melissa Massey (1840-1935), at Amarillo. Whether L. D. Massey was her husband is not stated in anything seen, so that remains a lead. If the director was James, he did not stay to see the first term taught: by his own account he was in Warren County, Kentucky, in 1875.

stories.title: Proposed by J. P. Thompson: Joseph in the council records, 1890–1904
stories.hook: Joel remembered his father as a lawmaker for years, but no council record naming him had been found. The printed acts of the October 1904 session have one line that does: 'Proposed by J. P. Thompson.'

subject.name: Joseph Perry Thompson in the Choctaw General Council

body: An 1891 sketch of Joseph, printed while he was still under thirty, says he began as a schoolteacher, was appointed county clerk of Cedar County in 1889, and "the year following he was elected representative to the lower House," where he was "one of the youngest members of the legislature." His son Joel later added that he served as county judge and about six years as a senator. Until now none of this had been matched to a record of the General Council itself.

The council Joseph joined in 1890 passed several laws for his own county. A compilation of Choctaw laws printed in 1894 includes an act approved 31 October 1890 that redrew the line between Cedar and Nashoba counties along Ward's Creek, an act approved 15 October 1891 that set up an election precinct "at or near the Gilbert Cooper place" in Cedar County, to be called Lick precinct, and an act approved 3 December 1891 that moved the Cedar County court ground from Pine Hill to Sulphur Spring, the court ground Joel later remembered his father presiding over. The compilation does not print who proposed these acts or how anyone voted, so it shows what Joseph's council did, not what he did in it.

The clearest entry comes at the end. The Acts and Resolutions of the General Council for the October 1904 session, printed at Hugo, open with a run of resolutions giving each committee a clerk. Bill No. 3 authorized the chairman of the Committee on Petitions to appoint a clerk "to make and keep a full record of the work of said committee," at four dollars a day, paid by warrant of the National Auditor. It closes: "Proposed by J. P. Thompson." Like the bills around it, it took effect "by statute of limitation" on 13 October 1904 (the printer set the year as 1604), over the name of Principal Chief Green McCurtain, attested by J. W. Conser, recording secretary.

The book gives initials only. In the Dawes final-roll index, the only adult Choctaw citizen named Thompson whose given names begin with J. P. is Joseph P. Thompson, Roll No. 3487, of Card 1283, who was 40 on the final roll. That makes the identification probable rather than proven. The volume does not say whether J. P. Thompson sat in the House or the Senate, or which county sent him.

It is a small bill, but it places Joseph in the council when the Nation's land had already been divided: the year before, he had gone to Atoka to select the family's allotments. The printed acts of the 1902 and 1903 sessions, read for this story, contain no bill proposed by a Thompson, so the dates of his House term, his years as county judge and his time in the Senate are still to be found.

stories.title: Goodland court ground: Kiamitia County's seat in the Pisachubbes' years, 1889–1902
stories.hook: Eunice Pisachubbe's 1899 card gives her post office as Goodland. For thirteen years Goodland was also where Kiamitia County held court, until the council moved it three miles south to the new railroad town of Hugo in December 1902.
body: Goodland began as a Presbyterian mission station. George Ainslie, a missionary who had served there, answered questions about it in a letter to Sue McBeth that the Chronicles of Oklahoma printed in 1939. He put it about twelve miles southwest of Goodwater and eighteen miles from Doaksville, and said its church was "a colony from Goodwater." When he first saw it in 1852 it was "a pretty and pleasant station" of a mission house and a church that also served as the school, "surrounded by forest with no prairie near." In the same letter he notes that Goodland had only a day school.

The railroad changed its place in the county. On 28 October 1889 the General Council passed two acts for Kiamichi County, as the laws spell it. One moved the Clear Springs election precinct to "Good Land station" and set the first election there for the first Wednesday in August 1890. The other removed the county court ground from Clear Springs to "Good Land station on the St. Louis & San Francisco railway," with court to sit on the first Monday of every month beginning in January 1890. The county judge was to sell the old courthouse at Clear Springs and set the money aside for a new one at Good Land.

That is the Goodland of the family's records. On 10 May 1899 the Dawes clerk made out Card 1580 for Kiamitia County, post office "Goodland, I.T.": Eunice Pisachubbe, 49, her sons William H. and Robert, and her ward Edward. The Secretary of the Interior approved their enrollment on 12 December 1902.

A week later the court ground left. In an extra session in December 1902 the council moved the Goodland election precinct to Hugo, "about three miles south of the present site," with the first vote there in August 1903 (Bill No. 23, approved 18 December). Bill No. 28, approved 19 December, removed the county court ground "from its present site, at Goodland" to Hugo, told the county judge to choose a house in the town, and set the first term for the first Monday in February 1903. Bill No. 30, approved the same day, let the judge sell "the building formerly used as a court house at Goodland" and buy a building in Hugo "at the junction of the Arkansas & Choctaw Railroad and the St. Louis & San Francisco Railroad." All three were proposed by Jeff Fulton. The volume itself was printed at Hugo, by the Husonian Press, in 1903.

Hugo became the family's town. William Harrison Pisachubbe's funeral in 1937 was held near the Long Creek school house, Robert and Lizzie lived at Speer and then with Simon and Frances at Jeter, and Simon and Frances are buried at Long Creek Cemetery near Hugo, as their stories tell. The records here do not say where on the Goodland road Eunice's own house stood.

stories.title: A corporal named Edward Tims: a Confederate clothing roll, 1862
stories.hook: One card in the Confederate service records names an Edward Tims, third corporal in a Choctaw company in 1862. It gives no age and no home, so whether he was Betsy's uncle Edward is still an open question.

subject.name: Edward Tims, Company G, 1st Choctaw Mounted Rifles

body: The site's story of the 1865 surrender at Doaksville leaves open whether any relative served in the war. The National Archives' compiled service records for units raised directly by the Confederate government (microfilm M258, roll 83) hold a small file for "Tims, Edward" of Company G, 1st Choctaw Mounted Rifles, "also known as Cavalry." The jacket gives his rank as corporal and lists a single card, with no medical cards and no personal papers.

The card is a War Department copy of one line on a pay roll. "Edward Tims," "3d Corpl," of Capt. Coleman E. Nelson's Company, 1st Regiment Choctaw Mounted Rifles, appears on a roll of enlisted men for commutation of clothing "for the last six months of the year ending November 23, 1862." The sum is twenty-five dollars. The roll date is written "Aug 13, 1862," which falls before the end of the period it covers; the card does not explain that. A printed note says Nelson's company was also known as Company G.

Nelson's own file sets the regiment's scene. As captain of Company G of the 1st Choctaw Regiment he signed a petition dated at Fort McCulloch in June 1862, from officers of the Indian regiments in Confederate service, asking that their colonel, Sampson Folsom, be made a brigadier general in the Provisional Army. On the clothing roll, the card notes, his name appears only as the signature to the certificate.

The obvious candidate is Edward Ward Tims of Towson County. His Dawes card of 1899 gives his age as 58, so he would have been about twenty in 1862, and he is the only Edward Tims in the Choctaw by Blood index of the final rolls. But the war card names no county, father or age, nothing seen ties Nelson's company to Towson County, and none of the later records in his own story mentions service. Under the site's rules this stays a lead.

One place to check came up empty. The Oklahoma State Archives' index of Confederate pension applications has a single Tims, Mary Amanda, the widow of Francis Marion Tims, whose regiment is given as Texas; it has no application from Edward or from his widow Willie Jane, who died four months before him in 1922. A muster roll for Nelson's company, if one survives, would be the next record to find.

stories.title: Born in Fannin County: Benjamin F. Hulsey signs on at Cedar Glades, 1864
stories.hook: His own enlistment paper, signed with his mark, names the north Georgia county where he was born.

subject.name: Benjamin F. Hulsey, Company D, 4th Arkansas Cavalry (Union)

body: The compiled service record of Benjamin F. Hulsey, private, Company D, 4th Arkansas Cavalry, is a Union record from the War Department files, now digitized in the National Archives catalog. Besides eleven cards copied from the regiment's rolls, it holds the two papers he made when he joined. On the volunteer enlistment, sworn at Cedar Glades, Arkansas, on 14 January 1864 before Lt. J. B. Spiva of the 4th Arkansas Cavalry, he stated that he was "born in Fannin Co in the State of Georgia," aged eighteen, a farmer, and volunteered for three years. On the declaration of recruit he signed "Benjamin F Hulsey, his mark." The form for a parent's consent in the case of a minor was left blank.

The papers describe him as having black eyes, black hair and a dark complexion. They do not agree on his height: the enlistment gives five feet nine inches, while the descriptive roll and the company descriptive book both give five feet three. He was mustered into service at Little Rock on 17 February 1864. The detachment roll assigns him to Company L, but every company muster roll carries him in Company D. He brought his own mount: the rolls credit him with pay "for use and risk of horse and equipments" from enlistment to 20 June 1864.

He was present on every muster roll from enlistment through April 1865. In November 1864 he was on daily duty "at work on stables," and in February and March 1865 he was on detached service in the quartermaster's department as a teamster. He was mustered out with the company at Little Rock on 30 June 1865, still recorded as eighteen. A War Department card of 1891 in the file adds that the regiment, "late Inf," had been ordered disbanded by Special Orders No. 121, Department of Arkansas, of 2 June 1864, "the War Dept not sanctioning the raising of a one year Regt"; his rolls nonetheless run on to June 1865.

Fannin County was created in 1854 from parts of Gilmer and Union counties. A boy of eighteen in January 1864 was born about 1845 or 1846, before the county existed, so the name he gave is most likely the county his birthplace lay in by the time he enlisted. In the 1850 census of Union County a Benjamin, three, was in the household of the blacksmith Salathiel Hulsey, and in 1880 the B. F. Hulsey of Center Township, Montgomery County, gave his age as 32 and his birthplace as Georgia. The three ages differ by a year or two. The Fannin County birthplace fits the Union County household and is the first record seen in which Benjamin himself names where he was born, but it names no parent.

He was not the only family name on that day's list. On the same 14 January 1864, at Cedar Glades and before the same Lieutenant Spiva, Gillam Graves, 45, born in Randolph County, North Carolina, signed his own enlistment into the same company. Gilliam Graves was the grandfather of Sarah Rebecca Graves, who in 1901 married George Washington Hulsey (see "A horse lost near Harrold and two months' pay").

stories.title: A horse lost near Harrold and two months' pay: Gilliam Graves's service record
stories.hook: On the day Dr. Brown of Cedar Glades was shot, the enemy took Gilliam Graves's horse in a fight in his own county.

subject.name: Gilliam Graves, Company D, 4th Arkansas Cavalry (Union)

body: The compiled service record of Gillam Graves, private, Company D, 4th Arkansas Cavalry, holds twenty images, among them his own volunteer enlistment. Sworn at Cedar Glades on 14 January 1864 before Lt. J. B. Spiva, it says he was born in Randolph County, North Carolina, was 45 years old and a farmer, with black eyes, black hair and a dark complexion, five feet ten inches tall. He was mustered into the service at Little Rock on 17 February 1864. The company descriptive book repeats Randolph, N.C., as his birthplace. Until now this site has had that birthplace only from the Graves family genealogy; the enlistment is his own statement. The cards note that his name "also appears as Gillman Graves."

Like most of the company he rode his own horse, and the rolls pay him for its use from enlistment. A War Department notation of 7 May 1869 explains a gap in that pay: "Horse and equipments captured by the enemy while engaged in action near Harrold Montgomery Co. Ark. March 1st, 1864," so that he was "not entitled to pay for use of horse from March 1st, 1864 to April 10th, 1864." The first of March 1864 is the day the Union men of Montgomery County said Dr. Brown of Cedar Glades was shot down, and the day the army lists a skirmish at Cedar Glade (see the story of the March 1864 petition). Harrold is spelled as on the card; the place has not been identified.

The later cards give the rest of what the family genealogy had summarized. The return for September 1864 has him absent without leave, and in October he "Deserted Oct. 12/64 at Little Rock," with $18 stopped for arms and accoutrements. He returned on 25 December 1864, "in arrest" on one roll and "restored to duty without loss of pay" on the next. He was then tried by a general court-martial for absence without leave and sentenced to forfeit two months' pay and allowances, under General Orders No. 8 of the Cavalry Division, 7th Army Corps, dated 28 December 1864, as the muster-out roll records. He was present on the rolls for early 1865 and was mustered out at Little Rock on 30 June 1865, last paid to 30 June 1864.

He did not serve alone. Benjamin F. Hulsey enlisted the same day before the same officer, and Alson Graves, eighteen, who is probably the Alison Graves of the orphaned household Gilliam had in his guardianship, was in Company D as well (see the stories on each).

quotes.t: Horse and equipments captured by the enemy while engaged in action near Harrold Montgomery Co. Ark. March 1st, 1864
quotes.c: War Department notation, 7 May 1869, service record of Gillam Graves

stories.title: Alson Graves, the ward who enlisted at eighteen
stories.hook: One of the orphans in Gilliam Graves's guardianship turns up beside him in the same Union company.
body: In January 1854, and again in April 1861, Gilliam Graves was named guardian of the minor children of Samuel and Sarah Graves of Montgomery County, Arkansas. The 1860 census, as the Graves genealogy gives it, lists them in a household of their own: William (Riley), 22, Alley, 17, Ursa, 15, Alison, 14, and Madison, 11, all born in North Carolina ("Gilliam Graves and the orphans of Samuel and Sarah").

A compiled service record filed as "Graves, Allison," with the name on the cards as Alson Graves, carries the story forward. Alson Graves, eighteen and a farmer, volunteered at Little Rock on 21 November 1863 for three years, enlisted by William Brown, recruiting officer of the 4th Arkansas Cavalry, before Capt. Geo. H. Hand. He signed by his mark. He was six feet tall. He first appears on a detachment muster-in roll of Lieut. Vance's company, 3rd Arkansas Cavalry, dated at Benton, Arkansas, on 6 December 1863, whose card notes that the organization afterward became part of the 4th. He was mustered into Company L of the 4th Arkansas Cavalry at Little Rock on 21 April 1864, and from then on the company rolls carry him in Company D.

The papers disagree about where he was born and what he looked like. The enlistment and the detachment roll say New Hanover County, North Carolina, with black eyes, black hair and a dark complexion. The company descriptive book says Randolph County, North Carolina, with grey eyes, dark hair and a fair complexion. Randolph County is where the Graves genealogy places the 1837 marriage of Samuel Graves and Sarah Cole.

He was present on every roll from enlistment to April 1865. His first roll notes "No horse," and later rolls pay him for the use of a horse. He was mustered out with the company at Little Rock on 30 June 1865, his age still given as eighteen. His guardian Gilliam Graves served in the same company, which he had joined at Cedar Glades on 14 January 1864.

The name, the age (fourteen in 1860, eighteen in late 1863), the North Carolina birth and his service in his guardian's company all fit the Alison of the 1860 household and the 1861 guardianship, and nothing seen contradicts them. How Samuel and Sarah's children were related to Gilliam remains unknown.

stories.title: W. E. F. Stevenson of the Third Tennessee: Fort Donelson, Camp Douglas and back
stories.hook: Abner Stevenson's eldest son went to war at nineteen with a Giles County company and spent the summer of 1862 in a prison camp in Chicago.
body: William Elam Fletcher Stevenson was the eldest son of Rev. Abner A. Stevenson and Martha S. Watson, born on 9 April 1842 according to the family history that lists their fifteen children ("Fifteen children at Bee Spring"). His initials, W. E. F., are unusual enough to follow. A Confederate compiled service record for W. E. F. Stevenson, private in the 3rd (Clack's) Tennessee Infantry, shows that he enlisted on 17 May 1861 at Nashville, mustered by Inspector Scudder for twelve months. One card describes the regiment as first organized at Lynnville, Tennessee, on 16 May 1861.

Goodspeed's 1886 history of Giles County says the Third Tennessee was organized at Lynnville, "this county," on 16 May 1861, and that five of its ten companies came from Giles County. Among them was Company K under Capt. F. C. Barber, which at the reorganization in September 1862 became Company A. Stevenson's cards carry him first in Company K and then in Company A, exactly as that company was renumbered.

The regiment went to Fort Donelson in February 1862. W. E. F. Stevenson was captured there on 16 February and appears on a roll of prisoners of war at Camp Douglas, Illinois, of 1 August 1862. A roll dated at Camp Douglas on 7 September 1862 lists him among the prisoners sent to Vicksburg to be exchanged; its endorsement records that 824 prisoners were received on board the steamer Jno. H. Done near Vicksburg on 23 September 1862. The regiment was reorganized at Jackson, Mississippi, three days later.

He was present on every muster roll from August 1862 through February 1864, once noted as absent from Chickasaw Bayou on detached duty, and by early 1864 his term was entered as "war." He drew clothing on 30 April 1864, signing "E F Stevenson," and again on 7 June 1864, when the receipt has only a mark. A hospital register shows him admitted to the 1st Mississippi C.S.A. Hospital at Jackson, Mississippi, on 28 October 1864 with intermittent fever, and returned to duty on 22 November. The cards stop there. The regiment was merged into the 4th Consolidated Tennessee Infantry about 9 April 1865 and paroled at Greensboro, North Carolina, on 1 May 1865, but no parole card is filed for him.

His younger brother Frank, the family's 2nd great-grandfather, was born in Giles County in November 1861, six months after William enlisted. The record answers, at least in part, the question left open in the story of their cousin Coleman Stevenson of the 32nd Tennessee: one of Abner's own sons did serve.

quotes.t: five of which were supplied by Giles County

stories.title: A Georgia-born Robert Hulsey loses an eye: a Confederate discharge, December 1862
stories.hook: Two years before Benjamin F. Hulsey rode for the Union, a Robert Hulsey of the right age was sent home from a Confederate hospital half blind.

subject.name: Robert Hulsey, Company B, 8th Battalion Arkansas Infantry (Confederate)

body: The Confederate compiled service record of Robert Hulsey, private, Company B, 8th Battalion Arkansas Infantry, is short: an index card, a jacket and his certificate of discharge. The certificate, written at the General Hospital "Okolona" at Meridian, Mississippi, on 15 December 1862, says he was enlisted by Capt. Imboden on 5 March 1862 to serve three years, at a place in Arkansas that reads like "Cordova." It gives his birthplace as Habersham County, Georgia, his age as 30 and his height as five feet six inches, with a dark complexion, blue eyes and dark hair, a farmer.

The examining board of three surgeons found him unable to serve "because of chronic ophthalmia & loss of one eye and serious injury of the other," and recommended his discharge under General Order No. 72. He was honorably discharged at Marion, Mississippi, on 21 December 1862. A clerk's jacket in the file is headed "Discharge of Priv. Robt. Hulsey according to general orders No. 72, Marion, Miss., Dec. 15th 1862."

Why this Robert matters is his age and birthplace. Thirty in 1862 places his birth about 1831 or 1832. The Robert in Salathiel Hulsey's Union County, Georgia, household was 17 in November 1850, and the Georgia-born Robert Hulsey of Hempstead County, Arkansas, was 27 in 1860; both point to about 1833.

Nothing in the file names his parents, his wife or his home county in Arkansas, and the record of where Company B was raised has not been examined here. He may be Salathiel's son Robert and the Hempstead County farmer, and so a possible older brother of the Benjamin F. Hulsey who joined the Union 4th Arkansas Cavalry in 1864, but none of those links is proven.

quotes.t: chronic ophthalmia & loss of one eye and serious injury of the other

stories.title: Elected at Richwoods, dismissed at court-martial: D. H. Grimes, 1862–1863
stories.hook: A 33-year-old Tennessean in Izard County was elected lieutenant within six weeks of enlisting and was dismissed by court-martial eight months later.
body: The Confederate service file of "D. H. Grimes," Company I, 27th Arkansas Infantry, is short, nine cards in all, but it holds the only description of him yet found. He enrolled on 6 July 1862 at Richwoods, in Izard County, under Captain Riggs, "for the war." The muster-in roll, made at Camp Bragg, Arkansas, on 31 July 1862, lists him as second corporal of Company I in what was then the 1st Regiment of McBride's Brigade, and gives his age as 33. The regiment was also known by its colonel's name, as Shaler's Regiment.

Six weeks later his company chose him as an officer. A roll for July and August 1862 notes "Promoted to Jun. 2nd Lt. Aug. 18, 1862," and a statement of the officers of the 5th (Tappan's) Brigade, Price's Division, dated 6 April 1863, records him as elected on 18 August 1862, aged 33, from Izard County, Arkansas, and born in Tennessee. Two rosters of Hindman's Division for February 1863 list him as third and second lieutenant, and the second of them marks him "Absent sick." A company roll dated 28 February 1863 says instead "Absent without leave."

By the roll for March and April 1863 he was present but "In arrest," and a register of the Provisional Army's commissioned officers closes his record: "Dismissed Court Martial Apr. 4, 1863." The file does not say what the charge was. It may be connected with the absence without leave noted a few weeks earlier, but no card says so.

Whether this lieutenant is Hannah Moffitt's father is still open. David H. Grimes of the family tree was born in 1829 in Wayne County, Tennessee, which fits a man of 33 in 1862 who was born in Tennessee, and Hannah's own 1900 census entry gives Tennessee for both her parents. Against that, the same tree places David in the lower Mississippi country of Arkansas in the 1850s and has him dying there in 1876, far from Izard County, and nothing in the file names a wife or child. The research guide quoted in "Two uniforms, two pension claims" says a widow of a David H. Grimes of this regiment later sought a Union pension; that file, if it can be found, is the record most likely to settle the question.

stories.title: The Turtle Paws: Marshall Moffitt, who died at Greenville in 1863
stories.hook: William C. Moffitt's son Marshall, whose 1863 death the family tree recorded without a cause, was a private in a Chatham County company of the 44th North Carolina.
body: The story of William C. Moffitt's family on this site notes that his son Marshall died in 1863, "which fits the Civil War, but no record of his service has been seen." The record exists. A Confederate service file in the National Archives for "Marshall D. Moffitt" places him in Company E of the 44th North Carolina Infantry, a company raised in neighboring Chatham County and known as "The Turtle Paws."

The company's muster-in and descriptive roll, made at Camp Mangum near Raleigh on 3 April 1862, says he was born in Randolph County, was 23 years old and stood 5 feet 10 inches. He had enrolled in March, at Lows Store according to that roll and at Pittsboro according to the muster rolls, for three years or the war, and he signed the oath of allegiance to the State of North Carolina himself, as "M. D. Moffitt." He was present on the company's rolls from March through August 1862 and again on the roll for January and February 1863, last paid to 31 December 1862.

A register of Confederate soldiers who died of wounds or disease records his death on 28 March 1863 at Greenville, North Carolina. The state's Roll of Honor gives his county as Randolph, his entry into service as 4 March 1862 and his age as 21, and says simply that he "Died April 1863 of Disease."

His age of 23 in 1862 fits the birth year of 1839 given for William C.'s son Marshall, and the Randolph birthplace and the 1863 death agree, so the identification is probable. The cards do not name his parents. His file also holds a stray card for a "W. D. Moffitt," captain of Company H of the same regiment, who resigned on 16 July 1862, and the regiment had another Randolph-born private, Milo M. Moffitt, 18, in the same company; neither is identified here, and Milo is too young to be William C.'s son of that name, born in 1828.

stories.title: Three days apart at Raleigh: the Rains brothers of the Randolph Rangers, 1862
stories.hook: Two of Lydia Moffitt Rains's sons enrolled on the same day in March 1862 and died of disease at Raleigh within three days of each other that May.

subject.name: Nathan, Daniel and Alfred E. Rains

body: On this site's page for Nathan Moffitt's sisters, a family-tree note says that two of Lydia Moffitt Rains's sons, Nathan and William Anderson, "died in the Civil War," and that the units were not checked. The Confederate service files in the National Archives tell a somewhat different story. They show a Nathan Rains and a Daniel Rains, both born in Randolph County, who enrolled together and died within days of each other in the spring of 1862.

Both men enrolled for active service on 5 March 1862 at Holts, in Randolph County, in Captain O. W. Carr's company, the "Randolph Rangers," which became Company G of the 46th North Carolina Infantry. The company's muster-in and descriptive roll, dated at Camp Mangum near Raleigh on 16 April 1862, lists each as a farmer born in Randolph County; Nathan stood 5 feet 11 1/2 inches and Daniel 5 feet 9 3/4. Each signed the state oath of allegiance, "N. Rains" and "D. Rains." No ages are given.

Neither left Raleigh. The North Carolina Roll of Honor says Nathan "Died May 14 1862 of Disease at Raleigh" and Daniel died there of disease on 17 May. The Confederate register of deaths agrees on both dates, and a register of the Pettigrew General Hospital, No. 13, at Raleigh, lists N. Rains under "Discharges on Surgeon's certificates and deaths" with a death date of 18 May 1862. The cards do not name the illness.

A third brother came later and came home. Alfred E. Rains (also carded as A. Rains and A. C. Rains) was enlisted for the war at Camp Holmes on 19 August 1864 by Colonel Mallett, and served as a private in Company G of the 38th North Carolina Infantry. He drew clothing in November and December 1864, signing by mark, and he was paroled at Greensboro on 19 May 1865 as one of the men surrendered with the Army of Northern Virginia. No service file for a William Anderson Rains was found in this search, so whether he also died in the war remains unconfirmed.

stories.title: Robert Livesay’s land at Beaucoup
stories.hook: Three federal patents put Robert Livesay on 320 acres in the Beaucoup timber, in the same section as the cemetery where his infant son Jasper was buried in 1841.
body: Until now Robert Livesay was known on this site only from a descendant’s sketch, a cemetery line and a court paper copied into that sketch. The federal government’s own land records add something firmer. The General Land Office index lists three patents to a Robert Livesay for land in Washington County, Illinois, each a cash sale through the land office at Kaskaskia. The first, dated 1 August 1838, covered 200 acres: the southeast quarter of the southeast quarter of Section 11 and the east halves of the northeast quarters of Sections 14 and 23, all in Township 2 South, Range 2 West of the Third Principal Meridian. The second, dated 10 October 1840, added 80 acres in Section 24, and the third, dated 10 March 1843, another 40 acres in Section 11.

Those are the dates the patents were signed, not necessarily the dates Robert chose the land or paid for it; cash entries were often patented a year or more after the sale. Together the three gave him 320 acres, half a square mile, in one block of adjoining sections. The patents themselves would not open when this story was written, so the details come from the index entries.

The township is Beaucoup. The volunteer transcription of Beaucoup Cemetery places the cemetery in Section 23 of Township 2 South, Range 2 West, the same section as part of Robert’s first purchase, and the Bethel (Darter) Cemetery transcription confirms that this township and range is Beaucoup Township. In that cemetery a stone lists Jasper L. Livesay, who died on 16 August 1841, as “son of Robert & Lydia.” The family sketch gives Jasper’s birth as 15 February 1841, so he lived six months. David P. Livesay, the lead for Floyd Livesay’s father, was buried in the same cemetery in 1904.

The sons followed. On the same day as Robert’s third patent, 10 March 1843, William E. Livesay, named first among Robert’s heirs in 1856, received 40 acres in Section 13 of the same township, next to his father’s land in Sections 14 and 24, and in 1848 he and Demsy Kennedy took 80 acres in Section 12. Jackson M. Livesay’s patent of 1 February 1850 lay a few miles east, in Section 8 of Township 2 South, Range 1 West, the Richview township. No patent to David P. Livesay appeared in the index.

Robert died on 15 February 1855, according to the sketch. The county’s probate index lists an estate file for him, which has not been seen. These patents are the earliest records found so far that place him on the ground, and they make the Beaucoup neighborhood the home place of the family Floyd Livesay grew up among.

A Robert B. Livesay of Nashville, born about 1825, was too young to buy land in 1838. Floyd stays unlinked from David P. and from Robert.

stories.title: Robert and Lydia’s heirs, checked one by one
stories.hook: An 1856 release names eight living heirs of Robert Livesay. County registers, land patents and a bank’s loan book confirm most of them, and one son the family sketch counts is missing from the list.

subject.name: The children of Robert and Lydia Livesay

body: After Robert Livesay died in February 1855, his older children signed a release in favor of the younger ones. The family sketch of Jackson Monroe Livesay copies it: William E., Lorenzo M., Jackson M. and David P. Livesay, and Unity Jane with her husband, gave up their claims on the personal estate until the three minors, Nancy P., Daniel M. and Elbert T. Livesay, had each received $125. All eight are called “heirs at law” of Robert. The paper is known here only from that transcription; the county’s probate index confirms that an estate file for Robert exists, but it has not been opened.

The adults can be checked against the county’s marriage registers, which volunteers have transcribed. William E. Livesay married Emily Goodner on a license of 1 August 1844. Lorenzo M. Livesay married Margaret Jane Thompson on 22 October 1845. Jackson M. Livesay married Lucinda A. Thompson on 15 November 1849, and James L. Logan married Unity J. Livesay the next day. The sketch says the Thompson brides were daughters of Isaiah and Hannah (Phillips) Thompson; the registers give only names and dates. William E. and Jackson M. also appear as federal land patentees, William beside his father’s land at Beaucoup in 1843 and Jackson near Richview in 1850.

The minors are harder. The sketch gives Nancy Paulina’s birth as 19 June 1838, Daniel Marion’s as 25 July 1842 and Elbert Trumbell’s as 7 February 1845, but only the censuses, described next, show them together. One small trace may be Daniel’s. The Hoyleton loan book records two personal notes written on 7 March 1879 and numbered one after the other: no. 17, $60 for D. P. Livesay, and no. 18, $50 for D. M. Livesay, the second marked paid on 14 May 1880. The book, presumed to be the Hoyleton bank’s, gives no relationship, so the D. M. who borrowed beside D. P. is only probably his brother Daniel.

The censuses do. In the 1850 enumeration of Washington County, the household of Robert Livesay (written “Livesy”) lists Lydia, 43, and David P., 20, Thomas N., 15, Nancy P., 13, Daniel M., 8 and Elbert T., 6. In June 1860, five years after Robert’s death, a household headed by Lydia Livesay, 52, born in Tennessee, in the same township lists David, 28, Thomas, 24, “Palina,” 20, Daniel, 17 and “Trumbull,” 15. The names are the sketch’s middle names: Nancy Paulina and Elbert Trumbell. The ages run seven to nine years above the 1850 ages, a little more than ten years would require, so the match rests on the order of the names and the middle names, not on exact ages. The census does not state relationships in either year, and a four-year-old, Floyd H. Livesay, is in the 1860 household too (see “Floyd Livesay in Lydia’s household, 1860”).

The list also has a gap. The sketch counts ten children and says nine survived Robert, yet the release names only eight. Jasper died in 1841, which accounts for one. The other missing child is Thomas Newton Livesay, born 22 February 1836 according to the sketch. He may have died before 1856, received his share another way, or been left off the copy; the sketch does not say, and nothing found here settles it.

None of this names Floyd Livesay. It does show that the sketch’s account of Robert and Lydia’s family holds up wherever an independent record can be found, which strengthens, without proving, its placement of David Pinkney among their sons. The Civil War rosters in the 1879 county history list several Livesays in the 49th and 60th Illinois Infantry, but none of the sons named in the release.

Lydia is not named in the release; she is linked as their mother on the strength of the sketch and Jasper’s stone. David P. is linked to Robert and Lydia as a probable son on the same footing (named in the release; his stone’s 1831 agrees with the sketch), though his being Floyd’s father remains a lead. Daniel M. is added as a lead only, and Nancy P., Elbert T. and Thomas N. are not added. Floyd stays unlinked.

stories.title: Lorenzo M. Livesay across the county line
stories.hook: In 1860 and 1870 the census taker found David P. Livesay’s older brother farming in Jefferson County, the county where Tabitha Livesay is buried.
body: Lorenzo Mastin Livesay was the second of Robert and Lydia’s sons in the family sketch, about five when the family left Maury County, Tennessee. He married Margaret Jane Thompson in Washington County on 22 October 1845, and in 1856 he signed the release as one of his father’s heirs at law.

By 1860 he had crossed into Jefferson County, the next county east. On 12 June 1860 the census taker for Township 2 South, Range 4 East, with a Mount Vernon post office, listed Lorenzo M. Livesay, 34, a farmer born in Tennessee, with real estate worth $2,000. With him were Margaret J., 32, also born in Tennessee, and three children born in Illinois: Ephraim J., 11, Mary C., 4, and Elizabeth P., 1. The ages fit the sketch’s account of a boy born in Tennessee about 1825.

Ten years later, on 29 July 1870, he was in Webber Township, in the same township and range, with a Lynchburg post office. Lorenzo M., 44, farmer, born in Tennessee, now held real estate worth $2,400. His wife was Sarah S., 36, born in Kentucky, so Margaret had probably died, though no record of her death was found. Mary C., 14, Elisabeth P., 11, Wilburn W., 9, Elva M., 6, and Lafaetta S., 5, were at home. In the dwelling listed just before his lived a Jasper Livesay, 21, and his wife Belle; the census does not say how they were related.

Lorenzo’s move matters for Floyd’s story because it puts a Livesay household in Jefferson County in the 1850s, the county where Tabitha J., “wife of David P. Livesay,” was buried at Gilead in 1856. Gilead lies in Grand Prairie Township, while Lorenzo’s 1870 home was in Webber Township, so the two were not in the same township. The households show that Robert’s sons moved freely across the county line; they do not explain how David P. came to marry a Jefferson County woman.
The census entries were read in a volunteer transcription of the Jefferson County returns. The originals were not examined.

stories.title: Tabitha J. Flannigan, aged 20
stories.hook: Six years before her stone was cut at Gilead, a Tabitha J. was living in Jefferson County with Thomas and Patsy Flannigan, whose own stones stand in the same cemetery.
body: Earlier stories on this site reported that Find a Grave and a family tree give Tabitha J. Livesay’s maiden name as Flannigen or Flannigan, and that the Gilead Cemetery transcription lists a Thomas H. Flannigan and a Martha Flennigen, “w/o Thomas,” near her. Nothing connected them. The 1850 census of Jefferson County, now read in a volunteer transcription, comes close.

On 8 August 1850 the census taker Robert Wingate listed household 443: Thomas A. Flannigan, 54, a farmer born in North Carolina; Patsy, 48, born in Georgia; Tabitha J., 20; James R., 18, a farmer; and Maria, 16, all three born in Illinois. Two Copple children, Amanda, 4, and Martha L., one month old, were also in the house. Two of the households just before it were Baldridges, a family well represented among the Gilead stones.

The fit with the Gilead record is close. Tabitha J. Livesay’s stone says she died on 14 February 1856 aged 27 years, 2 months and 4 days, which places her birth about 10 December 1828; a woman born then would have been 21 in August 1850, one year more than the census gives. Thomas H. Flannigan’s stone gives his death on 28 January 1853 at 58 years and 11 days, a birth in January 1795, within a year of the census age of 54. Patsy was the usual nickname for Martha, and Martha Flennigen, “wife of Thomas,” died on 9 July 1862. The census initial A and the stone’s H for Thomas do not agree, which may be a misreading in either transcription. A Thos. Flanagan also headed a Jefferson County household in 1830, and a Thos. A. Flanagan in 1840.

The 1850 census did not record relationships, so it does not say that Tabitha J. was Thomas and Patsy’s daughter, and it does not give her surname as anything but the household’s. No marriage record for David P. Livesay and Tabitha has been found in the Washington County register transcriptions; the Jefferson County marriage transcriptions found online stop at 1829. On the present evidence Thomas A. and Martha Flannigan are the most likely parents of Tabitha J. Livesay, and therefore possible great-grandparents of Floyd, but both links were leads when this story was written. Later stories (the 1840 page, the Whites of Jefferson County and the Gilead burials) strengthened the first, and Tabitha J. is now linked to Thomas A. and Patsy Flannigan in the tree as a probable daughter. Her being Floyd’s mother, or Thomas and Patsy being Floyd’s great-grandparents, remains a lead.

If the identification holds, Tabitha married David P. Livesay between August 1850 and the 1855 state census, which counted a woman aged 20 to 30 in D. P. Livesay’s Washington County house. She died in February 1856, and was buried among her own family at Gilead rather than with the Livesays at Beaucoup.

stories.title: Carters and Livesays: from Tennessee to the Beaucoup timber
stories.hook: The family sketch says Robert Livesay came to Illinois with his parents, aunts, uncles and cousins. Land patents and the 1879 county history show that clan arriving, while Robert’s and Lydia’s own parents stay out of reach.

subject.name: Robert and Lydia Livesay’s parents and kin

body: The family sketch of Jackson Monroe Livesay gives Robert Livesay’s parents as John and Rebecca (Carter) Livesay. It says John’s sister Alice married Rebecca’s brother Robert Carter, both couples in Franklin County, Virginia, in the 1780s; that the families moved to Maury County, Tennessee, some time after 1809; and that about 1830 more than fifty of them moved on to Washington County, Illinois, with the Carters going first. For Lydia it gives parents Edmund Fitzgerald and Sarah “Sally” Dodson and a birth on 16 October 1807 in Williamson County, Tennessee. None of those Virginia or Tennessee claims could be checked here: the Maury County marriage transcriptions on the USGenWeb archives would not load, and no Fitzgerald or Livesay record from Williamson County was found. A small family burial ground called the Edmund Fitzgerald Cemetery is recorded in Maury County, about nine miles north of Columbia, but nothing found says who that Edmund was.

The Illinois end of the story is better documented. The earliest federal patent found for this family in the state was issued on 10 December 1823 to Livesay Carter and Robert Carter jointly, for 160 acres in what is now Clinton County, through the Edwardsville land office. The 1879 county history says that Livesay Carter, a native of Virginia, went to Tennessee in 1807, came to Illinois in 1818, lived about four years in what became Clinton County and then settled near Nashville. Livesay Carter took his first Washington County patent in 1826, and a Carter Livesay his first in 1831. A Lorenza D. Livesay was patented 80 acres in Section 21 of Township 2 South, Range 2 West on 11 November 1831, and John W. Livesay land in Section 31 in 1834. All of it lay in the same township where Robert bought in 1838.

The county history fills in the community. It lists the Livisays and Carters among the families of the Beaucoup settlement, names Livesay Carter and L. D. Livesay among the first settlers of Nashville precinct, and lists John Livesay among the Methodists meeting at Alexander Anderson’s house in 1832. It records that William B. Livesay laid out the town of Richmond, later Richview, on Section 10 in 1839, and that J. M. Livesay and L. D. Livesay later laid out an addition to it. Lorenzo D. Livesay served as a private in J. Burns’s company in the Black Hawk War of 1832.

A volunteer list of Washington County veterans calls Lorenzo Dow Livesay a son of “John C. & Rebecca (nee Carter) Livesay.” If that is right, and if the sketch is right that Robert was a son of John and Rebecca, then Lorenzo Dow was Robert’s brother and William B., the sketch’s eleventh child of John, another. The list gives no source for the parentage, and its birth estimate for Lorenzo, about 1815, is hard to square with a land patent in his name in 1831. The 1855 Illinois state census points the other way: it counts L. D. Livesay’s household with one man aged 50 to 60, which would place his birth between about 1795 and 1805, close to Robert’s own.

For now Robert’s parents, his possible brother Lorenzo Dow and Lydia’s parents remain leads, and they are not linked in the tree. The best next steps are the Washington County estate files for Rebecca Livesay (numbered 26 and 36 in the probate index) and the Maury County marriage books, which may hold Robert’s own marriage to Lydia, probably in the early 1820s, since the sketch has the eldest son born about 1823 and Lydia born in 1807.

The patents and county history show Carters and Livesays settling the same township from 1823 on, which fits the sketch’s account of a clan migration but does not prove any one relationship. stories.title: Old Settlers Cemetery and the 1890s settlers
stories.hook: Floyd Livesay reached Pearland in the town’s first years, when a land campaign was drawing families from the North. The cemetery begun in 1894 is where he and Alice were buried.

subject.name: Floyd and Alice Livesay at Pearland

body: The Texas Historical Commission’s marker for Old Settlers Cemetery, placed in 1988 on Halik Road in Pearland, gives the town’s beginnings in a few lines. Settlement followed the railroad through northern Brazoria County in 1882. The townsite, first known as Mark Belt, was platted in 1894 and named Pearland for its pear orchards, and an advertising campaign praising the farm conditions “brought many settlers to the area in the 1890s.” Storms and freezes discouraged some of them, the marker says, but many stayed.

Floyd Livesay was one of those 1890s settlers. A Houston notice at his death in 1932, cited in an earlier story, put his move from Illinois to Pearland about 37 years before, and the 1900 census found him in Brazoria County with children born in Illinois and a daughter born in Texas about 1898. He came, then, within a year or two of the townsite’s platting.

The cemetery began with the burial of Echolean C. Ackerly on 11 August 1894, and four years later her plot and the land around it were dedicated as a community burial ground. The marker describes the early ways of marking graves there, from earth scraped over the grave to cement paving, gravel and brick, and stones ranging from plain markers to carved tombstones. It remained Pearland’s main cemetery until 1936.

Three of the Livesays belong to that period. William Paul Livesay, Floyd and Alice’s son, died in San Antonio in 1915 and was brought back to Pearland for burial. Alice died in 1922 and Floyd in 1932, and earlier stories on this site report that they lie side by side in Old Settlers Cemetery; Floyd’s death certificate records burial at Pearland on 6 May 1932. When Floyd was buried, the graveyard had four years left as the town’s principal cemetery, and the family’s later burials are elsewhere, at Alvin and in East Texas.
The marker does not name the Livesays, and the burial details here come from records cited in earlier stories rather than from a new examination of the stones.
