stories.title: The James Walker household in 1850
stories.hook: The original 1850 census page for Beaucoup puts a nineteen-year-old William P. Walker in the home of James and Etheldra Walker, and gives both parents’ birthplaces for the first time.
body: The 1850 federal census of Washington County was taken in District No. 20 by assistant marshal Gabriel Jones. The microfilmed schedules are scanned on the Internet Archive, and dwelling 148 appears near the foot of image 220 of reel 131. It is headed by James Walker, 50, a farmer with real estate worth $1,000, born in Tennessee. Below him are Etheldra, 45, born in Virginia; William P., 19, a farmer; Etheldra J., 17; a boy of 10 whose name most likely reads James H.; and a girl of 8 whose name is too faded to read. The household runs over to the next page, which is dated 23 August 1850, with Sarah E., 5. All five children were born in Illinois.

The ages match the Beaucoup stones closely. Rev. James Walker died in April 1857 aged 57, so he was born in March 1800; the older Etheldra’s stone points to 1804 or 1805; William P. Walker was born on 15 March 1831; and the younger Etheldra J., wife of Simeon Walker, was born on 31 July 1833. Censuses before 1880 do not state relationships, so this page does not prove that William was James and Etheldra’s son. But a William P. of exactly the right age, living in their house the year before his marriage, together with his naming of his eldest daughter Mary Ellen Etheldra, is enough to treat them as his probable parents. A register transcription records her marriage as Mary E. E. Walker to Andrew J. Scott on 22 November 1871. On that basis, this archive now links William to Rev. James and Etheldra in the tree.

The page also answers where the couple came from, at least in outline: James from Tennessee and Etheldra from Virginia. That agrees with the 1879 county history, which says the first Beaucoup settlers came from Tennessee. Etheldra’s maiden name is still unknown. Find a Grave calls William’s mother Etheldra Jane Ballard, and an earlier story suggested that the name might blend the two Etheldras. It is worth noting that the very next household, dwelling 149, was headed by John Ballard, 36, a farmer whose birthplace the marshal wrote as “unknown,” with Henry, 21, born in Tennessee. Living next door proves nothing about kinship, so the Ballard name stays a lead.

Several other Walker households were counted in the same district in 1850. Simeon Walker, 48, headed dwelling 280 with Sally and a son Simeon, 19. George W. Walker, 23, with Elizabeth and the baby Frances C. E., lived at dwelling 432; Levi S. Walker, 20, and William H. Walker, 22, lived at 435 and 436; and John W. Walker, 25, with Lavina E. and an infant son, lived at 460. John W. and George W. were born about 1825 and 1827, old enough to have been older sons of James and Etheldra who had already married and left home, but no record opened here says so. The only siblings this page supports for William are the children still at home: Etheldra J., the boy of 10, the girl of 8 and Sarah E.

The county’s probate index, compiled from the courthouse files before 1910, lists an estate for James Walker (index number 18) and one for “Ethaldra” Walker (number 96). Neither file has been examined. Rev. James died in 1857 and Etheldra in 1878, so either packet could name heirs and settle the relationships that this census only implies.

stories.title: Abigail Shank, sixteen, born in New York
stories.hook: Eighteen months before a William Walker took out a license to marry Abigail Schanck, the census found a sixteen-year-old Abigail Shank living with a young Beaucoup family. She was born in New York, not Illinois.
body: The same 1850 census district that holds the James Walker household also holds dwelling 462, on a page dated 9 September 1850. Its head was David S. Jack, 32, a farmer born in South Carolina with real estate worth $600. With him were Ruth D., 25, born in New York; Elizabeth A., 1, born in Illinois; and Abigail Shank, 16, female, born in New York. The original page was read for this story.

Abigail Walker’s family stone at Beaucoup gives her birth year as 1833, which fits a girl of 16 in the summer of 1850. A register transcription records a license for William F. Walker and Abigail Schanck on 25 February 1852, and Shank and Schanck are ordinary spellings of the same name. So the census adds a second record of an Abigail Schanck or Shank of the right age in the right neighborhood. It still does not join her to William P. Walker: the license gives the groom’s middle initial as F., and no record found names Wm. P. Walker’s wife as a Schanck.

The New York birthplace sharpens an old conflict. Alice Walker Livesay’s 1922 Texas death certificate, examined in an earlier story, names her mother as Addie Bruce, born in Illinois. If Alice’s mother was this Abigail, the Texas informant, who signed as F. C. Livesay, gave the wrong maiden name and birthplace decades later and far away. That happens often on death certificates, but it cannot be assumed. The Beaucoup Cemetery transcription has only one Bruce, Mary Ann, wife of Samuel, who died in 1846 at 19, and the probate index has an estate for a James Bruce. Neither is connected to Abigail by any record opened here.

Why Abigail lived with the Jacks is not stated. Ruth D. Jack was also born in New York, so she may have been a relative, but the census does not say. The Jack family was among the early Beaucoup settlers named in the 1879 county history, and the families were already tied to the Walkers: the marriage register records Isaac Berry Jack marrying Elizabeth C. Walker on 3 April 1845. The 1860 Washington County census, scanned on the same site, should show where Abigail Walker said she was born; it was not searched page by page for this story.

stories.title: Was Rev. James Walker a circuit rider?
stories.hook: An 1883 history of Illinois Methodism describes a James Walker who rode southern Illinois circuits in the 1830s and then preached locally for decades. Some of it fits the Beaucoup preacher, and some of it does not.
body: The Beaucoup records already show Rev. James Walker as a Methodist preacher and teacher from the early 1820s, a later owner of the “Rock Chimney” farm, a minister to the Richview church, and a local elder who performed a marriage in 1845. James B. Leaton’s History of Methodism in Illinois, from 1793 to 1832 (1883) adds the Illinois Conference records for a James Walker. At the conference of 1831, held at Indianapolis, a James Walker was among eleven men received on trial as traveling preachers, and a James Walker was also among the local preachers elected to deacon’s orders. That year’s appointments in the Kaskaskia District list “Mt. Vernon, James Walker.”

Leaton’s sketch of him is short. It says that James Walker “was a native of Georgia,” was sent to Mt. Vernon Circuit, spent the next two years on the Brownsville Mission and 1834 on the Wabash Circuit, and was then elected to elder’s orders and allowed to locate at his own request. He was readmitted the next year and sent to Fairfield Circuit, located again in 1837, and “for about thirty years labored quite extensively as a local preacher” until his death, “a good Christian man, enjoying the confidence of all.”

Parts of this fit Beaucoup. A local preacher and elder named James Walker was active in Washington County in the 1840s, and Mt. Vernon, in Jefferson County, lies just east of Washington County. Leaton also records that Simeon Walker, the other Methodist Walker of the Richview area, followed on the Mt. Vernon Circuit in 1832. But two details do not fit. The 1850 census gives the Beaucoup James Walker’s birthplace as Tennessee, not Georgia. And thirty years of local preaching after 1837 would run to about 1867, ten years after Rev. James of Beaucoup died in April 1857. Leaton’s round number may be loose, or the itinerant may be another James Walker. It was a common name.

Captain Simeon Walker's own sketch of 1894 adds one line that bears on this. It says his wife, “Miss E. J. Walker,” born in Washington County on 28 July 1834, “was a daughter of Rev. James Walker, who was also a circuit rider of this state.” That is a family statement that Etheldra's father rode circuit, which fits Leaton's James Walker, although it still does not say which circuits. It also gives her birth a year and three days later than the 31 July 1833 in the tree.

So the circuit rider stays a lead. The identification would be settled by a record that joins the two, such as an obituary of the Beaucoup preacher in a Methodist paper of 1857, which might name his circuits, or his estate file, listed as number 18 in the county probate index.

stories.title: The camp ground at Beaucoup
stories.hook: Before there was a church building in most of the county, the Methodists of Beaucoup had a log meeting house and a camp ground. The Walkers preached there and the Livesays sat in the congregations.
body: The 1879 History of Washington County carries a chapter on early Methodism by the Rev. L. F. Cullom, then the pastor at Nashville. He wrote that about 1819 Daniel and Joseph Whittenburg, John Phillips, George Lowe and their families came from East Tennessee and settled near Beaucoup. Daniel Whittenburg, a local minister of the Methodist Episcopal Church, organized the first society of that church in the county, and the settlers set apart the ground where the Beaucoup church still stood in 1879 for both a church and a camp ground. The first building was of logs. Cullom called Beaucoup the “headquarters of Methodism in this part of Illinois,” and said its yearly camp meetings drew people from forty and fifty miles away.

The same book’s list of pioneer ministers says that Whittenberg and Rhodum Allen served the Methodists at Beaucoup as early as 1820 and that Revs. Horatio Burns, Lewis Pate and James Walker came soon afterwards. Cullom’s list of men who served the Richview church as pastors or local preachers includes Rev. Simeon Walker, Rev. James Walker and Rev. Levi S. Walker. That church began in Samuel White’s home and built its first church house in old Richview in 1842; among its first members were the families of Thomas Livesay and William Livesay. George Lowe told Cullom that in 1832 there was a society at Alex Anderson’s home whose members included John Livesay. Until 1852 these societies belonged to the Illinois Conference; from that year they were under the new Southern Illinois Conference.

Later memories agree. Dr. John Thomas Foster (1841–1927) recalled camp meetings at Mt. Zion, Beaucoup, Liberty and Locust Creek, where families brought food for themselves and for strangers, and named Simeon Walker as a well-known local preacher who was “frequently at our home”. The county’s 1968 sesquicentennial book said that at Beaucoup “the Methodists predominated,” while the Baptists led at Elkton, and listed Walker and Livesay among the old Beaucoup family names.

For this family, the camp ground was the center of the neighborhood. Rev. James Walker preached and taught there, the cemetery beside it holds his stone and those of his wife, his probable son William P. and his probable daughter Etheldra J., and the Livesays who later married into the Walker family worshiped in the same circuit. Cullom admitted that he had come to the county only a few months earlier and had gathered his facts by “careful gleaning,” so his dates are best taken as approximate.

stories.title: Etheldra J. Walker and Captain Simeon
stories.hook: William P. Walker’s probable sister married a son of the other Methodist Walker family. Her husband was the captain of William’s company in the Civil War, and the stones at Beaucoup keep the names of their small sons.
body: In August 1850 Etheldra J. Walker, 17, was living with James and Etheldra Walker and William P., 19. Three weeks later the census taker reached dwelling 280, the home of Simeon Walker, 48, with Sally, 54, and children including Simeon, 19. The register shows Simeon Walker marrying Sally Whittenburg on 11 August 1846, and Simeon Walker Jr. marrying Etheldra Jane Walker on 15 September 1852. The Beaucoup Cemetery transcription lists Etheldra J. Walker, born 31 July 1833, died 29 April 1903, wife of Simeon, and Simeon Walker, born 3 March 1831, died 11 October 1909. A veterans compilation gives his death as 29 April 1905 instead, a conflict that only the stone or a death record can settle. The 29 April of the compilation’s date is the day and month the cemetery list gives for Etheldra J.’s own death, in 1903, which may be a coincidence or a copying slip.

The couple buried several young children at Beaucoup. The transcription lists James H. (12 June 1855 to 21 August 1856), Simon G. (28 July 1857 to 1 January 1858) and Elmer D. (4 January 1861 to July 1862), each called “son of S. & E.,” and on the same stone Wilbert F. (6 October 1853 to 9 August 1854) and Harry E. (11 February to 11 March 1869). The name James H. repeats the name of Etheldra’s father, and probably of the brother aged 10 in the 1850 household.

Simeon and Etheldra’s family was bound up with William P. Walker’s. Simeon was captain of Company C, 60th Illinois Infantry, from December 1862, so he commanded the company that William joined in March 1864. If Etheldra was William’s sister, as the 1850 census suggests, the captain was also his brother-in-law. A loan book from Hoyleton, transcribed by a volunteer, records a loan of $56 to Simeon Walker of Richview on 12 January 1860, with J. W. Walker and G. W. Walker as his securities.

Simeon came from the other Methodist Walker family. The memoir of Levi Sharpe Walker in the 1921 minutes of the Southern Illinois Conference says that Levi was born in Clinton County on 14 September 1829, the son of Simeon and Elizabeth Sharpe Walker, and that his father was an itinerant Methodist preacher. Levi was licensed to preach at Richview in 1856, served three years as chaplain of the 60th Illinois, William’s regiment, and died on 6 April 1921; he was buried at Richview. Leaton’s 1883 history gives the father, Simeon Walker Sr., a birth in Jackson County, Georgia, in 1802. Captain Simeon’s place in that family rests on the “Jr.” in the register and on the 1850 household, which does not state relationships, so he is not linked to a father here. The county probate index lists separate estates for Simeon and for Simeon Jr.

stories.title: Lieutenant George W. Walker of Beaucoup
stories.hook: The Beaucoup Walker who led men to Mexico in 1847 lived beside the Livesays in 1850, and his daughter later married one. Whether he was Rev. James Walker’s son is the open question.
body: In July 1847 a company raised in Washington County left Nashville, marched to Alton and was mustered in on 18 July as Company H, 2nd Regiment of Illinois Foot Volunteers, for the war with Mexico. The 1879 county history gives its officers as Captain James Burns and Second Lieutenant George W. Walker, among others. Its privates included three Livesays, Carter A., Alfred and John C., and four Walkers, Thomas, John Sen., John Jun. and Ezekiel. The company landed at Vera Cruz on 31 August 1847, skirmished at San Juan on 18 September, wintered at Jalapa, moved to Puebla and was discharged at Alton on 22 July 1848. Ezekiel Walker died at Vera Cruz on 10 September 1847.

The marriage register transcription records George W. Walker marrying Elizabeth Walker on 21 December 1848. In the 1850 census, on a page taken in early September, dwelling 432 holds George W. Walker, 23, a farmer with land worth $400, Elizabeth, 21, and Frances C. E., aged 8 months, all born in Illinois. Frances’s stone gives her birth as 19 September 1849, and her age in the census agrees, which fits a December 1848 marriage. The next two households were those of Lorenzo M. Livesay, 25, and William C. Livesay, 26, both born in Tennessee; William’s household included Jackson L., 4, the same name as the Jackson L. Livesay who later served with William P. Walker in Company C.

Frances C. E. Walker married Charles M. Livesay and died on 18 February 1874, according to the Beaucoup Cemetery transcription; her sister Eudora B. A. died as a child in 1854. A Nashville Journal notice of October 1902, as transcribed, says that Rev. George Walker died at his home near Beaucoup on 20 October 1902, having lived on the farm for fifty-four years, that he was a Mexican War veteran, and that three children survived him: Mrs. A. B. Stephens, D. A. Walker and J. E. Walker. It gives his marriage to Elizabeth Walker as December 1828, which cannot be right for a man born about 1826 and is probably a garbled date. The county death index lists an Elizabeth Walker in Beaucoup Township on 11 February 1920, which fits his widow’s stone (1829–1920). The probate index has an estate and an administrator’s bond for G. W. Walker.

George W. Walker was born about 1826 or 1827 in Illinois, close to the Beaucoup settlement, and by 1860 he stood security for Simeon Walker together with J. W. Walker. He could have been an older son of Rev. James and Etheldra who had married and left home by 1850, but no record opened here names his parents. He is therefore not added to the tree, and this story is a lead for the Walker and Livesay connection.

stories.title: James T. McCormack, teamster, Anderson, 1893
stories.hook: A city directory printed in the year of Sadah’s birth puts a James T. McCormack in Anderson, joining the “James” of one census and the “J. T.” of her death certificate.

subject.name: James T. McCormack
subject.rel: Probable father of Sadah McCormick Livesay

body: Knight & Co. published a city directory for Anderson and Madison County, Indiana, for the years 1893 and 1894. On page 134 of its Anderson city section is the line “McCormack James T, teamster, A S P Co, h. cor Vine and 1st.” He drove a team for a firm the directory abbreviates as A S P Co, and his house stood at the corner of Vine and First streets. The directory’s own pages did not expand the initials in the parts searched, so the employer is left as printed.

The entry matters because of when and where it was printed. Sadah Livesay Vaughan’s 1978 death certificate, described in the earlier story on her Indiana beginnings, gives her birth as 13 August 1893 in Anderson, Indiana, and names her father as J. T. McCormack. The 1900 census, seven years later, lists a James McCormack with a daughter Sadie born in August 1893, and the 1910 census calls the same household’s head Jay T. The directory is the first record found that puts the full name James and the initial T together, and it does so in Anderson in the very years of Sadah’s birth. That is the bridge the earlier research lacked between “James” and “J. T.” It does not explain the 1910 “Jay T.”, and no record seen says what the T stood for.

The directory also shows how easily two families of the name could be confused. The same page lists Edward McCormack, a file worker, and Louise A. McCormack, both at 53 East Lynne, and a separate McCormick household at 237 South Central Avenue: Elizabeth, a widow, with James and Susan. Emerson’s Anderson directory of 1891 has that Central Avenue family already in place, with a James McCormick working at Kilgore’s factory and Mrs. Lizzie McCormick, widow of John, but it has no James T. McCormack. The teamster therefore appears between the 1891 and 1893–4 editions. Nothing on the page says whether Edward or Louise were his relatives.

By June 1900 James and Frances McCormack were farming in Stony Creek Township, on the western edge of Madison County, as the next story follows. A directory line names no wife or children, so the identification of the Anderson teamster with Sadah’s father rests on the agreement of name, initial, town and date. It is probable, not proven. Sadah’s parent links in the tree are still left empty, as the earlier research decided.

stories.title: From a Stony Creek farm to a Brazoria fruit farm
stories.hook: Between 1900 and 1910 the McCormacks left a mortgaged Indiana farm for a fruit farm of their own in Brazoria County, Texas, the county next to the one where Sadah married.

subject.name: The McCormack family
subject.rel: Probable family of Sadah McCormick Livesay

body: The 1900 census page for the McCormacks was read again for this story from the National Archives microfilm, which the Internet Archive has put online. On sheet 2B of enumeration district 112, Stony Creek Township, Madison County, Indiana, the head is James McCormack, a farmer born in June 1863 in Indiana. His father was born in West Virginia and his mother in Indiana. His wife Frances was born in January 1862 in Indiana, as were both her parents. They had been married seventeen years, and Frances had borne seven children, five of whom were living. The farm was their own but mortgaged. Cleveland, fifteen, was working as a farm hand; Hazel, Sadie, Pernell and Dewey were at home.

Stony Creek Township lies on the western edge of Madison County, along the Hamilton County line. The county history of 1914 describes twenty-eight square miles, part of them once a heavily timbered tract called the “Dismal,” long since cleared and drained into some of the most productive farms in the county. Lapel and Fishersburg were its only towns, and the Central Indiana railroad ran through it.

Ten years later the family was in Texas. On sheet 1B of enumeration district 10, Justice Precinct 5, Brazoria County, the 1910 census lists Jay T. McCormick, 41, and Frances, 40, with Clevand, 25, Hazel, 20, Sadie, 17, Purnell, 14, Dewey, 9, and William, 7. Everyone was born in Indiana. Jay T. was a fruit farmer working on his own account, and the farm was owned free of mortgage. Cleveland worked on the home farm. Hazel and Sadie were both out at work as housekeepers for private families. The neighbors on the page were fruit farmers too, among them a family whose parents were recorded as Holland Dutch.

William, born in Indiana and seven years old in April 1910, is the new child since 1900. Frances now counted eight children, six living, which agrees with one more birth. His Indiana birth means the family was still in Indiana in about 1902 or 1903, so the move to Texas came between then and 1910. The two censuses also disagree. James aged five years in the decade, Frances only two. The marriage had lasted seventeen years in 1900 but twenty-five in 1910. Dewey, born in November 1898 by the first count, was only nine in the second. And the father’s birthplace, West Virginia in 1900, became Indiana in 1910. None of these conflicts is resolved here.

Sadie was seventeen and working in a Brazoria County household in April 1910. Eighteen months later, on 10 October 1911, Lester W. Livesay and Sadah H. McCormick married in neighboring Harris County, with a note that a mother’s consent was on file. Sadah’s later death certificate names her father J. T. McCormack and gives her birth in Anderson in August 1893, the month and year of Sadie’s birth in both censuses. The run of records is now close and consistent, which makes James T. and Frances McCormack Sadah’s probable parents. Apart from the certificate’s “J. T. McCormack,” though, no record yet seen names her parents, and Frances’s maiden name is still unknown.

Treating the 1900 and 1910 households as one family is probable: the parents’ names, Indiana births and five of the children’s names agree, though ages, marriage length and the father’s birthplace conflict. Their link to Sadah is not entered in the tree; it remains a strong but unproven identification of Sadie with Sadah. James McCormack was not found in the pages of the 1880 Stony Creek Township census that were read; his parents and Frances’s maiden name are still unknown.

stories.title: Clinton Whitfield in Sevier County, Arkansas, 1900
stories.hook: A six-year-old named Clinton, born in July 1893, turns up in a Sevier County household headed by W. F. and Emma Whitfield.

subject.name: W. F. and Emma Whitfield
subject.rel: Probable parents of Oliver Clinton Whitfield

body: Until now, everything this archive knew about Clint Whitfield’s parents came from Find a Grave pages read in earlier research. They named his father William Franklin “Frank” Whitfield and his mother Emma Ward Whitfield and placed his birth at Chapel Hill, Sevier County, Arkansas. The story on the thread from Glover to Sevier County suggested the 1900 census of that county as the place to test the lead. The Census Bureau’s card index to the 1900 census of Arkansas, filed by sound code, has a card for a W. F. Whitfield in Sevier County, Monroe Township, volume 36, enumeration district 151, sheet 5, line 33. The card lists his wife Emma and four children, the first of them a son named Clinton.

The original page agrees with the card. The enumerator in Monroe Township wrote the family as dwelling 82, family 83. W. F. Whitfield, white, was born in January 1868 in Mississippi and was 32. He had been married eight years. His mother was born in Mississippi; for his father the enumerator wrote “unknown.” Emma, his wife, was born in November 1874 in Arkansas and was 25. She was the mother of four children, and all four were living. Her parents’ birthplaces are also entered as unknown.

The children were Clinton, a son, born in July 1893 and six years old; Willie G., a daughter, born in March 1895; Robbie W., a son, born in February 1897; and Fannie I., a daughter, born in October 1898. All four were born in Arkansas. The last line of the household is a boarder surnamed Ward, a farm laborer born in August 1871 in Arkansas to parents born in Texas. His given name is hard to read.

Clint Whitfield’s gravestone at Glover gives his birth as 27 July 1893. The census Clinton was born in July 1893. The man went by Clint, and the boy is listed only as Clinton. The parents’ initials and Emma’s name and birth year match the memorial leads, and a Ward living in the house fits the lead that Emma was born a Ward, though the census calls him only a boarder. Taken together these make it probable that this is Oliver Clinton Whitfield’s family, and that Willie, Robbie and Fannie were his younger brother and sisters.

It is not yet proof. The page does not give Clinton a first name of Oliver, and no record that names his parents outright, such as his 1915 marriage or a death record from 1941, has been examined. For that reason W. F. and Emma are added to the tree with their three younger children, but they are not linked to Oliver as his parents. The page does not name a community, so the Chapel Hill birthplace also remains a lead.

The tree link is withheld until a record names his parents.

stories.title: Alonzo and Emma Box in Van Zandt County, June 1900
stories.hook: The original census page shows a farm family of five children, a mother who had borne eight, and parents from four different states.
body: Earlier research found Tyro Box in his parents’ household in 1900 through an online index. The original page fills in the rest. On 8 June 1900 the enumerator for Justice Precinct No. 6 of Van Zandt County, Texas, reached dwelling 71 and wrote down the household of Alonzo Box, on lines 54 to 61 of sheet 4B in enumeration district 134.

Alonzo was born in December 1850 in Arkansas and was 49. His father was born in Alabama and his mother in Mississippi. He was a farmer and owned his farm, which carried a mortgage. Emma, his wife, was born in July 1860 in Mississippi and was 39. Her father was born in Virginia and her mother in Mississippi. They had been married 23 years, which places the wedding about 1877, when Emma was about sixteen or seventeen. She was the mother of eight children, six of them living.

Five children were at home, all born in Texas: Walter, born March 1885, and Tyro, born May 1888, both working as farm laborers; Claudy J., born August 1891; Flossie B., born August 1894; and Archie W., born November 1896. A boarder, Charlie, a married farm laborer of 25, completes the household; his surname is hard to read. The Soundex card made from this page copies Archie’s birth year as 1894, but the page itself reads 1896. With six living children and five at home, one living child was elsewhere, and two had died.

The page gives the clues for going back a generation: Alonzo’s parents from Alabama and Mississippi, and Emma’s father from Virginia. It does not give Emma’s maiden name. A family note calls her Emillie Wilkerson, and that is still the only source for the name. The Soundex cards for the 1880 census of Texas and of Arkansas were searched under code B200 for an Alonzo Box, without result; the family may be indexed under another form of his name.

Van Zandt County was growing fast. The Handbook of Texas says its population reached 25,000 by 1900 and that the number of farms rose from 2,345 in 1890 to 4,208 in 1900. Canton was the county seat. Within a few years Annie Logan came north from Mount Pleasant to McCurtain County, and by 1942 Tyro, Claude and Archie were all living around Millerton and Valliant. Flossie is buried at Wheelock.

stories.title: Tyro Box registers at Millerton, April 1942
stories.hook: At 53, Violet’s father filled in a draft card that gives a third birthplace for him and a clear picture of the man.
body: In April 1942 the Selective Service held its fourth registration, for men born between 28 April 1877 and 16 February 1897, too old for the earlier calls. Tyro Box registered with McCurtain County’s Local Board No. 1 on 25 April 1942, before the registrar Howard Pratt at Valliant. The National Archives now publishes Oklahoma’s cards from that registration online.

His card gives his name as Tyro Steven Box, his home and mailing address as Millerton, McCurtain County, and his age as 53. He was born on 22 May 1888, the same day his 1967 obituary gives. For his birthplace he wrote Rockwall County, Texas. The person who would always know his address was Mrs. T. S. Box of Millerton, and the line for an employer is struck through. He signed it Tyro S. Box. The registrar described him as a white man about 5 feet 9 inches tall and 182 pounds, with gray eyes, gray hair and a light complexion.

Rockwall County is a new birthplace for him. His obituary says Pittsburg, Texas, the 1930 census says Oklahoma, and the 1900 census says only Texas. Wikipedia notes that Rockwall County was formed in 1873 from part of Kaufman County, where his brother Claude said he was born. The card, in Tyro’s own words, is the strongest of these, but the conflict is left standing.

Eight years later the census taker found him at home. In April 1950 Tyro S. Box, 61, and Annie F. Box, 63, both born in Texas, were listed in Kirk Township, McCurtain County, on a page marked as the Wheelock Community school bus route. Their daughter Violet and her husband kept a store near Golden at the same time.

stories.title: Claude and Archie Box: two brothers at Valliant
stories.hook: Two of Tyro’s younger brothers farmed around Valliant, and their own 1942 cards tie them back to the Van Zandt County household.

subject.name: Claude Joel and Archie W. Box

body: The 1900 census of Van Zandt County lists two younger sons of Alonzo and Emma Box, Claudy J., born in August 1891, and Archie W., born in November 1896. Forty-two years later, in the same Oklahoma registration that caught their brother Tyro, two Box men at Valliant filled in cards that fit them.

Claude Joel Box, 50, of Valliant gave his birth as 26 August 1892 at Kaufman, Texas, which the registrar spelled Coffman. He worked for himself, and his contact was Mrs. C. J. Box of Valliant. Archie W. Box, 45, also of Valliant, gave 11 April 1896 and Van Zandt County, Texas, written Vanzant. He farmed for himself, and his contact was Mrs. Erma Box. Each card matches the census boy in name, middle initial and county of origin; each differs from the census in the year or month of birth. Tyro’s 1967 obituary, as transcribed in earlier research, names a surviving brother, Arch Box. That fits Archie.

In 1950 Archie W. Box, 53, born in Texas, and his wife Erma L., 45, born in Oklahoma, were counted in Kirk Township, McCurtain County, in the same enumeration district as Tyro and Annie. Their younger household members are not named here.

Valliant itself was a young town. The Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture says the townsite was surveyed in 1902 for the Arkansas and Choctaw Railroad and named for the railroad official Frank W. Valliant. Its economy rested on farming, with cotton first, and by the early 1920s it had two banks and nineteen other businesses.

Other Box men registered in McCurtain County that April: Terrell Inge Box of Valliant, born 20 December 1896 at Canton, Texas, the Van Zandt county seat; Andrew Clarence Box of Broken Bow; and Ernest Box of Goodwater. Terrell came from the same county, but he cannot have been a full brother of Archie if both men’s birth dates are right, and he is not in Alonzo’s 1900 household. How, or whether, these men were related to Tyro is not known.

stories.title: Birdie Box James of Wheelock
stories.hook: Tyro’s little sister Flossie Belle was widowed at 33 and lived another half century; she lies at Wheelock, where Violet and Annie are buried.
body: In the 1900 census of Van Zandt County, Flossie B. Box was five, the only daughter at home with Alonzo and Emma Box. She was born in August 1894 in Texas, between her brothers Claudy and Archie.

The Wheelock Cemetery listing on the Oklahoma Cemeteries website, a volunteer transcription of the stones, records her as Flossie Belle “Birdie” Box James, born 4 August 1894 and died 14 November 1979. Beside her is her husband, Raphael B. “Rafe” James, born 20 February 1893 and died 5 January 1928. When he died, Birdie was 33. She outlived him by nearly 52 years.

Tyro Box’s 1967 obituary, as transcribed in earlier research, names his sister Mrs. Byrd James. Byrd is probably her nickname Birdie. With the 1900 census entry and the birth day on her stone, that makes her identification probable. She is buried in the same Wheelock Cemetery as her sister-in-law Annie and her niece Violet.

stories.title: Other Whitfields in McCurtain County: leads
stories.hook: A Sevier County-born Whitfield farmed at Valliant in 1942, and an Arkansas-born J. D. Whitfield lived in the county in 1950. Neither is yet tied to Clint.
body: Once Clint Whitfield’s probable family turned up in Sevier County, Arkansas, the Oklahoma records were checked for other Whitfields who might be his kin. The National Archives’ 1942 draft cards for Oklahoma include the Whitfield men registered in the state who were born between 1877 and February 1897. Two lived in McCurtain County.

John Grover Whitfield, 53, farmed for himself at Valliant. He gave his birth as 6 July 1888 in Sevier County, Arkansas, written “Sever Co.,” and his contact as Ida Whitfield of Valliant. He was born in the same county as Clint, but four years before W. F. and Emma Whitfield married, when Emma was thirteen, so he was not her son. Whether he belonged to W. F.’s family some other way is unknown. The other card, for William McKinley Whitfield, gives McCurtain County with a Route 2, Arkinda, Arkansas, mailing address; he was born in 1897 at New Boston, Texas, and shows no tie to Sevier County.
No card was found for a Robbie or Robert Whitfield, Clint’s probable brother, born in February 1897, right at the edge of the age range; he may have been born too late, or lived elsewhere.

The 1950 census of McCurtain County, district 45-45, lists a J. D. Whitfield, 46, born in Arkansas, with his wife Bessie, born in Texas, and two daughters. He was born about 1903 or 1904, after the 1900 census, so he could be a younger child of W. F. and Emma, but no record seen here connects them. The 1910 census of Sevier and McCurtain counties is the next place to look.

stories.title: Card 5754 read: Peter and Ellen Durant
stories.hook: The Dawes card that earlier research could only find in an index has now been read. It names Bessie’s parents, and Louis’s too.
body: The story “Card 5754: the record that may name Bessie’s parents” explained why the census card was the key to Bessie Merry’s line and why it had not been read. The National Archives Catalog has since given up both the card and the forty-page application jacket behind it. The card is headed Choctaw Nation, Choctaw Roll, field number 5754, residence Choctaw Nation, post office Glover, I.T. It lists three people: Louis Merry, 30 by the later index but 27 on the card, an intermarried white man; Bessie, his wife, 19, three-quarters Choctaw; and Ida May, their daughter, one year old, three-eighths. The date of application is 26 April 1899.

The columns for the parents answer the question. Bessie’s father is Peter Durant and her mother Ellen Durant. Both are marked dead, and both are given Bok Tuklo as their county, one of the Choctaw Nation’s counties. Louis’s parents are Calvin Merry and Elizabeth Merry, both dead and both “non-citiz,” that is, not Choctaw citizens. For Ida May the clerk simply wrote “No 1” and “No 2,” pointing back to her parents on the lines above.

The notes down the middle of the card add more. Louis was on the 1896 Choctaw roll as Lewis Merry and Bessie as “Betsy,” both in Eagle County, numbers 14822 and 8644. Ida’s proof of birth was filed on 9 May 1899; the day of birth in the note can be read as June 12 or June 17, 1898, while the affidavits in the jacket give the twelfth. The family’s case had first been carried on a card numbered D 128, and was transferred to card 5754 on 21 March 1904. Stamps show that the Secretary of the Interior approved Bessie’s and Ida’s enrollment on 9 May 1904 and Louis’s on 14 March 1905. A last note refers to letters from Principal Chief Green McCurtain and the Choctaw auditor Peter J. Hudson about 1893 leased district money for Bessie, filed on 2 April 1904.

The Calvin and Elizabeth Merry of the card fit the memorial lead that names Louis’s parents as John Calvin Merry and Eliza Jane McGregor, but the card gives no middle name, maiden name or place, so that lead is still unproved and his parents are not added to the tree. Bessie’s parents are a different matter: her own enrollment card names them, so Peter and Ellen Durant are entered here as her parents. Other cards, told in the stories that follow, show that she had a brother, Ben, and that the family belonged to the Bok Tuklo household of a woman named Wilsey Clay.

stories.title: A wedding at Lukfata, 7 September 1896
stories.hook: Louis Merry paid the Choctaw Nation one hundred dollars for the right to marry Bessie Durant. The license burned, but the certificate survived in the Commission’s files.
body: Earlier stories knew only that a letter of 18 January 1908 returned Louis and Bessie Merry’s marriage license and certificate, and that its date was not their wedding date. The enrollment jacket for card 5754 holds a handwritten copy of the certificate. It says that Louis Merry of Lukfata, I.T., and Bessie Durant of Lukfata were joined in marriage at Lukfata on 7 September 1896, “according to the ordinances of God and the laws of the Choctaw Nation.” It is signed by Rev. J. H. Sleeper, with J. W. Costelow and Chas. J. Gaffney as witnesses. The Commission’s decision of 10 January 1905 states the same date.

A white man who wished to marry a Choctaw woman and gain rights in the Nation had to do it under Choctaw law, and the jacket shows what that meant in practice. R. W. Thomas, a Choctaw by blood living at Lukfata, swore in August 1904 that he was clerk of Bok Tuklo County until 1 October 1896, that Louis Merry applied to him in September 1896 with a petition in proper form signed by ten Choctaws by blood, that he gave Louis the oath of allegiance to the Choctaw Nation, and that he took the regular fee of one hundred dollars and issued him a license to marry Bessie Durant. Louis himself testified in 1902 that he paid one hundred dollars and that Sleeper was a missionary.

The license did not last. At Atoka on 7 December 1900, Louis, giving his name as Lewis and his age as 28, told the Commission that he lived at Lukfata and had lived in that country about eight years, that the license had been shown to Commissioner Ben Watkins when he was put on the 1896 roll, and that it burned in December 1897 when “the house and all its contents were burned.” Ben Watkins, seventy years old, confirmed in a separate statement that he had seen the license and enrolled Louis in 1896.

The two clerks did not agree on one point. Joe A. James, who succeeded Thomas as county clerk on 1 October 1896, testified in November 1902 that he had recorded the license and certificate and handed them back to Louis. In his own affidavit of August 1904 he said he could not now be certain but did not think he had recorded them. Thomas swore that it was not the custom in that county to record marriage licenses at that time. Either way, the Commission accepted the marriage, and the certificate copy now in the file is the best record of the day.

stories.title: Louis Merry against the Choctaw Nation, 1900–1905
stories.hook: The Choctaw Nation contested Louis Merry’s claim. It took five years, three hearings and a threatened farm before he was enrolled.
body: In August 1900 the Commission wrote to Louis Merry at Lukfata that the Choctaw Nation, through its attorneys, had filed a protest against the enrollment of Louis, Bessie and Ida May Merry. The case was heard at Atoka in December 1900 as Choctaw D 128, with Melvin Cornish appearing for the Nation and J. G. Ralls for the family. Louis testified about the marriage and the burned license, and John M. Hodges testified about Bessie’s father, Peter Durant. The family’s lawyer asked for a copy of the evidence in January 1901.

The case moved slowly. Notices of February and March 1902 called it for final consideration at Muskogee on 4 April 1902, when it was submitted on the record. Letters from that year are addressed to J. L. Merry at Glover, and the one of 27 March 1902 speaks of “yourself and your wife, Bessie Merry and your child, Ida May Merry.” That settles a question earlier stories could only call probable: within this one case file, J. L. Merry of Glover and Louis Merry of card 5754 are the same applicant. In November 1902 Louis, now 30 and living at Glover, testified again at Garvin. He said he had lived in the Nation ten years, claimed rights through his wife Bessie Durant, a “full blood Choctaw” in his words (the Commission’s own census card enrolls her as three-quarters Choctaw, and that recorded figure is the one used on this site), and admitted that they had separated on 18 June 1902 and that she came back about a month later.

By 1904 the delay was costing him. On 30 September 1904 the Commission acknowledged his letter reporting that on 5 April 1904 a man named Hopper Watkins had filed on his farm in Section 4, Township 6 South, Range 23 East, and that he did not want to lose it. Affidavits from the two Bok Tuklo clerks were filed that August. On 10 January 1905 the Commission ruled in his favor: he had married Bessie under Choctaw law on 7 September 1896, both were residents in good faith, they had lived together except for about a month in 1902, and he was on the 1896 roll in Eagle County as number 14822. The Secretary of the Interior approved his enrollment on 14 March 1905.

The file says nothing about the later parting implied by Ida’s obituary or about his later marriages. It does show him writing persistently, by letter and through lawyers, for the citizenship that would let him keep his land, while serving as Glover’s postmaster under the name Joshua L. Merry, as the story about the Glover post office describes.

stories.title: Ben Durant, Bessie’s brother
stories.hook: A second Dawes card names the same parents as Bessie’s: Peter and Ellen Durant of Bok Tuklo. Their son Ben died at twenty.
body: The National Archives Catalog’s name index to the Dawes cards turned up a second card naming Peter and Ellen Durant as parents. Card 655 was made on 21 April 1899 for the household of Wilsey Clay at Red River post office in Bok Tuklo County, and its third line is Ben Durant, her grandson, 18, three-quarters Choctaw. His father is Peter Durant and his mother Ellen Durant, both marked dead, both of Bok Tuklo, exactly as on Bessie’s card 5754.

The notes say Ben was on the 1896 roll twice, in Blue County as number 3569 and, as Benj. Durant, in Bok Tuklo County as number 3404. He did not live to be enrolled. He died on 28 September 1901, proof of his death was filed on 25 March 1902, and in 1905 his name was struck from the card with the stamp “DEAD.” His blood degree matches Bessie’s three-quarters on her card, and his age, a year younger than hers in 1899, fits a brother.

The Merry case file preserves a memory of these two children. At Atoka on 7 December 1900, John M. Hodges, aged fifty and a Choctaw by blood, said that he knew Peter Durant, that Peter “had two little kids” when he left that part of the country in 1877 or 1878, a girl and a boy, not yet named that he recalled, and that the children “showed the Choctaw blood.” The county he named is typed “Matoon County” in the transcript, a name that does not match any Choctaw county in the records used here. He thought Peter was “about a quarteroon” and his wife about half Choctaw.

Hodges’ estimates do not fit the cards neatly, and his dates would make the girl born by about 1877, a little earlier than Bessie’s own ages suggest. Still, a girl and a boy, with parents named Peter and Ellen, matches Bessie and Ben. Because the brother link rests on the shared parents across two cards and not on a record that calls them siblings, it is entered as probable.

stories.title: Wilsey Clay’s household at Bok Tuklo
stories.hook: Bessie’s grandmother was a full-blood Choctaw woman whose children carried three surnames: Clay, Gavner and Durant. The Dawes cards and one witness’s answers let her family be put together.
body: Wilsey Clay applied for enrollment on 21 April 1899, when she was 58. Card 655 calls her full blood and places her in Bok Tuklo County, with Red River as her post office, on the 1896 roll as number 2573. Her parents are given as Joe Cahn and Patsey Cahn, both dead, of Eagle County, the county along the Arkansas line where Louis Merry was enrolled in 1896. With her on the card were her daughter Ida, 18, whose father was Charles Gavner, a non-citizen, and two grandchildren, Ben Durant, son of Peter and Ellen Durant, and Licey Durant, 14, daughter of Thomas and Melinda Durant.

Two neighboring cards fill in the family. Card 656, made the same day, is the household of William A. Durant, whose wife Laura, 19, had been on the 1896 roll as Laura Clay; her parents are Charles Gavener and Wilsey Clay. Card 507, made on 18 April 1899, belongs to Abner H. Clay, 27, of Lukfata, three-quarters Choctaw, son of Henry Clay, dead, and Wilsey Clay. Lukfata is where Louis and Bessie were married in 1896.

The link from Wilsey to Bessie comes from the Merry case. At Atoka in December 1900, after John M. Hodges described Peter Durant, the Choctaw commissioner Judge Lewis asked whether that woman was the mother of Abner Clay. Hodges answered that “Peter Durant was the son of Woolsey Clay,” and agreed that Abner was a half brother to Peter. The transcript’s wording is a little tangled, but read with card 507 it makes Wilsey the mother of both men, and with card 655 it explains why Peter’s son Ben was living in her household as her grandson.

That makes Wilsey Clay Bessie Merry’s paternal grandmother and Joe and Patsey Cahn her great-grandparents, the furthest the line now reaches. Because the parent link between Wilsey and Peter rests on one witness’s sworn answers supported by the cards, it is entered as probable. Peter’s own father is not named anywhere in these records, and the card gives no later dates for Wilsey; she was alive when her enrollment was approved on 12 December 1902, and she was still living in May 1906, when she gave sworn testimony at Lukfata, as the story “Wilsey Clay swears, May 1906” tells. Her stated ages differ: 58 in April 1899 points to a birth about 1841, and 67 in May 1906 to about 1839; the tree uses about 1841 and records the difference.

stories.title: The 1893 money: Bessie and her cousin Lizzie
stories.hook: In 1902 J. L. Merry wrote to the Choctaw chief about money still owed to two young Durants. The answer came as two warrants of $143.16.
body: Card 5754 refers to letters from Green McCurtain and Peter J. Hudson about 1893 leased district money, and both letters are in the jacket. On 17 December 1902 Green McCurtain, Principal Chief of the Choctaw Nation, wrote from Tushkahomma to “Mr J. S. Merry,” Glover, that he had passed on Merry’s letter about the amount due “Ben and Lizzie Durant, in the money paid in 1893,” to the national treasurer, George W. Scott, at Sans Bois. Ben Durant had died fourteen months earlier.

On 27 March 1903 Peter J. Hudson, auditor of the Choctaw Nation, wrote from Tushkahomma to “Mr. J. L. Merry, Glover, I.T.,” as “Dear Friend,” enclosing two warrants: number 44 for Bessie Merry and number 45 for Liza Durant, each for $143.16 from the leased district fund, $286.32 in all. Each was a pro rata share of $103.00 with four percent interest from 10 June 1893 to 10 March 1903. Merry sent both letters to the Commission, which filed them on 2 April 1904 with his own application.

Who was Liza or Lizzie? The Dawes cards suggest an answer. Licey Durant on Wilsey Clay’s card 655, daughter of Thomas and Melinda Durant, is noted there as a duplicate of Lizzie Durant on card 966. That card, dated 27 April 1899, the same day Bessie swore to Ida’s birth, places Lizzie at Wheelock Seminary, full blood, the daughter of Thomas Durant of Bok Tuklo, with a later note giving her post office as Glover on 8 December 1902. By then she was the wife of Fred Gibbs, a non-citizen, with a son born on 30 August 1902.

So in the winter of 1902 a granddaughter of Wilsey Clay was getting her mail at Glover, and her share of the 1893 money was collected through J. L. Merry alongside Bessie’s. That makes Lizzie close kin, probably Bessie’s first cousin. The cards alone did not say whether Thomas Durant was Wilsey’s son or Melinda her daughter, but the jacket for card 966 settles it: sworn at Lukfata on 9 May 1906, Wilsey Clay answered “Yes” when asked whether she was the mother of Thomas Durant, Lizzie’s father, as the story “Wilsey Clay swears, May 1906” tells. The cousinship with Bessie still depends on Peter Durant also being Wilsey’s son, which rests on John M. Hodges’ testimony of 1900. The letters also show that the man the Commission knew as Louis was J. L. to the Choctaw officials who knew him personally.

stories.note: The identification of Hudson’s “Liza Durant” and McCurtain’s “Lizzie Durant” with the Lizzie of card 966 is probable, based on name, family, date and the Glover post office; no record states it. Why McCurtain names Ben, who had died, and not Bessie is not explained; the warrants went to Bessie and Liza. McCurtain’s “J. S.” is taken as a typing slip for J. L. Lizzie, her husband and son are not added to the tree.

stories.title: A Logan and a Wedgeworth in Greene County, 1850
stories.hook: The 1850 census puts a three-year-old Dudley Logan nine doors from a nine-year-old Sarah A. E. Wedgeworth. It is a promising lead, not a proof.
body: Dudley Timothy Logan’s memorial says he came to Titus County, Texas, from Greene County, Alabama, and the tree gives his wife’s full name as Sarah Anne Elizabeth Wedgeworth. The USGenWeb Census Project’s transcription of the 1850 census of Greene County, made from the microfilm and proofread, has both names on the same stretch of road. On page 316A, dwelling 1122, is Stephen Wedgeworth, 41, a farmer born in North Carolina, with Nancy M., 31, and Sarah A. E., 9, both born in Alabama. On page 316B, dwelling 1131, is Clement Logan, 33, a farmer born in South Carolina, with Mary A., 28, Elizabeth H., 8, Dudley, 3, and Martha, six months.

Other Logans live in between. Martha Logan, 71, born in South Carolina, heads dwelling 1120, two doors before the Wedgeworths, and Elizabeth Logan, 30, with four children, dwelling 1124. Leroy Logan, 49, and Willis Logan, 44, both born in South Carolina, are on either side of Clement. It looks like a cluster of related Logan households, and a Wedgeworth family among them.

The fit is not perfect. The census does not state relationships, so Clement and Mary A. are not proved to be Dudley’s parents, and Dudley’s memorial instead names James Clement Logan and Martha Calhoun. A child born in January 1846 should be four in June 1850, not three. The initials Sarah A. E. match Annie’s full name exactly, but at nine in 1850 she was born about 1841, five years before the 1846 the tree now gives. Until a marriage record or a later census ties these children to the couple who went to Texas, the households stay a lead and no parents are linked.

Two other searches belong with this lead. The Alabama Department of Archives and History’s Civil War service database lists several Logans from Greene County and the Black Belt, including an A. Logan in the Greene County militia, but no Dudley or D. T. Logan, so his widow’s pension claim of Confederate service is still unexplained. And a Dudley Logan, with a John Logan and a T. M. Logan, took the voter registration oath in Tuscaloosa County, Precinct 24, in 1877, on a page that also has a J. T. Weaghworth from 1875. Tuscaloosa County borders Greene, so this may be the family on its way west, but the register gives no age or residence to prove it.

stories.title: Alfred Livesay: Tennessee boy, Mexican War private, Marion County farmer
stories.hook: A 1909 county biography, two marriage registers and a state census follow one Tennessee-born Livesay from the Beaucoup settlement to Marion County. His parents, John Wesley and Margaret Lyons, may belong to the family of Robert Livesay.
body: Alfred Livesay was born in Tennessee on 15 February 1822, according to the Biographical and Reminiscent History of Richland, Clay and Marion Counties (1909). The same biography says he came to Washington County, Illinois, at seven, so about 1829, which is the time the family sketch of Jackson Monroe Livesay gives for the Livesays’ move from Maury County, Tennessee, to the Beaucoup country. It names his parents as John Wesley and Margaret (Lyons) Livesay, both natives of Tennessee who later settled in Marion County, Illinois, and spent the rest of their lives on one place. It adds that Alfred was a cousin of Dr. Thomas Livesay, a leading physician of Marion County.

The county’s marriage registers add a wife the biography leaves out. A volunteer transcription of the early registers lists Alfred Livesay and Nancy A. Darter on a license of 6 December 1842 (book A, page 12). A second transcription of later books lists Alfred Livesay and Hannah Logan on 26 February 1846, the date the biography gives for his marriage to Hannah, who was born in Washington County on 30 September 1830. The biography does not say what became of Nancy. It is likely that the same Alfred made both marriages, since no other Alfred Livesay appears in either transcription, but no record opened here says so.

In 1847 Alfred enrolled at Nashville in Company H of the 2nd Illinois Volunteers, a Washington County company, and served about thirteen months in the Mexican War. The biography says he contracted a sickness there from which he never fully recovered. Later, the 1855 Illinois state census lists an “Alford Livesay” in Washington County with a man aged 30 to 40, a woman aged 20 to 30 and five children under ten, which fits Alfred (aged 33), Hannah (24) and a young family, though the transcription’s count of eight people does not match the seven it lists, and a state census names no relationships.

The biography describes him as a Democrat who never sought office, a farmer and stock raiser, and for some years a Methodist preacher. About 1866 he moved to Patoka Township, Marion County, where he improved his farm. He died on 22 April 1883 and left his family about six hundred acres. Hannah was still living in 1909, managing 134 acres and drawing a pension of twelve dollars a month; the biography names thirteen children, whom this site does not list.

Whether Alfred belongs to Robert Livesay’s generation of the family is the open question. The Livesay file in which the Jackson Monroe sketch appears also carries a notice for a published line on John Wesley Livesay (A132), son of John and Rebecca (Carter) Livesay, and the sketch calls John Wesley John’s second son. If Alfred’s father is that John Wesley, Alfred was a nephew of Robert Livesay and a first cousin of Jackson Monroe, David Pinkney and their brothers. The biography does not give John Wesley’s parents, so this remains a lead. The tree carries John Wesley and Margaret as Alfred’s parents and does not link them to John Livesay of the Carter kin story.

stories.title: Captain Burns’s companies: Livesays in the Black Hawk and Mexican wars
stories.hook: A Washington County company went to the Black Hawk War in 1832 with Lorenzo D. Livesay in the ranks. In 1847 another company under a Captain James Burns took three more Livesays to Mexico, and one did not return.
body: The 1879 history of Washington County prints two rosters that name Livesays. The first lists the county’s company in the Black Hawk War, enlisted on 25 May 1832 from the recollection of two old veterans and led by Captain James Burns. Its privates begin with Lorenzo D. Livesay. The veterans’ list calls him a son of John C. and Rebecca (Carter) Livesay and gives a birth about 1815, which the earlier story on the Carter and Livesay kin found hard to square with his land patent of 1831. He is the only Livesay in that roster.

The second roster is the muster of Company H, 2nd Regiment Illinois Volunteers, commanded by Colonel James Collins, which was mustered into service on 18 July 1847 and gathered at Alton. Its captain was a James Burns. Among the privates the 1879 history prints Carter A. Livesay, Alfred Livesay and John C. Livesay; the volunteer transcription spells the last “Livesay” and the book “Livesey.” A Nicholas H. Darter, the name of the man who married Mariah Livesay on 16 September 1841, is also among the privates.

The three men are not one family branch that can be sorted from the roster alone. Alfred was a Tennessee-born farmer and later preacher, whose story is told separately. Carter appears as “Carter H.” in the veterans’ list and in the early marriage register, where Carter H. Livesay and Frances Eliz. Anderson took out a license on 1 October 1841; the roster’s middle initial A may be a misprint, and a different Carter Livesay took out a license with Mabel Perkins in 1836 (an older, Virginia-born man, by a 1901 Kansas sketch of his son A. C. Livesay). John C. Livesay is the one whose fate is recorded. The roll of those who died lists him with the line “John C. Livesay died at Jalapa, May 1848,” among men who died at Vera Cruz, Puebla and Jalapa, at San Juan, and on shipboard.

Nothing opened here says that Captain James Burns of 1847 is the Captain James Burns of 1832; the name and county make it likely, and a James Burnes appears in the 1855 state census a few lines from Livesay Carter. It is also not shown that John C. of 1848 is related to the John C. said to be Lorenzo Dow’s father, who would have been well over sixty in 1848. The roster does show the Livesays and their in-laws entering the county’s militia and volunteer companies from the first decade of settlement.

stories.title: Livesay Carter: a surname used as a first name
stories.hook: A stone listing at Nashville, Illinois, a county sketch and a neighbor’s biography put dates and a household around Livesay Carter, the Carter whose given name echoes the family sketch’s story of two cousins.
body: The family sketch of Jackson Monroe Livesay says that John Livesay and his sister Alice married Rebecca Carter and her brother Robert Carter in Franklin County, Virginia, and that “both couples named their first sons after their families,” so that Carter Livesay and Livesay Carter were first cousins. The earlier story on the Carter kin put the Carter land patents of 1823 and later beside the Livesay patents. This story adds what the Carter side itself records.

The Masonic Cemetery transcription at Nashville lists “Livesay, Carter” with birth 15 November 1799 and death 17 October 1875, filed under L, and Mary Carter, 4 February 1800 to 24 October 1873, and Dr. William D. Carter beside them in the same block. The order is probably the transcriber’s slip for Livesay Carter. The 1879 county history confirms the man: in its sketch of Dr. William D. Carter it says his father Livesay Carter was a native of Virginia who went to Tennessee in 1807, came to Illinois in 1818, lived four years in what is now Clinton County, and then settled at Nashville, where he lived until his death in 1875, farming and raising stock. The same history credits him with a tread sawmill built in 1830 two miles east of the site of Nashville, and names him among the commissioners who chose Nashville as county seat.

His wife is identified by a second biography in the same book. George T. Hoke, born in Harrison County, Indiana, in 1819, says that his widowed mother, a Moore from Jefferson County, Kentucky, came to the county with her people in 1822, met Livesay Carter near Covington and married him in July 1823. They lived together more than fifty years, “when she died,” and Mr. Carter followed in about two years. The Masonic dates fit that account exactly: Mary died in October 1873 and Livesay Carter in October 1875. The sketch of Dr. Carter gives her as Mrs. Mary Hoke, native of Jefferson County, Kentucky, and says they had eight children, five boys and three girls, the doctor the seventh. The doctor’s birth is 12 January 1838 in the history but 2 January 1838 on the cemetery list.

Two details do not fit neatly. The 1855 state census lists a household headed by “Livesay(?) Carter” with nine people, six men of militia age and property valued at $3,670, the highest value among the Livesay and Carter households on the transcription. But it counts a woman aged 60 to 70, while Mary, born in 1800, would have been fifty-five. And a man born in 1799 cannot have been the first son of a marriage of the 1780s, as the sketch says of Livesay Carter. Either the sketch’s dates are loose, or Livesay Carter was not Robert Carter’s first son, or the stone’s year is wrong.

So the record shows a prosperous Virginia-born settler named Livesay, whose given name makes a Livesay-Carter connection plausible and whose arrival, in 1818 and 1823, matches the family sketch’s account of Carters going first. It does not name his parents, and nothing opened here connects him by record to John and Rebecca (Carter) Livesay. The Carters are kept out of the Livesay line in the tree.

stories.title: Three more Livesays of the 1830 generation
stories.hook: Cemetery lists, an obituary and a marriage register bring three more Livesays into view, born in the 1820s, two of them known to have been born in Tennessee. None can yet be tied to Robert Livesay’s house.

subject.name: Robert B., John W. and Lydia Jane Livesay

body: Robert Livesay of Beaucoup and his sons are not the only Livesays who came from Tennessee. The Bethel (Darter) Cemetery listing in Beaucoup Township, built from probate and newspaper records, gives two. Robert B. Livesay died on 7 June 1891 at his daughter’s home at Locust Creek. The listing says he and his wife Nancy were born in Tennessee about 1825, married in Perry County, Illinois, on 26 May 1842, and had children including Sarah J., Charlotte Ann and Delila. A daughter, Charlotte Ann, died on 23 January 1852 aged 6 years, 6 months and 11 days, and her stone survives. The veterans’ list adds that he was a carpenter at Nashville, born in Maury County, Tennessee, who enlisted on 4 February 1865 in Co. I of the 154th Illinois Infantry and was mustered out at Nashville, Tennessee, on 18 September 1865. An earlier story set this Robert B. aside as too young to have bought land in 1838.

John W. Livesay is the second. His obituary in the Nashville Journal, copied in the same listing, says he was born in Tennessee on 19 September 1826, “settled SE of Nashville in 1830,” married Mrs. Elizabeth M. Logan Sanders on 21 December 1848, and died at the home of a son in Nashville aged 79 years, 11 months and 10 days. The marriage register lists John W. Livesay and Elizabeth M. Sanders on that date. The obituary counts eight sons and a daughter. The age works out to late August 1906, but the transcription says September, so the exact day of death is not settled. He is easily confused: Alfred Livesay’s father was also John Wesley, and a John Wesley Livesay born about 1834 served in the 60th Illinois.

The third is a woman. The Richview Township Cemetery transcription lists Lilly Jane (Livesay) Thompson, 14 July 1824 to 4 December 1887, beside William Thompson, 24 October 1819 to 27 February 1879. The marriage register lists William Thompson and Lydia Jane Livesay on a license of 28 January 1841, when she was sixteen. A family biography of their son Thomas Benton Thompson says he was born near Richview on 24 January 1842, the first son and second child of eleven, served in the 49th Illinois from August 1862, and died on 3 February 1890. A first child, then a son within twelve months of the license, is a squeeze, so either the biography’s birth year is wrong or the first child was born before the marriage.

None of the three names a parent. They fall in the same years and townships as Robert’s children, and John W.’s obituary says he settled in 1830, but nothing opened here ties them to Robert’s house or to John and Rebecca’s. They stay in the tree as unlinked people. The records that could place them are the estate files for Rebecca Livesay (numbered 26 and 36 in the county probate index), a Maury County marriage book or tax list, and the 1850 census of Washington County, whose partial online transcription at Genealogy Trails shows no Livesay.

Relationships to Robert Livesay, to John and Rebecca (Carter) Livesay or to each other are not established, and none of these people is linked to the Livesay line. The Richview listing also carries a Jackson Livesay (1842–1917) and Mary A. (1847–1930); he cannot be Jackson Monroe Livesay, who died in 1871 according to the sketch, and was not added.

stories.title: Ten Livesay households and one Carter in the 1855 state census
stories.hook: The 1855 Illinois census of Washington County names ten Livesay heads of household and Livesay Carter. Set beside the registers, several fit known men; one does not appear at all.
body: The earlier story on D. P. Livesay used the 1855 state census for one household. The same transcription lists ten Livesay heads and a Livesay Carter: George W., “Jesse(?),” A. C., L. D., J. W., Alford, D. P., James M., I.(?) M., L. M. and, a few lines on, Livesay(?) Carter. The enumerator recorded only the head by name and counted the rest by sex and age group, with the militia count, the value of property and livestock. The transcriber warns that the script is faint and that initials are hard to read, and several totals do not equal the sum of the age groups.

Some of the heads fit people known from other records. “Alford Livesay” has a man aged 30 to 40, a woman aged 20 to 30 and five children under ten, which suits Alfred (born 1822) and Hannah Logan (born 1830), married in 1846, property valued at $375. “D. P.” is David Pinkney, whose household was described earlier. “L. D.” has one man aged 50 to 60, with no property, which suits Lorenzo Dow. “I.(?) M.” has a man aged 20 to 30, a woman aged 20 to 30 and three children under ten, which suits Jackson Monroe (aged 27) and Lucinda, whose Bible, as the sketch reports it, records Lydia Laura in 1850, Harvey in 1853 and Effie in May 1855. “L. M.” has a man and a woman aged 20 to 30 and three children under ten; the three children found for Lorenzo M. in 1860 were different ages, so that match is on initials alone. “J. W.” has a man and a woman aged 20 to 30, four children under ten and property valued at $325, which fits John W. Livesay (born 1826), who married in December 1848.

Others cannot be placed. George W. is aged 30 to 40, which suits the George Washington Livesay of Richview, a mechanic born about 1824 in the veterans’ list, but a George Washington Livesay is also named in the Livesay file as a son of Carter Livesay. “Jesse(?),” “A. C.” and James M., aged 20 to 30 with two men of militia age, are unidentified, though James M. may be the carpenter and later lieutenant of the 49th Illinois the veterans’ list places at Nashville. Livesay Carter’s household is far larger, with nine people, six men of militia age and $3,670 in property.

Two absences stand out. No household is headed by a W. E. or a William E. Livesay, although William Edmund, the eldest of Robert’s sons, had land patents and a marriage on the registers; “A. C.” may be a misreading, but nothing here shows it. And no household is headed by Lydia Livesay, whom the sketch makes Robert’s widow after his death in February 1855; if she was living, she was counted within a son’s household or missed. The census cannot settle either point, and it is no use for Floyd’s parentage, because it records no names beyond the head.

Carter); volunteer transcription, original not examined; read 4 Nov 2026: https://www.genealogytrails.com/ill/washington/1855census.html

stories.title: Twenty-five Livesay weddings in the county registers, 1831–1877
stories.hook: The Washington County marriage registers list twenty-five licenses that name a Livesay, from a December 1831 wedding to one in 1877. Read together they sketch a clan marrying into the Andersons, Darters, Thompsons, Whittenburgs and Logans.
body: Volunteers have transcribed two overlapping sets of Washington County marriage records. The “Early Marriages” list, from book A and the first pages of later books, gives the date of license and the book and page. A second list, from books A, B, D and E, gives the date of marriage and sometimes ages. Together they hold twenty-five entries with a Livesay as bride or groom. The earlier story on the sketch used six of them to test the family of Robert and Lydia.

The earliest is Alex Anderson and Sally Livesay, a license of 28 December 1831 returned on 15 February 1832. The 1879 county history says that in 1832 a society of Methodists met at the home of Alex. Anderson, with John Livesay among its principal members; if that is the same Anderson, John Livesay may have been a relative of the bride, which is a lead only. In the 1830s and early 1840s the book A list has Carter Livesay with Mabel Perkins (21 November 1836), Thomas W. Livesay with Elizabeth Thompson (22 February 1841), William Thompson with Lydia Jane Livesay (28 January 1841), Nicholas H. Darter with Mariah Livesay (16 September 1841), Carter H. Livesay with Frances Eliz. Anderson (1 October 1841), Alfred Livesay with Nancy A. Darter (6 December 1842), William E. Livesay with Emily Goodner (1 August 1844) and Henry Whittenburg with Margaret Rebecca Livesay (31 July 1844).

The later list adds Lorenzo M. Livesay and Margaret Jane Thompson (22 October 1845), Daniel Whittenburg and Mary Livesay (16 March 1846), Alfred Livesay and Hannah Logan (26 February 1846), John W. Livesay and Elizabeth M. Sanders (21 December 1848), David A. White and Elizabeth Livesay (29 October 1848), Jackson M. Livesay and Lucinda A. Thompson (15 November 1849), James L. Logan and Unity J. Livesay (16 November 1849) and Terry W. Nichols and Nancy Livesay (18 December 1849). It runs on through Ambrose H. Smith and Rebecca E. Livesay (1851), James M. Livesay and Margaret E. Johnson (1851), Parker Dillinger and Frances E. Livesay (1852), William Livesay and Margaret McKelvy (1853), David B. Livesay and Elizabeth D. Jack (1857), Cornelius R. Rhine and Martha R. Livesay (1857) and James R. Breeze and Sarah A. Livesay (1858), and ends with Charles M. Livesay and Theresa E. Tate in 1877.

A few entries invite checks. David A. White’s own county biography gives his third marriage, to “Mrs. Elizabeth Livesay,” as 20 October 1848, nine days before the register date, and does not say whose widow, if any, she was. The Thompsons recur: Lorenzo M. and Jackson M. married Thompson brides, Thomas W. Livesay married an Elizabeth Thompson, and a William Thompson married Lydia Jane Livesay. The registers do not give parents, so they cannot say which of these brides and grooms were Robert’s children, John and Rebecca’s, or from other branches. The Nancy Livesay who married in 1849 is not Nancy Paulina, whom the sketch gives as born in 1838.

One of those early licenses can now be placed. A 1901 county history from Kansas prints a sketch of A. C. Livesay, a farmer of Montana Township, Labette County, who was born in Maury County, Tennessee, in 1825 and came with his parents to Washington County, Illinois, in 1832. It names his father as Carter Livesay, born in Virginia, who “was married three times”: first to Elizabeth Wright, a native of Tennessee, mother of Charlotte, Polly, Thomas, Jesse, William, Caroline, George, Jane, A. C., Robert, Martha and John; then to Rachel Phillips, mother of a daughter Rachel; and last to Mabel Perkins, mother of James, Nelson and Louis. That makes the Carter Livesay who married Mabel Perkins in November 1836 the Virginia-born father of a large Tennessee family, and so probably not the Carter H. Livesay who married Frances Anderson in 1841, who may have been one of the next generation. A. C. himself married Delinda Finch of Jefferson County and moved to Kansas in 1873. How this family joins the Livesays of the tree is not yet shown.

What the list does give is a count and a calendar: nineteen of the twenty-five licenses fall between 1841 and 1853, the years when the children who arrived around 1830 came of age. For Floyd’s line the registers stop too early; a marriage of 1880, to Alice Walker, has not been found online.

The registers name only couples, so no relationship to Robert Livesay or to Floyd is claimed. The Alex Anderson of the 1831 license and the Alex. Anderson of the 1832 Methodist society are not shown to be the same man, so no tie between Sally and John Livesay is claimed.

stories.title: Two Beaucoup-born Livesays in Texas, in the First World War draft lists
stories.hook: A volunteer list of draft registrations from Washington County, Illinois, names a Lester William Livesay living at Pearland and a Melvin Livesay working in the Texas oil fields. Both were born at Beaucoup. The first is Floyd and Alice’s son; the second may be his brother.

subject.name: Lester W. Livesay and Melvin Livesay

body: The Washington County genealogy volunteers have compiled World War I and World War II draft registrations for men born or tied to the county, in columns by war. The list for surnames L includes Lester William Livesay, born on 8 November 1895 at Beaucoup, aged 22, married, a farmer residing at Pearland, Texas. That is the Lester W. Livesay Sr. of the tree: Beaucoup, the November birthday and Pearland all match, and his marriage to Sadah McCormick in 1911 explains the status of “married.”

The birth year does not match the stone. Lester’s headstone at Alvin gives 8 November 1894, and the 1900 census, as the earlier Illinois-to-Texas story reports, listed him as born in November 1894; the list says 1895. If the age of 22 is right, the registration was made after his birthday in 1917, which fits the registration of September 1918 better than the first call of June 1917; the transcription gives no date for him, though it does for others.

The same list holds a second Beaucoup birth in Texas: Melvin Livesay, born on 15 October 1891 at Beaucoup, aged 26, single, an oil field worker, residing in Texas. The Beaucoup birth and the Texas residence make a family link plausible, because Floyd and Alice lived in Illinois until the mid-1890s and then left for Brazoria County with children, among them Lester and, soon after, a daughter born in Texas about 1898. No Melvin is named in the stories already on this site, but they name only Walter, William Paul, Lester and Ruth. The 1900 census household and the 1910 census would show whether a Melvin was in it.

The list is silent on two other sons. Walter, born about 1880, died in January 1912, and William Paul, born about 1883, died in April 1915, so neither could have registered; their absence is what the draft ages predict. The list does include several other Livesays born in the county, among them men at Ashley and Richview, who are from other families and are not discussed here.
