1900 U.S. census, Brazoria County, Floyd and Alice Livesay household, as cited in the earlier story “From Illinois to the Texas Gulf Coast” (not re-examined): https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:M32B-JSM
stories.note: Lester’s identification is probable, since three details agree. Melvin is a lead only: the surname and the Beaucoup birth are common to several families, and the list names no parents. Melvin is not added to the tree. The birth year for Lester (1894 on the stone and in the 1900 census as reported earlier, 1895 on the list) is not reconciled; no original registration card was examined.

stories.title: Walkers in a row: Richview, July 1860
stories.hook: On 3 July 1860 the census taker at Richview wrote down five Walker households within a few dwellings of one another, and gave William P. Walker's wife Abigail a birthplace of New York.

subject.name: William P. Walker and his Walker neighbors

body: The 1860 federal census of Washington County is scanned on the Internet Archive as reel 235 of the National Archives series M653 (358 images). Pages 62 and 63 of the Richview post office, Township 2 South, Range 1 West, were taken on 3 July 1860 by the assistant marshal, whose surname reads Blankenship. The county's volunteer transcriptions of the 1860 census are partial and do not cover these pages, so the original images were read here, name by name.

William P. Walker's household is dwelling 453, family 420, on page 63. Wm P. Walker, 29, is a farmer born in Illinois. With him are Abigail, 27, Mary E E, 5, Alice May, 1, and Carrie Ida, 1, with Illinois written as the birthplace of every child. For Abigail the enumerator wrote something quite different: “N York.” The ages fit the Beaucoup stone, which gives her birth year as 1833, and they fit the Abigail Shank, 16, born in New York, whom the 1850 census found in a neighboring household. Alice May at 1 agrees with the headstone date of 11 January 1859.

Three households on the same page stand close by. Dwelling 452, directly above William's, is John W. Walker, 35, a farmer, with Lavina E., 30, and four children aged 10, 6, 5 and 2 whose first names are hard to read. A John W. Walker, 25, with Lavina E. and an infant son was dwelling 460 in 1850. Dwelling 456 is G. W. Walker, 33, a farmer, with Elizabeth, 31, and Frances C. E., 10, plus younger children, the same family as the Lieutenant George W. Walker of the earlier story, whose daughter had been eight months old in 1850. Page 62, just before, has Simeon Walker, 28, a farmer, at dwelling 449 and an Alex Walker, 24, a farmer, at dwelling 450 with Sarah A., 21, Wm H., 3, and Edwin F., 8 months, and a 20-year-old schoolteacher, Ellen Barns, in the house.

Simeon Walker's household, dwelling 449, is the one the cemetery stones lead one to expect, with one difference. Simeon, 28, is there with E. J., 26, who matches Etheldra Jane, born July 1833. But the page also shows a girl of 1, whose name reads Clara, and a Caroline, 12, born in Illinois. The Beaucoup stones list only sons for Simeon and Etheldra J. (Wilbert, James H., Simon G. and Elmer D.), and a daughter of 12 could not be Etheldra's, since Etheldra was herself 26. So the household held at least one girl who is not in the tree: a baby daughter who may have died young, or a relative, and an older girl whose connection is unknown. Neither is added as a person.

Five Walker households in eight dwellings fits the picture the earlier stories built: Rev. James Walker's probable sons and daughters had settled together near the old home place. George W. and John W. Walker had already stood security for Simeon Walker's Hoyleton bank loan in January 1860. Census pages do not state relationships, and no record opened here shows how Alex Walker, who is not in the 1850 James Walker household, was related to the others. Rev. James had died in 1857, and his widow Etheldra, then about 55, is not on the pages read (images n61 to n68, pages 58 to 65); where she lived in 1860 is not established.
quotes: Wm P. Walker, 29, Farmer, Illinois; Abigail, 27, N York; Mary E E, 5; Alice May, 1; Carrie Ida, 1 (1860 census, Richview P.O., dwelling 453)

The identifications of the households with the Beaucoup Walkers rest on names, ages, neighbors and the 1850 and 1870 pages. Abigail's New York birthplace here conflicts with Illinois in the 1870 census and on Alice’s death certificate; see the stories on the 1870 household and on Abigail’s birthplace.

stories.title: William P. Walker's household, Richview, 1870
stories.hook: By June 1870 William and Abigail Walker had six children at home, including a bracketed pair of twelve-year-old twins, and the census had changed Abigail's birthplace from New York to Illinois.

subject.name: William P. and Abigail Walker's household

body: The 1870 census of Washington County is on the Internet Archive as reel 287 of the National Archives series M593 (474 images). Page 70 of Township 2 South, Range 1 West, post office Richview, was enumerated on 20 June 1870 by John H. Barber, assistant marshal. Dwelling 548, family 531, reads: Walker, Wm P., 39, farmer, real estate $3,000, personal estate $1,500, born Illinois; Abigail, 37, keeping house; Mary E., 14; Alice M., 12; Carrie, 12, and Ellen A., 12, joined by a bracket and the word “twins”; Wm S., 6; and Charles, 3. Every name is given Illinois as a birthplace, Abigail's included.

Compared with 1860, the household grew by three children and lost none. Mary E E, 5 in 1860, is now Mary E., 14, and Alice May, 1, is 12, a year older than the headstone's 1859 birth would make her, which is an ordinary census drift. Carrie Ida, 1 in 1860, is Carrie, 12. Ellen A. is new, with no counterpart in 1860, and the twin bracket links her to Carrie, even though the 1860 page already showed two girls aged 1, Alice and Carrie. Either Ellen was missed or misplaced in 1860, or one of the 1870 ages or brackets is a slip. The two later children, Wm S. and Charles, were born in the 1860s; William was serving with the 60th Illinois from the spring of 1864 to July 1865, so William S., aged 6 in June 1870, may have been born while his father was away or just before he left.

The father's land is the other change. The 1860 page gives William's real estate and personal estate in figures too faint to read with confidence; the 1870 entry is $3,000 of real estate and $1,500 in personal property. The post office is the same, Richview, and the page is filled with farm households, not the railroad workers and merchants of the village pages.

A Washington County marriage register transcription records Andrew J. Scott and Mary E. E. Walker on 22 November 1871, a year and a half after this census, when the Mary E. of this page would have been about 16. The initials E. E. match the 1860 entry and the earlier story's reading of a name beginning Mary Ellen Etheldra. These children are added to the tree as probable children of William P. Walker. No mother is linked to them, because the question whether Abigail was Alice's mother, left open by Alice's death certificate, is still undecided.

One entry in this household is worth setting beside the earlier ones. Abigail is Illinois-born here, but the 1860 page gave her birthplace as New York, and the Abigail Shank of 1850 was also born in New York. The separate story on Abigail's birthplace sets out all the records that disagree.

stories.title: Abigail Walker: born in New York, or in Illinois?
stories.hook: Four records say where Abigail Walker, William P. Walker's wife, or Alice's recorded mother Addie Bruce, was born. Two say New York, two say Illinois, and no record yet names her parents.
body: The earlier story on Abigail Shank left a question to the 1860 census: where did Abigail Walker say she was born? The Richview page of 3 July 1860 answers it. Abigail, 27, in William P. Walker's household (dwelling 453), is given the birthplace “N York,” while her husband and children are all marked Illinois. That agrees with the 1850 census, where an Abigail Shank, 16, born in New York, lived in David S. Jack's household at dwelling 462 on a page that also holds John W. Walker's dwelling 460.

Ten years later the 1870 census, page 70 of the Richview post office, gives Abigail, 37, the same Illinois birthplace as everyone else in the house. Alice Walker Livesay's Texas death certificate of 1922 names her mother as Addie Bruce, born in Illinois. So the tally is two New York entries (1850 and 1860) against two Illinois entries (1870 and 1922). Either an enumerator carried the children's Illinois down onto the mother's line in 1870, or the 1860 entry is the slip, or two different women are in view; nothing in these pages decides among them.

The name is the second half of the problem. Abigail Shank (1850) and the Washington County marriage register's Abigail Schanck, licensed on 25 February 1852 to a William F. Walker, are the same surname spelled two ways. The register entry also lists a bondsman, William H. Walker, which shows a Walker standing for the groom, but the groom's initial F does not match William P. and no record found says that William P. Walker's wife was a Schanck. Bruce, on Alice's certificate, is a different name entirely. A married daughter's death certificate would normally give her mother's maiden name, so the children's records matter more than another census.

Several steps remain. The 1880 census, which asks for each person's parents' birthplaces, would show Abigail's and her husband's; it is on the Internet Archive as reels 256 and 257 for Washington County but the Richview district was not located here. The Illinois death certificates of the Walker children who lived past 1916 (Mary E. E. Scott or any of the daughters) should name their mother. And an 1852 Washington County marriage record, the original, would show whether the groom was William P. or William F. Until one of these is found, Abigail's birthplace is recorded as conflicting, her maiden name is not adopted, and she is not linked as Alice's mother.

Abigail, 37, F, Illinois (1870 census, Richview P.O., dwelling 548)

stories.title: Sergeant, lieutenant, captain: Simeon Walker in the state's roll
stories.hook: The state's own roster shows Simeon Walker rising from sergeant to captain of Company C, 60th Illinois, in ten months, and leaving the regiment two days before Averysboro.

subject.name: Captain Simeon Walker, Company C, 60th Illinois Infantry

body: The Report of the Adjutant General of the State of Illinois, volume 4, prints the roster of the 60th Illinois Infantry. Company C's officers are on pages 181 and 182. Simeon Walker appears three times. As a sergeant he is listed from Nashville, with an enlistment date of 10 February 1862 and a muster date of 21 February 1862; the remark reads “Promoted 2d Lieutenant.” As a second lieutenant his date of rank is 20 July 1862. As a captain his rank dates from 19 December 1862, the day the first captain, John R. Moss of Mt. Vernon, resigned; he was mustered in as captain on 16 April 1863 and mustered out on 14 March 1865. The residence column for the captains reads Mt. Vernon, with ditto marks for Walker.

The state's history of the regiment, on pages 207 and 208 of the same volume, gives the setting. The 60th was organized at Camp Dubois, Anna, on 17 February 1862 by Colonel Silas C. Toler. It went to Cairo, then to Island No. 10, the siege of Corinth, and by September 1862 to Nashville, where it was cut off from supplies until November. Toler died on 2 March 1863. The regiment fought at Chattanooga, wintered at Rossville and in February 1864 saw three-fourths of its men re-enlist as veterans; on 26 February it lost 42 killed and wounded at Buzzard Roost. It went through the Atlanta campaign, the March to the Sea and Savannah, then fought at Averysboro on 16 March 1865 and at Bentonville from 19 to 21 March, marched in the Grand Review on 24 May, and was mustered out on 31 July 1865 after provost duty at Louisville.

Simeon Walker's discharge of 14 March 1865 came two days before Averysboro. The same remark, “Mustered out Mar. 14, 1865,” stands beside several privates on page 182, while many of their comrades are marked “Re-enlisted as Veteran,” which suggests that the 14 March men were original enlistees who did not re-enlist. William P. Walker, by contrast, joined as a recruit in March 1864 and stayed to the end in July 1865, as the earlier story shows, so he was probably in the ranks at Averysboro and Bentonville, although the records opened here do not name his engagements.

The roster also confirms the regiment's chaplain, Levi S. Walker, whose residence is given as Richview; the earlier stories note him as a Methodist preacher of the other Walker family. A second point is a caution. The state's roster gives the sergeant's residence as Nashville and the captain's as Mt. Vernon, neither of them Richview, where a Simeon Walker, 28, with E. J., 26, appears in the 1860 census. The identification of Captain Simeon Walker with Etheldra J. Walker's husband rests on the Beaucoup stone's comment that he was a captain of Company C, 60th Illinois, and on the 1879 county history's Simon Walker of that company; the roll alone does not tie him to Richview.

stories.title: The lieutenant who resigned at Jalapa
stories.hook: The county history lists George W. Walker as second lieutenant of the Washington County company in the Mexican War. The War Department roster adds that he resigned at Jalapa on 17 December 1847, five months after the company left Nashville.

subject.name: George W. Walker, Company H, 2nd Illinois Volunteers

body: The story of Lieutenant George W. Walker of Beaucoup used the 1879 county history, which names him among Company H's officers. The Record of the Services of Illinois Soldiers in the Black Hawk War and in the Mexican War, an 1882 printing of the War Department's rolls, gives each man's remarks. On page 259, Company H of the Second Regiment lists Captain James Burns, First Lieutenant Malachi Jenkins and, under Second Lieutenants, George W. Walker, all enrolled at Nashville, Illinois, on 10 July 1847. Beside Walker's name the remark reads: “Resigned at Jalapa, Mexico, Dec. 17, 1847.”

That date matters because the regiment was then in winter quarters at Jalapa, according to the county history, and the company's Mexican service ran until July 1848. Walker therefore served about five months, through the voyage to Vera Cruz in August, the fight at San Juan on 18 September and the first months at Jalapa, and did not come home with the company. The 1902 obituary of Rev. George Walker, as transcribed, calls him a Mexican War veteran, and the 1850 census finds him farming at Beaucoup, so the resignation did not end his life there.

The roster also lists two privates named Walker, John and Thomas, enrolled at Nashville on 10 July 1847, and one man who did not return: Ezekiah Walker, whose remark is “Died at Vera Cruz, Mex., Sept. 10, 1847.” The county history spells him Ezekiel and gives the same date. No record opened here says whether any of these men was kin to George W. Walker or to Rev. James Walker's family; the 1850 Walker households named in the earlier stories do not include an Ezekiel.

Two small discrepancies between the printings are worth noting. The county history names James K. Finch as third lieutenant and as dying at Vera Cruz on 12 September 1847; the War Department roster lists a second lieutenant James R. Lynch with the same death date and place, so either one printing gives a different name for the same man or two men died there that day. And the roster lists an Isaac B. Jack, promoted second lieutenant on 28 February 1848, where the county history shows him only as a private; the register records an Isaac Berry Jack marrying Elizabeth C. Walker on 3 April 1845, but whether this is the same Isaac B. Jack is not shown.

stories.title: Abner Clay and Mattie Denson, 20 May 1897
stories.hook: Wilsey Clay’s son Abner took a second wife under Choctaw law. The license, written in Choctaw, survives in the Dawes jacket with an English translation made six years later.

subject.name: Abner H. Clay
subject.rel: Half-brother of Peter Durant and half great-uncle of Ida May Merry

body: Choctaw census card 507, made on 18 April 1899 at Lukfata, is headed by Abner H. Clay, 27, three-quarters Choctaw, the son of Henry Clay (dead) and Wilsey Clay. Under him it lists Mattie, 26, an intermarried white woman, and three children, Abner Henry, Mattie Lorena and Myrtle Eugenia, the last two entered after their births in 1899 and 1902. The jacket behind the card, thirty-eight page images in the National Archives Catalog, tells how the household came to be.

Abner and Mattie married on 20 May 1897 at Lukfata. The license was issued that day by J. A. James, county clerk of Bok Tuklo County, to “Mattie Denson a United States citizen” and “A. H. Clay a Choctaw citizen.” It was written in Choctaw, and in August 1903 the Commission’s interpreter L. G. Battiest swore at Atoka that his English translation was true. A handwritten certificate in English, signed by R. W. Thomas as judge of Bok Tuklo County, says the same couple were united “according to Regulation and Laws of the Choctaw Nation.” This is the same Thomas who, as county clerk until October 1896, had taken the oath and the hundred-dollar fee from Louis Merry eight months earlier.

Mattie testified at Wister on 16 December 1902 that she was then 32, that she had lived at Lukfata seven years, that she had never been married before, and that Abner had a first wife, Mabel Clay, who had been dead about four years when they married. Her parents, Joseph H. and Mattie E. Denson, are named on the card as non-citizens. Abner and Mattie’s children were born at Lukfata: Abner Henry on 29 March 1898 and Mattie Lorena on 25 September 1899, and Myrtle Eugenia on 8 March 1902, the last of them sworn to at Shawneetown in October 1902, after Mattie had left. The midwives were Amanda Butler in 1898 and Jane Butler in 1899 and 1902.

For the Merry and Durant line the household matters in two ways. Abner is the half-brother of Peter Durant, Bessie’s father, so his three children are probably half first cousins of Bessie, and his marriage was handled by the same county officers at the same place and under the same law that made Louis Merry’s marriage valid. The two files let a reader compare what a white spouse had to do to marry into the Nation in 1896 and in 1897. The next story, about the separation, follows the same jacket to 1904.

stories.title: Abner Clay, Mattie and the allotment letters, 1902–1904
stories.hook: A marriage that ended in October 1902 left the Commission a year of letters about who could choose land for three small children.
body: The jacket for card 507 is mostly letters from the Commission to Choctaw Nation officers and to Abner and Mattie Clay. They show a family dividing just as the Nation’s land was being surveyed for allotment. Mattie told the Commission on 16 December 1902 that she had lived with Abner until 9 October, that he had shot her through the arm and beaten her, and that he was living with another woman. She had gone to Lockesburg, Arkansas, in October, and the Commission wrote to her there until February 1904. Abner wrote on 10 December denying the charges, and on 12 January 1903 the Commission wrote that it would take any evidence he offered within thirty days.

The questions put to Mattie show what was at stake. As an intermarried white woman she could be enrolled only if she and her Choctaw husband had lived together as husband and wife in the Nation up to 25 September 1902, and the Commission wanted to know whether they had been divorced. She answered that neither of them had obtained a divorce and that she meant to return to the Nation “some day.” In January and again on 23 February 1903 Abner asked to give further evidence against her application; on 5 March the Commission told him he could appear at Atoka on 13 March, he did not, and on 21 March it acknowledged his letter of excuse. On 2 March 1904 the Commission decided in her favor, finding that they had married lawfully on 20 May 1897 and had lived together to the cutoff date. On 7 April 1904, answering her letter of 31 March from Garvin, Indian Territory, the Commission told her no protest had been filed by the Nations’ attorneys, and she was approved as an intermarried citizen on 7 May 1904.

Meanwhile the children’s land was in dispute. On 29 January 1903 Claude Denson of Shawneetown, who said he was Mattie’s brother, asked who had the right to select allotments for her three children. The Commission quoted the act of Congress that gave minors’ selections to “the father or mother, if members.” Mattie wrote on 9 February that Abner should not be allowed to choose for them, and in February 1904 the Commission passed her protest to the land offices at Atoka and Tishomingo. On 14 March 1903 the Commission also answered a letter in which Abner and other citizens proposed an organization to elect a committee of reliable men to select allotments at Atoka for members too poor or too ill to travel.

The file gives no end to the story, though it does show Mattie back at Garvin, in the Choctaw Nation, by March 1904. It does not say who selected the children’s land or whether the couple were ever divorced, and it does not say what became of Abner after 1904. It does show Abner Clay, Peter Durant’s half-brother, as an active citizen at Lukfata in 1903, writing to the Commission about the way the Nation’s land would be shared out.

stories.title: Wilsey Clay swears, May 1906
stories.hook: At sixty-seven Wilsey Clay stood before a Commission clerk and named another son, Thomas Durant. It answers a question the earlier stories had to leave open.

subject.name: Wilsey Clay
subject.rel: Great-grandmother of Ida May Merry Whitfield

body: The story of Lizzie Durant on card 966 began as a puzzle in the Merry file. Wilsey Clay’s household card, 655, listed a granddaughter named Licey, the daughter of Thomas and Melinda Durant, and noted that she was a duplicate of Lizzie Durant on card 966. Earlier stories could not say whether Thomas was Wilsey’s son or Melinda her daughter. The jacket for card 966 settles it.

In 1906 the Commission looked into the duplicate enrollment. Wilsey Clay was sworn at Lukfata on 9 May, with Jacob Homer as interpreter. She gave her age as 67 and said she was a Choctaw by blood. Asked if she was the mother of Thomas Durant, she said yes; he had died several years earlier; his wife was Melinda Durant; and he had two daughters, Jane and Lizzie or Licey, both living. She said Lizzie was one girl enrolled twice: the girl had enrolled herself, and when Wilsey went to Alikchi she enrolled her again under the other spelling. Lizzie, sworn five days later at C. W. Westbrook’s store five miles north of Glover, said the same.

The Department cancelled the Licey Durant entry on card 655 as an error. It recommended the cancellation in August 1906 and the Assistant Secretary of the Interior concurred on 19 September, leaving her enrolled once, as Lizzie, with an allotment already chosen.

The testimony makes Wilsey Clay the mother of three families: Abner Clay by Henry Clay, Ida and Laura by Charles Gavner, and Thomas Durant. The Durant surname of Thomas and of Peter Durant, whom John M. Hodges called Wilsey’s son in 1900, fits one household, but nothing read says whether the two men had the same father or were brothers by the same marriage. That keeps Peter’s own link to Wilsey probable, while Thomas’s is proven by her own sworn answer. It also makes Lizzie, whose 1893 money was collected with Bessie’s through J. L. Merry, a probable first cousin of Bessie Durant Merry.

Her age (67 in 1906) is a little higher than the 58 of 1899, a difference that is kept as written. The Department’s letter calls the witness “Wilson Clay” and dates the testimony 10 July 1906, which is the date of the typed transcript; the transcript itself dates the testimony at Lukfata to 9 May. Thomas’s relationship to Peter Durant is not stated in any record read and is not linked.

stories.title: Lizzie Durant: Wheelock, a wedding and a baby at Glover
stories.hook: A Wheelock schoolgirl on a Dawes card in 1899 was a wife and mother at Glover three years later, and her mail went through J. L. Merry.

subject.name: Lizzie Durant Gibbs
subject.rel: Probable first cousin of Bessie Durant Merry

body: Lizzie Durant was 13 when she was enrolled on 27 April 1899 at Wheelock Seminary, a Choctaw Nation boarding school, as a full-blood Choctaw whose father was Thomas Durant of Bok Tuklo County (card 966, roll 2580). She said under oath in 1906 that she had been a student there that April. Her grandmother Wilsey Clay had meanwhile enrolled her again as Licey on card 655, as the story of Wilsey’s testimony explains.

On 24 March 1902 the clerk of the United States court in Indian Territory issued a license for Fred Gibbs of Lukfata, 21, and Miss Lizzie Durant of Lukfata, 18. Milton A. Clark, a minister of the gospel, certified that he married them on 31 March 1902 and returned the paper on 2 April. Fred was not a Choctaw citizen, and the Commission later wrote to Lizzie asking for the license and certificate as authority for the change of her name on its records.

Their son Isaam was born on 30 August 1902. On 1 December 1902 Lizzie swore to his birth before J. L. Merry, notary public, with the midwife Susion Franklin’s affidavit taken the same day. The boy was approved as an infant citizen on 8 December, and the Commission’s letter of that date is addressed to Lizzie Gibbs at Glover. Later that month Principal Chief Green McCurtain wrote to Merry about the 1893 money of “Ben and Lizzie Durant,” the letter told in the story of the leased district money.

The allotment she mentioned in 1906 was already selected under the name Lizzie Durant. The jacket tells nothing about her after that year, and no record read gives a death date for her or for Fred Gibbs. If Peter Durant was Wilsey’s son, as John M. Hodges said in 1900, Lizzie and Bessie were first cousins, though no record read says how Thomas and Peter were related.

Lizzie’s age ranges from 13 to 23 across records dated 1899 to 1906. The boy’s name is spelled Isaam, Isaan and Isom on the documents. Several other records were not found: a marriage record from Fred’s side, and any later census.

stories.title: The notaries at Lukfata and Glover, 1899–1902
stories.hook: Gaffney, Sleeper and Merry each swore Choctaw families’ affidavits at Lukfata or Glover. The last signature is Louis Merry’s own.
body: Choctaw families had to prove births with sworn affidavits, and each one needed a notary public. The jackets for cards 507 and 966 show who held that job in the Lukfata neighborhood. On 1 May 1899 Mattie Clay and the midwife Amanda Butler swore to the birth of Abner Henry Clay before Chas. J. Gaffney, notary public. A Chas. J. Gaffney was also a witness on the certificate of Louis Merry and Bessie Durant’s wedding at Lukfata in 1896.

On 20 October 1899 Mattie Clay swore to Mattie Lorena’s birth before John H. Sleeper, notary public, at Lukfata. The same J. H. Sleeper, signing as Rev. J. H. Sleeper, performed the Merry wedding in 1896, and Louis Merry later described him as a missionary. So the man who married Louis to Bessie also witnessed oaths for neighbors three years afterward. In October 1902 the notaries were different again: Mattie Clay’s affidavit for Myrtle was sworn on 24 October before W. F. Nichols at Shawneetown, and the midwife’s on 29 October before a notary whose signature reads J. W. Costelow, the name of the other witness to the 1896 Merry wedding.

Then, on 1 December 1902, the notary was Louis himself. The birth affidavits for Lizzie Durant Gibbs’s son Isaam, her own and the midwife Susion Franklin’s, are both signed “J. L. Merry, Notary Public.” He was at Glover then, as postmaster and as the applicant whose own enrollment the Commission was still examining. A year earlier, in 1901, he had been appointed Glover’s first postmaster. In the notary’s signature the initials that the Commission used for him are written by his own hand, which fits the earlier story’s evidence that J. L. Merry of Glover and Louis Merry of card 5754 are the same man.

It also shows him doing a public job. A Choctaw woman whose husband was a United States citizen brought her sworn statement to Merry, who was himself still an applicant. The affidavit was filed with the Commission and the child was approved a week later.

Merry with Louis Merry is probable on the Glover address, the initials and the other J. L. Merry letters. stories.title: Laura Clay and William A. Durant at Red River
stories.hook: Laura, Wilsey Clay’s daughter, married into a household of three motherless boys on the Red River side of the Nation.

subject.name: Laura Clay Durant
subject.rel: Half great-aunt of Ida May Merry Whitfield

body: Card 656 was made on 21 April 1899, the same day as the card for her mother Wilsey Clay. It lists William A. Durant, 29, and Laura, 19, his wife, both one-half Choctaw, and three sons aged eight, six and five. The residence is Red River County and the post office Garvin, and Wilsey’s own card gives Red River as her post office in Bok Tuklo County, so the family was spread across the Nation’s counties.

The columns for the parents answer who is who. William’s parents are Allington Durant and Mary Durant, both dead and both of Red River. Laura’s are Charles Gavener, a non-citizen, and Wilsey Clay, enrolled in 1896 in Bok Tuklo. The boys, Gibby, Eddie and Louie, are William’s sons, but their mother is given as Sarah Durant, also dead and of Red River, not Laura, who at 19 was too young to be mother to an eight-year-old. A note on the card says William and Laura were on the 1896 roll as Wm. A. Durant and Laura Clay, he in Nashoba County and she in Bok Tuklo. The Secretary of the Interior approved all five on 12 December 1902.

Nothing in the card links William to Peter or Thomas Durant, whose mother was also Wilsey Clay. Durant was a very common Choctaw family name, and the family trees of the several Durant lines are not examined here. The card is kept because it fills out the household of Laura Clay and names William’s parents. Laura has the same parents on the cards as Ida Clay, so they were sisters, and she was a half-sister of Abner Clay and, probably, of Peter Durant.

stories.title: Lukfata, the White Clay settlement
stories.hook: Louis Merry’s wedding place was a Choctaw settlement older than the Nation’s Oklahoma counties, and a mission field before it was a county seat.

subject.name: Lukfata
subject.rel: Place of the Merry and Durant wedding, 1896

body: Muriel H. Wright, writing in the Chronicles of Oklahoma in 1950, gave the history of the name. Lukfata, also spelled Lukfahta and Lukfoata, means “White Clay.” It was the name of an old tribal village in what is now Kemper County, Mississippi, and the Choctaws who were removed to the West in 1832 to 1834 gave it to a new settlement in what is now McCurtain County, Oklahoma, about two and a half miles west of Broken Bow. A mission school of the American Board was opened there in 1835. Her notes name the Rev. Henry R. Wilson as the missionary who established the nearby Bok Tuklo mission in 1834, and place the mission about nine miles southwest of Broken Bow, on a creek forking in two. Bok Tuklo is Choctaw for “two creeks.”

The Nation later borrowed that name for a county. Bok Tuklo County lay in the Apukshunnubbee District, with Eagle County on the east, Red River County to the south and Towson County to the west, and its seat was Oak Hill. A county judge, sheriff and ranger were elected for two-year terms, and the county clerk kept the records of the county court. These are the offices that appear in the family’s files: R. W. Thomas as clerk until 1 October 1896 and county judge by May 1897, Joe A. James as clerk, and the licenses that they issued for Louis Merry in 1896 and for Abner Clay in 1897.

By the 1890s Lukfata was a post office and a place where Wilsey Clay’s children and grandchildren lived. Abner Clay’s card has Lukfata as his post office in 1899, Thomas Durant lived there, and Louis Merry gave it as his home in 1900. His 1900 testimony put him there about eight years. The people on these cards lived there just before the Nation’s land was divided into allotments. In 1905 the Sequoyah convention proposed that Bok Tuklo County become part of a new McCurtain County, and the Choctaw Nation’s counties disappeared when Oklahoma became a state in 1907.
This is a story about a place, not about a person; no record read says where Bessie Durant was born or raised, and Lukfata is where she married and where her grandmother’s family clustered.

stories.note: A context story. The place-name history and the mission dates are Wright’s; the county organization is from Wikipedia, which gives no sources of its own for it. The Sequoyah proposal and 1907 statehood are from the Wikipedia article and were not checked against another source. The family facts are from the Dawes jackets cited. Wright’s mission site (Section 2, T7S R23E) and Louis Merry’s farm described in 1904 (Section 4, T6S R23E) are different townships and are not claimed to be near each other.

stories.title: Calvin and Elizabeth Merry: what the records say
stories.hook: Louis Merry’s parents are named on one document, and nothing else about them has been found. The tree keeps them out on purpose.

subject.name: Calvin and Elizabeth Merry
subject.rel: Named parents of Louis Merry (not linked)

body: The only record read that names Louis Merry’s parents is Dawes card 5754, made on 26 April 1899. Its columns for his parents give Calvin Merry and Elizabeth Merry, both marked dead, both “non-citiz,” meaning that they were not citizens of the Choctaw Nation. Bessie’s parents, Peter and Ellen Durant, are given as of Bok Tuklo on the same card.

A burial-site memorial elsewhere names Louis’s parents as John Calvin Merry and Eliza Jane McGregor and his birthplace as Sevier County, Arkansas. The card’s Calvin and Elizabeth fit that, but the card has no middle name, maiden name or place, and a memorial posted by an unknown contributor is a lead and not a record. Elizabeth and Eliza Jane could be the same woman, but nothing read shows it. A common surname, a given name like Calvin and a Sevier County birth are the kind of match that a census or probate record would have to settle.

What the Commission’s own file adds is only a date. Louis told it in December 1900 that he had lived in the Choctaw Nation about eight years, which puts his arrival around 1892, when he was about twenty by his gravestone’s birth year. Where he was before that, and where his parents lived and died, is not in the file.

For these reasons Calvin and Elizabeth Merry are told here and not added to the tree: an existing test keeps Lewis Merry’s parents unlinked, and the records would not support more than a lead. What would settle it is a record that names Louis with his parents: the 1880 census of Sevier or a neighboring Arkansas county, a probate file for a Calvin Merry, or an obituary of Louis in 1932 that names his birthplace.
src: Choctaw census card 5754, Louis, Bessie and Ida May Merry, parents’ columns; National Archives, NAID 636187; examined 3 Nov 2026 (as read in the story “Card 5754 read”): https://catalog.archives.gov/id/636187

Testimony of Louis Merry, Atoka, 7 December 1900 (about eight years in the Nation), Dawes Enrollment Jacket for Choctaw by Blood, Card #5754, image 2185; as cited in the story “A wedding at Lukfata”: https://catalog.archives.gov/id/44362518
stories.note: A lead story. The memorial’s parents and Sevier County birthplace are an unverified lead from an earlier researcher and were not examined here. No census, probate or other record naming Calvin or Elizabeth Merry has been found. Lewis Merry’s father and mother stay unlinked in the tree, as the existing tests require.

stories.title: Dudley Logan, private, 7th Alabama Cavalry
stories.hook: A cemetery transcription in Mount Pleasant and a muster roll from Greene County, Alabama, both name a Private Dudley Logan of the 7th Alabama Cavalry. It is the first record to say where Dudley served.
body: The widow’s pension index told us only that someone thought Dudley Logan had been a Confederate. Two other records now say which army unit. The Masonic Cemetery in Mount Pleasant, Texas, has been transcribed for the Titus County TXGenWeb site, and its entry for Logan, Dudley reads January 8, 1846, to November 21, 1898, with the remark “Pvt 7th Ala Cav CSA.” The dates are the ones the tree already gives, so this is the same man as the Dudley Timothy Logan of the family memorial, and the inscription, or the funeral-home record it was copied from, names his regiment.

The second record is a muster roll on the Greene County, Alabama, GenWeb site: Company B, 7th Alabama Cavalry, headed “Muster Roll of the Broadfoots of Greene County” and submitted by a contributor, Scott Owens. Among the privates it lists Logan, Dudley, along with Logan, L. and Logan, Zach M. The page gives names and ranks only. It has no ages, no dates and no residences, and it does not say whether it is a first roll or a later one. The same site’s separate list of Greene County Confederate veterans includes Zachary M. Logan of Company B, 7th Alabama Cavalry, but it has no Dudley, so that list is plainly not complete.

Together the two records account for a puzzle left by the earlier work. The state archives’ own Civil War service database, searched for the earlier story, shows no Dudley Logan, yet his widow, Mrs. A. E. Logan of Titus County, filed Texas Confederate pension application 30414 in his name. A man born in Greene County, Alabama, in January 1846 who served in a company raised in Greene County, with a tombstone that names that regiment and a widow who later claimed his service, is a consistent picture. The roll and the stone are independent of each other, since one was compiled in Alabama and the other in Texas.

Two other Logans stand beside him on the roll, and the 1850 census of Greene County shows many Logan households, but nothing here says they were Dudley’s kin. Zachary and L. may be neighbors, cousins or uncles, or no relation. The roll also does not show whether Dudley was a boy of seventeen when he enlisted or joined later. The next records to open are the compiled service file for the regiment at the National Archives, the roll images at the Alabama archives, and the pension file, which the earlier story could not reach.
src: TXGenWeb Titus County, Masonic Cemetery transcription (compiler David Horton, from Bates-Cooper Funeral Home records, Lynch Harper’s 1960s survey and later surveys), read 4 Nov 2026: Logan, Dudley, January 8, 1846, November 21, 1898, “Pvt 7th Ala Cav CSA”: https://www.txgenwebcounties.net/titus/cemeteries/masonic_cem.html

Greene County, Alabama GenWeb (ALGenWeb), Civil War Units from Greene County: Company B, 7th Alabama Cavalry, “Muster Roll of the Broadfoots of Greene County,” submitted by Scott Owens; privates include Logan, Dudley, Logan, L. and Logan, Zach M.; transcription read 4 Nov 2026 (original roll not seen): https://magnoliasandpeaches.com/GreeneAlGenWeb/Military/CSA/CivilWarUnitsGreene7thCavalryCoB.asp

Greene County, Alabama GenWeb, Civil War Veterans, surnames G to L, entry Logan, Zachary M., Co. B, 7th Alabama Cavalry (no Dudley Logan listed), read 4 Nov 2026: https://magnoliasandpeaches.com/GreeneAlGenWeb/Military/CSA/CSAVetsGL.asp

Texas State Library and Archives Commission, Index to Confederate Pension Applications, application 30414, Mrs. A. E. Logan, Titus County, as described in “A widow’s pension application from Titus County” (index only, not re-examined here): https://www.tsl.texas.gov/apps/arc/pensions
stories.note: Probable, not proven. Both new records are transcriptions and neither gives an age or residence, so a second Dudley Logan cannot be ruled out. The tombstone wording has not been compared with the stone itself. The company roll is undated on the page. Confirm with the National Archives service file or the Alabama archives’ roll images.

stories.title: The Logan stones at the Masonic Cemetery, Mount Pleasant
stories.hook: Dudley’s grave is not the only Logan one in Mount Pleasant. Two boys who died a year apart, in 1888 and 1889, are marked as sons of “D. & Annie Logan.”
body: The Masonic Cemetery lies in the northwest part of Mount Pleasant. The county’s TXGenWeb pages say it has served the town and county since 1888, when a couple gave five acres to the Masonic Lodge, and that the earlier Old Mount Pleasant cemetery was judged too crowded and irregular to keep up. The page adds that people buried in the old Christian cemetery were reburied in the Masonic one, which is worth remembering when reading dates from before 1888.

Its transcription has several Logan entries that matter here. Dudley Logan, 8 January 1846 to 21 November 1898, is the soldier. Ernest C. A. Logan, 20 April 1876 to 15 August 1889, and Evan A. C. Logan, 23 February 1880 to 15 November 1888, are each described as “Son of D. & Annie Logan.” Ernest’s stone carries a short verse about a loss deeply felt, and the compiler notes that Evan’s monument is broken and unreadable. They were thirteen and eight when they died, and the stones place them in the same family as Dudley and the woman the family calls Annie Wedgeworth Logan.

Three more Logan entries lie close in the listing, and a fourth name is linked by marriage. Edd H. Logan, 25 October 1872 to 6 December 1947, is marked “Papa,” and Sallie G. Logan, 23 July 1879 to 9 May 1958, “Mama.” Dudley Edward “Dud” Logan, 25 February 1899 to 15 March 1981, was born three months after Dudley died. A Charles Homer Stewart, 1895 to 1980, has a note naming his wife as Eva G. Logan Stewart. None of these stones names a parent, so their place in Dudley’s family is only a guess. Edd was born in 1872, when Dudley was twenty-six, and the 1959 obituary of Annie Box lists her surviving brothers as Rob and Walter, not Edd, who had died in 1947. The infant Dud is probably a grandson, and Edd and Sallie are the most likely parents. These remain leads, and none is added to the tree.

What the transcription does not contain is a stone for Annie Wedgeworth Logan. There is no entry for her in the Masonic Cemetery under Logan, and a search of all 114 Titus County cemetery pages on the TXGenWeb site found no Wedgeworth and no other Annie, Sarah or Sallie Logan beyond those above. Either she is buried elsewhere, outside Titus County, or she remarried and is listed under another surname. Her 1923 death year, taken from family links on Find a Grave, is therefore still unverified.
src: TXGenWeb Titus County, Masonic Cemetery transcription (compiler David Horton, from Bates-Cooper Funeral Home records, Lynch Harper’s 1960s survey and later surveys), read 4 Nov 2026: entries Logan, Dudley; Logan, Ernest C. A.; Logan, Evan A. C.; Logan, Edd H.; Logan, Sallie G.; Logan, Dudley Edward “Dud”; Stewart, Charles Homer: https://www.txgenwebcounties.net/titus/cemeteries/masonic_cem.html

TXGenWeb Project, Titus County, Texas, Cemeteries index (about 115 cemeteries; 114 pages searched for Logan, Wedgeworth and related names), read 4 Nov 2026: https://www.txgenwebcounties.net/titus/cemeteries.html

McCurtain Gazette, 30 December 1959, Mrs. Tyro Box obituary (brothers Rob and Walter Logan), as described in “Alfreda Whitfield Sandridge and her Choctaw family” (Find a Grave memorial 180564131; not re-examined here): https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/180564131/annie_f-box
stories.note: The two boys are linked to Dudley and Annie at probable, because the stone says only “D. & Annie Logan” and was read in a transcription. Dates for the 1888 and 1889 burials may come from the reburials the cemetery page mentions. Edd, Sallie, Dud, Eva and Charles Stewart are leads and are not in the tree. Their dates are the compiler’s.

stories.title: Which Wedgworth girl was Annie?
stories.hook: The 1850 census has two Wedgworth girls who might grow into Annie Wedgeworth Logan: Sarah A. E., aged 9, and Ann E., aged 4. The second one fits the tree’s 1846 birth much better than the first.
body: The earlier story found Sarah A. E. Wedgeworth, 9, in Stephen Wedgeworth’s household in Greene County in 1850 and noted that nine years old does not fit a birth in 1846. The same page of the USGenWeb transcription has a second candidate. On page 263A, dwelling 298, Larkin Wedgworth is 39, born in South Carolina, a farmer with real estate worth $2,400. With him are Sarah J., 36, born in Tennessee, Ann E., 4, and Julia J. T., six months, both born in Alabama. A girl of four in the 1850 census was born about 1846, exactly the year the tree gives, and Ann E. could be read as Anne Elizabeth.

Next door, in dwelling 297, are Elizabeth Wedgworth, 48, with property listed at $4,800, and Stephen B., 26, a teacher, Middleton, 22, John M., 19, and Martha J., 17. Stephen Wedgeworth, 41, of the earlier story is a separate household, dwelling 1122 on page 316A, with real estate of $3,200. The census does not state how any of these Wedgworths are related, and the spelling varies between Wedgeworth and Wedgworth even on one page.

By 1860 Larkin had moved. The Tuscaloosa County census for the Fosters division, page 684, dwelling 703, shows Larkin Wedgeworth, 49, a farmer with real estate of $2,100 and personal property of $17,721, and Sarah J., 43, with three children: Amanda E. L(?), 13, Julia I. F., 10, and John F. L., 8. The transcriber put a question mark after the eldest girl’s name. Julia’s age and the parents’ ages and birthplaces line up with 1850, so this is Larkin’s family, and the 13-year-old is probably the 4-year-old Ann E. under a different reading. Four dwellings away, at dwelling 707, are Thomas Harkee, 23, and Sarah A. E. Harkee, 20, born in Alabama.

That Sarah A. E. Harkee is a warning. A girl of nine in 1850 would be twenty in 1860, and a young wife of that age with her three initials is a natural fit for Stephen Wedgeworth’s daughter, now married. If so, she was not Dudley Logan’s wife. Two other Tuscaloosa County girls named Sarah A. E. were enumerated in 1860 as well, aged 19 and 14, so the name was common. Nothing here proves either girl was Annie. The point is that the Larkin Wedgworth family went from Greene County to Tuscaloosa County, where Dudley Logan took the voter’s oath in 1877, and that its elder daughter was the right age. A marriage record for Dudley Logan before 1880, probably in Tuscaloosa or Hale County, would settle which girl she was.

stories.note: Lead only. Three candidates for Annie, none proved. Because Annie’s own birth is unsourced (1846 comes from Find a Grave family links), either the age in the tree or the Wedgeworth identification may be wrong. No parent links are made. Original census images should be checked, in particular the first name of the eldest girl in Larkin’s 1860 household, which the transcriber was unsure of.

stories.title: New Prospect: Logans and Wedgworths on the same roads
stories.hook: Planters named Logan and Wedgworth both appear at New Prospect in a directory of Greene County, and the 1875 voter register at New Prospect, by then in Hale County, still has both names.

subject.name: Logan and Wedgworth families of Greene County

body: A list of Greene County’s early settlers on the county GenWeb site draws on Snedecor’s directory for 1855 and 1856, county marriage books and the land office at Old St. Stephens. In it, Isaac Logan appears with an 1818 date as a planter at New Prospect, and Stephen Wedgworth and Larkin Wedgworth appear as planters at New Prospect, in section 1 of township 21 north, range 3 east. These are the two Wedgworths whose households stand in the 1850 census, and the Logan listing may be the Isaac Logan, 70, born in South Carolina, who heads a large household on page 278A of that census.

The Wedgeworth family is older than 1850 in Greene County. The same early-settlers list has two James Wedgeworths, senior and junior, entering land at Old St. Stephens in December 1823, and marriage entries for Caroline in 1824, Daniel in 1825, Jane in 1825 and Mary in 1826. For the Logans it lists Zachary and James entering land in December 1823 and January 1824, and Isaac marrying Matilda McGehee in 1824. These are only entries in an index, and they do not tie any of them to Dudley or Annie.

Alabama created Hale County in 1867 from parts of Greene and neighboring counties, and New Prospect became a precinct in it. Its 1875 voter registration oaths include a John Logan, a farmer, entered 5 June 1875, and Diggs Wedgeworth, who worked for Mrs. Haley, entered 29 June 1875. Neither is shown to be related to the Texas couple, but it confirms that both surnames were still there a generation later.

For this family, the useful part is the place. New Prospect is where to look for Clement Logan’s land, for a Stephen or Larkin Wedgworth deed, and for church or cemetery lists. A Wedgeworth Cemetery near Mount Zion in Hale County is recorded on page 66 of Greene County Alabama Records by Mrs. S. M. Marshall, according to the county GenWeb cemetery page, though no burials were read.
src: Greene County, Alabama GenWeb, Early Settlers of Greene County, K to L (Logan, Isaac; Logan, Zachary; Logan, James; Logan, Willis; Logan, Priscilla) and U to Z (Wedgeworth, James Sr. and Jr.; Wedgeworth, Caroline, Daniel, Jane, Mary; Wedgworth, Larkin; Wedgworth, Stephen), from Snedecor’s Directory 1855–56, marriage records and Old St. Stephens land entries, read 4 Nov 2026 (U to Z page): https://magnoliasandpeaches.com/GreeneAlGenWeb/History/EarlySettlers_UZ.asp; K to L page: https://magnoliasandpeaches.com/GreeneAlGenWeb/History/EarlySettlers_KL.asp

Alabama Department of Archives and History, voter registration oaths, Hale County vol. 1: Logan, John, New Prospect, Precinct No. 2, entry 3, 5 June 1875 (farmer), and Wedgeworth, Diggs, entry 15, 29 June 1875, item records read 4 Nov 2026: https://digital.archives.alabama.gov/digital/collection/voter/id/1442 and https://digital.archives.alabama.gov/digital/collection/voter/id/1444

stories.title: An Alabama Logan family at Mount Pleasant in 1860
stories.hook: Titus County had Alabama-born Logans before the war. The 1860 census at Mount Pleasant lists a J. H. Logan, 32, and his family, born in Alabama.
body: Dudley Timothy Logan’s memorial says he came to Titus County from Greene County, Alabama. But in the 1860 census of Titus County, Precinct 3, post office Mount Pleasant, enumerated between 10 July and 15 September by W. S. Stephens, a Logan household was already there. J. H. Logan is 32, a farmer born in Alabama. N. A. Logan, 26, is born in Alabama, as are M. J., 10, a girl, and P. H., 8, a boy. All four are listed as born in Alabama, and the eldest child was born about 1850, so the parents may have come to Texas only in the last decade.

No Dudley Logan appears in the 1860 index for Titus County, and none, aged 14, in the 1860 index for Tuscaloosa County, though the Tuscaloosa schedule has other Logans, including a Ben Logan household on page 685. The 1870 Titus County transcription is partial and lists only a William Logan, 45, born in South Carolina. The partial 1900 index lists Logan households, but they are Arkansas-born families.

That makes J. H. Logan a possible forerunner for Dudley, though no record says so. He may be an older brother or a cousin. He was born about 1828, eleven years after Clement Logan, 33 in 1850, of the Greene County household that has a three-year-old Dudley. But there is nothing that links them beyond their surname and state of birth, and the families may be entirely separate. A probate or land record in Titus County that names Dudley beside J. H. would be the test.
src: 1860 U.S. census, Titus County, Texas, Precinct 3, page 193B (dwelling 163: J. H. Logan, N. A., M. J. and P. H. Logan), NARA M653 roll 1305; USGenWeb Census Project transcription by John Wardlow (original image not examined), read 4 Nov 2026: https://www.us-census.org/pub/usgenweb/census/tx/titus/1860/pg0193b.txt

1860 Titus County surname index (Logan: J. H., N. A., M. J., P. H.; L. W. and W. M. Logan of Georgia), USGenWeb transcription, read 4 Nov 2026: https://www.us-census.org/pub/usgenweb/census/tx/titus/1860/indx-l-o.txt
1870 Titus County census index (Logan, William, 45, South Carolina) and partial-transcription status, USGenWeb, read 4 Nov 2026: https://www.us-census.org/pub/usgenweb/census/tx/titus/1870/index.txt
1900 Titus County surname indexes (Logan entries are Arkansas-born households), USGenWeb transcription, read 4 Nov 2026: https://www.us-census.org/pub/usgenweb/census/tx/titus/1900/_indx-a-l.txt
stories.note: Lead only. The Titus transcriptions for 1870, 1880 and 1900 are partial, so the absence of Dudley from them says little. Nothing connects J. H. Logan to Dudley. Do not link.

stories.title: Another Whitfield household, a few doors from W. F.
stories.hook: On the next sheet of the 1900 census, a Mississippi-born Whitfield with eight children lives a few households from W. F., and nothing yet says how the two are related.
body: The page that holds W. F. and Emma Whitfield, sheet 5A of Monroe Township, Sevier County, Arkansas, ends at line 50. The census taker, Rufus J. Nelson, carried on to sheet 5B, and at dwelling and family 87, lines 55 to 64, he wrote down a second Whitfield household. The head is a farmer born in May 1844 in Mississippi, aged 56, whose father and mother were both born in North Carolina. His initials are hard to read on the scan and look like R. H. He owned his farm. His wife Rachel was born in June of a year the scan gives as about 1849 and was 50; she and both of her parents were born in Georgia.

Eight children follow, all single and at home. The oldest, Luther, was born in July 1870 in Mississippi and worked as a cattleman. Minnie, born October 1874, is the first child entered as born in Arkansas, and she taught school. After her come a son whose name is only initials, born March 1877 and entered as a mill owner; Daisy, born February 1879; a son whose name looks like Roth, born March 1881; Ollie, born April 1883; Manda, born January 1886; and John, born July 1888. Every child gives a Mississippi father and a Georgia mother. The birth places place the family’s move from Mississippi to Sevier County in the years between Luther’s birth in 1870 and Minnie’s in 1874.

W. F. Whitfield, whose household is on the sheet before and four households earlier, was also born in Mississippi, in January 1868, and the census gives his mother as Mississippi-born and his father’s birthplace as unknown. The two men are both Mississippi-born Whitfields living in the same township, and that is all the page proves. The older man’s own parents were born in North Carolina, so he could be W. F.’s father only if he was a Mississippi-born son of Carolina parents who had a first marriage to a Mississippi-born woman that the 1900 page does not mention, and that is a guess, not a finding. He could as easily be an uncle, a cousin or an unrelated neighbor. The census does not mark either household as related to the other.

What the Whitfield question needs is a record that names W. F.’s parents, such as a Mississippi marriage or probate record, his death record, or the 1870 and 1880 censuses of the Mississippi county where he was born. The 1900 pages give no county. The 1880 census Soundex for Mississippi is on microfilm at Internet Archive, but a card for a W. F. or William F. Whitfield aged about twelve would have to be found among the Whitfield (W314) cards for the state, and no such card was identified in this round.

For the family line the point is narrower. Oliver Clinton Whitfield is still kept unlinked from W. F. and Emma in the tree, because no record that names his parents has been examined. This story adds one more Whitfield household to the neighborhood, and it adds no link.
src: 1900 U.S. census, Sevier County, Arkansas, Monroe Township, ED 151, sheet 5A (W. F. Whitfield, lines 33–39) and sheet 5B (second Whitfield household, dwelling and family 87, lines 55–64); NARA T623 roll 76; Allen County Public Library microfilm scan, Internet Archive, images n385 and n386, examined 4 Nov 2026: https://archive.org/details/12thcensusofpopu0076unit/page/n386/

imgs.cap: 1900 U.S. census, Monroe Township, Sevier County, Arkansas, ED 151, sheet 5B: a second Whitfield household, a Mississippi-born head with wife Rachel and eight children, on lines 55 to 64. NARA T623 roll 76, via Internet Archive. Public domain; downscaled only.

stories.note: Lead only. The head’s initials and some children’s names are hard to read on the scan and are given as read. No relationship between this household, W. F. Whitfield and Oliver Clinton Whitfield is established, and nobody from this household is added to the tree.

stories.title: Looking for Alonzo Box’s people
stories.hook: The 1900 census says Alonzo’s father was born in Alabama and his mother in Mississippi. A search of Mississippi and Van Zandt County records for his own parents found other Box families and no connection.
body: Alonzo Box’s own record is the 1900 census page, and it gives three clues. He was born in December 1850 in Arkansas. His father was born in Alabama and his mother in Mississippi. His children’s page entries agree: each of the five at home, all born in Texas, is entered with an Arkansas-born father and a Mississippi-born mother. Emma’s father was born in Virginia and her mother in Mississippi, and Emma herself in Mississippi in July 1860. A family born in Arkansas in 1850 to an Alabama father and a Mississippi mother fits a move west along the usual route from Mississippi into Arkansas and then Texas, but no record seen so far names the parents.

The neighbors on sheets 4A, 4B and 5A of Justice Precinct No. 6 do not help. The households around Alonzo’s are named Vance, Hanks, Hill, Reeves, Carter, Wright, Cade, Jackson, Malone, Maxfield and Tunnell. The only name near it that looks like Box is a merchant on sheet 4A, a Texas-born man of 33 with Georgia-born parents, whose surname reads as Boon or Bonn. No relative of Alonzo’s is on those three sheets.

Because Emma and Alonzo married about 1877 and had a child early, a household with them in 1880 would have a Soundex card, which indexes only families with children under ten. The earlier search covered Texas and Arkansas. This round covered Mississippi: in the 1880 Soundex for the state, volume T757 for B-000 to B-260, the Box surname codes as B200, and in the run of B200 cards that fall between Alex and Anderson (images 790 to 808 of the film scan) no card for an Alonzo appears. The cards are ordered by given name only roughly, so this is a negative result that is not conclusive. The film for the other surnames in that code was not searched card by card.

Other Box families turn up in the printed county histories. Wentworth Manning’s 1919 Some History of Van Zandt County, in its account of the early courts around Buffalo, lists a Thomas Box among the jurors summoned for the district court on 12 November 1849; the passage is part of the history of the court that served Henderson County, from which Van Zandt was cut. Jack Geddie’s 1963 history of Colfax, a community in the county, summarizes the 1880 census and lists James R. Box, born in Alabama, with his wife Sarah M. and six children: Charlie O., Mattie E., Mary E., Lou M., William B. and Ada T. The same book lists the Box families of the community as John, Booster, Bill, Cranfil, Elliot, Dr. John, Jim and Terrell Box, notes a W. J. Box as a Masonic officer, and records the 1895 marriage of Miss A. M. Box to H. D. Fountain.

None of this ties Alonzo to anyone. James R. Box was born in Alabama, like Alonzo’s father, but the book gives no date for him, and Alonzo was born in Arkansas. The Terrell Box on the Colfax list may be the Terrell Inge Box of Canton whose 1942 draft card is cited in the brothers’ story, a man who is not in Alonzo’s household and who may belong to this Colfax family. The Alonzo of 1900 is not mentioned in either book, and the Colfax list is undated. For now Alonzo and Emma remain the end of the line.
src: 1900 U.S. census, Van Zandt County, Texas, Justice Precinct No. 6, ED 134, sheets 4A, 4B and 5A, enumerated 8 and 9 June 1900 by Wm. B. Tunnell, Alonzo Box household at lines 54–61 of sheet 4B; NARA T623 roll 1675; Internet Archive, images n724 to n726, examined 4 Nov 2026: https://archive.org/details/12thcensusofpopu1675unit/page/n725/

1880 census Soundex index, Mississippi (NARA T757), volume B-000 to B-260 (Internet Archive item soundex1880ms003), images 790 to 808, B200 cards between Alex and Anderson, no Alonzo found; examined 4 Nov 2026: https://archive.org/details/soundex1880ms003

Wentworth Manning, Some History of Van Zandt County (Des Moines: The Homestead Co., 1919), p. 94, jurors summoned for the court at Buffalo, 12 November 1849; Internet Archive, text read 4 Nov 2026: https://archive.org/details/somehistoryofvan01mann

Jack Geddie, Colfax (Colfax Homecoming Committee, 1963), chapter “1880 Census Reveals Old Settlers” and the list of heads of families, with notices of W. J. Box and the 1895 marriage of A. M. Box; Internet Archive, text read 4 Nov 2026: https://archive.org/details/colfax00gedd
stories.note: Lead only. No Box named in these books is shown to be a relative of Alonzo Box. The Thomas Box of 1849 and the James R. Box of 1880 are not added to the tree, and Alonzo’s and Emma’s parents stay unknown.

stories.title: Looking for Esther’s Voris family: one Brazoria household in 1950
stories.hook: The only record naming Esther Voris is her half of a headstone. A search of the 1950 census finds one Voris household in Brazoria County, and nothing yet shows that it is hers.

subject.name: Esther Voris Livesay
subject.rel: Lester W. Livesay Sr.’s second wife

body: What the tree holds about Esther Voris Livesay comes from one stone. The double marker for Lester W. Livesay Sr. in the Confederate Cemetery at Alvin reads “Esther Voris, Aug. 9, 1910,” with no death year carved. Surname, birth date and a place within a few miles of Alvin are the only handles. No parents, siblings or marriage record for her have been opened, and Voris is treated as her maiden name only because the stone gives it that way.

For this round the National Archives’ 1950 census search was tried for Voris and for the spelling Vories in Brazoria, Galveston and Harris counties. It searches the machine-read names on each sheet, so it misses and misreads many entries, and a blank result proves nothing. In Brazoria it returned a single Voris household, in enumeration district 20-21. The sheet was read as an image. Lines 29 and 30 show Voris, Lester E., head, white, male, 38, married, born in Texas, working as a body mechanic in a garage, and Ruby J., wife, aged 30, also born in Texas. The sheet is stamped as started on 7 April 1950. A marginal note beside the household mentions an airport road and a highway, but the sheet does not name the town, and the place within the county was not worked out.

Lester E. Voris is the right age to be a brother, cousin or other relative of a woman born in 1910, and he lived in the county where she is buried. That is all. His age implies a birth about 1911 or 1912, so he could not be an older brother, and nothing in the sheet mentions Esther or Livesay. Nothing here links the household to her, and it is recorded as a lead only, not as a relative. The same name search listed other Voris entries in Harris County, which were not opened.

The ways forward are records not reachable here: Esther’s Texas death record (the stone carries no year), the marriage record that Find a Grave dates to 1942, the 1920 and 1930 censuses of Brazoria County, and the Alvin newspapers. A birth in Alvin was reported by an earlier researcher but could not be checked. Until one of those turns up, her parents remain unknown and no Voris parents are added to the tree.
quotes: Esther Voris, Aug. 9, 1910 (headstone, Confederate Cemetery, Alvin)
src: 1950 U.S. census, Texas, Brazoria County, enumeration district 20-21, sheet 7, lines 29–30, Lester E. Voris household (original sheet image read), National Archives, read 4 Nov 2026: https://1950census.archives.gov/iiif/2/1950census%2F43290879-Texas%2F43290879-Texas-047258%2F43290879-Texas-047258-0008.jpg/info.json

stories.title: Beaucoup in 1879: a post office, a store and Logan Livesay’s sawmill
stories.hook: The 1879 county history describes Beaucoup as a village laid out only in 1870, with one store, a post office and a sawmill run by a Logan Livesay, whom no other record here identifies.

subject.name: The village of Beaucoup
subject.rel: Home settlement of the Livesay and Walker families

body: The earlier stories here follow the Beaucoup settlement of the 1820s: the Methodist camp ground, the cemetery, Robert Livesay’s land patents and the farm Rev. James Walker bought at the Rock Chimney. The 1879 History of Washington County, Illinois, has a second Beaucoup that those stories do not use, the railroad village. Under its account of Nashville’s neighbors it says the village of Beaucoup lies on the St. Louis and South-eastern railroad, east of Nashville in Ashley precinct, and was laid out in 1870 by James Garvin and Daniel Hay as proprietors. The book, printed in 1879, counts in the village a post office, one store, kept by E. Patterson, and a sawmill belonging to Logan Livesay. A shorter note in the precinct descriptions agrees that Beaucoup is a small village in Ashley precinct, four miles east of Nashville.

So by the year the history was printed, the name Beaucoup belonged to two things: the old timber settlement on Beaucoup Creek, where the history says the Whittenburgs, Whites, Livesays, Lyons, Henrys, Carters, Rev. James Walker and others made it the strongest settlement in the county by numbers, and a village that was nine years old. A volunteer-compiled list of Washington County post offices, printed in modern times, gives the office name Beaucoup as open from 1815 to 1957. That span is odd for a place whose village was platted in 1870, and the list is a secondary compilation, so it is quoted here only to show that the office long outlived the plat. The county history itself says nothing of a postmaster for Beaucoup in 1879 beyond the single line. Its pioneer register, a roll of old settlers, appears to list an E. A. Patterson at Beaucoup as railroad express agent, postmaster and merchant, with his wife, which would fit the E. Patterson of the store; the register’s columns are hard to read in the scanned text.

The surprise is the sawmill. The tree lists Robert Livesay’s sons, from the family sketch used in earlier stories, as William Edmund, Lorenzo Mastin, Jackson Monroe, David Pinkney and others, and the tree has no Logan among them. The tree does carry a Lorenzo Dow Livesay, who died in 1876 and so cannot have been the miller of 1879, and a Lorenzo Mastin Livesay, who was farming in Jefferson County, Illinois, in 1860 and 1870 according to the census entries cited in his own story. The name Logan may be a nickname or a middle name of one of these men or of a son or nephew of the next generation, or the compiler may have set down a different Livesay. The 1855 state census lists a number of Livesay households near Beaucoup, but not a Logan. One link in the family is a Logan, since Robert’s daughter Unity Jane married James L. Logan; that is a fact about the family, not evidence about the miller.

None of the three Washington County census transcriptions read for this story (1860, 1870, 1880 excerpts on Genealogy Trails) contains a Livesay, so no census confirms that a Logan Livesay lived in the county in 1870 or 1880. For that reason the sawmill is treated here as a lead: a Livesay was running a mill at Beaucoup in the year the county history went to press, and one more document, such as the 1880 census of Ashley precinct, the county’s land transfer index or an obituary, would say whose son he was. The Walker farm and the camp ground lay in the same timber, so the families that had arrived in the 1820s were still at Beaucoup, in business as well as on the church rolls, a generation after the first settlers.
quotes: It contains at the present (1879) a Post Office, one store, by E. Patterson, and a saw-mill, by Logan Livesay. (History of Washington County, 1879)

stories.title: Anderson in the gas boom: Vine Street and a strawboard mill
stories.hook: The 1893 Anderson directory that lists James T. McCormack on Vine Street also shows a town built in a few years on natural gas, with a strawboard mill on First Street and neighbors who worked in it.
body: The earlier story on James T. McCormack reads his one line in Knight & Co.’s directory: a teamster for “A S P Co,” living at the corner of Vine and First. The rest of the same book describes the town around that line. Its preface says the canvass found 8,114 names, reduced to 6,166 after firms and duplicates, and multiplied by three to estimate Anderson at 18,498 people, counting Park Place and North Anderson. That is the directory publisher’s own estimate and not a census, but it is the size of the town where Sadah was born in August 1893.

The directory’s list of companies shows what made a town of that size in the Indiana gas field. The Anderson Natural Gas and Oil Company and the Citizens’ Gas Company were both incorporated in 1887, with capital of $20,000 and $50,000. A Columbia Encaustic Tile Company followed in 1889 and the Anderson Paper Company in 1892 with $200,000. The book also lists the Anderson Land and Gas Company, the Hazlewood Gas Company, the North Anderson Gas Company, the East Lynne Gas Company, a Gas Belt Supply Company and a maker of gas regulators, along with a long run of gas fitters. This story does not repeat any history of the boom; it rests on what the 1893 book itself prints, which is a town where gas companies, glass and tile works and mills sat side by side.

The directory also helps with the unexplained employer. “A S P Co” is not spelled out anywhere in the book, and a text search of the book found no firm under those initials. But Vine Street was a mill street. The American Straw Board Company, general manager M. R. Williams and superintendent F. Millspaugh, is listed as manufacturing straw board on the north side of First Street, west of Milton. Its workers lived close by. H. H. Coburn, an engineer for the company, lived at 84 North Vine, and Clemens Herricks, who worked there, lived on the south side of First Street, three doors east of Vine. A teamster who lived at Vine and First, at the end of the street, could well have hauled straw and board for that mill. The initials do not obviously stand for the American Straw Board Company, so this is only a possibility: a reading of “A S P” as a different firm cannot be ruled out from this book.

What the directory does show is how McCormack’s world looked in 1893. His house stood in a street of workers, his likely employer one of several firms burning cheap gas, and the town was growing fast in the year Sadah was born. By the June 1900 census the family was farming in Stony Creek Township, and by April 1910 it was in Brazoria County, Texas, so the Anderson years were brief.
quotes: McCormack James T, teamster, ASP Co, h. cor Vine and 1st (Anderson directory, 1893–4)
src: Knight & Co.’s Anderson, Ind. and Madison County Biennial Directory, 1893–4: preface (8,114 names; population estimate 18,498), company lists (Anderson Natural Gas & Oil Co and Citizens’ Gas Co, both incorporated 1887; Columbia Encaustic Tile Co, 1889; Anderson Paper Co, 1892; Anderson Land & Gas Co; Hazlewood Gas Co; North Anderson Gas Co; East Lynne Gas Co), the entry “American Straw Board Co … n s 1st w of Milton,” and the name entries for McCormack James T, Coburn H H and Herricks Clemens; full text read 4 Nov 2026, Allen County Public Library copy via Internet Archive: https://archive.org/stream/knightcosanderso00knig/knightcosanderso00knig_djvu.txt
Earlier story on this site, “James T. McCormack, teamster, Anderson, 1893” (page 134 image and the 1900 and 1910 census households), not reopened here.

imgs.cap: Anderson, Madison County, Indiana, Sanborn fire insurance map, September 1895, sheet 30: the works of the American Straw Board Co., with its rotary room, stock room, beater room, machine room and paper warehouse, and nearby the J. W. Sefton Mfg. Co. and the Anderson Cathedral Glass Co., marked not in operation. Library of Congress, Geography and Map Division, Sanborn Maps Collection, public domain; unaltered service JPEG. The map is two years after the 1893 directory and names no one; it does not show where James T. McCormack worked or lived, and this story leaves open whether his “A S P Co” was this company.

Whether “A S P Co” means the American Straw Board Company is not established; the neighbors’ employment is an observation about the street, not a proof about his job. stories.title: Eagle, Bok Tuklo and Towson: the Choctaw counties in the family’s papers
stories.hook: The Merry and Durant papers name three counties of the old Choctaw Nation, and the towns where later generations registered and were buried, Valliant and Millerton, lay in the same country.

subject.name: Choctaw Nation counties
subject.rel: Merry, Durant, Clay and Box families

body: Before 1907 the Choctaw Nation was divided into three districts and many counties, each with a judge, a sheriff and a clerk, and every Dawes card gives a person’s county. Reading the family’s papers together shows how the counties fit. On card 5754 Louis Merry and Bessie are on the 1896 Choctaw roll in Eagle County, as numbers 14822 and 8644. Bessie’s parents, Peter and Ellen Durant, are of Bok Tuklo County, and so is her grandmother Wilsey Clay on card 655, while Wilsey’s own parents, Joe and Patsey Cahn, are of Eagle County. Ben Durant, Bessie’s brother, was on the 1896 roll twice, once in Blue County and once in Bok Tuklo.

The wedding, as the earlier story shows, was in Bok Tuklo County: the clerk who issued Louis’s license was clerk of that county until 1 October 1896. Wikipedia’s articles on the two counties, which rely on the Chronicles of Oklahoma and an atlas, describe Eagle County as the county along the Arkansas line with Eagletown as its seat, bordered on the west by Bok Tuklo, and Bok Tuklo as named for Lukfata Creek and Yasho Creek, with its seat at a meeting ground called Oak Hill. Both lay in the Apukshunnubbee District. The two counties the Merrys appear in are therefore neighbors, which fits a couple married at Lukfata but enrolled in Eagle County.

The same sources put Nashoba County to the north of both, and the Merry file has a puzzle that may touch it. A witness in 1900 said Peter Durant left “that part of the country” in 1877 or 1878, and the typed transcript gives the county as “Matoon County,” a name found in no list of Choctaw counties read here. Nashoba is a neighbor of the two counties, but nothing in the record says the witness meant it, and no Durant or Clay card read here names Nashoba County, so this stays a question.

The later family’s towns sit on the same ground. Wikipedia says Valliant was founded on 2 June 1902 for the Arkansas and Choctaw Railway and then lay in Towson County, the next county west of Bok Tuklo; Tyro Box and his brothers registered there in 1942. Millerton, near Wheelock, is where Tyro’s draft card gives his home, and Wheelock Academy, according to Wikipedia, is three miles east of it. Violet Whitfield was killed in 1962 on the Oak Hill road near Golden; the old county seat of Bok Tuklo was a place named Oak Hill, but no record read here says the road is named for it, so the coincidence is noted without being claimed. After statehood in 1907 the counties disappeared, and the Bok Tuklo country now lies within McCurtain County.

Choctaw census card 655 (Wilsey Clay household; Bok Tuklo; parents of Eagle County) and the 1896 roll entries for Ben Durant (Blue County, number 3569; Bok Tuklo, number 3404), as read in the earlier stories “Wilsey Clay’s household at Bok Tuklo” and “Ben Durant, Bessie’s brother”.
