stories.title: Esther Sandridge and Steele’s Creek, 1909
stories.hook: Clinton Sandridge’s first wife drowned in a creek near Prescott trying to save a five-year-old boy. Three newspapers told the story, and one named her father.
body: Clinton Sandridge’s story records that his first wife, Esther Margaret Bolls, died in 1909 and was buried at Midway Cemetery near Prescott, in Nevada County, Arkansas, but not how she died. Prescott’s newspapers, digitized by the Library of Congress from the Arkansas State Archives’ microfilm, answer that. On the afternoon of Monday, 10 May 1909, “Mrs. Clint Sandridge” drowned in Steele’s Creek, about three miles west of Prescott near the Washington road, while trying to save a five-year-old boy, August Dierks Jr.

The Nevada County Picayune of 13 May gives the fullest account. Mrs. Sandridge and Mrs. W. H. Siders had taken about eight small children to the creek to fish and had split into two groups. The Dierks boy fell into the water near Mrs. Sandridge, and she waded in after him. Instead of turning back the way she had come, she tried to cross the stream and was soon over her head. Mrs. Siders heard the screams and ran to them with a fishing pole, but could not pull them out, and both went down. One of the older boys ran to the mill to raise the alarm, and a crowd recovered the bodies and carried them home.

Both Prescott papers place the two families at the Ozan Lumber Company. The Picayune calls Clint a carpenter for the company. The Prescott Daily News of 11 May says he worked in the mill’s carpenter gang, that the boy’s father, August Dierks, was its foreman, and that both families lived in the western suburbs of Prescott. The accounts differ on the hour: the Daily News first says about one o’clock and later about four, while the Picayune and a Prescott dispatch printed in the Washington Telegraph and the Mena Weekly Star say four. The water was six to eight feet deep.

The Picayune adds the detail that matters most for the family: “Mrs. Sandridge was a daughter of the late lamented H. C. Bolls,” and she left a husband and three children. The Daily News says one of the three was an infant. She was buried at Midway on Tuesday evening, and the boy at DeAnn Cemetery. None of the notices prints her given name, but the husband, the Midway burial, the year and the three young children all match Esther Margaret Bolls Sandridge, and the Bolls surname matches the one her memorial gives. Her father had died before May 1909; nothing more about H. C. Bolls has been found yet.

The death was remembered beyond the family. A week later the Picayune’s correspondent at Artesian wrote that it had been a sad day in the community when Mrs. Clint Sandridge and little August Derks were “called away so suddenly.” On 13 December 1909 the Prescott Daily News reported that the Carnegie Hero Fund Commission was making inquiries about the drowning of Mrs. Sandridge, “who gave her life in an effort to save” the boy. Whether the commission made an award is not known. A search of its website on 4 November 2026 did not find her, but that search may not reach every early case.

Her three children were Clinton Everett, called Chat, then about seven; Nobie, about five; and Mildred, the infant, according to the memorials recorded in Clinton’s story. Their school years in Prescott are told in the next story. Thirteen months after the drowning, on 19 June 1910, Clinton married Maggie.

stories.title: Everett, Nobie and Mildred in Prescott, 1915–1916
stories.hook: Six years after their mother drowned, Clinton Sandridge’s older children appear on Prescott school honor rolls and in the newspaper’s letters to Santa Claus.
body: After Esther Sandridge drowned in May 1909, Clinton married Maggie in June 1910, and Lemuel was born in December 1911, at Prescott according to his memorial. The family stayed in Prescott for several more years. The Prescott Daily News printed the public school honor rolls through the school year, and Esther’s children are on them.

In January 1915 the grammar school list names Everette Sandridge among the first-honor pupils of the first grade and Nobie Sandridge among the first-honor pupils of the second grade. The March list has both names again, with Everett now on the second-honor list. Everett appears again in April and in December 1915. The paper gives no ages or parents, and the grades are the school’s own divisions, so they are not used here to estimate ages.

At Christmas 1916 the Daily News printed children’s letters to Santa Claus. Mildred Sandridge asked for “a tablet and a doll and an apple that is good.” Everett Sandridge asked for ten packages of firecrackers, ten Roman candles, a bicycle, a freight train, a jumping jack, an air gun, a football and a Christmas book. The letters ran on 12, 14 and 16 December.

Everett, Nobie and Mildred are the names that memorials recorded in earlier research give to Clinton and Esther’s three children, and in 1909 the newspaper said that Mrs. Clint Sandridge left three children, one an infant. The Prescott papers of these years name no other Sandridge children. These items therefore probably record Clinton’s children, though none of them names a parent. Lemuel, Maggie’s son, was too young to appear. By February 1918 Clinton was working at a lumber mill in Malvern, and in 1919 he moved to McCurtain County. Nobie’s later life has not been traced, and Nobie is not entered in the tree because no record seen here states whether Nobie was a son or a daughter.

stories.title: Lon and Clint Sandridge, from Prescott to the Moline mill
stories.hook: Newspapers from Prescott and Malvern follow Clinton Sandridge and the brother his death notice named, Lon, through the 1910s, first in the same town and then on the same mill’s lists.
body: Clinton Sandridge’s 1961 death notice named a surviving brother, Lon, of Little Rock. Memorials recorded in earlier research list a Lon P. Sandridge (1889–1974) among the sons of William D. and Mary E. Sandridge of Beirne, Clark County, with Clinton, Joseph Burton and Lawrence Lafayette. The Library of Congress’s digitized Arkansas newspapers show a Lon Sandridge, and a Burton Sandridge, in Prescott in the same years as Clint.

In February 1908 the Prescott Daily News printed the results of a school examination, and Burton Sandridge scored 92 in the seventh grade. That September the Daily Picayune reported, under the heading “Soldier Arrested,” that Lon Sandridge had been arrested for wearing government clothes. When he was taken before J. B’Shers for trial, First Sergeant Garland Leverett dropped the case once Sandridge turned over all the government property he had. On 27 March 1912 the Daily News announced that Lon P. Sandridge and Miss Willie Denson had been married on the Saturday afternoon before, at the home of the bride’s parents, Mr. and Mrs. Jim Denson, by Squire B’Shers.

By 1917 Lon was in Malvern, the seat of Hot Spring County. On 14 June 1917 the Malvern Times-Journal printed the names of the men registering for the draft in the county, and “Sandridge, Lon P.” is under Ward Four of Malvern, a few names after “Denson, Thomas Monroe.” In January 1918 the paper listed Lon P. Sandridge of Malvern, number 756, among the registrants to whom the local exemption board was mailing questionnaires.

Clint was in Malvern too. On 16 February 1918 the Malvern Daily Record listed the Christmas Red Cross members from the town’s industrial plants. Under the Moline Lumber Company it gives “Lon Sandridge $1; C. L. Sandridge $1,” with Monroe Denson and J. M. Denson among the D’s. On 28 February the Times-Journal printed the Moline employees who had given to the Salvation Army fund: L. P. Sandridge, Monroe Denson and J. M. Denson near the top, and “Clint Sandridge 50c” further down. In 1909 Clint had been a carpenter at the Ozan mill in Prescott; in 1918 he and Lon were on the same mill’s lists.

None of these items says that Lon and Clint were brothers or names a parent. What they add is a working life in common: the same two towns in the same years, the same mill, and the Denson family moving with them. With the 1961 notice, they make Lon a strong match for the brother Clinton’s family remembered. The notice also named a brother “L. P.” in California. Because the Malvern lists use “Lon” and “L. P.” for what looks like one Moline worker, which initials belonged to which brother is not settled here. William D. and Molly Cole Sandridge remain unconfirmed as the brothers’ parents.

stories.title: William A. Nelson’s first family, Little River County, 1900
stories.hook: Sixteen years before he married Julia Myers, William A. Nelson was farming just across the line in Arkansas with a wife named Francis and two small daughters.
body: William A. Nelson married Julia Myers at Idabel in 1916, when he was forty-six, and his 1920 household held children who were not Julia’s. His memorial, read in earlier research, lists an older daughter, Rosa Isabel Nelson Flowers, born in 1894. Until now no record had placed William anywhere before 1916. The National Archives’ card index to the 1900 census of Arkansas, scanned by the Internet Archive, has a card for William A. Nelson, born in May 1871 in Arkansas, in Lick Creek Township, Little River County. The census page it points to, enumeration district 73, sheet 10B, lines 64 to 67, is on the same microfilm series and was read for this story.

William A. Nelson was the head of the household, a white man of 29, born in May 1871 in Arkansas and married seven years. He farmed on rented land and could read and write. He gave his father’s birthplace as Texas and his mother’s as Mississippi. His wife, written “Francis E.,” was 29, born in April 1871 in Mississippi to parents from South Carolina. She had borne three children, two of them living: Rosa B., born in August 1894 in Texas, and Minnie M., born in December 1897 in Texas.

The index card adds a fifth person, Harriet McLaren, about 70, born in Maryland, as William’s mother-in-law. Her line was not among the lines read on the sheet, and her Maryland birthplace does not agree with the South Carolina birthplace given for Francis’s mother, so McLaren is not adopted as Francis’s maiden name.

This is probably the William of Redland. The name and initial, the birth month, the Arkansas birthplace and a daughter Rosa born in 1894 all match his gravestone and memorial, and Little River County has McCurtain County, Oklahoma, on its western side and Bowie County, Texas, on its southern. Two details differ. The census gives 1871 where his stone has 1870, and it writes Rosa’s middle initial as B., where the memorial calls her Rosa Isabel.

The household explains part of the later story. Married about 1893, William and Francis had their first children in Texas and were in Arkansas by 1900. What became of Francis is not known. Homer E. Nelson, born in 1902 according to his memorial and named in Julia’s 1956 notice, is not on this page and was probably born after it, but no record seen here names his mother. For Audrey, born in 1917, Rosa and Minnie were half-sisters more than twenty years older. The father William named as born in Texas is not identified; whether that answer can fit the memorial lead naming Aaron Burr Nelson (1815–1888) is taken up in the next story.

stories.title: Julia Stevens and Charley Ratcliff, neighbors in 1950
stories.hook: Four months before they married, the census taker found Julia Stevens and Charley Ratcliff living a few doors apart in Broken Bow.
body: Julia’s story follows her through the surnames Myers, Nelson, Stevens and Ratcliff. Its last links are an Arkansas marriage record of 19 August 1950, in which Julia Ann Stevens, 76, married Charles M. Ratcliff, both of Broken Bow, and a 1956 newspaper notice for Mrs. C. M. Ratcliff. The 1950 census, taken that April, shows where the two were living before the wedding.

On 4 April 1950 the enumerator for district 45-4 in Broken Bow filled in sheet 5. On line 14, the only person in his household, is Charley M. Ratcliff, 68, white, widowed, born in Missouri. Three dwellings further on in the enumerator’s round, on line 19, is Julia A. Stevens, 76, white, widowed, born in Texas, also living alone. Neither was recorded as working that week. The National Archives’ name index reads her surname as “Stevend,” but the page shows Stevens.

The page adds two small facts to Julia’s record. Her age, 76 in April, fits the 17 November 1873 birth date in her 1956 notice and the age on the August marriage record, and so weighs against the 72 printed in that notice. And she is described as widowed, where the index to the 1930 census called her divorced. The page cannot tell whether a former husband had died in the meantime or whether the answer reflects how Julia chose to describe herself.

Charley Ratcliff’s line gives the tree its first facts about Julia’s last husband: born in Missouri about 1881 or 1882, and already a widower by 1950. His first wife is not named. Julia was his neighbor that spring and his wife by August, and she died in 1956 as Mrs. C. M. Ratcliff. Her daughter Audrey was living elsewhere in Broken Bow with Lemuel and their sons, on another enumerator’s sheet.

stories.title: Looking for three sets of parents in the Arkansas census indexes
stories.hook: The 1880 and 1900 census index cards for Arkansas were searched for the parents proposed for Clinton Sandridge, Maggie Sandridge and William Nelson. What they show, and what they do not, narrows the next search.

subject.name: Clinton Sandridge, Maggie Sandridge and William Nelson

body: The National Archives microfilmed card indexes, filed by a sound code called Soundex, to the 1880 and 1900 censuses, and the Internet Archive has scanned the Arkansas rolls. The 1900 index has a card for every head of household. The 1880 index covers only households that included a child aged ten or younger. Three parent leads in these stories, all taken from memorial pages read in earlier research, were checked against them: William D. Sandridge and Mary E. “Molly” Cole as Clinton’s parents, James L. Cash and Maxie Ann McClure Cash as Maggie’s, and Aaron Burr Nelson as William Nelson’s father.

No card for a W. D. or William D. Sandridge was found among the S536 cards for heads with W given names, in either the 1900 or the 1880 Arkansas index. Molly Sandridge died in 1897 according to her memorial, and by 1900 Clinton was about eighteen, so the family could have been split up, living in another household, filed under a misspelled surname, or out of the state. The search does not disprove the lead. It means that the census index cannot yet confirm it.

The 1900 index has one card for a James L. Cash in Arkansas, and it does not fit. He was 41, born in November 1858 in Arkansas, and lived in Caddo Township, Clark County, with his wife Martha J. and children Christina, a daughter whose name looks like Rita, Maggie L., born in January 1893, and three sons. Maggie Sandridge’s gravestone gives 2 May 1891 and the initial A., and the memorial names her mother as Maxie Ann. Cards filed under the initials J. L. were also checked, without a match. It is a coincidence worth recording that this household was in Clark County, where Clinton was born; nothing ties it to him. Maggie’s maiden name stays a lead, and her birthplace is still Texas in 1930 and Arkansas in 1950.

The 1880 index has no card for an Aaron Nelson as head of an Arkansas household. William would have been ten in June 1880, young enough for his household to be indexed if it was in Arkansas. In 1900, as his own story shows, William gave his father’s birthplace as Texas. Either the family was outside Arkansas in 1880, or William was in a household under another head. The Aaron Burr Nelson link stays a lead.

The next records to try are the 1880 population schedules for Clark County, where Beirne lies, the Texas indexes for the Nelsons, and Clinton and Maggie’s June 1910 marriage record. A search of the Prescott Daily News issues of 18 to 22 June 1910 did not find a report of that marriage.

stories.title: Three doors, one family: Flannigan, Dolson and the widow White, 1850
stories.hook: On 8 August 1850 the Jefferson County census taker went from Thomas and Patsy Flannigan’s door to Allen Dolson’s and then to a house where a 74-year-old North Carolina woman named Sarah White lived with the elder Dolsons. Two county biographies say these were a preacher’s daughters and his widow.

subject.name: Martha “Patsy” White Flannigan and her family

body: The earlier story on the 1850 household of Thomas A. and Patsy Flannigan stopped at page 64 of the Jefferson County census, dwelling 443, and could say only that a Tabitha J., 20, lived there. It did not say who Patsy was before she married. The next two dwellings on the same page answer much of that. Dwelling 444 is Allan Dalson, 45, a farmer born in New York, with Mary L., 40, born in Georgia, and eight children, among them Sarah, 20, Robert W., 19, Elizabeth, 16, Melville, 14, Mary J., 12, Christina, 10, William, 5, and Issac H., 3. Dwelling 445 lists Sarah White, 74, born in North Carolina, with Peter Dalson, 75, and Rachel, 73, both born in New York. The census taker, Robert Wingate, recorded Patsy herself as 48 and born in Georgia. Three dwellings back, at 440, he had listed James C. Baldridge, 38, with Tabitha, 39, born in Illinois, and ten children listed under the surnames Casey and Baldridge.

Two county histories put names on these households. The sketch of James C. Baldridge in the 1883 History of Jefferson County says that he married Mrs. Tabitha Casey, widow of Isaac Casey and daughter of Robert White, on 8 January 1846; that Robert White was born in South Carolina and came to Madison County, Illinois, in 1810; that Tabitha was born on 10 July 1811 in Chambers’ Fort; and that her mother, Sarah Holt, was a native of North Carolina who was “married in Georgia.” In 1909 Brinkerhoff’s History of Marion County printed the sketch of the Baldridges’ son George Pliney Baldridge, which lists the children of Rev. Robert White, a Methodist Episcopal minister with a large circuit: Robert, who was drowned in Madison County; Martha White, who married Thomas Flannigan and had a daughter Martha, who became the wife of Eli Copple; Louisa White, who married Allen Dolson and had a daughter Sarah, who became Eli Copple’s second wife; and Tabitha White, who married Isaac Casey and then James Clark Baldridge.

Laid beside the census page, the details agree. A North Carolina widow of 74, born about 1776, fits Sarah Holt, and she is listed in the dwelling next to Louisa’s, two doors from Patsy’s. Patsy, born in Georgia, and Mary L. Dalson, also born in Georgia, fit daughters of a mother who was married in Georgia, and Tabitha, born in Illinois in 1811 a year after the family’s arrival, fits the census’s “IL.” Eli Copple’s 1909 sketch calls Allen Dolson a native of New York, a son of Peter and Rachael (Quinby) Dolson, both New Yorkers, and says Allen’s wife was born in Georgia; the census gives exactly those birthplaces. The sketch’s list of Dolson children (Sarah, Robert, Elizabeth, Melville, Mary, Christina, William and Harvey) overlaps the census list, and the Harvey of the sketch may be the Issac H., 3, of the census. Sarah Dalson, 20, matches the Sarah Dolson whose Gilead stone gives 8 December 1829. The 1840 census transcription also puts Thos. A. Flanagan, J. C. Baldridge and Peter Dolson on one page, with Allen Dolson on the next, so these were neighbors a decade before.

The Gilead Cemetery transcription holds the rest. It lists Tabitha Baldridge (10 July 1811 to 13 April 1899) and James C. Baldridge (10 December 1811 to 16 May 1897), whose dates match both sketches; a “White, Rev. R.,” who died on 14 May 1828 aged about 55; Thos. H. Flannigan, who died on 28 January 1853, and Martha Flennigen, “w/o Thomas,” who died on 9 July 1862; Martha Copple, who died on 1 June 1850; and Mary A. Casey Noleman (6 June 1836 to 8 February 1911), who fits the Mary A. Casey, 14, in Tabitha’s household in 1850. The Whites, Baldridges, Copples and Flannigans share one burial ground in Grand Prairie Township.

What is not settled is narrow but real. The stone for Rev. R. White is tied to Robert only by the initial, the title and the township. The two sketches disagree about his earlier life: the 1883 sketch has him in South Carolina and Madison County, the 1909 sketch has him living early in Indiana before Marion County. The 1909 sketch gives Thomas Flannigan no initial and never calls Martha “Patsy,” and the census records no relationships, so Sarah White, 74, is identified from her name, age, birthplace and neighbors. Sarah’s later life is not known; she is not in the Gilead listing. Martha and Louisa’s mother is not named in any source, so only Tabitha is linked to Sarah. The new link from this family to Tabitha J. Livesay is weighed in the next story.
quotes: a minister in the Methodist Episcopal church, having a large circuit (Brinkerhoff, 1909, p. 834)
WHITE, Sarah 74 F NC / DALSON, Peter 75 M Farmer NY / Rachel 73 F NY (1850 census, Jefferson County, dwelling 445, as transcribed)

stories.note: Probable. The census page, the two county sketches and the Gilead stones agree on names, birthplaces, ages and neighbors, and nothing contradicts them, but no single record says that the census’s Patsy Flannigan and Sarah White were the daughter and widow of Rev. Robert White. The sketches are compiled county biographies written decades after the events. Rev. Robert White, Sarah Holt, Tabitha, James C. Baldridge, Louisa, Allen Dolson and Sarah Dolson Copple are added with the links the sources support.

stories.title: Was Tabitha a Flannigan? The 1840 page and a namesake aunt
stories.hook: The 1850 census put a Tabitha J., 20, in Thomas and Patsy Flannigan’s house but named no relationship. The 1840 census, a namesake aunt three doors away and a family of Whites at Gilead now make the case that she was their daughter.
body: The earlier stories left Tabitha J. Livesay as a lead. Her stone at Gilead says she was “wife of David P. Livesay” and died on 14 February 1856 aged 27 years, 2 months and 4 days, which puts her birth about 10 December 1828. The 1850 census of Jefferson County lists a Tabitha J., 20, born in Illinois, in the household of Thomas A. and Patsy Flannigan, and Find a Grave was reported to give her maiden name as Flannigan. Three things not used before bear on that.

The first is the 1840 census. The Jefferson County ILGenWeb transcription, page 309a, lists Thos. A. Flanagan with seven people in age bands: males, one under 5, one 5 to 10 and one 40 to 50; females, one 5 to 10, two 10 to 15 and one 30 to 40. The 1850 household fits the bands. Thomas, 54 in 1850, and Patsy, 48, are the man of 40 to 50 and the woman of 30 to 40. James R., 18, would have been 8, and Maria, 16, would have been 6. A girl of 20 in 1850 would have been about 10 in 1840, one of the two girls aged 10 to 15. The page also shows a boy under 5 and a second girl of 10 to 15 who are not in the 1850 house. A band count names no one, so this shows only that the 1850 household was the same family at an earlier stage and that a girl of Tabitha’s age was in it.

The second is a name. Patsy’s sister Tabitha White, born on 10 July 1811, was Mrs. James C. Baldridge, and in 1850 she lived at dwelling 440, three doors before the Flannigans at 443 on the same census page. A girl named for her aunt is an ordinary naming pattern. It is not proof, but it is one more point of agreement, and no record contradicts it. The third is the grave. The Gilead listing places Tabitha J. Livesay among the Whites, Baldridges and Flannigans, in Jefferson County, and not with the Livesays of Beaucoup in Washington County where David P. is buried.

Taken together, a Tabitha J. of the right age in the household, in the 1840 bands, with a namesake aunt next door and a grave among the family, are enough to call Thomas and Martha Flannigan her probable parents, and the tree now links her to them at that level. Several gaps remain. No marriage record for David P. Livesay and Tabitha has been found, and the Jefferson County marriage list read here stops at 1850. No record names her father. The census initial A and the stone’s H for Thomas still disagree, and the Find a Grave maiden name was not rechecked.

None of this reaches Floyd Livesay. Floyd’s headstone gives 5 February 1856, nine days before Tabitha’s death, and his Texas death certificate gives 5 February 1857 with both parents unknown, so Tabitha cannot be called his mother on any record. If the stone is right he was a newborn when she died, which fits the possibility but proves nothing. Floyd stays unlinked from his parents in the tree.

The earlier lead story, “Tabitha J. Flannigan, aged 20,” is left as written.

stories.title: Eli Copple and two cousins: a widower’s second marriage at Grand Prairie
stories.hook: Eli Copple’s first wife was Patsy Flannigan’s daughter Martha, and his second was Martha’s cousin Sarah Dolson. Two biographies, a marriage list and the Gilead stones follow him from 1839 to 1905.
body: Eli Copple was born in Washington County, Indiana, on 8 June 1820, according to his 1894 biography and his Gilead stone; the 1909 sketch gives 8 January. He was the son of the German-born David Copple and Lavina Huckleberry, and he was twelve when the family came to Marion County, Illinois, and settled on Seven Mile Prairie. His father gave him a quarter section of land when he started out. By 1909 he was remembered as thrifty and successful, at one time the owner of as much as two thousand acres, and as a man who in 1874 went to France and brought back a large number of Norman horses.

The Jefferson County marriage list, a volunteer transcription that its compiler says is not complete, shows Eli Copple and Martha Flanagan on 5 December 1839. The two biographies date the marriage to 1840, and the 1909 sketch calls her “Martha Flannagan, a native of Jefferson county, Illinois, who died in 1850.” The Gilead transcription lists Martha Copple, “w/o E.,” with the date 1 June 1850. The 1909 sketch of George Pliney Baldridge, a son of Patsy Flannigan’s sister Tabitha, supplies her parents: Thomas Flannigan and Martha White, a daughter of Rev. Robert White. Two daughters grew up. The sketches call them Arminda, who married William Dolson, and Loretta, who married A. J. Hartley of Irvington.

The 1850 census puts two Copple children in Thomas and Patsy Flannigan’s house on 8 August: Amanda, 4, and Martha L., aged “1/12,” one month. The names are close enough to Arminda and Loretta to suggest the same girls, though the transcription’s spellings and the sketches’ differ. The stone and the census do not quite fit. If Martha died on 1 June, a baby of one month on 8 August would have been born in early July, after her death. Either the stone’s day, the baby’s age or the birth date is misread, or the baby was a little older than the census taker wrote. The simplest reading is that Martha died in childbirth or soon after, and her grandparents took in the girls.

In February 1851 Eli married Sarah Dolson, the daughter of Allen and Mary Louisa (White) Dolson. The 1909 White sketch says Sarah was the cousin of his first wife, which makes them first cousins through the sisters Patsy and Louisa White. In 1850 Sarah, 20, lived at dwelling 444, next door to the Flannigans at 443, so Eli’s girls and his future wife were neighbors in the same month. The couple had seven children: Charles, Mary, Julia, Willis, Elmer, Robert and Ada. The 1909 sketch says two of the daughters married Baldridges, which kept the Copples tied to the family on the other side of the White sisters. Eli died on 14 August 1905, according to the sketch and his stone. His widow was living in Centralia Township in 1909, and a Sarah Copple, 8 December 1829 to 24 October 1915, lies beside him at Gilead.

stories.title: Lorenzo M. Livesay: a Webber Township sketch and two stones
stories.hook: The 1883 history of Jefferson County prints a short sketch of the man the earlier story found in the 1860 and 1870 censuses: his birth, both marriages, the death of Margaret in 1868 and his own in June 1876. A cemetery in Webber Township adds a conflict.
body: The earlier story on Lorenzo M. Livesay ended with two gaps: no record of Margaret Jane’s death and none of Lorenzo’s. The History of Jefferson County (1883) fills both in its Webber Township biographies, on page 75. It reads, in summary: Lorenzo M. Livesay, deceased, was born in Tennessee on 9 October 1825, came to the county in the fall of 1856 and died there on 6 June 1876. He was twice married, first to Margaret J. Thompson on 22 October 1845, by whom he had twelve children, of whom four were living in 1883: Mary C., Ephraim J., Elizabeth P. and Lafayette S. Mrs. Livesay died on 28 October 1868, and on 16 May 1869 he married Sarah S. Lane, daughter of the late Henry Lane. She was born in Caldwell County, Kentucky, and came with her parents to Clinton County, Illinois, in 1840. The sketch ends that he was “a faithful Methodist, and a useful, honest man.”

Each part of the sketch can be checked. The marriage date is exactly that of the Washington County license for Lorenzo M. Livesay and Margaret Jane Thompson, 22 October 1845. His arrival in the fall of 1856 fits the 1860 census, which found him in Jefferson County that June, and the family sketch’s report that he signed his father’s heirs’ release in Washington County in 1856, the day left blank. The second wife is the Sarah S., 36, born in Kentucky, whom the 1870 census lists in his house. The names Mary C., Elizabeth P. and Lafayette S. match children in the 1860 and 1870 households, and Ephraim J., 11 in 1860, is the first. Two 1870 children, Wilburn W. and Elva M., are not among the four living in 1883, so they probably died young. The family sketch, which puts Lorenzo Mastin at about five when the family came to Illinois in 1830, agrees with a birth in 1825.

The Black Oak Ridge Cemetery transcription, Webber Township, section 28, lists “Livesay, Lorenzo M.” with 3-9-1823 and 6-11-1876, and “Livesay, Margaret” with 6-20-1828 and 10-28-1868. Margaret’s death date agrees exactly with the sketch, and her birth year agrees with the 32 years the 1860 census gave her. Lorenzo’s entries do not. The sketch gives 9 October 1825 and 6 June 1876; the transcription gives a birth in 1823, in March or September depending on how the figures are read, and a death on the 11th of June. The census ages of 34 in 1860 and 44 in 1870 and the family sketch all point to 1825 or 1826, so the 1823 on the transcription is the outlier, whether from the stone or from the transcriber. The cause of the five-day difference in the death date is not clear. Both give June 1876, which is what the tree now records.

Several Lane stones stand in the same cemetery, among them Spencer Lane (1799 to 13 September 1888) and William M. Lane (8 January 1836 to 22 August 1898). The 1860 census lists a William M. Lane, 24, a farmer born in Tennessee, with Mary A., 23, born in North Carolina, and a daughter, in dwelling 388, the house next to Lorenzo’s at 387. Nothing says how these Lanes relate to Sarah Lane, whom the 1883 sketch places in Clinton County, and the Tennessee birth does not match her Kentucky one. Another Livesay couple lies at East Hickory Hill Cemetery in the same county: William G. (1827 to 1887, “Co. E 80 IL Inf.”) and Margaret (1829 to 1876). They are not shown to be related to Lorenzo. The twelve children are still not added as people.

The sketch, the marriage license and the census entries agree on who this Lorenzo M. was, but no document names his father, so his place as Robert’s son still rests on the name, the Tennessee birth about 1825 and the 1845 marriage. stories.title: Lorenzo Dow Livesay of Virginia, told by his son Evan
stories.hook: An 1894 biography of a Washington County farmer named Evan Carter Livesay names his father, Lorenzo Dow, and his grandfather, John Livesay, and gives the birth year and the death place that the veterans’ list got wrong.
body: The earlier story on the Carters and Livesays left Lorenzo Dow Livesay as a lead. A Washington County veterans’ list called him a son of John C. and Rebecca (Carter) Livesay, a Black Hawk War private, born about 1815 and died in 1876, a date the earlier story found hard to square with a land patent of 1831 and the 1855 state census. His own son’s biography now settles the date. The Portrait and Biographical Record of Clinton, Washington, Marion and Jefferson Counties (1894, pp. 555–556) prints a sketch of Evan Carter Livesay, of section 24, Ashley Township, Washington County, born near Nashville, Illinois, on 4 March 1830, the fourth child of Lorenzo Dow and Delilah (Mayse) Livesay.

The sketch says the father was a native of Virginia who at twelve moved to Tennessee with his father, John Livesay, and that John’s father, Thomas, came from England in 1748 and settled in Virginia. Lorenzo D. spent some years in Tennessee, came to Illinois in 1827 and settled near Nashville; later he went to Kansas, where he died in 1876. It adds that he was born in 1806, so he was about seventy when he died, and that his wife died two years earlier. The death year agrees with the veterans’ list. A birth in 1806 puts him at 25 at the 1831 patent and 26 in the Black Hawk War company of 1832. It makes him 48 or 49 at the 1855 census, which the transcription counts as one man aged 50 to 60 with a woman of 40 to 50, a year or two off. The woman fits Delilah.

Evan Carter Livesay farmed 115 acres, was a Methodist and a Populist, held school offices, and in 1849 married Martha D., daughter of John and Sarah (Coten) Carter, who came from South Carolina by way of Georgia and Tennessee to Illinois. They had nine children, two of whom had died by 1894. His middle name and his wife’s surname both recall the Carter families of the district, but nothing in the sketch ties Martha’s Carters to Livesay Carter.

The tradition of the descent does not fit everything else known. The family file of the Livesay Historical Society begins with a Thomas Livesay, born in Lancashire in 1730, married in 1749, with children born in England through 1757 and a first American record, a Pennsylvania deed of 1760. The 1894 sketch has a Thomas arrive in 1748 and settle in Virginia. If he is the file’s Thomas, the year and the colony are off; if not, the sketch’s Thomas is not in the file. Nothing opened here decides it. The sketch, which presumably draws on Evan’s own account (he was John’s grandson), is also the only source for Lorenzo Dow’s father by name apart from the veterans’ list, which names John C. and Rebecca (Carter). The two agree on John and on Virginia and Tennessee, and the family file has a John Livesay and a Rebecca Carter who married in Virginia and went to Tennessee, so Lorenzo Dow is linked to John at probable. The sketch names no mother, so Rebecca is not linked. John’s link to Robert Livesay is still a lead.

The Portrait and Biographical Record of Clinton, Washington, Marion and Jefferson Counties, Illinois (Chapman Publishing Co., 1894) has a sketch of Evan Carter Livesay, a farmer on section 24 of Ashley Township in Washington County. He was born near Nashville, Illinois, on 4 March 1830, the fourth child of Lorenzo Dow and Delilah (Mayse) Livesay. The sketch says his father was a native of Virginia who left it at twelve to settle in Tennessee with his own father, John Livesay, and that John’s father, Thomas by name, came from England in 1748 and settled in Virginia. The England date is a family tradition as the writer heard it. Nothing else opened for this story supports it.

Lorenzo Dow, the sketch goes on, spent some years in Tennessee, moved to Illinois in 1827 and settled near Nashville, and later went to Kansas, where he died in 1876. It gives his birth as 1806, so he was about seventy, and says his wife died two years before him. That fills a gap in the earlier research. The Washington County veterans’ list calls Lorenzo Dow a Black Hawk War private, names his parents as John C. and Rebecca (Carter) Livesay, and gives a death in 1876, but it guesses a birth about 1815. A birth in 1806 makes him twenty-six in the Black Hawk War of 1832, when the 1879 county history lists a Lorenzo D. Livesay among the privates of Captain James Burns’s company, and about forty-nine in 1855. The earlier story on the Carter kin noted that a birth about 1815 was hard to square with a federal patent issued to Lorenzo D. Livesay in 1831, which was not reopened here. The 1855 state census transcription lists L. D. Livesay’s house with six people, among them one man aged 50 to 60 and one woman aged 40 to 50. A man born in 1806 would have been a year or so short of that bracket, which is no worse than the fit with 1815.

The sketch and the veterans’ list agree on the man’s name, on Nashville and Washington County as his place, on a father named John and on a death in 1876. That is enough to treat them as one person, and Lorenzo Dow, who was already in the tree as an unlinked name, now has a wife and a son. Evan married in 1849 Martha D. Carter, daughter of John and Sarah (Coten) Carter, who the sketch says came from South Carolina to Georgia, then Tennessee, and finally Illinois. They had nine children, two of them dead by 1894. The sketch names the living ones, among them a son Lorenzo D. of Ashley, who had married first Alice McEnalley and then Alice Cundiff, and daughters in Pennsylvania and Chicago. Evan held 115 acres, voted with the Populists and served as a school officer, and his wife belonged to the Christian Church.

Because the sketch and the veterans’ list both name John as Lorenzo Dow’s father, the tree now links Lorenzo to John Livesay as a probable son. The sketch does not name John’s wife. Only the veterans’ list calls her Rebecca Carter, so she is not linked. Neither source says that this John was the father of Robert Livesay of Beaucoup. The family sketch has John and Rebecca moving from Virginia to Maury County, Tennessee, some time after 1809, and a Virginia departure about 1818 would fit that, but a date that fits does not make the two Johns one man. John’s link to Robert stays a lead.

Two cautions. Evan’s middle name Carter is tempting, because the family sketch says the Livesay and Carter families named sons for one another. But his wife was a Carter from a different line, nothing in the sketch ties his mother, Delilah Mayse, to the Carters of Nashville, and a given name alone proves nothing. And Lorenzo Dow, who died in Kansas in 1876, must not be mixed up with Lorenzo M. Livesay, Robert’s son, who died in Jefferson County in the same year; the next story on the 1883 county history sets the two apart.

The 1894 sketch is a biography of a living man, presumably from his own account, and it is the only direct statement of Lorenzo Dow’s parentage, birth year, move and death place. Its descent from Thomas of 1748 conflicts with the Livesay Historical Society’s file, and John’s wife is named only by the veterans’ list. Lorenzo Dow is linked to John at probable and not to Rebecca. His children other than Evan are not added.

stories.title: Jackson L. Livesay: Robert’s grandson, Company C, and a Centralia store
stories.hook: A 1909 Marion County biography names the parents of the Jackson L. Livesay who enlisted at Richview on 20 March 1864, the same day as William P. Walker: William E. and Emily (Goodner) Livesay, whom the register and the family sketch tie to Robert Livesay’s eldest son.
body: Brinkerhoff’s History of Marion County (1909, pp. 719–720) says Jackson L. Livesay, then in his sixty-third year and a well-known figure in Centralia, was born in “Washington, Illinois,” on 28 September 1845, the son of W. E. and Emily (Goodner) Livesay. William E. was a native of Tennessee who came to Illinois at seven with his parents, settled on a farm in Washington County and married Emily Goodner, of an Illinois family. Both died in Kansas, he in 1872 and she in 1874, after the family moved there in 1871 to farm and keep a store. They raised eight children, five boys and three girls, and Jackson was the eldest. The sketch is the first record found that gives William E.’s death, his wife’s family and one of his children. The family sketch has William Edmund about seven at the move from Tennessee in 1830, the Washington County register has William E. Livesay and Emily Goodner on a license of 1 August 1844 (book A, p. 15), and a first child in September 1845 fits.

The Adjutant General’s roster of the 60th Illinois, volume 4, page 184, Company C, lists “Livesay, Jackson L.,” of Richview, with enlistment on 20 March 1864, muster on 17 April 1864 and the remark “Mustered out July 31, 1865.” A few lines lower, “Walker, William P.,” also of Richview, carries the same three dates, so the two enlisted together. A volunteer abstract of the muster rolls adds that Jackson L. was a farmer, 5 feet 6 inches tall with light hair and blue eyes, mustered in at Centralia and out at Louisville, Kentucky; the sketch says he joined at Centralia, in the spring of 1864, under Colonel William Anderson of Mount Vernon and Captain Simeon Walker. Simeon Walker, Etheldra Jane Walker’s husband, was the company’s captain from December 1862 to March 1865, according to the roster page described in an earlier story. The sketch says Jackson followed Sherman to the sea, was mustered out at Louisville and came home in August 1865 with the First Brigade, Second Division, Fourteenth Army Corps. On the same page John W. Livesay, “Washington co.,” enlisted on 29 August 1862 and was discharged for disability on 16 February 1865; nothing found links him to Jackson.

After the war Jackson took up a claim in Kansas for a short time, returned to Washington County for two years, clerked at Richview for J. V. Holcomb & Co., and with his uncle William Shanks bought the firm out and moved the stock to Montana and Kansas, where they stayed eight years. They then farmed for three years, came back to Richview and, after three months, settled at Centralia. There he worked for several firms for twenty years and then eleven years for himself, at a store at 103 South Locust Street, eighty feet by twenty-four. He married Emma Ingram, daughter of H. P. Ingram and Millie Tyler of Richview, on 12 June 1871, and they had nine children, six boys and three girls. One daughter, Ruby, married William Severns, and the Marion County marriage list has William Servens and Ruby Livesay on 5 July 1900. He belonged to the Modern Woodmen and the Grand Army of the Republic, voted Republican and was a Methodist.

Some points disagree or are open. The sketch says he was born at “Washington, Illinois,” which most likely means Washington County, and the muster-roll abstract says Jefferson County. The sketch puts the family’s move to Kansas in 1871, the year of his own marriage, and its dates for his own years there are loose. An earlier story found a William C. Livesay, 26, with a Jackson L., 4, in the 1850 census beside the Walkers; the C may be a misreading of E, but that page was not reopened here. The sketch’s uncle William Shanks is not placed. Abigail Walker, William P. Walker’s wife, is called Shank or Schanck in other records, and nothing opened here connects that family to William Shanks, though Jackson served beside William P. at Richview, so the name is worth checking. The Marion County death index for 1916 to 1950 lists a Jackson Lafayette Livesay who died at Centralia on 25 August 1930, with no age. He would have been 84, and the match rests on the name and place.

stories.title: Alfred Livesay’s thirteen children, and two lists that do not match
stories.hook: Two 1909 Marion County sketches name Alfred and Hannah Livesay’s thirteen children, and the marriage lists, a land list and a death index confirm some of them. The two sketches disagree about which thirteen.
body: The earlier story on Alfred Livesay said that his 1909 biography names thirteen children and listed none. Two sketches do. The one for Alfred (Biographical and Reminiscent History of Richland, Clay and Marion Counties, pp. 548–549) names William T., a druggist at Stanley, Iowa, married to Eliza Seward; Elizabeth R., single and caring for her mother; Isaac B., married to Leticia Rock, in Kansas; Pearl, married to Joseph Larimer; Hester A., married to Perry Davidson; Ransom P., married to Louisa Suter; Marshall A., married to Rachael Walton, with nine children; Liddie, deceased, married to Robert Quale; Harvey R., married to Mollie Chick; Allen H., who stayed single and died at forty-four; Daniel R., married to Laura Cruse; Etta, married to James Smith; and Clinton O., married to Elvira McHaney. The sketch of Harvey R. Livesay in Brinkerhoff’s History of Marion County (pp. 746–747) lists them “in order of birth”: William, Lizzie, Berry, Hester, Ransom, Marshall, Lydia, Harvey R., Allen, Daniel, Clinton, Etta, and Eddie, who died young.

Records outside the sketches support part of this. The Marion County marriage list, a volunteer transcription, has William T. Livesay and Eliza A. Seward on 16 November 1871; Perry G. Davidson and Hester A. Livesay on 2 November 1876; Marshall A. Livesay and Rachel C. Walton on 20 January 1880 and again, as a second entry, on 20 January 1881; and Daniel R. Livesay and Laura O. Cruse on 7 August 1889. The sketch of Orville T. Walton names his sister Rachel as the wife of Marshall Livesay of Foley, Missouri, and a daughter of Iradell and Louisa (Foster) Walton. The sketch of J. R. Quayle, a teacher and township officeholder, says he married Lyda E. Livesay, “the accomplished daughter” of Alfred and Hannah, on 8 January 1889, that two of their four children had died by 1909, and that she herself died in June 1906.

The two lists conflict in places. Alfred’s sketch has Isaac B. in Kansas and Pearl married to a Larimer and no Eddie; Harvey’s has Berry, a merchant near Odin, Illinois, and Eddie and no Pearl. Berry may be Isaac B., but Kansas and Odin are different places, and a Pearl with a husband and two children cannot be a child who died young. Both say thirteen. The Marion County marriage list also gives a James R. Livesay and Louisa M. Souter on 5 October 1880, where the sketches have Ransom P. and Louisa Suter, and Lydia’s husband is Robert Quale in the sketches of Alfred and Harvey but J. R. Quayle in his own sketch. Rachel’s double entry is probably a repeat. These are left as found.

The family’s move is documented in the land list. The Marion County early land sales list shows Alfred Livesay buying two tracts on 16 March 1867, SESW-24-04N-01E and NWSE-06-03N-02E, 40 acres each by the descriptions. Harvey’s sketch says Alfred bought six hundred acres, mostly unimproved government land, in Patoka Township, and Alfred’s own says he left six hundred acres of improved land. The tracts listed are a small part of that, and Harvey’s sketch adds that Alfred went to Missouri in 1866 before coming to Marion County. Alfred died on 22 April 1883, and Hannah, then in her late seventies, farmed 134 acres on the old place in 1909. The death index for 1916 to 1950 lists a Hannah Livesay who died at Patoka on 28 August 1924, an Elizabeth R. Livesay who died at Patoka on 16 March 1934 and a Daniel R. Livesay who died at Centralia on 28 March 1946, none with an age; they fit Hannah, Lizzie and Daniel, but only by name and place.

Harvey R., born on 10 May 1861, became Supervisor of Foster Township, married Mollie Chick of Foster Township in February 1883, lost her in 1895, and farmed in section 29 with five children at home. He is the one child whose own sketch survives. His sketch also names his maternal grandfather, James R. Logan, whom the next story follows. Six children are added here, each with a second record or an account of his own: William T., Elizabeth R., Marshall A., Lydia E., Harvey R. and Daniel R. The other seven are named in the sketches and not added as people.

stories.title: Hannah Logan’s father: James R. Logan, local exhorter, died 1860
stories.hook: Alfred Livesay married Hannah Logan in 1846 and Robert Livesay’s daughter Unity Jane married James L. Logan in 1849. The sketch of Hannah’s son names her father, and a few county records show where he and the Logans stood.
body: The sketch of Harvey R. Livesay, Hannah’s son, says that his maternal grandfather, James R. Logan, was born in South Carolina and lived in Tennessee until he came to Washington County, Illinois, where he had a well improved farm and lived on it until his death, which occurred in 1860. He was a member of the Methodist church and a local exhorter. Hannah was born in Washington County on 30 September 1830, the year the Livesays and many of their Tennessee neighbors arrived, and the Livesay family sketch lists Logan among the families, with Whittenburg, Lowe, Phillips, Thompson and Darter, that founded the first Methodist church at Richview in 1842.

Three county records touch him. The 1879 history of the county says a man who was long a church member at Richview told the author that in 1832 he found a society of Methodists at Alexander Anderson’s house, whose principal members were Alex. Anderson, “Roberson Logan,” John Darter and John Livesay. The name may be a different Logan, or a form of Robertson or of a James R., and it is a lead only. The probate index for the county lists “Logan, Jas. R., Estate,” in line with a death in 1860. The 1855 state census, in a volunteer transcription, lists a James R. Logan with seven people in the household and property of $775, next to Henderson Darter’s household. The transcription’s columns make it hard to say which of the age groups are men and which are women, so no age is drawn from it.

The marriage lists show how the families crossed. Alfred Livesay and Nancy A. Darter took out a license on 6 December 1842, Alfred Livesay and Hannah Logan married on 26 February 1846, and James L. Logan and Unity J. Livesay married on 16 November 1849, when Unity Jane was sixteen. If James L. was Hannah’s brother, her brother married the daughter of the family into which Hannah married, and Alfred and Unity would be cousins if Alfred was Robert’s nephew, as the earlier story suggests. No record opened here says that James L. was James R.’s son, and the second Logan in the 1855 census, a “James L.(?)” with a household of three, valued at $35 and enumerated next to Enoch Tate, fits a young couple with a child but is a transcriber’s guess.

What remains is a gap. Unity Jane Livesay, born on 3 November 1833 according to the family sketch, is named with “James I. Logan” in the heirs’ release of 1856, and nothing found follows the couple afterward. The Washington County census transcriptions read here, which are partial, show no Livesay in 1850, 1860, 1870 or 1880, and the Perry County census transcriptions for 1850 and 1860 and the marriage transcription for 1868 to 1896 on the Internet Archive list no Livesay. The best next records are the Washington County estate file for Jas. R. Logan, the Logan names in the 1850 census, and the 1860 and later censuses for James L. and Unity.

stories.title: Dr. T. N. Livesay of Patoka: a physician, a drugstore and a newspaper
stories.hook: A cousin of Alfred Livesay practiced medicine at Patoka in the 1880s, sold drugs and helped start a newspaper. The family sketch lists a Thomas Newton Livesay, born in 1836, whom no record places after 1855. Nothing yet says they are the same man.
body: The sketch of Alfred Livesay in the 1909 county biographies says he was a cousin of “Dr. Thomas Livesay, one of the leading physicians of Marion county.” The 1881 History of Marion and Clinton Counties finds a T. N. Livesay at Patoka. Its business list for the village names seven physicians, among them T. N. Livesay and J. B. Lewis, and a drug business called Livesay & Lewis, “They also publish a newspaper.” The paper was the Patoka Enterprise, whose first number was issued on 5 August 1881, “edited and published as an auxiliary by Dr. J. B. Lewis and T. N. Livesay,” a six-column folio “independent on all subjects.” The same history names Dr. T. N. Livesay first among the present elders of the Patoka congregation of the Cumberland Presbyterian church, and lists a Mrs. D. O. Livesay (the initials are uncertain in the scanned text) as a Patoka milliner, whom it does not identify.

The 1894 sketch of Dr. J. B. Lewis fills in the partner. Dr. Lewis graduated from the Eclectic Medical Institute at Cincinnati in 1878 and began to practice at Patoka, gave up medicine in 1884 when he was elected clerk of the circuit court, and, for five years, “was engaged in the drug business in Patoka in company with Dr. T. N. Livesay.” The Marion County marriage list has Thomas N. Livesay and Mrs. Annie M. Watts on 27 October 1886. The 1909 sketch of her brother, the real-estate man George B. Simcox, names “Anna M., the widow of Dr. T. N. Livesay” near Patoka among the children of W. K. Simcox, a Pennsylvania-born merchant who came to Patoka in 1866. So Dr. Livesay died between 1886 and 1909, and the volunteer death lists for Marion County read here do not show him.

The question is whether he was kin to Floyd’s Livesays. The family sketch lists a Thomas Newton Livesay, born on 22 February 1836, among the ten children of Robert and Lydia, and Alfred’s sketch calls the doctor Alfred’s cousin, which would fit a son of Robert if Alfred’s father John Wesley was Robert’s brother. The release that Robert’s older children signed in 1856 names eight heirs and not Thomas Newton, who would have been 20; the earlier story could not say whether he had died, had been paid, or had been left off the copy. A medical student in 1856 would fit the last but proves nothing. Against the identification, other Thomas Livesays lived in Washington County, among them the Thomas W. Livesay who married Elizabeth Thompson on 22 February 1841, and “cousin” need not mean a son of Robert.

Several records could settle it: the 1870 and 1880 censuses for Patoka Township, which give his age and birthplace; a death notice or an obituary in the Patoka or Salem papers; the Eclectic or other medical registers, which may give his school and year; and the Washington County estate file for Robert, which should list his heirs. Until then the doctor is added as a person and is not linked to Robert or to Alfred.

stories.title: George T. Hoke, the stepson who drove the oxen
stories.hook: Livesay Carter’s wife brought a son from her first marriage to Nashville, Illinois. He drove the oxen that hauled the logs for his stepfather’s sawmill, opened a store at Nashville in 1844, and was raised in the Nashville Masonic lodge in its first chartered year, with his stepfather and a Carter son.
body: The 1879 History of Washington County prints a sketch of George T. Hoke, of Richview Township. His father, John Hoke, was a native of Kentucky and his grandfather, George Hoke, of Pennsylvania; his mother’s father, Thomas L. Moore, was “a revolutionary soldier” whose people came from Maryland. George was born in Harrison County, Indiana, on 1 October 1819. His father died at Baton Rouge in 1821 on a trip to New Orleans, and his mother went back to Jefferson County, Kentucky, and came with her people in 1822 to Washington County, where she settled about two miles east of old Covington and met Livesay Carter. They married in July 1823, lived two miles east of Nashville for over fifty years, and Mr. Carter followed her in about two years.

A passage in the county’s early history makes the stepfather’s mill concrete: in 1830 Livesay Carter built a tread saw mill two miles east of the site of Nashville, which sawed the lumber for the first buildings in the town, and George T. Hoke, then a small boy, drove the oxen that hauled the logs. Hoke farmed and went to school in winters, peddled merchandise, and in 1844 opened a store at Nashville with five hundred dollars, which at the time had the whole trade of the place. He married Rebecca Fulton on 4 October 1844. In 1851 he sold the store to Dr. Lucas, joined Judge Watts and Sheriff Jack in buying the press of the Nashville Era, the county’s first paper, and sold his share after four months to David Logan. After leasing the mill in 1852 he moved in 1853 to Richview, clerked for Dr. Lucas, opened his own store near the depot in 1856 and kept it until 1874. He was elected Justice of the Peace in 1856, and by 1879 had been re-elected five times, was appointed notary public by Governor Yates and three times reappointed, and was elected county commissioner in 1876. He was a Republican, a Methodist and a Mason.

The Masonic history of Nashville gives the family together. Washington Lodge No. 55 began as Hardin Lodge under a dispensation of 21 July 1847 and received its charter on 4 October 1848. It raised seventeen members in its first year under the charter, and the list includes George T. Hoke, S. M. Carter and Livesay Carter. The history adds that most of the early members had died by 1879 but that a few “old land marks” remained: George T. Hoke, S. M. Carter, Lewis N. Farmer and J. J. Swanwick. Livesay Carter, born in 1799 according to the Masonic Cemetery list, was then about forty-nine. A third passage in the county history puts the same names in the field. About 1840, it says, a company armed with guns and pistols went from Nashville to the “Little Muddy” settlement, later Richview, to protect the House and Carter families against old settlers who had threatened to burn Hansel House’s new house. The men named include G. T. Hoke, Robert P. Carter and Livesay Carter. They camped half a mile south of the later town, and the threat collapsed when the old squatters learned of them.

S. M. Carter links this story to Dr. William D. Carter. The 1879 sketch of Dr. Carter says that about 1858 he began his medical study in the office of his brother, S. M. Carter, of Pinckneyville. The 1883 history of Perry County lists an S. M. Carter among the five trustees chosen on 26 March 1857 when Pinckneyville incorporated, and the early members of the Nashville lodge include an S. M. Carter. The initials, the town and the lodge make these one man, probably, but the given name is not stated. Perry County transcriptions show a Samuel M. Carter in 1850 and an S. M. Carter, with Malissa and four children, in 1860. They give names only. So S. M. Carter is added as a son of Livesay Carter and Mary at probable, and George T. Hoke is linked to his mother, Mary Moore Hoke Carter. The father, John Hoke, and Rebecca Fulton Hoke are not added.

stories.title: Livesay Carter’s first land: Lake Township, Clinton County, 1818
stories.hook: The 1881 history of Clinton County lists Livesay Carter among the first men to enter land in what became Lake Township, on 26 February 1818, five years before the joint patent with Robert Carter that earlier stories found.

subject.name: Livesay Carter
subject.rel: Livesay Carter (kin to the Livesays, unconfirmed)

body: The earlier stories on Livesay Carter used his 1879 sketch in Washington County, which says he went to Tennessee in 1807, came to Illinois in 1818 and lived four years in what is now Clinton County, and a federal patent of 10 December 1823 to Livesay Carter and Robert Carter for 160 acres at Edwardsville. The Clinton County side now has a record. The 1881 History of Marion and Clinton Counties describes Lake Township, which until 1875 was part of Crooked Creek Township, in the southeast of the county on the Washington County line, and prints “Land Entries,” the first lands entered “as taken from county records.” In that list, on “Feb. 26th, 1818, Livesay Carter entered S. E. ¼ Sec. 7.”

The neighbors in the list are the first families of the township. William Morrison and Pierre Menard entered in September 1816, John Wakefield in January 1817, Robert C. McEver in April 1817, John Bradford on 29 January 1818, Seborn Wadsworth on 9 March 1818 and Wingate Maddux on 21 May 1818. B. Stephenson entered land for the Bank of Edwardsville and James Mitchell took 277 acres in 1818, and the list ends with John D. Patton in 1819. The township’s history adds that it was first settled in 1817, that Robert C. McEver came from Georgia, that the first death in 1818 was that of a man named Hull, killed felling trees and buried in what became the Wadsworth burial ground, and that the township “settled very slowly” and was almost empty by 1830. Livesay Carter’s four years there, from 1818 to about 1822, fit that account.

The entry raises a question the stone at Nashville had already raised. The Masonic Cemetery list gives Livesay Carter’s birth as 15 November 1799, which would make him eighteen on the day of the entry. The family sketch, which makes him the first son of a marriage of the 1780s, implies a birth a decade or more earlier. Either the stone’s year is late, or the Livesay Carter of the 1818 list was an older man than the stone allows, or he is not the man buried at Nashville. The 1881 text gives the quarter section and section but not the township and range, so the tract cannot be placed on a plat from it.

George T. Hoke’s sketch says that his mother, a widow, came with her people in 1822 to a place two miles east of old Covington, where she “became acquainted with Livesay Carter,” and that after their marriage in July 1823 they settled two miles east of Nashville. Dr. Carter’s sketch says his father lived four years in Clinton County and then went to Nashville. The dates fit together: an entry in February 1818, about four years in Clinton County, a meeting in 1822 or 1823 and a move to Nashville after the wedding. The 1818 entry is the earliest documentary date found for him, five years before the marriage and the joint patent.

stories.title: The regiment Company H joined: Collins’s Second Illinois, 1847–1848
stories.hook: The state’s 1882 roll and its historical notes say what became of the Washington County company that Alfred Livesay served in: a voyage to Vera Cruz, garrison duty, and a death list that took about one man in four.
body: The Record of the Services of Illinois Soldiers in the Black Hawk War and in the Mexican War, printed by the state in 1882 from War Department rolls, opens its Mexican War section with short historical notes. They say the Second Regiment, enlisted “during the war,” was organized out of the overflow of companies raised for the Fifth Regiment, after Lieutenant Colonel Hicks and others asked the Secretary of War for leave to raise another. It was organized at Alton on 3 August 1847, with James Collins elected colonel, and sent by steamer to New Orleans, where it was divided in two. Companies A, D, E, F and H went under Collins to Vera Cruz, arriving on 31 August 1847. The notes say they were soon in a skirmish with guerrillas but saw no further actual service beyond camp and garrison duty. The other five companies, under Hicks, were sent to Tampico. Both battalions, the notes say, lost heavily to sickness, and the regiment was mustered out at Alton between 20 and 25 July 1848.

Company H is the Washington County company the earlier stories follow. Its roll, on pages 259 to 261, gives Captain James Burns, First Lieutenant Malachi Jenkins and four second lieutenants, all enrolled at Nashville, Illinois, on 10 July 1847, and the last line says the company was discharged at Alton on 22 July 1848. By my count of the printed lines the roll has 97 names: 6 officers, 9 sergeants, corporals and the musician, 38 privates who carry no remark, 23 sergeants and privates listed as dead, 2 deserters, 18 discharged for disability and 1 man transferred. Two of the officers also carry death remarks, Second Lieutenant James R. Lynch at Vera Cruz on 12 September 1847 and First Lieutenant Jenkins on the Gulf of Mexico on 26 June 1848, on the way home. That makes 25 deaths, about one name in four. Only one is called killed in action, Private John Field at San Juan on 18 September 1847. Deaths began before the company left Illinois, with one man dead at Alton on 3 August 1847, and two more died on the Gulf of Mexico on 28 and 29 August, before the landing at Vera Cruz. The transferred man, Private Stephen G. Hicks, was elected lieutenant colonel of the regiment on 3 August 1847, so Company H supplied its second-in-command.

Three Livesays are on the roll. Alfred Livesay, a private enrolled on 10 July 1847, has no remark, which on this roll means he is not among the men listed as dead, discharged, deserted or transferred; he stayed with the company until the discharge at Alton. That fits the county biography’s account of about thirteen months of service and of a sickness he never shook off, since the roll’s own dates make twelve and a half months. Carter H. Livesay is on the list of privates discharged. His remark is dittoed from the line above, for Thomas Lossom, which reads as Jalapa, Mexico, 4 February 1848, and the final column of that list is dittoed “disability” all the way down. That is my reading of the ditto marks, and the printing is cramped. John C. Livesay is on the list of privates who died. His remark reads Jalapa, Mexico, May, and a day number whose second digit is damaged in the scan, either 11 or 14. The 1879 county history gave only “May, 1848.”

Other names on the roll echo the family’s neighborhood. Nicholas H. Darter, a private, shares a surname with Alfred’s first wife, Nancy A. Darter, and with the man who married Mariah Livesay in 1841. Richard P. Carter, a corporal, and Emanuel C. Carter, a private, are Carters; James B. Logan, a corporal, is a Logan. Ezekiah Walker, a private, died at Vera Cruz on 10 September 1847, and two privates named John Walker appear, one on the list of men who stayed and one among the men discharged. No record opened here says any of these men was kin to the Livesays or the Walkers of Beaucoup. The roll shows only that the families’ surnames were in the same company.

What the roll does not give is as telling. It states no cause of death except the one killed in action, and no residence beyond the place of enlistment. The only later trace of Alfred’s service found so far is in the county biography, which says his widow Hannah drew twelve dollars a month in 1909. A pension file or a bounty-land record would be the next thing to look for.

stories.title: Dr. William D. Carter of Nashville, surgeon in the 44th Illinois
stories.hook: Livesay Carter’s seventh child was commissioned in the 44th Illinois a week before Perryville and stayed until the regiment was mustered out in Texas in September 1865.

subject.name: Dr. William D. Carter, 44th Illinois Infantry

body: The Illinois adjutant general’s report prints the field and staff of the 44th Illinois Infantry on page 296 of volume 3. William D. Carter, of Nashville, appears twice. As second assistant surgeon his rank and his muster both date from 1 October 1862, and the remark reads “Promoted.” As first assistant surgeon his rank dates from 25 May 1863, and the remark is that he was mustered out on 25 September 1865. The residence is Nashville both times, the town where the 1879 county history says Dr. Carter practiced after the war. A different William D. Carter, of Oxville, a private in another regiment, is in volume 1 and is not this man.

The county history’s sketch, on pages 65 and 66, supplies the person. William was born in Washington County on 12 January 1838, the seventh of eight children, five boys and three girls, of Livesay Carter and Mrs. Mary Hoke. He read medicine in the office of his brother, S. M. Carter, at Pinckneyville, and then at Rush Medical College in Chicago, from which the sketch says he graduated on 4 February 1862. It says he volunteered, was appointed assistant surgeon of the 44th Illinois, served more than three years, spent most of the time on detached service and for part of it was on the Division Operating Staff in the Atlanta campaign. A second Chicago degree, from Chicago Medical College on 10 March 1866, is placed in a sentence that muddles its own dates, so it is not relied on here. In December 1869 he married Laura A. Lecompte of Nashville; by 1879 three children had been born, two of them living, and none is named.

The regiment’s history, printed in the same volume on pages 326 to 328, says where the regiment was. The 44th was organized at Camp Ellsworth, Chicago, in August 1861 and mustered in on 13 September. It fought at Pea Ridge in March 1862. In September it was at Cincinnati and Covington and then at Louisville, and it was in the battle of Perryville on 8 October, a week after Carter’s commission began. It entered Nashville in November. At Stones River, at the turn of the year, it lost more than half its number in killed and wounded, in the history’s words. In 1863 it was at Hoover’s Gap and Tullahoma, marched back to the field in time for Chickamauga on 19 and 20 September, and was foremost in the charge up Missionary Ridge on 25 November. In 1864 it passed through nearly all the battles and skirmishes of the Atlanta campaign, fell back before Hood to Franklin and took part in the battle of Nashville on 15 and 16 December. After service in Alabama and East Tennessee it went to New Orleans in June 1865, then to Texas, landing at Port Lavaca on 23 July. It was mustered out on 25 September 1865, the same day as Carter, and reached Springfield on 15 October for final payment.

The history does not name the regiment’s surgeons, so these dates show the setting of Carter’s service and not what he did in it. They do show that the Nashville physician’s war was the long one, from the Kentucky campaign to the last garrison in Texas. His father, Livesay Carter, had come to Illinois from Virginia by way of Tennessee, and the county’s Mexican War and Civil War companies carried other Livesay and Carter names.

stories.title: Two chaplains and a captain: the Walkers in the state’s rolls
stories.hook: The adjutant general’s report names Chaplain Levi S. Walker of the 60th Illinois and, in another regiment, a Chaplain Simeon Walker of the 15th Illinois Cavalry. With the county histories they point to a preacher’s family behind Captain Simeon Walker.

subject.name: Rev. Simeon Walker and his son Levi
subject.rel: Probable father and brother of Captain Simeon Walker

body: Volume 4 of the adjutant general’s report lists the field and staff of the 60th Illinois on page 174. The chaplain is Levi S. Walker, of Richview, with rank from 12 February 1862, muster on 17 February 1862 and the remark that he was mustered out on 14 March 1865. That is the day Captain Simeon Walker left the regiment, as the earlier story of the captain shows from the company pages. Both men therefore joined in February 1862, one as chaplain and one as a sergeant, and both left on the same day, two days before Averysboro. Levi’s memoir in the 1921 Southern Illinois Conference minutes describes his army service as three years as chaplain of the 60th.

Volume 8 holds a second chaplain. The field and staff of the 15th Illinois Cavalry, on page 488, lists as chaplain Simeon Walker, with rank from 5 June 1863, muster on 23 July 1863 and the remark that he was mustered out on 25 August 1864. No residence is printed. James Leaton’s History of Methodism in Illinois (1883) tells the same story from the other side. Its sketch of the Rev. Simeon Walker says he was born in Jackson County, Georgia, on 13 April 1802, was received into the conference in 1830, had six children by 1834, when failing health and money made him take a location, returned to circuits in 1856, and in 1863 “entered the army as chaplain of the Fifteenth Illinois Cavalry.” He died, the sketch says, at his son’s residence at Carbondale on 22 February 1880.

The county histories put this Rev. Simeon Walker in the family’s own neighborhood. The 1879 History of Washington County names a Rev. Simeon Walker as the pastor who visited the first Methodist class at Nashville about 1833, lists him among the ministers who served the church at Richview, and says he filled out the Nashville year of 1855–56 after the appointed pastor died. Of Richview it adds that he still lived there, in the home of his son, and describes him spending the evening of his life in quiet. It does not name the son. Levi, the one son the records name, was then chaplain of the Southern Penitentiary at Chester, according to the same book’s sketch of an Okawville merchant whose wife, Flora, was Levi’s daughter, so the son at Richview may have been another.

The 1850 census adds a household. At dwelling 280 in District 20 are Simeon Walker, 48, a farmer with real estate worth $2,000, with Sally, 54, Simeon, 19, John, 17, Thomas, 10, and Eliza, 7, and two more people whose names I could not read with confidence. I read the enumerator’s birthplaces as Kentucky for the older Simeon, South Carolina for Sally and Illinois for the children. The age fits the preacher born in 1802, and the marriage register’s Simeon Walker and Sally Whittenburg of 11 August 1846 would explain a wife of 54 in a household with children of 10 and 7. The Kentucky birthplace conflicts with Leaton’s Georgia; Leaton says the family went to Kentucky in 1810, so the census may give the place he grew up.

Levi’s memoir gives the preacher’s family from the son’s side. Levi Sharpe Walker, son of Simeon and Elizabeth Sharpe Walker, was born in Clinton County, Illinois, on 14 September 1829. He married Martha Henrietta Barnes at Mascoutah on 29 December 1849; she died on 2 April 1886, and on 29 September 1887 he married Mrs. Emma P. McCracken of Richview. He was licensed to preach at Richview on 30 August 1856, served the 60th as chaplain for three years and the penitentiary for three, and died on 6 April 1921, aged almost ninety-two, with funeral and burial at Richview. The memoir names grown children who survived him; none is added here.

The captain settled the question himself. His sketch in an 1894 county biographical review, written while he lived at Carbondale, says he was born in Clinton County on 3 March 1831, the son of Simeon Walker, who had been brought from Georgia by his mother in 1811, who was appointed chaplain of the 15th Illinois Cavalry by Governor Richard Yates, and who rode circuit in Peter Cartwright's day. His mother was Elizabeth Sharp. Of the twelve children, it says, five sons became preachers and six went to war: William H., a captain in the 111th Illinois; Samuel, a lieutenant in the same regiment; Levi S., chaplain of the 60th; Thomas C., a private in the 111th; the captain himself; and John B., whom the sketch calls a captain of the 40th Illinois killed at Shiloh, a claim no roster seen so far confirms. Four were still living in 1894: Rev. Samuel of Carlyle, Rev. William H. of Kansas, Rev. Levi S. of Chester, and the captain, who drew a pension of $24 a month.

The pieces fit one family. If Captain Simeon was one of the preacher’s sons, as the 1850 household, the “Jr.” in the 1852 marriage record, the preacher’s long residence near Richview and the brothers’ same-day discharge all suggest, then Company C of the 60th Illinois was commanded by a chaplain’s brother and a cavalry chaplain’s son, and William P. Walker served under him. No record opened here says so outright. A county biography or an obituary of Captain Simeon would. The tree therefore links Captain Simeon to the Rev. Simeon at the probable level, and links Levi to both parents, and this story stays probable and not proven.
