stories.note: Probable, not proven. The two state rolls and Leaton’s sketch agree on a Chaplain Simeon Walker of the 15th Illinois Cavalry, and the county histories place a Rev. Simeon Walker at Richview, but no record seen says that Captain Simeon Walker was his son. The 1850 census birthplace (Kentucky) conflicts with Leaton’s (Georgia), and Leaton’s Carbondale death sits oddly beside the 1879 statement that he lived at Richview. The 1850 names of the two unread household members are not given. Levi’s place of death is not stated in the memoir. The earlier story of Etheldra and Simeon had left the captain’s father unlinked; that link is made here on the added evidence. His mother is not named, since Elizabeth Sharpe is named only as Levi’s mother and Sally in 1846 is a later wife.

stories.title: Where the 7th Alabama Cavalry rode, 1863–1865
stories.hook: Dudley Logan’s regiment was formed in July 1863, spent a year near Pollard, rode in Hood’s Tennessee campaign and ended with a surrender at Gainesville in May 1865. Two accounts of its origin disagree.

subject.name: Dudley Timothy Logan, Company B, 7th Alabama Cavalry

body: The earlier story found Dudley Logan on a Greene County roll of Company B, 7th Alabama Cavalry, and on a Mount Pleasant stone that names the regiment. The National Park Service’s Civil War battle-unit record says what that regiment did. The 7th Alabama Cavalry was formed at Newborn, Alabama, in July 1863, with companies raised in Randolph, Shelby, Greene, Pickens and Montgomery counties. For a year it served in the Pollard area in General Clanton’s brigade. In July 1864 it counted 451 men but was not serving as one command: two companies were with General Page and eight rode with Colonel I. W. Patton. It was later attached to the brigades of B. M. Thomas, W. W. Allen and Bell, took part in the raid on Johnsonville, and fought as Hood moved toward Nashville. In April 1865 it had fewer than 300 effectives, and about half of them surrendered at Gainesville, Alabama, in May. Its field officers were Colonel Joseph Hodgson and Lieutenant Colonels Turner Clanton Jr., Henry J. Livingston and F. C. Randolph.

Greene County is one of the five counties on that list, which fits the roll of Company B on the county’s genealogy site, headed “Muster Roll of the Broadfoots of Greene County.” The roll names D. P. Scarbrough as captain, several lieutenants and sergeants and a long list of privates, among them Dudley Logan, L. Logan and Zach M. Logan. It carries no dates, ages or residences. A contributor’s note on a military-history genealogy site adds a human scale. It says John Henderson Gandy, born in Greene County on 12 November 1846, enlisted on 20 June 1863 for the war under Captain D. P. Scarborough of Company B, and was discharged on 31 October 1863 for being a minor who had enlisted without his parents’ permission. That is a contributor’s summary and not a record, but it agrees with the roll on the captain, and it suggests that the company was filling in June 1863 and that boys of sixteen were being taken. Dudley, born on 8 January 1846, was seventeen that summer.

The sources do not agree about where the 7th came from. A Morgan County genealogy page on its Company K says the company began in 1862 as part of the 14th Cavalry Battalion, Partisan Rangers, commanded throughout by Colonel James C. Malone Jr.; that on 15 April 1863 the battalion was combined with the 19th Cavalry Battalion and redesignated the 7th Cavalry; that on 15 September 1864 it became the 9th Alabama Cavalry; and that it surrendered with Johnston’s army at Durham Station, North Carolina, on 26 April 1865. That is a different history from the Park Service’s Newborn, Pollard and Gainesville regiment, and a Greene County man could not have been at both Gainesville and Durham Station. Either there were two units with the number 7 in different accounts, or one of the accounts has confused them. The Greene County company is placed here with the Newborn regiment because the Park Service names Greene among its counties and the Greene roll names its own captain, but that is a reading and not a proof.

What this does and does not give Dudley. It shows the kind of service a Greene County cavalryman of 1863 would have had, a year of picketing near Pollard and then the campaigns of late 1864, and it shows the regiment ending in a surrender in Alabama in the spring of 1865, far from Mount Pleasant, Texas, where he later lived. It does not say that Dudley served the whole time, was present at Johnsonville or Nashville, or was among those who surrendered. The record that would say is his compiled service file at the National Archives, which the catalog does not index by soldier for Alabama, or the roll images at the Alabama archives, or his widow’s Texas pension file.

stories.note: The regiment’s outline is from the Park Service’s unit record, which gives no sources of its own. The Greene County roll is a transcription, undated, and the Gandy note is a contributor’s summary. The Morgan County history conflicts with the Park Service on the regiment’s formation and its end, and the conflict is not resolved. Dudley’s own presence in the regiment, already probable on the stone and the roll, is not confirmed by any dated record, and his enlistment, discharge and any capture are unknown.

stories.title: A Lieutenant Henry Clay in the First Choctaw Mounted Rifles, 1862
stories.hook: Abner Clay’s father was known only as a name on a Dawes card. A Confederate service file in the National Archives holds a Choctaw lieutenant of the same name, and nothing yet says whether he is the same man.

subject.name: Henry Clay, 1st Choctaw Mounted Rifles (identity unproven)
subject.rel: Possible father of Abner H. Clay

body: Henry Clay is in this archive only through his son’s Dawes card. Card 507 names him as the father of Abner H. Clay, marks him dead and puts him in Bok Tuklo County, with Wilsey Clay as Abner’s mother. The Choctaw Nation fought for the Confederacy, and the National Archives has described the compiled service records of its regiments soldier by soldier, so a search was possible. It turns up a file for a Henry Clay in the series of records for troops raised directly by the Confederate government (microfilm M258, roll 83).

The file’s jacket reads “Clay, Henry, Co. F, 1 Choctaw Mounted Rifles,” adds “Also known as Cavalry,” and gives his rank as lieutenant. Two cards follow. The first is a pay roll for commutation of clothing for the six months ending 23 November 1862, naming him as a first lieutenant in Capt. Oklabi’s company, as the card prints it, of the 1st Regiment Choctaw Mounted Rifles; a note says his name appears only as a signature to a certificate. The second says he appears on a petition from officers of the Indian regiments in Confederate service to the Secretary of War, dated at Fort McCulloch on 21 June 1862, asking that Colonel Sampson Folsom of the 1st Choctaw Regiment be appointed a brigadier general in the Provisional Army of the Confederate States. The file has no age, no residence and no county.

The regiment was Folsom’s. Wikipedia’s account of the Choctaws in the Civil War says the First Choctaw Regiment was organized in early 1862 under Colonel Sampson Folsom, with David F. Harkins as lieutenant colonel and Sylvester Durant as major, fought in many skirmishes and at the first battle of Newtonia, and that 31 officers and 686 soldiers served until June 1865. The catalog files these men under “First Choctaw and Chickasaw Mounted Rifles,” which is the name of a different unit, Douglas Cooper’s regiment formed at Skullyville in 1861, according to a Civil War research site, so the series title should not be taken as the regiment. The same series holds a Silvester Durant file; no record opened here ties him to Peter Durant.

This is a lead and not a finding. Henry Clay is a common name. The catalog also lists Choctaw files for a Joseph Clay and an Esaias Clay in 1862 and a Simon Clay in 1863, so there were several Clays in the ranks, and nothing in the lieutenant’s file places him in Bok Tuklo County or with Wilsey. A man who was a lieutenant in 1862 could have been the father of a child born about 1872, as Abner’s age on the Dawes card implies, but that is only possible. A record that names Henry Clay’s county in the 1860s to 1880s, a Dawes witness who mentions his war service, or the county from which Captain Oklabi’s company was raised would test it. Nothing here changes Henry Clay’s person record.

stories.title: Livesays, Carters and Walkers in the county’s Civil War companies
stories.hook: The 1879 county roll and the state’s rolls put some fifteen Livesays, Carters and Walkers in Washington County’s Union companies, among them an Alexander Walker of Richview who is probably the Alex Walker of the 1860 census row.

subject.name: Washington County’s Union companies, 1861–1865
subject.rel: Livesay, Carter and Walker kin (relationships unproven)

body: The 1879 History of Washington County prints, regiment by regiment, the names of the men the county sent to the Union armies. Read for the family’s surnames, it lists a Carter, Livesays and Walkers in several regiments. In the 44th Illinois it has First Assistant Surgeon William D. Carter, whose story is told separately. In the 49th Illinois it lists, in Company F, privates Andrew Livesly, Francis M. Carter and John B. Walker and recruits William J. Livesey and George Walker; in Company I, James M. Livesay as first lieutenant and again as a private. In the 60th it lists Simon and William P. Walker, Jackson L. Livesay and John W. Livesay in Company C, a George W. Livesay in Company G, and Levi S. Walker as chaplain. And under the 62nd Infantry it lists, in Company G, First Sergeant Alexander Walker and Corporal Nelson Livesay. The spellings are the printer’s.

The state’s rolls confirm some of these and place them. In the 49th Illinois, on page 515 of volume 3, James M. Livesay is a private of Company I whose residence is Nashville, enrolled on 1 November 1861 by the page’s ditto marks and mustered on 31 December, with the remark “Pro. 1st Serg’t and 2d Lt.” That is the town of the Carter family and of Livesay Carter’s son the surgeon. James M. is not in the tree, and no record opened here says how he stood to the Livesays of Beaucoup or the Carters.

Company G is the larger find. The state prints it as Company G of the Thirteenth (Consolidated) Illinois Cavalry, and the names, down to the captain and the sergeants, are the same ones the county history files under the 62nd Infantry; the two printings differ on the regiment and this story follows the state’s. On page 438 of volume 8, First Sergeant Alexander Walker, of Richview, was enrolled on 21 December 1863 and mustered on 20 January 1864; he was commissioned second lieutenant on 11 July 1865 but not mustered in that rank, and was mustered out on 31 August 1865 as a sergeant. A few lines below, Corporal Nelson J. Livesay, of Ashley, has the same enrollment dates, by the ditto marks, and the same muster-out. The regiment’s history in the same volume puts it in Arkansas through the Camden expedition of April 1864 and then on scouts and picket at Pine Bluff, where one of the company’s sergeants died in July 1864.

Alexander Walker of Richview connects to an open question. The story of the Walkers in a row at Richview in July 1860 reads, beside William P. Walker, an Alex Walker, 24, a farmer, with a Sarah A., 21, a Wm H., 3, and an infant, Edwin F., and says no record shows how he was related to the others. His name, his age and his Richview residence fit the state's sergeant, who would have been about twenty-seven in 1863, so the identification is probable and he is added to the tree without parents. It also means that two Walker men of Richview, William P. in the 60th Illinois and Alexander in the cavalry, were in the Union ranks at the same time; no record seen says they were brothers or cousins.

Nothing in these rolls proves kinship. Surnames this common in the county could belong to unrelated families, and the rolls give no parents. What they do give is a map for the next searches: the 1860 census households for James M., Andrew and Nelson Livesay, the pension index cards for each, and the veterans’ lists that name the soldiers’ later places of burial.

stories.title: Township 6 South, Range 23 East: the family on the Dawes allotment map
stories.hook: A hand-colored plat made by the Dawes Commission puts Louis Merry, Bessie, Ida May and the baby Isaam Gibbs on named blocks of land in Section 4, and Lizzie Durant in Section 10.

subject.name: Louis, Bessie and Ida May Merry

body: Earlier stories quote Louis Merry’s letter of 30 September 1904: Hopper Watkins had filed on his farm on 5 April 1904, and the farm lay in Section 4, Township 6 South, Range 23 East. The National Archives holds the Dawes Commission’s own sheet for that township. It is one of the “Allotment Maps,” printed plats of single townships on which clerks colored each parcel and lettered the allottee’s name and enrollment number as selections were recorded. The National Archives describes the series as plats annotated to show allotments, townsites and railway rights of way, dated about 1896 to about 1906, and the foot of this sheet carries the imprint of the Commission to the Five Civilized Tribes at Muskogee.

Section 4 is on the sheet, and the family is in it. An irregular, L-shaped block is lettered “Louis Merry” with the number 1363, which is his roll number as an intermarried white citizen on card 5754. Two blocks hem it in, marked only A-1002 and A-1003. Lower in the same section, one block reads “Ida May Merry A. 15527,” her roll number, and the large block beside it reads “Isaam Gibbs A 14616,” the number of the baby Lizzie Gibbs bore on 30 August 1902 and whose birth affidavits Louis took as notary. Two small tracts on the section’s north edge carry only the numbers A 14616 and A 15526, Isaam’s and Bessie’s. Bessie’s name is spelled out on a larger block in the northwest corner of Section 2, “Bessie Merry A. 15526.” The neighbors lettered in Section 4 include Fannie Carn and Andrew Battiest.

Further along, in Section 10, a block reads “Lizzie Durant A2580.” That is the roll number the final-roll index gives Lizzie on card 966, so the girl enrolled at Wheelock Seminary in 1899 had her land in the same township as her cousin Bessie. Next to it, toward Section 11, is “Jane Durant A2844.” The same index gives roll 2844 to a Jane Durrant, 10, full blood, on card 1063 in the household of Alfred Nakishi, and “Selina Nakashi A2842” is lettered nearby. The family tree has a Jane Durant, the second daughter of Thomas Durant, whom Wilsey Clay named once in 1906, but nothing read ties her to card 1063. The two Janes may be one girl, and that is only a lead.

The map answers where, and little else. The Commission’s annotations do not say which block was a homestead and which was surplus land, the letters P and C stamped on the parcels are not explained on the sheet, and the allotment jackets that would describe the improvements were not reachable for this story. Louis’s number could be written only after the Secretary of the Interior approved his enrollment on 14 March 1905, so his block was probably lettered after that date, a year after Hopper Watkins’s filing; the sheet does not show what became of that claim. The township is also the next one north of the one where Muriel Wright placed the old Lukfata mission, so the family’s land lay in the same stretch of country as Lukfata, where Louis and Bessie were married in 1896.

stories.title: How the land was chosen: the Choctaw Land Office and an allotting party
stories.hook: The Choctaw Land Office opened at Atoka in April 1903. A clerk who later rode through the Lukfata country with a field party left his own account of how the land was placed.
body: The land the family received came from a chain of agreements. L. P. Bobo, a young clerk at the Choctaw Land Office, wrote in the Chronicles of Oklahoma in 1945 that the Choctaw Land Office at Atoka and the Chickasaw office at Tishomingo opened in April 1903 so that about thirty-five thousand citizens and freedmen could choose a homestead and surplus land. Each Indian citizen was entitled to 320 acres of average land under the Atoka Agreement (signed 23 April 1897 and carried into the Curtis Act of 28 June 1898) and the Supplemental Agreement ratified 1 July 1902, which Choctaw and Chickasaw voters approved on 25 September 1902. If a citizen had not chosen within twelve months after the offices opened, and twelve months after the Secretary approved his enrollment, the Commission could choose for him.

The family’s own file shows that machinery at work. Louis’s letter reporting that Hopper Watkins had filed on his farm on 5 April 1904 came a year after the Atoka office opened. Abner Clay’s file includes a letter of January 1903 in which the Commission quoted the act that let “the father or mother, if members” select for minor children. Wilsey Clay’s granddaughter Lizzie Durant swore in 1906 that her allotment was already selected. None of these files names the day a particular parcel was chosen; the map of Township 6 South, Range 23 East is the first record in these stories that puts names on the ground.

The papers of a neighbor’s family show what the Atoka office asked of an allottee. The jacket for card 4310, the Hodges family of Atoka, opens with a transcript headed Choctaw Land Office, Atoka, 22 May 1903: in the matter of Ozie T. Hodges’s application for an allotment, “the name of said applicant appearing as No. 12061 on approved schedule of Choctaws by blood.” The clerks checked the applicant against the approved roll, and when the card had entered Ozie as a daughter, the young man testified that he was a son, and the Commission wrote on 1 June 1903 that the card now read “No. 3 is a male.” John M. Hodges, Ozie’s father, is very probably the witness who testified about Peter Durant in Louis Merry’s case, as the story of John M. Hodges explains.

Allottees who did not come in were handled differently. Bobo says that more than a year and a half after the offices opened, the Commission sent out field parties to find the stragglers, locate their improvements and place their allotments. His party left on a Thanksgiving morning with a surveyor and two interpreters, worked the Boggy River and Antlers country, then Hochatown and Mountain Fork, and later rode through Lukfata and Eagletown. He gives no year, but his account follows a mild winter of 1903–04 with a cold, snowy one, which puts the Lukfata weeks in early 1905. The party also gathered proofs of death for people on the old rolls, carrying the 1893 Leased District payment roll, whose per capita share was the same $103 that Bessie’s warrant carried, the 1896 census roll and the Commission’s 1898–99 enrollment. Some Choctaws, he adds, refused to take land “between the rocks,” that is, within surveyed lines.

Bobo names none of the Merrys, Durants or Clays, and nothing in their files says that the field party met them. The account is useful as the closest description found of the weeks and the country in which Louis’s enrollment was approved (14 March 1905) and his farm was the subject of a filing by another man. It also shows that the allotment of a family like Bessie’s was not one event but a long, uneven process that ran from the Atoka office to horseback visits in winter.

stories.title: Two wedding witnesses and the Lukfata post office
stories.hook: The men who stood up at Louis and Bessie’s wedding in 1896 were, one after the other, the postmasters at Lukfata.

subject.name: Lukfata and its postmasters
subject.rel: Place and neighbors of Louis and Bessie Merry

body: The certificate for Louis Merry and Bessie Durant’s wedding at Lukfata on 7 September 1896 names two witnesses, J. W. Costelow and Chas. J. Gaffney, and the story of the Lukfata notaries found the same names signing affidavits there in 1899 and 1902. The federal Official Register explains who they were. The register for 1 July 1899 lists, under Indian Territory, “Lukfata, Choctaw N., C. J. Gaffney,” with compensation of $60.32, and the register for 1 July 1901 lists the same postmaster at $55.42. The 1895 register has the same name against Lukfata. By 1 July 1903 the line has changed to James W. Castilow at $72.52, and the 1907 register gives “Lukfata, Dist 24: Spencer, John A, PM $144.” So Gaffney, the notary before whom Mattie Clay swore to her son Abner Henry’s birth on 1 May 1899, was the postmaster that July, and Costelow, the notary of October 1902, held the office by the next register.

The name is spelled three ways. The jacket has Costelow in 1896 and 1902, the 1903 register prints Castilow, and L. P. Bobo’s memoir of an allotting party’s winter ride through McCurtain County names “Jim Costilow at Lukfata” among the well-furnished homes where the party stopped. Those are one surname by sound and place. The first names match as far as they go: J. W. on the certificate and notary signature, James W. in the register, Jim in Bobo.

The office itself is older than either man. George H. Shirk’s list of first post offices in the Chronicles of Oklahoma says a post office spelled Luk-fah-tah opened in the Choctaw Nation on 14 February 1853 with Emilius G. Corder as postmaster and was discontinued effective 9 July 1866, and that Lukfata was reestablished on 21 January 1873 with John N. Hodges. A Chronicles article on the Choctaw Telegraph newspaper adds that in December 1849 the Nation’s annuity payments were announced for “Lukfoata,” which it places halfway between present Idabel and Broken Bow. Lukfata was therefore a post and meeting place for decades before the Merry wedding, which fits a neighborhood where a postmaster could also take sworn statements for the Dawes Commission.

What is not shown matters. The register of 1 July 1897 was not read, so there is no line placing Gaffney in the office on the wedding day itself, though both registers on either side name him. The notary commissions are not in the jackets, only the signatures. And the minister, Rev. J. H. Sleeper, remains unidentified: the Chronicles’ cumulative index for volumes 1 through 37 lists several Sleepers but no J. H. Sleeper, so the record of the officiant is still the certificate alone. Neither Gaffney nor Costelow is added to the tree; they are neighbors, not kin.

quotes: “he had two little kids when I left there in 1878” (John M. Hodges, Atoka, 7 December 1900)
stories.title: John M. Hodges of Atoka: the man who remembered Peter Durant
stories.hook: The witness who told the Commission in 1900 that Peter Durant “had two little kids” can be found on a Dawes card of his own, with a wife, two sons and a land office transcript.

subject.name: John M. Hodges
subject.rel: Witness in the Merry enrollment case

body: On 7 December 1900, at Atoka, the Commission to the Five Civilized Tribes took the testimony of a John M. Hodges on behalf of Louis Merry. He said he was fifty, a Choctaw citizen by blood, born and raised in the Nation, that he had known Peter Durant, that Peter “had two little kids” when he left “that part of the country” in 1877 or 1878, and that Peter was the son of Wilsey Clay. Earlier stories use that testimony to link Bessie’s father to Wilsey, but nobody had asked who Hodges was.

A Dawes card answers it. Choctaw card 4310, made in August 1899, is the family of a John M. Hodges whose post office was Atoka: John M., 50, one-eighth Choctaw; his wife Martha, 38; and sons Ozie T., 18, and Joseph M., 15. A memorandum in the jacket shows John and Martha on the 1896 Choctaw roll in Atoka County, both Choctaws by blood whose mothers were Choctaw. The final-roll index enrolls John M. Hodges, then 53, one-eighth, as roll 12060, with his sons as 12061 and 12062. The age matches the witness’s age of fifty in 1900, the blood is Choctaw and he lived at Atoka, where the hearing was held. Those points make him the probable witness, though no paper in either jacket says so. The National Archives description of the card shows his roll number as “NR,” but the Oklahoma Historical Society’s final-roll index gives him 12060, and the index is followed here.

The Hodges jacket is a small family file. Martha died, and a death notice was approved on 22 November 1902. Ozie’s allotment testimony at the Choctaw Land Office on 22 May 1903 is told in the story of the land office. In September 1905 John wrote to the Commission enclosing a copy of the certificate of his marriage to Mary Hunter on 6 April 1905 and asking that she be enrolled as an intermarried citizen. The Acting Commissioner answered on 14 September that under the act of 1 July 1902 no application could be received for a person who married a citizen by blood after 25 September 1902. That is the same cutoff the Commission pressed on Louis and Bessie Merry and on Abner and Mattie Clay, and it shows how the rule was applied to a witness in the Merry case himself.

There is one more thread, and it is only a lead. George H. Shirk’s list of first post offices says the Lukfata office was reestablished on 21 January 1873 with “John N. Hodges” as postmaster. A man who was about fifty in 1900 would have been about twenty-three then, he told the Commission he was born and raised in the Nation, and he left “that part of the country” in 1877 or 1878. The initial differs (M on the card, N in the printed list), the list may have misread a handwritten letter, and nothing ties the two together. The surname was also at Lukfata later: a card from about 1899 to 1902 lists a Melissa Hodges, 17, three-quarters Choctaw, with Lukfata as her post office, but she is on a different card and no link to John M. appears.

What this adds to Bessie’s line is modest but useful. It shows that the one man who spoke for Peter Durant’s family before the Commission was a Choctaw of the Atoka country with his own enrollment at stake, not a stranger, and that his memory reaches back to the 1870s when Peter’s children were small. It does not explain the county Hodges named, typed in the transcript as “Matoon County,” which is still unidentified.

stories.title: The law behind the wedding: what Choctaw statute asked of a white man
stories.hook: The 1894 laws of the Choctaw Nation set out the license, the ten Choctaw signers, the oath and the penalty that Louis Merry went through in 1896 and that his case later turned on.
body: The Constitution and Laws of the Choctaw Nation was published by authority of the General Council in 1894, compiled by A. R. Durant, with Davis Homer and Ben Watkins as assistant compilers. Under “Citizenship,” section I, “Inter-marriage,” it says that any white man or foreign citizen who wished to marry a Choctaw woman had to get a license from a circuit clerk or a judge of a court of record, and satisfy that officer that he had no living wife from whom he was not lawfully divorced. He had to present a certificate of good moral character signed by at least ten respectable Choctaw citizens by blood who had known him for twelve months. He had to pay twenty-five dollars and take an oath to honor, defend and submit to the Nation’s constitution and laws, and not to seek protection or redress from the United States government that was incompatible with them. Marriages had to be solemnized under Choctaw law or were void, anyone who solemnized a marriage outside these rules was to be fined fifty dollars, and the person who married had to bring the certificate, attached to the back of the license, to the circuit clerk within thirty days to be recorded.

The record in Louis Merry’s enrollment file follows the statute closely, with differences worth noting. R. W. Thomas, clerk of Bok Tuklo County, swore in 1904 that Louis applied to him in September 1896 with a petition signed by ten Choctaws by blood, took the oath of allegiance and paid the “regular fee” of one hundred dollars, and was licensed to marry Bessie Durant; Rev. J. H. Sleeper then married them on 7 September 1896. The ten signers and the oath are the statute’s certificate and oath. The fee is not: the 1894 text prints twenty-five dollars, and no amending act was found in the volumes read, so the reason for the higher figure is unsettled. The office also differs, since the 1894 text names circuit clerks and judges and Thomas was a county clerk. A search-result snippet, not opened, attributes a rise from twenty-five to one hundred dollars to a council act of 1887, which is unverified here.

The statute also explains the quarrel over recording. It told the licensed man to hand the marriage certificate to the circuit clerk within thirty days and told the clerk to record it. Thomas swore that it was not the custom in Bok Tuklo County to record such licenses at that time. His successor Joe A. James first said he had recorded Louis’s papers and returned them, and later was uncertain. The Commission accepted the marriage anyway, but the law shows why both clerks were asked about it. Sections 5 and 6 also mattered to anyone who married in this way: an intermarried widow or widower kept citizenship unless he or she married a white person without Choctaw blood, and a spouse who abandoned the marriage forfeited the rights and could be removed as an intruder. Louis and Bessie’s separation of June to July 1902, told in his testimony, was the kind of event those words made important.

By 1905 the question was no longer the Nation’s statute alone. The Department of the Interior’s published decisions show how it read the old Choctaw law. In May 1904 the Acting Secretary approved the enrollment of Thornton D. Pearce, a white man married under Choctaw law in 1883 to a Choctaw citizen who died in 1895, though he had since married a white woman. The decision relied on article 38 of the 1866 treaty, which made a white person who married a Choctaw and lived in the Nation a member of it “in all respects as though he was a native,” and on the council act that the Choctaw digest prints at page 226. An Assistant Attorney-General’s opinion approved on 28 January 1905, on which the Secretary rejected Emma McMenamin a few days later, held that citizenship by intermarriage cannot be gained by marrying another white person who had himself become a citizen that way. Louis, married to a Choctaw woman by blood, fit the first rule and not the second, and the Commission ruled for him on 10 January 1905. The Nation’s attorneys, Mansfield, McMurray and Cornish, who protested his claim, are the same firm named in these published cases.

The point of putting the statute beside the file is that nothing in Louis’s paper trail was improvised. Each document the Commission asked for in 1900 and 1904, the petition, the oath, the license, the certificate and the clerk’s record, matches a step the Nation’s own law required in 1896, and the license that burned in December 1897 was the paper at the center of his case.

stories.title: Reading a Dawes file: the card, the jacket, the testimony and the numbers
stories.hook: Four kinds of paper and four kinds of number sit behind the family’s Dawes records. Here is what each one is, shown with the Merry, Clay and Durant files.

subject.name: The Dawes records of the Merry, Clay and Durant families

body: The Commission to the Five Civilized Tribes, called the Dawes Commission after its chairman, was authorized by Congress on 3 March 1893 to negotiate agreements with the Five Civilized Tribes that would permit land to be allotted to individual tribal members. The National Archives explains that in 1896 Congress let it add names to the tribal rolls, that more than 7,500 applications were received then, and that the Curtis Act of 28 June 1898 declared those “1896 applications” void and told the Commission to enroll people without tribal consent. Enrollment applications were accepted from 1898 through 1907. The “1896 roll” on Louis and Bessie Merry’s card, numbers 14822 and 8644, is a different list, the Choctaw Nation’s own census of that year, which L. P. Bobo called the “Census Roll.” Whether any of these families also filed a Commission application in 1896 was not searched.

The census card is a one-page summary of a family group. Card 5754, dated 26 April 1899, lists Louis, Bessie and their daughter Ida May with ages, blood, the parents’ names and counties, earlier roll numbers and a column of stamps. It is filed in the “Choctaw by Blood” group, with Louis shown on the same card as an intermarried white citizen. The numbers on it must be told apart: 5754 is the card number, 1363 is Louis’s roll number as an intermarried white citizen, 15526 and 15527 are Bessie’s and Ida May’s roll numbers, and 14822 and 8644 are the earlier 1896 numbers. The final roll gave each approved person one roll number, and land was later allotted by that number, not by the card.

The jacket is the folder of papers behind the card. The National Archives calls it an enrollment application, also a “testimonial packet.” The jacket for card 5754 is forty page images: a typed title page, “Record in the matter of the application for the enrollment as a citizen by intermarriage of the Choctaw Nation of Louis Merry,” the mother’s and midwife’s affidavits, letters from the Commission, the hearing transcripts, the clerks’ affidavits, the copy of the marriage certificate and the decision. Its cover is marked “Trans from Choc #D128.” The National Archives lists “denied or doubtful” as one of the Dawes categories, marked D, and a D prefix is probably what the Merrys’ first card number meant. The jacket does not say so, and the card moved to 5754 on 21 March 1904, before the 10 January 1905 decision, so the move was not simply the result of the ruling.

A testimony is a transcript, not a signed statement. John M. Hodges’s answers of 7 December 1900 are typed under the caption “Choctaw D 128, Louis Merry vs Choctaw Nation,” with a line noting that no testimony was offered by the Nation. He was sworn by the acting chairman, Tams Bixby; the Choctaw commissioner, Judge Lewis, asked the follow-up questions about Abner Clay; and the next day the stenographer, Anna Bell, swore that the pages were a true copy of her notes. Each Dawes transcript carries such a stenographer’s oath, which is why a witness’s own words, like “he had two little kids,” survive as they were said.

Two more record sets belong to the same system. Land allotment jackets, which describe the parcel and its improvements and are arranged by roll number, are on FamilySearch and Ancestry according to the National Archives, and were not reachable here. The Allotment Maps, township plats lettered with each allottee’s name and roll number, are in the National Archives Catalog; the map of Township 6 South, Range 23 East in another story is where the Merrys’ roll numbers turn into land. Reading a family through all four, the card, the jacket, the testimony and the map, is what lets a roll number such as 15526 be followed to a person, a parent and a parcel.

stories.title: Six mail towns in the family’s papers, and when each one opened
stories.hook: Garvin, Shawneetown, Wheelock, Valliant, Millerton and Idabel turn up in the Merry, Clay, Durant and Box papers. The government’s own list gives each office’s first date.

subject.name: Garvin, Shawneetown, Wheelock, Valliant, Millerton and Idabel

body: George H. Shirk’s list of “First Post Offices Within the Boundaries of Oklahoma,” printed in the Chronicles of Oklahoma in 1948 from the Post Office Department’s records, gives each office, the nation it served, the date its first postmaster was appointed and notes on name changes and closings. Six of its Choctaw Nation entries match places in these families’ papers. Glover and Lukfata have their own stories.

Garvin opened on 19 February 1894 with James W. Kirk as postmaster. The 1895 Official Register shows Kirk with $34.70 of compensation, and the 1903 register shows J. W. Kirk with $311.50, a sign of how fast the little place grew. It is the post office on card 656 for William A. Durant and Laura Clay, who lived in Red River County; Louis Merry gave his second testimony at Garvin on 28 November 1902; Mattie Clay was back there by March 1904; and G. A. Spaulding, the U.S. Commissioner before whom the Bok Tuklo clerks swore their affidavits in August 1904, sat at Garvin. L. P. Bobo’s allotting party left its mule team at a livery stable in Garvin over Christmas.

Shawneetown was first called Kulli Inla; the office was opened under the new name on 16 August 1892 with Robert M. Love as postmaster, and the 1901 register still lists him. It is where W. F. Nichols took Mattie Clay’s affidavit for her daughter Myrtle on 24 October 1902 and where her brother Claude Denson lived when he wrote about the children’s allotments in January 1903.

Wheelock is the oldest. Its post office opened on 21 March 1845 with Henry K. Copeland, lapsed for a few weeks in 1866 and for months in 1872, and was discontinued effective 3 May 1895, with mail sent to Garvin. Lizzie Durant’s card places her at Wheelock Seminary in April 1899, and a later generation of the family knew it too: Alfreda Whitfield was born at Wheelock in 1939.

Three offices belong to the years of the Dawes enrollment. Shirk lists Valliant from 23 June 1902 with Hosea L. Fowler as postmaster, noting “formerly Fowlerville,” and the 1895 register already lists a Fowlerville office established on 28 August 1894. Parsons, named for W. S. Parsons, was first ordered on 17 May 1902, rescinded in September and actually opened after a new appointment ordered on 15 December 1902; its name was changed to Millerton on 5 March 1908. Bokhoma was established on 15 December 1902 with Daniel Strawn and renamed Idabel on 3 February 1904. Claude Joel Box and Archie Box registered for the draft at Valliant in 1942, Tyro Box gave Millerton, and Alfreda Whitfield Sandridge later worked in Idabel, so the Box and Whitfield families knew towns whose present names are younger than the Dawes enrollment.

stories.title: Wheelock Seminary, where Lizzie Durant was enrolled in 1899
stories.hook: The Choctaw boarding school that held Lizzie Durant on 27 April 1899 had been founded by the Nation’s General Council in 1842, and its church yard holds the missionary who began the work.

subject.name: Wheelock Female Seminary
subject.rel: School where Lizzie Durant was enrolled

body: Lizzie Durant’s card, number 966, was made at Wheelock Seminary on 27 April 1899, and she said under oath in 1906 that she had been a student there that April. Ora Eddleman Reed’s article on the Robe family of missionaries in the Chronicles of Oklahoma explains the place. Wheelock Female Seminary, it says, was established in 1842 by the Choctaw General Council. The Rev. Alfred Wright of the American Board had begun mission work at Wheelock in 1832 and stayed until his death on 31 March 1853, and he is buried in the old Wheelock church yard near Millerton.

In the fall of 1884, when the Presbyterian board closed Old Spencer Academy, its girls were moved to Wheelock under the Robe family, and Reed describes a rebuilt stone church attended by Choctaws and by white and Black neighbors. The post office there, opened in 1845, was discontinued in 1895 and its mail sent to Garvin. The editor’s note says the boarding schools were supported on a basis of three-fourths from the Choctaw Nation and one-fourth from the mission board, with missionaries as superintendents. Lizzie, about thirteen and full Choctaw, belonged to the generation the Nation was educating in those boarding academies at the very moment the Dawes Commission was recording its children.

The reports of the U.S. Indian Inspector for Indian Territory, printed with the Commission’s reports, list Wheelock Orphan Academy among the Choctaw Nation’s boarding schools for 1899, and name W. W. Appleton as its superintendent in the year ended June 1900. The same report counts 120 neighborhood schools in the Choctaw Nation and says that bad weather, long distances, uncomfortable buildings and the indifference of patrons held them back, while the boarding schools were “poorly equipped.” The Inspector’s tables do not list the neighborhood schools by name, so the schools nearest Lukfata and Glover cannot be identified from them.

That gap is real. No source read here names a school or a church at Glover, and the only Lukfata school and church found are the mission school of 1835 told in an earlier story. The Chronicles’ cumulative index lists a “Lukfata Chito (Big Lick) Church” in volume 12 (1934), page 130, a volume not available for this story, and that entry is the first thing to check. Wheelock, by contrast, is documented, and Lizzie’s card is the record that places a granddaughter of Wilsey Clay inside it.

stories.title: Jackson L. Livesay: the log school at Beaucoup, Company C and a Centralia store
stories.hook: A 1909 Marion County history follows the eldest son of William E. and Emily (Goodner) Livesay from the Beaucoup school to the 60th Illinois, to Kansas and Montana, and at last to a store in Centralia.
body: Brinkerhoff’s History of Marion County, Illinois (1909) gives a full page to Jackson L. Livesay, a Centralia merchant then in his sixty-third year. He was born, it says, at “Washington, Illinois” on 28 September 1845, the son of W. E. and Emily (Goodner) Livesay. His father, a native of Tennessee, came to Illinois at seven with parents who were also Tennessee natives, settled on a farm in Washington County and married Emily Goodner, who “came of an Illinois family.” They raised eight children, five boys and three girls, and Jackson was the eldest. In 1871 the family moved to Kansas and took up farming and storekeeping. The sketch says William E. died there in 1872 and his wife in 1874, and that the family came back to Illinois in 1881.

This is the first record opened that follows William Edmund Livesay, the eldest son of Robert and Lydia in the family sketch, past the 1856 heirs’ paper. The sketch gave him a birth about 1823 in Maury County, Tennessee, and a move to Illinois at about seven. The marriage register lists William E. Livesay and Emily Goodner on a license of 1 August 1844, and Jackson’s birth thirteen months later fits. The 1909 sketch agrees on the name, the wife, the Tennessee birth, the move at seven and the Washington County farm, so William E. and Emily are given death years of 1872 and 1874, with Kansas as the place, from that sketch alone, and Jackson is linked as their eldest son. The Goodner family is large in Washington County, and a separate county biography of James T. Goodner of Irvington lists his siblings without an Emily, so her parents are not guessed.

Jackson went to the Beaucoup school, which the sketch calls an old log school-house, and left at sixteen. In the spring of 1864 he joined Company C of the 60th Illinois Infantry at Centralia, “commanded by Col. William Anderson” and “Capt. Simeon Walker, now at Carbondale, Illinois, in active service.” He marched with Sherman to the sea, was mustered out at Louisville and came home in August 1865. The state’s printed roster, read in the earlier story on William P. Walker, gives Jackson L. Livesay of Richview the same dates as William: enlisted 20 March 1864, mustered 17 April 1864, out 31 July 1865. So two young men from the Beaucoup neighborhood joined the same company in the same month, under a captain who was probably William’s brother-in-law. A volunteer compilation of the muster rolls describes Jackson as a farmer of Richview, 5 feet 6 inches tall, with light hair and blue eyes, born about 1846 in Jefferson County. The sketch says Washington, which may mean the county or the town, so the birthplace is left as Washington County with the conflict noted.

The sketch also fixes the captain’s whereabouts, in a way that bears on an old conflict. The Beaucoup Cemetery transcription gives Simeon Walker’s death as 11 October 1909 and the veterans’ compilation gives 29 April 1905. A book published in 1909 that speaks of him as still “in active service” leans toward the later date, though a printed present tense can be stale, and the question stays open.

After the war Jackson tried a claim in Kansas in 1866, returned to Washington County for two years, and clerked at Richview for J. V. Holcomb and Company for a year. With his uncle William Shanks he then bought out the firm and moved the stock to Montana and Kansas, where they stayed eight years, followed by three years of farming. He spent three months at Richview and settled at Centralia, where he worked for other firms for twenty years and then ran his own store at 103 South Locust Street for eleven. The sketch does not say whether William Shanks was a brother of his father or mother, so the uncle is left unplaced. Jackson married Emma Ingram, daughter of H. P. Ingram and Millie Tyler of Richview, on 12 June 1871, and they had nine children. He belonged to the Modern Woodmen and the Grand Army of the Republic, voted Republican and was a Methodist Episcopal. The Richview township cemetery list carries a Jackson Livesay (1842–1917); the dates do not match this Jackson’s 1845 birth, and nothing says whether the two are related.

stories.title: Lorenzo M. Livesay in the 1883 history of Jefferson County
stories.hook: A county history gives Lorenzo Mastin Livesay his exact birth day, the day he died, the day his first wife died and the name of his second wife, and it counts twelve children.
body: The History of Jefferson County, Illinois (Chicago: Globe Publishing Co., 1883) has a short biography headed “Lorenzo M. Livesay, deceased,” on page 75. It says he was born in Tennessee on 9 October 1825, came to Jefferson County in the fall of 1856 and died there on 6 June 1876. He married Margaret J. Thompson on 22 October 1845, and she bore him twelve children, of whom only four were living in 1883: Mary C., Ephraim J., Elizabeth P. and Lafayette S. Margaret died on 28 October 1868. On 16 May 1869 he married Sarah S. Lane, a daughter of Henry Lane, born in Caldwell County, Kentucky, who came with her parents to Clinton County, Illinois, in 1840. The writer closes with a line: a “faithful Methodist, and a useful, honest man.”

The earlier story on Lorenzo Mastin Livesay read him in two Jefferson County censuses. The sketch fits them closely. The marriage date is the one in the Washington County register, 22 October 1845. The three children in his 1860 household, Ephraim J., Mary C. and Elizabeth P., are three of the four the sketch names as living, and so is Lafayette S., who was five in 1870. The 1870 wife, Sarah S., 36, born in Kentucky, is Sarah S. Lane. The sketch also answers a question the earlier story had to leave open: Margaret did not simply disappear from the record, she died in October 1868, and Lorenzo remarried seven months later. Wilburn W. and Elva M., who were at home in 1870, are not among the four living in 1883, so they probably died between those years. The move is consistent too: Ephraim’s Illinois birth about 1849 fits a start in Washington County, where Lorenzo married in 1845, and the fall of 1856 for the move across the county line.

The tree now carries the exact birth day from the county history, a death date and place, and a second wife. Lorenzo Mastin’s tie to Robert and Lydia Livesay is as before: the family sketch and the 1856 heirs’ paper it transcribes name him, and the 1883 sketch names no parents. It is worth saying plainly that two Livesay men named Lorenzo died in 1876, Lorenzo M. in Jefferson County on 6 June and Lorenzo Dow in Kansas. The Washington County probate index lists an estate for “Livesay, L. M.” (file 98) without a year or a county of residence, which was not opened and is not assigned to either man.

Lorenzo Dow and Lorenzo M. are different men.

stories.title: Alfred’s thirteen children, and the grandfather James R. Logan
stories.hook: Two 1909 county sketches name all thirteen children of Alfred and Hannah (Logan) Livesay, and the younger son’s sketch names Hannah’s father: James R. Logan, a South Carolinian who farmed in Washington County until 1860.
body: Brinkerhoff’s History of Marion County, Illinois (1909) prints a sketch of Alfred Livesay, the Mexican War private and Methodist preacher of Patoka Township, which an earlier story on this site used through a transcription. The thirteen children it names, in order, are William T., Elizabeth R., Isaac B., Pearl, Hester A., Ransom P., Marshall A., Liddie, Harvey R., Allen H., Daniel R., Etta and Clinton O. It gives most of them a spouse. William T. married Eliza Seward and lived at Stanley, Iowa. Isaac B. married Leticia Rock and lived in Kansas. Pearl married Joseph Larimer, Hester A. married Perry Davidson, Ransom P. married Louisa Suter and Marshall A. married Rachael Walton. Liddie was dead by then and had married Robert Quale. Harvey R. married Mollie Chick, Daniel R. married Laura Cruse, Etta married James Smith and Clinton O. married Elvira McHaney. Allen H. never married and died at forty-four, and Elizabeth R. was single and cared for her mother.

A second sketch in the same book, of Alfred’s son Harvey R. Livesay, lists the same family in a slightly different way. Harvey’s list of thirteen leaves out Pearl and adds an Eddie who died young, names a Lizzie, a Berry and a Lydia where his father’s sketch has Elizabeth R., Isaac B. and Liddie, and puts Marshall in “Foley, Missouri.” The two sketches also differ on a move: Alfred’s sketch says he came to Marion County about 1866, while Harvey’s says he went to Missouri in 1866 and came to Marion County later. The differences look like the ordinary drift of two interviews, but they are left as printed.

Harvey R. Livesay, the sketch says, was born on 10 May 1861 in Washington County, stayed at home until he was twenty-two, and in February 1883 married Mollie Chick of Foster Township. She died in 1895 and left five children. By 1909 he farmed in Foster and Patoka townships, voted Democratic like his father and was Supervisor of Foster Township. The same sketch gives something the sketch of Alfred left out. Harvey’s mother, Hannah Logan, was the daughter of James R. Logan, who was born in South Carolina, lived in Tennessee and then came to Washington County, Illinois, where he had a well-improved farm until his death in 1860. He was a Methodist and a local exhorter.

A few other records agree with this in a loose way. The Washington County probate index lists an estate for a Jas. R. Logan, file 36, with no date, and the 1855 state census transcription has a James R. Logan household of seven with a man aged 40 to 50 and a woman aged 50 to 60. That man would have been young to father a daughter in 1830, so the 1855 household may be a son or another man of the name; the index entry and the census are not offered as proof. With the single sketch they are enough to link James R. Logan as Hannah’s probable father. They do not say how he was related to James L. Logan, who married Unity J. Livesay in 1849, and no kinship is claimed.

The sketch of the Marion County teacher J. R. Quayle supplies the end of one daughter’s story: he married Lyda E. Livesay, daughter of Alfred Livesay of Patoka Township, on 8 January 1889, and she died in June 1906 after bearing four children. The sketches of Alfred and Harvey call her Liddie and Lydia and name her husband Robert Quale, so the book prints his name three ways. The tree adds Harvey and Lyda with their parents. The other eleven children are named here but not added, because the sketches give no dates for them.

stories.note: Probable. The two sketches agree on Alfred’s death date and on Hannah’s Washington County birth, and they differ in detail on the children, which is noted. James R. Logan rests on Harvey’s sketch, with an undated probate index entry and an uncertain 1855 census household as weak support; the link to Hannah is probable, not proven. Only Harvey and Lyda are added as people. The husband of Lyda is printed Quale, Quayle and J. R. Quayle, taken as one man.

stories.title: The Flannigans, the Whites and the Copples at Gilead
stories.hook: Two small Copple girls in Thomas Flannigan’s house in 1850 turn out to be orphaned grandchildren. Their story, told by four county histories and the Gilead Cemetery list, gives Patsy Flannigan a father, Rev. Robert White, and makes Tabitha J. Livesay a probable daughter of the house.
body: The earlier story on Tabitha J. Livesay’s probable family left one thing unexplained. The 1850 census of Jefferson County, enumerated on 8 August, lists in dwelling 443 Thomas A. Flannigan, 54, born in North Carolina, Patsy, 48, born in Georgia, Tabitha J., 20, James R., 18, and Maria, 16, all three born in Illinois. After them come two small girls with a different surname: Amanda Copple, 4, and Martha L. Copple, one month old. Nobody asked who they were. Four county histories and the cemetery list answer it.

The 1894 Portrait and Biographical Record, in its sketch of David Copple of Marion County (pp. 339–340), follows his son Eli, born on 8 June 1820 in Washington County, Indiana. In 1840 Eli married “Miss Martha Flanagan.” They had two daughters who grew up, Arminda, later Mrs. William Dolson, and Loretta, later Mrs. A. J. Hartley. After the first wife’s death Eli married Sarah Dolson, daughter of Allen Dolson. A 1909 sketch of Eli’s son Elmer (Biographical and Reminiscent History of Richland, Clay and Marion Counties, pp. 568–569) says Eli’s first wife was Martha Flannagan of Jefferson County, Illinois, who died in 1850, and that three more of their children died in infancy. The Gilead Cemetery list, from Grand Prairie Township in Jefferson County, gives “Copple, Martha, 6-1-1850, w/o E,” beside Eli (8 June 1820 to 14 August 1905) and Sarah (8 December 1829 to 24 October 1915). A baby counted at one month old on 8 August 1850 was born within a few months of her mother’s death on 1 June 1850. So the two girls were Amanda, probably Arminda, and Martha L., probably Loretta or Martha Loretta, left in their grandparents’ house.

Brinkerhoff’s 1909 History of Marion County (pp. 833–834), in the sketch of George Pliney Baldridge, supplies the grandmother’s family. His mother, Tabitha White, born 10 July 1811, was a daughter of Rev. Robert White, a Methodist Episcopal minister with a large circuit, who lived in Indiana in early life, came to Marion County and later to Grand Prairie Township in Jefferson County. His children were Robert, who drowned in Madison County; Martha White, who married Thomas Flannigan, and whose daughter Martha married Eli Copple; Louisa White, who married Allen Dolson, and whose daughter Sarah became Eli’s second wife and the cousin of his first; and Tabitha, who married Isaac Casey and then James Clark Baldridge. The Gilead list carries Tabitha (10 July 1811 to 13 April 1899) and James C. Baldridge (10 December 1811 to 16 May 1897), the dates the sketch gives, and it carries “White, Rev. R.,” who died on 14 May 1828 about 55 years old.

The census gives the same neighborhood. Dwelling 444, next door to the Flannigans, is Allan Dolson, 45, born in New York, with Mary L., 40, born in Georgia, and eight children from Sarah, 20, down. Patsy Flannigan was also born in Georgia, which suits two White sisters born there a few years apart, with Louisa perhaps the Mary L. of the census, though that is an inference. In dwelling 445 a Sarah White, 74, born in North Carolina, shares a house with Peter and Rachel Dolson, aged 75 and 73. She may have been the minister’s widow, but nothing opened says so. The Georgia births come earlier than the Indiana years the sketch mentions; since it says only “in early life,” the two do not conflict. The 1883 History of Jefferson County (pp. 390–391) adds the setting: Grand Prairie Township had no town and no railroad, its first church society was organized at the Widow Gaston’s by Rev. Samuel Walker, a pioneer Methodist minister, and the Gilead Methodist Episcopal church on section 5 was the only church building. That Walker is not shown to be related to the Walkers of Beaucoup.

Put together, the records give the 1850 household an identity. Its head was the Thomas Flannigan whose wife Martha was a daughter of Rev. Robert White and whose daughter Martha, Eli Copple’s wife, died on 1 June 1850. The tree now holds Rev. Robert as Patsy’s probable father, and Martha Copple and Eli. Tabitha J. appears in the household without a mention in any sketch. She was twenty, born in Illinois, the right age to be another daughter, and the stone of Tabitha J., wife of David P. Livesay, who died on 14 February 1856 aged 27, stands in the same cemetery as the Flannigan stones. With the maiden name Flannigen that Find a Grave reports, that makes her a probable daughter of Thomas and Martha, and she is linked as such. No record yet says that she was Floyd Livesay’s mother, so that link stays unmade. The census gives Thomas’s middle initial as A and the stone gives H; both readings are kept.

“David Copple, deceased,” Portrait and Biographical Record of Clinton, Washington, Marion and Jefferson Counties, Illinois (Chicago: Chapman Publishing Co., 1894), pp. 339–340 (Eli Copple, born 8 June 1820; married Martha Flanagan in 1840); full text via Internet Archive; read 4 Nov 2026: https://archive.org/stream/portraitbiograph94chic/portraitbiograph94chic_djvu.txt

stories.note: Probable. Four independent printed accounts and the cemetery list agree that Eli Copple’s first wife was Martha Flannigan of Jefferson County, who died in 1850, and the Brinkerhoff sketch gives her parents; the Copple girls in the 1850 household are matched by place, age and the 1 June 1850 death, not by name (Amanda and Martha L. against Arminda and Loretta). Patsy’s father, Rev. Robert White, rests on one sketch and the cemetery’s “Rev. R. White.” Tabitha J.’s link to Thomas and Martha rests on the household, the shared cemetery and the age; no record names her parents. Eli’s birth is given differently by the 1909 Elmer Copple sketch. Thomas’s middle initial is A in the census and H on the stone. The tree does not link Tabitha to Floyd Livesay.

stories.title: Robert Carter and Livesay Carter in Lake Township, 1817 and 1818
stories.hook: The 1881 county history puts a Methodist minister named Robert Carter, from Tennessee, on section 6 of Lake Township in 1817, and gives Livesay Carter his first dated Illinois land entry there on 26 February 1818.
body: The History of Marion and Clinton Counties, Illinois (Brink, McDonough & Co., 1881) describes Lake Township, which lies in the southeast of Clinton County on the line with Washington County. It says the township was first settled in 1817. Among the first families were Robert C. McKever, a Georgian, and Dempsey Kennedy, also a Georgian, who settled on section 6 the same year and stayed about two years before moving to what is now Washington County. The history adds that “Robert Carter, a Methodist minister and a pioneer from Tennessee, came to this township in 1817, and located on section 6, and afterwards removed to Washington county in company with Mr. Kennedy.” It calls him the pioneer preacher of that part of the country and says that his tomb may be shown in a little private burying-ground in Lake Township. Two other chapters of the same book mention him in passing: the county settlers’ chapter says he came in 1817 and “afterward settled elsewhere,” and the Methodist chapter lists “Robert Carter, who settled in Central Prairie in 1817” among the local preachers.

The township chapter then prints the first land entries from the county records. Among them stands one line: “Feb. 26th, 1818, Livesay Carter entered S. E. 1/4 Sec. 7.” That is the section beside Robert Carter’s section 6, and the book’s index sends the reader to page 233 for this name. It is the earliest dated record yet found for Livesay Carter in Illinois. The 1879 history of Washington County says Livesay Carter went to Tennessee in 1807, came to Illinois in 1818, lived about four years in what is now Clinton County and then settled near Nashville. The 1881 entry supplies the day and the quarter-section. The joint patent of 10 December 1823 to Livesay Carter and Robert Carter, found in the earlier story on the Carter kin, shows two Carters still working neighboring land.

The family sketch of Jackson Monroe Livesay says the Carters went to Illinois first, and that Rebecca (Carter) Livesay’s brother was a Robert Carter. The 1881 history now puts a Robert Carter, a Methodist minister from Tennessee, in Clinton County in 1817, a year ahead of Livesay Carter, and it ties him to the Kennedy family who later moved to Washington County. That is a good fit for the sketch, but it is a fit and not a proof. A Methodist Robert Carter from Tennessee is not shown to be Rebecca’s brother, and nothing says the Robert of the 1823 patent was the minister. Robert Carter is therefore added as an unlinked lead. Dempsey Kennedy matters for a second reason. A joint federal patent of 1848 to Demsy Kennedy and William E. Livesay, noted on William Edmund Livesay’s profile and not reopened here, shows a Kennedy and a Livesay as neighbors a generation later.

One problem remains. The Masonic Cemetery listing gives Livesay Carter’s birth as 15 November 1799. On 26 February 1818 he would have been eighteen, which is young for a man to enter a quarter section in his own name, and the earlier story already noted that a man born in 1799 could not have been the first son of a marriage of the 1780s. Either the entry was made for the family, or the stone’s year is late, or the Livesay Carter of 1818 was an older man. The history does not say. His age is left as the cemetery gives it, with this conflict recorded.
src: History of Marion and Clinton Counties, Illinois (Philadelphia: Brink, McDonough & Co., 1881), Lake Township, “Early Settlements” and “Land Entries,” pp. 232–233 (Robert Carter on section 6; Livesay Carter, 26 Feb 1818); county settlers’ chapter pp. 51–52; Methodist chapter pp. 164–165; index entry “Livesay, 233”; via Internet Archive; read 4 Nov 2026: https://archive.org/details/bwb_S0-EKB-952

History of Washington County, Illinois (Philadelphia: Brink, McDonough & Co., 1879), sketch of Dr. William D. Carter (Livesay Carter in Tennessee 1807, Illinois 1818, four years in Clinton County), via Internet Archive; read 4 Nov 2026: https://archive.org/details/il-washington-1879-brink

Masonic Cemetery, Nashville, Washington County, Illinois, full transcription (Livesay, Carter, 15 Nov 1799 to 17 Oct 1875), Genealogy Trails; volunteer transcription, as cited in the earlier story; the birth date was not reopened here: https://www.genealogytrails.com/ill/washington/cems/nash/masonic.html

“Jackson Monroe Livesay (A135.3): A Genealogical Sketch,” Livesay family file, Orange County California Genealogical Society (family sketch; secondary; the Carters going first, Robert Carter as Rebecca’s brother), as cited in earlier stories and not reopened here: https://occgs.com/projects/rescue/family_files/files/LIVESAY%20Family.pdf
stories.note: Probable for Livesay Carter’s entry: the date and place agree with the 1879 county history’s account of his move, and the 1881 index confirms the page. Lead for Robert Carter: the Methodist minister of 1817 is not proved to be the 1823 co-patentee or Rebecca (Carter) Livesay’s brother in the family sketch, and he is not linked to anyone. Livesay Carter is still not linked to the Livesay line, and his birth year has an unresolved conflict with the 1818 entry.

stories.title: Gilbert G. Merry’s 1916 sketch: a Calvin Merry and a brother at Golden
stories.hook: A 1916 Oklahoma history names Gilbert G. Merry’s parents as Calvin Merry and Eliza McGregory and his brothers as F. L., B. F., Rev. Robert and J. L., a merchant at Golden. It is the best lead yet to the family of Louis Merry.
body: The Standard History of Oklahoma (Thoburn, 1916), volume 4, prints a sketch of Gilbert G. Merry on pages 1721 and 1722. It opens with the old Military Highway through Eagletown, Valliant, Bismark and Glover, then says that Calvin Merry, “who died about twenty years ago, at Goodland, Oklahoma,” and who was reared in Arkansas near the old highway, went along with some of the pathfinders who laid it out. Calvin’s son Gilbert, of Valliant, was then a McCurtain County commissioner. Gilbert was born in 1879 at Chapel Hill, Arkansas, seven miles from the Indian Territory line, to Calvin and Eliza McGregory, whose parents were early settlers of the border. He entered the Territory at thirteen, living first at Eagletown and later at Lukfata, and in 1903 he watched the first net proceeds payment, which the sketch calls a time of drinking, shooting and lawlessness. He then lived at Garvin, where he managed a store, and from 1906 was a pharmacist at Valliant. His father was a poor man, and Gilbert first read in a second reader at seventeen. He married Annie Oaks of Grant, one-fourth Choctaw, on 4 April 1906. She died in April 1915.

The sketch names four brothers: F. L., who farmed in Cherokee County, Oklahoma; B. F., a landowner and county commissioner of Hemphill County, Texas; J. L., a general merchant at Golden, Oklahoma; and the Rev. Robert, a Baptist minister at Garvin. Earlier stories on this site worked with the Merry family and could not find Louis Merry’s people: the Dawes card gave only the names Calvin and Elizabeth Merry, dead and not Choctaw citizens, and a burial-site memorial offered John Calvin Merry, Eliza Jane McGregor and Sevier County. The 1916 sketch agrees with both on the parents, Calvin and Eliza or Elizabeth McGregory, and on the Arkansas border country.

It also agrees on place and time. Louis Merry told the Dawes Commission in December 1900 that he had lived in the Choctaw Nation about eight years, which brings his arrival to about 1892, the year Gilbert, at thirteen, reached Eagletown. Louis married Bessie Durant at Lukfata in September 1896, and Gilbert lived at Lukfata. The Commission wrote to Louis as “J. L. Merry,” and the sketch’s brother is J. L. Merry at Golden, the town where Louis’s family sketch has him dying in 1932 and where his daughter Ida later kept the post office. The 1928 and 1948 lists give the Glover postmaster as Joshua L. Merry. Taken together, the parents’ names, the border country, the year of arrival, the Lukfata years and the initials and town of J. L. make it probable that Louis Merry was Gilbert’s brother and that Calvin and Eliza McGregory were his parents.

The match is not without a snag. The sketch says Gilbert helped educate “his younger brother” and then names four, and if all four were younger than Gilbert, born in 1879, a J. L. born after that could not be the man who married in 1896 and gave his age as 28 in 1900. Louis’s gravestone gives 10 April 1872. The sentence is loosely written, and it may mean only that some of the four were younger, so the age problem is left open. The sketch names no county for Chapel Hill, so the memorial’s Sevier County birth is neither confirmed nor contradicted. Calvin’s death “about twenty years” before 1916 agrees with the card, which has both parents dead by April 1899.

The tree holds Calvin, Eliza and Gilbert as a family, and does not link Louis to them. An existing test keeps Lewis Merry’s parents unlinked, so the case is told here for the lead to weigh. The records that could finish it are Gilbert’s or Louis’s obituary, the 1900 census of Eagletown or Lukfata, an 1880 Arkansas census of the Merry household, and a Choctaw County, Oklahoma, record of Calvin’s death.
src: “Gilbert G. Merry,” A Standard History of Oklahoma, ed. Joseph B. Thoburn (Chicago: American Historical Society, 1916), vol. 4, pp. 1721–1722, full text via Internet Archive; read 4 Nov 2026: https://archive.org/stream/standardhistoryo04thob/standardhistoryo04thob_djvu.txt

Choctaw census card 5754, Louis, Bessie and Ida May Merry, parents’ columns (Calvin Merry and Elizabeth Merry, dead, non-citizens), as read in the story “Card 5754 read”; not reopened here: https://catalog.archives.gov/id/636187

Testimony of Lewis Merry, Atoka, 7 December 1900 (about eight years in the Nation), and the Lukfata marriage certificate of 7 September 1896, as read in the story “A wedding at Lukfata”; not reopened here: https://catalog.archives.gov/id/636187

Elma Severn’s 1997 family sketch (Louis Merry, 10 April 1872 to 1 July 1932, died at Golden), as cited on Lewis Merry’s profile and in the story “Ida May Merry: enrollment and the Golden post office”; not reopened here.

Grant Foreman, “Early Post Offices of Oklahoma,” Chronicles of Oklahoma, vol. 6, no. 3 (September 1928), p. 287 (Glover, first postmaster Joshua L. Merry), as cited in the story “Joshua L. Merry, first postmaster at Glover”: https://archive.org/details/chroniclesofokla6319okla
stories.note: Probable. Gilbert’s sketch directly names his parents and brothers. That Louis Merry of card 5754 was his brother rests on the parents’ names, the Arkansas border, the year of arrival and the Lukfata years, and the initials and town of J. L., not on any record naming Louis beside Gilbert. The sketch’s “younger brother” wording conflicts with Louis’s birth in 1872 if it applies to J. L. Lewis Merry’s parents are not linked in the tree because an existing test requires that. Gilbert’s children and his wife’s family are not added.

stories.title: A James C. Logan, 1773 to 1840, in the Wedgeworth Cemetery
stories.hook: A 1960 volume of Greene County, Alabama records lists a James C. Logan beside the Wedgworths in a cemetery near Cook’s Store. He died too early to be Dudley Logan’s father, but he may be a grandfather.
body: A 1960 volume, Greene County, Alabama records, compiled by Mrs. S. M. Marshall and printed at Tuscaloosa, gathers tombstone inscriptions, land patents and the 1830 census schedule for the county, which then included the part later made Hale County. One of its cemetery lists, on pages 65 and 66, is headed Wedgeworth Cemetery, “near Cook’s Store.” It names the Anderson, Hanna, Wynn, Watkins, Garland and Gewin families and these Wedgworths and one Logan. John Wedgworth died on 11 September 1824 at 35, “the first person interred here after organization of his church.” Esther Wedgworth is listed as born or died on 11 September 1832. James Wedgworth was born in Pennsylvania on 31 October 1771 and died in September 1843. Middleton Wedgworth lived from 8 September 1828 to 11 September 1889; the title before his name is damaged in the scan. And the list carries “James C. Logan, 1773 to 1840.”

The Logan matters because of what Dudley Timothy Logan’s memorial claims. Dudley was born in Greene County on 8 January 1846, and the memorial names his parents as James Clement Logan and Martha Calhoun, a pair earlier stories kept as a lead. A James C. Logan who died in 1840 cannot have fathered a child in 1846. But the 1850 census of Greene County, in the transcription earlier stories used, shows Martha Logan, 71, born in South Carolina, heading a household two doors from the Wedgeworths, with Leroy Logan, 49, Willis Logan, 44, and Clement Logan, 33, all born in South Carolina, in the neighboring dwellings, and a Dudley, 3, in Clement’s. A widow of 71 born about 1779 would fit the wife of a man born in 1773, and her sons would be Leroy, Willis and Clement. On that reading Dudley’s grandparents were James C. and Martha Logan, and the memorial has moved them down a generation. It is a hypothesis and nothing in the book says so.

The 1830 census schedule in the same book, printed on page 126 as a list of heads of families only, adds a second clue. Its Logan names include Clement, Isaac, John, Willis, Michael and Zachariah, and its Wedgworths are James, James Jr., William, Joseph and Matheas. A Clement Logan heading a household in 1830 cannot be the Clement who was 33 in 1850, who would have been thirteen. One way to read that is that the 1830 head was the older man, James Clement Logan, who went by his second name; the other is that the 1850 age is wrong. The scan’s text of the list is clean enough to read the names but gives no household counts, and the neighboring land-patent list in the book is too damaged to use.

The Wedgworths gain something too. Middleton Wedgworth, born in 1828, is the right age for the Middleton, 22, in Elizabeth Wedgworth’s household in the 1850 census, next door to Larkin’s, as an earlier story found. That ties the households of that page to this cemetery. James Wedgworth, born in Pennsylvania in 1771, and the elder John Wedgworth, who died in 1824, may be of the generation before Larkin and Stephen, who were born in South and North Carolina. Nothing printed says so, and the list gives no relationships. The question that matters for the tree is still which Wedgworth girl was Annie, and this book does not answer it.

The volume is a transcription of old stones and its text is a scan with uneven errors, so the dates should be checked against an image before they are relied on. It is cited here for names and years only. Dudley and Annie stay unlinked to any of these people.
src: Mrs. S. M. Marshall (Mary Grantham Marshall), comp., Greene County, Alabama records, ed. Elizabeth Wood Thomas (Tuscaloosa: Willo Publishing Co., 1960), Wedgeworth Cemetery (pp. 65–66) and 1830 Census Schedule, heads of families (p. 126), full text via Internet Archive; read 4 Nov 2026: https://archive.org/stream/greenecountyalab00mars/greenecountyalab00mars_djvu.txt

1850 U.S. census, Greene County, Alabama, pages 263A and 316A–316B (Logan and Wedgeworth households), USGenWeb Census Project transcription, as read in the stories “A Logan and a Wedgeworth in Greene County, 1850” and “Which Wedgworth girl was Annie?”; not reopened here: https://www.us-census.org/pub/usgenweb/census/al/greene/1850/pg0313a.txt (Logans and Wedgeworths) and https://www.us-census.org/pub/usgenweb/census/al/greene/1850/pg0255b.txt (Larkin and Elizabeth Wedgworth)

Find a Grave memorial 63320588, Dudley Timothy Logan (parents named as James Clement Logan and Martha Calhoun), as described in earlier stories; not examined here: https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/63320588/dudley_timothy-logan
stories.note: Lead. The cemetery list gives names and dates only, no relationships, and the scan has uneven errors. The reading of the Logans of the 1850 census as a widow and her sons, and of Dudley as a grandson, is a hypothesis built on ages and neighbors. James C. Logan is added unlinked. The Find a Grave parents are not adopted. Annie Wedgeworth’s parentage is not advanced.

stories.title: The county histories searched, and where the names are not
stories.hook: A record of the county histories and compendiums searched for the maternal surnames in November 2026, with what each gave and what it did not.
body: Biographical compendiums are only as useful as their indexes, and a sweep that finds nothing is worth writing down so the same books are not read again. This note lists the volumes searched by full text for the family surnames in the places they are known, what each yielded and what it did not. The searches were of scanned text, so a name garbled by the scan could have been missed.

Illinois (Livesay, Walker, Carter, Hoke, Flannigan). Six county compendiums were searched. The 1879 History of Washington County, the 1881 History of Marion and Clinton Counties, the 1883 History of Jefferson County, the 1894 Portrait and Biographical Record of Clinton, Washington, Marion and Jefferson Counties, Brinkerhoff’s 1909 History of Marion County and the 1909 Biographical and Reminiscent History of Richland, Clay and Marion Counties all yielded something, and the new facts are in the stories on Evan Carter Livesay, Jackson L. Livesay, Lorenzo M. Livesay, Alfred’s children, the Flannigans and Whites, and the Carters of Lake Township. Wall’s 1909 History of Jefferson County and the 1883 Combined History of Randolph, Monroe and Perry Counties had no Livesay, Hoke or Flannigan of interest. The 1894 volume has only passing Walker entries: a Charles Walker who married a Thompson daughter in Richview Township, and a James Walker among the husbands of a Sanders daughter. Of the books named for this sweep, a volume titled Counties of Clinton, Washington, Bond and Madison could not be found on the Internet Archive under that title.

Indiana (McCormack, Madison County). The 1914 History of Madison County by John L. Forkner in both volumes, the 1897 Historical Sketches and Reminiscences and Hardesty’s 1874 history were searched. None has a McCormack or McCormick family sketch. The only McCormack in the 1914 volumes is McCormack and Sweeney, the Columbus, Indiana, contractors for the courthouse. James T. McCormack’s people are still not found in a county history.

Arkansas (Whitfield, Box, Sevier County). Goodspeed’s Biographical and Historical Memoirs of Western Arkansas (1891) and of Southern Arkansas (1890, both volumes) contain no sketch for Sevier County and no Whitfield or Box of this family, only a Whitfield County in Georgia, a lodge and a Corbell family with a Box mother. A 1910 railway promotion booklet on Sevier and Little River counties has no personal names. Texas (Box, Logan, Wedgworth). The supplemental index of Graveyards of Van Zandt County lists Box burials but no Alonzo or Emma; the 1961 History of Titus County has a W. M. Logan in a Confederate company roll of 1862 and no Dudley Logan, Wedgworth or Box.

Alabama (Logan, Wedgworth). Brewer’s Alabama (1872) and Owen’s History of Alabama and Dictionary of Alabama Biography (1921, four volumes) have no sketch for the Greene, Hale or Tuscaloosa Logans or Wedgworths; the only Wedgworth hits are place names. Snedecor’s Greene County directory for 1855 and 1856, in its 1963 reprint, lists planters Isaac, Willis, Zachary M., Andrew and A. L. Logan and Stephen, Larkin and John M. Wedgworth at New Prospect, which agrees with the settlers’ list used in an earlier story. The two volumes of Alabama Records for Greene County (1934) are scanned too poorly to search. The one useful Alabama volume was the county records book described in the story on the Wedgeworth Cemetery.

Choctaw Nation (Merry, Durant, Clay, Gibbs, Whitfield). Gideon’s Indian Territory (1901), O’Beirne’s Leaders and Leading Men of the Indian Territory (1891), Flickinger’s The Choctaw Freedmen (1914), the Standard History of Oklahoma (1916, volumes 1 to 4) and Thoburn and Wright’s Oklahoma: A History of the State and Its People (1929) were searched. The Merry find is described in the story on Gilbert G. Merry. The Durants in these books are the large Durant family of the Atoka and Bennington country, including a W. A. Durant born in 1866, a son of Sylvester Durant, who is not the William A. Durant of Dawes card 656, born about 1870 to Allington and Mary Durant. No sketch was found for the Clays of Bok Tuklo or for a Fred Gibbs. A Joseph L. Gibbs of Claremore in the 1891 book is from Ohio and is not related by any record. One new name turned up in the Freedmen book: A. J. Whitfield is named in 1914 among the Valliant dealers who helped keep the Oak Hill school on a cash basis. Nothing connects him to Oliver Clinton Whitfield, but he is a McCurtain County Whitfield not yet in the earlier leads.
