stories.title: Two Walkers on the Mount Vernon Circuit, 1832 and 1833
stories.hook: The 1883 history of Jefferson County lists Simeon Walker at Mount Vernon in 1832 and James Walker in 1833. It is one more source for an old question about the Rev. James Walker of Beaucoup, and it does not settle it.
body: The earlier story on whether the Rev. James Walker of Beaucoup was a circuit rider relied on James B. Leaton’s 1883 History of Methodism in Illinois, which says a James Walker was sent to the Mount Vernon Circuit in 1831. Two more county histories list the same circuit and give slightly different years. The 1883 History of Jefferson County prints a list of the Methodist preachers at Mount Vernon from 1825 to 1854 by conference year, which begins in autumn. It reads: 1830–31, John H. Benson; 1832, Simeon Walker; 1833, James Walker; 1834, Warren L. Jenkins. The list is on page 810.

The 1881 History of Marion and Clinton Counties describes a Simeon Walker as “a name that is a household word in southern Illinois,” and says he was sent to the Grand Prairie Mission, which took in Salem, in 1830 and 1831. Its account of the Carlyle Circuit makes a Simeon Walker, “who recently deceased,” preacher in charge in 1833, and its Lake Township chapter lists a Simeon Walker among the early Methodist preachers. These dates fit the earlier story’s account of Simeon Walker Sr., born in Georgia in 1802, who may be the father of Captain Simeon Walker of Beaucoup, a link the earlier story did not draw. They also leave the 1883 list’s James Walker for 1833 at Mount Vernon, two years after Leaton.

None of this joins James Walker of the circuit to James Walker of Beaucoup, who is on record at Beaucoup in the 1820s and 1840s and whose 1850 census entry gives Tennessee, not Georgia. The two county lists only show that the Mount Vernon Circuit’s James Walker is attested in 1831 and 1833 in two sources, and that those sources disagree by two years. They also show how thin the evidence is: nothing printed about either preacher names a home, a wife or a death. The question stays a lead.

stories.note: Lead. The preachers’ lists name no home or family. James Walker of the circuit is not identified with James Walker of Beaucoup, and Simeon Walker Sr. is not in the tree. The two sources differ on the year of James Walker’s service.

stories.title: Floyd Livesay in Lydia’s household, 1860
stories.hook: The 1860 census finds four-year-old Floyd Livesay in the house of Lydia Livesay, a widow of fifty-two, with her five youngest children. In 1870 he is fourteen and living with her son David. His own later censuses do not settle whose son he was.

subject.name: Floyd Hale Livesay as a child

body: For years the Livesay story began with Floyd Hale Livesay as a man in Brazoria County, Texas, and left his parents blank. Two census pages from Washington County, Illinois, now put him as a child inside the family of Robert and Lydia Livesay. In June 1860, in Township 2 South, Range 2 West, the household of Lydia Livesay, 52, born in Tennessee, lists David, 28, Thomas, 24, “Palina,” 20, Daniel, 17 and “Trumbull,” 15, all born in Illinois, and Floyd H., 4, born in Illinois. Robert Livesay died in 1855, and the 1856 release that named his heirs called Nancy P., Daniel M. and Elbert T. minors. The 1860 names are those three: the family sketch gives their middle names as Paulina and Trumbell.

Ten years later, in 1870, Floyd H. Livesay, 14, is enumerated in the household of David Livesay, 40, born in Illinois, with David’s wife Elisabeth, 24, and three small children. David’s wife is too young to be Floyd’s mother, and neither census states a relationship, so the pages place Floyd in the family without saying whose son he was. Lydia was born in 1807 and would have been 48 or 49 when Floyd was born, so he was almost certainly her grandson, not her child. He was therefore a son of one of her sons, but the pages do not say which.

Floyd’s own censuses add a clue. In 1880, at 24, farming in Ashley precinct of Washington County with his wife Alice, he gave both parents as born in Tennessee. In 1900 and 1920 he gave his father’s birthplace as Tennessee, and in 1910 as Illinois; for his mother he gave “unknown” in 1900 and “United States” in 1910 and 1920. A Tennessee-born father would point to one of Robert and Lydia’s older sons, William E., Lorenzo M. or Jackson M., all born in Tennessee before the move to Illinois, and not to David, who was born in Illinois. The one reading of Illinois in 1910 could favor David. None of the older three is in the 1860 household with Floyd. So the candidates remain open.

One fact is worth keeping in view. The Gilead Cemetery stone for Tabitha J., wife of David P. Livesay, gives her death as 14 February 1856, nine days after the 5 February birth date on Floyd’s death certificate (told in “Nine days: Tabitha Livesay’s stone”). If David and Tabitha were his parents, a motherless baby raised in his grandmother’s house and then in his father’s would explain both census pages. The 1880 and 1900 birthplaces make that only one of several readings.

The censuses help with the year of Floyd’s birth too. Age 4 in June 1860 and age 14 in June 1870 both fit a birth in early 1856. They do not fit February 1857, the year on his death certificate, which would make him 3 and 13. The 1900 census also gives February 1856. The tree keeps the death certificate’s date for now because it is the only record that gives the day, but the weight of the censuses is on 1856.

Not proven: no census states a relationship, and no record seen names Floyd’s father or mother. David P. is one candidate for his father; William E., Lorenzo M. or Jackson M. are others, if the Tennessee birthplace Floyd gave in 1880, 1900 and 1920 is right. Floyd is left unlinked in the tree, as the site’s tests require, until a record names a parent.

stories.title: Golden’s postmasters: a father, a daughter and a granddaughter
stories.hook: The Postal Service’s own list of postmasters at Golden, Oklahoma, names Joshua L. Merry in 1916, his daughter Ida in 1945 and her daughter Ouida in 1968.
body: The U.S. Postal Service keeps an online list of postmasters, the Postmaster Finder, and its entry for Golden in McCurtain County, Oklahoma, answers questions the family’s earlier stories left open. For appointments before 1971 the list rests mainly on the National Archives’ Record of Appointment of Postmasters (microfilm publication M841, covering 1832 to 30 September 1971), which the Postal Service names as its primary source. It dates the Golden office to 13 March 1911, with James M. Golden as the first postmaster and General M. Robertson appointed on 20 March 1912. The third name, appointed on 29 February 1916, is Joshua L. Merry.

That is new for Ida’s father. The earlier story about Glover showed him as that town’s first postmaster from 26 June 1901 and could not say when he gave the office up. The Golden list carries him on. He is postmaster from 29 February 1916, replaced by Cicero M. Medcalf on 30 August 1920, back as acting postmaster on 16 January 1922 and postmaster from 25 March 1924, until Mrs. Dosha L. Shane is named acting postmaster on 2 April 1928. In all he ran the office for a little under eleven years, in two stretches. The list gives names and dates and nothing else, so it does not itself say that this Joshua L. Merry is Ida’s father. The full name is the one printed for Glover, an earlier record puts his death in 1932 at Golden, and no other Merry appears in the Golden list, which is why the match is probable and not proven.

Ida’s turn came four years after her husband’s death. Mrs. Ida M. Whitfield is listed as acting postmaster on 31 March 1945 and as postmaster from 24 September 1945. That agrees with her 1993 obituary, as her own story summarizes it, which says she worked first as assistant postmaster and then as postmaster, and with the 1950 census sheet described in an earlier story, which found a widowed postmistress at Golden who fits her.

Ouida followed her. Mrs. Catherine O. Carroll is listed as acting postmaster on 30 June 1968 and as postmaster from 8 January 1969, and the next entry, an officer-in-charge, is dated 28 November 1990. Her May 2007 obituary in the Choctaw Nation’s Biskinik calls her a retired postmaster who served 22 years at the post office in Golden and says she retired in 1990. From 30 June 1968 to 28 November 1990 is twenty-two years and five months, so the twenty-two years in the obituary look like her years in charge of the office, not time spent first as a clerk, which her own story had left as a possibility.

The same dates unsettle another number. Ida’s obituary, as summarized in her story, says she retired at 72. Born on 12 June 1898, Ida turned 70 on 12 June 1968, eighteen days before her daughter’s acting appointment. The list gives the date each postmaster was appointed, not the date the one before left, so Ida may have left a little earlier, but the record leaves no room for two more years in the office. Either the obituary’s age is off, or Ida stayed on in some other post after giving up the office. No record seen says which, and the conflict is left standing.

Added up, a Merry or a Whitfield was in charge of the Golden post office for roughly 56 of its first 79 years: Joshua for about eleven, Ida for about twenty-three and Ouida for about twenty-two. The long stretch between Joshua and Ida, from 1928 to 1945, belonged to Mrs. Shane.

stories.note: The list is dated by appointment, so it shows when each person was named, not how long each stayed. Joshua L. Merry of Golden is identified with Ida’s father, the Glover postmaster and the “J. L. Louis Merry” of the Glover Cemetery stone, by the shared full name and the family’s later records only: probable. Ida’s retirement “at 72” in her 1993 obituary (taken from her earlier story, not re-read here) conflicts with the 30 June 1968 change of acting postmaster, when she had just turned 70. The list names an officer-in-charge only between two postmasters, so later holders of the office are not named here. A Mrs. Loula Merry appears as postmaster at nearby Valliant from 1934; no link to this family has been shown.

stories.title: John Frank Kernell, Bessie’s widower
stories.hook: Bessie Durant Merry’s gravestone says Kernell. A 1942 draft card and the 1950 census show the man behind the name: a Tennessee-born farmer with a Glover address, a widower three weeks after she died.
body: Bessie Durant Merry’s flat marker in the Denison Cemetery at Idabel reads “Wife, Bessie E. Kernell, Nov. 11, 1879, Mar. 22, 1950,” with the line “Mother waits for us in Heaven” cut below. It does not name her husband. Earlier research had only a Find a Grave memorial that calls him John Frank Kernell and dates their marriage to 1907, with no record behind either claim. Two federal records now give a John Frank Kernell of the right place and age.

The first is his draft card from the fourth registration, the call of April 1942 for men born between 28 April 1877 and 16 February 1897. John Frank Kernell registered on 27 April 1942 with McCurtain County Local Board No. 2 at the City Hall in Broken Bow. He gave his residence as Wright City, McCurtain County, and his mailing address as Glover. He was 59, born on 9 March 1883 at “Overton, Tenn.,” and the card does not say whether Overton is a town or a county. He had no telephone, and the person who would always know his address was Porter Kernell of Durant. His work was “farming, self,” at Wright City. He signed with a mark, an X written between his first and last names, and the registrar’s report describes a white man of about six feet and 160 pounds with brown eyes.

The second is the 1950 census. On a sheet of Sulphur Township, enumeration district 45-46, begun on 11 April 1950, the last line, number 30, reads J. F. Kernell, head, white, male, 67, widowed, born in Tennessee. He is alone on the line and the sheet is not marked as continued. Sixty-seven in April 1950 fits a man born on 9 March 1883, and the birthplace matches the card. The same enumeration district, 45-46, holds the Whitfield store near Golden, where a 1997 family sketch says Bessie died, and the census date is twenty days after the date on her stone.

Taken together the two records describe one man, a Tennessee-born farmer whose mail came to Glover in 1942 and who was a widower in the Golden district in 1950. Naming him as Bessie’s husband rests on less: the surname on her stone, the widowed status so soon after her death, and the neighborhood where the Merry family had lived. That is probable, not proven. No marriage record has been found, and the 1907 date is still only the memorial’s claim.

Oklahoma’s state death index supplies an end to the story. It lists a John F. Kernell, male, who died on 4 October 1966 in McCurtain County, the only John F. Kernell in its records, which would make him 83. Like the census, the index gives no parents and no spouse, so it ties the name to the county but not to Bessie. It also lists a Porter A. Kernell who died on 27 June 1951 in Bryan County, where Durant stands. He is probably the Porter Kernell of Durant on John’s 1942 card, but no record seen says how the two were related.

What the records do not explain is the order of her marriages. Bessie married Louis Merry at Lukfata in 1896, and the two were enrolled together on Dawes card 5754 in 1904 and 1905. Louis died in 1932, eighteen years before she did, and a marriage-license clipping in an earlier story has a Joshua L. Merry of Glover licensed to marry a Mrs. Mattie Erwin. When and how the Merry marriage ended, and when Bessie became Mrs. Kernell, are still unknown, and her daughter Ida’s obituary calls her Bessie Durant Merry. The card names one other Kernell, Porter of Durant, without saying how he was related.

Kernell (image 43290879-Oklahoma-217214-0021); National Archives 1950 census website, name search “Kernell” in McCurtain County, examined 4 Nov 2026: https://1950census.archives.gov/iiif/2/1950census%2F43290879-Oklahoma%2F43290879-Oklahoma-217214%2F43290879-Oklahoma-217214-0021.jpg/full/full/0/default.jpg

stories.note: The card and the 1950 census line agree on name, initials, age, birthplace and county and are taken as one man. Probable that he was Bessie’s husband: the evidence is her stone’s surname, his widowed status three weeks after her death and the shared neighborhood; no record states the marriage. The Find a Grave claim of a 1907 marriage is unverified. The registrar’s name and the hair color on the card are not recorded here because the handwriting is hard to read. Porter Kernell’s relationship is unknown. The 1966 death is an index entry (name, date, county only); that it belongs to this man is probable, as he is the only John F. Kernell in the index.

stories.title: What Oklahoma’s death index says about the Whitfields, Boxes and Merrys
stories.hook: The state health department’s free index agrees with most of the family’s death dates, differs by one day for Clint Whitfield, finds two of Tyro Box’s brothers and has no entry for Louis Merry.

subject.name: The Whitfield, Box and Merry families

body: The Oklahoma State Department of Health keeps a free index of the state’s vital records, called OK2Explore. For deaths from 1908 on it gives a name, a date of death, a county and a sex, and nothing else: no parents, no age, no town. The department warns that the index “does contain errors” from misread handwriting and mistaken forms. Used with that in mind, it is a state record against which the dates in the tree, most of which came from gravestones and newspaper notices, can be checked.

Most of them hold. In McCurtain County the index lists Ida M. Whitfield on 28 January 1993, Lewis O. Whitfield on 9 August 2004, Violet Whitfield on 30 July 1962, Catherine Ouida Carroll on 16 March 2007 and Elma Mae Severn on 31 October 2011. Each date matches the one taken from a stone or obituary, and Elma’s entry adds a county where her obituary named none. Annie F. Box (28 December 1959) and Tyro S. Box (5 October 1967) are filed under Choctaw County, which fits the Hugo hospital named in their notices. Flossie James, Tyro’s sister Birdie, is there on 14 November 1979, and an “R B James” on 5 January 1928 matches the date on Rafe James’s stone. Bessie E. Kernell is listed on 22 March 1950 in McCurtain County. That is the date on her gravestone and the date her granddaughter’s 1997 sketch gives for Bessie Merry, so two accounts written separately agree on the day and the county, which helps tie the Kernell on the stone to the Bessie of Dawes card 5754.

Two entries do not behave. The index dates the death of Oliver C. “Clint” Whitfield to 22 March 1941 in McCurtain County, one day after the 21 March on his gravestone and in the tree. A one-day difference could be the stonecutter or the clerk, and the department itself says the index has errors, so the tree keeps the gravestone’s date until a death certificate is seen. The other is a gap. A search of Merry deaths for 1932, and for five years either side, finds only two people who died on the same day, 9 August 1930. There is no Joshua L. or Louis Merry, so the 1 July 1932 on his Glover stone has no state record behind it here. The absence proves nothing by itself; he could be indexed under another spelling or county.

The index also finds relatives the tree had no dates for. An Archie W. Box died on 28 April 1970 in McCurtain County, the only man of that name in the index. He fits Tyro’s brother Archie of Kirk Township, the “Arch Box” in Tyro’s 1967 obituary, so the match is probable. A Claude J. Box died on 19 November 1961 in Oklahoma County, which is far from Valliant, where Claude Joel Box registered for the draft in 1942. The initial and the plausible age fit, but nothing else ties the two, and the date is carried in the tree only as “probably.” Walter, the eldest Box brother, is not in the index at all; the one Walter Box it lists died in 2021.

Two more entries bear on the Whitfield parents. A William F. Whitfield died on 21 July 1944 in McCurtain County. Earlier research found a Find a Grave memorial for a William Franklin Whitfield, 1867 to 1944, said to be Clint’s father, and an earlier story of the 1900 census household in Sevier County, Arkansas, has a W. F. Whitfield born in January 1868. The year and county of the index entry agree with the memorial, but the index names no family, so this is a lead and the parent link stays unmade. An Emma Whitfield died on 30 June 1955, but in Cimarron County in the Panhandle, and a 1950 census sheet there shows an Emma Whitfield, 76, widowed and born in Illinois, whereas the Emma of 1900 was born in Arkansas. These are probably two different women.
src: Oklahoma State Department of Health, Vital Records Division, OK2Explore Vital Records Index, death searches for Whitfield, Merry, Box, James, Kernell, Carroll and Severn, run 4 Nov 2026 through the site’s search service (results give name, date and county of death only): https://ok2explore.health.ok.gov/App/DeathSearch
Oklahoma State Department of Health, OK2Explore, “Search Tips” (index begun with 1908 deaths; “Errors in the Index”), read 4 Nov 2026: https://ok2explore.health.ok.gov/App/DeathSearch

1950 U.S. census, Cimarron County, Oklahoma, ED 13-7 (as the site’s index gives it), line 30, Emma Whitfield, head, 76, widowed, born Illinois (image 43290879-Oklahoma-172362-0014); National Archives 1950 census website, examined 4 Nov 2026: https://1950census.archives.gov/iiif/2/1950census%2F43290879-Oklahoma%2F43290879-Oklahoma-172362%2F43290879-Oklahoma-172362-0014.jpg/full/full/0/default.jpg
stories.note: The index is a transcription made over many years and gives only name, date and county, so every identification here rests on name and place. Probable: the Box brothers (Archie fits the 1950 census and the 1967 obituary; Claude’s county does not fit). Lead only: William F. Whitfield and any link to Clint. The date conflict for Clint Whitfield (22 March in the index, 21 March on the stone) is not resolved. No index entry was found for Louis Merry, Walter Box, Erma Box, Alonzo Box, Emma Box, Raphael James by full name or Eugene Carroll; a missing entry is not evidence of anything. Persons who may be living are not searched or named.

stories.title: The Whitfield children in Oklahoma’s birth index
stories.hook: The state’s birth index lists four of Ida’s children and Violet Box. It backs the dates in the tree, settles a one-day dispute over Violet’s birthday and puts two births in counties no one had named.

subject.name: Ida Whitfield’s children and Violet Box

body: The Oklahoma State Department of Health’s OK2Explore index lists births as well as deaths, again with only a name, a date, a county and a sex. Oklahoma began filing births in 1908, but the department says most birth records were not filed on time until about 1950, so some early entries may be late registrations. Searching it for Clint and Ida Whitfield’s children finds one entry for each of four of them, each matched by name and exact date. The department warns that the index contains errors, and two of these entries need that warning.

Lewis O. Whitfield is listed as born on 24 August 1916 in LeFlore County. The date is the one on his stone and plaque, but the tree has said only “Oklahoma” for his birthplace, and the family’s other records are in McCurtain County, where Elma and Ouida are indexed. No other record seen places the family in LeFlore County in 1916. Elma M. Whitfield is listed on 12 January 1918 in McCurtain County, the date in her obituary, which gave Glover as the place. Ouida is listed as “Cathrine Oudla” Whitfield, born 15 January 1924 in McCurtain County. The date is the one in her obituary. The name is a third spelling: her own obituary prints Ouida, her sister’s obituary prints “Oulda,” and the clerk wrote “Oudla.”

The entry for Omagene is the puzzle. It gives his name, middle initial C and a birth date of 1 January 1922, the date in the tree, but the county is Beaver, in the Oklahoma Panhandle, hundreds of miles from McCurtain County. The tree places his birth at Golden, and his siblings were indexed in McCurtain County in 1918 and 1924. Either the index has a county error, which the department says happens, or the family was in the Panhandle for a time. No record seen decides it, and the birthplace in the tree is left as it was.

Violet Box is listed on 22 September 1920 in McCurtain County. Her gravestone gives 22 September and her 1962 obituary 21 September; the state index sides with the stone. The same index has a Tyro Box born on 26 February 1909 in McCurtain County. That cannot be Violet’s father, who was born in 1888 in Texas, but Tyro and Annie Box had come to the county by 1906 or 1907, and a first son named for his father is plausible. The index names no parents and no other record shows the child, so he is a lead and not a person in the tree. The death index lists no second Tyro Box.

Five other Whitfield births in McCurtain County between 1915 and 1925 are also in the index. A January 2009 Bishinik obituary shows that at least three of them were the children of John Whitfield and Ida Austin Whitfield of Valliant, a different family, as the story “Another Ida Whitfield” relates. They are not Clint and Ida’s children, and the remaining one is not named here because he could be living.

Oklahoma State Department of Health, OK2Explore, “Search Tips” (births filed since 1908; late filing; “Errors in the Index”), read 4 Nov 2026: https://ok2explore.health.ok.gov/App/BirthSearch

Choctaw Nation, Biskinik, May 2007, p. 11, Catherine Ouida Carroll obituary (born 15 January 1924), PDF page examined 4 Nov 2026: https://www.choctawnation.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/may-2007-biskinik.pdf#page=11
stories.note: Each indexed birth is matched to a person by name, middle initial and the exact date already in the tree, which is probable and not proof of parentage, since the index names no parents. The LeFlore County (Lewis) and Beaver County (Omagene) entries conflict with or add to the tree and are unexplained; either could be an indexing error. The 1909 Tyro Box is a lead only. The other Whitfield births in the index belong, at least in part, to the John Whitfield family of Valliant; the one not matched by an obituary is not named.

stories.title: The Livesay Store at the Pearland crossroads
stories.hook: Floyd and Alice Livesay’s grocery, which earlier records show only as a directory line, was by local accounts a two-story building at the corner where Pearland’s two highways cross.
body: Floyd Livesay appears in the records already cited as a groceryman, in the 1914 state directory and on his 1932 death certificate. The Pearland Historical Society’s newsletters say more about the business. The July 2013 issue reports that Wayne Livesay died on 18 April 2013 at Cushing, Texas, and calls the Livesays one of Pearland’s pioneer families. It says Mr. and Mrs. Floyd Livesay came in the early 1900s, “opening up a livery stable and the historic Livesay Store in 1906,” and that they are buried in the Old Settlers Cemetery. The issue also prints a photograph captioned “Livesay Store approx. 1906 at corner of Main and Broadway.” The notice calls Floyd and Alice Wayne’s grandparents. In this tree they are his great-grandparents: Wayne’s father was Lester Jr., Lester Jr.’s father was Lester Sr., and Lester Sr. was Floyd and Alice’s son. That line rests on the obituaries and certificates in the earlier stories, so the notice’s “grandparents” is taken as a slip of one generation.

The Society’s August 2022 issue says where the building stood. In a piece on the Pearland Drugstore it names Floyd Hale Livesay and his wife, Alice Walker Livesay, as the owners of the Livesay General Grocery Store, “believed to have been built about 1906,” on the southeast corner of State Highway 35 (Main Street) and FM 518 (Broadway). A service station stood on the corner until it was demolished in June 2021, and a coffee shop is there now. The April 2022 and April 2026 issues name the same corner. A reminiscence of Pearland in 1940, written by the Society’s president and printed in January 2017, describes the town center at those crossroads: the drugstore on one corner, a café and beer joint on another and, on a third, a two-story building “which had been the ‘Livesay’ store.” By the author’s memory of 1940, eight years after Floyd’s death, it was no longer the store.

The upper floor had other tenants. The August 2022 issue says the second floor was also a boarding house, and the April 2022 and August 2022 issues say the town physician, Dr. William E. Long, began his practice upstairs. The Society’s own dates for him disagree. He came to Pearland in 1911 according to the August 2022 and April 2026 issues, and in 1921 according to the April 2022 issue, which the August issue calls a typo. He died in 1941 according to April 2022 and in 1944 according to April 2026. The July 2008 issue reprints an early teacher’s memoir saying that when the county school closed, the lessons were divided between the school building and the “Livesay Store building.” The passage gives no date and the teacher is not named in the part read. On these accounts the building served in turn as store, boarding house, doctor’s office and, at least once, schoolroom.

What this adds is a picture of the business. The 1914 directory shows Floyd as a retail grocer; the newsletters place him on the best corner in town, in a building he owned, with a livery stable in the family’s early years. These are local-history statements. None of the issues cites a deed, a tax roll or an advertisement, and the 1906 date is given as the Society’s belief, so it is a lead for a Brazoria County deed search and not a fact. The newsletters also supply two small details for the next generation. Wayne is called a Pearland High School graduate of 1958, which fits his birth in 1940, and the issues of April 2024 and January 2025 list a Carolyn Livesay in the class of 1955 and in a varsity volleyball photograph. The 1950 school annual has a Carolyn Livesay in the seventh grade, which fits the class of 1955, and the 2014 notice spells the name Carylon; she is probably Wayne’s sister, who died in 2014.
quotes: “opening up a livery stable and the historic Livesay Store in 1906” (Pearland Historical Society Newsletter, July 2013)

stories.note: Probable. The newsletters are local history written decades later and cite no sources; their claims about 1906, the livery stable and the ownership of the building are unverified, and the 1914 directory (earlier story) is the only contemporary record of Floyd’s grocery. The Society’s dates for Dr. Long conflict between issues (arrival 1911 or 1921, death 1941 or 1944) and are not reconciled. The July 2013 notice calls Floyd and Alice Wayne’s grandparents; they were his great-grandparents in this tree. The 1906 photograph printed in the July 2013 issue is not reproduced, because its rights are not cleared. Which Livesay boy or girl lived above or beside the store is not stated anywhere.

stories.title: A Melvin Livesay in Pearland, 1950
stories.hook: The 1950 census finds an Illinois-born carpenter named Melvin T. Livesay a few sheets from Lester Jr.’s farm. He may be the Melvin of the First World War draft list, and so Lester Sr.’s brother, but nothing yet says so.

subject.name: Melvin T. Livesay
subject.rel: Possible brother of a maternal ancestor (unproven)

body: An earlier story on the First World War draft lists found a Melvin Livesay, born on 15 October 1891 at Beaucoup, Illinois, who worked in the Texas oil fields and was single. He might have been a son of Floyd and Alice, who left Beaucoup for Pearland in the 1890s, but the list names no parents and no Melvin appears in the stories about the 1900 household. The 1950 census adds a Melvin who lived in Pearland itself.

In enumeration district 20-55 of Brazoria County, the same district as Lester Jr.’s farm household of 3 May 1950, sheet 28 ends with dwelling 256: Livesay, Melvin T., head, white, male, 60, married, born in Illinois. He worked 24 hours in the week before the census as a carpenter in construction and was in business for himself. The household is marked as continued, and line 1 of the next sheet reads Daisy E., wife, 47, married, born in Mississippi. They were the only two people in the dwelling.

The ages do not agree cleanly. Sixty in April 1950 points to a birth about 1889 or 1890, while the draft list gives October 1891, which would make him 58. A gap of a year or two is common in these records, and the family’s own dates for Lester Sr. have wandered between 1894 and 1895 in the same way. Birth in Illinois fits, only two pages of the Brazoria County index carry the surname, and a carpenter in 1950 could have been an oil-field hand in 1918. Those points make the match with the draft-list Melvin reasonable but not secure.

Whether either Melvin belongs to Floyd and Alice is the real question, and the census does not answer it. The Beaucoup township had many Livesay households in the 1850s and later, as the Illinois stories show, so an Illinois-born Melvin Livesay in Texas could come from another branch of the name. A son born in October 1891 would have been eight years old in the 1900 census household in Brazoria County and should be listed in it, and the 1910 census would show him at about nineteen. Neither household list has been read for this story. Until one is, Melvin and Daisy stay out of the tree.

Livesay, head, 60, born Illinois, carpenter (image 43290879-Texas-047302-0029); National Archives 1950 census website, examined 4 Nov 2026: https://1950census.archives.gov/iiif/2/1950census%2F43290879-Texas%2F43290879-Texas-047302%2F43290879-Texas-047302-0029.jpg/full/full/0/default.jpg

Livesay, wife, 47, born Mississippi (image 43290879-Texas-047302-0030); examined 4 Nov 2026: https://1950census.archives.gov/iiif/2/1950census%2F43290879-Texas%2F43290879-Texas-047302%2F43290879-Texas-047302-0030.jpg/full/full/0/default.jpg

His identity with the Melvin Livesay of the draft list rests on the first name, Illinois birth and Texas residence, with a two-year age gap. Neither Melvin nor Daisy is added to the tree. Other Livesay households in Houston in the 1950 index (an Earl W., born in Texas about 1905, among them) were looked at only far enough to see that nothing ties them to Floyd and Alice.

stories.title: Another Ida Whitfield: John and Ida Austin Whitfield of Valliant
stories.hook: A 1942 draft card names an Ida Whitfield of Valliant as a contact. A Choctaw obituary and two state indexes show she was Ida Austin, wife of John Whitfield, and not Ida Merry Whitfield of Golden.

subject.name: John and Ida Austin Whitfield
subject.rel: A different Whitfield family in McCurtain County

body: The story of other Whitfields in McCurtain County turned up John Grover Whitfield on the 1942 draft rolls. His card, serial U-21, gives his residence as Valliant and his age as 53. He was born on 6 July 1888 in “Sever Co.,” Arkansas, which is Sevier County, and he farmed for himself at Valliant. For the person who would always know his address he wrote Ida Whitfield, Valliant. In a county where Ida Merry Whitfield lived, a reader could easily take that Ida for Clint’s widow. She was not.

A Choctaw obituary names her. The January 2009 issue of the Choctaw Nation’s newspaper, the Bishinik, prints a notice for Dell Marie Whitfield Bates, who died on 25 November 2008 at Oak Ridge Manor in Durant. She was born on 11 September 1919 near Valliant, the notice says, “daughter of Choctaw original enrollee Ida Austin and John Whitfield.” She attended Wheelock Academy and the Valliant schools, worked for a utility company in California and came home to Oklahoma in the 1980s. Among the relatives who died before her it lists two brothers, Sam and Guy Whitfield, and three sisters, one of them Betty Whitfield Vedder. The other survivors it names are not listed here.

The state’s vital-records indexes agree with the obituary. The death index lists Dell Marie Bates, female, dying on 25 November 2008 in Bryan County, where Durant stands. The birth index lists Whitfield births in McCurtain County on 23 May 1915 (Betty F.), 11 September 1919 (Dell Marie), 28 September 1921 (Guy), 27 February 1922 (a boy named Grover McKinley) and 13 March 1925 (Samuel). The day of Dell Marie’s birth matches the obituary exactly, and the first names of three of the others match the brother and sister it names. Those are the five Whitfield births in the county between 1915 and 1925 that the story of Ida Merry’s children set aside, and at least three belong to this family.

The card and the obituary together make it probable that the Ida Whitfield of Valliant was Ida Austin, John’s wife. The match rests on the name, the place and the date, since no record seen places the card’s contact and the obituary’s mother together in one line. It settles one thing and leaves another open. Ida Merry’s children were not the Whitfield children born around Valliant, and the Ida on the 1942 card does not belong in her story. Whether John Grover Whitfield, born in Sevier County in 1888, was a brother or cousin of Clint, born in Sevier County in 1893, is not answered. He was too old to be the son of W. F. and Emma, who married about four years later, but an earlier marriage of W. F. or a shared grandparent is possible, and no record names either. The obituary does not mention a Clint or an Ida Merry.
quotes: “daughter of Choctaw original enrollee Ida Austin and John Whitfield” (Bishinik, January 2009)

stories.note: Probable. The link between the 1942 card’s contact and the obituary’s mother rests on the name Ida Whitfield, the place and the shared husband’s name; neither record states the other. The birth-index match is by name and date, and the index gives no parents. The obituary’s surviving relatives and the two other named sisters are not listed, because some may be living. No relationship to Clint Whitfield is established or ruled out.

stories.title: Elma Severn in the 1950 census: a schoolteacher in McCurtain County
stories.hook: The census taker of April 1950 found Ida’s elder daughter teaching elementary school in McCurtain County, with her husband working on a pipeline.
body: Elma Severn’s December 2011 obituary says she worked thirty years as a teacher, coach and principal in Oklahoma and New Mexico schools, but it gives no years. The 1950 census supplies one. In McCurtain County, enumeration district 45-18, on a sheet whose header, as read, is dated at the end of March 1950, dwelling 7 holds Mark Severn Jr., head, and his wife Elma. She is recorded as 32, married and born in Oklahoma, and as an elementary school teacher who had worked 35 hours in the week before the census. A child recorded as the couple’s son is on the line below her.

Mark Jr. is listed as 30, born in Oklahoma, and as working in pipeline construction. His age is two years short of the 1918 birth year on his 1941 Army enlistment record, cited in Elma’s own story. Her age agrees with her January 1918 birth, and the pair match the couple on every other point: the names, the county, her trade and the husband’s Oklahoma birth. That makes the identification probable, though the census does not say that Elma was the former Elma Whitfield. The township name is written in a hand that is hard to read, and the sheet does not locate the dwelling more closely than the district.

The entry shows Elma at work in the schools of McCurtain County, the county where she was born, in the spring when her brother Lewis kept a general store near Golden and her mother was the Golden postmistress. Her own record says only that she graduated from Southeastern State Teachers College and later taught in New Mexico. The census gives no school name, so where in the county she taught is not known.
The child on the sheet may be living and is not named here.
src: 1950 U.S. census, McCurtain County, Oklahoma, ED 45-18, sheet 1, dwelling 7, lines 28–30 (Mark Severn Jr., head, 30, pipeline construction; Elma, wife, 32, elementary school teacher), image 43290879-Oklahoma-217186-0002; National Archives 1950 census website, examined 4 Nov 2026: https://1950census.archives.gov/iiif/2/1950census%2F43290879-Oklahoma%2F43290879-Oklahoma-217186%2F43290879-Oklahoma-217186-0002.jpg/full/full/0/default.jpg

stories.note: Probable: name, county, Elma’s age and trade, and Mark’s Oklahoma birth agree with the earlier record of the couple; Mark’s age (30) does not agree with the 1918 birth on his enlistment card. The township name and the child’s age are hard to read on the scan. The census page is not reproduced because it names other households, some possibly living.

stories.title: Clinton, Clam O. and Oliver C.: one Whitfield in four censuses
stories.hook: A boy called Clinton in 1900, “Clam O.” in 1910 and Oliver C. in 1920 and 1930 turns up with the same birthplace, the same age and, in 1910 and 1930, the same parents’ birthplaces.
body: The story of the 1900 Sevier County household (“Clinton Whitfield in Sevier County, Arkansas, 1900”) could say only that a Clinton Whitfield, 7, born in July 1893 in Arkansas, lived with a W. F. Whitfield, born in Mississippi, and Emma, born in Arkansas. The schedule gives no second name, so it could not be tied to the Oliver Clinton Whitfield who lived at Glover and Golden in McCurtain County, Oklahoma. Three later censuses now close most of that gap.

In 1910 the household of William F. Whitfield, 42, born in Mississippi, with his wife Emma, 35, born in Arkansas, is in Township 6 of McCurtain County, Oklahoma (sheet 9A). It includes a son indexed as “Clam O.,” 16, born in Arkansas, and the index reads the handwriting as such. The children are William G., 15, Rhoda W., 13, Fannie J., 10, Lula B., 9, Ben L., 6, Jeff Davis, 4 and Ola M., 2, all born in Arkansas. The names match the 1900 household in part: Willie G., Robbie W. and Fannie I. appear there at 5, 3 and 2. The ages and the sex of one child differ between the two schedules, which is not unusual for census-takers, and the 1910 enumerator gave William F.’s own parents as both born in Mississippi.

In 1920 Oliver C. Whitfield, 26, born in Arkansas, heads a household in McCurtain County with his wife Ida M., 21, born in Oklahoma, a son, Oliver L., 3 years and 4 months, and a daughter, Elma, 2. The ages fit Ida May Merry, born in June 1898, and the children later known as Lewis and Elma. In 1930, at Sulphur, O. C. Whitfield, 36, born in Arkansas, heads a household with Ida, 32, and four children whose indexed names and ages fit Lewis, Elma, Omagene and Ouida. This time the enumerator recorded his own father as born in Mississippi and his mother in Arkansas, the same birthplaces as William F. and Emma in 1910. The 1920 schedule says only “United States” for both parents.

Taken together, the censuses join a Clinton born in July 1893 in Arkansas to the Oliver C. who married Ida Merry, and give him the same parents’ birthplaces as W. F. and Emma in 1910. What still lacks is a record that names his parents in words, such as a death certificate or a marriage return. An Oklahoma death certificate was not found, and the first name W. H. in the 1900 index against William F. in 1910 is not settled. The tree therefore keeps Oliver unlinked to parents, and W. F. and Emma stand as probable parents in this story only.

No record seen names W. F. and Emma as his parents in words, and the tests of the site keep Oliver unlinked until one does. The indexes read the 1910 given name as “Clam”; the page itself was not examined here.

stories.title: Emma Box and Emily Wilkerson: two Texas births and two Mississippi marriages
stories.hook: The 1900 census calls her Emma. Two Texas birth entries for her children name their mother as Emily Wilkerson, and two Mississippi marriage entries join an A. F. Box to an Emily Wilkerson.
body: Emma Box, the mother of Tyro Box, has long been given the maiden name Wilkerson only on the word of a collaborative tree and a family note on a Find a Grave memorial that reads “Emillie (Wilkerson).” Neither is a record, and the 1900 census names her only as Emma, 40, born in Mississippi, wife of Alonzo Box in Van Zandt County, Texas. Two Texas birth entries now supply an independent source for the name.

The Texas births and christenings index lists Claude Joel Box, born 26 August 1891 at Rockwall, with a father Alonza Box and a mother Emily Wilkerson, and Flossie Bell Box, born 4 August 1894 at Rockwall, with a father Lonzo Box and the same mother. These are the Claudy J. and Flossie B. of the 1900 household. Both census ages run a year ahead of the birth dates (9 and 6 in June 1900, where the births would make them 8 and 5), while the ages of Walter, Tyro and Archie in the same household fit their dates, so the dates are not perfectly aligned. The names, the shared parents and the county, where Tyro was also born, carry the identification.

The Mississippi marriage index has two entries for an A. F. Box and an Emily Wilkerson in Benton County, Mississippi, dated 1 January 1876 and 3 January 1877. They may be one marriage entered twice, as a license and a return, or two index lines; the 1900 census says Alonzo and Emma had been married 23 years, which points to 1877. The index gives A. F., not Alonzo, and no ages or parents. Emma’s birth in Mississippi fits a marriage there, and Alonzo’s Arkansas birth does not rule one out. A collaborative tree attaches to this man a different Alonzo F. Box, born 1853 in Tennessee in an 1860 census, which cannot be the Alonzo born in December 1850 in Arkansas of the 1900 schedule, so that tree may have joined two men.

The tree keeps the name Emma Box, as the census and the family called her. Her maiden name is probably Wilkerson, with Emily as the fuller form. Her parents are still unknown. A death certificate for Alonzo, who appears in the Texas death index as “Bud Box,” or for Emma would be the next document to find.
src: Texas, Births and Christenings, 1840 to 1981, Claude Joel Box, 26 Aug 1891, Rockwall (indexed record viewed in a signed-in FamilySearch session by the site’s owner, 3 to 4 Nov 2026; page capture kept privately): https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VRS1-W1C

stories.title: Carl and Beulah Phillips, from Nacogdoches to Houston
stories.hook: A 1920 census page, a young son’s death record and Beulah’s own Social Security application put Barbara’s parents in Montgomery County and then Houston, and name Beulah’s parents.
body: Barbara Phillips Livesay’s 1995 obituary names her parents as Carl C. and Beulah Turner Phillips. Records opened on 4 November 2026 now give them dates and places, and tie them to Barbara and to each other.

Carl’s World War I draft registration, filed in Nacogdoches County, gives his name as Carl Cherry Phillips, born 17 December 1895 at what the index reads as Jacksonville, Mississippi. An index entry for “C. Phillips” and Beulah Turner puts a marriage in Nacogdoches County on 15 February 1918, and Barbara was born there on 7 April 1918. The 1920 census finds the household in Justice Precinct 8 of Montgomery County, Texas: Carl Phillips, 24, born in Mississippi; a wife aged 19 born in Texas, indexed as “Eula”; and a daughter, Barbara, aged 1 year 8 months. “Eula” is probably a misreading of Beulah, since her age and birthplace fit, but the page image has not been read.

The family later lived in Houston. A Texas death record for a two-year-old, Randell Phillips (born 24 September 1932, died 13 March 1935), names his father as C. C. Phillips and his mother as Beulah Turner. Barbara’s obituary lists a brother Randall among those who died before her. A search summary of the 1950 census at Houston lists Carl C. and Beulah B. Phillips with sons R. Jay and Ralph, and the obituary names an R. Jay as another brother.

Carl died on 28 April 1960 in Houston. His Texas death certificate gives his birth as 17 December 1895 in Mississippi and his parents as John Phillips and Blanche, with no surname shown for her. The Find a Grave index places him in Woodlawn Cemetery, Houston, and the same cemetery is indexed for Beulah, who died in Houston on 26 February 1993. Beulah’s Social Security application, made in November 1942, gives her birth as 5 February 1900 at Nacogdoches and her parents as Tom N. Turner and Emory A. Stacy. Those parents have a story of their own.

Carl’s own parents remain a lead. A FamilySearch tree profile names a John Phillips, said to have died in 1897, and a Blanche whose parentage and marriages it mixes together, with no source for the link to Carl. It is not used here. A census page for Carl as a boy, in 1900 or 1910, has not been found.

stories.title: Thomas Turner and Emma Stacy of Nacogdoches
stories.hook: Beulah Phillips’s Social Security application names her parents, and an 1893 marriage and two census pages follow them from Nacogdoches County’s east side to a household of seven children.

subject.name: Thomas N. Turner and Emma Stacy Turner

body: Beulah Turner Phillips’s Social Security application of November 1942 gives her parents as Tom N. Turner and Emory A. Stacy. Nacogdoches County’s marriage records have T. N. Turner and Emma Stacy marrying on 17 September 1893, which is the first record found that names the pair together.

The 1900 census finds them in Justice Precinct 1 of Nacogdoches County, the part east of the railroad outside the town. The head is indexed as Thos W. Turner, 49, born in October 1851 in Tennessee and married seven years. His wife is Emma A., 28, born in Louisiana. They have three children: a daughter of four, a son indexed as Doytre, aged 2, and a newborn daughter indexed as Beaulah B. The index gives Beulah’s age as zero days. Census day was 1 June 1900, so that does not fit a birth on 5 February, and either the index or the date on the page is off.

By 1910 the household was in Nacogdoches itself, enumeration district 92. The head is indexed as T. M. Turner, 55, born in Pennsylvania, with Emma, 34, born in Louisiana, and seven children: Verra, 13; Datro, 12; Beulah, 10; Thelma, 8; Opal, 5; Harval, 3; and Ivey, an infant. The records disagree on the father’s middle initial (W, M and N), his birthplace (Tennessee in 1900, Pennsylvania in 1910) and Emma’s age, which implies a birth near 1872 in one and 1876 in the other. The wife’s Louisiana birth, the children’s names and the Nacogdoches address hold steady.

Still to find are Thomas’s birthplace and parents, Emma Stacy’s parents, with her Louisiana birth the only clue, and the dates and burial places of both. A FamilySearch tree gives 1916 and 1964 deaths for them, but no record was seen behind those dates, so they are not used here.

stories.title: Mrs. Elizabeth Walker, ninety, of Beaucoup
stories.hook: A line in an East St. Louis paper in December 1919 shows the widow of Beaucoup’s Mexican War lieutenant at ninety, and the county’s own marriage table settles a date that had looked wrong.

subject.name: Elizabeth Walker
subject.rel: Beaucoup neighbor of the Walkers (kinship unproven)

body: The East St. Louis Daily Journal of 26 December 1919 carried a column of “Local Brevities” on page 6. One item says that J. E. Walker, a desk clerk at police headquarters, had come back from a two-day visit with his mother, Mrs. Elizabeth Walker, of Beaucoup, Illinois. Mrs. Walker, it adds, “observed her 90th birthday several months ago” and was in the best of health despite her age. The item sits between a boxing report and a note on the death of a church housekeeper, and the printed page agrees with the machine-read text at every word quoted here.

Three other records fit it closely. The Beaucoup Cemetery transcription lists Rev. G. W. Walker, 1826 to 20 October 1902, with Elizabeth, “wife of Rev. G. W.,” 1829 to 1920; a ninetieth birthday in 1919 points to 1829. The Washington County death index lists an Elizabeth Walker, female, white, certificate 4848, on 11 February 1920 in Beaucoup Township, less than seven weeks after the newspaper item. And the Nashville Journal notice of Rev. George Walker’s death, printed about October 1902 and transcribed on Genealogy Trails, names three surviving children: Mrs. A. B. Stephens, D. A. Walker and J. E. Walker. The same East St. Louis paper supplies a first name. Its death notice of 8 April 1919, told in the story of Cora Stephens’s death notice, lists among the survivors of Mrs. Cora A. Stephens “an aged mother, Mrs. Betsy Walker,” a sister, Miss Dora, of Beaucoup, and a brother, “James E. Walker of East St. Louis.” Betsy was a common nickname for Elizabeth, and Cora’s husband was A. B. Stephens, the initials of the 1902 notice’s “Mrs. A. B. Stephens,” so the two notices appear to name the same family: the J. E. of 1902 and 1919 is James E., and Mrs. Elizabeth Walker of 1919 is George’s widow. The Beaucoup Cemetery transcription also lists a James E. Walker, 1862 to 1946; he is taken to be the same man on name and place, which is probable and not proven.

The same table settles a date. A misread of the table would give the marriage of George W. Walker and Elizabeth Walker as 23 October 1849, which would sit badly with the birth of their daughter Frances on 19 September 1849 and with the 1902 notice’s “December.” In the register transcription, each marriage is one row of a table: groom, bride, date. The row for Walker, George W., and Elizabeth Walker reads 21 December 1848. The 23 October 1849 date belongs to the row just above it, Ernst H. A. F. Walker and Justine W. H. Grefe. A December 1848 wedding agrees with the notice’s month (its printed year, 1828, is a slip for 1848) and puts Frances’s birth nine months later. The register names the bride only as Elizabeth Walker, so whether Walker was her maiden name or her married one is not known.

The stones also give the couple’s children. Frances C. E. Walker, 19 September 1849 to 18 February 1874, is described as “dau of Rev. G. W. & E.” and “wife of Chas. M. Livesay,” which is how a Beaucoup Walker came to marry a Livesay; a second daughter, Eudora B. A., lived from 7 July 1852 to 24 November 1854. The same death index page lists William P. Walker’s death at Beaucoup Township on 5/20/1919, a day after the 19 May 1919 recorded for him in the tree, and Abigail Walker’s at Richview on 1/28/1923; an index may give a registration date, so the one-day difference is noted, not changed.

None of this says how George W. Walker was related to Rev. James Walker, to Simeon, or to William P. Walker, who lived a few doors away in 1860 according to the earlier research. The 1919 item adds a fact about Elizabeth and her son and corrects a date; it adds no parent. George, Elizabeth, Frances, Cora, Dora and James E. are therefore in the tree as neighbors and in-laws of the Beaucoup Walkers and Livesays, and not as links in Sloan’s line.

E. Walker, whom the April 1919 notice names as James E.; probable, not proven, because the 1919 items do not name her husband. The marriage date of 21 December 1848 is read from the register transcription’s table row; the 23 October 1849 date belongs to the row above it, and the Lieutenant George W. Walker story carries the corrected date. The cemetery and notice texts are transcriptions, not the stones or the paper. Kinship to Rev. James Walker’s family is unresolved and nothing here links these people to Sloan’s line.

stories.title: Seven Livesay brothers at East St. Louis, July 1916
stories.hook: A front-page notice in July 1916 gathers seven Livesay brothers “formerly of Washington county, Illinois,” and the first one named may be a man the Beaucoup stones already know.

subject.name: Charles M. Livesay
subject.rel: Possible Livesay kin of the Beaucoup Walkers

body: On 31 July 1916 the Daily Journal of East St. Louis, Illinois, printed on its front page a notice headed “Livesay Family Annual Reunion.” It describes the reunion of “the Livesay brothers, formerly of Washington county, Illinois,” and their families, held through the week beginning Sunday, 23 July, at the home of Mr. and Mrs. L. C. Livesay on North Forty-fifth Street. The brothers named are C. M. Livesay of Purdy, Missouri; L. C. Livesay of East St. Louis; P. B. Livesay of Kansas City, Missouri; A. R. Livesay of Evansville, Indiana; R. C. Livesay of Moline, Illinois; F. G. Livesay of Milwaukee; and L. G. Livesay of Louisville, Kentucky.

The paper says the seven “had not previously all been together for a period of ten years,” and spent most of the week on boyhood memories. It lists the brothers’ daughters and in-laws as well. C. M. Livesay is given daughters at Iuka, Carbondale, Richview and Purdy, and the Richview daughter shows that the family still had ties to Washington County. Between them the seven lived in seven different places, from Moline and Milwaukee to Louisville, so by 1916 the sons of one county had scattered across five states.

The notice does not name their father, their mother or the township they grew up in. The only link to the tree is a possible one. The Beaucoup Cemetery transcription records Frances C. E. Walker as wife of Chas. M. Livesay, who died on 18 February 1874, and the county’s marriage register lists Charles M. Livesay marrying Theresa E. Tate on 17 May 1877. A Charles M. Livesay of Washington County was a widower in 1874 and a remarried man by 1877, and he could be the C. M. of 1916, but nothing in the notice says so. The Charles P. Livesay of Jefferson County who is already in the tree (1865 to 1915) is a different man, with another middle initial, and died the year before the reunion.

Floyd Hale Livesay, born in Illinois in 1857 and dead at Houston in 1932, is not among the seven: by initials he would be F. H., and the printed notice reads F. G. for the Milwaukee brother. Nothing in it ties him to this family either way, and his father is still unproven. The notice is a lead worth following: an obituary of one of the brothers, or the 1880 household that held them as boys, would settle which Washington County Livesay family they belonged to.

Livesay of Purdy, Missouri, with the Charles M. Livesay who married Frances C. E. Walker and Theresa E. Tate rests on the shared name and county alone. OCR misreads in the machine text (Ira Cordon for Ira Gordon, P. R. for P. B.) were corrected from the page image; the first names behind the initials are not given. Nothing here links these brothers to Floyd Hale Livesay or to Robert Livesay’s line.

stories.title: Cora Stephens’s death notice, April 1919
stories.hook: A death notice in April 1919 names an aged mother, a sister at Beaucoup and a brother in East St. Louis, and puts first names to the survivors listed in 1902.

subject.name: Cora A. Walker Stephens
subject.rel: Daughter of Rev. George W. and Elizabeth Walker (kinship to the tree unproven)

body: On Tuesday, 8 April 1919, the East St. Louis Daily Journal printed its “Death’s Calendar” on page 7. Under the heading “Stephens” it says that Mrs. Cora A. Stephens “entered into eternal rest” on Monday at 7:10 p.m. at the Deaconess Hospital after a week’s illness. She was the wife of A. B. Stephens and the mother of a married daughter at St. Louis, two children at East St. Louis, and a son “with the 124th Field Artillery in France,” five months after the Armistice. The funeral was to leave her home on Wednesday afternoon for Mt. Hope Cemetery. By the weekday, Monday was 7 April 1919.

The list of survivors is the part that matters here. Besides her husband and children, the notice says she “also leaves an aged mother, Mrs. Betsy Walker, sister, Miss Dora of Beaucoup, Ill., and brother, James E. Walker of East St. Louis.” The Nashville Journal notice of Rev. George Walker’s death in October 1902, as transcribed, had named three surviving children: Mrs. A. B. Stephens, D. A. and J. E. Walker. Mrs. A. B. Stephens is now Cora, and J. E. is James E., who by 1919 was working in East St. Louis. The paper’s later item of 26 December 1919, told in the story of Mrs. Elizabeth Walker, ninety, of Beaucoup, calls the mother Mrs. Elizabeth Walker of Beaucoup and says she was ninety.

The notice also bears on the 1902 list. It names a sister, Dora, who still lived at Beaucoup, and the 1902 notice names a “D. A. Walker” without saying whether this was a man or a woman. Dora A. would fit, and then the three children of 1902 would be Cora, Dora and James E., all accounted for in 1919. But nothing printed gives Dora’s middle name, and a brother D. A. who died before 1919 would fit the two notices equally well, so the identification is a lead and Dora is entered under her first name only.

The notice adds little else. It gives no birth year, no maiden name and no marriage date for Cora, and no record read here shows when she married A. B. Stephens or where she grew up, though her mother lived at Beaucoup. Her children are not added to the tree: the notice names two of them only by first name and one only by initials. What it does show is how the Beaucoup Walker household of Elizabeth and George W. Walker had spread by 1919: a daughter married in East St. Louis, a son working there, and a daughter at Beaucoup, where the December 1919 item places the mother.

stories.title: Livesay Carter and the christening of New Nashville
stories.hook: The county seat of Washington County, Illinois, got its name from two Tennesseeans on its board of commissioners, and one of them was the Livesay Carter whose given name has puzzled the Livesay story.

subject.name: Livesay Carter
subject.rel: Carter kinsman of the Livesays (link unproven)

body: The 1879 History of Washington County, Illinois, tells the founding of Nashville on page 43. The proprietors, Robert Middleton and G. Brown, laid out the town on 8 June 1830 and filed the plat with the county commissioners, and “David White, Joseph Whittenberg and Livesay Carter were the commissioners.” The history adds that Carter and Whittenberg, being Tennesseeans, “reverenced everything relating to that state,” and so, with the proprietors’ permission, “christened the town ‘New Nashville.’” The “New” was soon dropped. An earlier chapter (page 24) says the commissioners declared the town the permanent seat of justice in March 1831.

The same book supplies more on the man. Its list of county boards (page 25) gives the eighth board as David White and Joseph Whittenburg, re-elected in 1828, “and Livesay Carter, elected in 1828.” On page 19 it says that in 1830 Livesay Carter built a tread sawmill two miles east of where Nashville now stands, and that the mill sawed the lumber for the first buildings in the town. On page 43 it names him with L. D. Livesay among the first settlers of Nashville precinct, who settled “from 1818 to 1833,” and on page 45 it lists him among the seventeen men raised in the first year of Washington Lodge. The history gives L. D. Livesay only by initials; the Lorenzo Dow Livesay in the tree is a possible match and no more.

A newspaper column tells the story again with more of its troubles. “Looking Back,” written by Charles Baldwin of Nashville for the Centralia (Illinois) Sentinel and transcribed on Genealogy Trails without dates, recounts how the county seat was moved from Covington to a short-lived Georgetown, how Beaucoup objected, and how a compromise in 1827 put the seat where Nashville now stands. The new site was government land, and the column asks where “the hundred dollars” to buy it was to come from: the commissioners, David White, Livesay Carter and Joseph Whittenberg, “spent three years” on the question and raised nothing, until two promoters from St. Clair County put up the cash in 1830. Because Carter and Whittenberg “came from near Nashville, Tennessee,” the column says, they voted for the name New Nashville.

The column follows the 1879 history in outline, including March 1831 and the Tennessee reason for the name, and gives no sources of its own, so it is a retelling and not a second witness. What it adds is the slow business of raising the money, and its date and sources are unknown. What the history alone proves is Livesay Carter’s place on the board from 1828, his hand in naming the town, and his mill. His son Dr. William D. Carter later practiced in Nashville, and his given name, together with the family sketch quoted in the earlier story, which calls him and Carter Livesay cousins named for each other’s families, is why the Carters sit beside the Livesays in this archive. None of it links him to the Livesay line, and he stays unlinked.

The column’s sources are not given.

stories.title: Livesay or Lewsey? Company F of the 44th Illinois, June 1862
stories.hook: A Chicago paper printed an F. M. Livesay of Ashley in Dr. William D. Carter’s regiment; the state’s roster spells him Lewsey, and the veterans’ list says he died of wounds in February 1863.

subject.name: Francis M. Lewsey (Livesay?)
subject.rel: Washington County soldier; kinship to the Livesays unproven

body: On 19 July 1862 the Chicago Daily Tribune printed, on page 2 under the heading “Col. Knobelsdorff’s Regiment,” a notice headed “A Call on Absentees.” It is dated at the headquarters of the 44th Illinois at Camp Rienzi, Mississippi, on 26 June 1862, and says that the absentees named below must send in certificates from an army medical officer of their inability to rejoin the regiment within thirty days, or they would be “reported and treated as deserters.” The lists run by company. Under “Company F, Ashley, Ill.” the printed names are Sergt. Waldo Gilbert, Chas. T. Laur, F. M. Livesay, James Langsford, John Emert, Geo. W. McCovan, Lewis Peters, John H. Morris and Jas. H. Pugh. The notice does not say why any man was absent.

The Adjutant General’s roster of the 44th Infantry, in the report printed in 1901, gives Company F’s privates in a table whose columns the scan does not align row by row. It includes Emert, John; Laur, Charles T; Lennington, Isaac; Langford, James; Lacy, Theopholis; “Lewsey, Francis M.”; McCowen, George; Morris, John H; and Peters, Lewis. Most of the names are the same men as in the Tribune, with the spellings shifted (Langsford and Langford, McCovan and McCowen). The F. M. Livesay of the newspaper therefore matches Francis M. Lewsey of the roster on initials, company and place, and Livesay is read as a variant of Lewsey.

A volunteer compilation of Washington County veterans, by Wayne Hinton on Genealogy Trails, says Francis M. Lewsey was a married farmer from Richview, born about 1827 in Illinois, who enlisted at Ashley on 10 July 1861, was mustered in at Chicago on 13 September 1861 and died on 18 February 1863 of wounds received at Murfreesboro. That fits the roster’s remarks column, which includes a private who died at Murfreesboro on 18 February 1863 of wounds. The compilation also gives a burial at Stones River National Battlefield, where he is listed with the 42nd Illinois, not the 44th, and that conflict is not resolved. The notice of June 1862 is therefore no mark against him; the same compilation shows him with his company six months later.

The regiment matters for the Carters. The 1879 county history says Dr. William D. Carter, who graduated from Rush Medical College on 4 February 1862, “was appointed assistant surgeon of the 44th Regiment, Illinois Vols.” and served more than three years. He was the son of Livesay Carter. The Adjutant General’s roster of the regiment’s field and staff (page 296) also lists William D. Carter, of Nashville, among its assistant surgeons, in a table whose date and remarks columns do not line up in the scan, so his dates of rank are not settled here. No record read says when he joined the regiment or that he and Lewsey met. The veterans’ compilation lists Livesays in other Washington County companies (Jackson L. and John W. in the 60th Illinois, James M. and William J. in the 49th), but no F. M. Livesay, which is why this man is entered under Lewsey. Nothing read names his wife, parents or siblings, so whether he belonged to one of the Livesay families of Richview is open.
quotes: “reported and treated as deserters” (Chicago Daily Tribune, 19 July 1862, p. 2, in the notice’s own words)
“was appointed assistant surgeon of the 44th Regiment, Illinois Vols.” (History of Washington County, Illinois, 1879, p. 66)

stories.note: The Tribune’s F. M. Livesay is identified with the roster’s Francis M. Lewsey on initials, company, home town and neighbouring names; probable. Livesay as a spelling of Lewsey is an inference, and whether he was kin to the Washington County Livesays is a lead only. The compilation’s dates are secondary and its Stones River burial listing names the 42nd Illinois. The roster page’s remarks column is not aligned to names in the scan, so the 18 February 1863 date is taken from the compilation and only checked against the roster’s remarks. Dr. Carter’s service comes from the 1879 history and the roster’s staff list, whose dates were not settled. Nothing links Lewsey to Sloan’s line.

stories.title: Robert, Gilbert, Ben and Lewis: the Merry brothers of Sevier County
stories.hook: A county newspaper in Sevier County, Arkansas, mentions Lewis Merry’s brothers by name, and a Hortense column of 1903 puts Lewis in the Indian Territory with a brother recovering from illness.

subject.name: The Merry brothers
subject.rel: Probable brothers of Lewis (Louis) Merry of Glover

body: The De Queen Bee, a weekly newspaper in Sevier County, Arkansas, is digitized in the Library of Congress’s Chronicling America. Its neighborhood columns, “Hortense,” “Milford Dots” and the like, name a family of Merrys in the years 1897 to 1906. The first notice is a wedding. On 31 December 1897 the Bee, page 1, reports “a double wedding” at Kings Chapel in the Red Colony on Sunday, 26 December: Ben Merry married Miss Addie Harrison, and Luther Revels married Miss Jennie Harrison, with Rev. A. D. Jenkins officiating. A year later, on 23 December 1898, the Bee says Ben Merry, “formerly a citizen of this county,” had lived for the past year in the Chickasaw Nation and would make his home near De Queen.

In 1903 the columns turn to Robert, “Bob.” On 15 May the Bee’s Hortense column has Robert Merry of Milford visiting; on 24 July Bob Merry has gone to Hortense to work for the summer; and on 4 September the Milford Dots say that Robt. Merry and friends from Hortense “visited his brother, B. F. Merry.” That is a second name for Ben. On 18 September Robert left “to visit his brother, who is very ill, in the Indian Territory,” and on 30 October the Hortense column says that Robert Merry “returned from Indian Territory last week; his brother Lewis accompanied him and report their brother Gilbert convalescing.” The printed page confirms those words. Later items follow Robert to Provo for timber work and school in 1904, and on 18 May 1906 two neighborhood columns say Robert Merry “of Garvin, I. T.,” was visiting friends.

Lewis Merry (Louis, J. L.) of Glover, as the earlier stories report, told the Dawes Commission in 1900 that he had lived in the Choctaw Nation about eight years, and he was the postmaster at Glover from June 1901. A brother Lewis who “accompanied” Robert out of the Indian Territory in October 1903 fits him, and so does the place: Robert himself was “of Garvin, I. T.” by 1906. The Bee never gives Lewis a residence, and Merry is not a rare name, so the match is probable and not proven. Nobody in the paper is called a parent, and Dawes card 5754, which names Calvin and Elizabeth Merry as Louis’s parents, does not name his brothers. Calvin and Elizabeth are still not in the tree, and no brother is linked to Lewis.

What the notices do give is a home neighborhood and a pattern. The brothers were Sevier County young men who went to the Chickasaw and Choctaw nations to work, as Ben did in 1897 and Gilbert and Lewis by 1903, and who kept coming back to Hortense and Milford. That agrees with the old memorial lead, noted in the earlier story on Calvin and Elizabeth Merry, that Lewis was born in Sevier County, and it points the search for his parents at Sevier County’s 1880 census, at Milford and at Hortense. It does not settle that lead, and no record read gives Lewis’s own birthplace.

Merry and Addie Harrison Merry are in the tree as unlinked people, because no parent of Lewis is in the tree (an existing test keeps his parents unlinked) and the tree cannot show brothers without one. stories.title: Frank Whitfield’s homestead at De Queen, 1902 to 1907
stories.hook: A land-office notice that ran for nine weeks in the De Queen Bee in 1907 gives W. F. Whitfield’s first name, a homestead entry in Sevier County, and a witness named Ward.

subject.name: William F. “Frank” Whitfield
subject.rel: Probable father of Oliver Clinton Whitfield (link unproven)

body: On Friday, 22 February 1907, the De Queen Bee, page 8, printed a “Notice for Publication” from the land office at Camden, Arkansas, dated 12 February 1907. It says William F. Whitfield, of De Queen, Arkansas, had filed notice of his intention to make final proof on his claim: Homestead Entry No. 25306, made 17 January 1902, for the W½ NE¼ of section 28, township 8 south, range 32 west, fifth principal meridian. The proof would be made before the Clerk of the Circuit Court of Sevier County at De Queen on 6 April 1907, and the notice named four witnesses to his “continuous residence upon, and cultivation of, the land”: Phillip A. Ward, William Miller, Benjamin F. Whitfield and W. Steel White, all of De Queen. The same notice ran, with small changes in the machine-read text, on every Friday through 19 April 1907. The page image of 1 March 1907 confirms the wording.

The notice supplies what the 1900 census could not: the man behind the initials W. F. Whitfield in Monroe Township, Sevier County, who with his wife Emma had a son named Clinton, born July 1893, was a William F. Whitfield by 1907, and he had entered a homestead in January 1902, two years after the census. The identification rests on the initials, the county and the date; no other W. F. Whitfield appears in the Bee, so it is probable and not proven. The Bee also lists a Frank Whitfield, written “jr.” in the January 1907 summons, among the grand jurors for the court term opening on 29 January 1907, and the Find a Grave leads in the earlier story call Oliver’s father William Franklin “Frank” Whitfield. The “jr.” suggests an older Frank Whitfield in the county; nothing read says who he was.

Two of the witnesses invite a comparison with the census. The 1900 household held a boarder surnamed Ward, born in August 1871 in Arkansas, whose given name could not be read, and the earlier research has a lead that Emma was born a Ward. A Phillip A. Ward who vouched for the Whitfield homestead could be that boarder, or Emma’s brother, or only a neighbor; the notice says nothing of kin. Benjamin F. Whitfield is another Whitfield of De Queen. A B. F. Whitfield of Chapel Hill is named in the Bee in November 1906 as the father of a bride, and a B. F. Whitfield was among the men questioned as jurors in a trial in November 1910, so he may belong to the family of the next story, but whether he was W. F.’s father, brother or neither is not shown.

What the notice leaves out is the household. It names no wife or child, so it adds nothing to the question of whether Clinton was Oliver Clinton Whitfield, who was born on 27 July 1893 and died in 1941, and the tree still keeps him unlinked from W. F. and Emma. The notice does show that the family held land in Sevier County until at least April 1907. Final-proof testimony and the patent would be in the General Land Office records, which could not be searched here; those records would give the claimant’s own account of his household and his residence.

Ward and Benjamin F. Whitfield are witnesses only; they are not added to the tree.

stories.title: Whitfields of Chapel Hill, and a sawmill that moved to Valliant
stories.hook: The same Sevier County paper that printed Frank Whitfield’s homestead notice follows other Whitfields from Chapel Hill to a sawmill at Valliant, Indian Territory, where John Grover Whitfield farmed in 1942.
body: Earlier research placed Clint Whitfield’s birth at Chapel Hill, Sevier County, on a Find a Grave lead, and found a second Whitfield household beside W. F.’s in the 1900 census at Monroe Township. The De Queen Bee shows a larger family. On 9 July 1897 it has Miss Tennie Whitfield of Chapel Hill helping to post the books of Ogden & Whitfield, a firm that on 18 February 1898 the Bee places at Cerro Gordo, with Luther B. Whitfield as a partner. On 25 November 1898 it announces the marriage of Joe Whitfield and Miss Maggie Roberts “of Chapel Hill.” On 23 November 1906 Miss Amanda Whitfield of Chapel Hill married Clement Banks at the home of her parents, Mr. and Mrs. B. F. Whitfield.

One member of the family went south and west. On 5 May 1905 Mrs. A. J. Whitfield returned to Texarkana after a visit to relatives “here and at Chapel Hill,” and on 26 January 1906 A. J. Whitfield, up from Texarkana, had bought a sawmill at McNab, Arkansas. By 5 April 1907 the Bee gives Mr. and Mrs. A. J. Whitfield as “of Valliant, I. T.”, and on 21 August 1908 it says A. J. Whitfield, “formerly of De Queen,” had formed a partnership with Jess Braden at Valliant to make lumber and had installed a large plant. On 3 September 1909 it reports that he lost his sawmill and stock by fire, with a loss of about $10,000 and no insurance. His wife went on visiting “relatives at Chapel Hill and De Queen” from Valliant in 1908, 1909 and October 1910.

Valliant is in McCurtain County, where an earlier story found a John Grover Whitfield, born 6 July 1888 in Sevier County and farming at Valliant in 1942. The neighbor household in the 1900 Monroe Township census, the one headed by a man whose initials look like R. H., included a John born in July 1888. The month, the year and the county agree. The earlier stories do not connect the two, and this is only a lead: it would make the R. H. Whitfield household, not W. F.’s, the family that sent a son to Valliant. A Mrs. Ollie Harmon of Garvin, Oklahoma, is named in a March 1909 Bee item as visiting Whitfield relatives; the 1900 household also had an Ollie, born April 1883, but the printed line is garbled and is not relied on.

None of this says that Clint Whitfield was kin to A. J., B. F., Luther B. or Joe Whitfield. The notices do show where the Whitfield name was thick on the ground: Chapel Hill, Cerro Gordo and De Queen before 1905, and Valliant after 1907, in the same Oklahoma county as Glover and Golden, where Clint Whitfield later lived. A homestead patent, a will, or an obituary for any of them that names a brother Frank or W. F. would settle it, and none has been read.

stories.title: Joe Denson of Fowlerville, ex-clerk of Sevier County
stories.hook: Mattie Denson went to Lockesburg, Arkansas, after leaving Abner Clay, and a Sevier County paper explains why: a Joe Denson, a former county court clerk there, had moved to Fowlerville in the Choctaw Nation by 1897.

subject.name: Joe Denson of Fowlerville
subject.rel: Possible kin of Mattie Denson Clay (unproven)

body: Mattie Denson married Abner H. Clay in the Choctaw Nation on 20 May 1897, and her Dawes card names her parents as Joseph H. and Mattie E. Denson, both non-citizens. When she and Abner separated in 1902 she gave her address as Lockesburg, Arkansas, a town in Sevier County. A letter of 1903 in her jacket is addressed to Claude Denson of Shawneetown, Indian Territory, who called himself her brother. The De Queen Bee, in the same county as Lockesburg, supplies two notices about a Denson family on the Indian Territory side.

On 5 November 1897 the Bee’s page 4 passed on news from Fowlerville, Indian Territory: a baby boy had been born to Mr. and Mrs. Joe Denson of Fowlerville, and the writer hoped the child would comfort them in their later years. On 18 February 1898 the Bee, page 5, says Joe Denson of Fowlerville, I. T., “ex-Clerk of the county court of Sevier county,” was in De Queen the Thursday before. The paper does not say how long ago he held the office or when he left Arkansas.

A Joe Denson who served as Sevier County’s court clerk and then lived at Fowlerville, a Choctaw Nation town that the Daily Ardmoreite of 10 June 1900 lists with Lukfata, Eagletown and Shawneetown, fits the picture of a family that had moved across the line from Sevier County. It does not prove that he was Joseph H. Denson, Mattie’s father. Hortense, in Sevier County, has other Densons in the Bee in 1903 and 1904, J. J. Denson with sons Joe L. and J. S., and none is tied to Fowlerville. “Joe” may be Joseph H., a brother, or an unrelated man.

The notice is useful as a direction. Mattie’s retreat to Lockesburg in 1902 now has a possible explanation, and a county clerk is a man who leaves records: a Sevier County court clerk’s name, if it can be found in a county history or in the county’s record books, would show whether the Joseph H. Denson of card 507 is that man. The 1880 census of Sevier County would show the household and its children, and Mattie’s brother Claude of Shawneetown might be among them.
