stories.title: Deer tags and a five-year pin: Junior in the Hugo papers, 1961–62
stories.hook: One November he lined up with the rest of Hugo for a deer tag. The next spring he got a pin from the glove factory.
body: Deer season in Oklahoma opened on a Wednesday in late November 1961, and Hugo took it seriously. On Tuesday, 21 November, The Hugo Daily News ran “Local Sportsmen Purchase Deer Tags” across the top of its front page. Tags were on sale at D. C. Patterson Hardware, Leard Hardware and Askew Service Station, and one seller, Mrs. Tom Baskin, had sold all 25 of hers by Monday. Many hunters had already moved into the woods to set up camp. The paper then printed the name and town of everyone who had bought a tag, a list that ran down several columns, from a 12-year-old to a 78-year-old. Partway down the second column is “William Thompson Jr., Hugo.”

Four months later, on 2 April 1962, a front-page photograph showed a crowd of employees of the Wells Lamont glove factory in Hugo receiving five-year service pins, standing with the assistant manager, Robert Bowen. The caption lists them by name, and among them is “Junior Thompson.” A five-year pin in April 1962 would mean he had been on the factory's payroll since about 1957, the year after his marriage license with Mary Ellen Hulsey was announced.
Neither item says much, but together they fill in an ordinary working life that the censuses skip: a young husband in Hugo with a factory job and a deer tag.
src: The Hugo Daily News, 21 Nov 1961, p. 1, “Local Sportsmen Purchase Deer Tags,” https://www.newspapers.com/image/602946740/; The Hugo Daily News, 2 Apr 1962, p. 1, photograph caption, Wells Lamont glove factory service pins, https://www.newspapers.com/image/632307107/.
kv: The Hugo Daily News, 21 Nov 1961, p. 1: “William Thompson Jr., Hugo” among the buyers of deer-hunting tags
The Hugo Daily News, 2 Apr 1962, p. 1: “Junior Thompson” among Wells Lamont glove factory employees receiving five-year service pins
stories.note: Both identifications are probable, not proved. Neither item gives an age, address or relative. William Thompson Jr. of Hugo fits the grandfather, who was living in Hugo in these years, and “Junior” was his name in the family and in the 1940 census, but another man of the same name cannot be ruled out. Several other Thompsons appear in the glove-factory caption, and none is identified as a relative. The 1957 start date is inferred from the five-year pin.
stories.place: Hugo, Choctaw County, Oklahoma

stories.title: Wildcat whisky: three and a half pints in Hugo, 1957
stories.hook: The sheriff counted it out to the half-pint. And yes, he drank it.
body: On the morning of Thursday, 30 May 1957, The Hugo Daily News reported that Johnny Moffitt, 31, of Hugo had pleaded guilty to a disorderly-house charge before Justice of the Peace Bert Bush. He had been arrested the night before by Sheriff Ed Thornton and Constable Lonnie Wright, who said they found one quart and three half-pints of “wildcat whisky” at his home.

“Wildcat” was the old word for liquor made without a license, and it has never sounded like anything you would want to drink. He drank it anyway. The sheriff, to his credit, counted precisely: one quart plus three half-pints comes to three and a half pints, so nobody could later argue about the arithmetic. That makes the half-pints sound less like a stockpile and more like a supply.

The law was the point. Oklahoma had been officially dry since statehood in 1907 and did not repeal statewide prohibition until 1959, so in May 1957 a cupboard with the wrong bottles in it was a matter for the sheriff and the justice of the peace. Four years later the same town’s paper reported a much more serious whisky case, told in “Moonshine and federal court in Hugo.” This one stayed small.
src: The Hugo Daily News, 30 May 1957, p. 1, https://www.newspapers.com/image/901891967/; Oklahoma Historical Society, The Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture, entry on prohibition in Oklahoma (statewide prohibition from statehood in 1907 until its repeal in 1959).

stories.title: Henry and Hannah's other children: a section hand, a plainsman and three sisters
stories.hook: Grady was the youngest. His brother Tom farmed next door to him in Oklahoma, and his brother Jesse went all the way to the Texas plains.
body: Henry and Hannah Moffitt started their family in Randolph County, Arkansas. The 1880 census at Janes Creek Township lists them with Josephine, 3, and Jesse, 1. Hannah later told the 1910 census taker she had borne seven children and that six were living, so one died young and left no record. By 1900 the family was in Franklin Township, Stone County, with Jesse; a daughter transcribed as “Gimsa,” born in August 1883; Bertha, born in March 1886; Tom; and the youngest, Woodford Grady. Josephine, who would have been about 23, was no longer at home.

Thomas Berry “Tom” Moffitt, born at St. James in Stone County on 17 February 1889, was the first of the children known to be born in Stone County. After his father died in 1901 he stayed with his widowed mother, and in 1910 he was working as a railroad section hand. By 1920 he had followed, or led, his brother across the Red River and was farming next door to Grady in Wilson Township, Choctaw County, Oklahoma. His wife Vesta died at Holdenville, Oklahoma, in October 1930, aged 38. Tom ended up at Paris, Texas, where he died on 21 March 1953; his grave marker is carved for service in both world wars.

Jesse Gee Moffitt (1879–1957) went the farthest, out onto the Texas plains. He is buried at Tahoka in Lynn County, and family notes place his death at Amarillo. Of the sisters, less is known. A Bertha May Moffitt Barham (1888–1930) is buried at Herpel Cemetery near her mother and may be the Bertha of the 1900 census, but that is not proved.

stories.title: Ten children of a preacher, from Hot Springs to Wright City
stories.hook: Oscar was the fourth of ten. Here is what the records say about the other nine, and where they go quiet.
body: George Washington Hulsey and Sarah Rebecca Graves married on 22 December 1901 and had ten children over twenty-one years. The first three were boys: William Roy in 1904, John Wesley in 1906 and Noah in 1908. In April 1910 the census found the young family in Mountain Township, Garland County, Arkansas, with “William R.,” “John W.” and Noah at home. Their father farmed, and the family remembers him as a preacher. Oscar arrived that October at Hot Springs.

Then the family started moving. Fred came in 1913 and Ruby Ellen in 1915, the first daughter after five sons. Grady was born in 1918, the year his father, whose home was at Story in Montgomery County, registered for the draft while working on the Camp Pike construction job near Little Rock. By 1920 the household had crossed into Oklahoma and was tenant-farming in Sulphur Township, McCurtain County, with six children at home. Louis Daniel was born at Bethel that May. Grace Irene followed in 1923, when her mother was about 39, and George Paul, the last, in 1925, when his father was nearly fifty. In 1930 the census found a renting household of ten near Wright City, deep in the sawmill country.

Their father died on 5 August 1935 and was buried at Breashears Cemetery near Story. The eldest, William Roy, was about 31; the youngest, George Paul, was nine or ten. Their mother later went west and died at Bandon, Oregon, in 1972. When Oscar died in 1982, his obituary counted four brothers and two sisters still living. Ruby, who married a Stipe, and Grace, who married a Dunagan, are the only daughters in the family list, so they were evidently those two sisters. Three of the ten had died by then, Louis Daniel among them.

After 1935 most of the siblings are hard to follow. Marriage indexes in McCurtain County show a John Hulsey (1929), a Noah Hulsey (1930) and a Roy Hulsey (1931), and a Roy Hulsey, 34, married in Montgomery County, Arkansas, in 1938. Any of them may be Oscar’s brothers, but none of those records names parents, so they are leads. Louis’s story is the one the records tell most fully: see “A gunshot near his mother’s farm, January 1948.”

stories.title: Kentucky, Minnesota and back: John C.'s brothers and sister
stories.hook: Their father took the family to Minnesota and brought it home again, and one brother married his brother's wife's cousin.

subject.name: John C. Satterfield's brothers and sister

body: James H. Satterfield's 1885 biography names six children of his first marriage, to Malissa Gibson: “Henry W., John C., Sidney R., James D., Martha A. and Mary C.” It also says that “in 1867 he removed to Dakota County, Minn., and in 1875 he returned to Kentucky.” Malissa died in 1877, soon after the move back, and James remarried in 1878.

Sidney Rufus, born 2 September 1865 and the third son named in the sketch, stayed in Kentucky and kept the family close. He married Eliza “Ancie” Johnson, a daughter of James P. Johnson and Martha J. Clark. Martha was the older sister of Melvina (Clark) Johnson, the mother of Samantha, who married Sidney's brother John C. in 1892. So two Satterfield brothers married first cousins from the same Clark-Johnson family. Sidney died at Richardsville, Warren County, on 19 November 1949, and Ancie in 1951; both are buried at Satterfield Cemetery near Jetson.

James Doiser was born in February 1867 in Allen County, the year the family left for Minnesota. He married in 1889, had five children, and went south to Arkansas; he died at Hickoria, Clay County, on 10 July 1929 and is buried at Redenbo Cemetery. The only child known to have been born in Minnesota was a daughter, A. M., on 23 July 1870. She married Calvin H. Coots in 1891 and died on 25 May 1892, only 21. Her Minnesota birth is the one piece of independent support so far for the family's Minnesota years.

stories.title: Pearl's brothers and sister: two soldiers, a Riddle wedding and a death at seventeen
stories.hook: John C. and Samantha Satterfield's children followed them from Kentucky to Texas to the Oklahoma side of the Red River, and most came home to be buried near their mother.
body: Wavey Lincoln Satterfield was the oldest surviving child. His World War I and World War II draft cards both give his birth as 28 December 1895 at Morgantown, Butler County, Kentucky; his headstone at Soper Cemetery says 9 January 1896, and the Find a Grave memorial treats the stone as the mistake. The stone is marked “TEXAS PVT. U.S. ARMY World War I,” which fits the family's move to Franklin County, Texas, about 1907. In 1925 he married Jewel Dale Weems, and they settled in Choctaw County, Oklahoma, near his mother. He died at Soper on 24 March 1952, aged 56, and lies in plot E4, the same plot as Samantha.

James Bethel was born on 12 May 1901 in Butler County and was about six when the family went to Texas. He married Alice Elizabeth Riddle, and they had seven children between 1922 and 1940; one, Charlie, died in 1940 at about ten. James died at Paris, Texas, on 7 December 1964 and was buried at Soper, near his mother.

Stella B., “little Stella” in the Hagansport household of April 1910, was born on 6 October 1907, one of the two children born after the move to Texas. She married Clifford Calvin Riddle. Whether her husband and her brother James's wife Alice were brother and sister is not shown in any record seen. Stella died on 25 January 1925, only 17, and was buried at Chillicothe Cemetery in Hardeman County, Texas, far from the rest of the family. No cause of death is given.

The two youngest were boys. Ira L. was born in 1905 in Kentucky, was five at Hagansport in 1910, served in World War II (his stone reads “AMRY WWII”), died in 1977 and is buried in plot B2 at Grant Cemetery, where Pearl and Charles Oscar Smith also lie. Jewel Thompson Satterfield, the last child, was born at Talco, Titus County, Texas, on 3 May 1912. He married Marie Nabors in 1929, when he was 17, had five children, and died at Hugo on 13 January 1995. He is buried at Mount Olivet Cemetery in Hugo.

stories.title: From Gadsden to Apache and California: Mamie's brothers and sisters
stories.hook: John Morgan and Lizzie Shackleford raised a big family that scattered from Alabama to the Pacific, and two obituaries twenty years apart count them off.

subject.name: Mary Tinsley Shackleford's brothers and sisters

body: In June 1900 the census at Gilbert, Etowah County, found John Shackleford, 37, and his wife Elizabeth, 28, married ten years, with five children, all living: “Balous,” 8; Myrtle, 6; May, 5, who was Mary Tinsley; Robert, 3; and Eddie, 8 months. More were born after the family moved to Texas, among them Hazel, born in 1908 at Rattan in Delta County.

Balis Anthony, the eldest, was born on 5 February 1892 in Alabama and went west. He married Bertha Mae Fox, and he died in Los Angeles County on 9 January 1982, nearly ninety, and is buried at Green Hills Memorial Park, Rancho Palos Verdes. Robert Yates, born at Gadsden on 25 October 1897, also ended up in California. When he died at Oroville in June 1961, aged 63, the Chico Enterprise-Record called him a World War I veteran (his stone carries a World War II marker) and named his survivors: brothers “Bayles of Los Angeles and Ed and John of Oklahoma,” and six sisters, among them “Mamie Moffett” of Oklahoma.

Hazel stayed closest to the Red River. She married John Wesley King, who died in 1968, and she died at Paris, Texas, on 22 December 1980. The Lamar County Echo named her parents as John Morgan Shackleford and Kathryn Elizabeth Newton and listed her surviving sisters, Mrs. Joe Haskell, Mrs. Beula Hutchings and Mrs. Helen Josey, all of Apache, Oklahoma, and Mrs. Eular Tillman of Lawton, and her brothers Balis of California and John S. and Edward of Apache. Three of her six pallbearers were Moffitts. Two of them, Donald and Odis, were very likely Mamie's sons and so Hazel's nephews, though the paper gives no relationships.

Apache in Caddo County was where much of the family landed: Lizzie moved there from Dawson County, Texas, in 1933 and is buried at Fairview Cemetery. Two of the 1900 children, Myrtle and Eddie, do not appear in either obituary; they may have died young or be known by other names. Josephine, Eulah and Beulah are known only by their married names, so their birth years and places are still open.

stories.title: Twenty-six divorces in one day, January 1946
stories.hook: Katie's divorce from Oscar went through on the day McCurtain County set a record for them.

subject.name: Oscar Franklin Hulsey & Katie Cornelia (Stevenson) Hulsey

body: After the war, the McCurtain County courthouse at Idabel was busy undoing marriages. On Saturday, 12 January 1946, the McCurtain Gazette reported on its front page that a county record had been broken that Wednesday: District Judge George R. Childers had granted 26 divorces in a single day, one more than the previous record of 25, according to the court clerk, Buel Grinage.

The paper printed every one of them, the first name of the spouse who filed followed by the other's full name: Addie from C. L. Mahon, Lorene from Jesse Ramage, Floyd from Mary Dimmitt, and so on down a column of twenty-six names. Near the bottom, between Rosa Bell from Lonnie Lewis and John from Dorothy Keiss, is “Katie from Oscar Hulsey.”

It was the second time the marriage had ended on paper. An Arkansas divorce had already been entered in Montgomery County in September 1941, and Oscar had remarried five weeks later. Katie's Oklahoma suit, case no. 12,652, had run as a notice by publication in the Gazette from late November to mid-December 1945, addressed “To: Oscar Hulsey.” The January list closes the file. The same front page, a column over, carried the homecoming notices of local men just out of the Army and Navy, which may explain why the judge had so much to do.
src: McCurtain Gazette (Idabel), 12 Jan 1946, p. 1, https://www.newspapers.com/image/747373903/; McCurtain Gazette, 24 Nov to 15 Dec 1945, legal notices, district court case no. 12,652; Arkansas, U.S., Divorces, 1923-1975 (1941, Montgomery County).
kv: 26 divorces in one day, breaking the record of 25 (court clerk Buel Grinage)
McCurtain Co. district court no. 12,652, notice by publication Nov–Dec 1945
stories.note: The article names the parties only as “Katie from Oscar Hulsey,” but the 1945 notice in the same county court names Katie Hulsey as plaintiff and Oscar Hulsey as defendant, so the identification is firm. The day the record was set is the Wednesday before the 12 January issue. The link between the postwar homecomings on the same page and the number of divorces is the paper's juxtaposition, not a stated cause.
stories.place: District court, Idabel, McCurtain County, Oklahoma

stories.title: Noah Smith: Kentucky farmer, Franklin County justice of the peace, Confederate pensioner
stories.hook: John B. Smith's father turns up in three censuses around Mount Pleasant and Hagansport, with his son beside him in two of them.
body: In the summer of 1870 the census taker for Titus County, Texas, post office Mount Pleasant, came to the farm of Noah Smith, 40, born in Kentucky, with land worth $1,200 and $200 in personal property. In the house were Mary, 16; John B., 11; and a girl, Annie L. The 1870 census does not give relationships, but the next one does.

In 1875 the southern part of Titus County became Franklin County, and in June 1880 Noah Smith, 51, was in its Precinct 2, listed as a farmer and a justice of the peace. His wife was Mary E., 25. The household was spelled out this time: John B. Smith, 20, son; Anna L., 11, and Eliza A., 8, daughters; Mary B., 5; George R., 2; and a baby boy a month old. Noah gave his father's birthplace as Maryland and his mother's as Virginia. Twenty years later John B. Smith, the 2nd great-grandfather of this family, was farming his own land in the same Precinct 2 of Franklin County.

On 5 July 1899, at about seventy, Noah applied to the State of Texas for a Confederate veteran's pension from Franklin County (file no. 08305). The 1900 census found him still on his own farm in Justice Precinct 2, now a widower, with two young daughters, Flora, 17, and Oma, 15. He died on 28 January 1906 and is buried at Smith Cemetery in Franklin County; his Find a Grave memorial gives his birth as 6 June 1831 in Greenup County, Kentucky.

Who John B.'s mother was is still open. Noah's wife in 1880, Mary E., was only 25, and a later Texas death certificate for their daughter Flora names her mother as Mary Keith. Born about 1855, Mary Keith cannot be the mother of a son born in the late 1850s. John B.'s mother was evidently an earlier wife, and no record seen so far names her.
src: 1870 U.S. census, Titus Co., Tex., roll M593_1606, p. 115A, dwelling 1443; 1880 U.S. census, Precinct 2, Franklin Co., Tex., ED 033, roll 1304, p. 420a, dwelling 83; 1900 U.S. census, Justice Precinct 2, Franklin Co., Tex., sheet 9, dwelling 161; Texas Confederate Pension Applications, 1899-1975, file 08305 (Texas State Library and Archives Commission, roll 2748), index via Ancestry; Texas Death Certificates, 1903-1982, Flora May Miller (parents Noah Smith and Mary Keith), index via Ancestry; Find a Grave memorial 230179746 (Noah Smith, Smith Cemetery, Franklin Co., Tex.).

stories.note: The 1880 census names John B. Smith as Noah's son. Identifying that John B. with the family's John B. Smith is probable: same name, same Franklin County precinct in 1880 and 1900, and a sister Annie L. carried from the 1870 household to the 1880 one. But his age does not agree: 11 in 1870 and 20 in 1880 point to a birth about 1859–60, while the family tree and the 1900 census use July 1856. Noah's own age also drifts (40 in 1870, 51 in 1880, 71 in 1900; Find a Grave says 1831), and his parents' birthplaces are Maryland and Virginia in 1880 but Kentucky in 1900. The pension file itself has not been read, so his regiment is not yet known. Ancestry family trees pair Noah with Mary P. Keith as John's parents; the records point instead to Mary Keith as a later wife.

timeline.t: Thomas Gaunt marries Susan Bate at Rotherham on 28 August; their son Peter is a proposed match for the later Sandwich settler.
Henry Croasdale, yeoman of Newhey in the Forest of Bowland, makes his will on 21 September and is buried at Waddington on 10 October.
Peter Gaunt tells the Plymouth Colony court at its March session that he knows of no public worship in the world he can join.
Peter Gaunt and three other Sandwich men are fined twenty shillings each on 2 March for appearing before the Plymouth court with their hats on; Thomas Butler is cleared.
Daniel Butler, brother of Dorothy Butler, is publicly whipped at Plymouth for rescuing a 'Strang Quaker' from the Sandwich marshal.
William Croasdale of Newhey dies on the 29th day of the 11th month and is buried at Settle Meeting, Newton.
Hananiah Gaunt marries Dorothy Butler at Sandwich, Massachusetts, on 10 May, a week after posting their intention at the Friends meeting.
The Plymouth court fines Thomas and Dorothy Butler after a search for their son Daniel, who had helped a Quaker escape the marshal.
The Plymouth court grants Thomas Butler land at Tassacausett after his purchase from Pampmumitt, also called Charles.
Plymouth Colony court records that Peter Gaunt of Sandwich hosted two visiting Quakers.
The Settle Meeting certificate of 7 June names the Cowgill and Croasdale families preparing to move to Pennsylvania. Later accounts differ over the ship they sailed on.
Ralph Cowgill arrives in the Delaware on 28 September on the Friend's Adventure, indentured to Randolph Blackshaw for four years and fifty acres.
Thomas Croasdale dies on 2 November on Neshaminy Creek; his goods, apart from 500 acres 'not prized,' are appraised at 47 pounds 9 shillings.
Hananiah Gaunt takes up 500 acres at Hananicon, Springfield Township, New Jersey.
George Hutcheson sells Hananiah Gaunt 'of Rhode Island, yeoman' 500 acres in the First Tenth of West Jersey on 11 May.
Anthony Champneys and Anne Pitts marry at St James, Duke's Place, London, on 23 September.
Agnes Croasdale dies on 20 October; her estate account lists livestock, household goods and 500 acres.
Hananiah Gaunt sells 100 acres of the 500 to William Bustill, a carpenter of Shrewsbury, on 18 May.
Land surveyed for William Biddle in Springfield, Burlington County, is described as adjoining the land of Hananiah Gaunt.
Dennis Garrett of Baltimore County dies on 2 September of a sword blow; his son-in-law John Cole and his widow Barbara Garrett are named as witnesses at the trial of John Oldton.
John Cowgill marries Bridget Croasdale at Neshaminy, Bucks County, on 19 October.
A 67-acre tract, Cole's Addition, is surveyed for John Cole on 29 May on the north side of the Patapsco, on the site of Baltimore.
John Chamness marries Ann Weary at St John's Church, Wapping, London, on 4 January.
Nottingham Friends begin meeting at the house of William Brown on the Nottingham Lots; Concord Monthly Meeting approves in the 2nd month of 1705.
Barbara Garrett Broad deeds land to her grandson Dennis Garrett Cole in Baltimore County, Maryland.
Anthony Chamness is born in East Smithfield, London, to John and Ann Chamness.
Elizabeth Cowgill of Duck Creek, daughter of the tanner John Cowgill, marries William Brown Jr. of Nottingham.
Hananiah Gaunt's will names his daughter Mahitable Staples.
Henry Stevenson marries Ann Curlett at Saul parish, Downpatrick, on 2 June.
Joseph Cole's will names his wife Susanna and daughter Sarah.
Anthony Chamness is indentured in London for service in Maryland.
Jacob Perkins Sr. of Willingboro dies intestate in May with a cane and sword in his inventory; Jacob Jr. makes his will on 26 October naming Henry Nordike as a debtor.
Mary Norton, daughter of Edward Norton of Armagh, marries Richard Brown at Nottingham Meeting.
Anthony Chamness marries Sarah Cole.
Robert Blackshaw deeds 100 acres at Little Creek, Kent County, Delaware, to 'My Son Alexander,' for the natural love he bears him.
Thomas Rogers marries Ann Staples at Upper Springfield Meeting, New Jersey.
John Cole, Senior, aged about 67, testifies in March at a Baltimore County land commission on the bounds of Cole's Adventure.
Edward Norton, son of Edward Norton of Armagh, Ireland, marries Elizabeth Brown at West Nottingham Meeting.
Agnes Blackshear is examined apart from her husband in the Kent County court on 14 May and says she freely agreed to the sale of their Delaware land.
William Kirk, widower of Margaret Davis, marries Mary Norton Brown, widow of Richard Brown, under the care of Fairfax Monthly Meeting in Virginia.
Anthony Chamness moves his family from Monocacy, Maryland, to Carver's Creek Meeting, North Carolina.
Cane Creek Monthly Meeting is organized, with Anthony Chamness as overseer.
Cane Creek Monthly Meeting is set up in the tenth month; the Davis family book names Charles and Hannah Davies as charter members, having come south from Radnor and Hopewell.

Robert Johnson marries Virginia Elmore of Louisa County, Virginia, on 19 November; in 1766 Cedar Creek Meeting sends them to North Carolina by certificate.
